WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD GRIER v. NORTHWOOD TEXTILE MILLS, INC. 

Workmen's compensation—Accidental injury—Wrist drop caused by use of cardboard punch.

A referee's award of compensation based upon his finding of an accidental injury will be sustained where claimant testified that in the course of his work punching holes in cardboard coupons, the punch which he was using broke, requiring him to use a lighter punch, to work much faster to do the required work, and to exert heavy pressure of the right hand following which he developed a wrist drop and paralysis of the right hand.

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Alessandroni, district no. 1, claim petition no. 106,866. Appeal dismissed. November 19, 1947. 

Maryland Casualty Co., insurance carrier. 

John F. Donohue, for claimant. 

Louis Wagner, for defendant.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

This is an appeal by defendant from an award of the referee.

Claimant, in his petition filed on November 21, 1946, set out that while punching holes in coupons, in the course of his employment on September 5, 1946, he developed a wrist drop and paralysis of the right hand, as a result of the puncher being too small to punch through the thickness

[84 Dep. Rep. 

of the coupons. Defendant's answer, filed on November 

27, 1946, denied the material averments of claimant's petition and alleged that claimant's disability did not result from an injury by accident suffered in the course of his employment. After hearing, the referee found that claimant had suffered an accidental injury in the course of his employment but that the partial disability lasting from September 5, 1946, to October 8, 1946, was not reflected in loss of earnings and, in accordance with such findings, entered an award in favor of claimant for medical expenses incurred by him. This appeal followed. 

The sole question raised in this case is whether the referee properly determined that claimant suffered an accident in the course of his employment. The sole testimony given on this point is that of claimant who testified that, on the day in question, it was his job to punch holes in cardboard coupons; that he had been using a large and heavy punch which enabled him to punch through six or seven cards at once and that, in so doing, pressure was applied to the whole body, from the shoulder; that this punch broke and the only other punch available “was a much smaller and lighter punch, which is the kind railroad conductors use for punching very thin tickets"; that in using this punch he could only punch two or three cards at a time and, in so doing, heavy pressure of the right hand was required, in addition, it was necessary for claimant to work much faster to do the required work. The following morning claimant noticed that the wrist seemed paralyzed and that he suffered from a dropped wrist. 

We are of the opinion that this testimony is sufficient to establish an accident within the meaning of the act. 

While it is true that claimant was doing his usual work, under the uncontradicted testimony set out above, it is equally clear that he was not doing such work in the usual manner. It is settled law that some unforeseen or undesigned circumstance may arise in the performance of the regular work which would constitute a compensable accident: Nye v. M. H. Baker & Co., 3 P. C. R. 27.

An injury by accident may occur in the course of the

1948] 

 normal duties of an employe and without overexertion when a strain, sprain or twist causes a break or sudden change in the physical structure or tissue of the body: Rudy v. Motor Freight Express, 2 P. C. R. 12; Davis v. Lacka wanna Linoleum Stores, 6 P. C. R. 58; Toman v. McKlveen, 3 P. C. R. 12. We are of the opinion, from a review of the testimony, that this is the situation in the instant case. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD VARGO v. LATTIMER COAL CORP. 

Workmen's compensation—Occupational diseases—Silicosis—Failure of claimant to give notice within statutory period. 

A referee's order dismissing claimant's petition for compensation as a result of silicosis which he suffered from exposure in defendant's mines will be affirmed where it appears that claimant failed to give notice of his disability until 124 days after he became totally disabled. 

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Olexy, district no. 2, claim petition no. 107,911. Appeal dismissed. 

October 29, 1947.

Coal Operators Casualty Company, insurance carrier. 

Roger J. Dever, for claimant. 

Nathan Hyman and R. H. Cunningham, for defendant.

KNOLL, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by claimant from an order of Referee 

Joseph P. Olexy, of the compensation district no. 2, dismissing his petition for compensation under The Pennsyl vania Occupational Disease Act. 

The petition alleged, inter alia, that claimant became totally disabled on October 17, 1946, as a result of silicosis and that notice of disability was given on February 20, 1947. The referee denied compensation upon finding that notice had not been given to defendant within 90 days, as provided by section 311 of the Occupational Disease Act. 

Claimant's testimony established that he quit work on 

October 17, 1946, because of shortness of breath; that he knew he was suffering from miners' asthma on that date; and that he knew in July 1945 that he had miners' asthma. 

Section 311 of the act provides as follows: 

"Unless the employe or someone in his behalf, or some of the dependents or someone in their behalf, shall give notice of disability to the employer liable for compensation under this article, within fourteen days after the disability begins, no compensation shall be due until such notice be given, and unless such notice be given within ninety days after the beginning of disability no compensation shall be allowed."

In the instant case, the notice of disability was given 124 days after the beginning of disability on October 17, 1946.

The statute of limitations begins to run from the time the employe is disabled and definitely knows he is disabled by the occupational disease: Roschak v. Vulcan Iron Works, 

157 Pa. Superior Ct. 227. This claimant, although he admitted knowledge of his disability from the occupational disease, failed to notify his employer within the statutory period. It is uncontradicted that claimant was exposed to a silica hazard in defendant's mines and that, as a result, he is totally disabled by silicosis. Under the circumstances, it is regrettable that his claim petition must be dismissed. 

However, we cannot extend the period of limitations merely

1948] 

 in aid of a meritorious claimant or to relieve against the hardship of particular circumstances. 

Accordingly, the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of dismissal are affirmed. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD KAPLAFKA v. HAMMOND COAL CO. 

Workmen's compensation-Disability-Concurrent payment of unemployment compensation and occupational disease compensation.

Where there was uncontradicted testimony that claimant was totally disabled from anthraco-silicosis, an award of compensation will be affirmed notwithstanding the fact that for the period during which compensation was payable claimant received unemployment compensation; claimant's certification to the Bureau of Employment and Unemployment Compensation that he was able to work during the period in question was of no probative value as to his true physical condition and defendant's liability could be discharged only by payment of compensation under the provisions of the Pennsylvania 

Occupational Disease Act. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Enterline, district no. 5, claim petition no. 105,133. Appeal dismissed. 

November 19, 1947.

Coal Operators Casualty Company, for insurance carrier. 

Roger J. Dever, for claimant.

Penrose Hertzler and Mr. R. H. Cunningham, for defendant. 

KNOLL, Commissioner: 

This case comes before the board on a second appeal by defendant from an order of Referee L. E. Enterline, of

the fifth compensation district, republishing an award of compensation to claimant for total disability from anthracosilicosis. On the first appeal, we remanded the record for the purpose of permitting defendant to offer evidence relating to claimant's petition for unemployment compensation payments.

Competent testimony of record shows that claimant became totally disabled from anthraco-silicosis on August 28, 1945. Notice of disability was given to defendant-employer when claimant was last exposed to a silica hazard, on September 6, 1945, and the claim petition was filed within the statutory period. The disability of claimant from anthraco-silicosis was not controverted. The referee awarded compensation from September 4, 1945.

The sole issue raised by defendant is whether or not claimant is entitled to concurrent payment of unemployment compensation and occupational disease compensation, the former being based upon his ability to work and the latter based upon his inability to work. 

According to the records of the Bureau of Employment and Unemployment Compensation, claimant received unemployment benefits from July 16, 1945, to November 5, 1945, a period of 16 weeks, at the rate of $20 a week. In order to receive unemployment compensation, claimant was required to sign the following certificate: "I register for work and make application for unemployment compensation; and certify that I am able to work and available for work and that all statements made in this. application are true and correct."

Defendant contends, in substance, that claimant's certification constitutes proof that claimant was not disabled from July 23, 1945, to November 5, 1945. In view of the positive uncontradicted medical testimony that claimant was totally disabled on August 28, 1945, we are unable to accept that contention. We believe that the certification was a self-serving misrepresentation of no probative value as to the true physical condition of the claimant.

1948] 

Finally, defendant asks that compensation be disallowed during the period while claimant received unemployment compensation payments and for the required waiting period thereafter.

The statutory liability of defendant to pay compensation to the claimant began after the seventh day of claimant's total disability. That liability could be discharged only by payments received and paid as compensation due to the claimant under the provisions of The Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act. The unemployment payments received by claimant were not earnings or wages; they were not paid by defendant and they would not have stopped the running of the statute of limitations of the Act. We see no difference between unemployment compensation payments and benefits payable from any association, society or fund. Under section 204 of the act, the receipt of such benefits does not bar recovery of compensation. While we agree that claimant should not be unjustly enriched, that is a matter of concern to the Bureau of Employment and 

Unemployment Compensation upon whom the alleged fraud was perpetrated. Defendant has cited no authority, and we find none which would permit the board to order the withholding from the claimant of legally due compensation payments.

Accordingly, the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and award are affirmed. 

The defendant's appeal is dismissed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD BAILEY v. CITY OF BRADFORD, SANITARY DEPARTMENT 

Workmen's compensation-Injury in course of employment off premises-Employe acting on orders prior to starting day's work.

A referee's award of compensation will be affirmed as against defendant's contention that claimant's accident did not happen in the

[84 Dep. Rep. 

course of his regular employment where it appears that claimant, employed by defendant as a helper on a garbage truck, was injured while he was servicing his truck at his home prior to starting work early in the morning, but at a time when he was trying on orders from his employer to get a man to assist him in the day's work. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Smith, district no 10, claim petition no. 107,876. Appeal dismissed. 

December 10, 1947. 

Accident & Casualty Insurance Co., insurance carrier. 

Thomas B. Wilson, for claimant. 

W. D. Gallup, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal from an award entered by Referee 

Smith May 22, 1947.

Claimant in the case is Albert L. Bailey who filed his petition February 24, 1947, alleging that on January 4, 1947, in the course of his employment with defendant, the City of Bradford, as a helper on a garbage truck, he sustained a brain injury in a fall on concrete which thereafter rendered him wholly unfit for work. The factual circumstances of the accidental injury introduced into the record through the testimony of claimant and J. L. McCutcheon, his immediate superior in defendant's sanitary department, are to all intents and purposes uncontradicted. From such testimony it appears that on the evening of January 3, 1947, claimant learned that the fellow workman with whom he regularly made his rounds would not be available to begin the next day's collections which should start at or before 4 o'clock in the morning; that in view of this prospect he called McCutcheon who told him to secure the services of one Floyd Sweet; that upon contacting Sweet about an hour before work was to begin claimant found him unwilling to work; that by reason of this he called for another man whose services might be secured; that upon being unable

1948] 

 to induce the latter to work claimant told another helper (Gifford) to call McCutcheon back for further instructions and that while Gifford was making this call and claimant was filling the radiator of his truck, he (claimant) fell and sustained the disabling injury complained of. The gist of 

McCutcheon's supporting testimony was that when the failure to get Sweet was reported to him, he left an order with claimant to keep on trying to get any man he could. 

The injury sustained resulted in hospitalization for about five days and was serious enough that Dr. J. A. Kervin, claimant's medical witness, prognosed continued total disability for some months subsequent to the hearing in the case. This doctor also expressed the opinion that the disability was due to the accident described to him. 

There is no serious dispute so far as the facts so outlined are concerned. Defendant called no witnesses of its own and failed, on cross-examination, to shake the account of the matter essentially as we have reviewed it. It chooses rather on this appeal to question whether or not the accidental injury was in the line of claimant's duty or, in other words, in the course of regular employment. On the issue posed it is argued that claimant was using his own truck; that he had not yet reported to the headquarters from which the garbage collection crews were dispatched and that, in any event, the use of his own truck to transport any helper he could secure would only constitute a personal convenience to the latter whoever he might be. 

In this connection defendant cites particularly the rule in 

Wolsko v. American Bridge Co., 158 Pa. Superior Ct. 339, but we cannot agree that the principle enunciated in that case is applicable here. Wolsko was found dead in a section of a shipyard at a place some distance from the work to which he was assigned and a reasonable inference was drawn to the effect that the death was due to a fall. The case turned, however, on the construction that the fatal fall occurred on the "premises" rather than merely the "property" of the named defendant.

[84 Dep. Rep. 

In the present case we are not dealing with a question which might be settled by reference to construction of the law as it draws the line of demarcation between the words "premises" and "property" in their legal meaning. Quite to the contrary, we are considering circumstances which involve a roving or "off the premises" employe and corollary thereto the particular circumstances which might bring such an employe on his way to work within the contemplation of the act which we administer. 

One of the earliest cases on the subject in hand had to do with a stenographer, who was injured crossing a street while on her way back to the office from her lunch hour, carrying a sandwich which her employer told her to get for him while she was out: Bridge v. Lomax, 69 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 109. The execution of the employer's simple order was the fact which brought her injury within the scope of her employment and, in our opinion, the same principle of law coming down to us unchallenged throughout the history of compensation law in this Commonwealth holds true in the case before us. It is now, of course, hornbrook law that disability from accidental injuries incurred going to or from work is not compensable. But an outside worker may come within the benefits of the act if, in either case, he is under orders. Bailey's position in this phase of the case is undeniably clear. He was not just on his way to work. 

He was running around his home neighborhood doing the personnel work for his superior, trying, on orders coming down to him through proper channels from his employer, "to get a man" to help at the task for the day. Had he ignored the directive he received from McCutcheon and driven to the place where his actual collections ceased the day before or the center from which new tours of duty were assigned, he might have found himself in hot water. 

He had to do what he was told and he was engaged in doing one of the incidental concomitants of that very thing when he was hurt.

Wherein the referee's conclusions are excepted to so far as this case concerns the interpretation of the law laid down

1948] 

 by the courts, we quote from Krchmar v. Oakland Beach 

Co., 155 Pa. Superior Ct. 430, as follows: “In general, where the accident occurs off the premises of the employer, the proofs must establish that the employee was actually engaged in furthering the business of the employer at the time of the injury. Palo v. Taylor- 

McCoy Coal & Coke Co. et al., 289 Pa. 401, 137 A. 625.

Otherwise, if the Act in which the employee was engaged when injured off the premises, was not connected with the employer's business it must appear that the employer ordered or directed the Act. Merely permitting the employee to do the Act without directing or ordering its performance will not support an award. Gibson v. Blowers Paint Serv. et al., 140 Pa. Superior. Ct. 216, 14 A. 2d 154. In the absence of a positive direction or order, we have held, even where the service is a part of the contract of employment, that there can be no recovery where the employee is injured while voluntarily performing the service off the premises after working hours. Haley v. City of Phila., 107 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 405, 163 A. 917. Cf. Cronin v. American Oil 

Co., 298 Pa. 336, 148 A. 476."

With the above quotation in mind it is clear to us that claimant was not only acting in furtherance of the business of his employer but also under positive orders. Thus he brought himself under not only one but two of the exceptions to the rule denying compensation for disability arising from injury sustained by "off premises" employes "going to or returning from" work.

The findings of fact, conclusions of law, award and bill of expense of Referee Smith dated May 22, 1947, are affirmed. 

The appeal is dismissed.

5 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD ANDRIOLI v. HUDSON COAL CO. 

Workmen's compensation—Injury in course of employment— 

Mine explosion—Violation of rules as to use of explosive— 

Burden of proof.

A referee's award of compensation claimed as a result of injuries sustained in a coal mine explosion will be affirmed where defendant alleged the explosion was caused by claimant's violation of positive orders in the use of an explosive, but where the referee further found that defendant had failed to comply with a rule of the Pennsylvania 

Anthracite Mine Law of June 2, 1891, requiring that the manner of charging and firing high explosives be in accordance with the special rules furnished by the manufacturer of the same and that said rules be endorsed with the manufacturer's official signature and be approved by the mine owner; in such case the burden of proving the rules and their violation by claimant so as to preclude an award was upon defendant, and the authentication of the manufacturer's rules and regulations for the use of powder products was not sufficiently proved where there was no evidence as to the time and place of the adoption or execution of the rules by the manufacturer. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Carmalt, specially presiding in the Second district. Claim petition no. 98,975. Appeal dismissed. November 19, 1947. 

Roger J. Dever, for claimant. 

Francis McMahon, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This case is before the board upon an appeal by defendant, Hudson Coal Company, from the order of Referee Carmalt awarding compensation to claimant, Carmen Andrioli, for accidental injuries sustained by him on March 13, 1944.

The record was before the board previously, upon an appeal by defendant from the referee's award (A-31443). After a careful study of the record in that case we were of the

1948] 

 opinion "that claimant was guilty of a violation of positive orders of his employers, thereby removing himself from the course of his employment and thus forfeiting any claims to compensation". Accordingly, we reversed the referee. 

Claimant then appealed to the Court of Common Pleas of 

Luzerne County. In an opinion by Judge Flannery, the court stated that it was "not satisfied that a so-called 'knowledge that it was a violation of the law' is sufficiently shown by the evidence, or if so shown that such would exempt the employer and the manufacturer from the obligations imposed by statute". The court points out that no specific findings were made as to the special rules furnished by the manufacture of the explosives used, their execution, authentication and posting. The court then remanded the record for such specific findings. Accordingly, the board remanded the record to the referee for the purposes indicated in the court opinion.

No additional testimony was offered at the remanded hearing before the referee. The referee added one addi tional finding of fact (8th) as follows: 

"Your referee finds as a fact that defendant has failed to comply with rule 29, article 12, of the Pennsylvania 

Anthracite Mine Law of June 2, 1891, in that special rules were not posted with proper execution and authentication as required by law."

Defendant's appeal challenges, in the main, the propriety of this finding under the remanding order of the court. 

We have again reviewed and made a careful study of the testimony of record, keeping in mind the directions of the court. We are satisfied as to the factual conditions present which we summarized in our earlier opinion. A fresh review of the record prompts no change or addition to our findings as to the circumstances attendant upon the accident. The particular question posed relates to the rules for the use of the explosive employed in the blasting charge. 

Rule 29, article XII, section 424 of the Pennsylvania Anthracite Mine Law of June 2, 1891, P. L. 176, provides:

"When high explosives other than gunpowder are used in any mine, the manner of storing, keeping, moving, charging and firing or in any manner using such explosives shall be in accordance with special rules as furnished by the manufacturers of the same. The said rules shall be indorsed with his or their official signature, and shall be approved by the owner, operator or superintendent of the mine in which such explosives are used."

The powder in question was manufactured by the E. I. duPont Company. The burden of proving the rules and violation of the rules by claimant so as to preclude an award is upon defendant, since the injury by accident is clearly established. Our prime inquiry is to determine whether the special rules of the manufacturer were duly executed, authenticated and posted. The measure of proof here approximates that required in criminal cases: Labuck v. Mill 

Creek Coal Co., 292 Pa. 284. In the Labuck case, involving an alleged violation of posted rules that a miner must not return to a misfire until the following day, the Supreme 

Court said (p. 286): "The Board was satisfied that the evidence did not show that the rules contained in the poster offered were the rules that were posted; nor did it show that the rules offered or posted were duly authenticated. Proof of both facts is required by the Act. They must be established either by direct evidence or by inference from proven circumstances if the employer wishes to succeed in his case." 

Wesley R. Stonebreaker, superintendent of defendant's

Baltimore colliery, testified that he furnished claimant with a copy of defendant's Rules for Miners and Laborers when he was hired on April 16, 1943, and that a copy of the Rules and Regulations of the duPont Company of Pennsylvania was duly posted at and prior to the date of the accident on the bulletin board, No. 5 shaft powder house. He identified the signature on the lefthand corner as his own. The superintendent stated that a copy of an abstract of the 

Anthracite Mining Laws of the Commonwealth was also

1948] 

 posted on the bulletin board at the colliery office. Counsel for defendant restricted the testimony upon the duPonts' Rules and Regulations to the genuineness of the facsimile signature of G. D'A. Belin, president of the E. I. duPont de Nemours and Company of Pennsylvania. Belin testified that he has been president of the corporation since 1918 and that the name "G. D'A. Belin" which appears in handwriting on the lower right hand corner of defendant's Exhibit 1 is a facsimile of his signature, which has been in use since 1918. The witness testified, under cross-examination, over objection by defendant's counsel, that he could not remember whether he was present at any meeting of the corporation where the rules were promulgated. The record is silent as to the authoritative source for offering the president's signature in the official capacity for the corporation. Nor is the corporate seal affixed to the rules. 

There is also no testimony of record as to the time and place of the adoption or execution of the rules for firing the explosives. Accordingly, we deem the testimony inadequate to prove that the rules in question were properly executed or authenticated by the duPont corporation. 

We ruled the case against claimant in our earlier opinion, principally on our 7th finding of fact that "the claimant had knowledge that it was a violation of law and defendant's rules and orders to drill or fire a misfired hole". 

The Common Pleas Court of Luzerne County stated in its opinion (p. 3): "We are not satisfied that a violation of the defendant's rules would be sufficient to defeat the claim", citing the following language from the case of 

Dickey v. Pittsburgh and Lake Erie R. R. Co., 297 Pa. 172, 175: . . . where the employee's duties included the doing of the Act that caused the injury, or where his duties were so connected with the Act that caused the injury that, as to it, he was not in the position of a stranger or trespasser. 

The violation of positive orders under these circumstances does not prohibit compensation for injuries sustained therefrom.'"

Violation of the orders given to claimant by defendant would not be fatal to his claim, under the circumstances attendant upon the injury in this case. The execution and authentication of the manufacturer's rules and regulations for the use of its powder product were not sufficiently proved to visit forfeiture of compensation benefits upon claimant. He is, therefore, entitled to compensation. We believe the referee's 8th finding of fact is adequate. 

The appeal of defendant is dismissed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD BRYANT v. CARNEGIE-ILLINOIS STEEL CORP. 

Workmen's compensation-Evidence-Accidental injury—Statement by claimant one month after occurrence. 

A referee's order dismissing claimant's petition for compensation will be affirmed where claimant alleged he suffered an accident resulting in a skull fracture and a spinal nervous injury, the testimony being to the effect that on the morning of the accident, claimant was apparently normal when he reported for work, that he performed various duties prior to 11 o'clock a.m., that he complained to a fellow worker that he had a pain in his head and about an hour later he entered the plant hospital, subsequent to which X-rays revealed a skull fracture and a spinal tap showed evidence of a cerebral accident, claimant thereafter being unable to speak; in such case, a statement made by claimant to his wife approximately one month after he entered the hospital when he had a lucid interval, that bricks had fallen on him on the morning of the occurrence was inadmissible as part of the res gestae.

1948] 

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Moore, district no. 8, claim petition no. 103,737. Appeal dismissed. 

November 5, 1947.

Sylvia Schlesinger, for claimant. 

C. E. Stewart, for defendant.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

This is an appeal by claimant from an order of the referee dismissing claimant's petition. 

Claimant's petition, filed on November 15, 1945, set out that while working as a metal liner in the course of his employment on December 11, 1944, he suffered an accident, as a result of which he sustained a "skull fracture and a brain and spinal nervous injury". Defendant's answer, filed on December 8, 1945, denied the material averments of claimant's petition. After hearing, the referee found that there was no proof that claimant had sustained an accident in the course of his employment and, in accordance with such finding, dismissed the petition. This appeal followed.

The testimony in this case is to the effect that, on the morning of the alleged accident, claimant was apparently normal when he reported for work; that, about 9:45 a.m., on being asked to bring two buckets to the liners whom he was helping, he asked for "small chains" but when told that it was buckets and not chains that were required, and upon being given a written order to procure same, he proceeded to the storeroom in the company of a fellow employe; that, at the storeroom, he talked and joked with a fellow employe and then returned, with the buckets, to the place where the ladle liners were working, where he worked without speaking until about 11:40 a.m. when his coworkers went to dinner; that, about 11 a.m. he complained to a co-worker that he had a pain in his head but thought

that it would be all right; that, about 11:50 he entered the plant hospital, at which time he was incoherent; that he was then removed to the Braddock Hospital where he was in a coma from December 11, 1944 until February 8, 1945. X-rays taken of claimant's skull on December 11, 1944, disclosed a fine line of fracture of the left temporal parietal region. On December 17, 1944, a spinal tap was made showing evidence of a cerebral accident. Claimant has been discharged from the hospital but is confused and unable to speak or work.

Testimony was given by witnesses for claimant that, upon visits to claimant, while in the hospital, bruises were noted upon claimant's head and elbow. This testimony was not corroborated by any of the medical witnesses who attended claimant immediately after the onset of his condition or while in the hospital. 

In addition, claimant's wife testified, under objection by counsel for defendant, that approximately one month after claimant entered the hospital he had his first lucid interval, at which time he stated to her that, on the morning of the occurrence, bricks had fallen on him.

After a careful review of the law applicable thereto, we are of the opinion that the statements made by claimant to his wife are not admissible as part of the res gestae. 

To be admissible as part of the res gestae, declarations must be the spontaneous utterances accompanying or immediately preceding the act in question, so near in point of time and place as to be in reality a part of it and not the designed statements of the actor or a recital of a past event. No fixed time with relation to the main event may be set up as a standard for the admission of hearsay declarations as a part of the res gestae; each case must depend on its own facts and circumstances: Riley v. Carnegie Steel 

Co., 276 Pa. 82; Ceccato v. Union Collieries Co., 1 P. C. R. 

65; Reeder v. Pittsburgh Collieries, 1 P. C. R. 34; Wagner v. Snyder, 6 P. C. R. 184.

In the instant case the testimony is to the effect that, about 11 a.m. on the day of the occurrence, claimant stated

1948] 

 to Charles Ryan, a co-worker, that he had a "very bad pain" in his head. There is no question that, at this time, claimant was conscious and able to speak coherently. It was at this time, if at all, that any statement made by claimant could be considered as part of the res gestae. The first statement made by claimant upon the recovery of consciousness or the ability to speak may be regarded as spontaneous even though some time has elapsed since the principal oc currence: Smith v. State Workmen's Insurance Co., 140 Pa. 

602. While it is true if the testimony of claimant's wife upon this point is to be accepted, that, at the time of his first lucid interval after the occurrence, claimant made the statement above set out, it cannot be considered as part of the res gestae in view of his statement made to Charles Ryan, immediately prior to his becoming incoherent and unconscious.

Deciding this point as we have, we are of the opinion that claimant has not proved the happening of an accident in the course of his employment. To constitute an accident, there must be some untoward occurrence aside from the usual course of events (Arhnaver v. Hodge & Webeck, 3 

P. C. R. 14) and claimant has the burden of establishing not only that an accident happened, but that he sustained injuries as a result thereof: Dougherty v. Altoona Con struction Co., 3 P. C. R. 34. Conversely, in order to recover compensation there must be proof of an accident. 

An accident cannot be inferred from an injury: Delaney v. 

Penna. Refining Co., 2 P. C. R. 9; Pelynsky v. Susquehanna 

Collieries, 2 P. C. R. 37; Ricci v. Vesta Coal Co., 3 P. C. R. 

78; Kirby v. Carnegie-Illinois Steel Corp., 1 P. C. R. 70.

While it is, of course, true that an award for compensation may be had even though there is no direct evidence of an accident, where the circumstances are such that an accident may logically and reasonably be inferred (Zborovian v. Suffolk Collieries Co., 93 Pa. Superior Ct. 320; Lario v. 

Pa. R. R. Co., 277 Pa. 382; Roth v. Locust Mountain State 

Hospital, 130 Pa. Superior Ct. 1) such rule can have no application to the facts of the instant case. Though the

testimony discloses that the onset of claimant's condition came while he was actually engaged in his duties for defendant, the testimony is to the effect that there was no actual physical evidence of the happening of an accident and, further, that during the entire time that claimant was working for defendant on the day of the occurrence, he was within observation of at least one of his co-employes, none of whom witnessed any accident involving claimant. Even more harmful to the claim of claimant is the testimony of the medical witnesses that the effects resulting from a fracture of the skull may not become apparent for a period of 24 hours or more after the fracture has been suffered. 

With the presence of such testimony, it would be impossible to infer that the condition suffered by claimant resulted from an accident suffered in the course of his employment.

PENNSYLVANIA SUPREME COURT SUN SHIPBUILDING AND DRYDOCK COMPANY v. 

UNEMPLOYMENT COMPENSATION BOARD OF REVIEW 

Unemployment compensation-Leaving employment without good cause-Entry upon private business venture-Unsuccessful termination of business-Section 802 of the

Unemployment Compensation Act. 

A person who voluntarily resigns from his employment in order to go into business for himself as an independent contractor will not be entitled to unemployment benefits upon the unsuccessful and involuntary termination of his private business venture; in such circumstances claimant's unemployment was due to his voluntarily

1948] 

21 leaving without good cause within the meaning of section 802 of the Unemployment Compensation Act, and he thereby became ineligible for compensation.

Appeal from Superior Court of Pennsylvania, October term, 1946, no. 230, affirming order of Unemployment Compensation Board of Review, September 10, 1946. Judgment reversed. Supreme Court of Pennsylvania, January term, 1947, no. 145. 

Harold Scott Baile and John D. M. Hamilton, for appellant. 

Roland M. Morgan, Associate Counsel; Charles R. Davis, Special Deputy Attorney General, and T. McKeen Chidsey, Attorney General, for appellee.

MAXEY, C. J.: 

This is the question to be decided: Is an individual who voluntarily resigns from his employment in order to go into business for himself as an independent contractor entitled to unemployment benefits upon the unsuccessful and involuntary termination of his private business venture? The Un employment Compensation Board of Review and the Su perior Court of Pennsylvania answered this question affirmatively.

Perkins Dawkins, claimant, was employed by the Sun 

Shipbuilding & Dry Dock Company, Chester, Pa., as a third-class sheet metal worker from October 20, 1942, until August 4, 1945, when he left appellant company's employ in order to engage in business for himself as a roofer. Claimant noted the following reason on his official separation slip: "Quit, going into business for myself."

From the date of his separation, claimant conducted a business as a roofing contractor, making about $35 per week, and he continued his private business until November, 1945, when he was forced to give it up because he could no longer secure necessary materials for carrying on his work.

The record establishes that on August 30, 1945, Dawkins filed a claim for unemployment benefits with his local unemployment compensation office. On that date claimant's "benefit year" began, his "base year" being the calendar year of 1944. The Bureau of Unemployment Compensation rendered a decision on December 7, 1945, declaring that claimant met all the requirements of the Unemployment Compensation Law and was therefore eligible to receive benefits. The Sun Shipbuilding & Dry Dock Co., Dawkins' 

base year employer, appealed from this decision and the case was referred to a Bureau Referee, who on February 27, 1946, conducted a hearing. In testifying at that time, Dawkins told how he had reached a decision to resign from his employment with appellant company, as follows: 66 . . the war was over and I hadn't been making any headway, I did some work and I figured I could do better on the outside doing roofing. I came out to work for myself, but I put in my resignation. I didn't walk off the job.

I gave them a whole month's resignation. . . . After the war was over I considered two things, first my age and I figured I would probably be one of the first ones to go because I was 57, so I took that into consideration and between time I built up myself a nice little business." 

The Referee concurred in the decision of the Bureau and affirmed its Findings of Fact, which consisted, inter alia, of the following: "2. A month previous to August 4th, 1945, claimant gave his employer notice that he was going to resign for the specific purpose of going into business for himself."

In his "Reasoning", the Referee made the following statements: "The Referee believes that this business of claimant's was a legitimate business and its failure to succeed was no fault of the claimant's and his separation therefrom can be construed as unemployed due to lack of work. The Referee must therefore conclude that claimant did not volun-

1948] 

 tarily leave his last place of employment without good cause within the meaning of the Law."

The appellant thereupon filed an appeal with the Unem ployment Compensation Board of Review and on August 

5, 1946, the Board of Review issued an order upholding the referee's Findings of Facts and Conclusion of Law award ing benefits to the claimant. The Board of Review stated: "On the basis of these Findings [which are "supported by the evidence"], the Referee properly concluded that the claimant cannot be disqualified under the provisions of Section 402 (b) of the Law. The unemployment for which claimant seeks benefits was due to the failure of a business enterprise and not to voluntarily leaving work, and for this reason he must be found eligible for benefits with respect to the provisions of the Unemployment Compensation Law."

A petition seeking "judicial review on the ground that the board erred in concluding as a matter of law that the claimant's act of voluntarily leaving his employment for the purpose of going into business for himself, constitutes 'good cause' within the meaning of the Unemployment Compensation Act" was filed by appellant with the Superior Court of Pennsylvania. A review was granted. The Superior Court sustained the decision of the Board of Review, saying, inter alia: "Under the definition, claimant clearly was not unemployed until his business failed. In the interim, between the date when he left his employment and the failure of his business, he was employed since he received remuneration for services rendered in his business." 

Appellant contends that claimant was an "independent contractor" after he severed his connection with appellant company and not an "employee" within the contemplation of the Unemployment Compensation Act and thus was disqualified from receiving the benefits conferred by the act; that if claimant's "employee" status was not forfeited by virtue of his resignation, he was nevertheless ineligible for benefits under section 802 of the Act, 43 PS Supp., which

reads: "An employe shall be ineligible for compensation for any week—(a) . . . (b) In which his unemployment is due to voluntarily leaving without good cause . . ." As amended April 23, 1942, Ex. Sess., P. L. 60, sec. 4; May 21, 1943, P. L. 337, sec. 1; May 29, 1945, P. L. 1145, sec. 9. Effective

June 1, 1945. 

Apparently this case is sui generis. We find no case like it in either this or other jurisdictions. Our decision must be based on reasoning and not on authority. 

The decision under review is based on the postulate that the "unemployment for which claimant seeks benefits was due to the failure of a business enterprise and not to voluntarily leaving work, and for this reason he must be found eligible for benefits with respect to the provisions of the 

Unemployment Compensation Law". This rationale we do not accept. The initial question is: Was Dawkins an "employee" within the purview of the Unemployment Compensation Law? The Pennsylvania Unemployment Compensation Act defines "employe" as follows: 66 ''Employe' means every individual, whether male, female, citizen, alien or minor, who is performing or subsequent to January first, one thousand nine hundred thirtysix, has performed services for an employer in an employment subject to this act." 43 P. S. Supp. 753 (i) 

Dawkins while in the service of Sun Shipbuilding and Dry

Dock Company was an "employee". But subsequently he changed his status from that of an employee to that of an "individual engaged in an independently established business".

At this point it is pertinent to quote certain sections of the Unemployment Compensation Act. Section 753 (1) (I) states: 

66 'Employment' means (i) all service performed prior to the first day of January, one thousand nine hundred forty-five, which was employment as defined in this section prior to the effective date of this amendment, and (ii) all

1948] 

1 service performed after the thirty-first day of December, one thousand nine hundred forty-four, which is employment as defined in this section as hereby amended . . . (2) The term 'Employment' shall include an individual's entire service performed within or both within and without this Commonwealth, if-(A) ... (B) ... 'An individual performing services for remuneration in an employment subject to this act shall be deemed to be performing such services for wages, unless and until it is shown to the satisfaction of the department that-(a) such individual has been and will continue to be free from control or direction over the performance of such services both under his contract of service and in fact; and (b) . . . (c) that such individual is customarily engaged in an independently established trade, occupation, profession or business": 43 P.S. 

Supp (i), As amended, April 21, 1943, Ex. Sess., P. L. 

60, sec. 1; May 21, 1943, P. L. 271, No. 125, sec. 1; May 27, 1943, P. L. 717, sec. 1; May 29, 1945, P. L. 1145, sec. 1. 

Effective January 1, 1945.

Subsections (u) and (x) of section 753, as amended, May 

29, 1945, state: "(u) 'Unemployment'-An individual shall be deemed unemployed with respect to any week during which he performs no services and with respect to which no remuneration is paid or payable to him . . ." Effective June 1, 1945. "(x) 'Wages' means all remuneration for employment paid with respect to all services performed prior to 1. That remuneration means wages is clear from a consideration of the applicable section of the Act before its amendment. There it was stated ". . . An individual performing services for remuneration in an employment subject to this act shall be deemed to be performing such services for wages, unless and until it is shown to the satisfaction of the department that (a) (b)... (c) that such individual is customarily engaged in an independently established trade, occupation, profession or business." 43 P.S. 753 (j), Dec. 5, 1936, Second Ex. Sess., P. L. (1937) 2897, art. I, sec. 4; May 18, 1937, P. L. 658, sec. 1; June 20, 1939, P. L. 485, sec. 1; May 16, 1940, Extra 

Sess., P. L. 

No. 9, sec. 1. .... ...

January first, one thousand nine hundred and fortytwo..." Effective June 1, 1945.

It is provided in the Act, 43 P. S. 802, as amended, 1942, on April 23, P. L. 60, sec. 4; 1943, May 21, P. L. 337, sec. 

1; 1945, May 29, P. L. 1145, sec. 9, as follows: "An employe shall be ineligible for compensation for any week-(a) . . .; (b) In which his unemployment is due to voluntarily leaving work without good cause: • • 99 In discussing the phrase "good cause" the Superior Court says, ". . . it must be a good cause which animates a man to seek the fullest expression and amplest development of his highest skills and capacities, and to strive for steady employment, be it in his own business or in service for others." It may be conceded that this statement is an expression of sound social philosophy, but the "good cause" thus referred to is not the "good cause" which under the Act justifies an employee voluntarily leaving his work. If an employee left his work to fight for his country on the field of battle his act would be praiseworthy but his patriotic motive and his willingness to sacrifice his life would not constitute the good cause which as a motive for leaving his work would maintain his eligibility for compensation benefits afterwards. By "good cause" as used in the Act is obviously meant such a cause as justifies an employee's voluntarily leaving the ranks of the employed and joining the ranks of the unemployed. For example, if an employee was compelled to work in a position where his life was constantly menaced by a heavy object over his head which was suspended from the ceiling by a palpably inadequate or defective chain, he could successfully plead "good cause" for voluntarily leaving his employment. The same would be true if he was compelled to work under inexcusable conditions which were palpably detrimental to his health, such as working in a mine or factory where the supply of fresh air was obviously insufficient to sustain life. 

In Dames Unemployment Compensation Case, 158 Pa. 

Superior Court 564, the Superior Court held that a woman

1948] 

 who left her employment to marry could not have that praiseworthy motive accepted as a good cause for leaving her employment. In that case Judge Reno said, "No legal obligation rested upon the claimant to marry or to join her fiance" (who was in the Armed Forces). This case is an example of the fact that a laudable motive for leaving employment and a "good cause" within the meaning of the Act are entirely different things. 

In Teicher Unemployment Compensation Case, 154 Pa. 

Superior Court 250, the claimant left her employment to live with her husband who was in the Armed Forces. All seven judges of the Superior Court held that that claimant by voluntarily leaving her work and moving to Alexandria to be with her husband made herself "unavailable for work" and was therefore not entitled to compensation. Five members of the Court declared that the claimant in leaving her job in order to be with her husband left her work "with good cause". This latter conclusion was not necessary to a decision of the case. We express no agreement with the dictum that such a "humanly justifiable cause" as "the impulse which induces a devoted wife to spend with a husband, who is a member of the Armed Forces in time of war, what may prove to be the last days they shall ever be together on earth" (as the Superior Court expressed it) constitutes a "good cause" for leaving a job, within the meaning of the Act. 

In Sturdevant Unemployment Compensation Case, 158

Pa. Superior Court 548, it appeared that a married woman, employed as a skilled machine operator in an industrial plant left her work to join her husband in the armed forces near a city other than that in which she was employed; that she registered for work in the nearby city, stating that she was available for a 30-day period only; and that in the new locality there were no demands for her particular skill; it was held, apparently on the authority of the dictum in the Teicher case, supra, that claimant was entitled to unemployment compensation benefits. In this Sturdevant case Judge Reno said:

- 

"Of course, 'good cause' and 'personal reasons' are flexible phrases, capable of contraction and expansion, and by construction, all meaning can be compressed out of them or they may be expanded to cover almost any meaning. 

However, in whatever context they appear, they connote, as minimum requirements, real circumstances, substantial reasons, objective conditions, palpable forces that operate to produce correlative results, adequate excuses that will bear the test of reason, just grounds for action, and always the element of good faith. .. When we approach the problem of a married woman who leaves her work to join her husband we realize immediately that we are in the presence of a compulsion which readily supplies a personal reason and a good cause. Under our law, it is the legal right of the husband to select the marital domicile and it is the legal duty of the wife to reside with him. Hence, when a husband moves the marital domicile to a distant point where he secures work and his wife voluntarily leaves her work to accompany him, her compliance with the duty which the law casts upon her satisfies the requirements of 'good cause'."

To hold that a married woman who quits her job to join her husband in a new domicile is voluntarily becoming "unemployed" for a "good cause" within the meaning of the Act is to open the door to so much fraud on employers that one may doubt that such a construction of the Unemployment Compensation Act conforms to the canon that "all laws should receive a sensible construction": per Field, J. in United States v. Kirby, 7 Wall 482, 486, cited with approval in Watson v. Witkin, 343 Pa. 1, 6. In this last cited case we quoted with approval what Judge Cardozo said in In re Rouss, 221 N.Y. 81, 116 N.E. 782, as follows: "Statutes must be so construed, if possible, that absurdity and mischief may be avoided." If a woman can quit her job in order to follow her husband into another domicile where work for her will not be available, and then become entitled to the benefits of this Compensation Act, and

1948] 

 if a workman can quit his job to go into private business and then when that business fails he can still reap the benefits of this Compensation Act, the latter will in many instances be used as a "short cut" to a temporary pension. While the good faith of the claimants in such cases is always open to attack, whoever makes such an attack has the burden of proving bad faith and in this class of cases it will be a difficult burden to maintain. 

No principle applicable to the interpretation of statutes has been more widely used than the principle enumerated in Heydon's Case, 3 Coke 7a, 14 Eng. Rul. Cas. 816, cited in 25 R.C.I.. 1016, section 254, as follows: 66 for the sure and true interpretation of all statutes in general four things are to be discerned and considered: '(1) What was the common law before the making of the act? (2) What was the mischief and defect for which the common law did not provide? (3) What remedy the Parliament hath resolved and appointed to cure the disease of the commonwealth. And (4) the true reason of the remedy.' 999 

These second and fourth "things" should be considered in solving the question before us. The "mischief" to be remedied was the condition of involuntarily out of work laboring men in an era when wages were such that it was difficult for them to save money for the proverbial "rainy day". Such unemployed workmen frequently became indigent and their families were left without the necessities of life. The "true reason of the remedy" provided in the Unemployment Compensation Act is clearly set forth in the intendments of the Act, inter alia, in Section 3 (43 P.S. 752), as follows: 

"a. That the economic insecurity which the act seeks to avoid is the 'Involuntary unemployment and its resulting burden of indigency' which falls with crushing force upon the unemployed worker . . .” "b. That this insecurity can best be met 'by the systematic setting aside of financial reserves to be used as compensation for the loss of wages by employes 99

"c. That the Commonwealth is justified in exercising its police powers 'for the compulsory setting aside of unemployment reserves . . This reserve is of course to be set aside by the employer and is 'to be used for the benefit of persons unemployed through no fault of their own"." 

These intendments make it clear that those within the protection of the Act are "unemployed workers". By that last quoted phrase is meant those who while working for wages become unemployed. In that class there is not included those who did not work for wages but who voluntarily removed themselves from the latter class to become independently engaged in a business of their own. 

When this claimant voluntarily quit his job as an employee for wages to become an independent contractor he took himself out of the class entitled to the protection of the Act now under consideration. He became a businessman at his own risk. He could not assume his new status with the legal assurance that if his expectations of more favorable economic results from his new status was realized he would be the sole gainer while if his venture failed he could fall back on the compensation benefits which were his when he was a worker for wages. The law does not make Pennsylvania employers the insurers to any extent whatsoever of the private ventures of their employees. In a free society any employee may quit his work for any reason which appears to him adequate, but if he "gambles" with his job as an employee in the hope of becoming a businessman and an employer himself he cannot expect to find that the "game" is one in which all the possible gains are to be his while the losses, if any, are to be borne chiefly by his last employer.

In his testimony claimant gives his reason for ceasing to be an employee and going into business for himself. He said: ". . . from the time I put in there and the way I put the time in I figured I wasn't getting the proper break I should have gotten." He added what is quoted in the third paragraph of the opinion. Without consulting his

1948] 

 employer and without seeking any information as to his probable employment tenure he decided that he would leave the ranks of wage earners and become a business man, and so on August 4, 1945, he became "customarily engaged in an independent business", that of roofing. He continued "on his own" from August until November, when he discovered that by his change of status he had worsened his economic position. If, for example, he had been admitted to the Bar just before the war and had at once, for either patriotic or economic reasons, become an employee of the Sun Shipbuilding Company and had on August 4, 1945, quit his job and entered upon the practice of law and then about three months later had decided that the law was not his field, he could not by abandoning his professional career have restored his eligibility to the Unemployment 

Compensation benefits he had voluntarily forfeited months before by renouncing his then status.

It is true that claimant was unemployed after he failed as a businessman, but since he had renounced his status as a "wage earner" in order to become a "businessman" his failure in the latter role did not automatically restore him to the status of an "unemployed employee" any more than a manumitted slave's failure to gain a livelihood on his own piece of land would automatically restore him to the status he had before his manumission. Claimant can be restored to his former status of an employee only by again performing as an employee "services for an employer in any employment subject to this Act". The "good cause" which compelled claimant to terminate his career as an individual contractor cannot be used as a substitute for the not-good cause which impelled him to leave the employ of the Shipbuilding Company.

An individual wage-earner is within the protection of the Unemployment Compensation Act only as long as he has the status of an employee as that term is used in the 

Act. His idleness immediately following his employment does not affect his status. He is still an employee, though

out of work, if (1) his being out of work was not willed by himself, or (2) if his being out of work was voluntary but was based on a "good cause" within the meaning of the Act. The "good cause" which justifies an employee's terminating his relations with his employer must, other than in those exceptional cases where reasons "personal to the employee" may under a certain state of facts be adjudged "good", be one connected with his employment. He certainly is not within the "good cause" provision if he quits his employment in order to comply with the wishes of his wife, or in order to marry a girl who made his quitting his employment a condition precedent to the marriage, or because of some whimsical desire or fancy or ambition of his own. See Barclay White Co. v. Unemp. Comp. Bd., 356 Pa. 43, 48, 50 A. 2d 336, where we emphasized the fact that Article 1, section 3, of the Unemployment Compensation Law of December 5, 1936, P.L. (1937) 2897, as amended, was enacted "for the benefit of persons unemployed through no fault of their own". In that case we also said (p. 48): “It is impossible to give a general definition of 'good cause'. The meaning of those words must be determined in each case from the facts of that case." 

We added: "good cause' must be so interpreted that the fundamental purpose of the legislation shall not be destroyed." Even in matters connected with his employment there must be some limit to the legally approved list of "good causes" for quitting employment. The quitting must be for such a cause as would reasonably motivate in a similar situation the average able-bodied and qualified worker to give up his or her employment with its certain wage rewards in order to enter the ranks of the "compensated unemployed".

An employee may contend that the character and habits of his fellow employees are distasteful to him, he may contend that the work he is engaged in (such as the making of war munitions or alcoholic beverages) offends his religious or moral principles, or he may contend that his family ob-

1948] 

 jects to his working in a job in which he becomes begrimed with dirt, yet these and similar reasons cannot be legally accepted as a "good cause" for leaving one's employment.

If an employee leaves his position as a wage earner so that he may become a professional man or a business man or any other sort of "free-lance" he cannot successfully contend that he left his former employment for a statutorily "good cause" and that if he fails at his independent work he is immediately restored to his status quo ante. 

We do not agree that since this claimant's ambition to be independently self-supporting was a "laudable" one, such ambition must be adjudged a "good cause" for leaving his then employment. In most civil cases requiring the adjudication of rights and liabilities the laudability of an actor's motive has no bearing on the legal appraisal of his act. If every reason which appeals to an employee's head or his heart is to be accepted as a "good cause" for his or her voluntarily leaving a job in a locality where there is no other work available, the Unemployment Compensation Law will become in many instances an invitation to a compensated rest.

This claimant on August 4, 1945, voluntarily took himself out of that class which is under the protection of this law for a cause which cannot legally be recognized as "good". He took an economic risk when he left the employer-employee field with the expectation of succeeding as an independent contractor and then becoming an employer. 

When his private venture failed he did not ipso facto become an unemployed employee-he became an unemployed businessman.

The judgment of the Superior Court is reversed and the order of the Unemployment Compensation Board of Review affirming the decision and order of the bureau and the referee granting the claimant unemployment compensation benefits, is set aside.

Dissenting Opinion 

JONES, J. (dissenting):

I think the opinion for the Superior Court fully and correctly justifies the decision made in this case by the Unemployment Compensation Board of Review which I would affirm on the able opinion of Judge Reno. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD RZEPLINSKY v. STATE WORKMEN'S INSURANCE FUND ET AL. 

Workmen's compensation-Occupational Disease Act-Acceptance by employer prior to employe's death from silicosis but after termination of employment.

A referee's award of compensation to claimant, as dependent widow of a decedent, who died from silicosis contracted during the time of his employment by defendant coal company, will be set aside where it appears that decedent stopped working on May 29, 1946, that he died July 21, 1946, that during the entire period of his employment with defendant, the latter had rejected the Occupational Disease Act though it subsequently agreed to accept the provisions of the act under a contract with decedent's union effective May 31, 1946; since decedent performed no services after the time the contract became effective, he was not an employe within the definition of that term as set forth in section 104 of the act. 

Appeal by Commonwealth of Pennsylvania from award of Referee Enterline, district no. 5, claim petition no. 

107,863. Appeal sustained. December 23, 1947.

State Workmen's Insurance Fund, insurance carrier. 

Roger J. Dever, for claimant. 

Ralph H. Behney and Mr. C. E. Bottiger, for defendants.

1948] 

 MURPHY, Chairman: 

The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania has appealed from the referee's award of compensation to claimant as dependent widow of John Rzeplinsky, who died July 21, 1946.

Exposure to a silica hazard for the statutory period and silicosis as the cause of death are not disputed. The question before us is whether decedent's employment with defendant was covered by the Occupational Disease Act of 1939, as amended July 1, 1945. The referee found that it was; we believe it was not.

Decedent had worked for defendant, and its predecessor company, from 1934 to May 29, 1946, when he ceased work because of an attack of bronchial pneumonia. He recovered from that disease but was unable to resume work because of the anthraco-silicosis, from which he died July 21, 1946. 

During the entire period of decedent's employment with defendant, the latter was a rejector of the Occupational 

Disease Act. By virtue of a contract between defendant and decedent's union, defendant agreed to accept the provisions of the Occupational Disease Act, effective May 31, 1946. This contract was entered into after decedent quit working for defendant, but before his death. 

The contract between the union and defendant was not a contract of hire; it merely set forth the terms under which, after its effective date, defendant would hire members of the union. There was no contract of hire between decedent and defendant after its effective date, and therefore no employment of decedent after that date.

Perhaps upon the theory that decedent continued as an employe during his illness the referee found that decedent was entitled to the benefit of the terms of the new contract between his union and defendant. Had decedent reported for work after May 31, 1946, and been accepted by defendant or had he performed any services for defendant there would have been no question as to his status; but even though he be considered to have been a potential

employe, he had no contract of hire into which the terms of the accepted Occupational Disease Act could be read. 

Section 104 of the act defines the term employe as follows: "The term 'employe', as used in this act, is declared to be synonymous with servant, and includes all natural persons who perform services . for another for a valuable consideration. . . ." (Italics supplied.) 

Clearly decedent "performed" no "services" on or after 

May 31, 1946, nor until the date of his death on July 21, 1946. During that period, therefore, he was not an "employe" within the definition in the act. 

It is a matter of sincere regret that we are constrained to so rule, but if we are to decide cases on judgment rather than emotion we have no alternative. Any other ruling would lead to an incongruous result. Any employe prevented by total disability from working for defendant subsequent to May 31, 1946, if he be a "continuing employe❞ would be entitled to the protection of the act. In case of death his dependents would be entitled to compensation, limited only by the three-year death period in the act. Thus a valid rejection of the act would be swept aside. In the instant case decedent missed "performing services" by a period of only two days, but if the principle be sound, a period of two years would make no difference. No such result was ever contemplated by the parties nor does it follow under the law.

The referee's 1st and 2nd findings of fact are affirmed. 

The 3rd finding of fact is set aside and in lieu thereof we substitute the following findings of fact: 

Finding of fact "3. Decedent performed services for defendant, Philadelphia & Reading Coal & Iron Company, from 1934 until May 

29, 1946, on which date he was stricken with pneumonia.

1948] 

He recovered therefrom, but due to bronchial and allied conditions remained at home until July 21, 1946, on which date he died. From May 29, 1946, until July 21, 1946, claimant did not perform services for defendant." 

The remaining findings of fact are affirmed. 

We strike out the referee's conclusions of law and in lieu thereof make the following:

"1. On May 29, 1946, defendant had rejected the provisions of the Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act of 

1939 and its amendments of 1945. 

2. Decedent, having performed no services for defendant, Philadelphia & Reading Coal & Iron Company, subsequent to May 29, 1946, until his death on July 21, 1946, was not an employe of said defendant during that period, within the meaning of the Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act of 1939 and its amendments of 1945. 

His dependents are therefore not entitled to receive compensation."

We strike out the referee's award, and substitute therefor the following:

Order "Claimant's petition is dismissed."

The appeal of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania is sustained.

SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA HAUG v. UNEMPLOYMENT COMPENSATION BOARD OF REVIEW 

Unemployment compensation-Refusal to accept new job at lower rate-Reasonable time within which to find suitable work. 

An order of the Unemployment Compensation Board of Review disallowing compensation to a claimant will be affirmed where it appears that, after being unemployed for approximately 10 months, claimant was offered work which she refused to take on the ground that the rate of pay was insufficient, but where it further appeared that she had made no attempt to obtain employment between the time when she was laid off and the time when the work at the lower rate which she was capable of performing was offered to her; under the circumstances, her refusal to work was without good cause. 

Appeal from decision of Unemployment Compensation 

Board of Review, dated April 18, 1947, at appeal no. B-44- 

99-D-1519. Affirmed January 8, 1948. Superior Court of 

Pennsylvania, October term, 1947, no. 170.

Roland M. Morgan and T. McKeen Chidsey, Attorney General, for appellee.

RHODES, P. J.: 

This is an unemployment compensation case in which the bureau disqualified claimant, the referee reversed the bureau, and the board of review reversed the referee, and entered an order disallowing compensation. In support thereof, the board of review specifically found the following facts: Claimant's last employment, with the Aldan Rubber

Company as clerk inside the plant at a wage of 90 cents per hour, was terminated by lay-off on August 31, 1945. She had previous work experience as sales clerk in a dry goods store. On June 20, 1946, claimant was referred to the J. B. 

Smith Company (iron works), which offered a position

1948] 

 placing nuts and bolts in vents at a wage of 55 cents per hour. After interviewing the prospective employer, claimant refused the position on the grounds that the wage rate was insufficient, and that the work was not in conformity with her prior training and experience. The board of review concluded: "Inasmuch as claimant had been unemployed approximately 10 months at the time the work was offered to her, it is the opinion of this board that she had been given ample opportunity to find employment of the standard she desired and, therefore, her refusal to accept the work offered was unwarranted."

From the action of the board thus disqualifying her for compensation, claimant has taken this appeal. 

The facts in the case are undisputed, and the only question presented is whether they form a sufficient basis for concluding that claimant was offered suitable work and that she refused it without good cause. 

In the broad sense, "suitable work" is not synonymous with "want of good cause" in refusing work; rather, they are to be treated as separate and distinct concepts: Bar clay White Co. v. Unemployment Compensation Board of 

Review, 356 Pa. 43, 48, 50 A. (2d) 336. A claimant who refuses to accept referred suitable work without good cause is ineligible for compensation under the statute: Unem ployment Compensation Law of December 5, 1936, P. L. 

(1937) 2897, sec. 402 (a), as amended by the Act of May 

29, 1945, P. L. 1145, sec. 9, 43 PS §802. But in the present case, claimant has assigned as "good cause" for rejecting the proffered employment two factors which the legislature has designated (among others) for consideration in reaching a determination as to whether or not particular work is "suitable": (1) Prior training and experience, and (2) previous earnings of the employe: Unemployment Compensation Law of December 5, 1936, P. L. (1937) 2897, sec. 

4 (r), as amended and relettered section 4(t), by the Act of 

May 29, 1945, P. L. 1145, sec. 1, 43 PS §753. Consequently,

we are of the opinion that the finding of the board of review that claimant's refusal of the work was "unwarranted" or without "good cause" was also a finding by necessary implication that the proffered work was "suitable." 

We have recognized that, where an employe is referred to a position which pays a wage materially lower than the wage last earned, the employe may be justified in refusing such a referral while seeking employment at a rate of pay more commensurate with his previously demonstrated earning capacity. The right to decline work for this reason is not, however, without qualification; the employe is entitled only to a reasonable opportunity to obtain work at a satisfactory wage rate. In Fuller Unemployment Compensation 

Case, 159 Pa. Superior Ct. 74, 46 A. (2d) 510, we held that in the circumstances 19 days did not allow claimant a reasonable time within which to secure suitable work; and in 

Davis Unemployment Compensation Case, 159 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 77, 46 A. (2d) 512, where claimant refused an offered employment because the salary was too low, we sustained the board in holding that, in the circumstances prevailing at the time the offered employment was refused, five days in which to find suitable work was not a reasonable time. 

In the present case it appears from claimant's own testimony that she made no attempt to obtain employment (except to ascertain that at the store where she had previously worked they did not need any additional help) between 

August 31, 1945, when she was laid off, and June, 1946, when she filed her second registration for work with the bureau and reopened her claim for a second benefit year. 

We believe that claimant had ample opportunity, of which she did not choose to avail herself, to seek and obtain employment at a rate of pay satisfactory to her. Her refusal of work at the lower rate, after the lapse of a 10month period, was therefore without good cause. 

Claimant also objected to the proffered work on the ground that it was not in conformity with her prior training and experience. We attach little weight to this objec-

1948] 

 tion. She admitted that she was capable of performing the work and that she would have accepted the position except for the wage rate and her assumption that there was "no chance of advancement." A reference to claimant's testimony in which she described more particularly her duties with the Aldan Rubber Company, the last employer, shows that the duties were performed not in the office but in the shop, and consisted of placing tickets on rolls of cloth which passed through the plant in the course of a process of rubberizing. While this task differs somewhat from that of placing nuts and bolts in vents, we are not convinced that the difference was so great as to render the proffered work unsuitable. 

Decision is affirmed.

SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA BOYERTOWN BURIAL CASKET COMPANY v. UNEM- PLOYMENT COMPENSATION BOARD OF REVIEW, ETC. 

Unemployment compensation-Compensation to employes on strike 

Unemployment Compensation Law-Constitutionality. 

The Pennsylvania Unemployment Compensation Law does not violate the Federal or Pennsylvania Constitution in providing that employes may be entitled to unemployment compensation under certain circumstances in labor dispute cases nor may such compensation be denied because the payment thereof will cause an employer's contribution to the unemployment compensation fund to be increased under experience rating.

Appeal from Unemployment Compensation Board of Re view dated February 10, 1947, decision no. B 44-98-B-330. 

Affirmed. January 8, 1948. Superior Court of Pennsylvania, October term, 1947, no. 119.

Lewis H. Van Dusen, Jr., and Henry S. Drinker, for appellant.

ARNOLD, J.:

In this unemployment compensation case the employes of the Boyertown Burial Casket Company, after failure of negotiations as to wages, hours and conditions of employment, went out on a strike on May 1, 1946.

Claimant, and his associates, were awarded unemployment compensation, after the expiration of the four weeks' waiting period, under section 402 (d) of the act as amended 

(43 PS §802), which reads: 

"An employe shall be ineligible for compensation for any week— ... (d) in which his unemployment is due to a voluntary suspension of work resulting from an industrial dispute, at the . premises at which he . . . was last employed: Provided, That this disqualification shall apply only to . . . [the] period beginning with the day on which such suspension occurs and ending with (i) the last day of the fourth calendar week immediately following such suspension or (ii) the day on which such suspension was terminated, whichever is the earlier." The employer as intervenor appeals.

Under the original Unemployment Compensation Act of 

December 5, 1936, P. L. 2897, sec. 401 (e), it was provided: "If the employe's total unemployment is due to a voluntary suspension of work resulting from an industrial dispute, then he shall be ineligible for compensation for a further waiting period of three weeks . . ."; thus making a waiting period of six weeks in the industrial dispute cases. In the same section it was provided: "Compensation shall be payable to any employe who is or becomes totally unemployed..." upon meeting certain conditions of earnings, registration for work, the making of a claim, and his ability and availability for work, after a waiting period of three weeks. The original act, section 4 (s) defined "total unemployment" as meaning that an employe, during a particular week, has had no work for which wages are payable to him.

1948] 

The original act was amended in 1942, P. L. 60; 1943, P. L. 337 and P. L. 717; and 1945, P. L. 1145,¹ and the legislature adhered to the policy of paying unemployment compensation where a voluntary suspension of work resulted from an industrial dispute; but the waiting period was reduced to four weeks, and the method was changed by taking the proviso from section 401 and placing the sub stance of it in section 402 (d) (43 PS §802)—"Ineligibility for compensation"; and in section 401 the words "totally unemployed" were changed to "unemployed"; and in section 4 (u) "unemployment" was defined in substantially the same words as the original act defined "total unemployment."

Compensation is therefore payable to any employe who, after meeting the qualifications of section 401, is unemployed, i. e., has performed no services for which remuneration was payable; unless he is rendered ineligible under section 402 (43 PS §802): Sturdevant Unemployment Com pensation Case, 158 Pa. Superior Ct. 548, 45 A. (2d) 898.

Under section 402 (d) this claimant was only rendered ineligible for the first four weeks following the voluntary suspension of work.

Appellant adduces many arguments that unemployment compensation ought not to be granted in the labor dispute cases, but we must again state that the legislature possessed and exercised the sole power to determine the social and economic policies involved in unemployment compensation, and embedded them in the Unemployment Compensation Law as it was from time to time amended.
