Where an employe voluntarily left his employment in a jurisdictional strike in which an American Federation of Labor union attempted to supplant a Congress of Industrial Organization union as the bargaining agent of employes in the employer's plant, his unemployment as a result thereof was voluntary and not the result of an industrial dispute and was without good cause as defined under section 402 (b) of the Unemployment Compensation Law, hence he was not entitled to compensation. 

Appeals from decision of Unemployment Compensation

Board of Review awarding compensation. Appeals sus tained. January 8, 1948. Superior Court of Pennsylvania, April term, 1948, nos. 88 and 89. 

Mulvihill, Gollmar, Herron & Grier, for appellants.

Richard H. Wagner and T. McKenn Chidsey, for appellee. 

HIRT, J.: 

These appeals, which as test cases will govern a number of other claims for unemployment compensation, raise a single legal question on facts which are identical in material respects. The referee modified the decision of the bureau in claimants' favor, on a finding that these claimants had voluntarily left their work without good cause and accordingly were ineligible for compensation under section

402 (b) of the amendment of the Unemployment Compen sation Law of May 29, 1945, P. L. 1145, 43 PS §802. 

The Unemployment Compensation Board of Review, on appeal, however, concluded that claimants' absence from work was the result of an industrial dispute. On that finding the decision of the referee was reversed and claim credits for benefits were allowed subject to the disqualification period under section 402 (d) of the above act. A recital of the undisputed facts will demonstrate that the referee was right in refusing all benefits in these cases. The orders of the board will be reversed. 

For some years the breweries in the Pittsburgh area were parties to a closed-shop labor agreement with the executive board of Local No. 144 and two other local unions, affiliates of International Union of United Brewery, Flour, Cereal and Soft Drink Workers of America. 

The agreements governed the terms of employment of workers in the bottling departments of the breweries and were in full force and effect during the period involved in this appeal, and would not expire thereafter until April 1, 1947. At the time these agreements were entered into, the 

International union was independent and was not associated either with the American Federation of Labor or the Congress of Industrial Organizations. Claimants were members of Local No. 144. In July 1946 a majority of the entire membership of the International union voted to affiliate with the Congress of Industrial Organizations. As a protest against the referendum which resulted in affiliation 

Local No. 144, joined a new Local Union No. 232, affiliated with the C. I. O., claimants, with other former members of with the Teamsters Union of the A. F. of L. Claimant,

Peter Loerlein, became president of the new local union and Patsey Stella was a provisional member. Early in October 

1946 the executive committee of Local 232 ordered its members to stop work. Picket lines were then established by this local at the plants of appellants and were maintained until April 2, 1947, when the strike ended, by agreement

1948] 

 between appellants and the joint council of the teamsters' unions, which included Local 232, A. F. of L. Stella did not work after October 7, 1946; Loerlein left the employ of 

Duquesne Brewing Company on October 10, 1946 and did not work thereafter. From the testimony in these cases it is clear, as the Board of Review found, "that the work stoppage by members of Local Union No. 144 of the International union who were also members of Local No. 232 of the teamsters' union, was part of an effort to give effect to their unit determination to affiliate with the American Federation of Labor and to avoid the effect of the referendum by which the International union determined to affiliate with the Congress of Industrial Organizations". The strike was in no sense against appellant employers. The workmen who participated in the work stoppage had no grievances against the breweries as to working hours, rate of pay or other conditions of their employment. The sole purpose of the strike was to compel appellants and other breweries in the Pittsburgh area to recognize the Teamsters Union No. 232 of the A. F. of L. as the authoritative bargaining agency for the employes in their bottling departments, instead of a certified union affiliate of the C. I. O. In this situation appellants were hurt, but they were not in position to do anything about it; they were under contract with an established C. I. O. bargaining agent which precluded any negotiations by them with the striking A. F. of L. affiliates. In this contest the aggressors sought to recoup a part of their loss of earnings in the form of unemployment compensation benefits from contributions of former employers who were in no sense parties to the controversy. 

Claimants' unemployment was voluntary, but the testimony is wholly insufficient to support the finding of the board that their suspension of work resulted from an industrial dispute. This was exclusively a jurisdictional contest for labor control in which an A. F. of L. union attempted to raid the C. I. O. in a vain effort to attain recog-

nition as the bargaining agent of employes in the bottling departments of the breweries. To amount to an industrial dispute a controversy need not necessarily be between employer and employes. "It may be between the employees and their Union or bargaining agency, provided it involves the employer and affects the terms or conditions of employment": Miller v. Unemployment Compensation Board, 152 

Pa. Superior Ct. 315, 31 A. (2d) 740. Cf. Dorrington et al. v. Manning et al., 135 Pa. Superior Ct. 194, 205, 4 A. (2d) 

886. In the instant cases the controversy had nothing to do with the relationship between employers and employes, as to terms or conditions of employment, and therefore did not present a single aspect of an industrial dispute. Claimants clearly are not entitled to compensation under section 

402 (d) of the act.

It is equally clear, under the facts of these cases that claimants are barred under section 402 (b) of the act because their voluntary unemployment was without good cause. Section 3 of article I of the Act of December 5, 

1936, P. L. [1937] 2897, 43 PS §752, which has never been changed by amendment or otherwise, "constitutes a Declaration of Public Policy with respect to the aims and purposes of the legislature in establishing a system of unemployment compensation. It is not a mere preamble to the statute, but a constituent part of it and is to be considered in construing or interpreting it . . . And the basic principle at the root of the Act, justifying the exercise of the police powers of the Commonwealth in its enactment, is that the reserves thus set aside from the enforced contributions of employers are to be used for the benefit of persons unemployed through no fault of their own": Keller, P. J., in Department of Industry, etc., v. Unemployment 

Compensation Board, 148 Pa. Superior Ct. 246, 24 A. (2d) 667. 

What is "good cause", of course, must be determined in the light of the facts of each particular case but a cause to be good in the sense of section 402(b), must be "real,

1948] 

 not imaginary, substantial not trifling, reasonable not whimsical, circumstances [which] compel the decision to leave employment": Barclay White Co. v. Unemployment Compensation Board, 356 Pa. 43, 50 A. (2d) 336, quoting from the opinion of Judge Reno in Sturdevant Unemployment 

Compensation Case, 158 Pa. Superior Ct. 548, 557, 45 A. (2d) 898. Cf. Baigis Unemployment Compensation Case, 160 

Pa. Superior Ct. 379, 51 A. (2d) 518. No "outward pressures" compelled the stoppage of work in these cases. And even though the strike was ordered by claimants' Local 232, their participation in it must nevertheless be regarded as voluntary. "It would do great violence to the clear and unequivocal wording of the statute to hold that a labor or any other organization can control payments of unemployment benefits to its members by merely forbidding them to work at wages less than those set by it, or with certain persons, or at certain places, or under certain conditions": Barclay White Co. v. Unemployment Compensation Board, supra. Claimants were members of Local 144 when it became a party to the existing agreements with their employers. That local then was claimants' agent and the agreements entered into by it on behalf of its members became claimants' contract and was binding upon them. 

Claimants' voluntary unemployment, which resulted in a violation of an existing contract made on their behalf, offended against the declared public policy of the act and was without "good cause". One who voluntarily leaves his work in violation of an existing contract between his duly certified union and his employer is not within the coverage of the unemployment compensation law. 

Decision reversed.

[34 Dep. Rep.

 WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD WITTLINGER v. BOROUGH OF MILLERSVILLE Workmen's compensation—Injury in performance of duties—Volun teer fireman-Injury while removing property used for fire company festival—Act of June 21, 1939, as amended. 

A referee's order disallowing a claim for compensation on the ground that the injuries for which claimant, a member of a volunteer fire company, sought compensation did not arise while going to or returning from a fire nor while doing other duties authorized by defendant borough will be affirmed where it appears that claimant was injured while assisting in removing bleachers from the fire company premises which had been used for a festival held by the company for the purpose of raising funds; under the circumstances, where there was no evidence that the borough authorized the holding of the festival, although it raised no objection thereto, claimant did not come within the provisions of the Act of June 21, 1939, as amended by the Act of July 2, 1941, extending compensation protection to firemen while performing any duties as such authorized by a borough.

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Graybill, district no. 4, claim petition no. 107,456. Appeal dismissed. December 23, 1947. 

New Amsterdam Casualty Ins. Co., insurance carrier. 

Randolph C. Ryder, for claimant. 

Harvey B. Lutz, for defendant. 

Theodore Brubaker, for Manufacturing Casualty Ins. Co.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

This is an appeal by claimant from an order of disallowance by the referee.

Claimant, in his petition filed on January 17, 1947, alleged that while hauling bleachers which were used by the fire

1948] 

 company in raising funds, in the course of his employment as a member of the volunteer fire company on August 20, 1946, he suffered a fracture of the first lumbar vertebra. 

Defendant's answer, filed on February 5, 1947, denied the material allegations of claimant's petition and defended upon the further ground that claimant was an employe of the Township of Manor, which carried compensation insurance covering the volunteer fire company of which claimant was a member. After hearing, the referee found that claimant did not come within the purview of the Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 566 or its amendments, since the accident did not occur while going to or returning from a fire or while doing other duties "authorized" by the municipality, and dismissed claimant's petition. This appeal followed.

After a careful review of the entire record in this case, we regretfully concluded that the action of the referee was proper and must be affirmed.

The Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 566, as amended by the 

Act of July 2, 1941, P. L. 222 states that: 

"In addition to those persons included within the definition of the word 'employe' as defined in Section 104 of the Act of 1915. . . there shall be included all members of volunteer fire companies or volunteer fire departments of the various cities, boroughs, incorporated towns and townships, who shall be and hereby are declared to be 'employees' of such cities, boroughs, incorporated towns or townships for all purposes of said act and shall be entitled to receive compensation in case of injuries received while actually engaged as firemen or while going to or returning from any fire which the fire companies or fire departments of which they are members shall have attended or while performing any other duties of such companies or fire departments authorized by such cities, boroughs, incorporated towns and townships".

The testimony in this case is to the effect that claimant is a member of the volunteer fire company of the Borough

206 

 [84 Dep. Rep. 

of Millersville and also a director and secretary of the company. On August 20, 1946, while assisting in removing from the fire company premises bleachers, which had been used for a horse show and festival held by the fire company for the purpose of raising funds, to the Manor Township High School, claimant fell backwards off the truck containing the bleachers and fractured the first lumbar vertebra. 

The Millersville Fire Company is a volunteer fire company, chartered in 1911, its purpose being "To provide a means for the purchase and maintenance of fire engines, hook and ladder truck and any other fire extinguishing apparatus for the protecting of the Village of Millerville and the surrounding community from fire". The volunteer fire company held festivals on its property, with the knowledge and consent of the burgess, for the purpose of raising necessary monies and, on occasion, received contributions from defendant borough to carry on their work of fire fighting.

Since it is clear from the testimony presented that claimant did not suffer his accidental injuries while actually engaged in fighting, or going or returning from a fire, the question for our consideration is whether the accidental injury suffered by claimant is covered by that part of the 1941 amendment to the Act of 1939, which adds compensation protection to a volunteer fireman injured "while performing any other duties of such companies or fire departments authorized by such . . . boroughs. ." After a careful review of the entire testimony, we are of the opinion that it is not. While the municipality raised no objection to the holding of the festivals, there is nothing in the testimony from which we could conclude that the municipality did authorize them to be held as a duty. Under the act, to make injuries, suffered by a volunteer fireman, compensable where he sustained such injuries while performing duties other than going to or returning from a fire or while actually engaged

1948] 

 in fire fighting, it must affirmatively appear that such duties were authorized by the municipality. 

As was stated in the case of Shindledecker v. New Beth lehem Borough, 145 Pa. Superior Ct. 73: 

"Many kinds of gratuitous services are accepted by a borough from its citizens, among them the services of volunteer firemen. Parades, exhibitions, conventions and the like all, directly or indirectly, contribute to the efficiency of a volunteer fire company and to the benefit of the borough. But they who thus give of their services do not, thereby become employees of the borough. Liability for compensation without negligence on the part of the borough can arise only by virtue of a statutory enactment. 

There is no public policy of the Commonwealth as to compensation except as expressed in the compensation statutes. 

De Felice v. Jones and Laughlin Steel Corp., 137 Pa. Su perior Ct. 191. Courts can only sustain such compensation awards as are within the scope of the liability so imposed by the Legislature. Versellesi v. Elizabeth Township, 136

Pa. Superior Ct. 362. Injury, to be compensable, must have occurred within the restricted circumstances which alone give rise to the right under the Act. Casual injuries incident to other activities of the volunteer fire company were not contemplated by the Act, except to be executed by necessary implication as to risks which must continue to be assumed by the members. See also Lees v. State Workmen's 

Insurance Fund, 146 Pa. Superior Ct. 70." 

The bleachers which claimant was helping to remove at the time of the accident were there by virtue of having been used by the fire company for its own entertainment and for the purpose of raising money to aid its conservation. 

While it is, of course, true that the borough received the benefit of the funds so raised, in that such funds resulted in a more efficient and better equipped fire department to fight fires occurring in defendant borough, since there was no proof of authorization by defendant borough and since there can be no liability on the part of a borough in such a

ཙ་ matter as the instant case except by virtue of statutory enactment which requires such authorization, no award can be made.

  

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD SANTO v. STATE WORKMEN'S INSURANCE FUND Workmen's compensation—Evidence-Death certificate—Basis of finding as to cause of death.

A death certificate is admissible as evidence, in a compensation case, of the cause of death as stated therein and is sufficient evidence upon which to base a finding by a referee where the facts stated in the certificate are not contradicted or explained by the opposing party. 

Appeal by Commonwealth of Pennsylvania from award of Referee Phillips, district no. 3, claim petition no. 107,319. 

Appeal dismissed. December 23, 1947.

State Workmen's Insurance Fund, insurance carrier. 

Roger J. Dever, for claimant. 

Ralph H. Behney, for defendant and Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

This is an appeal by the Commonwealth from the action of the referee in entering an award in favor of claimant, widow of Dominic Santo, and minor children of the parties. 

An appeal (A-33186) from the action of the referee has also been taken by the State Insurance Fund, which appeal has been determined by us in a separate opinion. 

The record discloses that claimant, in her petition filed on January 10, 1947, in which she set out the dependency of herself and her minor children averred that her husband, Dominic Santo, had died on November 9, 1946, as a result

1948] 

 of anthraco-silicosis contracted in the course of his employment with defendant. Both defendant and the Commonwealth filed responsive answers denying the allegations contained in claimant's petition. After hearing, the referee found that claimant's death resulted solely from anthraco-silicosis contracted after an exposure of more than five years and which had reached a point of disablement on October 28, 1946, and, thereafter, entered an order in accordance with such findings. This appeal followed. 

The sole question for our consideration in this case is whether claimant has properly proven that her husband's death, on November 9, 1946, resulted solely from silicosis.

We are convinced that the record, in its present state, is sufficient to sustain the award made.

The only medical witness called in this case was Dr. 

James F. Forest, who testified that he was not decedent's attending physician and that he had treated him but once, about October 1, 1946, at which time decedent was suffering only from anthraco-silicosis. The witness further testified that, at the time of decedent's death, he was being treated by Dr. McCarron, who issued the death certificate, giving as the cause of death bronchial pneumonia due to anthraco-silicosis. The death certificate was then introduced in evidence. 

Thereafter, the following testimony was given: "By the referee: "Q. Doctor, you saw the man on October 1st. You didn't see the man between October 1st and the 28th? "A. I did not. "Q. Can you state the cause of death without having more information than you have? "A. I can't state the cause of death at all. "Q. You are depending solely on the death certificate are you? "A. Yes, sir."

Thus the question for our determination is whether the mere introduction of a death certificate, without more, is

conclusive proof of the cause of death and is a sufficient meeting of the burden of proof imposed upon a claimant under the law, where the facts stated therein are not contradicted or explained by the opposing party. In our opinion it is. 

A death certificate setting forth the causes of death is admissible in evidence but by no means conclusive. Findley v. Craftex Mills, 2 P. C. R. 305; Romanick v. Pine Hill

Coal Co., 4 P. C. R. 270; Borgon v. Hancock Life Insurance 

Co., 99 Pa. Superior Ct. 377; Griffin v. National Coal Mining 

Co., 127 Pa. Superior Ct. 588. Such certificates are prima facie evidence of any fact stated therein and are open to explanation and contradiction by the opposing party. Even though it is not a very high grade of evidence, since it is not given under oath and is not subject to cross-examination, where it is not contradicted, denied or explained, it may be accepted by the referee as a basis for his findings and conclusions. As was stated by the court in Bozicevich v. Kenilworth Mercantile Co., 58 Utah 458: "Moreover, if the (plaintiff) in a case like the one at bar, is not satisfied with the statement contained in the certificate of death, he may always contradict the record by any proper evidence". 

To the same effect, see Cohasset v. Moors, 204 Mass. 173; 

Broadbent's case, 240 Mass. 449 and Krapp v. Metropolitan Life Insurance Co., 143 Mich. 369.

We, are, therefore, of the opinion that, where a certified death certificate is introduced in evidence and the facts stated therein are not contradicted, denied or explained by the opposing party, it is not error on the part of the referee to accept the facts set forth therein, without more, as verity and as a basis for any findings of fact, conclusions of law and order he might make.

1948] 

 WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD KLEIN v. A. M. BEYERS COMPANY Workmen's compensation-Disability from dermatitis-Death from endocarditis-Causal connection. 

A referee's award of compensation to claimant on account of the death of her husband will be affirmed where it appears that decedent suffered a dermatitis of both arms and hands while employed by the defendant, that this ailment resulted from his exposure to certain oils attendant upon his job, that while the immediate cause of his death, which ensued more than a year later, was endocarditis, the dermatitis persisted during the entire period of his employment until shortly before his death, there being definite evidence that a bacteremia from the poison he was absorbing damaged his heart. 

Appeal by Commonwealth of Pennsylvania from award of Referee Curtis, district no 8, claim petition no. 106,805. 

Appeal dismissed. January 14, 1948.

Ralph F. Smith, for claimant. 

V. C. Short, for defendant. 

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This case involves a death claim. It is before the board upon an appeal by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania from an award of Referee Curtis to claimant, Mrs. Blanche M. 

Klein, for the death of her husband, August Klein, on November 18, 1945. Defendant, A. M. Byers Company, has also appealed. (A-33181.) The record discloses that decedent suffered a dermatitis of both arms and hands while employed by defendant, resulting in disability on July 7, 1944, and compensation was paid for total disability from

886 

July 14, 1944, to February 26, 1945. Decedent's record of employment shows that he was employed by defendant as a docket tapper in 1929 and continued in that employ, with some interruption, until August 22, 1943. That work involved exposure to oil. Decedent's next employment for defendant was three months as a ball grinder, from August 23, 1943, to November 28, 1943. He then worked as a general laborer until February 20, 1944. From February 

29, 1944, until August 1, 1945, Klein was employed as a blacksmith helper. From August 2, 1945, until November 

9, 1945, the last day of employment, he worked as a ball 

Robert E. Langdon, defendant's employment supervisor, who testified as to the periods of decedent's employments, also explained the exposure to oil attendant upon the various jobs. He stated that the work of a socket tapper only involves an exposure to oil. In the other duties, there is a small amount of oil and grease. 

The sole question involved in this case is whether decedent's dermatitis was a responsible factor in the death. 

This is primarily a medical question and there is considerable testimony in this connection, which we have carefully reviewed and considered. The death certificate states inexarteric embolism as the cause of death but this term appears foreign to medical terminology. 

Dr. Francis P. Kenney, a dermatologist called by claimant, testified that decedent was under his care from July 

20, 1944, to October 19, 1945. At the time of the doctor's first examination, practically the whole of the patient's body was covered with a vesicular eruption and the hands and feet showed considerable edema. The doctor recommended hospitalization and decedent was hospitalized from 

July 20, 1944, to September 7, 1944. Upon discharge decedent's condition showed considerable improvement. Later, the doctor made patch tests which showed a positive reaction to the oils with which decedent worked. Dr. Kenney testified:

1948] 

"Q. Did this enlargement (glands in the epitrochlear region) indicate, doctor, an infection? "A. Oh, yes. That's why the glands were enlarged, because of this infection. He was absorbing a lot of toxic material from this skin condition. He had a very, very severe skin irritation and he was absorbing a lot of this into his system. He was gradually becoming weak, he was losing weight, and he couldn't sleep. Of course this condition at that time was very irritated, it was very pruritic, very itchy."

The doctor stated that he permitted the patient to return to work from February 1945 to October 1945 because he was badly in need of funds. The physician continued to treat him until about a month before the death. He stated that Klein's physical condition was very poor, which he attributed "to the absorption of these toxins he was getting from his skin". Dr. Kenney was of the opinion that this absorption was the only thing that could cause the endocarditis which eventually terminated in the death, if the cause of death stated in the death certificate was correct. 

The exact cause of death, according to the doctor, could be determined only by a blood culture or autopsy. The doctor further testified: "Q. This bacteriemia you talk about, doctor, that definitely came from this skin disease, did it not? "A. It did. "Q. And is that what pulled his whole system down? "A. That's right. "Q. And weakened him? "A. That's right. "Q. And is that why you didn't want him to work? "A. That's right. "Q. And did that weaken the heart and all the organs of the body? "A. Yes, sure. "Q. And is that why you're of the opinion, doctor, that this disease-this skin disease, that he suffered from which

you call a dermatitis, that hastened and accelerated his death? "A. That's right.”

The doctor also testified that the lesions had finally pretty well cleared up, but "they were red, eczematous sort of eruption still present". Dr. J. C. Mahan, called by claimant, testified that he treated claimant from March 1943 until January 1944 for an acute dermatitis due to working with his hands in grease and oil. He said that a toxic condition accompanied the inflammation of the skin and caused a systematic condition. In answer to a hypothetical question as to the causal connection between the dermatitis and the death, the doctor stated: "Well, I can state what I have in my mind, and my opinion is that in the event there was no other sickness, which I have no knowledge of, that this skin infection and irritation caused a lot of pain and physically reduced him, as I stated, and that a period of time with more or less absorption from the skin condition, and the previous absorption when it was severe, along with the pain and suffering and loss of sleep, a year or so's time, would greatly reduce him and also exhaust him; that an endocarditis could exist. In the event that there was no other sickness, and I know of none, in my opinion he would pass on because of a toxic condition."

Although Dr. Mahan last saw decedent about 22 months before his death, the tenor of his testimony is that the dermatitis deteriorated his physical condition to such an extent that the toxic condition definitely contributed to or accelerated the death. He was also of the opinion that the open dermatitis could be possible portals of entry for an organism of infection causing the endocarditis. 

Dr. Frederick B. Utley, called by defendant, testified in reply to a hypothetical question that, in his opinion, the skin disease had nothing to do with the endocarditis of the heart. The substance of the doctor's reasons for rejecting any causal connection was that endocarditis is

1948] 

 caused by the portal entry of an infectious germ and the disease is manifested within 10 days or two weeks after the entry. The doctor thought that if decedent was suffering from endocarditis at the time decedent was working, he would have had to stop work after only a few days, due to shortness of breath and associated weakness. Dr.

Henry Jew, who treated decedent in his last illness and who signed the death statement, testified in behalf of defendant that he could not say whether decedent had a dermatitis at that time. As to the cause of death, the doctor stated that decedent had an endocarditis but that he had no opinion as to any connection between the dermatitis and the death. The doctor could not readily recall the details of the last illness.

It is our considered opinion that the occupational dermatitis was responsible for an infection which hastened the death. Decedent's debilitated condition was further aggravated by his return to work in 1945. The death is readily traceable to the long standing dermatitis since it cannot be overlooked as the initiating factor. No other responsible agency is advanced as a possible cause of the endocarditis followed by an embolism, if that is accepted as the terminal cause. Medicine is not an exact science. In the instant case, the over-all testimony is clear that the severe dermatitis had a deleterious effect upon decedent's physical well being, in producing a toxemia danger. We are of the further opinion that the dermatitis, although it has subsided to a considerable extent, nevertheless persisted during the entire period of employment, or until November 9, 1945, and that decedent had some slight exposure to oils and greases until his last day at work. Claimant's case does not necessarily depend upon the premise that her decedent's death was due to lowered resistance alone. Compensation could not be entertained under the theory: Bunnell v. State 

Fund, 124 Pa. Superior Ct. 171; Smith v. Wm. Hodges & 

Co., 151 Pa. Superior Ct. 14. In the latter case, however, the court affirmed an award, quoting from Williams v. Sus-

quehanna Collieries Co., 148 Pa. Superior Ct. 540-543 as follows: 

"Unequivocal expert medical testimony that an injury is a marked contributory factor in an employee's subsequent death, or that such injury so aggravated a pre-existing condition that it accelerated his death is sufficient to establish the requisite relation or connection between the injury and the death and meets the requirements prescribed in the decisions of our Supreme Court and of this Court." 

In the case quoted, decedent suffered severe burns which never completely healed. There was medical testimony offered in behalf of claimant which the court reviewed as 

"He (Dr. Lueders) testified that he believed there was a connection between the burns decedent suffered and his death as the burn was very fertile field, or a culture medium, for infection. After stating that Smith's death was due to a subacute streptococcus viridans, endocarditis and septicemia, he was asked the following question: "And in your opinion was that connected with the original burn?' He replied: 'I said it was.' He testified further that as the burns never completely healed and as Smith had no other accident between the injury of January 18, 1938, and his death he could find no other condition which had caused his death except the burns."

Claimant's medical testimony is of a similar tenor. Nor are we unmindful of defendant's medical testimony that the entry of an infectious germ would be manifested within two weeks prior to the disclosure of the endocarditis and that claimant's employment until shortly before his death thus precluded such a possibility. However, Dr. Utley, who gave this testimony, never attended the patient. Dr. Kenney, who attended decedent over a long period of time, eliminated any other source or cause of the endocarditis except the absorption of toxins from the skin if this diagnosis given on the death certificate was correct. There was definite evidence, in any event, that a bacteremia from the

1948] 

The re- poison he was absorbing, damaged the heart. sponsible dermatitis thus materially contributed to the death and the referee's award is proper: Campbell v. Oakmont 

Boro, 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 283.

The appeal of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania is dismissed.

SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA STILLMAN ET AL. v. UNEMPLOYMENT COMPENSA- TION BOARD OF REVIEW 

Unemployment compensation-Voluntary unemployment-Refusal to cross picket line-Section 402(d) of Unemployment 

Compensation Law. 

A finding by the Unemployment Compensation Board of Review that appellants refused to work at their employer's plant because of the existence of picket lines around the plant, and an order based thereon denying unemployment compensation for four weeks after the waiting period of one week on the ground that their unemployment was due to the voluntary suspension of work resulting from an industrial dispute within the meaning of section 402 (d) of the Unemployment Compensation Law, will be affirmed where the evidence, though conflicting, fully sustained the findings of the board. Appeal from the Pennsylvania Unemployment Board of 

Review. Decision affirmed. January 8, 1948. Superior 

Court of Pennsylvania, April term, 1947, no. 114. 

Robert A. Wilson and Raymond P. Shafer, for petitionersappellants.

Richard H. Wagner and T. McKeen Chidsey, for appellee. 

F. Joseph Thomas, for Talon, Inc.

RENO, J.: 

The board denied appellants' claims for unemployment compensation for four weeks after the waiting period of one week, holding that their unemployment during that time was due to the voluntary suspension of work resulting from an industrial dispute.

The sole question presented by their appeal is whether the board's findings of fact are supported by the evidence. 

The act provides: 

"In any appeal to the Superior Court the findings of the board or referee, as the case may be, as to the facts, if supported by the evidence and in the absence of fraud, shall be conclusive, and in such cases the jurisdiction of the court shall be confined to questions of law. . .": Unemployment Compensation Law, sec. 510, 43 PS §830. See 

Bonner v. Unemployment Compensation Board of Review, 156 Pa. Superior Ct. 367, 40 A. (2d) 106; Hall v. The Unemployment Compensation Law, sec. 510, 43 PS §830. See 

Bonner v. Unemployment Compensation Board of Review, pensation Case, 160 Pa. Superior Ct. 501, 52 A. (2d) 362.

Where an act ascribes conclusiveness to evidentially supported findings, substantial evidence is contemplated, that is, evidence affording a substantial basis of fact from which the fact in issue can be reasonably inferred: N. L. R. B. v. 

Columbian Enameling and Stamping Co., 306 U. S. 292, 59 S. Ct. 501; Wilbert v. Com. of Pa. Second Injury Reserve 

Account, 143 Pa. Superior Ct. 37, 17 A. (2d) 732.

The pertinent statutory provision involved in this appeal is section 402 (d), 43 PS §802, added to the original legislation by the Act of April 23, 1942, P. L. 60, sec. 4, and reduced to the form by which these claims are to be adjudged by the Act of May 29, 1945, P. L. 1145, sec. 9. (The further amendment of July 2, 1947, Act No. 493, is not involved in this appeal.) The section provides: "An employe shall be ineligible for compensation for any week... (d) In which his unemployment is due to

1948] 

 a voluntary suspension of work resulting from an industrial dispute, at the factory establishment or other premises at which he is or was last employed: Provided, That this disqualification shall apply only to any week of unemployment which, in whole or in part, includes any part of a period beginning with the day on which such suspension occurs and ending with (i) the last day of the fourth calendar week immediately following the calendar week in which such suspension occurs, or (ii) the day on which such suspension was terminated, whichever is the earlier."

It will be seen when we examine the facts that appellants' unemployment undoubtedly "resulted from an industrial dispute." But was it also "due to a voluntary suspension of work"? In this section "voluntary" has not been modified in subsequent amendments by "good cause", and such cases as Teicher Unemployment Compensation, 154 Pa. Superior Ct. 250, 35 A. (2d) 739; Sturdevant Un employment Compensation Case, 158 Pa. Superior Ct. 548, 

45 A. (2d) 898, and others of like import, are irrelevant. "Voluntary" in this context connotes a suspension of work resulting from the decision of the employe, as distinguished from a dismissal or discharge or lay-off by the employer. 

Cf. Department of Labor and Industry v. Unemployment 

Compensation Board of Review, 133 Pa. Superior Ct. 518, 3

A. (2d) 211. The task of the board was to ascertain from the evidence whether appellants' suspension of work was due to their decision or to some action by their employer. 

The employer, Talon, Inc., operates plants in Meadville and Erie where it manufactures slide fasteners. At the time in question it employed 3,200 persons at its Meadville plant and 700 at Erie. Most of the employes were members of various craft unions affiliated with the American Federation of Labor. There were 10 of these unions, and the number of employes holding membership in them ranged from one in the pattern makers association, 350 in the tool and die makers, and 1,900 in the slide fasteners union. After a probationary period, union membership

was required by the employer as a condition of continued employment.

The tool and die makers had been engaged in negotiating a new working agreement, and conferences having failed to produce results, the union voted to strike, and on October 24, 1945, at about 1 p. m. walked out of the 

Meadville plant. Three shifts were maintained: 7 a. m. to 3 p. m., 3 p. m. to 11 p. m., and 11 p. m. to 7 a. m. Some employes continued to work until 3 p. m. but none reported for the 3-11 p. m. shift. The subsequent events are fairly described in the pivotal finding of the board: "8. After the members of the tool and die makers union established a picket line at the Meadville plant, the other employes, who were members of affiliated unions of the American Federation of Labor, failed to report for work because of their unwillingness to cross the picket lines. The employer company was at all times ready and willing to continue operations, and would have been able to do so to a very considerable extent for some time after the strike by the tool and die makers. No action was taken by the employer, nor was any authorized action taken on its behalf, to close the plant or to afford a basis for a reasonable belief on the part of any employes that the plant had been closed to them. The failure of the employes to work was not in any measure due to the fact that they were prevented from working; there was no violence nor were there any threats of violence on the picket line. Their failure and refusal to work was due to (a) their objections, based upon principle, to crossing a picket line, and (b) their unwillingness to risk the consequences which might be imposed by their unions by reason of crossing the picket line." 

The situation at the Erie plant was essentially similar to the conditions at Meadville, and it is covered by the finding: "9. The tool and die makers went out on strike at the 

Erie plant on or about November 8, 1945. The company also was ready, able and willing to continue operations at

1948] 

 this plant. The suspension at the Erie plant likewise resulted from the failure or refusal of the employes to report for work after the strike by the tool and die makers at that plant. Their failure to work was based upon their objections in principle or their apprehension with regard to crossing a picket line."

Claimants charged and testified that the supervisory employes sent them home and told them not to return until the strike was over or until they were notified to return, that the plant gates were closed, that their machines were broken and in the absence of the die makers there was not one capable of repairing them, and that upon making calls to the plant they were informed there was no work.

To the contrary, the employer contended and its witnesses testified that it did nothing to prevent or discourage employes from returning to their work, that indeed it urged them to return and was ready, willing and able to resume production, that the gates were open and the guards were instructed to admit all employes who displayed badges, that its supervisors sent no one home, and that it was informed by union officials that no union member would cross the die makers' picket line.

In the welter of the conflicting testimony the board could conceivably have found either way. But it found for the employer, and its findings are fully sustained and warranted by substantial and competent evidence, which requires no review beyond the above brief summarization. When we discover a rational basis for the findings of an administrative agency predicated upon substantial evidence our hand is stayed. The plain legislative mandate confines our review to questions of law, and we cannot disturb findings of fact even though the record may contain, as it does in this case, other competent evidence which, had it been accepted by the board, would have justified different findings. Nor are we at liberty to substitute our findings for those of the board even

when our reading of the testimony might have brought us to a different conclusion. The credibility of the witnesses, the weight of their testimony, and the reasonable inferences to be drawn from it are for the board. Our duty is performed by studying the testimony in the light most favorable to the party in whose favor the board has found, giving that party the benefit of every inference which can be logically and reasonably drawn from it. These principles governing appellate review of the decisions of administrative agencies were largely developed in workmen's compensation cases, a comparable area of the law, and are applicable to appeals from the Unemployment Compensation Board of Review. See, e. g., Kennedy v. Holmes 

Construction Co., 147 Pa. Superior Ct. 348, 24 A. (2d) 

451; McMillan v. Wm. S. Miller Co., 149 Pa. Superior Ct. 

241, 27 A. (2d) 735; Kasman v. Hillman Coal & Coke Co., 149 Pa. Superior Ct. 263, 27 A. (2d) 762; Carberry v. Reitz 

Furniture Co., 152 Pa. Superior Ct. 417, 33 A. (2d) 289; 

Kline v. Kiehl, 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 392, 43 A. (2d) 616.

The 24 appellants took a joint appeal. Some are die makers, some are members of the other unions, and two are not members of any union. The board did not distinguish · between them. It cannot be said that the nonunion employes and the members of the unions which had not formally voted to strike were in President Judge Keller's phrase in Miller v. Unemployment Compensation Board of 

Review, 152 Pa. Superior Ct. 315, 321, 31 A. (2d) 740, "innocent bystanders." If not all were deterred by the union tradition against crossing a picket line, they at least shared the strikers' viewpoint and, in the language of the Miller case, supra, p. 321, "act[ed] in concert to prevent a continuance of operations." Or as the board put it: "In short, the employes generally made the suspension by the tool and die makers their own voluntary suspension of work." The evidence substantially sustains that conclusion, and there is no basis in the record for distinguishing between the variant classes of appellants.

1948] 

The board moved to quash this appeal upon the ground that persons who have separate interests in the case may not prosecute a joint appeal. Cf. Schuetz's Estate, 315 Pa. 

105, 172 Atl. 865. Technically the board is correct, for although the unemployment may arise out of the same suspension of or separation from work each claimant is required to file a separate claim for benefits, and each claim is the basis for separate action by the bureau, the referee and the board. However, the board indicated its willingness to waive its objection, and we have accordingly decided the case upon its merits. We have also taken into account the fact that some agreement had been reached between the agents of the bureau and the employes whereby only a small number of representative claims were filed in order to reduce the paper work of the bureau and yet provide a sufficient basis for the adjudication of all phases of the controversy. We recognize that the board is a separate appellate agency and is not bound by agreements made by the bureau, and yet, in the interest of expedient justice, we venture to suggest that some modus operandi might be evolved, either by a rule of the board or by a joint rule of the board and the bureau, whereby representative cases could be presented to the board and this court, and decision upon them rule all other claims. Perhaps action by the legislature is required, but certainly each of 24 claimants should not in this class of litigation be required to incur the expense of prosecuting a separate appeal. And when, as in this instance, save for the wise action of the bureau, almost 4,000 appeals might have become necessary, the call for some action by some one in authority becomes all the more potent. 

Decision affirmed.

[84 Dep. Rep. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD ARISTA v. H. C. FRICK COKE CO. 

Workmen's compensation—Partial disability-Return to work at wages exceeding wages at time of injury-Suspension of payments.

An order of a referee suspending compensation payments to claimant until such time as his disability reflected itself in a loss in earning power will be affirmed where it appears that claimant, a coal miner, returned to work at a period subsequent to his injury at an average weekly wage in excess of his weekly wage at the time of the accident although he continued to suffer a partial disability; under such circumstances, payments of compensation will be suspended as long as claimant continues to receive wages in a weekly amount equivalent to those received at the time of his injury. 

Appeal by claimant from order of Referee Carmalt, district no. 8, awarding compensation under agreement no. 

4,084,272. Appeal dismissed. January 14, 1948. 

Samuel Krimsly, for claimant. 

Ira R. Hill, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This case involves an order of Referee Carmalt suspending compensation due claimant, Domenick Arista, for injuries sustained by him during the course of his employment by defendant, H. C. Frick Coke Company, on March 

28, 1942. It was before the board previously upon appeal of claimant from the referee's order of suspension (A-30530). 

We affirmed the referee. Claimant appealed to the County 

Court of Allegheny County, contending that employment conditions at the time of the hearing and the wages earned at the time of the accident are not comparable and that the order of the referee does not reflect the true loss in earning power sustained by claimant. The county court re-

1948] 

 turned the record to the board, directing the board, in determining "earning power", to consider the nature of the services, hours of employment and other relevant factors, as well as the amount of wages received. In remanding the record to the referee, we stated (p. 2): "Our application of section 306(b) is at variance with that of the court. However, the question raised is a legal rather than a factual one and we are constrained to accept the court's interpretation and application of the law." 

Accordingly, we remanded the record to Referee Carmalt for further hearing and determination. However, no witnesses were called by either side. It was agreed by counsel for the interested parties that if Dr. J. Huber Wagner, the attending physician, had been called as a witness at the hearing held on March 16, 1944, "he would have expressed the opinion that claimant is 40 to 50 percent disabled as far as coal mining is concerned". It appears claimant is still disabled. Defendant submitted a statement of claimant's earnings from April 15, 1946, to March 31, 1947, which indicates that claimant's work period coincides pretty closely to the period the plant worked. For the last quarterly period shown in the work statement, claimant's average weekly wage was $61.20. His average weekly wage at the time of the accident was $45.61.

The referee suspended compensation payments beginning December 2, 1945, until such time as claimant's disability shall reflect itself in a loss in earning power within the limitations of the act. Claimant has again appealed. Claimant contends that the referee failed to comply with the instructions of the county court in determining loss of earning power. Since the opinion of the county court was handed down, the Superior Court has had occasion to review the statutes and decisional law in regard to orders suspending compensation payments in the case of Holtz v. 

McGraw and Bindley et al., 161 Pa. Superior Ct. 371, decided September 20, 1947. The main question before the court in that case concerns the effect of a suspension order

[84 Dep. Rep. 

and the resulting burden of proof upon a subsequent loss of earning power. The opinion holds that a suspension order is not a termination order. The court points out that the controversial section (306) of the Act of 1939, P. L. 

520, reading: "The term 'earning power' as used in this section shall in no case be less than the weekly amount which the employe receives after the accident", was intended to prevent the receipt of both equivalent wages and compensation payments by a claimant, which had been held permissible under a line of earlier cases, notably Weinstock v. United Cigar Stores et al., 137 Pa. Superior Ct. 128;

Chubb v. Allegheny County Club et al., 147 Pa. Superior Ct. 

146; Johnston v. Butler Railways Co. et al., 149 Pa. Superior Ct. 404. In these cases, however, the wages were not wholly earned. Where claimant actually earns and receives equivalent wages he is not entitled to compensation for partial disability: Irwin v. Byllesby Engineering 

Corp., 119 Pa. Superior Ct. 449. In the Irwin case the court stated (p. 452): "There is evidence that during this period of five and one half months claimant earned wages equal to those he was receiving when injured. Therefore, he is not entitled to an award of any compensation for those weeks, even if the award is otherwise sustainable: Motte v. Carnegie C. Co. et al., 114 Pa. Superior Ct. 239, 173 A. 670”.

In the case of Keleman v. Reiber et al., 161 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 169, involving an accident under the Act of June 4, 1937, P. L. 1552, the court stated (p. 173): "The controlling consideration in this appeal is the finding of the compensation authorities, upon sufficient testimony, that claimant's residual physical disability from the accident, is not reflected in loss of earning power. To give effect to such finding the 1937 act, by necessary implication, must have intended a suspension of payments during periods when physical disability is not reflected in loss of earning power. The principle is not entirely new. In 

Scipani v. Pressed Steel Car Co. et al., 150 Pa. Superior Ct.

1948] 

410, 28 A. (2d) 502, we held that the amendment of section 

306(b) in the 1939 amendment by necessary implication supplies the ground for suspension of payments during periods when disability of an injured employe was not reflected in loss of wages."

The opinion of the county court stresses the fact that the amendment contained in the Act of 1939 does not exclude other competent and material evidence bearing upon the determination of "earning power". In effect, the court opinion directs the compensation authorities to consider the potential earning power, rather than his earning power as manifested by the wages which he actually earns and receives. In the Holtz case, the court stated (p. 377): "The amendment of 1939 as to equivalent wages under Section 306 in partial disability cases was not intended to be a final adjudication of whether disability had ceased. It was intended to relieve the employer from the payment of compensation to a claimant then partially disabled, but who then suffered no economic loss by reason of his injury."

In the light of the later pronouncement by our appellate court in the Holtz case, we feel constrained to agree with the referee that claimant suffered no loss of earnings since December 2, 1945. Since there was no additional material evidence produced that claimant's “earning power" was affected adversely by any other circumstances of which we may take cognizance, we necessarily conclude that he actually earned the wages which he received and there has been no attendant loss in earning power. 

The referee's order provides, inter alia, that "compensation payments are hereby suspended beginning with December 2, 1945, until such time as claimant's disability shall reflect itself in a loss in earning power, however, within the limitations of the act". This is really an order of termination since it places the burden of proving a change in disability or earning power upon claimant in order to reinstate compensation and is contra to the direction of the 

Superior Court.

[84 Dep. Rep. 

We hereby amend the referee's findings of fact by adding these additional 

Findings of fact 3. We find as a fact that following his return to employment after the accident, claimant earned and received wages equivalent to the wages received at the date of the accident. 

4. As of December 2, 1945, claimant suffered a 45 percent partial disability, which has not been reflected in a loss of earning power since that date.

The referee's other findings of fact are affirmed. We hereby affirm the referee's conclusion of law. 

We hereby amend the referee's order by vacating and setting aside that portion of the order reading "compensation payments are hereby suspended beginning with December 2, 1945, until such time as claimant's disability shall reflect itself in a loss in earning power, however, within the limitations of the act." 

In lieu thereof, we hereby substitute: 

All payments of compensation under the agreement executed July 25, 1942, as amended, are hereby suspended as of December 2, 1945; said suspension to continue as long as the employe continues to receive wages in a weekly amount which are equivalent to the wages received as of the time of the injury or in the amount of $45.61.

SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA PRENTICE v. UNEMPLOYMENT COMPENSATION BOARD OF REVIEW ET AL. 

Unemployment compensation-Unemployment caused by strike-Approval of strike by claimant's union—Voluntary suspension of work-Section 402(d) of Unemployment Compensation Law.

Claimant's unemployment was due to a voluntary suspension of work resulting from an industrial dispute at the premises where he

1948] 

 was employed, within the meaning of section 402 (d) of the Unemployment Compensation Law, so that claimant was disqualified from receiving compensation during the waiting period provided for therein where the miners' union to which he belonged and which had full powers of collective bargaining in his behalf took no steps to prevent a strike by members of a union of supervisory mine workers, which it had the power to prevent, the result of the strike being that the mines were shut down and claimant's employment suspended; because of his membership in the union, which approved and controlled the strike, the suspension of work, which caused claimant's unemployment, must be held to have been voluntary on his part. 

Appeal from Unemployment Compensation Board of Re view dated January 23, 1947 (appeal no. B-44-95-E-56) revising first decision of June 13, 1946. Affirmed. January 

8, 1948. Superior Court of Pennsylvania, April term, 1947, no. 169. 

Richard H. Wagner and T. McKeen Chidsey, Attorney 

General, for appellee. 

Jesse P. Long, Samuel Krimsly, Joseph M. Loughran, Anthony Cavalcante, for appellant.

DITHRICH, J.: 

This is an appeal from a decision of the Unemployment Compensation Board of Review (hereinafter referred to as the board), affirming the decision of the Bureau of Employment and Unemployment Compensation (hereinafter referred to as the bureau), denying claimant unemployment compensation.

It grows out of a work stoppage in the bituminous coal industry during the so-called "supervisors' strike" which extended from on or about September 22 to October 22, 1945. It is estimated that approximately 50,000 rank and file miners became unemployed due to the strike and either filed claims or were considered potential claimants for unemployment compensation.

The various claimants were employed at approximately 125 different mines or places of employment operated by approximately 63 employers. It is acknowledged by all parties that there was an industrial dispute between the 

United Clerical, Technical and Supervisory Employees 

Union (hereinafter called the UCT) and the coal operators. 

It is also acknowledged that the suspension of work by the supervisory employes developed when, following the refusal of the Jones and Laughlin Steel Corporation (hereinafter referred to as J. & L.) and other coal operators to recognize the UCT as their collective bargaining agent, supervisors in the employ of J. & L. voted to go out on strike as a means of enforcing their demand. Supervisory employes at other mines in the bituminous area then went out on strike in sympathy with the employes at the J. & L. mines. The coal operators were forced to shut down their mines because, due to the strike of the assistant foremen and fire bosses, the mines could not be fire-inspected, as required by the Bituminous Mine Code, and as a result of this suspension the rank and file miners became unemployed. 

They remained unemployed until they were ordered back to work by John L. Lewis, President of the United Mine Work ers of America (hereinafter referred to as the UMW). 

The board in its decision states: "The case of a single claimant has been selected for procedural reasons, viz., to simplify further appellate proceedings which are anticipated. However, while actually deciding only one claim, we include for the purpose of review the basic facts of the entire controversy as it affected all the claims before the board. We have pursued this course for the following reasons. Obviously the important question for determination is not the rights of a single claimant or employer, or even all appellants now before the board, Ultimately at stake is the contested right of some 50,000 employes to receive, and the Commonwealth's liability to pay, benefits for a period of four weeks. 

Contingent upon this determination also is the effect which

1948] 

 the payment of benefits may have on the employers' contribution rate under the merit rating provisions of the law. 

For, even though each and every one of the individual appeals before the board. were decided, the bureau's responsibility would only then commence with respect to the thousands of other miners, potential claimants for an aggregate sum of approximately $4,000,000. . "We have selected the claim of James Prentice for determination because he is a member of that group of claimants (see group (d), finding no. 14) as to whom there is the least indication of personal participation in the strike. 

Claimants in this group, as hereinafter stated, reported for work on the day the strike commenced and were told by management to go home because the mines could not be operated. The specific case of James Prentice has been chosen because counsel and witnesses were present at the referee's hearing, with the result that a better than average record was developed. Furthermore, because of the special efforts which the parties made to 'fix the blame for the miners' unemployment', we believe that this record better than any other reveals the true circumstances in which the parties generally found themselves during the strike." 

Claimant, James Prentice, was employed as a coal loader at Yatesboro No. 5 mine of the Rochester and Pittsburgh

Coal Company at Nu Mine in Armstrong County. He is president of the local union of the UMW. He worked on 

September 23rd but did not work thereafter until October 22nd.

The issue thus being essentially one of fact and not of law, arising out of a situation which involves a voluminous record, the facts so far as essential to a determination of the issue may be briefly culled from the "findings of fact" by the board: "1. The circumstances which finally culminated in the unemployment of the miners arose out of a suspension of work by supervisory employes throughout the bituminous coal area.

"2.

As to the background in the controversy, the follow ing appears: . . . Sometime in 1942 the Mine Officials 

Union petitioned the UMWA for admittance and, on February 5, 1943, after the passage of an amendment to the Constitution of the UMWA . . . authorizing its admittance, the petition was finally accepted, to become effective 

March 31, 1943. "3. On February 20, 1943, the UMWA issued a letter of instruction to all district and local officers setting forth the manner in which supervisory employes were to be granted membership in the union. This letter stated [inter alia]: "a. Between this date and March 31, 1943, each mine foreman, assistant mine foreman, dock boss, night boss, fire boss, mine examiner, watchman, coal inspector, mine clerk and all other employes heretofore exempted from membership shall be presented application blanks for membership in the UMWA and requested to join this union. ""b. When such petitions for membership are signed, they shall be held by the local union until the first day of April, 1943, at which time a special meeting of the local union can be called. Signers of the petitions accepted shall be given the obligation and inducted into membership in the UMWA.' 

"The letter further states: ""The officers of each local union are requested to give their full consideration and coöperation in the execution of this policy and under no circumstances should the instructions contained in this letter fail to receive their immediate and constant attention until the task herein outlined is completed.' 999 Following unsuccessful efforts on the part of the international executive board of the UMW during 1943 and 

1944 to have the operators recognize the Mine Officials 

Union, sometime in 1945. 67. • • the president of the UMWA. stated in a message to an operator;

1948] 

""I acknowledge your wire in reference to several idle mines. This office is advised that the officers of District 5 are doing everything possible to correct the situation and insure continuance of operation. I call your attention to the fact that present unrest in the district over the question involved in this strike have been super-induced by the negligent and arrogant attitude of the operators' representatives in your association in refusing over a period of years to coöperate with the UMWA in the adjustment of the mine foremen and supervisors question.' "8. The UCT is a division of District No. 50 of the 

UMWA, . . . District No. 50 is the organization commonly called the 'catch all' district of the UMWA and includes construction workers, building trades and other employes. . . The miners' locals and the UCT locals each have their own officers; they meet separately, and to date the UCT locals have not admitted rank and file miners to membership nor have rank and file locals admitted supervisory, clerical and technical personnel to membership. Upon joining their respective locals both miners and supervisors take the same oath and obligation. "9. The UCT has no separate constitution apart from that of the UMWA, no separate charter or bylaws, no separate rules or regulations. Local unions of the UCT are issued a charter by the UCT and have local bylaws which must not be in conflict with the UMWA constitution, or the UMWA rules and regulations. . . . Dues from the local UCT union are forwarded to the UCT officials in Pittsburgh where they are divided. Part is returned to the locals, part is retained, and the greatest portion is sent to the international union of the UMWA. . . . "10. . . . The president and secretary-treasurer of the

UCT... the only full-time officials, were not elected by the UCT members but were appointed by the international officers of the UMWA. . . . The salaries of these officials are paid by the international union of the UMWA. Their salaries and expenses are included in the semi-annual re-

[84 Dep. Rep. 

ports of the international secretary-treasurer and the international auditors of the UMWA, where these individuals are listed among the officers and employes of the UMWA. "(The facts contained in the findings No. 1 to 10, inclusive, were made the subject of a stipulation.)” "The board's findings of fact when supported by evidence are conclusive upon appeal, which is confined to conclusions of law": MacFarland v. Unemployment Compensation Board, 158 Pa. Superior Ct. 418, 420, 45 A. (2d) 423.

The board in its decision states: "After considering the organizational relationship between the UMWA and the UCT, together with the provisions of the UMWA constitution, it seems evident that the officers of the UMWA had the power to prohibit the strike. • • "It remains . . . to be determined whether or not the officers of the international organization of the UMWA took any steps to prevent the strike . . . there [is no] evidence that the officers of the UMWA took any measures to halt the strike until October 19th when the president of the UMWA and the president of the UCT directed their members to return to work. On the contrary, it must be inferred [as a fact] that the strike met with the actual approval of the UMWA.”

The board decided "that the strike by the members of the UCT not only was within the control of the officers of the UMWA, but that it was approved by the international organization of the UMWA" and "Since the . . . UMWA approved and supported the strike by the supervisors, the immediate consequence of which was to throw the rank and file miners out of work, the members of the UMWA must be deemed to have assented to the strike and the suspension of work must be considered voluntary on their part."

1948] 

The bureau based its decision on the theory that any employe is temporarily disqualified if his unemployment is "due to a strike in the establishment where he works," irrespective of claimant's participation in the strike and regardless of whether or not his employment is voluntary on his part, a construction still contended for by the operators. There is much to be said in favor of such a con struction. Section 402 (d) of the Unemployment Compen sation Law of December 5, 1936, P. L. (1937) 2897, as amended, PS §802, provides in part that an employe shall be ineligible for compensation for any week "In which his unemployment is due to a voluntary suspension of work resulting from an industrial dispute, at the factory establishment or other premises at which he is or was last employed." Cf. Baker v. Powhatan Mining Co., 146 Ohio 

State 600, 67 N. E. (2d) 714. The Ohio statute provides in part that "no benefits shall be payable to any individual who has lost his employment or has left his employment by reason of a strike in the establishment in which he was employed."

But in our opinion the board was on more reasonable ground than the bureau when it based its decision on the fact that "... the officers of the UMWA, in supporting the position of the supervisors and in approving the strike, acted as agents for the members of the UMWA." The soundness of this reasoning cannot be effectively questioned. 

Not only is it supported by the principle that a member of a union designates his union representatives to act for him as his agents in all matters pertaining to his employment, such as collective bargaining, but also on the principle that a person cannot claim the advantages of his voluntary acts, in this case joining the union, without at the same time assuming responsibility for their natural and probable consequences. As stated in Department of Industrial Re-

lations v. Pesnell, 29 Ala. 528, 199 So. 720 (certiorari denied by Alabama Supreme Court, Ex parte Pesnell, 240 

Ala. 457, 199 So. 726): "The appellee's situation was created by his duly selected bargaining agents. Their acts were his acts. It would be difficult for us to reach the conclusion that the appellee [claimant] could, under the law, bring about a cessation of work and then claim he was unemployed within the terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act." Quoted with approval in Baker v. Powhatan Mining Co., supra. See also decision of the Circuit Court of Allegany County, Maryland, 4 C. C. H. 23546, 23550.

True, the principles of the law of agency have not heretofore been applied to any case arising under the Pennsylvania statute, but that is merely because the facts in the earlier reported cases do not call for their application. 

But here the significant facts are the authorization of his agents by claimant and his acquiescence in the conditions imposed by them which prevented him from remaining at work. He knew, or must be presumed to have known, that his return to work had been conditioned by his agents upon the recognition of his union, the UMW, as the bargaining agent for the UCT, on an industry-wide basis. Not only did he acquiesce in failing to object to his union's action, but also by remaining away from work until notified by the president of his international union to return. "Acquiescence by the principal in conduct of an agent whose previously conferred authorization reasonably might include it, indicates that the conduct was authorized; if clearly not included in the authorization, acquiescence in it indicates affirmance": Section 43, Restatement of Agency. 

That the board was warranted in finding that the officers of the UMW had the power to prohibit the strike and in concluding that by failing so to do, they in effect sanctioned and supported it, is abundantly clear from the evidence. Article XVI, sec. 1 of the UMW constitution pro-

1948] 

 vides that "No district shall be permitted to engage in a strike involving all or a major portion of its members, without the sanction of an International Convention or the International Executive Board." Between international conventions, "the supreme executive and judicial powers" of the union are vested in the executive officers and the executive board. The constitution further provides that "The 

International Union shall have supreme legislative, executive and judicial authority over all members and subordinate branches, and shall be the ultimate tribunal to which all matters of importance to the welfare of the membership and subordinate branches shall be referred By delegating authority to his union officials to act for him lawfully within the scope of the union's objectives, claimant clearly made them his agents. By making them his agents he shared in the responsibility for the strike, which brought about his unemployment, thereby rendering it voluntary within the meaning of section 402 (d), supra. 

Notwithstanding his personal willingness to work and the fact that he would have done so had work been available, his unemployment was voluntary because he voluntarily joined the union and adhered to its principles and obeyed the orders of its officials. As said in Barclay White Co. v. Unemployment Compensation Board, 356 Pa. 43, 50, 50 

A. (2d) 336: "By what stretch of the imagination could it be said that such a person is involuntarily unemployed? Claimant entered into membership in his union of his own volition because he felt that his best financial interests would be served thereby. . . . No one can properly question the fact that a worker who joins a union and abides by its lawful rules, regulations and bylaws is within his legal rights. 

The public policy of the Commonwealth does encourage membership in labor organizations but retention of membership therein is not a surrender to circumstances of the kind and quality which will turn voluntary unemployment into involuntary unemployment."

Claimant “of his own volition" dealt with his employer collectively through his union agents. Full responsibility and authority for fixing the terms and conditions of his employment were delegated to them. No reasonable person in the present day and age would question his right of collective bargaining, a right which has come to be almost universally recognized. But he cannot delegate to others a responsibility he owes to the Unemployment Compensation Fund to pursue a standard of conduct manifesting his desire to work during the period for which he claims benefits. And his responsibility to the fund has not been met when the course of conduct of his union officials has not been consistent with his remaining employed. Claimant's unemployment was brought about as a direct result of his own chosen method of collective bargaining. No matter how wisely he may have chosen his bargaining agents, and no matter how dutifully they may have acted in his behalf, their acts were his acts, binding upon his union and binding upon him. To hold otherwise would be to ignore the way in which trade unions function through their international officers. "We think it pertinent to say here that we are in no way interfering with the practice and procedure of collective bargaining or with a worker's full freedom of association with his fellows in a labor or other lawful organization. Such considerations have no place here. We are called upon to decide merely whether or not under the facts presented claimant is eligible for compensation under the Unemployment Compensation Law": Barclay White Co. 

v. Unemployment Compensation Board, supra, page 49.

Whether or not the recognition of the UCT by the coal operators would benefit the rank and file miners of the UMW is beside the point. The point is that their international officers considered it of distinct advantage to the UMW, and that the rank and file miners, in acquiesc g in the suspension of work which their representatives obviously approved for their ultimate benefit, thereby became voluntarily unemployed.

1948] 

• • be- We agree with the conclusion of the board that ". cause of his membership in the union which approved and controlled the strike, the suspension of work which caused his [claimant's] unemployment must be deemed to have been voluntary on his part with the result that his claims are subject to the disqualification provided in Section 402 (d) of the Unemployment Compensation Law." 

Decision affirmed.

SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA AMERICAN STEEL & WIRE COMPANY OF NEW JERSEY v. UNEMPLOYMENT COMPENSATION BOARD OF THE COMMONWEALTH OF PENN- SYLVANIA 

Unemployment compensation-Voluntary suspension of work resulting from industrial dispute—Postponement of plant reopening following settlement of dispute—Eligibility for compensation-Section 402(d) of Unemployment 

Compensation Law. 

Where an employe became unemployed due to a voluntary suspension of work resulting from an industrial dispute at the plant where he was employed and the dispute was settled and the employe was willing to return to work within the maximum period of disqualification prescribed by section 402 (d) of the Unemployment Compensation Law, but by reason of the need to recondition equipment it was impossible for the employer to resume operations until several weeks later, the employe became eligible for unemployment compensation benefits as of the date on which the dispute was settled and he was ready to return to work. 

Appeal from decision of Unemployment Compensation 

Board of Review at no. 44-94-13-1237 and B-44-94-13-1133 to 1281. Affirmed. January 8, 1948. Superior Court of 

Pennsylvania, April term, 1947, no. 165. 

Paul E. Hutchinson, for appellant. 

Roland M. Morgan, for appellee.

RHODES, P. J.: 

This is an unemployment compensation case in which the employer has appealed from the decision of the Un employment Compensation Board of Review. The appeal involves the interpretation of section 402 (d) of the Unem ployment Compensation Law of December 5, 1936, P. L. 

(1937) 2897, as amended by the Act of May 29, 1945, P. L. 

1145, sec. 9, 43 PS §802, in order to ascertain the length of the period of disqualification provided for in that section where claimant's ineligibility for compensation is "due to a voluntary suspension of work resulting from an industrial dispute." The referee and the board held that claimant's disqualification ended the day the strike terminated. Appellant contends that claimant remained ineligible as long as the work stoppage continued, subject to the maximum period of ineligibility provided in clause (i) of section 402(d). 

Claimant was employed at the Rankin works of the 

American Steel and Wire Company of New Jersey, appellant. He became unemployed on January 21, 1946, by reason of an industrial dispute between the United Steel Workers Union and appellant. The dispute, which resulted in a suspension of work, or a strike, involved a controversy over wages. Claimant, as a member of the union, actively participated in the dispute and the resulting suspension of work.

The plant where claimant was employed was engaged in the manufacture of wire of various gauges, wire nails, and other wire products. The material used consisted of steel rods made up on bundles of approximately 48 inches in diameter, and weighing approximately 400 pounds each. 

Prior to being drawn into wire, the rods were pickled in sulphuric acid and then heated or baked at a high temperature for several hours. The bakers, in which the latter process is carried on, are rectangular ovens 60 feet long by 45 feet wide, which are heated by burners beneath the floor

1948] 

 level. Hot gases from combustion chambers pass through the bakers. The bakers are constructed of brick and the combustion chambers are constructed of firebrick. Upon leaving the bakers, the rods are conveyed to the wire drawing and finishing departments. Claimant in this appeal, Anthony Bonomo, and the other claimants whose claims are pending were employed in the wire drawing and finishing departments as distinguished from the rod bakers. 

The referee and the board found that the industrial dispute or strike was settled at 12:01 a.m. February 18, 1946, and that claimant was then ready, willing and able to return to work.
