However, at a meeting held at that time between representatives of the union and representatives of appellant, the latter "advised that the plant would not be ready to resume operations until March 4, 1946, due to lack of material and the necessity of repairing the bakers." 

The board affirmed the referee's finding that "The bakers were repaired and the plant ready to resume operations on March 4, 1946, at which time claimant was recalled." 

There was testimony to the effect that the bakers were in need of repair prior to the strike of January 21, 1946, and that this fact was known to appellant. There was also testimony that the bakers were further damaged by reason of the long cooling period caused by the strike, but the extent of damage due to any one cause does not appear. 

The referee and the board found that the union refused on January 28, 1946, to permit qualified men to enter appellant's plant to repair the bakers during the continuance of the strike. In this connection the board made an additional finding: "By reason of the nature of the processes involved in the plant of the employer company it was not possible for the company to resume operations immediately upon settlement of the dispute, and it was not in position to resume operations until March 4, 1946." The board did not make any finding fixing the blame upon either of the parties for the failure of the plant to resume opera-

tion upon the date set in the agreement for the termination of the strike.

The referee and the board held that claimant's ineligibility ended at 12:01 a.m. February 18, 1946. Appellant's contention is that claimant's ineligibility continued, under the proviso in section 402(d), until February 24, 1946, inclusive.

Section 402 (d) of the Unemployment Compensation Law, as amended by the Act of May 29, 1945, P. L. 1145, sec. 9, 43 PS §802, provides: "An employe shall be ineligible for compensation for any week-... (d) In which his unemployment is due to a voluntary suspension of work resulting from an industrial dispute, at the factory establishment or other premises at which he is or was last employed: Provided, That this disqualification shall apply only to any week of unemployment which, in whole or in part, includes any part of a period beginning with the day on which such suspension occurs and ending with (i) the last day of the fourth calendar week immediately following the calendar week in which such suspension occurs, or (ii) the day on which such suspension was terminated, whichever is the earlier . . ."

The real substance of appellant's contention is that the phrase "unemployment due to a voluntary suspension of work resulting from an industrial dispute" should be interpreted to mean that claimant is disqualified, subject to clause (i) of section 402 (d) as to the maximum number of weeks, not for the duration of the strike alone, but also for any additional time of unemployment caused by the strike, that is, the period of actual work stoppage. Appellant further contends, in relation to the limitation on disqualification in the proviso in section 402 (d), that the board erred in holding the "suspension" of work was terminated on the day the strike ended. According to appellant, the word "voluntary" in the phrase "voluntary suspension of work" in the first sentence of section 402 (d) is necessary to indi-

1948] 

 cate a strike, as opposed to a lockout, or some other action on the part of the employer, but that when the word "suspension" is used later in the proviso in section 402 (d) it means "work stoppage," and has no application to the termination of the strike.

The legislature, in our opinion, by the language used, intended that the period of the employe's disqualification should be measured by the day the strike or "voluntary suspension" of work ended. The unemployment compensation law is a remedial statute, and its provisions must be liberally and broadly construed so that its objectives may be completely achieved: MacFarland v. Unemployment Compensation Board of Review, 158 Pa. Superior Ct. 418, 45 A. (2d) 423. Its purposes are clear, and we shall not resort to a strained or narrow construction. 

Appellant makes reference to the declaration of policy in section 3, 43 PS §752, which makes the act applicable to those who "become unemployed through no fault of their own," and urges upon us the proposition that the strikers are responsible, subject to the limitation clause (i) in section 402 (d) as to the maximum number of weeks, for any unemployment due to or caused by the strike as well as for that unemployment necessarily included in the actual duration of the strike. But that takes too narrow a view of the applicable provisions of the statute. Besides, the general declaration of public policy, as it may relate to unemployment caused by the employe, must yield to the specific designation contained in section 402 (d): Com. ex rel. v. 

Macelwee et al., 294 Pa. 569, 572, 144 Atl. 751; Kolb v.

Reformed Episcopal Church of Reconciliation, 18 Pa. Su perior Ct. 477. For the same reason, where the legislature has made a specific designation as to the exact period of disqualification, we cannot extend that period, under the guise of interpretation, by finding an ambiguity where none exists, or by reading the doctrine of legal causation into this section of the statute. Statutory rights cannot be so readily destroyed. We think that the import of section

402 (d), considered in its entirety, is plain, and that it requires no extended interpretation. Disqualification exists, in the first instance, where a claimant's unemployment is "due to a voluntary suspension of work resulting from an industrial dispute." The words "such suspension" which occur thereafter three times in the proviso clearly refer, in our judgment, to the term "voluntary suspension" previously used. We do not believe that the legislature meant "voluntary suspension" in the one instance and "work stoppage" in the other. Moreover, where the meaning of a word or phrase is clear as used in one section of the act, it will be construed to mean the same thing in another: Commonwealth v. Stingel, 156 Pa. Superior Ct. 359, 362, 40 A. (2d) 140.

It is not without some significance that the legislature, since this controversy arose, further amended section 

402 (d) of the Unemployment Compensation Law by the 

Act of June 30, 1947, No. 493, making the employe ineligible for compensation "for any week . . . (d) In which his unemployment is due to a stoppage of work, which exists because of a labor dispute • · 

Finally, appellant contends that, even under the board's interpretation of "suspension" as a voluntary suspension on 

February 18, 1946, all of the fifth week, ending February 24th, must be included in the period of ineligibility. Stated briefly, appellant's view, as we understand it, is that where a strike extends beyond one week of seven consecutive days, and into a second or subsequent week of seven consecutive days, all of the subsequent "week," included within the seven-day period in which the strike (voluntary suspension) ends (counting from the day the suspension occurred), must be held a part of the period of ineligibility. 

Reduced to its simplest terms, the period of disqualification is "any week of unemployment which, in whole or in part, includes any part of" the period of voluntary suspension. It seems that the clear meaning of the language used is to disqualify in units of "weeks" of unemployment.

1948] 

Under section 402 (d) the legislature obviously intended to disqualify a claimant for a full week where a voluntary suspension occurs. Cf. Bonner v. Unemployment Compensation Board of Review, 156 Pa. Superior Ct. 367, 371, 40 A. (2d) 106, where, under the 1942 amendment to section 402 (d), a claimant was held disqualified for the entire claim week, although, under the findings, the voluntary suspension lasted only one day.

It is unnecessary for us to decide the question which appellant seeks to raise on this branch of the case. Under the facts of the present appeal as found, the strike was settled at 12:01 a.m. February 18, 1946, and claimant was ready, willing and able to return to work during all of February 18, 1946. The referee reasoned, and this reasoning was approved by the board, that "since the strike was settled at 12:01 a.m., February 18th, claimant's period of disqualification because of the industrial dispute had ended as of February 17th and his unemployment from February 18th to March 4th was due to the inability of the company to resume operations and not because of an industrial dispute existing at that time. The period from February 18th to February 24th would, therefore, constitute a full week of unemployment." It is evident therefore that the voluntary suspension ended with the expiration of February 17, 1946, and claimant became eligible for the claim week of 

February 18th to February 24th. Thus, the "voluntary suspension" ended exactly four full consecutive "weeks" of seven days after it began, and we are not confronted with the problem, which appellant attempts to inject, of a voluntary suspension ending when only a part of a subsequent week has passed. The interpretation placed by the board on the proviso in section 402 (d), as to the number of weeks of ineligibility, was correct. 

Decision is affirmed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD CLINGAN v. FAIRCHANCE LUMBER CO. 

Workmen's compensation—Partial disability—Earnings derived from operation of business-Performance of duties by members of claimant's family.

A referee's order dismissing defendant's petition for modification of a compensation agreement on the basis of a finding that claimant was still totally disabled will be affirmed notwithstanding the fact that claimant derived a substantial income from the operation of a grocery store, where it appeared that the income so derived resulted from the fact that no salary was paid to the members of claimant's family with the exception of one daughter, all of whom performed most of the duties of operating the store, it further appearing that it was necessary for him to rest from time to time during the day for which purpose he maintained a bed at his place of business, and that all the work which claimant performed required about one hour's time per day.

Appeal by defendant from order of Referee Foust, District No. 9, awarding compensation under agreement no. 

9,128,530. Appeal dismissed. January 14, 1948. 

Ocean Accident & Guarantee Corp., insurance carrier. 

Anthony Cavalcante, for claimant. 

James J. Burns, Jr., for defendant.

KNOLL, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by defendant from the order of Referee 

J. Ross Foust, of District No. 9, awarding compensation under agreement no. 9,128,530.

A study of the record discloses that claimant sustained certain injuries while acting within the course of his employment with defendant herein on October 23, 1939. A compensation agreement was entered into between the

1948] 

 parties, providing for the payment of compensation at the rate of $14.49 per week for an indefinite number of weeks. 

On November 4, 1942, defendant filed its petition for modification of the aforesaid agreement, averring that claimant's disability had resolved itself into that of 25 percent partial disability. The referee, by decision dated 

February 26, 1943, found as a fact that claimant was still totally disabled and dismissed defendant's petition. From this ruling defendant appealed to this board, which dismissed the appeal on September 3, 1943.

On December 7, 1945, defendant filed its petition for termination, averring that claimant has been engaged in the operation of a grocery store since August 1944 and was no longer totally disabled. The matter was again referred to Referee Foust before whom testimony was taken.

The referee found as a fact that claimant was still totally disabled and, based upon said finding of fact, dismissed defendant's petition. From this ruling, defendant appealed to this board, which, by opinion of July 31, 1946, sustained the referee's findings and dismissed the appeal. 

Thereupon, defendant appealed to the Court of Common 

Pleas of Fayette County (Clingan v. Fairchance Lumber 

Co., 59 D. & C. 698, 33 Dept. Rep. 183), which court, in an opinion by Carr, President Judge, dated March 21, 1947, remitted the record to the board for further hearing and determination in accordance with the opinion of the said court. The board was directed by the court to take into consideration the fact that claimant had been deriving substantial profits from his business and to find the comparative relation of his services to the profits thereof in order to determine the amount of his earning power, despite his injury; this for the purpose of determining the loss or impairment of earning power suffered by claimant by reason of his injuries. In accordance with the mandate of the court, this board, by order dated April 29, 1947, remitted the record to the referee for District No. 9 for

further determination in accordance with the opinion of said court.

At the hearing held before the referee, claimant was called as for cross-examination and testified that the net income from the business for the year ending December 31, 1946, was $3,134.41; that the net profit did not reflect the payment of any moneys to his wife and four children who played an active part in the operation of the business. 

Claimant also testified that his wife, in effect, ran the business and that his oldest daughter, who is 19 years of age, was a fulltime employe, but did not receive any compensation until August 1946, when she was paid $20 per week; that his two other daughters, aged 16 and 13, respectively, devoted all of their vacation time to the business and also spent time at the place of business after school. The youngest daughter, aged eight, also did some work in and around the business. In addition to his family, claimant also employed two full-time employes and four part-time employes, and during the year 1946 claimant moved the business into larger quarters.

Claimant further testified that he cuts most of the roasts and steaks, but that others did the cutting of all other meats; that he assisted in the keeping of books and payment of bills, and in purchasing of merchandise for the business, but that most of the purchasing was done by his wife; that many of the duties which he was able to perform in the original store, he was unable to perform now due to the size of the larger store; that his activities at the time of the hearing before the referee were more limited than they were at the time of the hearing held on January 22, 1946; and that all of the work which he performed in the said business required only about one hour's time. 

Claimant also testified that the condition of his leg had become progressively worse and that it was necessary for him to rest during the day and, for this purpose, a bed is maintained at the place of business.

1948] 

The referee found as a fact that claimant was still totally disabled and, based upon said finding of fact, dismissed the termination petition. From this ruling defendant has again appealed.

We have made a careful study of the testimony and are of the opinion that the ruling of the referee should be affirmed. While claimant receives a substantial income from the operation of the business, it is to be noted that this income results from the fact that no salary is paid to the members of his family, including his wife, with the exception of the oldest daughter. While claimant does some work in and about the business, it is of a very limited nature and, according to the testimony, does not require more than one hour per day.

We are convinced, from a study of the testimony, that claimant would be able to perform such duties only in his own place of business. It is necessary for this claimant to rest from time to time during the day and, for this purpose, a bed is maintained at the place of business. It is difficult to foresee any employer giving work to this claimant under these circumstances. We feel that claimant is not able uninterruptedly to do even light work due to his physical limitations.

If suitable work is available for such a person, it is incumbent upon defendant to show that fact; otherwise, claimant is entitled to payment for total disability. Nor has defendant introduced any medical testimony whatsoever to show that there has been a change in the physical condition of this claimant and we have reason to believe that if such testimony were available, defendant would have introduced it. Considering the testimony in its entirety, we have concluded that claimant is, for all intents and purposes, totally disabled and, by reason thereof, the referee properly dismissed defendant's petition for termination.

We, therefore, affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of dismissal. 

The appeal of defendant is dismissed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD GERRINGER v. FOLLMER TRUCKING CO. 

Workmen's compensation-Accidental injury—Disability resulting from drenching in rain storm—Award for hospital expenses. 

1. A referee's award of compensation on the basis of a finding of an accidental injury will be sustained where claimant, employed as a truck driver by defendant whose duties required him to drive from terminal to terminal but not to load or unload merchandise, was exposed to a heavy rain storm for a period of an hour or more when he happened to approach the scene of an accident that involved a tractor-trailer of the defendant where he performed duties as a result of which he suffered chills and developed pleurisy and thrombo-phlebitis causing disability; in such circumstances, the acts performed by the claimant at the scene of the accident were unusual, outside of his course of duty, and the exposure suffered by him as a result thereof constituted an accident within the meaning of the 

Workmen's Compensation Act. 

2. A referee's order limiting recovery of hospital expenses to the sum of $150 will be set aside and an award entered in a larger amount for hospital treatment incurred during the first 60-day period after claimant's disability began; section 306 (ƒ) of the Workmen's 

Compensation Act provides for hospital treatment and services at the prevailing charge in the hospital for the 60-day period in addition to medical services, medicines and supplies, the cost of which latter services shall not exceed the amount of $150. 

Appeal by claimant from award of Referee Olexy, District No. 2. Claim petition no. 108,587. Appeal sustained. 

January 21, 1948.

Globe Indemnity Company, insurance carrier. 

Hemingway & Wagner, for claimant. 

John F. Donohue, for defendant.

KNOLL, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by claimant from the order of award of Referee Joseph P. Olexy, of District No. 2.

1948] 

On April 30, 1947, claimant filed his petition, averring, inter alia, that he sustained certain compensable injuries while acting within the course of his employment with defendant herein on October 10, 1946. To this petition a responsive answer was filed by defendant, denying the allegations of the said petition. 

Claimant, on his own behalf, testified that he was employed as a driver by defendant herein and that on October 10, 1946, he was driving a truck from Philadelphia, Pa., toward Danville, Pa., with another truck of defendant company preceding him on the highway; that as they approached Elizabethtown, Pa., at or about 1:30 o'clock a.m., they came to the scene where another truck of defendant company had been involved in an accident; that there was no parking place near the scene of the accident, and claimant and the other driver drove their trucks to the Farm Diner and ran back to the scene of the accident. Their investigation disclosed that a tractor-trailer of defendant company had been in an accident and, as the result thereof, the trailer was partly obstructing the highway, and a pole of the Pennsylvania Power and Light Company had been knocked down. Claimant and a fellow-employe, a Mr. 

Stump, immediately placed fuses and flares on the highway at the scene of the accident so as to give adequate warning to other persons using the highway. Claimant then called the office of the highway patrol, notifying them of the accident, and also called the terminal at Danville, Pa., and was directed to stay at the scene of the accident until a call was received from the terminal office; and he then called Mr. Rossen, president of the trucking company, and was directed to remain at the scene of the accident until the highway patrolmen arrived. Claimant also testified that, following the placing of the fuses and flares, he was engaged in a search for way bills which were scattered in and about the scene of the accident; that during this period of time, it was raining heavily and the sweater which he was wearing became soaked; that he returned to

his truck, removed the sweater and turned the heater on, because he had become chilled and his teeth were chattering; and that he then went to a diner in Elizabethtown to get something warm to eat. The record discloses that, following this occurrence, claimant worked until October 20, 1946, at which time he suffered severe pains in the area of the back and had difficulty in breathing. Following this attack, claimant called Dr. Carl to administer treatment who directed claimant to go to bed. A few days later, claimant began to suffer from pain in the area of the right leg, and he again consulted a doctor and was removed to the Geisinger Memorial Hospital, where he was confined for a period of 51 days. Following discharge from the hospital, claimant was confined to his home and was able to resume his work on April 7, 1947.

In reference to the notice given to defendant company, claimant testified that on October 20, 1946, he notified Harry Davis (the jockey), whose duty it was to obtain another man for a particular trip if the scheduled driver was unable to take the trip. Claimant testified that he told Mr. Davis that, by reason of the occurrence heretofore referred to, he had contracted pleurisy. Claimant also testified that, while he was confined to the hospital, a Mr. 

Donahue, the general manager of defendant company, visited him at the hospital, at which time he told Mr. Donahue what had happened and that he had been suffering from pleurisy. This took place during the first three weeks that claimant was confined to the hospital. 

Dr. Wendell J. Stainsby, called on behalf of claimant, testified that claimant was confined to the hospital from 

October 26, 1946, to December 16, 1946, at which time a diagnosis of acute thrombo-phlebitis was made; that claimant made a slow but definite recovery and left the hospital in good shape to continue his convalescence. The doctor was of the opinion that the chilling which claimant received during his exposure to the rain and the elements produced

1948] 

 an infection in the chest, resulting either in pleurisy or pneumonia and, as a result thereof, an inflammation developed in the veins of the leg, causing the thrombophlebitis. The doctor testified that an examination disclosed no varicose veins or other infections which would have produced the thrombo-phlebitis and that phlebitis was frequently caused by pneumonia or pleurisy. The doctor concluded that, while phlebitis can be caused from factors other than those present in this case, the chilling which claimant suffered was in all probability 99 percent of the cause of the phlebitis.

Harry F. Davis (the jockey), called on behalf of claimant, testified that he was advised by claimant on October 20, 1946, as to the disability from which claimant was suffering and that he immediately notified the dispatcher of the same.

Claimant offered into evidence the bill of the Geisinger Memorial Hospital in the sum of $541.70, and also testified that he paid the sum of $22 to Dr. Carl for medical services rendered.

The referee found as a fact that, as a result of the exposure to the rain of October 10, 1946, claimant developed pleurisy which resulted in acute thrombo-phlebitis, by reason of which claimant was totally disabled from October 20, 1946, to and including April 6, 1947. The referee further found as a fact that claimant sustained an accident in the course of his employment with defendant herein. Based upon said findings of fact, the referee awarded compensation to claimant at the rate of $20 per week for the period beginning October 27, 1946, to and including April 6, 1947.

The referee further directed that defendant pay to Dr. 

Carl the sum of $22 and the Geisinger Memorial Hospital the sum of $150. From the order directing the payment of $150 to the Geisinger Memorial Hospital, claimant has appealed, contending that he is entitled to payment of $150 for medical services received and that, in addition thereto, to such sums expended for hospital treatment at the Geis-

inger Memorial Hospital during the statutory period of 60 days. According to the calculations of claimant, the treatment at the hospital exceeded the 60-day period by one week and claimant has petitioned the board for additional allowance of the hospital expenses for the said one-week period.

Defendant has filed a cross appeal, contending that claimant did not sustain an accident within the meaning of the 

Compensation Act. 

We have made a careful study of the record and are of the opinion that the ruling of the referee, to the effect that claimant sustained an accident within the meaning of the Compensation Act, should be affirmed. We are of the opinion that the referee was in error in limiting the recovery of the hospital expenses to the sum of $150. 

The testimony in this case discloses that on October 10, 1946, claimant, while acting within the course of his employment was driving toward Danville, Pa., and when he reached Elizabethtown, Pa., approached the scene of an accident. An investigation disclosed that a tractor-trailer of defendant company had been involved in an accident as a result of which the trailer obstructed a portion of the highway. Claimant immediately parked his truck, ran to the scene of the accident and, with a fellow-employe, placed fuses and flares on the highway so as to give adequate warning to other persons using the highway, and likewise notified defendant company, at which time he was directed to remain at the scene of the accident until the highway patrolmen arrived. Pending the arrival of the patrolmen, claimant was engaged in the search of way bills which were scattered in and about the scene of the accident. 

During this period of time, it was raining heavily and claimant's sweater and clothes became wet, and when claimant returned to his truck, he was compelled to remove the wet sweater, as he was suffering from chills and his teeth chattered. Claimant then drove to a diner where he ordered a bowl of hot soup in order to obtain some warmth. The

1948] 

 testimony further establishes the fact that claimant was able to work for a period of 10 days when pleurisy developed and, as a result of the said pleurisy, claimant developed acute thrombo-phlebitis by reason of which condition he was totally disabled to April 6, 1947. The medical testimony in this case conclusively establishes the fact that the acute thrombo-phlebitis from which claimant suffered was a direct result of the chill and pleurisy arising out of claimant's exposure to the rain and other elements. 

We are convinced that there is sufficient competent testimony presented to warrant the referee's finding that claimant sustained an accident on October 10, 1946, while acting within the course of his employment with defendant herein as the result of which claimant was totally disabled from 

October 20, 1946, to April 6, 1947.

If pneumonia or pleurisy is contracted by exposure to cold or water under conditions which usually prevail, the general rule is that it is not compensable. On the other hand, if one is exposed in the course of his employment to unusual conditions, and pneumonia, chilling or pleurisy result therefrom, there is an accidental injury. The testimony in this case discloses that claimant drove from terminal to terminal and that it was not part of his duties to load or unload the merchandise; hence, claimant while acting in the course of his employment, was generally protected from prevailing weather conditions and would not be exposed to rain for a period of one hour as was present in the case at issue. We are of the opinion that the acts performed by claimant at the scene of the accident were abnormal and unusual, and outside of claimant's course of duty, and hence, we have an accident within the meaning of the Compensation Act. See Roth v. Locust Mountain

State Hospital et al., 130 Pa. Superior Ct. 1; Rathmell v. 

Wesleyville Borough, 154 Pa. Superior Ct. 351; Parks v. 

Miller Printing Machine Co., 336 Pa. 455.

Section 306 (f) of the Workmen's Compensation Act of 

1915, as amended, provides that, during the first 60 days

after disability begins, the employer shall furnish reasonable surgical and medical services, medicines and supplies, the cost of which shall not exceed the sum of $150. The act further provides that, in addition to the above service, hospital treatment, services and supplies shall be furnished by the employer for the said period of 60 days except that the board, upon petition of claimant, may grant an additional 30 days. The cost for such hospital treatment, service and supplies shall not in any case exceed the prevailing charge in the hospital for the like services to other individuals.

The record in this case discloses that claimant is indebted to Dr. Carl in the sum of $22 for medical services rendered within the statutory period and to the Geisinger Memorial Hospital for services rendered for the period beginning October 26th and terminating December 16, 1946, in the sum of $541.70. Since claimant's disability began on October 26, 1948, the statutory period of 60 days runs from October 26, 1946; hence, the said debt was incurred within the statutory period of 60 days. We are of the opinion that, in addition to medical expenses incurred during the statutory period not exceeding the sum of $150, defendant is liable for hospital treatment furnished this claimant during the said 60-day period. By reason thereof, the referee was in error in directing that the sum of $150 be paid to the Geisinger Memorial Hospital. 

We, therefore, affirm the referee's findings of fact and conclusions of law, set aside the order of award and, in lieu thereof, substitute the following:

Order Defendant, Follmer Trucking Company and/or its insurance carrier, Globe Indemnity Company, is directed to pay compensation to claimant, Raymond E. Gerringer, at the rate of $20 per week for the period beginning October 27, 1946, to and including April 6, 1947, at the ex-

1948] 

 piration of which period all payments of compensation shall cease and determine. 

Defendant, Follmer Trucking Company and/or its insurance carrier, Globe Indemnity Company, is further directed to pay the following medical and hospital expenses incurred by claimant during the statutory period: 

Dr. Carl, $22; George F. Geisinger Memorial Hospital, for medical services rendered, $123; Geisinger Memorial 

Hospital, for board, treatment and general services rendered to the claimant during the statutory period, $418.70. 

This award to bear interest at the rate of six percent per annum on all deferred payments, in accordance with the provisions of section 410 of the act. 

The appeal of claimant is sustained. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD ULSHOFER v. J. S. THORN COMPANY Workmen's compensation-Permanent partial disability-Return to work at same rate of pay-Reduction in work week- 

Suspension of payments.

Where claimant suffered a serious permanent injury to his foot for which he was paid compensation during a period of total disability, subsequent to which he returned to work at the same wage rate as he earned at the time of his injury, although he received reduced wages due to the fact that the work period of defendant's plant had been reduced from a six-day week to a five-day week, the referee did not err in suspending compensation payments and in refusing claimant's petition for reinstatement for the reason that his reduced wages were not attributable to his injury but solely to the reduction in the working period. 

Appeal by claimant from order of Referee Alessandroni, District No. 1, dismissing petition for reinstatement under compensation agreement no. 443613. Appeal dismissed. 

February 11, 1948.

Penna. Manufacturers Association Casualty Ins. Co., in surance carrier. 

David L. Ullman, for claimant. 

Paul H. Ferguson and H. M. Engell, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

Claimant, John Ulshofer, suffered an admitted accident on April 21, 1944, in the course of his employment by defendant, J. S. Thorn Company. A compensation agreement entered into by the parties describes the accident and nature of the injury as follows: "Climbed onto machine to oil same without turning off machine causing amputation of the distal one-third of the right foot". Compensation was paid for total disability until June 11, 1944, at which date Referee Alessandroni entered an order suspending compensation upon defendant's petition for termination of compensation liability. On May 7, 1948, claimant filed a petition for reinstatement alleging that his disability "results in a loss of earning power which is now reflected in wages". 

Defendant filed a responsive answer. Upon hearing held, the referee concluded that claimant's loss "of earning power" was not related to the accidental injuries and dismissed claimant's petition. This appeal has followed. 

Claimant described his work duties as lifting and setting heavy dies, weighing from 75 to 130 pounds, operating manually a foot lever for the press and acting in a supervisory capacity over other employes. Ulshofer testified that upon his return to work after the accident, he required the assistance of friendly employes to lift the dies, that he had to operate the press pedal by crossing over with the left foot, which retarded his work, and that he was relieved of his supervisory duties. Claimant stated that he had a feeling of "pins and needles" in the instep, has difficulty in climbing stairs and the left foot tires because of the added

1948] 

 strain and weight. Dr. Charles Rosenfeld, claimant's witness, testified that he examined claimant's right foot on 

July 22, 1947, and the examination disclosed "approximately one-third of the foot gone, involving the toes and portions of the metatarsal bones". The doctor elicited pain and tenderness at the distal ends. He was of the opinion that claimant's complaints of pain, discomfort and distress, were the direct result of the accident and amputation. 

Defendant called no witnesses in its behalf. The record discloses that claimant's average weekly wage at the time of the accident was $58.14 and following his return to employment, his average weekly wage at the same wage rate, was $49. The reduced wage is due to the fact that the work period of defendant's plant has been reduced from a six-day week to a five-day week. Claimant's reduced wages are on a parity with those received by able-bodied employes in the plant.

It is obvious that claimant suffered a serious permanent injury that will remain with him throughout his life. The sole question involved here is whether claimant's loss in wages is compensable? 

Section 306(b) of the Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 520, states that "the term 'earning power', as used in this section, shall in no case be less than the weekly amount which the employe receives after the accident". In the frequently cited case of Scipani v. Pressed Steel Car Co. et al., 150 

Pa. Superior Ct. 410, the court held that the amendment of section 306(b) in the Act of 1939 by necessary implication supplied the ground for suspension of payments during periods when disability of an injured employe was not reflected in loss of wages. See Keleman v. Rieber et al., 161 

Pa. Superior Ct. 169. "Wages" and "earning power" are not necessarily synonymous. However, loss of earning power must be reflected in a loss of wages in order for an

injured employe to receive compensation. Where the loss in earning power is not responsible for the reduction in wages, we are of the opinion compensation cannot be allowed. We are satisfied that claimant presently earns the wages which he receives. It is also true that if claimant had not suffered the accident in question and continued in his employment for defendant, he would be receiving exactly the same wages which he is now receiving. It necessarily follows, then, that the reduced wages which he now receives is in no wise attributable to his injury and leads us to the inescapable conclusion that his recognized physical disability is not reflected in a present loss of earning power, or wages, although the amount of wages actually received is less than those received at the time of the accident. Our attention has been directed to the recent case of Holtz v. McGraw and Bindley, 161 Pa. Superior Ct. 371 (decided September 30, 1947). We had occasion to consider this opinion in the case of Arista v. H. C. Frick Coke 

Co., A-33120 (Board 1947), in which we said (p. 2): "The main question before the Court in that case concerns the effect of a suspension order and the resulting burden of proof upon a subsequent loss of earning power. 

The opinion holds that a suspension order is not a termination order."

We have again reviewed and considered the language of the court in the Holtz case and do not believe that case is analagous to the instant case. We believe that the court opinion is predicated upon a realistic premise that the reduction in wages is due to the physical disability entirely and not, as here, to the curtailment of the work week. We have likewise considered arguments advanced by claimant's counsel and deem them inapplicable to the facts presented in this case. The suspension order now in effect does not terminate claimant's right to future compensation benefits.

The door is still open, within the limitations of the act, to obtain compensation if and when his disability reflects itself in a loss of earning power.

1948] 

When the case was before the referee on November 29, 1944, the referee found that "claimant has been suffering an undetermined degree of partial disability as a result of the condition of his right foot, but this condition has not caused him to suffer a loss of earning power to the present time" and suspended compensation payments "until such time as the claimant's disability is reflected in a loss of earning power". Neither party took an appeal. The referee's later opinion is of the same tenor. We believe that there is sufficient and satisfactory evidence upon the record to enter a finding that claimant's overall disability from the accident is a permanent partial disability of 25 percent. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's second finding of fact and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following: 

Findings of fact 

2. That from June 11, 1944, claimant has a permanent partial disability of 25 percent as a result of the accident on April 21, 1944. 

3. That the loss in wages suffered by claimant since September 1, 1944, has been due entirely to a reduction in the work week and is not in any way related to the 25 percent partial disability which claimant suffers as a result of the accident of April 21, 1944.

The referee's first finding of fact is affirmed. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's conclusion of law and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following: 

Conclusion of law 

Since claimant's loss of 25 percent partial disability is not presently reflected in a loss of earning power, he is not entitled to compensation payments.

The referee's order of dismissal is affirmed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD SCHRECENGOST v. O. K. HEILMAN TRUCKING COM- PANY Workmen's compensation—Claim petition-Limitations—Tolling of statute-Payment of compensation—Necessity for payment within year of accident.

Under section 315 of the Workmen's Compensation Act, provid ing for limitations upon filing claims for personal injuries but further providing that where payments of compensation have been made, the limitations shall take effect only after the expiration of one year from the date of the last payment of compensation, “payments of compensation” mean wages, benefits or other relief apart from the act, but do not include a loan made by an employer to an employe to help him out until he obtained other funds; in any case, the statute may be tolled only by payments made within one year after the accident and a payment made by an employer to employe after the expiration of said period did not afford the basis for the subsequent filing of a claim petition. 

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Carmalt, District No. 8, claim petition no. 99,446, accident no. 

4,407,092. Appeal dismissed. February 4, 1948.

Zurich General Accident & Insurance Co., insurance car rier. 

John B. Nicklas, Jr., for claimant. 

Irwin M. Ringold, for defendant.

KNOLL, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by claimant from an order of Referee 

Galdstone A. Carmalt, of Compensation District No. 8, dis missing his claim petition on the ground that claimant had not filed his petition within the statutory period provided by the Workmen's Compensation Act. 

Claimant's petition, filed June 27, 1944, alleged, inter alia, that he was struck in the left eye by a piece of metal

1948] 

 in October 1941, as a result of which he had lost the vision of the left eye.

Section 315 of the act bars claims for personal injuries unless, within one year after the accident, the parties agree upon compensation, or a claim petition is filed. Where, however, payments of compensation have been paid in any case, the limitations take effect only after the expiration of one year from the date of the last payment of compensation.

Claimant, on appeal, contends that the referee's dismissal was in error since claimant had an oral compensation agreement with defendant and had received compensation from defendant on October 14, 1943.

The record shows that claimant worked, without any apparent disability, with average weekly wages of $45, until August 1943, when he first consulted an eye specialist.

He was hospitalized from September 23, 1943, to October 9, 1943, when it was found that an intraocular foreign body in the left eye had destroyed the vision of the eye. Claimant returned to work on October 15, 1943, and was in defendant's employ at the time of hearing on December 30, 1946. 

Claimant testified that defendant paid him $40 on October 14, 1943, for the two weeks which claimant had off, and that defendant said that he would take up the case with the insurance company.

Defendant admitted that he had given the $40 to claimant, but he denied any conversation with claimant regarding workmen's compensation insurance. He testified that he gave the money in order to help out claimant until "he obtained some more funds."

The referee rejected the credibility of claimant's testimony relating to the alleged conversation and agreement with defendant. He accepted defendant's explanation of the circumstances under which he gave the money to claimant and we believe that he exercised proper judgment.

"Where Section 315 refers to 'payments of compensation' as extending the time within which the limitation provided for in the Act shall take effect, it means payments by way of wages, benefits, relief or other voluntary or informal compensation, apart from the Act . . .": Tinsman v. Jones & Laughlin Steel Corp., 118 Pa. Superior Ct. 516, 523.

Clearly, claimant did not receive "wages", "benefits", "relief" or any form of compensation, but did receive a gratuity which, in our opinion, did not toll the statute of limitations.

Further, we are of the opinion that the statute may be tolled only by payments made during the one-year limitation set forth in the act. In this case, the right of claimant to file a claim petition had expired before the receipt of the money from his employer. The statute was not tolled during the period of one year after the alleged accident and after the expiration of one year there was no effective procedure left to claimant.

Accordingly, the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of dismissal are affirmed. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD MACKLEY v. PHILADELPHIA & READING COAL & IRON CO. 

Occupational disease compensation—Occupational Disease Act of 

1939—Rejection of act by employer-Section 302(a) of the act-Necessity for reposting rejection on renewal of hiring. 

1. Under section 302 (a) of the Occupational Disease Compensa tion Act of June 21, 1939, providing that in contracts of hiring made after October 1, 1939, and in every contract renewed or extended after said date, it shall be conclusively presumed that the parties have accepted the provisions of the act unless the employer shall post at his place of business a notice of his intention not to pay compensation, a notice of rejection posted by the employer on

1948] 

 the premises at the time of the hiring of an employe is sufficient to constitute a rejection of the act, and the employer is not required to post a new notice each time a new contract of hiring is thereafter entered into or an old contract of hiring is renewed. 

2. An agreement entered into by an employer with a miners' union covering the working conditions of employes in the employer's mine was not a "contract of hiring" referred to in section 302 (a) of the Occupational Disease Act of 1939, providing that employers shall be presumed to have agreed to be bound to pay compensation under the act unless they shall have posted notice of rejection thereof. 

3. Compensation will be denied to claimant, a widow, for the death of her husband as a result of silicosis contracted in the course of his employment by defendant, where it appears that on December 31, 1944, the date when decedent was employed by defendant, the latter had posted on its premises a rejection of the Occupational Disease Act, and that decedent was last employed by defendant on September 15, 1945; notwithstanding the fact that decedent was hired, discharged and reëmployed at various times within the overall period of his employment, defendant was not required to post and repost a rejection notice at each subsequent hiring or renewal thereof, nor did the fact that defendant entered into a contract with decedent's union in May of 1945 require it to repost its notice of rejection to avoid a presumption that the parties accepted the pro visions of the Occupational Disease Act. 

Petition for rehearing filed by counsel for defendant. 

C. A. 4,936,509. Order of Referee Enterline dismissing claim petition. Appeal dismissed. February 4, 1948. 

Thomas Waltz, for claimant.

Penrose Hertzler and Mr. C. E. Bottiger, for defendant. 

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This case was before the board upon appeal by claimant, Mrs. Anna Mackley, from the order of Referee Enterline dismissing her claim for compensation for the death of her

husband, John Mackley, on April 24, 1946. Upon appeal to the board (A-32842), we vacated and set aside the referee's findings of fact and conclusions of law and remanded the record to the referee for hearing upon the merits of the case. In effect, we sustained the appeal. Before further hearing by the referee, defendant petitioned the board for a reargument. In view of the fact that the case was one of first impression and involved a question of paramount importance to an industry as a whole, the petition was granted. 

The case is again before us for determination. We have carefully considered the provisions of the act and the arguments of counsel. We are in agreement that the referee's original order of disallowance was proper and should be sustained. Mackley's last employment by defendant was on September 15, 1945.

We recognize that silicosis is an insidious disease which takes years to develop to a stage of total disability: Roschak v. Vulcan Iron Works, 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 227. Mindful as we are of the humane purposes of the Occupational Disease Compensation Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 566, we, nevertheless, believe that a realistic consideration of all of the facts in the instant case compel the conclusion that defendant, Philadelphia & Reading Coal & Iron Co., had rejected the provisions of the act at the time. However, there are prescribed rights and liabilities in the act in question, which must be applied to the particular facts in a given case before compensation can be awarded. It is our considered opinion that the act must be applied to the legal relationship existing between decedent and defendant as of September 15, 1945, the date of his last employment, as prescribed by section 301 (c). Mackley's death on April 

24, 1946, was also prior to the acceptance of the act by defendant. What, therefore, were the rights and liabilities on September 15, 1945? In order to arrive at a proper conclusion, we must review the facts from December 31, 1944, to September 15, 1945. The referee found that decedent was employed by defendant on December 31, 1944,

1948] 

 the date when defendant posted, on its premises, the rejection of the Occupational Disease Act. This rejection, as of that date, appears to be proper in its form and valid under the Occupational Disease Act. The referee, in his findings, stated: "The parties were unable to agree as to whether decedent was not effective as to him and, therefore, also not effective in paragraph 1 hereof. Claimant contends that if the periods were not continuous and decedent were reëmployed at one or more times during said period that the rejection was in continuous employment during the periods set forth as to claimant, his widow, who filed her petition on December 30, 1946, alleging his death on April 24, 1946, unless personal notice was given to decedent or additional posting prior to each contract of reëmployment was made." 

Let us agree, for the benefit of claimant's contention, that decedent was hired, discharged and reëmployed at various times by defendant during the aforesaid period of time. In addition to this employment and reëmployment of decedent, defendant and the United Mine Workers entered into a contract in May 1945, which has been considered as the contract of hiring.

We, therefore, have a decedent who was working prior to and after December 31, 1944, to September 15, 1945, for a defendant who had rejected the act on December 31, 1944, and, as the testimony reveals, rejected the act prior thereto; a decedent who worked at various times for defendant during the aforesaid period of time; and a new 

United Mine Workers' contract which contained new provisions and changes of working conditions entered into on May 19, 1945. The legal question now presented is whether the aforesaid facts were such as to defeat the legality of the rejection of the Occupational Disease Act made by defendant on December 31, 1944, and raise a presumption that defendant accepted the act. Section 302 (a) of the 

Occupational Disease Act reads as follows:

"In every contract of hiring made after October first, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-nine, and in every contract of hiring renewed or extended by mutual consent, expressed or implied, after said date, it shall be conclusively presumed that the parties have accepted the provisions of article three of this act, and have agreed to be bound thereby, unless the employer shall post at his plant, office or place of business a notice of his intention not to pay such compensation . . ."

This section appears to require a posting of the rejection of the act whenever a contract is made, renewed, or extended; however, the presumption of the acceptance of the act may be rebutted by the latter part of said section which reads: “... unless the employer shall post at his plant, office or place of business a notice of his intention not to pay such compensation". If the words "shall post" mean that every employer must post the rejection notice after the contract of hiring was entered into, then the purpose of the first part of section 302 (a), supra, would be defeated, because decedent would have no notice of rejection and, as stated in the act, it would be conclusively presumed that the parties have accepted the provisions of this act and have agreed to be bound thereby. If the employer posts the notice prior to the time that the contract of hiring is entered into, then the purpose of the act can be carried out, because the employe will receive his notice prior to the time he enters into the contract and he knows that defendant will not pay compensation in accordance with the act. For us to say that the posting of the notice must take place immediately before the contract of hiring is entered into, would be setting a limitation of time upon defendant, which is not contained in the act. Furthermore, it would not be a reasonable interpretation of the act to say that the posting of the notice must be made at any specific time as long as the notice is posted before the execution of the contract of hiring. With this in view, what must defendant do in order to keep the rejection of De-

1948] 

 cember 31, 1944, in legal form and enforcible? Must it post a similar notice in the same place where a notice was posted on December 31, 1944, every time a condition in the contract is changed or a United Mine Workers' contract is entered into, renewed or extended? While we must read the law as it is enacted, yet we are not expected to arrive at an absurd and ridiculous conclusion. If section 302 (a) should require a defendant to post a new notice every time a new contract of hiring takes place, it would be a repetition of what is already in existence. Defendant posted a notice on December 31, 1944, "in a wooden frame with a glass over same" and if the act required defendant to do the same thing every time a new contract of hiring took place, then all the defendant would have to do would be to have the clerk open this glass case, take the notice out and put it back up again. This would have to be done every time defendant employed a new employe. In addition thereto, every time an employe is hired, another notice would have to be sent to the Workmen's Compensation Bureau, all of which forces us to arrive at an absurd and ridiculous interpretation of section 302 (a) of the Occupational Disease Act.

The other act committed by defendant, which we refer to in the first part of this opinion, is the fact that defendant entered into a contract with the United Mine Workers on May 19, 1945, which, it is contended, renewed and extended the contract of hiring and, since defendant did not repost its notice of rejection, it is presumed that the parties accepted the provisions of article three of the Occupational Disease Act. It is our opinion that the United Mine Workers' contract is not the contract of hiring contemplated by section 302 (a) of the Occupational Disease Act, supra. 

The contract of hiring was between the employer and employe, "master" and "servant" as defined by the Occupa tional Disease Act and the United Mine Workers' contract was only effective as to the conditions under which the employe and employer were to maintain their working rela-

1 

tionship: Kalish v. Lehigh Valley Navigation Coal Co., 33 Dept. Rep. 555. The legal contract of hiring in the with in case took place prior to December 31, 1944, when, in plain words, decedent got a job from defendant. If he quit his job and was subsequently rehired, a new contract of hiring was entered into. But, as we stated above, it would be an unreasonable interpretation of the act to compel defendant to post and repost a rejection notice every time an employe was hired, "fired" or rehired. As long as there is a notice of rejection posted on the premises at the time of the contract of hiring, it is sufficient to reject the 

Occupational Disease Act. 

The absurdity of compelling employers to post a new notice every time a contract of hiring is entered into can be more fully appreciated when we try to comprehend the vast number of employes engaged in the extensive industries within the confines of our Commonwealth. It is, therefore, our opinion that, when decedent was last employed by defendant on September 15, 1945, the rights and liabilities of the parties were fixed as of that date and defendant's rejection, as posted on December 31, 1944, was in full force and effect and claimant is not entitled to compensation in accordance with the provisions of the Occupational Disease Act of 1939, as amended. 

Our order of June 25, 1947, is vacated and we hereby affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of disallowance.

1948] 

 WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD STEINER v. CRAMP SHIPBUILDING CO. 

Workmen's compensation-Death-Accidental injury-Exposure to fumes in welding process.

A referee's award of compensation to claimant for the death of her husband will be reversed where it appears that decedent, employed by defendant as a welder, became ill from the brazing and welding fumes to which he was exposed in tank compartments where he worked during a period of three months, which illness resulted in his death; since death was attributable to exposure to conditions existing over an extended period of time and not to any single occurrence or act, proof of an accidental injury was lacking. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Alessandroni, District No. 1, claim petition no. 97,298. Appeal sustained. January 28, 1948.

Daniel Marcu, for claimant. 

J. Paul Erwin, for defendant. 

Ralph H. Behney, for Commonwealth.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

Claimant, Mrs. Bella Steiner, filed a claim petition on 

October 29, 1943, for the death of her husband, Norman

Steiner, under the Occupational Disease Compensation Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 566. At the hearing before Referee Alessandroni, claimant requested and was given leave to amend the petition to bring it under the Workmen's 

Compensation Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 520. The referee awarded compensation and defendant, Cramp Shipbuilding

Company, has appealed. Steiner was employed as a pipefitter's helper from late January 1943 to April 17, 1943.

when he ceased work because of his physical condition. He died on May 26, 1943. The testimony, introduced in behalf of claimant, is quite lengthy. Claimant established marriage and dependency. She testified that her decedent had been engaged in business as a paper hanger from 1926 until the fall of 1942 and that he then did no work except for a few days, until placed with defendant by the State Employment Service. She stated that her decedent had been in excellent health prior to his last employment and weighed approximately 195 pounds, but after such employment he lost considerable weight, complained about his health and became nauseous. Claimant testified that her husband returned from work on Saturday, April 17, 1943, appearing very sick, that "he just dragged his feet; didn't have enough strength to lift them," that he was very weak. He saw a neighborhood physician, Dr. Nathan Shapiro, the following

Monday, who treated him for several days, and was next attended by Dr. Frank Glauser, who immediately ordered him to the Jewish Hospital. Raymond Fletcher, a registered plumber, testified that he had 36 men under his supervision as a leaderman, and that decedent worked in the outside tanks of submarines. He described the location, shape, size, working area of the fuel tanks, and operations that were carried on at the time of decedent's employment. 

At times, a welder, silver brazer, pipefitter and a helper would be working simultaneously in the tank. After the pipefitters fitted up the pipe, the silver brazers coated the piping with a brazing flux. Fletcher testified: "Q. Did they require heat for that (brazing)? "A. Positively. "Q. Would that give off fumes? "A. It would. "Q. How about the welding? "A. The same way. "Q. Any fumes given off there? "A. Give you 'galvo' fumes. "Q. Was Steiner subject to those fumes while he worked there?

1948] 

"A. He was. "Q. Did it ever, to your knowledge, affect him? "A. It did. I gave him quite a number of passes to the dispensary."

The testimony of the witness clearly and positively establishes that Steiner became ill from the brazing and welding fumes in the confined, poorly ventilated tank compartments and complained to Fletcher about the fumes. The leaderman identified the fumes as a "dose of galvo", which he said caused "a sweet taste or sweet sensation in the throat that makes you sick or vomit at times". He stated that other employes engaged in the same type of work were similarly affected.

Ronald P. Hubbard testified that he was employed by defendant as a welding foreman during the period of decedent's employment and has been associated with welding about 25 years. The witness stated that in welding the galvanized coating of pipe, which is zinc and lead, metallic fumes are diffused, which is known in the welding fraternity as "galvo". He said copper pipe was used mostly in submarines and galvanized pipe in cruisers. William M. 

Grandahl, foreman of the pipe and copper shop, testified there was galvanized pipe used in the tanks of submarines and some welding done. He also identified the fumes given off as "galvo". Grandahl testified: "Q. Was any silver used? "A. Silver solder, yes. "Q. Where was that used? "A. All over the shop-different places in compartments. "Q. Was it used right on the tanks of submarines? "A. Yes, on the tanks of submarines. "Q. Do you know the reaction of silver when it is heated on these electric welding machines? Yes or No. "A. Yes. "Q. And what is the reaction? "A. Well, the reaction we had on some of it was due from the flux-of breaking out on your body as a rash. "Q. Do fumes come off?

"A. Fumes come off the flux used to silver-solder."

This witness also testified from daily time sheets for Steiner that decedent worked on submarines, tugs and cruisers. Dr. Harold Lipshutz, a urologist, testified that decedent was hospitalized from April 30, 1943, until May 26, 1943. The doctor's diagnosis was an acute breakdown of both kidneys "due to the exposure to the chemical fumes in his occupation". The doctor testified: "It is my honest opinion in this case without any bias, not having known this man before in my life, but only as a major consultant in the Jewish Hospital, that this man died through acute pathology of his kidneys caused by exposure to chemical fumes."

Philip Sadtler, a consulting chemist, specializing in industrial chemistry, testified at some length in regard to welding and brazing operations. He explained that brazing is a form of welding where brass is used as the welding metal and is frequently done as a preliminary to common steel welding. He said the flux used generally is silver solder, which melts in a very low temperature and is used to remove oxides of metal and dirt which are present at most joints when they are brazed or welded. The chemist testified that to the best of his knowledge all silver solder fluxes contain fluoride and that fluoride fumes are considered the most toxic in industrial fumes or gases, harmful to all forms of animal and vegetable life. Sadtler stated that fluorine poisoning is productive of vomiting, nausea and related symptoms and can easily prove fatal. Under cross-examination, the chemist testified: "Q. So that in order to arrive at your conclusion that fluorine gas was disseminated by the operations, you would have to know what the type of flux was that was used? "A. I have known from experience beginning in college that you have to have a fluoride to get a low melting point and the flux is not satisfactory and will not clean unless it is molten, and the best way and the most common way is to use a fluoride; and I have not heard of a flux of this type without a fluoride.

1948] 

"Q. I see. Would that be the only gas given off? "A. No. It would be the most harmful gas given off." 

He stated that fluorine quantities less than half a part per million have been known to cause damage to humans and to animals.

After a careful review and study of the entire record, we are fully convinced that Steiner's death was due to the inhalation of the brazing and/or welding fumes, to which he had been exposed during the period of his employment by defendant. Is the death compensable? Claimant tacitly admits that the claim does not come within the purview of the Occupational Disease Act, by amending the claim petition to bring it within the Workmen's Compensation 

Act. Section 108 of the Occupational Disease Act lists the occupational diseases for which compensation may be claimed. The instant claim does not fall within any of the enumerated diseases. The only reference to fumes, gases or vapor is paragraph (i) as follows: "Infection or inflammation of the skin due to oils, cutting compounds, lubricants, dust, liquids, fumes, gases, or vapor, in any occupation involving direct contact with, handling thereof, or exposure thereto." (Italics supplied.) 

Does decedent's exposure to the fluorine fumes constitute an accident within the meaning and intendment of the 

Workmen's Compensation Act? Defendant cites,a long line of cases of our appellate courts defining an accident: 

Gausman v. Pearson Co., 284 Pa. 348; Lacy v. Washburn & 

Williams Co., 309 Pa. 574. The law is well established that an accident means a happening by chance or unexpectedly, casual or fortuitous occurrence aside from the usual course of events: Gausman v. Pearson Co., supra. In the frequently cited case of Lacy v. Washburn & Williams Co., supra, the court said (p. 577): "The word accident-as used in the act-must be interpreted in its usual, ordinary, popular sense. Webster has defined it as 'an event that takes place without one's foresight or expectation; an undesigned, sudden, and unexpected event; chance; contingency'. Many courts have

quoted this definition and some have added to or embellished it, but in reality few have improved upon it. It would answer no good purpose to call attention to the many immaterial variations and additions. Our decisions interpreting the word as used in our compensation law have substantially clung to this meaning." 

It is claimant's contention that the inhalation of the poisonous fumes by her decedent constituted a compensable accident, citing Sinkiewicz v. Susquehanna Colliery Co., 115

Pa. Superior Ct. 377. The facts in that case are not at all analagous to the situation here. In that case decedent, on a particular occasion, March 17, 1932, was engaged, with others, in firing charges of dynamite. Decedent, who had previously been in good health, returned to the site of the shots and was immediately taken ill. He died early the next morning. The court said (p. 380): "While the mere fact that the decedent was taken ill while on the premises of the defendant is not sufficient to support an award of compensation (citing cases), the decedent before the accident was in good health and as soon as he inhaled the air where the dynamite had been discharged was taken ill and died in less than twenty-four hours."

In the present appeal, claimant's decedent was subject to the harmful conditions during the entire period of three months employment by defendant. The effects were readily apparent, as claimant testified, in Steiner's tiredness, noticeable loss of weight and nausea. It was necessary for decedent, on several occasions, to visit defendant's dispensary for relief. How can any date be designated for the necessary accidental occurrence, or any element be set up as the lighted match which initiated the death? The cumulated exposure to the fluoride fumes, inadequate ventilation and the time element conspired to effect a final and fatal breakdown on April 17, 1943, which culminated in the death on May 26, 1943. There is not an iota of evidence that anything of an unforseen or fortuitous nature occurred on that day which could be deemed accidental. There is

1948] 

 no hint or implication that upon decedent's last day of employment, the working conditions were any different than during the entire period of his employment. It appears to us that the death is attributable to the continued unfavorable conditions existing during his three months' employment and not to any single occurrence or act: Micale v. 

Light et al., 150 Pa. Superior Ct. 399. In the case of 

McCauley v. Imperial Woolen Co., 261 Pa. 312, 328, the 

Supreme Court said: "When, however, death results from germ infection, to bring a case of this character within the Act of 1915, supra, the disease in question must be a sudden development from some such abrupt violence to the physical structure of the body as already indicated, and not the mere result of gradual development from long continued exposure to natural dangers incident to the employment of the deceased person, as in cases of occupational diseases, the risks of which are voluntarily assumed." 

The case was ably tried and it is unfortunate that, under the law, claimant must be denied compensation for the death of her husband, which we found was due entirely to his employment. However, we have no alternative, under the limitations of the Workmen's Compensation Act, as interpreted by our appellate courts.

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's fourth finding of fact and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following: 

Finding of fact 4. Claimant's decedent became totally disabled on April 

17, 1943, and died on May 26, 1943, due to inhalation of welding and brazing fumes, which inhalation did not constitute an accident.

The referee's other findings of fact are affirmed. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the second and third paragraphs of the referee's conclusions of law and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following:

Conclusion of law 

Since claimant's decedent did not sustain death by accident, claimant and her dependent children are not entitled to compensation.

The first paragraph of the referee's conclusions of law is affirmed.

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's award and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following:

Order 

Claim petition no. 97,298 is hereby dismissed.

The appeal of defendant is sustained. 

COURT OF COMMON PLEAS NO. 3 OF PHILADELPHIA COUNTY FEENEY v. NEEDHAM'S MOTOR SERVICE, INC., ET AL. 

Workmen's compensation—Award—Interest. 

Under section 410 of the Workmen's Compensation Act, as amended by the Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 520, providing that the amount of compensation due claimant at the time the first payment is made after an award shall bear interest from the date such claim is presented, an award for the loss of use of a leg made following claimant's petition for modification of an agreement based on partial disability will bear interest from the date the petition for modification was presented rather than from an earlier date to which defendant was credited by the board's award on account of prior payments of compensation.

In the Court of Common Pleas No. 3 of Philadelphia 

County, No. 54, September term, 1947. Appeal from opinion of Workmen's Compensation Board. Appeal sustained. Jan uary 19, 1948. 

Lester J. Schaffer, for claimant. 

George H. Detweiler, for defendant.

1948] 

 PER CURIAM: 

On July 16, 1940, claimant was injured while in the course of his employment as a truck driver for defendant. He suffered, inter alia, a fracture of the left hip. On July 30, 1940, he entered into an open agreement with the insurance carrier for defendant for payment of compensation on a total disability basis which provided for payment of compensation at the rate of $18 a week. This was based on an average weekly wage of $37.27. The compensation was paid under this agreement for 67 weeks or $1,260.¹ On January 

21, 1942, defendant filed a petition for modification of the compensation agreement with the Workmen's Compensation 

Board averring that claimant's disability had now changed to the extent that he is able to fill a steady position and "... has been working steadily as a clerk . . ." Claimant answered the complaint claiming that his position "is not steady". A hearing was had before a referee who found that claimant is "now working and has been working since October 17, 1941, earning $30 a week, thus suffering a loss in earning power of $7.27 per week". The referee concluded that "claimant's disability has been changed, and defendant's petition for modification should be granted." On April 

14, 1942, an award was made for the payment of 662% percent of $7.27, the loss in earning power, or $4.85 per week, "to continue until such time as claimant's disability shall cease or change in extent within the meaning of the provi sions of the Workmen's Compensation Act." On May 11, 

1942, the parties entered into a formal agreement that the disability of claimant changed on October 17, 1941, as follows: "On that date employee returned to work and has continued there at earning $30.00 per week; . . . that on and after October 17, 1941, compensation shall be payable to the said employee at the rate of $4.85 per week, for 

235-5/7 weeks . . ." It was further agreed "that employee 

1 In addition he was paid for hospital and other medical expenses and for special appliances from time to time. The total of these additional payments ultimately amounted to $2,488.35.

made a settlement with the third party responsible for his injury, $1100 of said settlement to be credited to Needham's Motor Service, Inc. on account of compensation and medical expense that employee may be entitled to subsequent to 10/17/41." At the hearing on the petition for modification hereinafter mentioned (December 6, 1946) counsel for claimant stated that "the $1,100 at the rate of $4.85 a week would have been used up at May 2, 1946." It is thus apparent that claimant was really paid in advance for the compensation currently due, and from October 17, 1941, was employed at $30 a week.

On January 22, 1947, the referee awarded compensation at the rate of $18 per week from July 24, 1940, until September 6, 1944, a period of 215 weeks, and, after crediting appellee for payments of $1,306 made under the above agreements, and $1,100 received by claimant in the third-party settlement, or a total of $2,306, there remained due claimant the sum of $1,564, or $18 per week from January 3, 1943, to September 6, 1944, a period of 86-6/7 weeks. The Workmen's Compensation Board awarded accrued interest of $80.13 on $18 per week from January 3, 1943, to September 6, 1944, and also awarded simple interest of $231.94 on the sum of $1,564 from September 6, 1944, to February 

14, 1947, the date of payment of the principal.

The present appeal is from the award by the Workmen's 

Compensation Board of these two interest items. Paragraph 

2 of section 410 of the Workmen's Compensation Act, as amended by the Act of June 21, 1939, P. L.

520, reads as follows: 

"Whenever any claim for compensation is presented to the Board, and is finally adjudicated in favor of the claimant, the amounts of compensation actually due at the time the first payment is made after such adjudication shall bear interest at the rate of six per cent per annum from the date such claim is presented, and such interest shall be payable to the same person as the compensation is payable." 

Does the interest begin to run from January 3, 1943, the date to which payments were made or credited under the

1948] 

 last adjudication of the board as set forth above, or does it begin April 4, 1946, the date when claimant filed his petition for modification of the previous agreement? We believe the assessment of interest on an award of compensation is intended to be a penalty on a defendant for failure to make prompt payment and to compensate claimant for loss of the use of the money during the period of the delay in the payment thereof caused by defendant. There appears to be nothing in this case to indicate that defendant purposely delayed any payment, and it was only upon petition of claimant on April 4, 1946, that defendant had knowledge that it would be called upon to pay for a permanent injury. In fact, claimant, at the hearing on December 6, 1946, before the referee, where the testimony was introduced showing he had lost the industrial use of his left leg, testified that he was still working as a clerk and earning $40.90 a week. No act of defendant delayed claimant in the presentation of his claim for total disability as to the use of his leg. Defendant should not be penalized merely because the Workmen's Compensation Board in its judgment awarded compensation for a period preceding the date of petition for modification. 

The Workmen's Compensation Act as amended, supra, specifically provides that interest shall be calculated from the date such claim is presented. It is our judgment that the spirit and letter of the Workmen's Compensation Act is met when interest is calculated only from the date the claim is presented, irrespective of what form the petition embodying the claim takes. In this case, the claim for the total loss of use of claimant's leg was presented as a petition for modification of an agreement based on partial disability. Consequently, the interest should be calculated from the date petition or claim for modification was presented, i. e., on 

April 4, 1946 (which was when claimant presented his claim for a change from partial to total disability with respect to the industrial use of his leg) and not from January 3, 1943, when claimant, defendant and the board were agreed that his claim was only for partial disability as to which compensation had been paid.

[84 Dep. Rep. 

In an analogous case, Angelo v. Keystone State Construction Co., 134 Pa. Superior Ct. 255, 263, the court said: "Our general conclusion is that judgment should have been entered upon the award but not for the full amount thereof as calculated by the Board-principal $663.40, plus accrued interest to June 1, 1926, $23.35, and plus interest to the date of award, $456, or a total of $1142.75. "As above indicated, claimant permitted his case to lie dormant for five years and, in our opinion, is not justly entitled to the above mentioned second item of interest. "A judgment, as of September 15, 1937-the date of the

Board's calculation-for the first two items thereof, aggregating $686.75, will give the claimant the compensation to which he is entitled under the letter and spirit of the statute."

We, therefore, sustain defendant's appeal and modify the award of the compensation in the following 

And now, to wit, January 19, 1948, the exceptions of defendants are sustained. Appeal taken in this matter is sustained and the award of the Workmen's Compensation 

Board is herein modified. 

Judgment is entered for William Feeney against Needham's Motor Service, Inc., defendant, and Jamestown

Mutual Insurance Company, insurance carrier, for accrued compensation amounting to $1,564, with interest on the above sum from April 4, 1946, until the date of payment. 

Judgment is further entered for William Feeney against 

Needham's Motor Service, Inc., for one half the costs of these proceedings.

1948] 

 WORKMAN'S COMPENSATION BOARD KWIECIEN, ETC., v. JOHNSTOWN COAL & COKE CO.
