Workmen's compensation-Death-Miner-Violation of law-Use of improper support in mine-Act of June 9, 1911, P. L. 821-Nonresident alien dependent-Interest on award. 

1. A referee's order disallowing compensation on the ground that plaintiff's decedent, who was fatally injured when struck by falling coal which he was mining, had violated article 25, special rule I, of the Act of June 9, 1911, P. L. 821, requiring a miner to set sprags under the coal while undermining will be reversed and an award entered where it appeared that the type of sprag used by decedent was insufficient but where it further appeared that defendant had permitted improper sprags to be at decedent's place of work and where there was further no evidence that he had been instructed, as the act required, by his mine foreman, how to place the sprags. 

2. Under section 5 of the Act of April 13, 1927, P. L. 186, interest may not be allowed upon an award to a nonresident alien dependent. 

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee 

Schwing, District No. 7, claim petition no. 72,641. Appeal sustained. March 10, 1948. 

R. J. Lucksha, for claimant. 

Francis A. Dunn, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This is a death case which dates back to 1936. There is little or no dispute as to the facts. On December 1, 1936, Andy Janik, a miner employed by Johnstown Coal & Coke Co., defendant, was fatally injured during the course of his employment with defendant when he was struck by falling coal which he was undermining. He was survived by his widow, Marianna Janik, the real claimant here, who lived in Poland; a claim petition was filed on her behalf by the 

Consul General of Poland at Pittsburgh, Pa.

[84 Dep. Rep. 

The proceedings have been long delayed due to the fact that letters rogatory were issued and answers to the same were delayed by reason of World War II.

The referee found that claimant widow was dependent upon her husband, Andy Janik, at the time of his death, but compensation was disallowed on the ground that decedent had violated the Bituminous Mining Laws of this Commonwealth, to wit, the Act of June 9, 1911, P. L. 821. Article 

25, special rule I of that act provides inter alia: ". . . It shall be the duty of the miner to mine his coal properly before blasting, and to set sprags under the coal while undermining, to secure it from falling. . . ." Article 4, sec. 9, relating to the duties of a mine foreman, provides, inter alia: "He (the foreman) shall also direct that the miner set sprags as often as necessary, at a distance not exceeding seven feet apart under the breast of undermined or center mined coal, for safety. . . ."

The evidence discloses that decedent was undermining coal in a "room" somewhat over 22 feet wide, that he had undercut about 15 feet of coal. Decedent had placed only one sprag and this was not the type which should have been used. The usual sprag, it appears, is about three and one half feet long. The sprag is placed into the undercut as far as it can go, and it is supported by a post, usually a four by four, about 10 feet long. Although the proper sprags were nearby, decedent had used for a sprag a small round tie about three inches thick. After the accident, this was found broken in pieces, due to the fall of coal. There was also some testimony to the effect that defendant company knew that improper sprags were being used in the mine, that following the accident, defendant was ordered to use bigger sprags by the State Mine Inspector. 

If decedent violated article 25, special rule 1, of the mine law, the violation was purely technical. The rule merely requires the miner to set sprags. The sprags are furnished by the company. If defendant allowed improper sprags to be at claimant's place of work, it cannot now reject responsibility arising from usage of the same. Apparently the use

1948] 

 of that kind of sprag was not unusual in defendant's mine prior to the accident. Moreover in using the wrong type sprag, Janik was not doing an act wholly foreign to his employment or of such a nature as to take him out of the course of his employment. See Bucci v. Lincoln Coal Co., 140 Pa. Superior Ct. 538.

The other section of the act quoted above sets forth a duty upon the mine foreman to instruct the miner as to the placing of sprags. There is no testimony as to Janik having been ordered or instructed how or where to place sprags. But had Janik been instructed to place them seven feet apart, he was hardly beyond the point where the second sprag would have been placed. There is also some testimony here that the accident may have been due to a slip of coal, although it was never so proved, and not due to decedent's particular undercutting of the coal.

We do not believe that compensation must be denied here under the law and we conclude that an award is proper to Janik's alien widow, claimant here, according to the Act of 

June 2, 1915, P. L. 736, 77 PS §563. As claimant is a nonresident alien dependent, no interest upon this award is allowable, according to the Act of April 13, 1927, P. L. 186, sec. 5.

We vacate the referee's eighth finding of fact, second conclusion of law and order of disallowance, substituting the following and affirming the balance of the referee's findings of facts, and conclusions of law: 

Findings of fact 8. The board finds as a fact that it was not unusual to use in defendant's mine the type of sprag which decedent used. 

 2. The board concludes as a matter of law that claimant is entitled to compensation as her decedent was in the course of his employment when injured.

[84 Dep. Rep. 

Order 

The Workmen's Compensation Board hereby directs 

Johnstown Coal & Coke Co., defendant, to pay to Roman 

Kwiecen or his successor, Consul of Poland, attorney in fact for Marianna Janik, the sum of $5.07 per week beginning 

December 10, 1936, for a period of 300 hundred weeks, without interest on deferred payments, in accordance with the 

Workmen's Compensation Act. 

Defendant is also directed to pay to Harold F. Buck, the sum of $150 for funeral expenses.

Defendant is directed to pay to the Memorial Hospital at Johnstown, Pa., the sum of $96.65 for hospital treatment rendered to Andy Janik. 

Claimant's appeal is sustained.

COMMON PLEAS NO. 1 OF PHILADELPHIA COUNTY SCHWARTZ v. PHILADELPHIA DRESSED BEEF COMPANY ET AL. 

Workmen's compensation-Accidental injury-Collapse in performance of duties-Burden of proof. 

Evidence that claimant, employed by defendant meat dealer to operate a refrigerator, went into the room where the temperature was approximately 32 degrees to rearrange the meat and came out about 25 minutes later in a state of collapse, that he was taken to a hospital where it was found that he had suffered a thrombosis as a consequence of which he was paralyzed and unable to speak, was insufficient to support a finding of an accidental injury where it appeared that he had suffered for a number of years from hardening of the arteries and high blood pressure, there being no evidence that anything had taken place in the cooler, except that some crates of meat weighing possibly between 900 and 1,200 lbs. had been moved.

Appeal from Workmen's Compensation Board. Appeal sustained. February 11, 1948. C. P. No. 1 of Philadelphia 

County, June term, 1947, no. 2591.

1948] 

W. Kendall, for claimant. 

G. R. Gitman, for defendant, Philadelphia Dressed Beef Co. 

S. H. Torchia and R. H. Behney, for defendant, State

Workmen's Insurance Fund. 

PER CURIAM: 

This is an appeal from the Workmen's Compensation 

Board.

The referee found as a fact that claimant was overcome by exposure to cold while employed in defendant's cooler; that such exposure accelerated the cardio vascular disease from which he suffered and this constituted an accident occurring in the course of his employment. The award was affirmed by the Workmen's Compensation Board, which added that claimant had collapsed due to an unusual strain. 

From these findings and conclusions we have this appeal. 

Claimant was employed by a meat dealer to operate a cooler or refrigerator, a room in which the temperature was kept at about 32 degrees. In the ordinary exercise of his duties he was required to take meat to the cooler, arrange it there, and fetch it out as it was needed. In this task he was sometimes assisted by others. On the date in question it was necessary for him to rearrange the meat in order to make room for an expected consignment of poultry. He was seen to go into the room and after about 25 minutes, come out in a state of collapse. He was taken to a hospital where it was found he had suffered a thrombosis, in consequence of which he was paralyzed and unable to speak. Nothing is known of what took place in the cooler but a fellow employe observed that some crates containing hams had been moved from the position they formerly occupied and he estimated the total of the different joints of meat moved to be between 

900 and 1,200 pounds.

There is no evidence that claimant moved any unusual or excessive weight or that the objects he may have moved were any different or any heavier than he customarily handled every day. There is no evidence that the temperature was other than that he encountered daily when at his work and in any case, 32 degrees can hardly be considered extreme cold.

It is conceded that claimant had suffered for a number of years from hardening of the arteries, and had very high blood pressure. The medical witnesses for both sides agree that he might have had a stroke at any time whether he was in a state of activity or quiescence. 

A doctor, whose testimony was relied on by the referee and the board, was of the opinion that moving a number of weighty objects in a low temperature for such a length of time, all tended to show that claimant's injury happened as the result of an unusual combination of circumstances and that the extra exertion under such circumstances was a contributing cause to the hemiplegia. Dr. LaPlace was called in by the referee and while unfortunately his testimony does not appear in the record, the referee has found that he was of the same opinion. Medical evidence to the contrary we need not consider, as it was the province of the referee to determine which he would accept. 

The finding of accidental injury is based apparently upon the theory that evidence that a man with hardened arteries, who is doing unusual and strenuous work that requires him to exert himself to an uncommon degree causing a break in a diseased artery, will support a finding of an accident occurring in the course of his employment. This is undoubtedly the law of Pennsylvania (Murphy v. Philadelphia & 

Reading Coal & Iron Co., 98 Pa. Superior Ct. 108), but we find nothing in the record that will permit its application. It seems to us that the case is ruled by Palinski v. State Workmen's Insurance Fund, 140 Pa. Superior Ct. 522 and the decisions there cited. The burden was on claimant to prove that his disability resulted from an accident or at least that

1948] 

 the accident was a contributing cause; but the fact that he was stricken in the course of his employment raised no presumption of the existence of an accident. The opinions of the medical witnesses, which the fact-finding tribunals accepted, appear to us to be based merely on the assumption that there was an accident and so are insufficient to sustain an award.

Exceptions to the findings and conclusions of the Workmen's Compensation Board are sustained and judgment is entered for defendant. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD KOZAK, GUARDIAN, v. LEHIGH VALLEY COAL CO. 

Workmen's compensation-Occupational disease-Period of employment prior to acceptance of act by employer. 

A referee's award of compensation to claimant for disability resulting from anthraco-silicosis acquired during his employment with defendant from 1935 to 1943 will be set aside and the claim disallowed where it appears that defendant had rejected the Occupational Disease Compensation Act prior to May 31, 1946; the fact that claimant became totally disabled subsequent to May 31, 1946, on and after which date defendant accepted the act, did not make the claim compensable as the whole of claimant's employment occurred prior to claimant's acceptance of the act. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Patterson, District No. 6, claim petition no. 106,387. Appeal sustained. 

January 28, 1948. 

F. B. Wickersham and H. F. Dowling, for claimant. 

J. C. Valentine, for defendant.

[84 Dep. Rep. 

MURPHY, Chairman: 

On October 2, 1946, claimant filed a petition for compensation in which he alleged that he became totally disabled on November 10, 1945, the result of anthraco-silicosis acquired during his employment with defendant from 1935 to 1943 and with the Bethlehem Steel Company from 1943 to 1945. 

Defendant employer filed an answer denying liability on the ground that it had rejected the Occupational Disease Act until May 31, 1946. On January 27, 1947, claimant by his guardian filed an amended petition alleging total disability on August 10, 1946, and his confinement at the Harrisburg 

State Hospital from November 17, 1945, to May 11, 1946, and readmitted on July 28, 1946. Defendants again denied liability. The referee, although he found as a fact that defendant had rejected the act prior to May 31, 1946, and that claimant had last been exposed to the silica hazard on April 3, 1943, concluded as a matter of law that defendant was bound by the provisions of the act and made an award against the Lehigh Valley Coal Co., defendant and the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. Appeals by defendants followed. Claimant has also taken an appeal from the award because the referee had only awarded the total sum of $3,600 stated in the Act of 1939 rather than the sum of $4,000 provided for in the Act of 1945 which applied to this claim.

We have carefully reviewed the entire record and although we agree with the referee's findings of fact, the conclusions of law and the award must be set aside. The referee found as a fact, based on competent and substantive evidence, that the Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act was rejected by the Lehigh Valley Coal Company, defendant, prior to May 31, 1946, and was first accepted by defendant on and after May 31, 1946. The last day of claimant's employment by defendant was April 3, 1943. Claimant had no employment with defendant while claimant and defendant were bound by the provisions of article III of the Occupational Disease Act and his employment only prior to the acceptance of the act does not justify the award.

1948] 

If there had been no rejection we believe that claimant would have been entitled to receive compensation for total disability because he had at least four years' employment during a period of eight years next preceding his disability, in an occupation having a silica hazard and defendant was the last employer in whose employment the deceased was exposed to the hazard.

Accordingly, we affirm the referee's findings of fact but we vacate the conclusion of law and the award. We make the following

1.

Claimant and defendant were not bound by the pro visions of article III of the Occupational Disease Act of 

1939, as amended. 

2. That since claimant was employed by defendant solely during the period of rejection of the Occupational Disease Act and became disabled after defendant's acceptance, claimant is not entitled to receive compensation. 

We make the following

Order The claim petition is dismissed and compensation is disallowed. 

Defendant employer's appeal is sustained.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD WALLACH v. KARL Workmen's compensation—Accidental injury-Pain in back following lifting in the performance of usual duties. 

A referee's order disallowing compensation will be affirmed where it appears that claimant employed by defendant in a furniture store to perform warehouse duties felt a sharp pain in his back following which a doctor made a diagnosis of a pulling of the muscular attachments on the sides of the spine; since claimant was performing his

usual work in the usual manner without any evidence of his slipping, stumbling or falling, there was no evidence that he sustained an accidental injury.

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee 

Alessandroni, District No. 1, claim petition no. 108,766. 

Appeal dismissed. January 14, 1948. 

Penna. T. F. Mutual Casualty Ins. Co., insurance carrier. 

Philip J. Franzese, for claimant. 

Robert C. Duffy and J. G. Feinour, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This case comes before the Workmen's Compensation Board upon an appeal by Martin Wallach, claimant, from an order of disallowance of compensation. Defendant is 

Samuel Karl (Karl's).

The facts are not in great dispute. Claimant was employed by defendant in his juvenile furniture store to wait on trade and perform warehouse duties. On April 15, 1946, a delivery of furniture arrived; claimant lifted a coach and felt a sharp pain in his back around the sacroiliac region. 

Claimant was taken to a hospital where his back was strapped. He continued to work, but testified that he did very little. On August 26, claimant avers, he was moving a set of furniture when he felt a sharp pain in his back. On 

September 6, 1946, claimant visited Dr. John G. Striegel who received a history of claimant having received a pain in his back while moving heavy furniture. The doctor made a diagnosis of a pulling of the muscular attachments on the sides of the spine. The doctor gave claimant diathermy treatment, and when he last examined claimant October 26, 1946, he felt claimant's condition had improved; on that date there were no objective symptoms of disability.

1948] 

The sole question necessary for our determination here is whether claimant sustained an accidental injury within the meaning of the Workmen's Compensation Act on April 

The evidence discloses that claimant was performing his usual work in the usual manner when he felt a pain in his back. Claimant did not slip, stumble or fall. There was no strain, sprain, or twist. It does not appear that any unusual occurrence took place. We are bound to conclude, as did the referee, that claimant failed to sustain an accidental injury within the meaning of the Workmen's Compensation 

Act.

An accident cannot be inferred merely from an injury; there must be other evidence, direct or circumstantial: 

Baston v. Stoher & Fister, 151 Pa. Superior Ct. 618; Moyer v. Union Boiler Mfg. Co., 151 Pa. Superior Ct. 477; Hoon v. State Workmen's Insurance Fund, 149 Pa. Superior Ct. 

236; Powell v. Hills Garage, 150 Pa. Superior Ct. 17.

We affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order. 

SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA BOGAVICH, DECD., ETC., v. WESTINGHOUSE ELECTRIC AND MANUFACTURING COMPANY Workmen's compensation-Death from explosion-Violation of law- 

Decedent's possession of explosives-Findings by board.

Findings by the compensation board in reversing a referee's award that claimant's husband died during working hours on the premises of his employer as a result of an explosion of a device carried on his person and that decedent by his possession thereof violated the Act of July 1, 1937, P. L. 2681, as amended, as well as the Federal Explosive Act of December 26, 1941, as a consequence of which compensa-

tion was barred, will be affirmed where the findings of the board were supported by sufficient legally competent evidence; in such case the lower court was without power to reverse the order of the board and to reinstate the referee's award. 

Appeal from order and judgment of County Court of 

Allegheny County at no. A-359 of 1946. Appeal sustained. 

March 8, 1948. Superior Court of Pennsylvania, April term, March 8, 1948, no. 3. 

Gilbert E. Morcroft and James H. Brennan, for appellee. 

James J. Lawler, Leo Daniels, for appellant.

HIRT, J.: 

Claimant's husband came to his death during working hours at his accustomed working place on the premises of defendant employer. He died from the effects of an explosion, under most unusual circumstances. Based on a finding of an explosion, "the cause of which is unknown", the referee concluded that claimant was entitled to compensation and made an award accordingly. The board set aside the finding and substituted the following: "The explosion which caused the death of claimant's decedent was caused by a device of his own making carried upon his person". The board's "appraisal of the factual situation [was] that claimant's decedent constructed an explosive device out of materials he illegally possessed in his own home; that he carried to work on his person illegally on January 6, 1945 . . ." and that his death resulted from an explosion of the device. The board dismissed claimant's petition for compensation on the ground that the death of claimant's husband from accident was not compensable because it was the direct result of his violation of law, in carrying explosives on his person. On appeal the lower court reversed the order of the board and reinstated the award of the referee. The judgment entered thereon must be reversed.

1948] 

Rudolph Bogavich left his home, according to daily custom, at 7 a.m. on the morning of January 6, 1945, and reported for work in section D-1 of defendant's plant in East Pittsburgh at the usual time. The hours of his shift were from 7:30 to 3:30 p.m. Within the building there was a railroad track on which cars were placed for loading shipments of defendant's products. Decedent was in charge of flat car loading. On the morning of decedent's death a flat car and a gondola, coupled together, were on the track inside the building. A large condenser had been loaded on the flat car and wooden housing had been built over it by workmen during the preceding night shift. At 8 a.m. claimant was on the flat car and by means of a mechanical stapling machine was covering the condenser with waterproof paper, preparing it for shipment. Shortly thereafter claimant ran out of staples. He got down from the flat car and walked along the passageway, 52 feet wide between the factory wall and the tracks, in the direction of a cupboard to get more staples. 

He had gone only a short distance, about to the middle of the gondola, when a loud explosion was heard and dense blue smoke was seen to rise from underneath the freight car. Nearby workmen immediately went to the scene of the explosion. Bogavich was found face down on his right side upon the floor. He was dead. The left side of his body between the hip and the shoulder was entirely blown out; the body was eviscerated and the liver, kidney, heart and other organs were disrupted and torn. According to the coroner's physician the damage to his internal organs was so great that there was little left to examine. The left hand was torn off and was found separate from the body; the left forearm was not found intact. There was tearing of the left hand and some laceration of the right hand. Pieces of flesh, bones and clothing were found near the body and on the nearby factory wall as high as 40 feet above the floor. No damage was done to the building nor to the gondola car nor to any of defendant's machinery or equipment.

In decedent's home were found a coil of black powder safety fuse; one electric detonator; two railroad torpedoes; two Eveready flashlight batteries dated for "use before 

Jan. 1944"; a quantity of heavy copper and iron wire and a box containing six detonating caps. In or near decedent's torn side, as he lay on the shop floor, were found two pieces of wire; pieces of a battery case and of a zinc battery shell and small pieces of an Eveready flashlight battery. Of more significance were pieces of blue and red paper, part of the flashlight battery wrapping containing the notation "Eveready flashlight, use before Jan. 1944".

Decedent was familiar with explosives and had the material in his home from which a small bomb could be constructed. The county detective testified that a railroad torpedo could be exploded by contact of a battery with a detonator cap and that it is a reasonable inference from the physical facts that death resulted from such device exploded in that manner. It is of no real significance that the detective was unable to set off a torpedo with an electric detonator cap found in decedent's home for the reason that the cap was defective. There was nothing defective in the detonating material which did cause the fatal explosion. 

What decedent intended to do with the device admits of no satisfactory answer. His home life apparently was happy; he had no financial or other serious problems and it is agreed that the question of suicide is not in the case. He had been in the employ of the defendant for 25 years and was highly regarded as a capable, trustworthy and loyal employe. Sabotage is not suspected and in fact this small bomb could not have done serious damage to any machinery or manufactured products in defendant's plant. Every fact and circumstance raises the reasonable inference that the electric contact which set off the explosive was accidentally made. But the absence of an apparent motive does not impeach the finding of the board that claimant carried the device on his person.

The compensation board, in common with juries and other fact finding agencies, may make findings from direct

1948] 

 proof, from circumstantial evidence or by inference from other facts within the limitation that the inferences from the facts and circumstances and conditions directly proved, must be reasonable: Yowkoski v. Hudson Coal Co., 159 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 256, 48 A. (2d) 80. From the nature of decedent's torn body, the testimony will support no other conclusion than that Bogavich came to his death as the result of the explosion of a device carried on the left side of his person under his clothing. A piece of his clothing, completely cut out in the shape of the wound, was found some distance away from the body, clearly indicating that the explosion occurred on decedent's person and under his clothing. All of the circumstances support the finding of the board as to the cause of death.

Explosives were not used in defendant's plant and nothing relating to claimant's employment justified his possession of the device. The board found that decedent by his possession of explosives violated the Act of July 1, 1937, P. L. 2681, as amended by the Act of April 27, 1939, P. L. 34, 73 PS 

§151, as well as the Federal Explosive Act of December 26, 

1941, 50 U.S.C. §121, et seq. Violation of law amounts to an abandonment of employment (Shoffler v. Lehigh Valley 

Coal Co., 290 Pa. 480, 139 A. 192) and is a complete bar to compensation for resulting injury: Section 301 of article III of the Workmen's Compensation Law, as amended June 

21, 1939, P. L. 520, 77 PS §431. Violation of law will result in forfeiting compensation if because of the violation the workman is injured.

The burden was on defendant employer to establish by a clear preponderance of the evidence that decedent's fatal injury resulted from his violation of law: P. Gima v. The 

Hudson Coal Co., 106 Pa. Superior Ct. 288, 161 A. 903; 

Yowkoski v. Hudson Coal Company, supra. That burden has been met in this case. In fact the evidence will admit of no other conclusion. All of the findings of the board are based upon sufficient legally competent evidence and the award of the referee could have been affirmed by the board

[84 Dep. Rep. 

only by a capricious disregard of the compelling probative force of undisputed facts. 

The findings of the board are consistent with each other and with its conclusions of law and its order. Cf. Schrock v. 

Stonycreek Coal Co., et al., 152 Pa. Superior Ct. 599, 33 A. (2d) 522; Walsh v. Penn Anth. Mining Co., 147 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 328, 24 A. (2d) 51. And since the findings are based upon sufficient legally competent evidence, the lower court was bound by the action of the board and was wholly without power to reverse the board and reinstate the award of the referee. The lower court in effect set aside the findings of the board and reinstated the findings of the referee on its appraisal of the weight of the evidence. In so doing in this case its action was extravagant beyond the bounds of its authority: Corrento v. Ventresca, 144 Pa. Superior Ct. 358, 19 A. (2d) 746; Osterritter v. Moore-Flesher Co., 150 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 236, 27 A. (2d) 262.

Since the lower court was bound by the findings of the board we must regard the judgment before us on this appeal as a nullity. The action of the lower court could not affect the validity of the order made by the board. In reversing the lower court therefore the record need not be remitted for further proceedings.

The judgment is reversed, in effect reinstating the order of the board.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD WALKER v. NU-CAR CARRIERS, INC. 

Workmen's compensation-Course of employment-Car driver-In juries while returning home after delivery of vehicle. 

A referee's award based on his finding that claimant's husband was injured fatally in the course of his employment by defendant will be affirmed where it appears that decedent was a driver employed by

1948] 

 defendant in transporting motor vehicles from and to various destinations, that at the time of the accident which resulted in his death, he was returning to his home by motorcycle carrying with him documents in connection with the delivery of a motor vehicle which he was required to return to his employer; it appearing that decedent had no regular hours of employment, that he was still on the errand to which he had been assigned by his employer, he was acting in the course of his employment at the time. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Patterson, District No. 6, claim petition no. 104,807. Appeal dismissed. 

February 11, 1948.

New Amsterdam Casualty Co., insurance carrier. 

Wm. W. Mentzinger, Jr., for claimant. 

Raymond A. White, Jr., for defendant.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

This is an appeal by defendant from an award of compensation made to the dependent widow and minor children of James Kenneth Walker, deceased.

Defendant is a corporation engaged in the business of delivering motor vehicles from one location to another. During World War II defendant had entered into a contract with the United States Army wherein they agreed to transport or have delivered Army motor vehicles from and to various destinations. Defendant provided drivers or its equipment as required. The drivers were licensed by the 

State and also received permits from the Quartermaster 

Corps known as "GI".

Decedent entered defendant's employ on or about February 4, 1945, as a driver and had received the necessary licenses. Certain regulations were issued prohibiting speed in excess of 35 miles per hour and the carrying of cargo or hitchhikers. Defendant paid its drivers for their time on a mileage basis during the time they operated or trans-

ported Army vehicles. The drivers also received railroad or bus fare from Chambersburg, Pa., to the point where they would start transporting and from the destination back to Chambersburg, Pa. On March 29, 1945, decedent received instructions at Chambersburg to go to Richmond, Va., pick up a motor vehicle and drive it to Newport News, Va. He was paid the railroad fare from Chambersburg to Richmond and from Newport News back to Chambersburg. Defendant also entrusted decedent with delivery of documents or bills of lading which were to be acknowledged by the Army upon delivery of the equipment in good order and decedent as well as other drivers were specifically instructed to return these documents to Chambersburg. The pay of the driver was then computed and defendant would then forward the documents to its home office at Chester, Pa., where bills were issued to the United States Government. It was the practice of the drivers to return these documents in person, but occasionally other means for their return were used when the driver was not returning or failed to continue in his employment. Defendant was, however, interested in having these receipted documents returned as expeditiously as possible. 

Decedent proceeded on his assigned work and after arriving at Richmond, Va., was instructed to make the delivery to Newport News, Virginia, and then to return to Richmond, Va., and make another delivery to Carteret, N. J. While en route to Newport News, Va., he exceeded the speed limit of 

35 miles per hour and was given a "ticket" for driving 50 miles per hour. He completed the delivery, however, and returned to Richmond, Va., where he picked up a truck and drove it to Carteret, N. J., in accordance with defendant's instructions. On his return trip from Carteret, N. J., the decedent was riding a motorcycle owned by him which he had apparently taken with him from Chambersburg. An automobile collided with him on Lancaster Pike, Montgomery County, Pa., and he died as a result of the injuries sustained.

Defendant contested the claim of compensation and based its defense on the grounds that decedent had taken himself

1948] 

 out of the course of his employment, first, when he exceeded the speed limit of 35 miles per hour while en route to Newport News, Va., and, second, when he used a motorcycle for his return trip contrary to the alleged instructions given decedent when he started out on his trip. These violations, defendant contends, had severed the relationship of employer and employe so that decedent, when fatally injured, was not entitled to compensation.

We have carefully reviewed the entire record and are of the opinion that the referee has properly decided this claim. 

The following principles of law are here applicable:

Every violation of law or positive order of an employer does not ipso facto deprive the employe of compensation. 

An employe cannot be denied compensation unless the violation is the proximate cause of his injury: Kolonik v. Hudson 

Coal Co., 160 Pa. Superior Ct. 491. "A violation of positive orders is an affirmative defense and the burden of proof is upon the defendant": Kostello v. Kostello, 159 Pa. Superior Ct. 194, 196.

Assuming that decedent violated the speed limit of 35 miles per hour while en route from Richmond, Va., to Newport News, Va., his violation did not immediately sever the relationship of employer and employe. He continued in his work and it is equally clear that this violation was not the proximate cause of his injury and death. The question of fact then arises whether any instructions prohibiting the use of the motorcycle were given to decedent. If we believe that decedent was not permitted to use the motorcycle and was restricted as to his mode of travel, then the question of the alleged violation of instructions would arise. Claimant's evidence indicates that the drivers, including decedent, were permitted to use any means they desired in returning to Chambersburg, as long as they returned the documents with great dispatch. Defendant's witnesses testified that decedent was instructed not to use the motorcycle and that he was ordered to return by bus or train. This issue of fact was decided by the referee adversely to defendant and we see

no error in this decision since it was based on competent and credible evidence.

We are confronted by the question as to whether or not decedent was acting in the course of his employment while on his return trip to Chambersburg, Pa. We believe he was.

Decedent had no regular hours of employment and his duties did not cease when he had made a delivery of a motor vehicle. 

He was subject to call at any time when commissioned to go to another city for his employer. On completing the delivery at Carteret N. J., he still had to report the fact of the delivery and return the receipted documents to his employer. He was so engaged in delivering the documents required by his employer when injured. This activity at the time of the injury was not foreign to any concept of his employment. He was still on the errand to which he was assigned by his employer: Haddoch v. Edgewater Steel Co., 263 Pa. 120, and Bauman v. Ehmke Co., 126 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 108.

As we view the record we believe that when decedent was returning to Chambersburg, Pa., from Carteret, N. J. he was actually engaged in the performance of some as yet incompleted business of the employer. The return of the documents was connected with the employer's business because these documents were the basis on which the employer was paid by the United States Government. He was thus furthering the interests of his employer, although he may have also furthered his own interest in returning to 

Chambersburg, where he resided.

Decedent's employment had not terminated at the time of his fatal injury and we therefore affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and award.

1948] 

 WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD ANGOTT v. TRI-STATE ENGINEERING CO. 

Workmen's compensation—Hernia-Notice-Sufficiency-Act of May 

18, 1945. 

Under the Act of May 18, 1945, P. L. 671, providing that where a claim is made for hernia, claimant must notify the employer or representative of the employer within 48 hours after the occurrence of the accident, notice need not be given by the claimant himself but may be given by some other person at his request; however, the notice must be sufficient to inform defendant that claimant has suffered an accident by hernia, and where the only notice given within the statutory period was a telephone call by claimant's former wife to someone at defendant's office stating that her husband fell last night and hurt himself and was sick, the notice was insufficient to sustain an award. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Carmalt, District No. 8, claim petition no. 108,273. Appeal sustained. 

February 11, 1948. 

Employers Liability Assurance Corp., insurance carrier. 

Francis Patrono, for claimant. 

G. M. Berg, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

Referee Carmalt awarded compensation to claimant, Pete Angott, for an accidental hernia suffered by him on February 5, 1947, during the course of his employment. Defendant, Tri-State Engineering Co., has taken this appeal. 

From a careful review of the record, we are convinced that the hernia was traumatic in origin. The sole question to be considered is whether the required notice was given defendant within 48 hours after the occurrence as required by the 

Workmen's Compensation Act of May 18, 1945, P. L. 671. 

Claimant contends that notice was given the next day following the accident by his ex-wife, Leona Angott. Defendant admits that Mrs. Angott called, but claims she merely in-

formed its office representative that claimant was "sick". 

Claimant's former wife testified that she called defendant on February 5, 1947, at claimant's request. Her account of the conversation is as follows: 

"A. Well, I went up to Murphy's Five and Ten Cent Store and called up the Tri-State Engineering Company and when they came to the phone they said, 'Tri-State', and I said, ‘I am calling to report Pete Angott off work. He asked me to tell you he fell last night and hurt himself and he was sick and he can't come out to work until he got to feeling better.' "Q. Who were you talking to at the Tri-State? "A. I do not know, he told me when I went to telephone to go before Trump or Bill goes out, either one of them will answer the phone and when I talked to the party they said, 'Who did you say?' and I said 'Pete Angott' and he said, 'that is perfectly Okay' and before I got a chance to say any more he hung up on me and I don't know whether he was Trump or Bill or who he was. I called down at the Tri-State 

Engineering plant down on Jefferson Avenue." 

William F. Wells, defendant's witness, admitted that a lady called the office on February 5, 1945, that claimant would be off work. Wells testified: "Q. Can you tell us who called? "A. Well, I don't remember whether they said it was a lady and I couldn't say as to who they said it was at this time, but a lady called and said he was sick and wouldn't be out."

Paul O'Brien, an investigator employed by defendant's insurance carrier, Employers Liability Assurance Corp., testified that he obtained statements from claimant and his former wife. Claimant's statement, defendant's Exhibit 2, describes the accident and contains the statement "The next morning I told my wife to call up the office and tell the timekeeper that I will not be out to work as I am sick". Exhibit 

3, the wife's statement, states, inter alia, "I am calling to report Pete Angott sick". The investigator stated that he did not read the statements to the parties and he could not

1948] 

 recall whether they read the statements. Claimant signed the statement prepared by the investigator. 

In view of our conclusions that claimant sustained an accidental hernia, we would indeed be reluctant to reverse the referee's award except in the light of convincing testimony that claimant failed to comply with the statutory provision relative to notice. The Act of 1945 has omitted the postulates contained in the Act of 1939, P. L. 520. It is significant, however, that the requirement of notice within 48 hours in hernia claims has been retained. The act provides: "Where a claim is made for hernia, claimant must notify the employer, or a representative of the employer, within 48 hours after the occurrence of the accident." 

No particular form of notice is required, so long as the employer, or his proper representative, has information from which he knows, or should know, upon reasonable inquiry, that a hernia injury is claimed. In our opinion, it is immaterial whether notice is given by the claimant himself of the hernia or by some one at his request. So long as actual notice is communicated, the requirement of the act is satisfied. There may be instances where an employe suffers such a severe injury that his physical condition would prevent personal notice from him to his employer. Certainly, a deserving claimant ought not to be penalized on that account, so long as the employer is made aware of the accidental origin within the required time: Romesburg v. Gallatine 

Market, 114 Pa. Superior Ct. 388, 393. While we are reluctant to set aside the award in this case since we are convinced that claimant suffered a hernia by accident, we are constrained to accept defendant's contention that adequate notice was not given within the necessary 48 hours. Omitting for the moment, the negative and contradictory testimony relative to notice offered in behalf of defendant, we are of the opinion that claimant has failed, by the quality of the testimony submitted, to meet the statutory requirements and to discharge his necessary burden of proof: 

Condron v. Philadelphia & Reading Coal & Iron Co., 78 Pa.

[84 Dep. Rep. 

Superior Ct. 133. The legislature, in the past, has seen fit to set apart hernia claims from other accidents and to require a higher and more exacting measure of proof for allowing compensation. While the Act of 1945 has deleted the postulates for proof of a hernia, the notice of claim for a hernia must still be made within 48 hours after the occurrence of the accident. Claimant admits that he personally did not contact defendant's office until about one week after the accident. Claimant's whole case of notice may be summed up in the language of his former wife that she told some one at defendant's office on the telephone that Angott "fell last night and hurt himself and he was sick". We have carefully reviewed the cases cited by claimant's counsel in support of his contention that proper notice was given and find those cases are not analogous and, therefore, not controlling. 

The case of Uditsky v. Krakovitz, 133 Pa. Superior Ct. 186, involved a "paralysis of the left hand, arm and the left side of the body", and notice was given immediately to the foreman by claimant that “. ;". I feel sick, my head hurt me and my face and hand. I have no strength in my hand". The court said (p. 189): "That he (foreman) knew whatever injury claimant suffered had occurred in the course of his employment at the shop, some time during the five or ten minutes after claimant left the foreman to carry out his orders and before reporting back to him. Being fully aware that each case must necessarily depend upon the particular facts for its ultimate determination, we consider the extent of the foreman's 'actual knowledge' (the equivalent of notice under the act) together with the notice given him by claimant under the immediate circumstances. Adopting a rule of liberal construction as a guide in construing the provision requiring notice of the injury, we are agreed that claimant has substantially complied with the particular provision."

1948] 

Department Reports of Pennsylvaina 

The instant claimant admitted that he did not seek out his foreman and report the occurrence although the foreman was still on the premises. In the frequently cited case of Palermo v. North East Preserving Works, Inc., 141 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 211, the main question involved was whether the hernia was accidental in origin. Upon the question of notice, the opinion points out that claimant sustained the occurrence at 3 p. m. and complained of a pain in his right side to a fellow employe. Claimant's foreman testified that he came to him “around 3:30 and said he just felt he couldn't do anymore, that he complained of a pain in his right side". 

The following day, claimant's doctor informed him that he had a hernia and advised him to go to the office of the insurance carrier, which he did the same day. In Barbaryka v. 

Henderson Coal Co., 154 Pa. Superior Ct. 402, the claim involved a back injury and notice was given to a foreman by claimant telling him: “I was lifting rock and I hurt my back". Each case necessarily depends upon its own particular facts.

In the instant case, accepting Mrs. Angott's statement at full value that she told defendant's representative that claimant "fell last night and hurt himself", we deem it insufficient to apprise defendant that claimant suffered an accident by hernia. The information is lacking as to where the fall took place or where claimant was injured. It may just as well have indicated that claimant fell at home or en route home and that he hurt his arm, back or head. We cannot say that this information constituted notice of a hernia as provided in the act. To sustain the award would be tantamount to setting aside the legislative provision and usurping a legislative function. In the case of Rought v. 

Watkins, 33 Dept. Rep. 429 (1947), in an opinion by Chairman Murphy, we affirmed the referee's order of disallowance in a hernia claim, where claimant, upon the day following the accident, notified his employer that he "hurt his back": 

Hart v. Elliott Trucking Co., A-30507 (Board 1944); Winnicki v. Pressed Steel Car Co., Inc., A-30142 (Board 1944).

[84 Dep. Rep. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's 5th finding of fact and in lieu thereof we substitute the following 

Finding of fact 5. We find that claimant failed to give proper notice to defendant of the hernia within 48 hours after its occurrence.

The referee's other findings of fact are affirmed. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's 2nd conclusion of law and in lieu thereof we substitute the following 

Conclusion of law

Having found that claimant failed to give proper notice of the hernia accident to defendant within the statutory period, claimant is not entitled to recover compensation payments therefor.

The referee's first conclusion of law is affirmed. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's award and in lieu thereof we substitute the following 

Order of dismissal 

Claim petition of Pete Angott, no. 108,273, is hereby dismissed. 

The appeal of defendant is sustained.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD PAUL v. JOHNSTOWN COAL AND COKE COMPANY 

Workmen's compensation Occupational disease Death Claim by widow-Limitations.

A referee's order disallowing a widow's claim for compensation on the ground that it was barred by section 301 (c) of the Occupational Disease Compensation Act will be set aside and the claim allowed

1948] 

Department Reports of Pennsylvaina where it appears that decedent in his lifetime filed a claim petition for total disability as a result of anthraco-silicosis incurred in the course of his employment with defendant, which petition was disallowed on the finding that death was caused solely by tuberculosis, it appearing however in the hearing on the widow's petition that the medical autopsy had established anthraco-silicosis as the primary cause of death; notwithstanding the fact that decedent's death did not occur within three years after the date of his last employment, the filing by decedent of a timely claim in his lifetime tolled the statute in favor of his widow's right to file a claim in her own name for his death.

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee 

Schwing, District No. 7, claim petition no. 107,422. Appeal sustained. February 4, 1948.

S. R. DiFrancesco, for claimant. 

Albert L. Allen Co., for defendant. 

Francis A. Dunn, for defendant. 

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

Claimant, Matilda Paul, is the dependent widow of 

Michael Paul, who died on December 28, 1946. Decedent was employed by defendant, Johnstown Coal and Coke Company, from 1929 to December 4, 1940, when he became totally disabled. During his lifetime Paul filed a compensation claim for total disability, alleging anthraco-silicosis as the cause. Referee Schwing denied compensation, holding that the claim petition, filed June 25, 1941, was barred as it was filed more than one year after total disability began, which was stated to be in April 1940. Upon appeal to the board, we held that total disability began on December 4, 1940, and, therefore, the claim petition was filed within the statutory period (A-27857). We thereupon remanded the record to the referee for further hearing. The referee then heard the

case upon its merits, including the testimony of an impartial physician as to the cause of disability. The referee found tuberculosis to be the sole and primary cause of the disability and dismissed the claim. An appeal was taken to the board and we affirmed the referee (A-29963). 

The present claim petition was filed on January 20, 1947. 

Testimony of Dr. H. B. Anderson, claimant's witness, discloses that he performed an autopsy on decedent's body on December 28, 1946, and that he was of the opinion that anthraco-silicosis was the primary cause of death. Dependency is established. The referee concluded as a matter of law that "since the death of decedent, which was the primary result of anthraco-silicosis, occurred more than three years after the date of decedent's last employment in an occupation having a silica hazard, claimant is barred from the recovery of any compensation under the provisions of the Occupational Disease Act." This appeal has followed. Is the present claim petition filed too late? 

Section 301 (c) of the Occupational Disease Compensation 

Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 566, provides: "Compensation for the occupational diseases enumerated in this act shall be paid only when such occupational disease is peculiar to the occupation or industry in which the employe was engaged, and not common to the general population, and occurring within one year after the date of his last employment in such occupation or industry. Wherever death is mentioned as a cause for compensation under this act, it shall mean only death resulting from occupational disease and occurring within three years after the date of his last employment in such occupation or industry." 

We are reluctant to hold that this language of the act precludes a recovery in the case. The purpose of the act is clearly to prevent stale claims. It is an unfortunate result, in the instant case, that it operates to prevent a meritorious claim. We had occasion to consider the applicability of the language of the section in question in the case of Toffalori v. Donatelli Granite Co., A-29727, Cross Appeal 29731

1948] 

Department Reports of Pennsylvaina 

(Board 1944). We held that widow claimant was not barred from filing her separate and independent claim for compensation more than three years after date of her decedent's total disability as decedent's claim for compensation had been recognized and payments made to him during his lifetime. In our dissenting opinion, we said (p. 3): "Thus it seems to me that Section 301 (c) applies to such cases where a decedent had not been totally disabled by an occupational disease prior to his death, which occurred more than three years after the date of his last employment in such occupation or industry. In that event, a widow would be precluded from a recovery."

The present case is different in that compensation benefits were denied to claimant's decedent during his lifetime. The 

Superior Court, in the Toffalori case, 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 

311 affirmed our view. The appellate court distinguished the case before it from Meyers v. Moxham Coal Co., 293 Pa. 

7, in that the claim petition in the Meyers case filed after the expiration of the statutory period, was an original claim and the "cause of compensation" was death. The court said 

"But in the instant case, the claim petition was not an original claim. The original claim had been filed by the decedent during his lifetime and the 'cause for compensation' was total disability, not death. Upon this claim, compensation had already been paid. The present petition was in effect a claim for continuation of the payments of compensation that had already been awarded for total disability. 

Since the claim was not an original claim, and since death was not the cause for compensation, the claim was not barred. In our opinion the words of Section 301 (c) 'Wherever death is mentioned as a cause for compensation . . .' are applicable in a case where no claim is made during the employee's lifetime for compensation for disability. In such a case, where the first claim is filed after the employee's death, death is the cause for compensation. If the employee

[84 Dep. Rep. 

dies more than three years after the date of his last employment, the claim is barred."

Here, a claim petition was filed by the employe, but after mesne proceedings, it was disallowed. There was error in the disallowance as subsequent events established that decedent was suffering from anthraco-silicosis and not tuberculosis. This was shown by post mortem. Medical opinion is generally in agreement that the presence of silicosis can best be established by autopsy. The posting confirmed the original diagnosis of anthraco-silicosis of Dr. Marcy, claimant's witness, which had been rejected by the compensation authorities in the light of contra opinion from defendant's medical expert and an impartial physician appointed by the board. It would be unjust to persist in a refusal of compensation where the evidence is convincing that death was due to an occupational disease incurred in the course of defendant's employ, if such a miscarriage of justice can be avoided. From the language of the Toffalori case, we believe that the filing of the claim petition by Paul tolls the statute in favor of the widow's right to file a claim in her own name for his death. We held earlier that the employe filed his claim petition within the one-year period. While the widow's claim is for death as the cause of compensation, her right necessarily remained inchoate until the death occurred. A silicotic condition does not improve. Since decedent was removed from the hazard after 

1940, it is only logical to assume that the silicotic condition found at autopsy was present at the date he ceased work for defendant. It seems to us that higher humanitarian grounds require an award to the widow for the death. In so deciding, we can, in part, correct the injustice in denying decedent compensation in his lifetime.

The referee's 10th finding of fact is unnecessary and we hereby vacate and set it aside. The referee's other findings of fact are affirmed.

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's conclusion of law and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following

1948] 

Department Reports of Pennsylvaina Conclusion of law 

Having found that decedent filed an original claim petition for total disability as a result of anthraco-silicosis incurred in the course of his employment by defendant, Johnstown Coal and Coke Company, we conclude that claimant is thereby not barred from filing her separate and independent claim petition for her decedent's death more than three years after the date of decedent's last employment in an occupation having a silica hazard. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's order of disallowance and in lieu thereof, we enter the following Award

The board accordingly awards to Matilda Paul, claimant, widow of Michael Paul, decedent, and against Johnstown

Coal and Coke Company and the Commonwealth of Penn sylvania and/or State Workmen's Insurance Fund, defend ants, compensation at the rate of $12 per week, beginning December 28, 1946, not to exceed $3,600 within the limitations of the act.

This award to bear interest in accordance with section 

410 of the act.

Defendants are further directed to reimburse claimant in the amount of $200 on account of funeral expenses incident to the burial of decedent. 

Defendant employer shall be liable for, and pay 80 percent of the compensation above awarded and the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, 20 percent thereof.

Defendant company is further directed to pay the following 

Dr. H. B. Anderson 

Johnstown, Pa. 

Bill of costs
