WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD COYLE v. HUDSON COAL COMPANY Workmen's compensation—Occupational discase-Anthraco-silicosis— 

Exposure inside mine-Sufficiency of evidence.

A referee's order disallowing compensation for the death of claimant's husband allegedly due to anthraco-silicosis will be reversed and an award entered where the question at issue was whether decedent had been exposed to a silica hazard for a sufficient period preceding the date of his disability and whether anthraco-silicosis was the sole cause of death, there being evidence that decedent had been employed for defendant for a period in excess of 20 years prior to his death, that he worked near the foot of a mine shaft where cars of coal and rock created dust conditions, and there was medical testimony to the effect that anthraco-silicosis caused decedent to suffer from bronchial asthma which in turn brought on a heart attack causing death. · 

Before the Workmen's Compensation Board. Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Phillips, District 

No. 3, claim petition no. 107,751. Appeal sustained. January 

28, 1948. 

Roger J. Dever, for claimant. 

Francis D. Mahon, for defendant. 

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This case involves a death claim. It is before the board upon appeal by claimant, Mrs. Mary Coyle, from the order of Referee Phillips disallowing compensation for the death of her husband, Lawrence Coyle, on December 6, 1946, allegedly due to anthraco-silicosis, incurred in the course of his employment by defendant, Hudson Coal Company. The appeal poses two questions:

1948] 

Department Reports of Pennsylvaina 

1. Was decedent exposed to a silica hazard for a period of four years during a period of eight years next preceding the date of disability?; and, 2. Was the anthraco-silicosis the sole cause of death within the meaning and intendment of the statute?

Marriage and dependency of claimant are admitted. The record reveals that decedent worked for defendant from 1923 until November 23, 1946, and that his work record up to that time was good. David James, called by claimant, testified that he worked with decedent within a distance of 500 feet from the foot of the mine shaft for a period of seven or eight years, in an air intake zone. He stated that it was not too dusty there, but that there was "a certain amount of dust". Karl Miller, a dust engineer, employed by defendant, testified in considerable detail regarding a number of dust count tests which he made in 1942 and 1943 in the three working areas where decedent was employed, the 

14-foot vein near the shaft of the Marvine Colliery, the

Clark vein near the shaft and the Diamond bed, also near the shaft. Decedent was employed as a runner first class, running empty cars in the three beds mentioned. The engineer stated that the maximum dust count per cubic foot was 6,500,000, made on February 19, 1943, near shaft in the Clark bed. The engineer testified that the largest percentage of particles was coal dust although no test was made to separate the coal dust from the silica bearing dust. 

The tests, according to Miller, showed that the dust hazard was not harmful, based upon a tolerance maximum of "50,000,000 particles of coal and 10,000,000 particles of rock". He said that no further tests were made after 1943 while decedent was employed because the air is comparatively free in the area where Coyle worked. However, tests made on June 21, 1947, while loading coal at the Clark vein showed a dust count of 15,400,000 and in the same vein 200 feet from the shaft, the sample showed 12,400,000. Miller testified, under examination by the referee:

"Q. Then in your professional opinion state whether or not in the areas in which you made these tests, to wit, the 14-foot bed, Clark bed and Diamond bed in the areas in which the deceased worked he was exposed to a silica hazard? "A. It is a slight silica hazard, yes."

Miller estimated that out of 300 loaded cars, not more than 30 percent would be rock and possibly one fourth of these would be nonfree silica bearing. 

Joseph Legenza, section foreman at the Marvine Colliery, testified that he made weekly tests in the three locations near the shaft where decedent worked to determine the quantity of air passing at those locations and that at the 14-foot vein there was 15,740 cubic feet of air passing at intake, 7,980 cubic feet at the Diamond bed shaft and at the Clark bed a total of 45,440 cubic feet. The witness stated that the maximum legal requirement is 200 cubic feet per area per minute for each man working in that area. The foreman also testified that decedent never made any complaint and worked steadily during the five-year period he was under the foreman's supervision. The foreman's testimony establishes a sufficient supply of air in decedent's working place and nothing more. It does not eliminate a silica hazard. James, decedent's fellow employe, previously testified that the air "was pretty strong at that point", but that there was "a certain amount of dust". Miller described decedent's duties at the shaft as follows: "Oh, they are hoisting coal or pulling it through the shaft; they are engaged in transportation, you might say, to the shaft or cars in the shaft to take outside."

He stated that the cars loaded with coal contain some impurities and that "the air coming down the shaft rushing over the coal cars . . . would have a tendency to disperse any loose dust on top or in the cars". We are of the considered opinion that a realistic view of the operations performed by decedent compels the conclusion that he was exposed, in some degree, to a silicosis hazard during his

1948] 

Department Reports of Pennsylvaina employment inside the mines. In the case of Kruskie v.

Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Co., 33 Dept. Rep. 

528, we awarded compensation where claimant's decedent was employed outside the mine on a conveyor line. We said: "A realistic view must be taken of the existing facts and circumstances in this case. Section 301 (c) of the Act of 

1939 provides for compensation payments 'when such occupational disease is peculiar to the occupation or industry in which the employe was engaged and not common to the general population . . . Silicosis and its companion disease are now well established as peculiar to the anthracite coal industry."

We have given due consideration to the tests made by defendant's dust engineer, but we are not convinced in the instant case that the statutory presumption (301 (f)) that the anthraco-silicosis "arose out of and in the course of his employment" has been rebutted. No tests were made for several years prior to Coyle's death. Several months after the death the dust count was shown to be comparatively high. 

The silica content, although admitted, was never computed: 

Jaloneck v. Jarecki Manufacturing Co., 157 Pa. Superior

Ct. 609, 614. Cars of coal and other cars of rock created dust conditions in and about decedent's place of employment and, in our opinion, constituted a continuing occupational hazard. 

We are of the opinion that the first question as to necessary exposure must be resolved in favor of claimant. 

Dr. Anthony G. Zale, called in behalf of claimant, testified that he saw decedent on November 30, 1946, and found the patient totally disabled due to an advanced anthraco-silicosis. 

The doctor stated that he also found a mild myocarditis, which, in his opinion, was caused by the anthraco-silicosis. 

Dr. Zale saw decedent only upon the one occasion. The doctor thought that the death on December 6, 1946, was caused by the anthraco-silicosis. 

He testified: "Q. . . . Isn't it a fact, Doctor, that the actual cause of

Mr. Coyle's death in this case was bronchopneumonia which he contracted after you saw him on November 30, 1946?

"A. No, I would say that anthracosilicosis was the cause of his death and he finally died with bronchopneumonia or as we call it or what we call a hypostatic pneumonia, is the terminal event or just before death the lungs become congested and what is termed medically bronchopneumonia." 

Dr. F. A. Carroll, claimant's witness, testified that he attended Coyle immediately prior to his death. He testified the "basic cause of death was anthraco-silicosis. The complication of bronchopneumonia, bronchial asthma and heart failure killed him". The doctor explained that the bronchial asthma was caused by the anthraco-silicosis and it, in turn, brought on the heart attack. Dr. Carroll stated that the death certificate made by him showed no reference to anthraco-silicosis "through oversight". The doctor testified: "Q. Well, Doctor, it would be quite possible wouldn't it that this deceased was suffering from bronchial asthma that would have no connection with anthraco-silicosis? "A. Not in this case. "Q. Why not, Doctor? "A. I have known him for 30 years and I have seen him going down hill getting that miner's asthma. Look, when you are practicing up there-up and down the valley for 30 years and seen loads and loads of cases you can pick them out on the street. I know from my statistics of the 

Metropolitan that every man in the mines 25 years dies from it." 

He further testified: "Q. Well, Doctor, if it is a terminal type of congestion you might get it in any particular case even a case of a man not suffering from anthracosilicosis, isn't that true? "A. No, it is not true. This man has been through a terrific marathon for two weeks, breathing, suffering and trying to hold on and I am giving him digitalis, medicants to try to keep that heart pumping and get him over the goal line see, but in failing to get over the goal line his heart starts to go and that's when you get that hypostatic con-

1948] 

 gestion. The heart is failing, which I put down. Heart failure, get it."

Defendant offered no medical testimony. The medical testimony of record permits a fair and logical inference that the advanced anthraco-silicosis set in motion the combination of complications precipitating the death. Dr. Carroll's explanation of the terminal factors, in the absence of any opinion to the contrary, is entirely credible. We believe the facts of record warrant an award.

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's 8th, 9th, 10th, 11th, 12th and 14th findings of fact and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following: 

Findings of fact 8. We find that in his employment by defendant company from 1923 to November 23, 1946, decedent was exposed to an occupation hazard of anthraco-silicosis. 

9. We find that decedent was exposed to an anthracosilicosis hazard for a period of four years out of the eight years next preceding November 23, 1946, the date disability commenced. 

10. We find that decedent incurred the anthraco-silicosis in the course of his employment by defendant. 

11. We find that decedent worked for defendant until 

November 23, 1946, when he ceased work, and that he died on December 6, 1946. 

12. We find that the sole cause of the total disability and subsequent death, was anthraco-silicosis, producing a fatal congestion of the lungs and a heart failure.

The referee's other findings of fact are affirmed. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's 2nd and 3rd conclusions of law and in lieu thereof, we substitute the 

2. Having found as a fact that claimant's decedent was exposed to an anthraco-silicosis hazard for a period of eight

[84 Dep. Rep. 

years next preceding disability and that the death on December 6, 1946, was caused solely by anthraco-silicosis, claimant is entitled to compensation. 

The referee's 1st conclusion of law is affirmed. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's order of dismissal and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following: Award

Defendant employer, Hudson Coal Company, and the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania are hereby ordered and directed to pay compensation to claimant, Mrs. Mary Coyle, at the rate of $12 per week, beginning December 6, 1946, and continuing within the limitations of the act, but not to exceed the total amount of $3,600. 

The weekly payments of compensation shall be appor tioned as follows: 

The Hudson Coal Company shall pay 80 percent of each installment and the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania shall pay 20 percent of each installment.

This award to bear interest in accordance with section 

410 of the act.

Defendants above named are further directed to reimburse claimant in the same proportion in the sum of $200 for funeral expenses incurred by her.

The appeal of claimant is sustained. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD WERNER v. CARNEGIE-ILLINOIS STEEL CORP. 

Workmen's compensation—Claim petition—Statute of limitations— 

Tolling Statement by defendant's physician to claimant. 

A referee's order dismissing claimant's petition for compensation on the ground that it was filed beyond the period of the statute of limitations provided for in the Workmen's Compensation Act will be

1948] 

 affirmed where it appears claimant injured his foot on the premises of his employer, that subsequently a gangrene process set in necessitating the amputation of his leg, that defendant's physician, according to claimant's testimony, told claimant when he first saw him several weeks after the date of the injury that he "was done" when advised that claimant's injury had occurred on his way out of the plant after the deposit of his time slip, the physician himself having testified that he told claimant defendant was not responsible if his injury occurred on a public street; in any case the physician's advice could not be held to charge the defendant with misconduct or to estop it from setting up the defense that the claim was filed too late. 

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Moore, District No. 8, claim petition no. 104,651. Affirmed. January 

14, 1948. 

John E. Evans, Jr., for claimant. 

C. E. Stewart, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal from an order of dismissal entered by 

Referee Moore April 15, 1947.

According to the petition filed in the case March 13, 1946, the accidental injury complained of occurred February 3, 1945, and the legal significance of the period which expired between those dates, more than a year, raises the principal issue in this appeal.

In his testimony claimant, Adam S. Werner, a man over 

70 years of age, explained that after he had turned in his time card and taken a few steps beyond the gate of the Homestead plant of defendant, the Carnegie-Illinois Steel Co., at about midnight on the date above mentioned, he was stopped by a picket who told him he would not work the next day and emphasized the remark by stamping upon claimant's right foot. According to a plan of the plant introduced as an exhibit, the incident occurred on a portion of defendant's plant entrance between the public street and the chain stretched across the entrance at the place where

[84 Dep. Rep.

 the police gate was located and it is not seriously disputed that the spot was on the premises of the employer. 

After the injury claimant worked about two weeks but was then forced to quit. A gangrene process had set in around the second toe and showed a tendency to spread. 

This required admission to the South Side Hospital from 

March 13 to April 14, 1945, and from May 31, to July 20, 1945. In the first period of hospitalization Dr. B. L. Jones amputated the gangrenous toe and in the second Dr. 

J. H. Curran found it necessary to remove the right leg about two and one-half inches above the knee. 

At the hearing the factual issues were somewhat beclouded by claimant's hazy recollection of dates and names but was sufficiently certain of the substantial circumstances to convince the referee and we have found nothing in our review of the record which would constrain us to alter the resultant findings of fact. Wherein credibility is involved in this phase of the matter the case falls in that class which the hearing officer is in a better position to judge: Isherwood v. American Steel Foundries, 98 Pa. Superior Ct. 164; Smith v. Smith, 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 582. Defendant did do some cross-examining as to the possible effect that some new work shoes purchased by claimant might have had in producing the trouble which disabled him but the referee gave little weight to the implications so developed and we see no reason to disagree.

The testimony having to do with the principal issue relates chiefly to a pronouncement attributed to the plant physician, Dr. E. V. McCormick, who first saw claimant 

March 10, 1945. According to claimant, this doctor told him he "was done" when advised that the attack had occurred after deposit of the time slip on the way out of the plant. But the doctor, called as a witness, denied the exactness of this and insisted that he had told claimant defendant was not responsible if the incident occurred on the public street when claimant was on his way to work. Such a remark or statement, whichever recollection of it should be correct,

1948] 

 would not be of the type that holds forth a false promise or which would tend to mislead claimant. Quite to the contrary it would be the kind of statement which should put claimant on notice that he would have to prove his case if he thought he had one. Thus it cannot be said that Dr. McCormick's advice lulled claimant into a sense of security and that by reason thereof the statute of limitations was tolled: See 

Mackanitz v. Pittsburgh & West Virginia Railway Co., 157

Pa. Superior Ct. 359. Although plant physicians are largely concerned with the treatment of employes who come to them sick or injured, they cannot escape the incidental duty of classifying the cases they diagnose as compensable or noncompensable and when in doing so they are unequivocal the action so taken cannot be charged to the employers who hire them as misconduct.

We have reviewed this record with the utmost sympathy so far as claimant is concerned. He is up in years and has suffered a severe loss. However, our hands are tied. The law is plain and to deliberately misconstrue it would be to prostitute it. We are not at liberty to do so. The petition was filed too late.

The findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of 

Referee Moore dated April 15, 1947, are affirmed. 

The appeal is dismissed.

SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA SHEAFFEL v. PENN DAIRIES, INC., et al. 

Workmen's compensation-Dependency-Widow living with husband at time of death-Necessity of living together in the same house- Finding by board-Power of common pleas to reverse. 

1. The Workmen's Compensation Board is the exclusive fact-finding tribunal even where the testimony is free from conflict, hence a court on appeal may not find facts contrary to findings of fact made by the

board, but it may remand the case to the board for the purpose of making more specific and sufficient findings of fact. 

2. Where it appeared that claimant was married to decedent just a few months prior to his death, that she, at the time of their marriage, was employed and living with her invalid parents who were dependent upon her, that after the marriage, she continued to live with her parents but saw her husband each day either at her home or his boarding house in the same town, that he contributed to her maintenance from the time of their marriage until his death, the board erred in disallowing an award where its finding that the parties were not living together within the meaning of section 307 of the Workmen's Compensation Act rested solely upon the circumstance that they did not occupy the same living quarters; however, the court on appeal had no power to enter an award but should have remanded the record to the board for further consideration. 

In the Superior Court of Pennsylvania, October term, 1947, no. 198. Appeal from judgment of C. P. of Lancaster 

County, April term, 1947, no. 18. Record remitted. January 

8, 1948. 

B. M. Zimmeman, for claimant. 

Frank R. Ambler and Paul A. Mueller, for defendants.

RENO, J.: 

The referee refused compensation to claimant upon the ground that her husband had died of natural causes and not from an accidental injury. The board found that his death resulted from an accidental fall, but refused compensation because claimant was not "living with" the deceased at the time of his death. The court below reversed the board, awarded compensation, and from its judgment the employer and its insurance carrier appealed. 

The case turns upon the meaning of section 307, 77 PS 

$562, of the Workmen's Compensation Act: 

"No compensation shall be payable under this section to a widow, unless she was living with her deceased husband at the time of his death, or was then actually dependent upon

1948] 

 him and receiving from him substantial portion of her support. 

The board found: "10. Decedent left to survive him a widow, Lillian M. Sheaffer, claimant herein, who was not living with him nor dependent upon him and receiving from him a substantial portion of her support." A conclusion of law, similarly phrased, was the basis for its refusal of an award.

The evidence was that claimant and her husband were married on November 15, 1941, and returned on the same day to their respective homes in Mount Joy. He died on 

January 12, 1942. They had never set up a home of their own, or lived in a room or rooms under the same roof. Each continued to live in separate rooms in the houses in which they had dwelt before the marriage. In a narrow and severely literal sense of the phrase, claimant was not "living with" deceased at the time of his death.

The evidence was and, depending upon its appraisal of claimant's credibility, the board could have found that claimant's parents were invalids, she was their sole support, and to avoid administering a shock to them she and her husband determined to keep their sudden marriage a secret until by their constant association together at her home her parents became reconciled to the idea of her marriage. They saw each other daily, either at her home or his boarding house and, as soon as her parents could be safely advised of her marital status, they planned to have him move into her home, when she would discontinue work and give her eyes needed rest and treatment. Although she continued to work and support her parents, he contributed to her maintenance, purchasing some of her clothing, paying several dollars. weekly for groceries, and supplying fuel oil for the heating of her house.

There was no evidence of a repudiation of marital obligations, no break in the connubial relations, no legal separation, no release of matrimonial duties, no estrangement, and if proof of intercourse is lacking it may be inferred or sup-

[84 Dep. Rep. 

plied. If the nature and the character of their married life and their intention respecting it are examined it is apparent that while they were not living in the same place and under the same roof they were in substance and in spirit "living with" each other. "Living with" does not always import physically dwelling together in the same house: Icenhour v. Freedom Oil Works 

Co., 136 Pa. Superior Ct. 318, 7 A. (2d) 152; 145 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 168, 20 A. (2d) 817; Dietrich et al. v. Hudson Coal Co., 117 Pa. Superior Ct. 193, 177 Atl. 606. Whether parties are "living with" each other is a question of fact, but it is to be determined, not by consulting only one facet of the relationship, but by inspecting the whole picture. And where it is found that for the convenience of the parties, or for some other moving and reasonable motive they dwell in separate homes without estrangement or repudiation or release of their legal obligations, and with constant recognition of the marital tie, it is no strain upon logic or credulity to find that they were "living with" each other. Cf. Creasy v. Phoenix 

Utilities Co., 276 Pa. 583, 120 Atl. 659. For in this class of cases, we look beyond the form to the substance, from outward appearances to the realities behind them. 

The board, as its finding indicates, construed the phrase too narrowly, and having discovered the one fact that the parties did not occupy the same living quarters, rested its finding that they were not living together solely upon that circumstance. If the board had found the facts indicated by the evidence which we have recited, assuming that claimant's testimony was credible, we believe it might have inferred the ultimate fact that claimant lived with deceased. 

Its error consisted in concentrating its attention upon one item of the proof, ignoring the rest of the testimony, and without finding the specific facts, reached a conclusion which upon its face indicates failure to consider all the evidence. 

The court below properly construed the meaning of the phrase, "living with," but unfortunately and, as we think, inadvertently stepped beyond the bounds of its authority.

It found as facts the circumstances to which we have ad-

1948] 

 verted, and upon the basis of its factual finding entered an award and judgment. The board is the exclusive fact-finding tribunal even when, as here, the testimony is free from conflict, and the case should have been and must be remanded to it for the purpose of finding all the facts, as well as the ultimate fact, in the light of the legal meaning of "living with" as herein construed. 

Both sides relied upon the Icenhour case, supra. The case was here twice, and in its several aspects it supports both parties, and reinforces this opinion. In the first opinion 

Judge, now President Judge, Rhodes said (p. 322): ". . . and if the living apart is merely for the mutual convenience or for the joint advantage of the parties, and the obligation of the husband to support her is recognized, the right of compensation exists as if they were living together." 

The second appeal was unavailing because the board had found against the widow upon the facts. In both cases there was recognition of the fact-finding function of the board, and of the power of a reviewing court to remand a claim for more specific and sufficient findings of fact. Our disposition will enable the board to reconsider the case, to take further testimony if deemed necessary, and to find the facts with greater specificity. What its findings shall be, and what inferences it shall draw from the testimony are within its exclusive control.

The judgment is vacated and the record is remitted to the court below with directions to remand it to the board for further consideration and proceedings not inconsistent with this opinion.

[84 Dep. Rep. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD MASHBURN v. MOORE et al. 

Workmen's compensation—Employe―Truck driver hauling freight— 

Return load for different hauler.

An award in favor of claimants, minor children of deceased, whose death resulted from carbon monoxide gas while driving a truck owned by one of defendants, will be affirmed where it appears that decedent was employed by the defendant in question who was engaged in the business of hauling freight in interstate commerce, that decedent was directed to deliver a load of freight from Reading to Detroit and required to secure a return load if one was available, that a return load was secured from the other defendant who was similarly engaged in the business of hauling freight, and that decedent fell asleep and suffocate in the cab of his tractor while on his return trip; as decedent received all his instructions from the defendant who hired him, was on the latter's payroll, and merely followed instructions of the other defendant as to the place of delivery and the route to follow with the return load, and as decedent's solicitation of the load was in the pursuance of directions given him by his employer, the latter was liable for compensation.

Appeal from defendant from award of Referee Graybill, District No. 4, claim petition no. 106,279. Affirmed. March 

10, 1948.

Luther Heist, for claimant. 

George Eves, for defendant.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

Claimants are the minor children of William J. Mashburn, who died on January 4, 1946. Decedent was accidentally overcome by carbon monoxide gas on January 3, 1946, at 

Beaver Falls, Pa., when en route from Toledo, Ohio, to Carlstadt, N. J., while driving a truck owned by James W. 

Moore, one of defendants. Decedent was employed by James 

W. Moore, who was engaged in the business of hauling

1948] 

 freight in interstate commerce. On December 29, 1945, decedent was directed to deliver a load of freight from Reading, Pa., to Detroit, Mich. His instructions required him to secure a return load if one was available. Decedent inquired of 

Kramer Bros. (who were similarly engaged in the business of hauling freight) at their terminal in Toledo, Ohio. The equipment owned by James W. Moore was loaded and the trailer sealed. Kramer Bros. made an advance of some money for gas and turnpike toll, and gave decedent a road clearance card and instructed him as to the routes on which they were licensed to travel. When decedent reached Beaver 

Falls, Pa., he stopped his tractor and fell asleep in the cab at a service station with the motor running and was overcome by the escaping fumes of carbon monoxide. He was taken to a nearby hospital and died on January 4, 1946. 

James W. Moore was notified and a substitute driver was sent out to Beaver Falls to pick up the load and the delivery was completed as arranged by defendant with Kramer Bros. 

The referee made an award of compensation, finding as a fact that decedent sustained his fatal injury while an employe of James W. Moore and dismissed the claim against the Kramer Bros. Freight Lines. The sole question raised by this appeal filed by the insurance carrier of James W. 

Moore is whether decedent was at the time of the accident under the direction and control of this defendant. 

The record indicates that decedent was hired by James Moore, that he was on Moore's payroll, and deductions were made from decedent's wages for social security, withholding taxes, union dues and advances. Decedent was given his original directions by Moore and was also instructed to pick up any loads available on his return trip. Decedent followed these instructions and when he picked up the Kramer load the only direction he received was as to the place of delivery and the route to follow. Our further review of the record persuades us that Kramer had no control of the vehicle. nor were they concerned in the manner of operation other than the safe delivery of the load at its destination.

Kramer could not discharge decedent nor could he remove decedent from his equipment. The mere fact that Kramer paid Moore 65 percent of the gross charges made for the carriage of the freight less deductions did not change the relationship between decedent and Moore. The instructions given as to the route to be followed by decedent were limited to the roads which Kramers were permitted to follow under certificates issued to them as common carriers. Decedent's solicitation of the Kramer load was in pursuance of the directions given him by Moore and the performance of these duties did not transfer him to the employ of Kramer. 

We, therefore, are of the opinion that decedent was an employe of James W. Moore when overcome by the poisonous fumes. The relationship of master and servant still existed. 

Moore had selected decedent, he retained the power to remove and discharge decedent, he retained the right to direct what freight was to be carried and the manner in which it was to be done. Moore thus employed, paid and had full power to control decedent: Healey v. Carey, Baxter & Kennedy, Inc., 144 Pa. Superior Ct. 500; McGrath v. E. G. 

Budd Mfg. Co., 348 Pa. 619; Walters v. Kauffman Department Stores, 145 Pa. Superior Ct. 56.

Accordingly we affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and award.

The appeal of James W. Moore's insurance carrier is denied.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD NICKOLAY v. HUDSON COAL COMPANY Workmen's compensation—Occupational disease-Notice to employer of disability-Failure to give notice within 90-day period.

An award for disability due to anthraco-silicosis incurred in the course of claimant's employment by defendant will be reversed where

1948] 

 the testimony discloses that claimant was totally disabled on June 29, 1946, the last day of his employment by defendant, and gave no notice to defendant of his disability prior to the filing of a claim petition on December 11, 1946; failure of claimant to notify defendant within 

90 days after disability began, as provided by the Occupational Disease Compensation Act of June 21, 1939, necessitated dismissal of his claim petition.

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Olexy, District No. 2, claim petition no. 107,065. Reversed. January 

28, 1948. 

Roger J. Dever, for claimant. 

F. D. Mahon, for defendant. 

Ralph H. Behney, for Commonwealth.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

Referee Olexy awarded compensation in this case to claimant, Lewis Nickolay, for total disability due to anthracosilicosis incurred in the course of his employment by defendant, Hudson Coal Company. The referee found that claimant became totally disabled on December 5, 1946, and that notice was given by the filing of the claim petition on 

December 11, 1946. Defendant has appealed. The Common wealth of Pennsylvania has also appealed (A-33276).

Mindful as we are of the humane purposes of the Occupa tional Disease Compensation Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 

566, as amended, we are of the opinion that claimant failed to give the required statutory notice and that the referee's award must be reversed. It is most unfortunate that a meritorious claim, such as is represented here, must be disallowed because of failure to give notice to the employer within 90 days after disability. However, we cannot substitute sympathy for the legislative requirement. . While notice, by filing a claim petition is adequate, it is unusual to do so in occupational disease claim cases. From

[84 Dep. Rep. 

our extended experience in these cases, we find that an employe, disabled for further employment, almost invariably notifies his employer's representative that he is unable to continue at his work any longer. The preponderance of the evidence in this case establishes claimant's date of disability as June 29, 1946, when he ceased work, because he could not work. There is direct testimony by claimant, corroborated by his medical witness, to this effect. Claimant testified that he notified Mr. Connor, mine foreman, on December 5, 1946, that he was totally disabled and that Connor referred him to the mine superintendent. This notice on December 5, 1946, claimant admitted, was the first notice given to defendant. 

Claimant testified: "Q. When your work as company laborer finished up on 

June 29, 1946, did you ask for any other kind of work? "A. No, not right away. "Q. Did you ever go back to the colliery to look for any other kind of work? "A. I didn't. I didn't feel so good. I thought I get rest and feel better and I go back again, but I wasn't getting better; I was getting worse. "Q. That's all."

Claimant stated that he consulted a physician in July, 1946, a Dr. Ryhkiewicz, when he obtained his "security". 

Claimant further testified: "Q. Well, you could not work in July 1946, could you? "A. Not hardly. I looked around but could not get no easy job and by and by I got sicker. "Q. That's all."

Recross Examination: 

By Mr. Mahon : 

"Q. Mr. Nickolay, the reason you didn't work after June 

29, 1946, is because you could not work, isn't that so? "A. That's so. "Q. All right, that's all."

Dr. George Shuman, called by claimant, testified that he was not sure when he first saw claimant but thought it was

1948] 

"around October or September 1946" and that he saw him through the winter on various occasions for bronchitis and pleurisy. He stated that he notified Nickolay early in December 1946 that he was through working because of his physical condition. The doctor testified, under cross-examination: "Q. Didn't you review your file before you came into the court today, doctor? "A. No. "Q. At any rate, when you first saw him, you concluded, did you not, that he was totally disabled as a result of anthraco-silicosis? "A. Yes. I will retract that. There was some doubt in my mind from the beginning. I saw him getting progressively worse, losing weight, shortness of breath, poor appetite, dyspnea. "Q. When you first saw him, didn't you make a tentative diagnosis of total disability as a result of anthraco-silicosis? "A. Well, not the first time I saw him, no. "Q. When you first saw him, you took a history of the case? "A. Yes. "Q. Didn't it include a statement by him he quit work 

June 29, 1946, because he could not work any longer? "A. That's what he told me." 

Dr. Shuman further testified:

By the Referee: 

"Q. You don't know whether you saw him first in September or October? "A. Not positive. It was in the fall."

By Mr. D'Iorio: 

"Q. It could have been in August 1946, too? "A. It could have been late in August, toward the fall. 

I would have to look it up. "Q. From your first examination, you realized the original possibility of a total disability resulting from anthracosilicosis was confirmed. The very first time you examined

[84 Dep. Rep. 

him you knew he had it. He was totally disabled from that time. "A. Yes."

All this testimony adds up and points to the inescapable conclusion that claimant was totally disabled on the last day of his employment by defendant, June 29, 1946, and there is no credible testimony to support the referee's finding that the onset of total disability was on December 5, 1946. Guy 

Conner, defendant's mine foreman, denied that claimant notified him on December 5, 1946, that he was suffering from miner's asthma, or at any other time. The referee evidently did not accept claimant's testimony that he personally notified Conner on December 5, 1946, as the referee's finding was that notice was served upon defendant by filing of the petition on December 11, 1946. We agree that no notice was given until the later date in December. 

The burden of proof was upon claimant petitioner: Condron v. P. & R. C. & I. Co., 78 Pa. Superior Ct. 133. We cannot say that the quality of evidence offered by claimant satisfied his affirmative burden that total disability commenced on December 5, 1946. Claimant's cessation of work on June 29, 1946, his failure to engage in any employment after that date and the lack of any satisfactory evidence that he even sought any work subsequent to that date, convinces us that total disability began on June 29, 1946. Since notice was not given until December 11, 1946, claimant is barred by the act (section 311).

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's ninth finding of fact and in lieu thereof we substitute the following: 

Finding of fact 9. On June 29, 1946, claimant became totally disabled by anthraco-silicosis. He has been contracting this disease of anthraco-silicosis for more than five years prior to the last date of his employment in the mines. 

The referee's other findings of fact are affirmed.

1948] 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's second conclusion of law and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following:

Conclusion of law 

2. Since claimant became totally disabled on June 29, 1946, and did not give notice to defendant within 90 days thereafter, he is not entitled to compensation. 

The referee's first conclusion of law is affirmed. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's award and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following: 

Order of disallowance

The claim petition of Lewis Nickolay, no. 107,065, is hereby dismissed. 

The appeal of defendant is sustained.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD FELTEN v. MELLOTT Workmen's compensation—Employe or independent contractor-Haul ing coal with own truck-Supervision by defendant. 

An award to claimant, dependent widow of a deceased person, will be affirmed where defendant claimed that decedent was an independent contractor, not an employe, and where it appeared that decedent together with his truck was hired on an hourly basis to assist other employes of defendant in hauling coal, that in carrying out his employment decedent received the same supervision and performed the same services as defendant's other employes who worked with defendant's trucks, that he worked only when his services were required and in accordance with the instructions received from the defendant's supervising employe.

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Patterson, District No. 6, claim petition no. 106,904. Affirmed. March 

10, 1948. 

Paul A. Koontz, for claimant. 

Paul E. Beaver, for defendant.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

This is an appeal by defendant from an award of the referee.

The record discloses that, in her claim petition filed on November 25, 1946, claimant alleged that she was the dependent widow of Ross Felton, who died on June 24, 1946, as a result of injuries suffered by him in the course of his employment with defendant. Defendant's answer filed on

December 28, 1946, denied the material averments of claimant's petition and, in addition, denied the existence of an employer-employe relationship between decedent and defendant, alleging that decedent was an independent contractor.

After hearing, the referee found that decedent met his death as a result of accidental injuries suffered by him in the course of his employment with defendant and, in accordance with such findings, entered an award in favor of claimant. This appeal followed.

The sole question raised by this appeal is whether decedent was an independent contractor, in which event his widow would not be entitled to compensation under the Workmen's Compensation Act, or whether he was an employe of defendant, in which event his widow would be entitled to the compensation provided for by the act. Whether one is an employe, entitled to compensation, under the definition of the act, or an independent contractor, not within the act, often presents a close legal question: Bradley v. Chester 

Materials Co., 3 P. C. R. 184. The statements of law upon this matter are quite clear:

1948] 

"The chief things to consider in determining the relationship are the payment of wages, control over the claimant, manner of entering into the contract of hire, and the general classification of claimant on the basis of the nature of the services performed": Capelli v. Freitick, 3 P. C. R. 248. "The relation of employer and employee exists where the employer has the right to select the employee, to direct both what work he shall do and the manner in which it shall be done, and to remove and discharge him. Where a contract is entered into and no control is reserved over the means and manner of accomplishing the work but merely the result, the employment is an independent one": Shields v. Freihofer, 2 P. C. R. 224. "Where the employer controls the means of accomplishment of the work either personally or through the agency of a foreman, the party so controlled is an employee and not an independent contractor". Johnson v. Narehood, 2 P. C. R. 

95 but "the mere fact that a party retains the right to supervise and inspect the work during performance does not change the relationship from independent contractor to master and servant where the mode and means of performance are within the control of the one designated as the independent contractor": Adams v. General Machine

Works, 2 P. C. R. 106. 

The difficulty, however, arises in the application of the above quoted general principles of law to the facts of a particular case. 

In the instant case, the facts are as follows: Defendant was and is engaged in a coal stripping operation in Bedford County, Pa. In this coal stripping operation he used trucks to haul coal from the shovel to the loading ramp. Some of these trucks were owned by defendant and operated by his own permanent employes, who were classified as truck drivers and received $.85 per hour. When there was no driving to be done, these employes were either assigned to other duties or were "laid off" for short periods of time. In addition to these trucks and drivers, defendant had in operation

trucks that were hired with an operator on an hourly basis. 

On June 24, 1946, the date on which decedent suffered his fatal injuries, there were 14 trucks in operation hauling coal from the shovel to the loading ramp, a distance of approximately four miles, eight trucks were owned by defendant and six were hired with an operator on an hourly basis. 

For a period of approximately two years, decedent had been engaged in hauling coal, for defendant, from the coal stripping operation to the loading ramp. Decedent furnished his own truck, which he operated himself, and was paid on an hourly basis of $3 for the time he worked. When there was no coal to be removed, decedent did no work for defendant and received no remuneration. Decedent was told by defendant to report at the coal stripping operation at 7 o'clock in the morning, was directed to one of seven shovels in operation, and was directed to which ramp to haul the coal. Thereafter he continued to haul coal during the normal working day, which in the summer time was 10 hours and in the winter was 9½ hours. In doing this work, he was doing the identical work done by defendant's own trucks and truck drivers and was under the same supervision and instructions as they. He worked regularly when there was work, although there was at least one time when he left before the designated quitting time. Evidence was presented to show that he also did work for others but there was no evidence to show that this other work was done during the time and hours that defendant had work available for him. 

On June 24, 1946, while hauling coal for defendant, decedent suffered accidental injuries from which his death resulted. 

Applying the above-quoted law to the facts of the instant case, we are of the opinion that the findings of fact, conclusions of law and award of the referee were proper and must be affirmed. As counsel for claimant has properly stated in his brief filed in this appeal: "To create the relationship of independent contractor two requirements must be met; first, there must be a separation of the business of the contractee and a delegation of such

1948] 

 separated part to the contractor; second, the performance of such separated portion of the contractee's business must be placed under such control of the contractor that he has complete charge of the manner of performance as distinguished from the result to be accomplished."

In the instant case, neither of these requirements has been met. Summarizing the testimony presented, we find that decedent, together with his truck, was hired on an hourly basis to assist other employes of the defendant in hauling coal; he was not designated any particular portion of defendant's business nor was any definite work set aside as that over which he would exercise control; in carrying out his employment, decedent received the same supervision and performed the same services as defendant's other employes and, in addition, he worked only when his services were required and in accordance with instructions received from the defendant's supervising employe.

In our opinion, this case is controlled by McCall v. Bell 

Telephone Co., 79 Pa. Superior Ct. 505. In that case it was held that a teamster, who owned and drove his own team, working for defendant without any contract, but upon an engagement to do any and all work required, under the control of defendant's foreman as to the extent, character and manner of his services was an employe of defendant and not an independent contractor. See also Smith v. State Workmen's Insurance Fund, 262 Pa. 286; Kelly v. 

Delaware, Lackawanna & Western Railroad Co., 270 Pa. 

426. To our mind, the fact that, in the case cited, claimant engaged "to do any and all work required", while in the instant case he merely hauled coal, does not remove the instant case from the law set out in the McCall case, in view of the fact that, in the instant case, decedent was doing the same work, in the same manner and under the same instructions and supervision as other employes of defendant. 

We have carefully reviewed the decision of the Superior Court in the case of Healey v. Carey, Baxter and Kennedy, 144 Pa. Superior Ct. 500, cited by counsel for defendant in

support of his argument that decedent was an independent contractor and not an employe, and, in our opinion, this case does not aid the position taken by defendant. In that case, the court properly found that defendant company, Carey, while engaged in a coal stripping operation, did no hauling, the hauling being done by other defendant, Yesu, with whom the Carey Company had entered into a verbal contract for the hauling of its coal from its stripping operation. Yesu 

Brothers sent claimant one of its trucks to do the work. 

It employed claimant, paid his wages and had full power of control over him. Carey Company could not have discharged the claimant and, conversely, could not have demanded that Carey Company send only claimant, rather than some other driver to do this work. Under such facts, the court properly found that claimant was an employe of Yesu and not of the Carey Company. A comparison of the instant case with the Healy case shows that there is no similarity between them as to the facts. 

We, therefore, affirm the findings of fact, conclusions of law and award of the referee. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD REED v. WESTINGHOUSE ELECTRIC CORP. 

Workmen's compensation 

Claim petition · 

Limitations 

- Tolling

Advice by foreman to continue working-Payment of medical expenses by employer. 

1. A referee's award of compensation to claimant will be set aside where it appears that a claim petition was filed three years and seven months after the date of the accident and the only reason for the delay offered by claimant was an alleged conversation with his foreman advising him to keep on working because he would not get much out of compensation; the alleged conversation did not constitute improper conduct on the part of the defendant and was not a promise relating to continued employment conditioned upon the nonfiling of a petition.

] 227 

2. The furnishing of and payment for medical treatment by an employer does not stop the running of the limitations on filing a claim petition provided for in the Workmen's Compensation Act. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Clayton, District No. 1, claim petition no. 108,068. Appeal sustained. 

February 11, 1948. 

Philip J. Franzese, for claimant. 

Thomas P. Mikell, for defendant.

KNOLL, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by defendant from an order of Referee 

A. Harry Clayton, of Compensation District No. 1, awarding compensation. 

Claimant's petition, filed March 12, 1947, alleged, inter alia, that he was injured on August 2, 1943, while working on an elevator and described the accident and injury as follows: "left wrist broken, when lever became loose and

I was hit on arm by bar. Arm was broken on two occasions, later, to reset same, and am now losing industrial use of left arm."

The answer of defendant denied all the material allegations of the claim petition, excepting the accident. 

After hearing, the referee awarded compensation, on a basis of 25 percent partial disability, from August 9, 1943, until cessation or change of disability.

The record shows that claimant lost only a few days of work as a result of his accidental injury; that he continued at his work as an elevator operator for several hours each day and acted as a watchman and car cleaner for the balance of the day; that he earned his regular salary, with an increase in wages from 7012 cents per hour to 9512 cents per hour, until his discharge from work on February 22, 1947; that the discharge of claimant was due to union seniority and was beyond defendant's control, and that claimant secured other employment on May 29, 1947.

The record presents a conflict as to the extent of claimant's injury, claimant having testified that he suffered a broken wrist, while defendant's medical witness testified that X-ray examination revealed a disclocation of the wrist and no fracture. However, it appears that claimant had lost some of the industrial use of his left arm, as evidenced by limited use of the fingers of the hand and atrophy of the muscles of the arm. Claimant offered no medical testimony as to causal relationship between the physical condition of the arm and the alleged accident of August 2, 1943.

The claim petition was filed three years and seven months after the accident, a delay which claimant alleges was due to a conversation with his foreman advising him to keep on working because he would not get much out of compensation and "the best thing to do is keep on working". 

It is our opinion that the claim petition in this case should be dismissed because it is barred by the statute of limitations of the act. Claimant received his regular wages from the date of the accident to the date of his discharge from work. 

The payments were for services rendered and because they were received as wages they did not toll the limitations of the act: Chase v. Emery Manufacturing Co., 271 Pa. 265; 

Hickey v. Cudahy Packing Co., 153 Pa. Superior Ct. 45, Elkins v. Cambria Library Assn., 82 Pa. Superior Ct. 144.

The alleged conversation of claimant with his foreman does not constitute improper conduct and was not a promise relating to continued employment conditioned upon the nonfiling of a claim petition. Further, the furnishing and payment of medical treatment does not stop the running of the limitations of the act: Guy v. Stoecklein Baking Co., 133 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 39.

Accordingly, the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of award are hereby set aside. Order 

Claimant's petition no. 108,068 is hereby dismissed. 

Defendant's appeal is sustained.

1948] 

 WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD GEHRET v. SURE-FIT PRODUCTS COMPANY Workmen's compensation—Accidental injury-Rash caused by lint from product handled by claimant. 

An award of compensation to claimant as a result of disability caused by a severe rash will be reversed where it appears that claimant worked in defendant's plant on a material known as crasoite used in the manufacture of mattresses and that the lint from this product fell on various parts of her body causing the rash; it appearing that claimant was doing the same character of work in the manner as she was accustomed to without any unusual occurrence constituting a fortuitous happening when she became disabled, there was no accident within the meaning of the Compensation Act and likewise there was no evidence that would support an award under the Pennsylvania 

Occupational Disease Act. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Phillips, District No. 3, claim petition no. 106,436. Reversed. March 10, 1948. 

Philip J. Franzese, for claimant. 

Frank R. Ambler, for defendant. 

Ralph H. Behney, for Commonwealth.

KNOLL, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by defendant from the order of Referee 

David W. Phillips, of the Compensation District No. 3, awarding compensation to claimant herein.

On October 8, 1946, claimant filed a petition, averring that on February 20, 1946, as a result of working on material, she suffered a severe rash on the inner side of both thighs and both hands, by reason of which condition she was disabled for a period of time. To this petition responsive an-

swers were filed by defendant and by the State Workmen's Insurance Board, custodian of the Occupational Disease Fund, denying the material allegations of the said petition. 

Claimant, on her own behalf, testified, that, in the course of her employment with defendant herein, a rash broke out in the area of her limbs and arms and began to spread all over her body until the condition was checked by her doctor; that this condition originally was temporary in nature and disappeared only after a poisonous lotion and powder were applied to the affected area; that on February 20, 1946, the condition became such that she was compelled to seek medical aid and to temporarily terminate her employment with defendant herein. Claimant further testified that she was originally disabled on February 20, 1946, to March 13, 1946, and thereafter from April 20, 1946, to June 8, 1946; that upon her recovery from the condition on June 9, 1946, she obtained employment with another company and has not been affected with the condition since the time. 

It is claimant's contention that the rash heretofore referred to is the result of lint falling on her body from a product described as crasoite or crassoide used in the manufacture of mattress covers and pillow tops for hay fever sufferers.

The referee found as a fact that, as a result of the rash from which claimant suffered, she was totally disabled from February 20, 1946, to March 12, 1946, inclusive, and thereafter from March 13, 1946, to April 19, 1946, inclusive.

Based upon said findings of fact, the referee made an award to claimant herein, pursuant to the provisions of The Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act, even though the claim. petition was filed on the form designated for claims arising out of the Act of 1915, its amendments and supplements. 

From this ruling defendant has appealed.

While the petition filed by this claimant was on the form designated for claims arising out of the Act of 1915, its amendments and supplements, the referee had the authority

1948] 

 to treat the claim petition and award compensation pursuant to the provisions of The Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act, if claimant met the requirements of the act. 

The record discloses that on February 20, 1946, at which time claimant became disabled, claimant was doing the same character of work, in the same manner as she was accustomed to and there was no unusual occurrence constituting a mishap or fortuitous happening so as to constitute an accident within the meaning of the Compensation Act: Kusevich v. H. J. Heinz Company, 149 Pa. Superior Ct. 232.

Hence, claimant's remedies, if any, are under the provisions of The Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act. 

The testimony in this case discloses that claimant worked on a material known as crasoite or crassoide used for the manufacture of mattresses and pillow covers for people suffering from hay fever and that the lint from this product fell on various parts of her body, causing a rash. The testimony further discloses that claimant received treatment in the form of a lotion and powder which caused the condition to disappear until February 20, 1946, at which time claimant became disabled. There is no testimony as to the ingredients of the product or the characteristics of the lint which fell on the body of claimant. Claimant's rights, if any, are under section 108 (i) of The Pennsylvania Occupational Disease 

Act, which provides for compensation resulting from "infection or inflammation of the skin due to oils, cutting compounds, lubricants, dust, liquids, fumes, gases or vapor in any occupation involving direct contact with handling thereof or exposure thereto". There is not a scintilla of evidence which would warrant an award to claimant under this section of the act. Accordingly, we are of the opinion that the referee was in error in awarding compensation to claimant herein.

We, therefore, set aside the referee's third conclusion of law and order of award and, in lieu thereof, substitute the 

---

3. That, since claimant's disability is not the result of an accident within the meaning of The Workmen's Compensation Act, and since claimant's disability is not the result of any condition for which compensation is provided for under the provisions of The Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act, the claim petition filed by this claimant must be dismissed.

Order 

Claim petition no. 106,436, filed by claimant, Olive Seifert 

Gehret, be and the same is herewith dismissed.

The findings of fact and remaining conclusions of law of the referee are herewith affirmed. 

The appeal of defendant is sustained.

COMMON PLEAS NO. 7, PHILADELPHIA COUNTY ROHNER v. FOX PRODUCTS et al. 

Workmen's compensation-Occupational disease-Lead poisoning— 

Contributory cause of death-Award. 

1. Medical testimony to the effect that claimant's husband died from pulmonary tuberculosis which was aggravated and accelerated by lead poisoning was sufficient to sustain an award for compensation under the provisions of the Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act where it appeared that decedent had been employed in the lead plating department of defendant's plant for a period of five years immediately prior to his death; unlike disability or death due to silicosis, anthracosilicosis or asbestosis, compensation is payable under the act where the occupational disease other than those named, is a contributory or accelerating cause.

In the Court of Common Pleas No. 7 of Philadelphia 

County, no. 1532, June term, 1947. Appeals from decision of Workmen's Compensation Board. Appeals dismissed. 

March 25, 1948.

1948] 

David L. Ullman, for claimant. 

George H. Detweiler, for employer and its insurance carrier.

S. H. Torchia, for State Workmen's Insurance Fund. 

CRUMLISH, J.: 

Claimant, the widow of Franklin Rohner, filed her petition for benefits under the Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 566, sec. 101, et seq., 77 PS §1201 et seq., for the death of her husband. The referee awarded her compensation, and the Workmen's Compensation Board affirmed that award. The employer and its insurance carrier have appealed the award, as has the State 

Workmen's Compensation Fund, custodian of the Occupational Disease Fund (Pennsylvania Occupational Disease 

Act, sec. 308, as amended, June 12, 1941, P. L. 125, sec. 1, 77 PS §1408). 

Claimant's evidence established her marriage and her dependency upon deceased at the time of his death. Deceased's employment and wages were not in dispute. Claimant's further evidence showed that deceased had been employed by defendant from November 10, 1936, until January 

19, 1942, in the lead plating department, first as a wire-up man assembling plates on wires for dipping, and later as a tank man at the lead dip tanks. Defendant's business included manufacturing lead plates for batteries. The plating department was housed in a separate building, and contained three lead baths. Deceased's chief employment was at the lead tanks, and he worked on lead most of the time. 

His work at the tanks required him to lean over the sides of the tanks to put plates in and to take them out. 

Deceased was in good health up to the summer of 1941. 

He then began to lose weight, became jaundiced, developed a lead line in his teeth at the gums, had a metallic taste in his mouth and lost muscular coördination in his hands and

feet. He suffered loss of appetite, had cramps and nausea, and in the latter weeks of his life, developed a serious cough. 

His health declined until he was forced to stop work, January 19, 1942. His family physician diagnosed the condition as lead poisoning, and the employer arranged for deceased's admission to the Germantown Hospital, Philadelphia, on January 28, 1942, where he died a week later. The cause of death given was pulmonary tuberculosis.

When the referee awarded compensation, he based it upon a finding that the employe died as the result of lead poisoning. The Workmen's Compensation Board amended this and substituted its finding that death was due to pulmonary tuberculosis which was aggravated and accelerated by lead poisoning, and affirmed the award. Thereupon an appeal was entered by the employer and its insurance carrier, and also by the State fund. Discussion The respective appeals require discussion of the following three questions: 

1. Is there evidence of a substantial and competent nature to support the findings and conclusions upon which the award was based? 

2. Does death from pulmonary tuberculosis come within the provisions of the Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act when the condition is aggravated and death accelerated by lead poisoning? 

3. Is the evidence sufficient to warrant a finding that employe's exposure was of sufficient duration in point of time? 1. 

Before discussing the evidence upon which the compensation authorities made their findings, it would be well to remark that the only duty of this court is to determine whether the findings of fact as made by the referee and the board are based on legally competent evidence: Harmon v.

1948] 

Knoll, 129 Pa. Superior Ct. 390 (1937). Our review is limited to questions of law, which includes, in cases where the board has found in favor of the party having the burden of proof, whether there is competent and substantial evidence to justify the findings: Smith v. Wm. Hodges & Co., 151 Pa. Superior Ct. 14 (1942). When there is such evidence, the findings of the board are conclusive on the courts, and the evidence must be considered in a light most favorable to that party: Franks v. Point Marion Bridge Co., 128 Pa.

Superior Ct. 269 (1937). Considered in this light, the evidence supports the findings and award. The conduct of the employer's business exposed the employe to the lead hazard. 

Defendant's medical expert testified he examined employer's premises some four years after the employe's death. At this time it was admitted that conditions there were better than they had been at the time of deceased's employment. For one thing, at the time of inspection there was only one lead tank in the department, whereas at the time of deceased's employment there were three. The doctor testified there was exposure to lead. The testimony of Charles Kramer, deceased's foreman, brought out that deceased was exposed to this hazard in placing the plates in the tanks and removing them after plating. This same witness testified deceased worked most of the time at the lead tanks.

Deceased's family physician, Dr. Marks, testified that deceased was suffering from lead poisoning. His diagnosis was based upon the history of exposure to the lead hazard, the distinct dark line at the base of the teeth, the metallic taste in the mouth, the jaundice, tremor of the hands, nausea, cramps, restlessness and loss of weight. The doctor states that it was his opinion the lead poisoning aggravated the tuberculosis and accelerated death. His testimony was corroborated in this respect by that of defendants' medical expert, Dr. Aussprung. Dr. Aussprung was asked about the effect of lead poisoning on tuberculosis by claimant's counsel, as follows:

“Q. If you feel this is a proper question, all right; if you don't feel so, tell me so and I will simply drop it: Are you able to tell us, Doctor, whether it isn't a fact, a pretty well accepted fact, that if there be chronic lead poisoning present -and I am asking you to assume a chronic lead poisoning and I am asking you to assume a tubercular condition-that the effect of the chronic lead poisoning, with the various deleterious effects that it has on a human body, is to aggravate the effective of the T.B. and to hasten its progress? 

That is true, isn't it? "A. That is true."

Based on this evidence, then, it is clear that the compensation authorities had competent and substantial evidence before them to enable them to find, successively, that there was a lead hazard at his place of employment as the result of exposure to which employe contracted lead poisoning; that because of the lead poisoning, the employe's tuberculous condition was aggravated and his death accelerated. 2. 

Having concluded the evidence supports the findings and award of the compensation authorities, we come to the second problem, namely, whether death which is accelerated by the aggravating effect of lead poisoning on pulmonary tuberculosis comes within the provisions of the Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act. The employer and its insurance carrier argue, by analogy to the silicosis, anthracosilicosis and asbestosis section of the act (section 301 (e)) that occupational diseases which are the contributing or accelerating cause of death are not compensable, citing

Stuffer v. Hubley Manufacturing Co., 151 Pa. Superior Ct. 

322 (1943). These specified diseases have been treated differently for the reasons set forth in Rando v. State Work men's Insurance Fund, 145 Pa. Superior Ct. 36 (1941). This precise problem was before the Superior Court in Plaugher v. American Viscose Corp., 151 Pa. Superior Ct. 401 (1943).

1948] 

There, the analogy was discarded, and the opinion stated, at p. 407: "We must note here that unlike disability or death due to silicosis, anthraco-silicosis, or asbestosis, compensation is payable where the occupational disease-due to carbon disulphide et al.-is a contributory or accelerating cause. 

See Williams v. Susquehanna Collieries Co., 148 Pa. Superior Ct. 540, 541-543. The provision excluding contributory or accelerating causes as the basis for compensation for disability or death due to silicosis, anthraco-silicosis and asbestosis (See Stauffer v. Hubley Manufacturing 

Co., 151 Pa. Superior Ct. 322), does not apply to carbon disulphide and the other diseases catalogued in section 2, paragraph (a) to (j) inclusive." 

It is true that the Plaugher Case, supra, was decided under the Occupational Disease Compensation Act of 1937, but the same distinctions drawn there have been incorporated into the present act. The similarity of the wording employed by section 301 (c) of the Pennsylvania Occupa tional Disease Act to section 301 (c) of the Workmen's Com pensation Act (77 PS §411) compels us to follow the

Plaugher Case, supra, which, in turn follows the rule in industrial accident cases laid down in Williams v. Susquehanna Collieries Co., 148 Pa. Superior Ct. 540 (1942), as follows: 

"Unequivocal expert medical testimony that an injury is a marked contributory factor in an employe's subsequent death, or that such injury so aggravated a preëxisting condition that it accelerated his death is sufficient to establish the requisite relation or connection between the injury and the death, and meets the requirements prescribed in the decisions of our Supreme Court and of this court." 3.

Finally, the State Workmen's Compensation Fund, as custodian of the Occupational Disease Fund, takes the posi-

tion that the evidence does not support the finding that the employe's exposure was of sufficient duration to warrant contribution under section 308 (a). The evidence shows that deceased was employed in the lead plating department during the entire time of his employment, from 

November 10, 1936, until January 19, 1942, a period in excess of five years.

Order 

And now, March 25, 1948, the exceptions of the employer,

Fox Products, and Employers Liability Assurance Corpora tion, insurance carrier, defendants, and the exceptions of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania Occupational Disease 

Fund, codefendant, are severally overruled, the appeals are dismissed. The order of the Workmen's Compensation Board affirming the referee's award granting compensation is affirmed.

Accordingly, it is ordered and decreed that judgment be entered in favor of Laura Rohner, widow of Franklin Rohner, and against defendants, Fox Products, and Employer's

Liability Assurance Corporation, and codefendant, Common wealth of Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Fund, in the total sum of $3,300, to be paid at the rate of $11 per week for 300 weeks, beginning the seventh day after death, 60 percent of such compensation or the sum of $6.60 per week to be paid by Fox Products and Employers Liability As surance Corporation, and 40 percent of such compensation or the sum of $4.40 per week to be paid by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Fund, together with simple interest at six percent per annum from the respective date the weekly instalments were payable until the date on which payment thereof is actually made in accordance with this judgment.

It is further ordered and decreed that defendants, Fox 

Products and Employers Liability Assurance Corporation, and codefendant, Commonwealth of Pennsylvania Occupa-

1948] 

 tional Disease Fund shall pay on account of the expense of burial the sum of $200, 60 percent, or the sum of $120, to be paid by Fox Products and Employers Liability Assurance 

Corporation, and 40 percent, or the sum of $80, to be paid by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania Occupational Disease 

Fund. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD WADDEL v. MERCK & COMPANY Workmen's compensation-Medical and hospital expenses-Claimant covered by Blue Cross hospitalization-Employment of own doctor. 

1. A referee's award to claimant for medical and hospital expenses incurred by him as a result of an injury will be affirmed notwithstanding the fact that claimant had Blue Cross hospitalization, which organization paid his hospital expenses under its agreement with him. 

2. A claimant who had been receiving treatment from defendant's physician as the result of an injury and who suddenly became very ill, as a result of which he consulted his own physician, will be entitled to reimbursement for medical expenses, although he did not request his employer or insurance carrier to furnish such medical treatment. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Alessandroni, District No. 1, claim petition no. 107,615. Appeal dismissed. 

February 11, 1948.

American Mutual Liability Ins. Co., insurance carrier. 

Henry W. DeLuca, for claimant. 

Frederick L. Fuges, for defendant.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

Claimant was injured on January 9, 1947, while in the course of his employment. He and a group of men were carrying an iron lid weighing about 1,200 pounds when two

of the men slipped. The weight of the lid was shifted to claimant who sustained a severe strain of the back. The occurrence was immediately reported to the employer and claimant was sent to defendant's first aid dispensary where he was treated by defendant's physician. Claimant was sent home, told to stay in bed and rest. Although defendant's physician, who had prescribed heat and sedation, believed that claimant's condition became improved and he advised claimant's return to work, claimant's condition did not improve. Clamant became very ill on January 14, 1947, consulted his own physician and was referred to the Jeanes 

Hospital where he remained until January 21, 1947. Claimant lost wages from January 16, 1947, to January 27, 1947; he paid his own physician $50 and $76.54 to Jeanes Hospital. 

The referee awarded compensation for 11 days and directed defendant to reimburse claimant for his medical and hospital expenses. This appeal by defendant followed.

Defendant contests the hospital expenses because claimant did not actually pay this bill out of his own pocket. 

Claimant had Blue Cross hospitalization. This organization paid his hospital expenses under its subscription agreement with claimant. The mere fact that claimant had arranged with another person to pay those expenses, which defendant was obligated to pay, does not relieve defendant of liability. 

We are also of the opinion that claimant's sudden illness created an emergency which required immediate action. To require contacting the employer or its insurance carrier when one is suddenly stricken before seeking immediate medical treatment would be unreasonable. Claimant had been receiving treatment from defendant's physician without much avail. We believe that under the circumstances of the present case the medical and hospital expenses were properly established and should be paid by defendant. 

Accordingly, we affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and award.
