 COMMON PLEAS OF LACKAWANNA COUNTY TUMELEAVICH v. MOTLEY COAL COMPANY Workmen's compensation—Occupational disease—Rejection of provisions of Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act of 1939-Denial of claim by Workmen's Compensation Board—Action in common pleas—Alleged contractual liability of defendant to accept act— 

Collective bargaining agreement-Jurisdiction. 

1. A court has jurisdiction over an action against an employer to recover for damages arising from an occupational disease only on the theory that defendant has rejected the provisions of the Occupational Disease Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 566, as amended: It has no jurisdiction over an action to recover for such damages upon the theory that though at the time disability rose defendant had rejected the provisions of the act, it was under a contractual obligation to accept them by reason of a collective bargaining agreement with the union of which plaintiff was a member. 

2. It seems that the Workmen's Compensation Board should, under section 423 of the Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act of June 21, 1939, as amended, permit a claimant to take an appeal after the time therefor has expired from an order of a referee denying compensation for an occupational disease on the ground that defendant had rejected the provisions of the Occupational Disease Act, where claimant failed to contend before the referee defendant was under a contractual obligation to accept the provisions of the act and subsequently mistakenly raised that contention in a court action.

In the Court of Common Pleas of Lackawanna County, September term, 1947, no. 1098. Preliminary objections to complaint. Action dismissed. October 31, 1947. 

Pearson M. Judd, for claimant. 

Frank M. McDonald and Joseph T. McDonald, for defendant.

HOBAN, J.: 

The complaint according to its form is in assumpsit, but the fact upon which it is based, to wit, disability arising

from an occupational disease, would make the case one of trespass if it could be the subject of direct litigation in this court. Plaintiff alleges that he was disabled by anthracosilicosis as of July 26, 1946, after more than four years' employment with defendant company under conditions exposing him to a silica hazard. Plaintiff on January 7, 1947, within one year from the date of his disability, filed a claim against defendant with the Workmen's Compensation Board. 

By an order filed March 25, 1947, Referee David W. Phillips, of the Third District, dismissed plaintiff's claim petition for want of jurisdiction, for the reason that at the time the disability occurred defendant company had rejected the elective provisions of the Pennsylvania Occupational Disease 

Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 566, as amended, 77 PS §1401 

et seq., and that defendant did not accept the elective provisions of the act until October 1, 1946. In the opinion of the referee, the Workmen's Compensation Board has no jurisdiction to consider this claim under the circumstances. 

In this complaint plaintiff alleges that as a member of the United Mine Workers of America he ought to have the benefit of certain provisions of the contract between the 

United Mine Workers and the Anthracite Coal Operators, to which defendant is a party, of June 7, 1946. The provisions of the contract in question are set forth in the complaint as follows: 

"5. It is agreed that for the duration of this Agreement each signatory operator shall accept the Workmen's Compensation Law and the Pennsylvania Occupational Disease 

Law of June 21, 1939 as amended May 18, 1945." "10. This agreement is an integrated instrument and its respective provisions are interdependent and shall be effective from May 31, 1946 subject to approval of appropriate 

Governmental Agencies."

It is plaintiff's theory that by the provisions of the contract quoted above, defendant committed itself to accept the provisions of the Occupational Disease Act as to elective compensation from May 31, 1946, and the amount of money

1948] 

 he claims is the limit authorized by section 301 of the act as amended by Act of May 18, 1945, P. L. 661, 77 PS §1401.

It does not appear from the opinion of Referee Phillips, nor from the complaint, that the provisions of the contract above cited were brought to the attention of the referee or the board, and no appeal apparently was taken from the decision of the referee to the Workmen's Compensation Board. Obviously, if the contract is not to be considered, the decision of the referee was correct, for no jurisdiction was given to the Workmen's Compensation Board to determine cases arising under the elective compensation features of the act unless both parties in accordance with the act had accepted article 3. But the question raised by the complaint ought to be litigated. Our difficulty is that it cannot be determined in this proceeding for if, as a matter of fact, plaintiff is entitled to the benefits of the elective compensation features of the act, the procedure to determine his rights must be taken in accordance with the act and facts found by the compensation board to determine the cause, extent and duration of the disability claimed. It seems to us that the proper procedure would have been to appeal from the decision of the referee and argue the question of defendant's liability to pay elective compensation before the Workmen's Compensation Board in the first instance, and if compensation was denied there, then to appeal to the court of common pleas. This court has no power to act as a fact-finding agency in a claim for elective compensation benefits. If a claim is brought into this court for damages by reason of an occupational disease, it must be based on the theory of nonacceptance of the act and pleaded as in trespass. 

The preliminary objection here is in the nature of a demurrer, and as to this action of assumpsit it must be sustained. But plaintiff is not without a remedy. While the time for appeal from a decision of the referee to the board has passed, section 423 of the act authorizes the board to extend the time provided for taking an appeal upon cause shown, and in view of the importance of the question in-

volved it would not seem probable that the board would deny this plaintiff the right to take his appeal simply because he has mistaken his remedy in an effort to secure a determination of the legal question involved. 

Now, October 31, 1947, the preliminary objection in the nature of a demurrer is sustained for the reason that the complaint does not state a cause of action cognizable in this court, and the action is dismissed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD JONES v. JOHN WOOD MFG. CO., INC. 

Workmen's compensation-Dependent-Posthumous illegitimate child -Act of May 18, 1945. 

A referee's award to the guardian of a posthumous child of decedent based on his finding that the child was a member of decedent's household at the time of his death and dependent upon him for support will be set aside where it appears that the child was illegitimate; under section 307 of the Act of May 18, 1945, P. L. 671, defining the class of dependents and providing that the term "child" shall include posthumous children, a posthumous illegitimate child is excluded. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Clayton, District No. 1, claim petition no. 107,298, accident no. 4,773,506. 

Award vacated. February 18, 1948.

Liberty Mutual Insurance Co., insurance carrier. 

Herbert C. Nelson, for claimant. 

J. Paul Erwin, for defendant.

1948] 

 JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by defendant, the John Wood Manufacturing Co., from that portion of an order entered by Referee 

Clayton, July 22, 1947, which directs payments of compensation to be made in behalf of an illegitimate posthumous child.

Harvey Jones died on January 23, 1946, as a result of an accident which occurred January 16, 1946, in the course of his employment with defendant. His wife, who bore him a son, Robert, November 12, 1936, now living with his grandmother, Minnie Kitte (See petition no. 107,453), predeceased him by five or six years. Thereafter he took up common abode with Sarah R. Jones, who lived with him in meretricious relationship from September 26, 1944, until the date of his death. Of this union which admittedly has the benefit of neither formal nor common-law marriage ceremony, two sons were born. They were named Harold and Harvey 

Jones. Harold was born June 22, 1945, and decedent supported him in his home and assumed a natural parental attitude toward him. Harvey, however, was born July 21, 1946, after his father's death and decedent, therefore, never had the opportunity to so evidence acceptance of him as a son.

On the basis of the state of facts above mentioned, as to which no substantial dispute is discernible, defendant has appealed from the award to a guardian for Harvey, and has assigned as error the referee's fifth finding of fact upon which the award objected to was made. The finding of fact referred to is stated as follows: "5. Harold Jones born June 22, 1945 and Harvey Jones, posthumous child, born July 21, 1946, were children of 

Sarah and Harvey Jones. Harold was a member of decedent's household at the time of his death and dependent upon him for support."

In our opinion the quoted finding of fact which sets forth the actual situation on the basis of the evidence in the record, does not support the award under the law as it has

been construed by the authorities to which we are amenable. 

The portion of the Act of May 18, 1945, P. L. 671, applicable to the case is the 7th paragraph of section 307. The sentence therein defining the class of dependents with which we are concerned here reads: "If members of decedent's household at the time of his death, the terms 'child' and 'children' shall include step children, adopted children and children to whom he stood in loco parentis, and shall include posthumous children."

That sentence has remained the same in context in all the amendments except that the amendment of June 21, 1939 P. L. 520, took the clause "If members of decedent's household at the time of his death" out of its original position between the word "parentis" and the clause having to do with posthumous children and placed it where quoted above, thus sacrificing some grammar to the danger of legal misconstruction. The courts have held that the word "child" so used means only and exclusively a legitimate child. (Overseers v. Overseers, 176 Pa. 116) and that a posthumous illegitimate child, as such, is not within the contemplation of the legislation (Gierak v. L. & W. B. Coal Co., 101 

Pa. Superior Ct. 397) particularly because of the impossibility of proving that such a child was a member of a decedent's household at the time of his death or had become the recipient of the necessary parental attention (Smrekar v. Jones & Laughlin Steel Corp., 137 Pa. Superior Ct. 183).

In the face of such judicial pronouncements there is nothing we can do but very reluctantly strike out the portion of the award complained of by defendant. The 5th finding of fact as it is stated is consistent with the action we must take under the law and must therefore stand. 

The findings of fact and first conclusion of law of Referee 

Clayton dated July 22, 1947, are affirmed.

The second conclusion of law of Referee Clayton dated July 22, 1947, is modified, substituting for the words "dependents are" the words "dependent son Harold is" and as so modified the said conclusion of law is affirmed.

1948]  

The following conclusion of law is supplied: 

3. Harvey Jones, born July 21, 1946, being a posthumous illegitimate child, is not entitled to compensation. 

The award of Referee Clayton dated July 22, 1947, is vacated and set aside and the following substituted therefor: Award

Defendant is ordered to pay compensation in this case as follows: 

To the guardian of Harold Jones $4.455 per week from 

January 30, 1946, to October 31, 1951, the end of the 300week period; then $3.50 per week from November 1, 1951, to November 12, 1952, when Robert B. Jones (see petition no. 107,453) becomes 16 years of age and then $4.453 per week from November 13, 1952, to June 22, 1961, when Harold Jones becomes 16 years of age. 

The appeal is sustained.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD GIANNETTI v. M. C. SEIB COMPANY Workmen's compensation-Award for partial disability-Suspension of payments—Application to reinstate-Time for making. 

Where, following an award for partial disability and suspension of compensation payments thereunder until claimant showed a loss of earning power, defendant filed a petition to terminate compensation as a result of which an award was entered for further payments to the end of the 400-week period during which compensation for partial disability was payable, the award was not barred because of claimant's failure to ask for it within one year from the date of the last payment of compensation nor because the 400-week period had expired before his application was filed to have the suspension order lifted.

Appeal by defendant from order of Referee Clayton, District No. 1, dismissing petition for termination under compensation agreement no. 9.058,536. Appeal dismissed. February 18, 1948. 

New Amsterdam Casualty Co., insurance carrier. 

A. F. Barbieri, for claimant. 

Raymond A. White, Jr., for defendant.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

On May 25, 1939, claimant was injured while in the course of his employment with defendant. On June 23, 1939, the parties executed an open agreement in which the accident and injury were described as follows: "Pulling rope on wheelbarrow, slipped on grass, and fell to ground. Fracture of lower third of tibia and neck of fibula, right."

Compensation for total disability was paid claimant at the rate of $15.60 per week until February 1, 1940, when defendant filed a petition to terminate. After hearing, the referee on October 24, 1941, found that claimant's disability changed on February 5, 1940, from total to 25 percent partial and ordered the payment of compensation at $3.90 per week from February 5, 1940, to May 21, 1941, when compensation was suspended until such time as claimant showed a loss of earning power. On March 4, 1947, defendant filed a petition to terminate alleging that claimant has sustained no loss of earning power from May 31, 1941, to date and that the 400-week period for the payment of compensation for partial disability had expired. Claimant filed an answer alleging that beginning March 9, 1943, claimant had again sustained a loss of earning power and requested compensation therefor. The referee awarded compensation for 25 percent partial disability to the end of the 400-week period. 

This appeal by defendant followed.

1948] 

Defendant contends that since the order of suspension was entered on October 25, 1941, and claimant did not request to have it vacated until March of 1947, the award is barred because the claim to reinstate was not filed first, within one year from the last payment of compensation and second, because the 400-week period during which compensation for partial disability was payable had expired.

The answer to defendant's first contention is found in the recent case of Holtz v. McGraw & Bindley et al., 161 Pa.

Superior Ct. 371. An order of suspension merely holds in abeyance the payment of compensation and agreements or awards made the basis of such payments until a change in disability or earning power is shown by the party on whom the burden rested when the order of suspension was entered. 

The one-year period of limitations is not applicable because the agreement or award has not been terminated and there has been no last payment of compensation: Stanella v. 

Scranton Coal Co., 122 Pa. Superior Ct., 505, 512, 513.

Defendant had instituted a proceeding to terminate its liability for compensation after payment of compensation was suspended. It does not contend that claimant was not entitled to compensation from March 9, 1943, but contends that he was too late in demanding payment. If claimant had applied for a reinstatement of compensation because his disability had increased and no order of suspension had been made we would be required to apply the bar of limitations. 

The order of suspension fixed defendant's liability for compensation on March 31, 1941.

In the cases of Stanella v. Scranton Coal Co., supra, and 

Angelo v. Keystone Construction Co., 134 Pa. Superior Ct. 

255, the petitions were filed by claimants more than one year after the last payments of compensation but awards were sustained because the compensation due had been held in abeyance. See Augustine v. Evert Lumber Co., 134 Pa.

Superior Ct. 167, where claimant's petition, filed after the 

300-week period, the maximum provided for in the earlier act, was held to be in time.

We are of the opinion that claimant's evidence showed a loss of earning power from March 9, 1943, that defendant's liability to pay compensation which had been postponed was then outstanding in the same fashion as if no payments had been made by defendant on an award of compensation. 

Accordingly, the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order are affirmed.  

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD UMBENHAUER v. BOYD Workmen's compensation-Employe-Independent contractor—Mining coal-Illegal enterprise.

A referee's order dismissing a claim petition will be affirmed where it appeared that claimant, who was injured while preparing to remove coal from a coal mine hole, had made an agreement with defendant, engaged in the trucking business, whereby the latter was to pay claimant a certain price for each ton of coal mined, it further appearing, however, that the land upon which the mining was conducted was owned by a county, and that neither defendant nor plaintiff had the right to remove coal; under the circumstances, the referee properly found that claimant was an independent contractor and as such not entitled to compensation; further than that, claimant being engaged in an illegal enterprise, of which fact he had knowledge, was barred from receiving compensation.

Appeal by claimant from order of Referee Enterline, District No. 5, dismissing claim petition no. 106,847, accident no. 4,864,057. Appeal dismissed. March 10, 1948. 

Joseph S. Lilienthal, for claimant. 

Ralph M. Bashore and Arthur H. Schrager, for defendant.

1948] 

 KNOLL, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by claimant from the order of Referee L. E. Enterline, District No. 5, dismissing the claim petition filed on behalf of claimant. 

On November 12, 1946, claimant filed his petition averring, inter alia, that he sustained certain injuries on April 12, 1946, while acting within the course of his employment with defendant herein. To this petition a responsive answer was filed by defendant, denying the allegations of the said petition.

The testimony discloses, and it is not denied, that claimant sustained an accident on April 12, 1946, resulting in claimant's suffering a fracture of the left femur and fracture of the tibia and fibula of the right leg, causing claimant to be totally disabled to January 6, 1947, and thereafter partially disabled to the extent of 25 percent. The sole issues in this case are whether or not claimant was an employe within the meaning of the Compensation Act, at the time of the accident, and whether or not claimant was engaged in an illegal enterprise at the aforesaid time.

There was testimony presented in this case, which, if believed by the referee, would warrant a finding that sometime prior to April 1, 1946, a meeting took place between claimant and defendant, at which time claimant requested information of defendant as to whether or not defendant knew a coal hole which could be worked by claimant; and that defendant advised claimant that there was a coal hole available which had previously been worked by two miners named Peterson and Fleming. There was also testimony to the effect which, if believed by the referee, would warrant a finding that, at the time of the aforesaid meeting, claimant agreed to work the mine hole and deliver the coal to defendant, who was engaged in the trucking business, and that defendant would pay claimant the sum of $7 for each ton of coal mined. There is also testimony to the effect that, pursuant to the said agreement, on or about April 1, 1946,

claimant and his son began to work on the coal hole in preparation for removing the coal in the said hole and that on April 12, 1946, while this work was being done, claimant was injured. It likewise appears from the testimony that, following claimant's removal to the hospital, claimant's wife was paid the sum of $35 for five tons of coal delivered to defendant, apparently pursuant to the agreement heretofore referred to.

It also appears from the testimony, and it is not disputed, that the land upon which the operation was conducted was owned by Schuylkill County by virtue of unpaid taxes and that neither defendant nor claimant had the right to remove the coal from the said land. There is likewise credible testimony to the effect that claimant knew that neither he nor defendant had the right to remove the coal from the said land.

We have concluded, from a careful study of the testimony, that there was sufficient competent testimony presented to warrant the referee's finding that claimant was an independent contractor at the time of the accident of April 12, 1946, and therefore, not an employe within the meaning of the Compensation Act. As was pointed out by the court in 

Coccaro v. Herman Coal Co. et al., 145 Pa. Superior Ct. 81, an employer as such is not entitled to compensation under the act, as one cannot become an employe of himself and thus occupy the anomalous position of both employer and employe, defined by the act as the equivalent of master and servant.

We have likewise concluded that, at the time of the accident, claimant was engaged in an illegal enterprise of which fact claimant had knowledge and by reason thereof, claimant is barred from the benefits of the Compensation Act: Garan sosky v. Chervanik, 29 D. & C. 88; Pepper v. Dorinzo, 9 

Schuyl. Reg. 149.

We, therefore, affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of dismissal.

1948] 

 WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD FRIEDERIKA v. ST. BONIFACE CHURCH Workmen's compensation—Jurisdiction of board-Person engaged in domestic service- -Insurance policy. 

The Workmen's Compensation Board does not have jurisdiction over a claim for compensation arising against an insurance carrier out of a policy issued by it covering a person exempted under the Workmen's Compensation Act of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, claimant being a member of a religious order employed in domestic duties in defendant church; jurisdiction of the board could not be conferred by consent or agreement of the parties nor did the evidence warrant application of the principle of estoppel. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Olexy, District No. 2, claim petition no. 87,927. Appeal dismissed. 

April 7, 1948. 

Desmond K. Kennedy, for claimant. 

Edward J. Kelley, for defendant. 

Walter W. Harris, for insurance carrier.

KNOLL, Commissioner: 

After our opinion in the within case was filed, the London Guarantee and Accident Company, the insurance carrier herein, petitioned the board for a rehearing. The petition for rehearing alleged: "7. In its decision, the compensation board concluded that your petitioner, as insurance carrier, had accepted a premium on its policy based on the employment of claimant as an employe of St. Boniface Church, and was therefore estopped from denying coverage under the policy, and from denying that the policy included claimant as a member of

an order, in accordance with a rider and agreement attached to said policy. "8. Your petitioner represents that the insurance policy, which is the subject of this suit, provided that the premium should be based upon a payroll audit, that the payroll was audited by the insurance carrier, your petitioner, in July of 1941, subsequent to the last hearing before the referee, and the premium in connection with this policy, as finally adjusted, did not include the wages or salary paid by the St. Boniface Church to claimant or other members of her order, so that your petitioner did not receive any premium based upon any employment or payment of wages to claimant or other members of the order alleged to have been employed by St. Boniface Church, named as employerdefendant."

Claimant filed an answer thereto, averring that a premium was charged by the insurance carrier and paid by the insured to cover compensation insurance for claimant; that testimony taken before a referee disclosed that the policy in effect was a nonaudit policy; that the premium was fixed especially by information submitted to the company in answer to a questionnaire; and that an audit was not necessary and no refund was ever made by the insurance carrier, because of alleged elimination of coverage of claimant, Sister Friederika.

The board granted the rehearing and testimony was subsequently taken before one of the members of the Workmen's Compensation Board. At this hearing, additional testimony was received which brought forth additional evidence pertaining to the workmen's compensation policy issued by defendant covering all of the parishes in the Scranton Diocese of the Roman Catholic Church. Before we discuss this additional testimony, we believe it would be of assistance to a better comprehension of our decision by quoting parts of our first opinion, which sets forth the facts and issues as set before us in the first instance, to wit:

1948] 

"Claimant was, on November 2, 1940, a member of a religious order, known as St. Boniface Roman Catholic Congregation of Williamsport-a teaching order, organized within the Roman Catholic Church. On the above date, the convent was comprised of 15 teaching nuns and three domestic nuns, to which latter class claimant belonged. The duties of claimant consisted generally in domestic functions, caring for the wants of the teaching sisters and laundering church linens. "The question before us is as to the interpretation of the contract between the defendant and its insurance carrier, the London Guarantee & Accident Company, Limited, as affecting accidental claims brought by individuals standing in the same relationship to defendant as did claimant herein. "At the outset it must be observed that a contract of insurance is, in law, no different from any other written contract and is subject to the same rules of interpretation which affect all agreements between individuals; though, by reason of public policy, contracts of insurance are subject to more rigid control and supervision. In the absence of ambiguity or provisions which fail to conform to the requirements of the Insurance Code or other regulatory legislation, the same are subject to sensible and literal interpretation by the courts of this Commonwealth. "The policy now under consideration was issued May 15, 1940, and was duly approved by the Insurance Commissioner of this Commonwealth. The insurance contract was, on May

""This endorsement becomes effective at 12:01 A. M. 

May 15th, 1940. ""This endorsement is hereby made a part of Policy No.

"The above endorsement became a part of said insurance contract under circumstances which are set forth in the following stipulation filed by counsel to this action: 66 ...9 "Now, 21 day of November, 1941, it is stipulated between counsel for St. Boniface's Church, Defendant, and counsel for London Guarantee Accident Company, Ltd., that for the purpose of this appeal before the Board, the Board may consider that the endorsement on the policy, known as "Roman Catholic Church Endorsement" found on page 17 of the record, was placed on said policy on August 1940, effective as of the date of the policy, namely May 15, 1940, and that said endorsement was promulgated by Pennsylvania Compensation Rating and Inspection Bu reau, Philadelphia, a department or bureau under the Insurance Commissioner of the State of Pennsylvania, and that said endorsement was attached to said policy by said company unwillingly on the orders of said Bureau and not at their own initiative and not at their own desire or desire of St. Boniface Church, or Bishop Hafey, acting for them as Trustee, but because said Bureau insisted that said endorsement must be on said policy. This stipulation is for the purpose of this case and may be considered as a fact as if the same had been testified to at a hearing held in the said matter.' Since the activity and work so conducted is diversified and subject to wide variance as to scope, it was customary to issue certificates of specific coverage which re-

This particular group was covered by a certificate, issued by the insurer, designed to cover this specific risk under the master policy. "The contractual obligations which existed between defendant herein and its insurer must be arrived at by a consideration of the master contract, the endorsement thereon, and the certificate above set forth."

At the hearing upon the petition for a rehearing, defendant, Elmer Lang, testified that he was resident manager of the London Guarantee and Accident Company and acted in that capacity on May 15, 1940, the date when the policy in question was issued. His testimony explains that when the present policy was originally written, it included an estimated payroll for the various sisters in the diocese. After the policy was written, a copy was filed with the Pennsylvania Rating Board, which board subsequently advised the insurance carrier that it was improper for them to issue a policy covering the sisters, because they were excluded under the Workmen's Compensation Act. Mr. Lang further testified that the aforesaid Rating Board required his company to issue what is known as the Roman Catholic Church endorsement, excluding the sisters as of the date of issue of the policy, and that said endorsement was to be attached to the original policy. When this endorsement was issued, a copy was sent to Edward F. C. McLaughlin, who was acting as agent for Bishop William J. Hafey of the Scranton Diocese.

Mr. McLaughlin, then called upon as a witness, explained that a portion of the deposit premium paid the insurance company applied to the coverage of the sisters in the sum of approximately $500, and that, since the policy was issued, certain accidents occurred and that the company had paid workmen's compensation in about the same amount as the premium paid. Mr. McLaughlin decided that the diocese would keep the money they received for the workmen's compensation for the injuries incurred by the various sisters and the insurance carrier would keep the premiums. This was the way a set-off was contemplated by the insurance carrier and defendant. The policy, however, was a master policy to cover all of the parishes and, in its audit, carried

1948] 

 eighteen sisters, which included Sister Friederika, claimant herein.

Defendant also called David LaRocque, who testified that he was in charge of the compensation underwriting department of the insurance carrier; and that he had charge of the audits of compensation policies for the carrier. He explained how the audits were made and, upon cross-examination, admitted that it was purely an oral arrangement between the insurance carrier and Mr. McLaughlin and that the final adjustment of the premium did not take place until the term of the policy had expired. 

Mr. McLaughlin testified that he was the insurance broker, that he was the agent for the London Guarantee and Accident Insurance Company; and that he had an oral agreement with Bishop Hafey to care for the premiums of various institutions and parishes. Mr. McLaughlin denied that he discussed the matter of a set-off of the premium with Mr. 

Lang and that he had any agreement with Bishop Hafey that this set-off should take place. 

The additional testimony brought forth the issue of a set-off affecting the validity of the policy covering the 18 sisters contained in the audit attached to the policy. It appears to us that the set-off was attempted to be made, but, in reality, was not carried out to completion until the policy had expired and bookkeeping of the insured and the insurance company affected the alleged set-off. 

The rehearing also gave us additional evidence which threw light upon the issue involved, to wit: Did the policy issued by the London Guarantee and Accident Insurance 

Company cover claimant, who was a domestic, for injuries received under the Workmen's Compensation Act?

As stated in our former opinion, claimant herein must be considered as a domestic. When the parties entered into the insurance contract, they insured St. Boniface Church for workmen's compensation and included a number of sisters who are considered as domestics and not covered by the 

Workmen's Compensation Act. What, therefore, is the lia-

bility in the event a policy is issued to cover persons who are exempt from workmen's compensation under the Work men's Compensation Act of the Commonwealth of Penn sylvania?

The general principle of law is that parties to a suit cannot, by consent, confer jurisdiction with respect to the subject matter of litigation either by stipulation or agreement; as jurisdiction is fixed by law, it is beyond the control of the parties. Wolf et al. v. Lewisburg T. & S. Deposit Co., 305 

Pa. 583, 558.

In Thompson v. Parke, 131 Pa. Superior Ct. 81, where a policy contained an endorsement with voluntary compensation coverage, which provided that the insurance carrier insure the employer of farm laborers against personal injuries sustained in the course of employment, in accordance with the liability for compensation benefits under the Workmen's Compensation Act, the claim petition was dismissed and the court said: "The endorsement did not and could not confer jurisdiction on the compensation board. The legislature unequivocally said that the Board is not authorized to hear and determine claims arising from employment in agriculture. That is decisive; its jurisdiction cannot be changed or enlarged by contract or consent. 'It is a well settled principle of law that parties to a suit cannot by consent confer jurisdiction with respect to the subject-matter of litigation, either by stipulation or agreement; as jurisdiction is fixed by law, it is beyond the control of the parties': Wolfe et al. v. Lewisburg T. & S. Deposit Co., 305 Pa. 583. See also Blumenthal's Est., 227 Pa. 268; Rosenberry v. Gillan Bros. et al., 130 Pa. Superior Ct. 469."

We have also taken into consideration the principle of estoppel and have carefully reviewed all of the acts and deeds of the respective parties and cannot conclude that the conduct of the insurance carrier, of claimant or of the representatives of the Scranton Diocese was such as to estop

1948] 

 the carrier from objecting to the jurisdiction of the workmen's compensation authorities. In the case of Rosenberry v. Gillan Bros., 130 Pa. Superior Ct. 469, the employe was engaged in agricultural employment. The insurance carrier, under the provisions of the policy covering personal injuries to insured's employes, paid compensation for the loss of claimant's middle finger. Later, on a claim petition, additional compensation was awarded for the loss of the use of the third finger. From this award defendant appealed, challenging the finding of fact and jurisdiction. Claimant pleaded estoppel. The court, in its opinion, said: 66 “As a general proposition, jurisdiction over the subjectmatter cannot be conferred by estoppel or even by agreement of the parties, particularly when the legislature has expressly withheld it from the administrative tribunal which seeks to exercise it: Wettengel v. Robinson et al., 288 Pa. 

362; Bluestone v. DeRoy et al., 298 Pa. 267. If claimant was engaged in agriculture, the Board and its referees never had jurisdiction to entertain her claim petition. Such a lack of jurisdiction could be raised at any stage of the proceedings." 

We also carefully reviewed the evidence pertaining to the set-off and, although the testimony is not quite clear, we are able to conclude that the Scranton Diocese finally got credit for the money paid to its respective parishes for compensation paid to other sisters. This set-off in premium has also led us to the conclusion that there was nothing in the conduct of the respective parties which might lead to an estoppel.

It is, therefore, our opinion that the Workmen's Compensation Board does not have jurisdiction over the within claim and we, accordingly, set aside our former opinion and herewith affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and his dismissal of the claim against the insurance carrier and the granting of the award against St. Boniface 

Church, defendant herein. 

The appeal of defendant is dismissed.

[84 Dep. Rep. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD HARTMANN v. STATE WORKMEN'S INSURANCE FUND Workmen's compensation-Volunteer fireman-Operation of own business-Compensation based on earnings from business. 

A person injured while acting as a volunteer fireman who operated his own business, receiving no wage excepting profits from his business, is entitled to have the earnings from his business taken into consideration in computing his average weekly wage to determine the amount of his compensation. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Clayton, District No. 1, claim petition, no. 109,859, accident no. 

4,980,281. Affirmed, April 28, 1948.

State Workmen's Insurance Fund, insurance carrier. 

Philip J. Franzese, for claimant. 

Ralph H. Behney, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This case is before the Workmen's Compensation Board upon an appeal by McKinley Fire Company, defendant, from an award in favor of Carl A. Hartmann, claimant. 

The facts are not in dispute. Claimant is a member of the McKinley Volunteer Fire Company of Abington Town ship, Pa. While operating a pumper on February 16, 1947, at the scene of a fire, a hose coupling blew off and a stream of steam and hot water struck claimant and scalded him. 

He sustained burns on both legs and his abdomen. Claimant is in the roofing and tinning business. Due to his injuries, he was unable to work for a period of six weeks; it was agreed that his weekly earnings for personal services rendered are over $30 per week.

1948] 

The sole question before us on this appeal is whether claimant's earnings from his business should be taken into account in computing his average weekly wage. Defendant concedes that claimant is entitled to the minimum compen sation, under the Workmen's Compensation Act. 

The question raised is unique on its particular factual situation. We find no appellate authority to govern us. 

We held in the case of Fitzgerald v. Muhlenberg Township School District (A-26583, 1941) that the earnings of a physician in his private practice may not be considered in computing his compensation where he was also a paid employe of the school board and sustained a fatal injury during the course of his employment. That decision does not bind us here for the reasons set forth hereinafter. 

Volunteer firemen have been given the status of employes by legislative enactment. See 77 PS §22 (a). The interest of the public so required. Volunteer firemen are the only group of persons, as a class, specifically designated as employes. Being so singled out was obviously no accident. 

These men serve the public and their community without pay and at great personal danger to themselves. They are a necessity in any community where, for economic reasons, no paid group of firemen exists. The welfare of the community dictated that they be given protection under the 

Workmen's Compensation Law. 

The wage earner who acts as a volunteer fireman, if injured while actually engaged as a fireman, may recover compensation based upon his earnings in his separate employment. We are compelled to hold that the volunteer fireman who operates his own business and receives no wage but profit from his business, is entitled to have his earnings from his business taken into consideration, if he is injured while acting as a fireman. An opposite ruling would tend to deter professional and business men from serving their community in the capacity of volunteer firemen. It is not our belief that the legislature intended to discriminate be-

[84 Dep. Rep. 

tween wage earners acting as volunteer firemen and professional and business men so acting. 

In the Fitzgerald case cited above, the deceased physician received a wage from the township. He received a financial remuneration for his employment; he was paid for his services to the township. We cannot place a volunteer fireman in the same category.

We affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and award. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD GREYER v. AIR COOLED WHEEL CORP. 

Workmen's compensation-Accidental injury-Death following inhalation of antimony fumes-Condition not incident to decedent's normal employment.

Evidence that decedent, a salesman employed by defendant, who was engaged in the abrasive grinding wheels business, helped to finish and refinish some wheels because of the urgent need for them on a certain date, as a result of which he inhaled antimony fumes and that his so doing either caused his death or aggravated a preëxisting anemic condition which thereby hastened his death would be sufficient to constitute an accident within the meaning of the Workmen's Compensation Act, as the work performed by defendant was not done in the normal and regular course of his employment; however, where the medical testimony was in irreconcilable conflict as to whether there was a causal relation between decedent's death and the inhalation of the antimony fumes, a referee's order disallowing compensation will be set aside and the case remanded for the appointment of an impartial medical expert to examine the record and thereafter testify.

Appeal by claimant from award of Referee Clayton, claim petition no. 99,489. Remanded April 7, 1948.

1948] 

Henry A. Frye, for claimant. 

Frank R. Ambler, for defendant. 

Ralph H. Behney, for Commonwealth.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

This is an appeal by claimant from an order of the referee dismissing her claim petition. 

The record discloses that, on July 5, 1944, claimant filed her petition, as dependent widow of Charles H. Greyer, in which she alleged that decedent died on March 24, 1944, as a result of a gastric hemorrhage resulting from monocytic leukemia and chronic antimony poisoning suffered in the course of his employment with defendant between November 10, 1943, and November 13, 1943. 

Defendant's answer, filed on July 21, 1944, denied the happening of an accident or of any accidental injury causing death. After hearings, the referee found that nothing of an accidental nature occurred in the course of decedent's employment and that an autopsy performed after decedent's death showed the cause of death to be hemohistioblastic leukemia and, in accordance with such findings, dismissed claimant's petition. This appeal followed. 

After carefully reviewing the entire record in the instant case, we are of the opinion that the interests of justice require us to secure the testimony of an impartial medical expert before making a final determination of the issue here raised.

From a review of all the evidence here presented, we are convinced that decedent was suffering from an anemic condition, for which he was being treated, during the period between July 10, 1943, and November 12, 1943; that, on 

November 12, 1943, he was exposed to the antimony fumes and, on the same evening, exhibited one of the symptoms of antimony poisoning; that, thereafter, his blood condition

became rapidly worse; that on December 28, 1943, a bone marrow biopsy showed megaloblastic anemia, together with depression of the leukocytes; that biopsy performed on 

March 10, 1944, also showed this condition, together with the fact that there was antimony present in decedent's system.

The testimony further shows that decedent was employed as a salesman by defendant company, who were engaged in the abrasive grinding wheels business and, in the manufacture of its product, defendant did the finishing and also attempted to correct wheels which had been rejected by the purchasers thereof for some defect; that, in refinishing the wheels it was necessary to melt the bushing, the metal of which was 88 percent lead and 12 percent antimony, so that it could be removed and replaced with another bushing; that in the doing of this work, lead and antimony fumes were given off; that, because of the urgent need for wheels, decedent helped to finish and refinish some on November 12, 1943.

The first question for our determination is whether, even if it be admitted that decedent did inhale antimony fumes and that his so doing either caused his death or aggravated his preëxisting anemic condition which thereby hastened his death, his so doing constitutes an accident within the meaning of the Workmen's Compensation Act. In our opin ion, the inhalation of antimony fumes by decedent in the course of his employment on November 12, 1943, was an accident and, if it resulted either in his death or the aggravation of a preëxisting condition, defendant would be liable for the payment of compensation under the act. As was stated by the court in Johnston v. Orcutt, 103 Pa. Superior

Ct. 503, in which case decedent, employed by defendant as an automobile mechanic, became ill of noxious gases while repairing an automobile and four months later died of endocarditis accompanied by blood stream infection and fibrosis and in which case testimony was given that a chronic lung ailment suffered by claimant prior to the inhalation of

1948] 

 the noxious gas and fumes had aggravated and accelerated the injury to the lungs and contributed directly to his death: "The issue is whether the death of the employee occurred in an ordinary way, natural to the progress of the disease with which he was afflicted prior to the time of the occurrence, or whether inhalation of noxious gases in the course of his employment on that date aggravated a preëxisting and chronic . . . condition . . . and accelerated its fatal termination. If his demise was brought about by an injury accidentally suffered during the course of his employment, the fact that he had a chronic ailment, which rendered him more susceptible to such injury than an ordinary person would be, will not defeat the right to compensation. Jones v. United Iron & Metal Co., 99 Pa. Superior Ct. 394."

In addition, it has been expressly held by our appellate courts that death resulting from carbon monoxide poisoning or from heat exhaustion constitutes an accidental injury within the meaning of the Workmen's Compensation Act, even where decedent, in the course of his employment has been subjected to such poisoning and noxious gases for a number of days: Gerst v. Smith-Faris Co., 107 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 30. See also Pataky v. Allen Motor Co. et al., 100 Pa.

Superior Ct. 343; DiMarcantonio v. State Fund, 15 D. & C. 

56; Clems v. Cornish, 295 Pa. 73; Matis v. Schaeffer, 270 

Pa. 141; Lane v. Horn & Hardart Baking Co., 261 Pa. 320.

To our minds, there is no distinction whereby the inhalation of carbon monoxide would constitute an accident but the inhalation of equally dangerous fumes of antimony would not. Thus, if there is present, and it appears to us that there is in this case, sufficient proof to show that decedent, who was then engaged in doing work for defendant other than that to be done in the normal and regular course of his employment, inhaled antimony fumes which either caused his death or aggravated a preëxisting condition, it is an accident within the purview of the act. 

In arguing that claimant has failed to prove the happening of an accident defendant has cited the cases of Micale

v. Light & State Workmen's Insurance Fund, 105 Pa. Su perior Ct. 399, and Kusevich v. H. J. Heinz Co., 149 Pa.

Superior Ct. 232. 

We have carefully reviewed those cases and are of the opinion that they are not controlling in this case. In both of those cases, the employe, on the date of the alleged accident, was doing the same character of work and in the same manner that he was accustomed to with no unusual occurrence constituting a mishap or fortuitous accident: Adamchick v. Wyoming Valley Collieries Co., 332 Pa. 401. Thus, the distinguishing feature between the cases cited by defendant and the instant one is the fact that, in the cases cited by defendant, there was no unusual occurrence or untoward happening aside from the usual course of events in the employe's work, or the disease resulting in death was not a sudden development from some abrupt violence to the physical structure of the body but was the result of gradual development from long continued exposure to natural dangers incident to the employment.

The remaining question to be determined in this case is whether there is sufficient proof to establish the causal relation of the antimony fumes inhaled by decedent and his death. As to this, the medical testimony was in irreconcilable conflict.

In the opinion of Dr. Max M. Strumia, claimant's medical witness, there is a connection between antimony poisoning and gastroenteritis and there is a similar connection between antimony poisoning and the depression of granulocytis or leukocytis in the bone marrow, and that a condition which disturbs the normal cell production in the bone marrow enhances the probability of a resulting leukemia. This witness was of the further belief that there was a possible relationship between antimony poisoning and leukemia but that positive proof of same was impossible. He did, however, express the opinion that chronic antimony poisoning was a contributing factor in decedent's death.

1948] 

Defendant's medical witness, Dr. Charles Michael Gruber, testified that, in his opinion, decedent did not have antimony poisoning for the reasons that the metal which decedent allegedly inhaled was composed of 88 percent lead and 12 percent antimony; that lead melts at 325 degrees centigrade and antimony at 430 degrees centigrade and yet no lead was found in decedent's urine; that lead excretes slowly while antimony is excreted very rapidly in the stool, urine and skin; that if decedent had inhaled antimony tracheitis would have been present; that the most common finding of chronic antimony poisoning is a rash similar to smallpox and decedent had aleukemia leukemia which is invariably fatal while antimony is never fatal or acute. 

In reviewing this witness' testimony, however, it must be noted that he refused to admit or deny the fact that decedent suffered from antimony poisoning but merely stated that he did not know whether decedent did or not. 

He further argued that the antimony appearing in various tests to which decedent was subjected might have come from certain laboratory utensils used in conducting such tests. That there was no basis for such assumption and that such assumption was incorrect, is apparent from a review of the stipulation as to the testimony which would have been given by the dietitian and laboratory technician of Bryn Mawr Hospital where decedent was a patient and where the tests were taken.

When it is considered that both of these medical witnesses are eminent in the particular field here involved, that the opinion of Dr. Strumia is based upon not only his medical knowledge but also the fact that decedent came under his care and that the various tests were made by him, while the opinion of Dr. Gruber apparently stems from the fact that there is nothing in medical literature to support the idea that antimony can cause leukemia and the further fact that certain assumptions as to the possible origin of antimony resulting from tests made of the decedent were incorrect, we are not prepared to say that his testimony

[84 Dep. Rep. 

was such that it must be accepted by the referee and by us. 

We are, therefore, of the opinion that, before a final determination of this issue is made by us, we should have the benefit of the testimony of an impartial medical expert. 

We, therefore, set aside the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of disallowance and remand this case to Referee A. Harry Clayton, District No. 1, for the appointment by this board of an impartial medical expert in the field of hematology and pharmacology who shall examine the entire record in this case and thereafter testify before the referee, subject to cross-examination by the parties, as to his findings and conclusions. The referee is further instructed to permit the parties to present such further relevant testimony as they may desire, subject to crossexamination and, at the conclusion thereof to make such findings of fact, conclusions of law and order as the entire record may warrant. 

Claimant's appeal is sustained.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD NARDELLI v. STATE WORKMEN'S INSURANCE FUND Workmen's compensation-Occupational disease-Death—Prior award to decedent-Act in effect at time of disability.

An award for compensation to claimant for herself and her minor children representing the difference between the amount paid to decedent in his lifetime and the maximum amount provided under the Occupational Disease Act of 1939 will be affirmed where it appears that deceased had become totally disabled as a result of anthracosilicosis following which he had filed a claim petition and been awarded compensation covering a period in excess of three years up to his death; in such case the claim petition filed by the widow was in effect

1948] 

 a claim for continuation of the payments for compensation that had already been awarded for total disability and the award was based not upon the death of the decedent but merely constituted an order to pay the balance of compensation to his dependent widow; compensation was therefore payable pursuant to the Act of 1939 which was in force at the time claimant became totally disabled rather than pursuant to the Act of May 18, 1945, in effect at the time of his death. 

Appeal by claimant from award of Referee Phillips, District No. 3, claim petition no. 110,156, accident no. 4,498,145. 

Affirmed April 7, 1948.

State Workmen's Insurance Fund, insurance carrier. 

T. L. Kennedy, Jr., for claimant. 

Ralph H. Behney, for defendant.

KNOLL, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by claimant from the order of award of 

Referee David W. Phillips, of Compensation District No. 3. 

On October 26, 1944, Baldo Nardelli filed a claim petition pursuant to the provisions of The Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act, averring, inter alia, that he became totally disabled as a result of anthraco-silicosis on July 22, 1944. The matter was duly referred to Referee Phillips before whom testimony was taken. The referee, by decision dated January 29, 1945, found as a fact that claimant became totally disabled on July 22, 1944, as a result of anthraco-silicosis, which developed to a point of disablement after an exposure of five or more years. Based upon said finding of fact, the referee made an appropriate award. 

No appeal was taken from the award of the referee. 

On September 15, 1947, Mary Nardelli, as the widow of

Baldo Nardelli, filed a claim petition, averring, inter alia, that her husband, Baldo Nardelli, died August 23, 1947, as a result of anthraco-silicosis. The matter was again referred to Referee Phillips, District No. 3, before whom

[84 Dep. Rep. 

testimony was taken. The referee, by decision dated November 21, 1947, found as a fact that decedent, Baldo Nardelli, died on August 23, 1947, and that the sole cause of death was anthraco-silicosis; and that decedent left to survive him his widow and four minor children. Based upon said findings of fact, the referee awarded compensation to claimant herein for herself and her minor children and, in addition thereto, the sum of $200 for payment of funeral expenses incurred.

Decedent, in his lifetime, had been paid compensation in the amount of $2,880 and the additional award of $720 made the total award amount to $3,600, the maximum under the Act of 1939. Claimant has appealed, contending that, insofar as decedent died on August 23, 1947, the award should have been made pursuant to the provisions of the 

Act of 1945. 

We have made a careful study of the record and are of the opinion that the award of the referee should be affirmed.

In the instant case, the claim petition filed by Mary Nardelli was not an original claim. The original claim had been filed by decedent during his lifetime and the "cause for compensation" was total disability, not death. Upon this claim, compensation had already been paid. The present petition was, in effect, a claim for continuation of the payments of compensation that had already been awarded for total disability. The award made on this petition was not based upon the death of decedent; death was not the "cause for compensation". The award was merely an order to pay the balance of the compensation due to decedent's dependent widow. See Toffalori v. Donatelli Granite Co. et al., 157 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 311.

Moreover, when the employer and employe here accepted the provisions of the Occupational Disease Act of 1939, their relations became contractual. The contract bound the employe's dependents as well; and if they are entitled to compensation for his death, it must be through him under the

1948] 

 contract. The statute in force at the time that claimant became totally disabled on July 22, 1944, namely, the Act of 1939, formed a part of the contract of employment, and governs the rate of compensation to deceased employe's widow and other dependents. Likewise, the obligation of the employer to pay compensation to the dependents of employe, in case of death of such an employe, being substantive, was fixed and determined by the statute in force at the time that claimant became totally disabled. To grant compensation to employe's widow in accordance with the provisions of an amendment adopted after the contract was entered into, and after the rights of the parties had been fixed, and where decedent was never employed after the effective time of the Act of May 18, 1945, would be, in effect, impairing the obligation of contract specifically protected by the Constitution of the United States and the Constitution of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. See Polk v.

Western Bedding Co. et al., 145 Pa. Superior Ct. 142. 

We, therefore, affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of award. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD ORRIS v. STATE WORKMEN'S INSURANCE FUND Workmen's compensation—Award—Error based on mistaken computation of wages-Power of the board to correct The Workmen's Compensation Board has the power to correct an error made in an award of compensation arising out of a mistake made by the referee in computing the wages earned by claimant prior to the date of his injury notwithstanding the fact that claimant took no appeal from the referee's order and filed no petition for rehearing within one year from the date of the order pursuant to the provisions of section 413 of the Workmen's Compensation Act.

Appeal by defendant from order of Referee Smith, District No. 10, awarding compensation under agreement no. 

3,751,085. Affirmed April 14, 1948.

State Workmen's Insurance Fund, insurance carrier. 

Howard N. Plate, for claimant. 

Ralph H. Behney, for defendant.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

When this matter was last before us upon appeal by claimant from the action of the referee in granting defendant's petition for modification, we affirmed the referee's action. 

Claimant thereupon appealed to the Common Pleas Court of Erie County which court in an opinion by Judge Elmer 

L. Evans, under date of May 5, 1947, agreed with the board in affirming the action of the referee but returned the case to the board for the determination by it of the sole question of whether claimant is entitled to adjustment of payments due him under the Workmen's Compensation Act because of error in computing the wages earned prior to the date of the injury, it not being denied that an error existed in the amount of compensation, as calculated, based on the wages received by claimant at the time of the injury. 

The board then remanded the matter to Referee Smith who, thereafter, found that claimant's average weekly wage prior to the accident was $28.22, and not the sum of $20 as set out in the original agreement, or the sum of $24.44, as determined by Referee Smith in an opinion dated January 22, 1942, and entered an order based upon the following finding of fact: "Claimant has previously been paid compensation, based on an average weekly wage of $24.44 as follows: Compensation for total disability at the rate of $16.29 per week, from 

October 29, 1940, to October 27, 1943, inclusive, a period of

1948] 

156 weeks and 2 days, total amount of $2,545.89, and compensation for 50 percent partial disability at the rate of $8.15 per week, from October 28, 1943, to July 26, 1945, inclusive, a period of 91 1/7 weeks, amounting to $742.81, total compensation paid to claimant, $3,288.70. "During this latter period from October 28, 1943, to July 26, 1945, inclusive, claimant should have received a compensation for only 25 percent partial disability, at the rate of $4.07 per week; consequently claimant was overpaid during this period."

No interest was allowed by the referee upon the award made.

In this appeal by defendant from the referee's award, defendant contends that the entering of an award is contrary to section 413 of the act and that claimant is not now entitled to a modification of his wages since such modification could be done only by an appeal from the order of the referee dated January 22, 1942, or within a year from said date by the filing of a rehearing petition. 

Claimant has also taken his appeal from the order of the referee, the basis for his appeal being that the referee erred in making the award of 25 percent disability retroactive to 

October 28, 1943, and allowing defendant a credit for overpayment of 25 percent from October 28, 1943, to July 26, 1945. Claimant's appeal (A-33433) will be determined by us in a separate opinion, this opinion being limited to the question raised by the appeal of defendant.

It is apparent, from a review of the record in this case, that an error was made, both at the time of the signing of the agreement between the parties and in the opinion of 

Referee Smith dated January 22, 1942, and August 28, 1942.

The question now being raised by defendant is whether this error can be corrected by us at this late date. The parties are both in agreement that such error does exist but it is the position of defendant that claimant not having appealed

from this part of the findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of the referee in his opinion of January 22, 1942, and not having filed a petition for modification within the period allowed, he is now barred from having the error corrected since the order of the referee being unappealed from, is now "res adjudicata”, citing Huha v. Frick Coke Co., 149

Pa. Superior Ct. 108, Michetti v. State Fund, 143 Pa. Superior Ct. 458.

We have carefully considered the argument advanced by defendant and, after such consideration, we are constrained to say that we can find no merit therein. In this case an obvious and admitted error has been made in determining claimant's average wage prior to the accident. We are a quasi-judicial body and as a court of law has the power to correct an obvious error at any time so also do we. This right and duty does not inure to us through any particular section of the Workmen's Compensation Act but follows the dictates of justice from time immemorial. To determine the issue here raised otherwise, would permit defendant to secure an improper advantage over claimant through no fault on the part of claimant. It is the duty of the courts and of any quasi-judicial body to see that appropriate justice is afforded to each of the litigants and it is for this reason that the right to correct an obvious error has always been recognized as being within the proper sphere of all judicial and quasi-judicial bodies without the necessity of such right or authority being expressly given.

1948] 

 WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD 

.

SQUARCIA v. INDUSTRIAL COLLIERIES CORP. 

Workmen's compensation-Final receipt-Petition to set aside— 

Claimant's inability to read.

A referee's order dismissing a petition to set aside a final receipt will be affirmed where it appears defendant forwarded the receipt to claimant by mail, that the latter executed it and that the only reason advanced by him for having it set aside was his testimony that he signed the receipt not knowing what it meant because he was unable to read, there being no evidence, however, that he was unaware of the full extent of his injuries at the time he executed it; claimant's illiteracy was not in itself sufficient grounds for setting aside the receipt. 

Appeal by claimant from order of Referee Carmalt, District No. 8, dismissing petition to set aside final receipt under compensation agreement no. 4346011. Affirmed. May 5, 1948. 

Samuel Krimsly, for claimant. 

Rufus S. Marriner, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

Claimant, Nicola Squarcia, sustained admitted accidental injuries on September 4, 1943, in the course of his employment as a coal loader by defendant, Industrial Collieries Corporation. The record shows that defendant filed a petition for termination on July 30, 1946, which was withdrawn on August 26, 1946. In the interim, or on August 20, 1946, a final receipt, executed by claimant, was filed of record. 

A few weeks later, on September 24, 1946, claimant filed his present petition to set aside the final receipt, alleging "final receipt was not explained to me, I did not know that it was to terminate my compensation. When final receipt was signed I was totally disabled and unable to return to work."

Referee Carmalt dismissed the petition and claimant has now appealed. Dr. Harry Epstein, called by claimant, testified that he examined claimant on September 19, 1946. The doctor's significant findings were that claimant "walks with a left limp . . . from a point beginning at the middle of the tibia to the ankle joint, the leg is swollen and pits on pressure motions of the ankle are normal except for eversion, which is 50 percent limited". X-rays, according to the doctor, indicated a fracture of the left tibia and fibula, which has healed in an abnormal bowing of both bones. The doctor was of the opinion that the deformity resulted in circulatory changes which prevented claimant from standing on his left leg too long, and was responsible for a permanent 60 percent disability. Claimant testified that he has difficulty and pain after walking for an hour or so and that the left leg swells up. Squarcia stated that he cannot read or write, except his name. He testified that he received the final compensation check in the mail and had it cashed at a beer garden. Claimant said that he signed the final receipt but did not know what it meant. He has not worked nor attempted to work since the accident.

Defendant called Dr. J. A. L. McCullough, who testified as to the examination and treatment made by Dr. Mawhinney and Dr. F. M. Goldsmith from September 7, 1943, to 

November 26, 1945. Dr. McCullough did not see the patient but was of the opinion there was no bowing in the tibia or fibula of any consequence and that the union between the fragments of these two bones was in a satisfactory position. 

Claimant was under the surgical care of Dr. Griffith from the date of the accident to December 6, 1943, when the doctor became ill. Dr. Griffith has since died. Dr. J. E. McClenahan, called by defendant, testified that he examined claimant on October 15, 1947, and upon previous occasions, dating from November 22, 1944. Dr. McClenahan's pertinent findings were:

1948] 

"The end result of the fracture was that he has had for quite sometime good bony union of both the tibia and the fibula. There is some fusion at the lower end of the fibula with the tibia. There is some slight angulation but in my opinion, this is of such a slight degree that it is not the cause of any disability. There is some moderate degree of thickening of the soft tissues in the region of the fracture side. The man has varicosities of his left leg but he also has varicosities of his right leg. The movements of his ankle joint, which incidentally was not involved in the fracture itself, are normal with the exception that there is slight limitation of eversion. He has full flexion and full extension. 

These movements are carried out without pain. There is no evidence of any pitting edema of the lower left leg at the time of this examination, this last examination." 

The doctor was of the opinion that claimant was fully recovered from his injuries as early as April 26, 1945. He felt that the abnormal bridging of the tibia and fibula did not interfere with the functions of the parts and that whatever deformity existed, did not cause any functional impairment. The doctor did not believe there was any justification for claimant's complaints of pain. He stated that any circulatory change might be secondary to bilateral varicosities. 

Claimant suggests the appointment of an impartial physician and ordinarily we would be in accord with this suggestion. However, medical opinion is not indicated as essential to the proper disposition of the case. It should be borne in mind that this case involves the setting aside of a final receipt under section 434 of the Workmen's Compensation 

Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 520, which provides as follows: "A final receipt, given by an employe or dependent entitled to compensation under a compensation agreement or award, shall be prima facie evidence of the termination of the employer's liability to pay compensation under such agreement or award: Provided, however, That the board, or a referee designated by the board, may at any time within two years from the date to which payment is made as evidenced by

such final receipt, set aside a final receipt, upon petition filed with the board, if it be conclusively proved that such receipt was procured by fraud, coercion, or other improper conduct of a party, or is founded upon mistake of law or of fact."

Our appellate courts have repeatedly held claimant to an exacting standard of proof on overcoming the prima facie evidence of the termination of an employer's compensation liability. It has been stated that "the evidence to overthrow a final receipt must be definite and specific and of the required quantity and quality": Eberst v. Sears, Roebuck and 

Co., 334 Pa. 505. Claimant's case stands wholly upon his single statement that he signed the final receipt "but I don't know what it means". We accept claimant's word that he cannot read, but this does not relieve him from his signed commitment. The burden was upon him, being illiterate, to ascertain the contents and import of the instrument before affixing his signature. Full opportunity was available to him by calling upon the members of his family, or his tradespeople. As a last resort, he could by himself, or through another, have made inquiry of defendant as to the character of the writing, which he voluntarily signed. Having failed to exercise this precaution, he cannot now avoid himself of the consequences. It is not contended that claimant was unaware of the full extent of his injuries at the time the final receipt was signed. There is no hint or intimation that defendant was guilty of fraud or improper conduct in the procurement of the final receipt. In fact, defendant had no direct personal contact with claimant in connection with it, as claimant acknowledges he received it in the mail. There is no duty imposed upon an employer by law to acquaint a claimant with the import of a final receipt. It is selfexplanatory upon its face. It is unfortunate that claimant may have prejudiced his legal rights to possible further compensation, but the misfortune is of his own doing. 

Mindful as we are of claimant's illiteracy, we cannot accept

1948] 

 that fact, per se, as grounds for setting aside the final receipt. To do so would render section 434 meaningless. 

Ignorance here does not constitute a mistake in law within the meaning and intendment of the act. 

We hereby affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of dismissal. 

SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA PARMLEY v. UNEMPLOYMENT COMPENSATION BOARD OF REVIEW 

Unemployment compensation-Employment outside Pennsylvania—

Insufficiency of wages earned in Pennsylvania-Section 401(a) 

of Unemployment Compensation Law. 

Unemployment compensation was properly disallowed where it appeared that claimant's earnings during the base year amounted to only $250 in Pennsylvania employment; in such case wages earned by him in another State, from an employer not subject to the Pennsylvania 

Unemployment Compensation Law, during three-quarter periods of the year that he resided there, cannot be considered in determining his eligibility for compensation under section 401 (a) of the act. 

In the Superior Court of Pennsylvania, March term, 1948, no. 13. Appeal by defendant from decision of Unem ployment Compensation Board of Review, November 13, 

1947, appeal no. B-44-IB-97-J-1595. Appeal affirmed, April 

13, 1948. 

Roland M. Morgan, for appellant. 

William L. Hammond, for Commonwealth.

T. McKeen Chidsey, Attorney General, for appellee.

RHODES, P. J.: 

This is an appeal by claimant from the decision of the 

Unemployment Compensation Board of Review disallowing unemployment benefits. The bureau and the referee previously disallowed the claim.

Claimant formerly resided in Pennsylvania but moved to Ithaca, N. Y., in January 1946, where he was last employed. He filed his application for benefits on February 3, 1947, against the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. It follows that his base year consisted of the fourth quarter of 

1945 and the first, second, and third quarters of 1946. See 

Unemployment Compensation Law of December 5, 1936,

P. L. (1937) 2897, sec. 4(a), (b), as amended by the Act of 

May 29, 1945, P. L. 1145, sec. 1, 43 PS §753 (a), (b).

Compensation was disallowed as claimant failed to establish eligibility for unemployment compensation benefits as required by section 401 (a) of the Unemployment Compensation Law, as amended by the Act of May 29, 1945, P. L. 

1145, sec. 8, 43 PS §801(a). This section provides that a claimant to be eligible must have been paid wages for employment within his base year equal to not less than 30 times his weekly benefit rate. His wages must have been for "employment" during his base year. "Services performed without this Commonwealth shall not be included within the term 'Employment' if contributions are required and paid with respect to such services under an unemployment compensation law of any other state": 

Section 4 of the Act of December 5, 1936, P. L. (1937) 2897, as amended by the Act of May 29, 1945, P. L. 1145, sec. 1 [section 4(1), (2) (B)], 43 PS §753 (1), (2) (B). Claim- ant first sought unemployment compensation based on his total earnings in Pennsylvania during the calendar year 1945. He subsequently modified his claim, and now states: "It is for the benefits of the last quarter of 1945 that I am contending."

During the last quarter of 1945, claimant earned in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania the sum of $250 for lo-

1948] 

 calized services. This amount, of course, is insufficient to establish eligibility for a claim against this state. When claimant appealed from the order of the referee he incorporated in his petition a statement of additional facts showing that he earned a total of $1,360.50 in the State of New 

York during the second and third quarters of 1946. Claimant's services during the first, second, and third quarters of 1946 were not in Pennsylvania employment. His New 

York employer obviously was subject to and paid contributions according to the provisions of the Unemployment Compensation Law of that State, as he concedes that he received benefits from the State of New York on his earnings during the year 1946. See section 402 (c) of the Unemployment 

Compensation Law, as amended by the Act of May 29, 1945, P. L. 1145, sec. 9, 43 PS §802 (c). Such services performed by him were localized in the State of New York. 1 It appears that claimant was invited to file a combinedwage report pursuant to the rules of procedure ¹ under the 

Interstate Benefit Payment Plan,2 and that he expressly declined to do so for the reason that he did not wish to complicate matters by involving New York in his claim against Pennsylvania. Claimant could have become a combined-wage claimant, but he preferred to file a separate claim in the State of New York and a separate claim in the 

Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. His earnings of $250 in covered Pennsylvania employment not meeting the eligibility qualifications of section 401(a), 43 PS §801 (a), claimant is not entitled to unemployment compensation benefits under the Pennsylvania Unemployment Compensation Law. See 

1 See 1 Unemployment Insurance Reporter, paragraphs 20502050.03, Commerce Clearing House, Inc. 

2 See section 312 of the Unemployment Compensation Law, as added by the Act of April 23, 1942, P. L. 60, sec. 4, and amended by the Act of May 29, 1945, P. L. 1145, sec. 7, 43 PS § 792, authorizing entry into reciprocal arrangements with authorized agencies of other States and of the Federal Government.

section 404 of the Unemployment Compensation Law, as amended by the Act of May 29, 1945, P. L. 1145, sec. 10, 43 PS §804. 

Decision of the board is affirmed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD ORRIS v. STATE WORKMEN'S INSURANCE FUND Workmen's compensation—Award-Credit for overpayment—Interest. 

1. A referee's order pursuant to defendant's petition for modification of an agreement making an award of 25 percent disability retroactive to a date as of which the referee found claimant's disability had changed from total to 25 percent and allowing defendant a credit for overpayments from the date as of which the referee found said partial disability began will be affirmed where it appeared that defendant during the period in question had made payments based upon a 50 percent disability and that defendant's liability to pay further compensation still continued. 

2. Interest upon an award pursuant to section 410 of the Workmen's 

Compensation Act will be allowed where no act on the part of claimant estops him from asserting his right thereto.

Appeal by claimant from order of Referee Smith, District 

No. 10, awarding compensation under agreement no. 

3,751,085. Amended and affirmed April 14, 1948.

State Workmen's Insurance Fund, insurance carrier. 

Howard N. Plate, for claimant. 

Ralph H. Behney, for defendant.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

This appeal by claimant is a cross-appeal to that taken by defendant (A-33419) and which cross appeal has already been determined by us in a separate opinion.

1948] 

Since the facts in both appeals are identical, it would serve no useful purpose to again repeat same here and we, therefore, incorporate that part of our opinion in defendant's appeal.
