In the instant appeal claimant argues: 1, That the referee erred in making the award of 25 percent disability retroactive to October 28, 1943, and allowing defendant a credit for overpayments from that date until July 26, 1945, and, 2, that the referee erred in not allowing claimant interest upon the award made. We shall discuss these objections in the order made. 

1. The record discloses that, on November 15, 1943, defendant filed its petition for modification with the board in which it alleged that, commencing on October 28, 1943, claimant's disability changed from total to 50 percent partial. At the hearing held before the referee on February 25, 1944, Dr. Arthur G. Davis, defendant's medical witness, testified that, as of the date of his examination of claimant, on October 28, 1943, claimant was suffering a 25 percent partial disability. In his award of June 21, 1945, the referee adopted this uncontradicted medical opinion and entered an award in accordance with same, an amendment requesting a change in the modification petition to read 25 percent partial rather than 50 percent partial having been made by counsel for defendant at the hearing. In his award, the referee further allowed defendant credit for payments made by it to claimant since October 28, 1943. Thereafter, upon appeal by claimant, we affirmed this action by the referee and upon appeal by claimant to the Common Pleas Court of Erie County, this part of our opinion was affirmed by Judge Elmer L. Evans. Claimant now argues that since defendant has already paid him compensation based upon a 50 percent disability during the period from October 28, 1943, to July 26, 1945, inclusive, it was error for the referee to allow defendant credit for the overpayment made by it during this period.

We find ourselves unable to agree with the logic or wisdom of this argument. This question has already been determined both by us and by the Common Pleas Court of Erie County in which the order of the referee awarding claimant compensation for a 25 percent partial disability from October 28, 1943, and allowing defendant credit for payments made since that time was affirmed. To do otherwise would result in penalizing a defendant who, under a mistake of fact as to the disability suffered by a claimant, overpaying a claimant and thereafter, while additional payments are still due, being unable to take credit for the amount of such overpayment. While we would feel constrained to hold otherwise where a claimant has received compensation for the full period of time that such compensation was due and defendant, thereafter, filed a petition requesting our aid in recovering back any overpayment made, it would be most unjust to refuse to permit claimant to recover back or receive credit for any overpayments while still compelling that defendant to continue paying compensation to claimant thereafter. 

2. We are of the opinion that the referee erred in not awarding claimant interest upon the award made. 

Paragraph 2 of section 410 of the Workmen's Compen sation Act provides: "Whenever any claim for compensation is presented to the board and is finally adjudicated in favor of the claimant, the amounts of compensation actually due at the time the first payment is made after such adjudication shall bear interest at the rate of six per centum per annum from the day such claim is presented, and such interest shall be payable to the same persons as the compensation is payable." 

Upon reviewing the entire record in this case, we can find no such action on the part of claimant that would estop him from asserting his right to interest upon the amount presently due him, in accordance with the above quoted paragraph of section 410 of the act.

1948] 

We, therefore, affirm the referee's findings of fact and conclusions of law.

We amend the referee's amended award to include the following paragraph: "Amended award "This amended award is to bear interest at the rate of six percent in accordance with section 410 of the Workmen's 

Compensation Act."

The balance of the referee's award is affirmed. 

The appeal of claimant is sustained. 

Affirmed as amended.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD BEVERIDGE v. VICTORY COAL COMPANY 

Workmen's compensation ·Dependency · 

Widow living apart from husband-Evidence-Burden of proof. 

Under the Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 520, sec. 307, providing that no compensation shall be payable to a widow living apart from her husband at the time of his death unless she was actually dependent upon him and receiving from him a substantial portion of her support, the burden was upon a claimant widow living apart from her husband at the time of his death to establish substantial contributions to her support; evidence that claimant and decedent lived together in West 

Virginia until about two years before his death, at which time claimant went to live in Ohio with their son, while decedent remained in Pennsylvania, where he worked, visiting his family about twice each year, was insufficient to sustain an award to claimant as dependent widow. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Dillman, District No. 8, claim petition no. 107,929. Appeal sustained. 

February 18, 1948.

Coal Operators Casualty Company, insurance carrier. 

A. J. Marion, for claimant. 

R. W. Smith, Jr., and Mr. R. H. Cunningham, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

The main question involved in this appeal is whether claimant, Mrs. Minnie N. Beveridge, was a dependent of her decedent, Alexander Beveridge, within the meaning and intendment of the Workmen's Compensation Act. The acci dental death of decedent on October 12, 1946, is admitted by defendant, Victory Coal Company. Referee Dillman resolved the question in the affirmative and this appeal by defendant has followed. Defendant has also taken exception to the rate of compensation awarded claimant. 

A review of the record reveals that decedent and a son, Alexander B., Jr., were employed by Joseph Nassar, doing business as the Victory Coal Company on Friday, October 11, 1946. The two men started to work on Saturday morning and within an hour or so, decedent was fatally crushed under a fall of rock. The son testified that his father dug the coal down and the son shoveled it into the wagon. He said two wagons were loaded at the time of the accident. The witness testified that arrangements were made with the employer for the use of a shanty near the mine and they purchased $5 worth of groceries on credit at a store operated by defendant. Under cross-examination, the son testified that he had been living with his mother, claimant, and a sister, Betty, and a half brother, Ray, at Massillon, Ohio, for about two years before entering defendant's employ. During his residence in Ohio, he was employed by the Enterprise Aluminum Company. He stated that he kept the house "going" but 

Ray paid claimant a weekly amount for room and board. 

Upon the pivotal question of dependency, claimant testified that she and her decedent were married on May 1, 1926, and

1948] 

 lived together mostly in the coal fields of West Virginia and at times in Western Pennsylvania until about two years. before the fatal accident. Claimant testified: "Q. Mrs. Beveridge, who supported you at the time that you were living with the deceased, Mr. Beveridge, after your marriage and during the period he was working, as you previously testified, in the coal mines? "A. Well, he did he supported us when he worked in the mines "Q. When did you last see Mr. Beveridge before his death?" "A. Just about five or six days before he was killed. "Q. And where did you see him at that time? "A. In Massillon, Ohio. "Q. He had come to Massillon? "A. Yes, to take us back to Pennsylvania with him. He was supposed to get us a home down here. We were going to move down here.' 

Claimant stated that she had no separate or independent income of her own. Since the death, she said, she had been dependent for support upon the son, Alexander Beveridge, Jr. Prior to his decease, the husband visited his family, according to the claimant, about twice each year. Claimant attributed the separation to the fact that decedent "always worked the coal mines all his life and that's the reason he liked Pennsylvania." While claimant's testimony is meager on the actual amount of support which her decedent contributed to her support, there is acceptable testimony of record that during the greater part of their married life, the parties lived together. Is the later period of separation fatal to her compensation claim as a dependent? Since claimant offered no testimony that decedent actually furnished her with any support or subsistence while she resided apart from him in Massillon, it necessarily appears to us that no contribution was ever made by him. The Workmen's Compensation Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 520, Sec. 307 (7) provides:

"No compensation shall be payable under this section to a widow, unless she was living with her deceased husband at the time of his death, or was then actually dependent upon him and receiving from him a substantial portion of her support."

The testimony, corroborated by her son, is to the effect that decedent spent five days with his family in Massillon, just before his death and that the purpose of his visit was to effect arrangements for the restoration of the family unit "just as soon as he found a home." Credence can be attached to this testimony because the son then left his job in Massillon, to join his father in seeking new employment in the Pennsylvania soft coal fields. The frequently cited case on the question of dependency is Morris v. Yough Coal and Supply Co., 266 Pa. 216, in which the court held that there is no absolute or rigid rule which can be laid down as to the quantity or quality of evidence necessary to establish dependency, but that each case necessarily depends upon its particular facts and circumstances. Under the line of cases prior to the Act of 1939; claimant here would be entitled to an award. The leading case on the question of dependency where the husband and wife were living separate and apart is Creasy v. Phoenix Utility Co., 276 Pa. 

583, cited by claimant's counsel, in which the court said (p. 586): "The criterion in cases of this character, consequently, must be whether or not a wife, living apart from her husband and dependent upon him, but not actually receiving support from him, has acquiesced in his action under circumstances amounting to a repudiation by him of his legal obligation to support his family." 

That case and others which followed it were authoritative law for the proposition that dependency does not depend upon the fact alone that a husband failed to provide support for his family, but rather whether the wife had acquiesced in the default. If the wife were indifferent to her husband's repudiation of his legal obligations, the claim of dependency

1948] 

 could not prevail: John v. Susquehanna Colliery Co., 113 

Pa. Superior Ct. 493; Feldman v. Pictorial Review, 122 

Pa. Superior Ct. 491.

However, under the provisions of the Act of 1939, supra, a claimant must establish substantial contributions to her support where living apart, as a necessary prerequisite to an award. The legally subsisting marriage relationship does not, per se, establish dependency. A fundamental concept of compensation legislation is to substitute compensation payments, in part, for wages lost by accident, and where death strikes down a home provider, in the course of his employment, the act makes some provision for those who depended upon him for support during his lifetime. Where such dependency did not exist, the need for compensation relief likewise fails. The legislature has deemed it expedient to exclude from the class of dependents, widows whose claims for compensation are founded upon irregular, infrequent and meagre contributions of support during decedent's productive period of life. The 1939 amendatory provision: "dependent upon him and receiving from him a substantial portion of her support" is clear and explicit. 

It means exactly what it says. No matter how favorable claimant's testimony of dependency in the instant case is viewed, it falls far short of meeting the statutory requirement. The links in her dependency claim are simply these:

That while they lived together in West Virginia, decedent supported her and that shortly before his death he came to Massillon and informed the family that he expected to obtain quarters for them in Pennsylvania. While they lived together in West Virginia in a single family household, dependency is assumed. But there is not a single iota of evidence that he made any contribution whatever during the period of separation, while claimant resided in Ohio. Nor is there anything of record that decedent had no means to provide support during the period in question. Claimant admitted that even his visits to the family were infrequent, "about twice a year." An open mind and a realistic view

compels the rejection of any "substantial contribution" made by decedent to claimant during the period of separation. Rather, it appears that claimant's support was provided, in toto, by her son and step-son. In the case of 

Hendricks v. Bethlehem Steel Co., 150 Pa. Superior Ct. 257, the court said (p. 259): "But under the Act of 1939 the fact that a wife, living apart from her husband, was actually dependent upon him at the time of his death is not sufficient in itself to establish the right of the widow to compensation; she is also required to affirmatively show as a fact that she was then receiving from him a substantial portion of her support. Her right to compensation has been made to depend upon the fact of receiving support at the time of his death." (Italics supplied.)

The award to claimant as the dependent widow must be reversed under the provisions of the act. We find no reversible error in the referee's computation of wages under section 309.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD ZBYSZNSKI v. BELMONT IRON WORKS Workmen's compensation-Disability-Total or partial-Inability to do light work in general.

A referee's award of compensation on the basis of a 75 percent partial disability will be held insufficient and total disability will be awarded to claimant where the weight of medical testimony was to the effect that his injury had produced physical disability of 75 percent and as a result thereof claimant was a nondescript not able to perform light work which would involve stooping, bending, lifting, or climbing stairs; total disability is warranted where claimant's injury incapacitates him from doing anything but special kinds of work not generally available.

1948]  Appeal by claimant from order of Referee Sheldrake, District No. 1, awarding compensation under agreement no. 

4166121. Modified. May 12, 1948.

David L. Ullman, for claimant. 

George D. Sheehan, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal from an order entered by Referee Sheldrake January 16, 1948, reinstating compensation payments on a 75 percent partial disability basis. The order is insufficient considering the facts in the case as we understand them and we propose to adjust it accordingly. 

On November 4, 1942, in the course of his employment with defendant, Belmont Iron Works, claimant, Stephen Zbysznski, was the victim of an accident in which a pile of heavy channels fell over on him. His fellow workmen extricated him alive and he regained consciousness for an interval about a quarter of an hour after the accident as he lay on a stretcher. He was then taken to the Graduate 

Hospital from which he was discharged about four months later. As set forth in the agreement accorded him under date of November 16, 1942, he sustained fractures of the seventh cervical and first dorsal vertebrae and twelve ribs on the right side; also dislocation of the second lumbar vertebra with fractures of the articular process, crush of the right muscular spiral nerve and pneumo-thorax.

Under date of March 20, 1945, a supplemental agreement providing for partial disability compensation was entered into by reason of claimant returning to work and earning a wage of $5 per week. Another supplemental agreement dated June 29, 1945, arranged for suspension of compensation because of the fact that claimant found employment

with the Independent Manufacturing Company at wages in excess of those paid to him by defendant. However, his work with the latter employer amounted to little more than putting in time and the cessation of hostilities in the late war put an end to his rather questionable usefulness. He then, being out of employment, filed the petition with which we are now concerned March 11, 1946. In the meantime he had put in some time trying to readjust himself with the help of the State Rehabilitation Service. 

In his own testimony claimant explained how he started himself back along the road to recovery by first working a few minutes at a time in a school for occupational therapy, then at washing walls for awhile and finally by getting back into industrial employment with the Independent Manufacturing Company above named. He submitted, however, that his services to the last named employer were actually of no value and insisted that even the United States Employment Service could find nothing for him that he might be able to do. He was also turned away on the several attempts he made to get jobs with private employers such as Gimbels, Lit Brothers, Cramps, S. K. F. and Snellenburgs. His com plaints were headaches, sleeplessness, inability to walk any considerable distance, numbness in the members on the right side and pain in the back. He demonstrated to the referee that he was wearing a prescribed brace which extended from his shoulder blades to his coccyx. He admitted that his headaches, with concomitant dizziness, usually let up during the day.

On the medical side of the picture Dr. Mulford K. Fisher, from X-ray pictures made March 16, 1946, read into the record a report which evidences considerable vertebral damage and Dr. William Gash, who examined claimant March 

8, 1946 and April 7, 1947, expressed an opinion to the effect that claimant is totally disabled. This was in answer to a hypothetical question which, as we have read it, contained all the facts reasonably to be inferred from the evidence which preceded it. This was competent enough but the

1948] 

 doctor went further and stated that claimant would be unable to do even light work. He stated that if claimant should be expected to do anything at all it would have to be at a job specially made for him and tailored to his limitations. 

Defendant's medical witness was Dr. James R. Martin. 

He examined claimant April 8, 1946. He found that claimant had 50 percent limitation of motion in all directions but thought that disability should be placed at 35 percent. He admitted, however, that for the type of work claimant was accustomed to by education and experience he was through for the rest of his life.

Being in doubt the referee arranged for the advice of an impartial specialist and the board named Dr. Eugene J. 

Garvin. This doctor's estimate of the situation, predicated upon an examination made July 9, 1947, and a review of the substance of the case up to that time, is, we think, the determinative evidence in the matter. He estimated physical disability at 75 percent, which is probably what led the referee to decide the case as it stands. But he went further than this. He categorically ruled out stooping, bending, lifting or climbing stairs and went along with Dr. Gash on the point that any work claimant could do would have to be tailormade for him. The best he could recommend for claimant was a sedentary job such as sorting. He could not approve anything suggested to him as ordinary light work.

Dr. Garvin's opinion is so closely in line with Dr. Gash's wherein the two touch upon the sparseness of the work available to claimant, considering his physical ability, that we think the referee in considering the percentages of disability has overlooked the true issue in the case. The latter, as we see it, has to do with whether or not claimant is in fact a nondescript and in our opinion the evidence indicates that he is. Our view of the matter is that if claimant is ever to work at all it will have to be at a job which is made for him. He has shown that he has searched fruitlessly for

[84 Dep. Rep. 

such light work as is generally available and his experience in this regard substantiates the pronouncements by his own doctor and the impartial physician that he could not handle such work.

The law in such a case is clear. We need but quote the opinion of the Superior Court in one of its most recent decisions on the subject in hand, wherein it was said: "The medical witnesses agree that the claimant is disabled and it is clear from a reading of their testimony that the claimant is not able to do light work in general but only 'selective' light work; light work that does not require 'lifting', 'bending' or 'stooping'. "In Babcock v. Babcock & Wilcox Co. et al., 137 Pa. Superior Ct. 517, 9 A. (2d) 492, this court stated that there is a fundamental distinction 'between those who are able to do light work in general and those who are so limited in capacity that they are only fitted to perform special service, a class of work not generally available'. It is in the latter class of cases where allowance of total disability is warranted, and it is clear that the claimant's disability brings him within this class. Consona v. R. T. Coulborn & Co. et al., 104 Pa. Superior Ct. 170, 158 A. 300; Osborn v. Franklin 

Hospital et al., 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 307, 43 A. (2d) 579; 

Naughton v. Kettl, 154 Pa. Superior Ct., 318, 35 A. (2d) 

527. Since the claimant is not able to do light work of a general character, the burden of showing availability of work which he can do was on the defendant (Jones v. 

Hazle Brook Coal Co., 119 Pa. Superior Ct. 409, 179 A. 783; 

Hale v. Susquehanna Collieries Co., 126 Pa. Superior Ct. 

342, 191 A. 225) and it made no effort to meet that burden":

Barckhoff v. Westmoreland Coal Co., 161 Pa. Superior Ct. 

146. 

The first, second, third, fourth and fifth findings of fact of Referee Sheldrake, dated January 16, 1948, are affirmed.

The sixth and seventh findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of Referee Sheldrake, dated January 16, 1948, are vacated and set aside and the following substituted therefor:

1948] 

"Findings of fact "6. The board finds as a fact that as of September 15, 1945, claimant is found to be in such physical condition due to the accidental injury in this case that he is not able to do such light work as is generally available. " "1. The board concludes as a matter of law that since claimant as of and after September 15, 1945, has been in such physical condition due to his accidental injury that he is incapable of doing types of light work generally to be found he is a nondescript and entitled to receive compensation on a total disability basis. "2. The board concludes as a matter of law that suspension of payments of compensation in this case provided for under supplemental agreement of June 29, 1945, should be lifted. "Order "Suspension of compensation payments in this case is lifted and defendant, the Belmont Iron Works and/or its insurance carrier, the Liberty Mutual Insurance Co., is directed to pay to claimant, Stephen Zbysznski, compensation at the rate of $18 per week beginning September 15, 1945, and continuing until such time as said claimant's disability ceases or changes within the limitations of the Workmen's Compensation Act; deferred payments to bear interest in accordance with the provisions of section 410 of the said act." 

The appeal is sustained.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD MARTIN v. CARRIEL ENGINEERING CO. 

Workmen's compensation-Common-law marriage—Evidence— 

Sufficiency.

A referee's order disallowing compensation to claimant based on a finding that claimant had failed to prove a common-law marriage with decedent, will be set aside and an award entered where claimant presented testimony that on a certain occasion decedent had said to her, "I take you as my wife," whereupon she said, "I'll take you as my husband and we'll live together as husband and wife"; that thereafter they lived together, that claimant was introduced by decedent as his wife to various members of his family, and that she was accepted and became known as his wife, her testimony as to cohabitation being corroborated by other witnesses; under the circumstances claimant's testimony did not indicate an intent to enter into a future marriage but rather an intent that the parties agreed and consented to become husband and wife forthwith.

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Clayton. Claim no. 107,686, accident no. 4,916,335. Reversed. 

April 14, 1948. 

United States Casualty Company, insurance carrier. 

Arthur S. Werblun, for claimant. 

Raymond J. Porreca, for defendant.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

This is an appeal by claimant from a disallowance of the referee. 

William Martin was accidentally killed on October 22, 1947, while in the course of his employment. Claimant 

Veronica E. Martin filed her petition for compensation alleging that she was the common-law wife of decedent. 

The referee dismissed the claim, finding as a fact that claimant failed to prove a common-law marriage with decedent.

1948] 

Claimant filed an appeal and we remanded the record for further hearing on the question of whether or not a common-law marriage was contracted. The hearing was held, the referee again dismissed the claim and the present appeal followed. The sole issue is whether claimant has proved a common-law marriage.

Claimant's evidence indicates that during September of 1937, decedent and claimant were discussing their relations in an automobile. Decedent said to claimant, "I take you as my wife" and "I'll take you as my wife and we'll live together as husband and wife". Claimant thereupon said, "I'll take you as my husband and we'll live together as husband and wife". Decedent also asked, "Shall we live together from this day?" and claimant replied, "Yes". The parties thereafter lived as man and wife at the home of decedent's sister. Claimant was introduced by decedent as his wife to various members of his family. She was accepted and known as the wife of decedent by his parents. They held themselves out as husband and wife, filed joint income tax returns as husband and wife, filed withholding tax returns as husband and wife and entered into an agreement for the purchase of real estate, title to which was to be held in their names as husband and wife, by entireties. 

Claimant called decedent's father and sister as witnesses.

Their testimony clearly indicated cohabitation and reputation and corroborated claimant's testimony in this regard. 

The parties were legally competent to marry. Claimant had never married before and decedent had been legally divorced.

Defendant contends that claimant's testimony indicates an intent to enter into a future marriage. We do not agree with defendant's contention. Although the language used may suggest future conduct, the decedent's language, "I'll take you as my wife" and "We'll live together" and the further expression of "Shall we live together", is not an absolute expression of futurity.

As stated in the case of Caddy v. Johnstown Firemen's 

Association, 129 Pa. Superior Ct. 493, 499: "Unlettered persons frequently become confused in the use of tenses and it is difficult to get them to testify to the exact language used in a conversation, in words of the first and second person and using the present tense, rather than their understanding of its import." "We think the testimony of the claimant, instead of establishing that no marriage contract was made between them, is entirely consistent with a finding that the parties agreed and consented then and there to become husband and wife and live together in that relation, without a marriage ceremony, and that following that agreement they cohabited together as husband and wife and were generally recognized and reputed to be such, until his death." 

We have carefully reviewed the entire record and are of the opinion that from September 1937, when the conversation above referred to took place, claimant was recognized by decedent as his wife, considered claimant as his wife and she considered decedent as her husband. See also McGraff's 

Estate, 319 Pa. 310, and Horton's, Estate, 357 Pa. 30.

Accordingly we vacate the referee's 6th finding of fact. the conclusion of law and the order. In lieu thereof we make the following: "Findings of fact "6. Claimant and decedent entered into a contract during

September 1937 wherein they agreed to take and took each other for husband and wife. Claimant and decedent recognized each other as husband and wife; they lived together as husband and wife, and were known to members of decedent's family as husband and wife. "7. Decedent and claimant entered into a common-law marriage during September 1937." " "1. The parties are bound by the provisions of article III 

of the Workmen's Compensation Act.

1948] 

"2. Since claimant, Veronica E. Martin, was the wife of decedent and living with him at the time of his accidental death she is entitled to receive compensation as his widow." "Award "Defendant, James E. Finegan, trading as the Carriel

Engineering Company, and/or his insurance carrier, the United States Casualty Company, are ordered to pay to claimant, Veronica E. Martin, the widow of William J. 

Martin, the sum of $12 per week from October 29, 1947, for a period of 300 weeks, a total sum of $3,600, in accord ance with the provisions of the Workmen's Compensation 

Act as amended, with interest on deferred payments in accordance with section 410 of the act. "Defendants shall also pay to claimant Veronica E. Martin the sum of $200 on account of the funeral expenses incurred." 

Claimant's appeal is sustained.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD WINTERHALTER v. DUQUESNE LIGHT COMPANY Workmen's compensation-Final receipt—Petition to set aside— 

Statute of limitations—Tolling by benefit payments. 

1. A referee's order dismissing claimant's petition to set aside a final receipt on the ground that the petition was barred by the statute of limitations since it was not filed within one year after the last payment of compensation to claimant, will be set aside and compensation awarded where it appears that within one year prior to the date of filing the petition claimant had received from defendant certain benefit payments in excess of the maximum compensation payments based upon claimant's tenure of service; under the circumstances the benefits were in lieu of compensation payments and tolled the statute of limitations. 

2. A final receipt will be set aside and compensation awarded where it appears that at the time claimant executed it he had not fully recovered from his accidental injuries of which fact defendant had knowledge. 

Appeal by claimant from order of Referee Moore, District No. 8, dismissing petition to set aside final receipt under

[84 Dep. Rep. 

compensation agreement no. 4,508,868. Reversed. May 26, 1948. 

Samuel J. Goldstein, for claimant. 

William J. Powell, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

Claimant, Charles E. Winterhalter, sustained admitted accidental injuries on July 13, 1944, during the course of his employment by defendant, Duquesne Light Company. 

The accident occurred on the Bakerstown-Culmerville Road in Allegheny County. The compensation agreement describes the accident and resulting injuries as follows: "Employe said that he had fallen from rear of truck and had struck his back, resulting in bruised ribs and fracture of 10th rib and contusion over kidney and hemorrhage under the skin of his back." 

Winterhalter received compensation until August 8, 1944, a period of 3-6/7 weeks, when he executed a final receipt. 

On May 8, 1947, claimant filed a petition to set aside the final receipt, alleging that the final receipt "was entered into by the parties under a mutual mistake of fact as to the true nature and extent of claimant's disability". Referee 

Moore held that the petition filed was barred by the statute of limitations since it was not filed within one year after the last payment of compensation to him, on August 8, 1944.

The record discloses that claimant suffered an earlier accident on October 30, 1941, when he was thrown from the back of a truck while cleaning street lights, in which accident he sustained a severe concussion of the brain, laceration of the scalp and fracture of the right wrist. Winterhalter was paid compensation to October 31, 1943. It appears also that claimant was injured at work at McKeesport on 

June 25, 1944. Following the third accident, claimant returned to work and remained employed until October 19, 1945. The referee found that claimant became totally disabled again on October 19, 1945, as a result of the first

1948] 

 accident and the aggravation of the head injuries due to the later accident and that he has been totally disabled since that time. From October 19, 1945, to October 19, 1946, claimant received certain benefit payments in excess of the maximum compensation payments under a welfare policy of defendant company based upon his tenure of service. 

Claimant contends that these payments under the welfare policy were made in lieu of the compensation payments and, therefore, the petition was filed timely within one year from the last payment of the welfare benefits. The question involved here was fully considered by the Superior Court in the case of Creighton v. Continental Co., 155 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 165, in which the court said (p. 173): "One thing is certain, and that is, that 'in lieu of compensation' does not mean 'by way of compensation'. 'In lieu of' means 'in place of' or 'instead of. "The decisions hold that when an employee is totally disabled and the employer, while denying any liability for workmen's compensation, nevertheless pays the employee regular stated amounts, weekly or monthly, either out of its own general funds, or out of sick or accident benefits or relief funds contributed by it, not as wages or salary for work performed, but in relief of the employee's incapacity to labor, on its being determined that the employee is entitled to workmen's compensation, the amount paid by the employer discharges its liability for compensation for the weeks in which its payments to him equalled or exceeded the compensation payable. Long v. Philadelphia, 140 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 631, 29 A. 2d 243; Somerton v. Bell Tele. Co., 111 Pa. Superior Ct. 264, 268, 169 A. 579; Cotton v. John 

Wood Manufacturing Co., 126 Pa. Superior Ct. 528, 191 A. 

189; Tinsman v. Jones & Laughlin Steel Corp., 118 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 516, 523, 180 A. 175; Hunter v. Mailey, 91 Pa. 

Superior Ct., 350; McGuirk v. Sun Shipbuilding Co., 80 Pa.

Superior Ct. 457. It is only where the employee is not totally disabled and actually performs some labor for which he is paid wages or salary (Chase v. Emery Mfg. Co., 271 Pa. 265, 268-9, 113 A. 840; Hickey v. Cudahy Packing Co., 153 Pa.

Superior Ct. 45, 33 A. 2d 285) that such payments will not extend the time within which the claimant's petition must be filed or discharge the employer's liability for compensation for the weeks in which its payments equalled or exceeded the compensation payable. "The board was wholly wrong in its conclusion that payments so made by the employer to the employee in excess of the equal compensation payable by it, could be credited on future installments of compensation. This is ruled by 

Chase v. Emery, supra, p. 270, and Long v. Philadelphia, supra, p. 635. In the former, the Supreme Court said 'Nor does the amount paid plaintiff over that allowed by law as compensation alter this conclusion. It was shown to be a pure gratuity'. In the Long case, this court said: 'During such weeks when the payments under the ordinance are equal to or exceed the equal amount due on the compensation award, liability on the award is discharged.'" (Italics supplied.)

It should be noted that the benefits paid to claimant were made by the defendant employer and were not received by claimant under an insurance policy taken out by him as a protection against loss of wages arising through sickness. 

In the case of Hickey v. Cudahy Packing Co., 153 Pa. Superior Ct. 45, anent the same question, the court, in discussing the voluntary payment of $40 weekly to a claimant following disability due to accidental origin, said (p. 47): "It is defendant's contention that these gratuitous payments were made under a fixed policy of the company to continue disabled employees on the payroll for a limited time. What prompted the payments is unimportant. Though equal to his former wages, they were not paid to him as wages, for he earned nothing during the period. They were intended to compensate him for loss of earning power and were as much workmen's compensation as if paid as such. by agreement. There is ample evidence to support the finding of the Board that the payments were received as compensation and not as wages. The finding is conclusive of the

1948] 

 question. Somerton v. The Bell Telephone Co. of Pa., 111 

Pa. Superior Ct. 264, 169 A. 579." (Italics supplied.)

The record clearly establishes, as the referee found, that claimant's disability subsequent to October 19, 1945, was attributable to the accident and that he was a patient in the St. Francis Hospital from January 10, 1946, until February 

26, 1946, where a diagnosis of post-concussional syndrome was made. Prior to and following this period of hospitalization, he received benefit payments from defendant. It is patent that these payments were intended in lieu of compensation although it is not necessary to inquire into the motives which prompted them. Mindful as we are of the humane purposes of compensation legislation, we necessarily hold that these benefits were in lieu of compensation payments and tolled the statute of limitations, which the referee erroneously invoked against claimant. 

Claimant also filed a petition to modify an existing compensation agreement (no. 90,376) and the referee's findings and conclusions dispose of both petitions. Claimant raises no challenge that the final receipt was obtained through improper conduct upon the part of the employer. It is claimed that the final receipt "was entered into by the parties under a mutual mistake of fact as to the true nature and extent of claimant's disability". The next question presented is whether claimant has satisfied the burden of proof resting upon him to set aside the final receipt. Evidence to set aside a final receipt must be of higher standard or quality than that upon which compensation is claimed in the first instance: Eberst v. Sears Roebuck & Co., 334 Pa. 505. The final receipt is prima facie evidence of the termination of the employer's liability to pay compensation under an agreement or award: Section 434 of the Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 520. Has claimant met this burden? Was there a mutual mistake within the contemplation and intendment of the act?

Claimant testified at some length concerning all three accidents. He identified the locale of the several accidents as Millvale (October 30, 1941), McKeesport (June 25, 1944)

[84 Dep. Rep. 

and the Bakerstown-Culmerville Road (July 13, 1944), successively. The McKeesport accident is not particularly involved in these proceedings since no claim was made for compensation, although claimant stated he suffered "two holes" in his head and an arm injury, when a safety sign for workmen fell from the truck and struck him. Testifying as to the circumstances attendant upon the execution of the second final receipt (1944), claimant said: 66 They come over there a couple of times and I would get all fussed up and Dr. Wagner put a stop said no one was to mention anything 'to him' about the light company. That was Dr. Cullegon, he insisted I sign. I said I couldn't sign, and he said, 'You will have to'. He said, 'Make an X'. He said, 'I'll take your hand'. And I think he did, but I can't recall. It seems to me he took my hand and got me to write, I'm not sure now."

The last money received by claimant from defendant was by a check dated March 5, 1947, in the amount of $68.64, marked "Pay Ending: February 28, 1947". Accompanying the check was a voucher notation reading: 

"RETROACTIVE WAGES JOB EVALUATION, $69.02. 

In addition to regular wages, this voucher includes the sum of $31.20 paid in accordance with the policy covering absence from work due to nonoccupational illness or injury." 

Claimant stated that about the last date that he worked for defendant, although he could not recollect the date, he came home feeling fine, but suddenly he felt "funny in the head" and then went to sleep for a period of three days.

He consulted Dr. J. Huber Wagner, who recommended hospitalization. He stated that he had worked "off and on" until he quit work. Winterhalter said that he was assigned such duties as his physical condition permitted. Claimant's wife, Marie Winterhalter, testified that she thought claimant last worked sometime in October 1945. She stated that claimant's nerves are "all shot" since then and that sometimes claimant will go to bed for a week at a time and at other times, he will spend most of the night in the basement and garage, hammering away.

1948]  Dr. J. Huber Wagner, claimant's witness, testified that claimant first came under his service in the hospital on October 30, 1941, for a cerebral concussion, laceration of the scalp and fracture of the right wrist and was discharged on November 22, 1941. The patient was readmitted to the hospital on November 29, 1941, for post-concussional headaches and discharged on December 10, 1941. He was a hospital patient again from May 21, 1942, to June 26, 1942, suffering from headaches, dizziness, lassitude and general weakness. Claimant was again hospitalized from January 9, 1946, to February 26, 1946, for the same complaints. Dr. 

Wagner stated that he last examined claimant on May 1, 1947, and that the patient still complained of headaches, weakness and exhaustion. The doctor was of the opinion that claimant is totally and permanently disabled and would consider him a nondescript on the labor market. Questioned as to any casual connection between claimant's present condition and the accidents, the doctor testified: "When I first saw this man he was very badly hurt, and in these brain injuries very often these people go on to a complete recovery; this man reported back showing the clinical symptoms of post-concussional syndrome, showing that he had a damage to his brain, and, after treatments, spinal air injection, rest, forced feeding, etc., we got him back to a point where he was able to do light work; then, following pressure and overexertion, he relapsed back to the point where he had to be rehospitalized, as you see here. 

This has gradually gone on so that the brain damage, although not demonstrable on an organic basis, is, in my opinion, definite, so that his mental reserve and general reserve is at a very low ebb. He becomes tired easily, and, as a man gets older, his age tendency isn't to improve, but rather to remain in status quo, or get a little worse, and I think that's what happened to this man." 

The doctor thought that the first accident is the primary cause of claimant's condition and was aggravated by the later accidents.

C. S. Hamilton, defendant's welfare and compensation manager, testified that claimant was paid a total sum of $4,743.72 for the first accident, representing medical expenses of $772.10, compensation of $1,735.65 and welfare wage reimbursement of $2,235.97. No compensation was paid for the second accident. Claimant received compensation of $51.42, representing 3-6/7 weeks and a welfare wage reimbursement of $87.28, or a total of $138.70 for the third accident. The witness stated that claimant signed three final receipts in all. He said that the last final receipt was handed to claimant in defendant's office on or about August 20, 1944, the content explained to him, and the check was cashed by claimant several days later. The compensation manager testified that the final receipt was prepared after receipt from defendant's medical department of information indicating recovery. The witness testified, under cross-examination: "Q. At the time of the execution of the final receipt based on the first accident you didn't know anything about this post-concussional syndrome. "A. That had been mentioned, yes, and I had the report of Dr. Wagner." 

William J. Zehfuss, general foreman of a construction crew, testified that claimant worked from December 27, 1943, until March 27, 1944, at various assignments. On the latter date, claimant was promoted to a lineman C, at which job he worked until October 19, 1945, when defendant's records show that "he reported off sick". The foreman said claimant's work was satisfactory and that he had no complaint from claimant or those working with him. The witness stated that claimant lost no time from work except two weeks' vacation and two weeks' jury duty. Mrs. Winterhalter contradicted this statement, claiming that her husband "was more home than he was working", but that he received his regular wages. Claimant also testified that he lost considerable time from work prior to October 19, 1945. 

M. J. Scheller, superintendent of operations, northern division, testified that he approved the request that claim-

311 

 ant be paid for nonoccupational illness, as he was reported to the office "ill with the grippe" on October 19, 1945.

Scheller's recollection was that claimant was paid benefits in excess of $18 per week until October 19, 1946. S. E. 

Claney, defendant's office manager, testified that the purpose of the policy governing wage allowances "during the time such employes may be absent from work due to nonoccupational illness or injury is to provide regular hourly and daily rate employes a greater economic security by providing wage allowances during those periods when such employes may be absent from work due to nonoccupational illness or injury”. He explained the schedule of benefits and gave a record of payments to claimant showing a final payment to October 31, 1946. Mrs. Winterhalter, recalled by claimant, denied that she reported claimant off to Scheller on October 19, 1946, on account of grippe, and claimed she told the superintendent it was on account of the head injury. 

Hamilton, recalled by defendant, testified that he explained to attorney William H. Markus in January 1946 that claimant's absenteeism and disability were not casually connected with any accident in the course of employment, but agreed to provide further medical and hospital care, purely as a welfare measure. However, the medical diagnosis upon admission to the hospital was the same as upon claimant's previous admissions. Claimant's uncontradicted medical evidence indicates that the accidental head injuries have resulted in a post-concussional syndrome manifested, as the referee found, "by general weakness, mental instability, dizziness and headaches". On August 8, 1944, when the final receipt was signed, the same post-concussional syndrome existed, even though he continued in employment until October 19, 1945, when he again became totally disabled. 

Claimant testified that he received preferential work assignments and that he was off work a good deal. Claimant's history in this case is not uncommon in cases involving a head concussion. Often, symptoms are arrested and then suddenly flare up and become active, causing disability. 

Although claimant's condition may have been dormant when

[84 Dep. Rep. 

the receipt was signed, it nevertheless existed, and we are of the opinion that defendant had knowledge of its existence. 

Even though both parties were aware of the sequelae, they were mistaken in fact as to its seriousness and disabling character. We believe that the quantity and quality of proof are sufficiently definite and specific to overcome the final receipt: McKissick v. Penn Brook Coal Co., 110 Pa. Superior

Ct. 444. When the final receipt was solicited, defendant's representative had before him a medical report from Dr. 

Wagner that claimant was suffering from a post-concussional syndrome. Defendant then knew or should have known that claimant had not made a complete recovery from his accidental injuries. Although defendant's representative stated that he had information from the company doctor that full recovery had been made by claimant, the statement, although unchallenged, was clearly inadmissible as violative of the hearsay rule. No medical testimony was offered in defendant's behalf to the effect that claimant had fully recovered. Under the circumstances a final receipt was improper and defendant should have proceeded with a petition for modification of compensation. A suspension order would then have been warranted. We are of the opinion, too, that claimant's petition to review an existing agreement may also be properly considered as a timely petition to reinstate compensation under the second paragraph of section 413 of the act upon grounds of a recurrence of disability. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's 10th, 11th, 12th and 13th findings of fact and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following: "Findings of fact "10. The board finds as a fact that claimant had not fully recovered from his accidental injuries when he executed the final receipt on August 8, 1944, of which fact defendant had knowledge and that the procurement of the final receipt by defendant at that time was improper. "11. Claimant suffered a recurrence of total disability on 

October 19, 1945, as a result of said accidental injuries and

1948] 

 such total disability has continued up to the present time." 

The referee's other findings of fact are affirmed. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's 2nd, 3rd and 4th conclusions of law. In lieu thereof, we substitute the following " "2. Having found that the final receipt was procured by improper conduct and that claimant has suffered a recurrence of total disability as a result of the accidents on 

October 30, 1941, and July 13, 1944, he is entitled to have the final receipt set aside and compensation reinstated under agreement no. 4,508,868."

The referee's first conclusion of law is affirmed. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's orders dismissing the petition to set aside final receipt and claimant's modification petition. We substitute the following "Order "Defendant, Duquesne Light Company, is directed to reinstate compensation payments under agreement no. 4,508,868 and to pay to claimant, Charles E. Winterhalter, compensation at the rate of $18 per week, beginning October 19, 1945, and continuing thereafter so long as claimant shall continue to be disabled, within the limitations of the act; defendant to receive credit for payments made to the claimant. "This award to bear interest in accordance with section 

410 of the act."

The appeal of claimant is sustained.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD STREPPA v. BEN CONSTRUCTION CO. 

Workmen's compensation-Partial disability-Injury to hand- 

Loss of use of two fingers.

A referee's order awarding partial disability as a result of injury to claimant's hand, will be set aside where the medical testimony was in accord that the partial ankylosis remaining in the index and middle fingers was attributable to the condition of the third and fourth fingers for the loss of use of which claimant had been paid; in such circumstances no additional compensation was due. 

Appeal by defendant from order of Referee Moore, District No. 8, awarding compensation under compensation agreement no. 4,882,282. Reversed. May 12, 1948.

Employer's Mutual Liability Insurance of Wisconsin, in surance carrier. 

Louis Rosenfield, for claimant. 

H. Y. Crossland, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

Claimant, Alfred J. Streppa, suffered accidental injuries on August 19, 1946, during the course of his employment by defendant, Ben Construction Company. The record indicates that claimant was paid compensation for 35 weeks under an open agreement and upon his refusal to execute a final receipt, defendant filed its petition to terminate on June 11, 1947, alleging that disability has resolved itself in loss of the ring and little fingers on the left hand. The record refers to a review petition filed by claimant which does not appear in the record. However, testimony was taken before Referee 

Moore upon both petitions. The referee found that claimant sustained a 25 percent partial disability as a result of the

1948] 

 accident and entered an appropriate award. Defendant has appealed.

Although the compensation agreement recites injury to fingers on both hands, no serious claim is made that there is any residual disability in the right hand. The controversy between the parties relates to the extent of disability resulting from the accident to the left hand. Defendant contends that the pain, inconvenience and disability which claimant experiences in the left hand is the natural and normal sequence which flows from the loss of the two fingers in question and that compensation for such specific loss under section 306 (c) of the Workmen's Compensation Act of June 

21, 1939, P. L. 520 terminates compensation liability. Lente v. Luci, 275 Pa. 217. Claimant, on the other hand, claims that he suffers disability to the left hand, separate and apart from the loss of the two fingers.

Each party produced medical testimony. Dr. George V. 

Foster, an orthopedic surgeon, testified in behalf of defendant that he examined claimant on January 20, 1947, and found that the thumb on the left hand had good motion, the index and middle fingers had about 75 percent of normal motion, and that claimant had lost the use of the ring and little fingers. The doctor's diagnosis was "compound fracture of the fourth and fifth fingers. In other words, the doctor felt that claimant's inability to use the two fingers in question caused some restriction of motion of the index and second fingers. The physician admitted that claimant had only about a 35 percent of normal grip in the hand. The doctor testified relative to loss of grip, as follows: "I feel that it's due to the industrial loss of the fourth and fifth fingers and the fact that those fingers are left on so that they cause a restriction of motion of the index and middle fingers." 

The doctor ascribed "shooting pains" into the wrist as due to injured nerves of the third and fourth fingers.

Dr. M. S. DeRoy, an osteopathic surgeon, called by claimant, testified that he made an examination of claimant on

June 27, 1947, which included X-ray. The doctor's pertinent findings and conclusions were "a residual disability of the left hand characterized by loss of active motion and control of these two fingers (third and fourth), with fibrosed partial ankylosis of the joints of the fingers and a loss of sensation in the ring finger". The doctor estimated that claimant had a residual permanent disability of 50 percent in the left hand. Questioned as to any benefit to be derived from amputation of the two fingers, Dr. DeRoy testified: "Well, it would be pretty radical treatment, but I think he would have real use of his first three fingers if the others didn't restrict him, but as long as the fourth is limited in flexion, you can't close the other fingers."

Under cross-examination, claimant's physician stated that aside from the condition found in the third and fourth fingers, he found the hand, "structurally", to be normal. The doctor further testified: "Q. Aside from the injury or disability of the fourth and fifth fingers of the left hand, is there any disability in the remainder of the hand which is separate, apart, and distinct from the disability to the fourth and fifth fingers? "A. Only by virtue of their proximity, and the fact that the tendons work in unison-they are dependent on one another, but, actually, if you can rule out these two last fingers, structurally there's nothing in the other fingers, but they are limited because they can move only as four fingers. "Q. Assuming, Doctor, that the claimant's fourth and fifth fingers had completely healed back to normal from this accident; with that assumption what would be your opinion as to the disability remaining in the left hand? "A. If the fourth and fifth fingers had become normal? "Q. Yes, sir. "A. I don't think he would have any disability."

The doctor admitted that, in his opinion, claimant does not have any disability unrelated to or connected with the third and fourth fingers. Claimant testified that he had difficulty in gripping with the left hand and that at times

1948] 

 he experiences pains in the hand, which "shoot right up" through the wrist. Claimant stated that he is reluctant to have an amputation because of appearances. 

The medical testimony is in accord that the stiffening in the index and middle finger are attributable to the condition of the third and fourth fingers and result in a reduction of the gripping power of the left hand and impedes claimant in the performance of work as a laborer. The sole question posed in this case is whether the partial ankylosis, or stiffening of the joints in the index and middle fingers, is due to the industrial loss of the other two fingers, or is an entirely separate, independent and unrelated result from the accident. Dr. DeRoy "ties in" the residual disability of the first two fingers mentioned as related to the condition of the ring and little fingers. The palmar surface of the left hand is sound. It is our considered opinion that the present disability of the claimant is wholly "wrapped up" with the loss of the two last fingers and no additional compensation is due therefor under the act and the decisions of our appellate courts. In the case of Niemi v. Asplundt Tree Expert Co., 154 Pa. Superior Ct. 600, claimant suffered the accidental loss of the index and middle fingers of the left hand by amputation. Compensation was improperly awarded for partial disability of the hand. The court said (p. 606): "The loss of the gripping power of the hand cannot be added to a partial loss of function of the remaining fingers to determine the extent of compensable disability. The amputation of the two principal fingers inexorably was responsible for a very substantial loss of gripping power. 

Whatever loss of such gripping power was caused by the amputation has been compensated for in the award for 65 weeks under Section 306 (c). Lente v. Luci, 275 Pa. 217, 119 A. 132; Priorello v. State Workmen's Insurance Fund et al., 133 Pa. Superior Ct. 373, 2 A. (2d) 864." 

In the recent case of Pellegrino v. Consumers Mining Co., 162 Pa. Superior Ct. 119 (January 8, 1948), claimant suffered "amputation of index finger at first phalange; and

middle finger lacerated on right hand". The referee awarded 

20 percent partial disability under section 306 (b) of the act. 

Upon appeal, the board modified liability to the loss of use of the index and second fingers and found "that other disability to the ring and little finger is the result of the injury to the second finger and the failure to have the same amputated". Upon appeal to the County Court of Allegheny 

County, the court remanded the record for "further hearing and determination of any additional disability and loss of earning power that may entitle the claimant to any additional compensation". The Superior Court held that the practical effect of the court's order was a mandate to the board "merely for the formality of an additional award for partial disability". The Superior Court affirmed the action of the board. President Judge Rhodes said (p. 123): "It was not shown that there was any other injury or any disability not resulting from the loss of the two fingers. See

Bordick v. John Conlon Coal Company, 144 Pa. Superior Ct. 

522, 529, 19 A. (2d) 536. But it does appear from the testimony, and the Board so found, that the condition concerning which appellant complains, restriction of movement of little and ring fingers of the right hand, is the result of the specific losses or permanent injuries for which compensation is fixed by Section 306 (c)."

It was thus determined that there was no separate and distinct disability apart from the two fingers. The instant case is similar in all respects. Compensation is due under section 306 (c) for a specific loss and the board is without authority to enlarge upon the statutory schedule of benefits. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's 2nd finding of fact and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following "Findings of fact "2. We find as a fact that claimant, as a result of the accident on August 19, 1946, has lost the use of the ring and little fingers of the left hand."

The referee's 1st finding of fact is affirmed.

1948] 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's 2nd conclusion of law. The referee's 1st conclusion of law is affirmed. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's order and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following "Order "The board, accordingly, awards to claimant, Alfred J. 

Streppa, and against defendant, Ben Construction Company, and/or its insurance carrier, Employer's Mutual Liability Insurance Company of Wisconsin, as total disability for specific loss of the use of the third and fourth fingers of his left hand compensation at the rate of $20 per week for a period of 35 weeks, beginning August 26, 1946, up to and including April 27, 1947, or in the total amount of $700. "This award is to bear interest in accordance with section 

310 of the act. "Further, defendant and/or its insurance carrier is directed to take credit against this award for compensation payments already made to claimant." 

The appeal of defendant is sustained.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD CHESTER CARR v. HOLLINGSHEAD & CHRISTIAN Workmen's compensation-Employe—Injury while working on defendants' silo-Casual employment.

An appeal from a referee's order of disallowance of compensation will be dismissed where it appears claimant when injured was engaged in work on defendants' silo on a farm operated by them; under the circumstances, the work being performed by claimant at the time of his injury was casual employment and not in the regular course of defendants' business.

An appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee 

Olexy, District No. 2, claim petition no. 108,267, accident no. 4,972,848. Modified-Affirmed. May 12, 1948.

[84 Dep. Rep. 

Penna. Thresherman & Farmers' Mutual Casualty Ins. 

Co., insurance carrier. 

Smith & Eves, for claimant. 

J. G. Feinour and E. C. Marianelli, for defendants.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal from an order of disallowance entered by Referee Olexy September 22, 1947.

The petition in the case was filed by Chester Carr, claimant, March 26, 1947, against Arthur W. Hollingshead and

Lucas A. Christian, trading as Hollingshead & Christian, defendants. Defendants conducted a drugstore in Bloomsburg but also were engaged in farming at two locations in the surrounding countryside. Shortly before the accident in the case, which occurred September 7, 1946, they were interested in having the inside of a silo on one of the farms, particularly the metal hoops, treated with linseed oil. With a view to this they contacted claimant's father, Elroy Carr, who, besides running his own farm, did some contracting work. The elder Carr advised them on September 5, 1947, that he could not do the work alone and there is some dispute evident in the testimony at this point in the story as to whether he or defendants suggested the younger Carr as a helper. In any event, father and son undertook the job and used equipment and materials supplied by the former. It is also quite clear that direction of the work was conceded to the elder Carr.

The mishap which gives rise to the case occurred at 3 o'clock in the afternoon of September 7, 1946. At that time the chain on a suspended chair broke and claimant fell to the floor of the silo breaking the femur of the left leg just above the knee and causing injuries to the left foot which would require operative procedure to correct the position of the left great toe. Thereafter he was in the Bloomsburg Hospital until November 24, 1946, incurring a bill of $542.96 and

1948] 

Dr. L. F. Bush, who examined him twice during the first week in April 1947, was permitted to state without contradiction that he was totally disabled at the time of the hearing. Healing of the femur fracture was complicated by the presence of osteomyelitis and the prognosis was for slow recovery.

At the hearing in this matter, the issue emphasized was whether or not claimant had been employed by his father or by defendants. On this point both father and son testified that immediately after defendants' inquiry, claimant had gone to the drugstore in Bloomsburg and been employed directly. In support of this, defendants' checks paying each of them separately appear with the record as exhibits and this manner of payment is admitted. But statements by both the Carrs taken at the Bloomsburg Hospital October 1, 1946, by R. B. Shutts, the adjuster for defendants' insurance carrier, indicate that the elder Carr hired claimant at the rate of $1.25 per hour. Both of them have admitted reading and signing these statements but now declare that the item last mentioned was a very plausible oversight. 

Before leaving our review of the testimony, it is necessary to point out that there is very little evidence directed to the purpose of showing that there was any connection between the operation of the drugstore and the farms owned by defendants. Claimant had a rather indefinite impression that lunches were served at the drugstore and Hollingshead admitted that some vegetables from the farm were used in the business conducted in Bloomsburg but stated that all the milk produced on the farm was sold to the R. R. DuBois Dairy.

The principal contention on appeal is that, since the referee has refused to accept as credible the denials by claimant and his father of that portion of the statements they signed which places the hiring between them rather than between claimant and defendants, then claimant became a statutory employe under his father and is, therefore, entitled to relief under section 203 of the Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 520.

But this is all beside the real point in the case. Whether or not claimant was either an employe, in the true sense of the work, or a statutory employe of defendants does not matter. 

The general factual situation as to which there is no dispute, is such, under the law, that neither the referee nor this board has any alternative. The same situation has been before the courts (Blake v. Wilson, 268 Pa. 469) and it has been held that a disabling injury sustained under circumstances so similar to those in the instant case as to be well nigh identical could not be considered compensable because it was incurred in casual employment not in the regular course of the employer's business. The referee has not included this conclusion in his decision. We, therefore, believe we are bound to modify his findings accordingly. 

The 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th, 9th and 14th findings of fact and order of Referee Olexy dated September 

22, 1947, are affirmed. 

The 10th, 11th, 12th and 13th findings of fact and conclusion of law of Referee Olexy dated September 22, 1947, are vacated and set aside and the following substituted therefor: "Findings of fact "10. The work being done by claimant for defendants was casual and not in the regular course of defendants' business. "Conclusion of law "1. Since claimant's accidental injury was sustained while doing work which was casual and not in the regular course of defendants' business, the disability resulting from such injury is not compensable under the law.” 

The appeal is dismissed.

1948] 

 COMMON PLEAS NO. 4, PHILADELPHIA COUNTY FORBES v. KEASBEY & MATTISON ET AL. 

Workmen's compensation—Accidental injury—Hernia-Occurrence while performing usual work in usual manner. 

An order of the compensation board dismissing a claim petition for compensation will be affirmed where the claim was based on disability resulting from a hernia which was first noticed by claimant at a time when he was doing his usual work in the usual manner which consisted of lifting, with the help of another employe, steel plates weighing approximately 115 pounds; under the circumstances, there was no evidence of an accident within the meaning of the 

Workmen's Compensation Act. 

Appeal from the Workmen's Compensation Board. C. P. 

no. 4, June term, 1947, no. 5522. Appeal dismissed. May 

12, 1948. 

S. H. Torchia, for plaintiff. 

F. L. Fuges, for defendants.

GUERIN, Judge: 

This is an appeal by claimant from the action of the 

Workmen's Compensation Board in refusing to make an award.

There is no dispute as to the facts, all of which appear from the following stipulation filed with the board: "On July 16, 1945, the above-named claimant was employed by the above-named defendant as a press machine operator. As part of the duties of this job he had to lift steel plates weighing 115 pounds and asbestos sheets weighing 50 pounds, but had another man to help with the lifting. "At 10:30 a. m. on July 16, 1945, while doing this work, he felt a pain in his left groin, and noticed a small swelling there. At said time he was doing his usual work in the usual manner. He continued working until quitting time,

at 2:00 p. m. on that day. He reported to the plant doctor at 4:00 p. m. on that day, and was subsequently furnished a truss. "In 1934 this claimant was operated on for a right femoral hernia. It is further agreed that notice was given by claimant in conformity with the provisions of the act, and that he was operated on for a left inguinal hernia November 2, 1945. At this time he was hospitalized for nine days, at no cost to him. "Doctor Jacobs operated and charged the claimant $100. 

As a result of this hernia claimant was disabled for 13 weeks, from November 2, 1945, when all disability terminated, 13 weeks following November 2, 1945. This claimant's wages were in excess of $60 per week.” 

The Workmen's Compensation Act of June 2, 1915, P. L. 

736, sec. 301, as amended, 77 PS §341, provides for "compensation for personal injury to . . . employee, by an accident, in the course of his employment, The amendment of May 18, 1945, P. L. 671, sec. 1, 77 PS §515, effective July 1, 1945, provides: "Where claim is made for hernia, claimant must notify the employer or a representative of the employer within forty-eight hours after the cccurrence of the accident." 

Claimant urges that the proof of the "accident" is found in the change in the physical structure of the body, rather than in external evidence of an untoward occurrence; and that in hernia cases, the rupture of the abdominal wall evidenced by the protrusion accompanied by pain, immediately subsequent to the lifting, is, in itself, sufficient from which to infer that this was the result of an accident. 

Claimant places great reliance upon Davis v. Jones & 

Laughlin Steel Co., 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 133 (1945).

In that case, claimant was engaged in lifting a steel rail when he suffered a hernia as he turned to throw the rail aside. As was pointed out in the opinion of the Superior 

Court, the circumstances embodied in the findings of the

1948] 

Workmen's Compensation Board, supported by strict proof, established an unexpected injury—an unusual result—from sudden effort or strain. The Superior Court construed the findings as those of an accident, though occurring in the course of the performance of claimant's ordinary duties. 

For this reason, the Superior Court held the claim compensable. The opinion emphasizes, however, the necessity for the claimant to prove the happening of the "accident". 

In Adamchick v. Wyoming Valley Collieries Co., 332 Pa. 

401 (1938), claimant, whose duties required him to carry railroad ties weighing between ten and fifteen pounds each, was stooping over in the act of picking up a tie when he got a pain in the shoulder. Nothing hit him, but "something just took" him in the neck as he started to pick up the tie. In reversing the Superior Court and entering judgment for the defendant, the Supreme Court held that the evidence negatived the idea of an accident. The opinion of Mr. Justice Schaffer reads in part (p. 403): 

"The Compensation Act (June 2, 1915, P. L. 736, Sec. 301, 

77 PS Sec. 431) provides for 'compensation for personal injury to, or for the death of, such employee, by an accident, in the course of his employment'. In Billo v. Allegheny Steel Co., 328 Pa. 97, 195 A. 110, speaking through 

Mr. Justice Maxey, we said (p. 101): "The conclusion is inescapable that only when an employee meets with an accident in the course of his employment do the provisions of the act become operative to him,' and in Gausman v. 

Pearson Co., 284 Pa. 348, 354, 131 A. 247, we declared: 'Disability, overtaking an employee at his work, is not compensable unless the result of accident . . . neither can death or disability overtaking an employee in the course of his employment and resulting from a natural cause; if it could, it would render the employer an insurer of the life and health of the employee."" 

In Crispin v. Leedom & Worrall Co., 341 Pa. 325 (1941), it appeared that claimant suffered of a chronic heart con-

dition. After he and an associate had pushed a heavy truck from an elevator which was an inch to an inch and a half below the floor level, claimant became ill, having strained a heart muscle. He had frequently performed the same act and the conditions under which the truck had been pushed were not unusual but ordinary. In reversing the referee, the board, the court of common pleas, the Superior Court, and the Supreme Court held that claimant was not entitled to compensation.

At page 328, the opinion of the Supreme Court reads: “Summarizing our judgment in the Adamchick case, we said (p. 410): 'After giving careful consideration to the provisions of the Workmen's Compensation Act, the policy which underlies it, our own decisions and those of the Superior Court, not all of which seem to be in full harmony, our conclusion is that to secure compensation there must be proof both of an accident and of an injury; an accident cannot be inferred merely from an injury. There must be some evidence of an accident, either direct or circumstantial, in the latter instance clearly and logically indicating it. In this case, there was none. Nor can an injury be inferred simply because there was an accident. There must be proof that the injury resulted from an accident.'”

In Good v. Pennsylvania Department of Property and 

Supplies, 346 Pa. 151 (1943), claimant, a pipe fitter, was engaged in lifting a bucket of pipe fittings to his shoulder. 

There was evidence that he lifted it on the day of the accident in a way different from that which he had employed on previous occasions. When he got the bucket, weighing anywhere from 60 to 100 pounds, from his knee to his shoulder, it was testified that the sweat started to pour out of him. Later he was found at a point 75 to 100 feet away from where the lifting took place, sitting on a pile of boards with his head slumped forward and the bucket, still full, in an upright position, was some five to ten feet away. 

Part of his duties as a pipe fitter necessitated the lifting of heavy pieces of pipe, quantities of fittings and couplings,

1948] 

 radiators and the like. He suffered a coronary occlusion which resulted in his death. Claimant, his widow, offered no evidence that her husband had ever before lifted such a heavy weight or carried weight on his shoulder. 

The Supreme Court in affirming the Superior Court denied claimant the right to recovery. It pointed out that compensation was payable for the death of an employe caused by an "accident" in the course of his employment. 

The opinion of the Supreme Court reads in part as follows (p. 154): "An accident is 'an occurrence which proceeds from an unknown cause, or which is an unusual effect of a known cause, and hence unexpected and unforeseen': Lacey v. 

Washburn & Williams Co., 309 Pa. 574, 578. The factor which is unexpected may lie either in the circumstances causing the injury or in the nature of the injury itself: 

Parks v. Miller P. Mach. Co., 336 Pa. 455, 458-9. In the first type, a fortuitous happening occurs, but the injury is the natural consequence of that happening. In the second type an ordinary event takes place, but results in an unforeseen injury, as, for example, in Wolford v. Geisel 

M. & S. Co., 262 Pa. 454, where a healthy piano mover while lifting a piano suffered an abscess, culminating in pneumonia. If an employee already afflicted with a disease suffers in the course of his employment an injury which is the natural result of the disease, there can be no recovery, for there is then neither the fortuitous event to cause the injury, required in the first type of case, nor an unexpected result of an ordinary happening, as in the second type: 

Monahan v. Seeds & Durham, 336 Pa. 67, 70. In the second class it is only where the cause of the injury was unexpected that an employee can recover for an aggravation of an existing ailment, but the fact of injury does not give rise to an inference that its cause was unexpected: Adamchick v. Wyoming Val. Col. Co., 332 Pa. 401, 410." 

In Turek v. Damalak, 161 Pa. Superior Ct. 84 (1947), it was held that there must be clear proof of an accident to warrant compensation. To the same effect is Rupchak v.

Westinghouse Electric & Mfg. Co., 161 Pa. Superior Ct. 

228 (1947). 

We are unable to find from the stipulated facts in the case any evidence sufficient to overcome the statutory presumption of fact that hernia is a physical weakness which ordinarily develops gradually, other than from accidental causes. There is no evidence of an "accident" within the meaning of the Workmen's Compensation Act and its Amendment. 

The exceptions and the appeal are therefore dismissed. 

Counsel will prepare a form of judgment.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD HOGG v. KEHOE-BERGE COAL COMPANY 

Workmen's compensation-Occupational disease-Anthraco-silicosis- Period of employment by defendant-Successive owners of mine— Liability of owner at time when disability occurred. 

A referee's order dismissing a claim petition for disability resulting from anthraco-silicosis, will be reversed and the record remanded where the referee denied compensation solely on the ground that claimant's period of employment by defendant was less than six months, it being admitted, however, claimant had been exposed to a silica hazard in the employ of successive employers for the required period, though the record failed to show affirmatively that claimant's employment had been continuous in the same mine for the requisite period, in which event he would be entitled to compensation from the employer who was the owner at the date disability occurred.

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Olexy, District no. 2, Claim petition no. 108,894, accident no, 5,015,607. Reversed and remanded. February 25, 1948. 

T. L. Kennedy, Jr., for claimant. 

Charles Shea, for defendant.

1948] 

JACOBY, Commissioner:
