This case is before the board upon appeal by claimant, James Hogg, from the order of Referee Olexy dismissing his claim for compensation for total disability resulting from anthraco-silicosis. Defendant is Kehoe-Berge Coal Company. 

The following significant facts were agreed upon by counsel for the interested parties, as follows (p. 3): "It is agreed between parties that James Hogg was employed by the Kehoe-Berge Coal Company from February 

16, 1946 to June 21, 1946; by the Panzetti Coal Company from August 30, 1945 to February 16, 1946; by the Pennsylvania Coal Company at the Euen Colliery from July 9, 1943 to August 1, 1945; at the Franklin Coal Company from 

1941 to July 1, 1943 and for the Sullivan Trail Company from 1935 to January 1, 1941."

Exposure to a silica hazard for the required period, total disability as a result of anthraco-silicosis, and proper notice are established. The referee concluded that "since the claimant's period of employment by defendant was less than six months, the claim petition must be dismissed".

The record of employment, as agreed upon, clearly establishes that claimant was employed by defendant from February 16, 1946 to June 21, 1946, a period slightly in excess of four months. No testimony was offered by the claimant in this connection. Section 301 (g) of the Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 566, provides: "The employer liable for the compensation provided by this article shall be the employer in whose employment the employe was last exposed to the hazard of the occupational disease claimed, regardless of the length of time of such last exposure: Provided, That when a claimant alleges that disability or death was due to silicosis, anthraco-silicosis, absestosis or any other occupational disease which developed to the point of disablement only after an exposure of five or more years, the only employer liable shall be the last

employer in whose employment the employe was last exposed to the hazard of such occupational disease during a period of six months or more after the effective date of this act; and in such cases an exposure during a period of less than six months after the effective date of this act shall not be deemed an exposure. The notice of disability or death and claim shall be made to the employer who is liable under this subsection, and his insurance carrier, if any." 

Counsel for defendant contends that the present case is ruled by the case of Silva v. Erie Forge Company, 149 Pa.

Superior Ct. 251 (1942), and is decisive of the question before us. The court said (p. 254): "It will be noted that section 301 (g) deals only with the liability of employers and is silent as to any rights which claimant may be entitled. The first part of this Section provides that the employer in whose employment the employe was last exposed to the hazard of the occupational disease claimed, regardless of the length of time of such last exposure, is liable for the payment of compensation. This, then, is general and applies to all, occupational diseases, except such as are specifically exempt from this provision. In the later half of the Section it is provided that silicosis, anthracosilicosis, asbestosis, or such other occupational disease that requires an exposure of five or more years, the only employer liable shall be the last employer in whose employment the employe was last exposed to the hazard of such occupational disease during the period of six months or more after the effective date of the Act, and that an exposure of less than six months shall not be deemed an exposure. This Section applies only to employers and designates the one that shall be liable under certain circumstances. By reason of the difference between disability caused by an accidental injury which can be traced to a single event and an occupational disease which develops gradually over a period of time, this Section was designed to protect the last employer in whose employment the employe had not been exposed for six months or more. Thus, if an employe has not been in the employ of the particular employer and exposed to the

1948] 

 hazard for six months or more after the effective date of the Act, then he must, under the Act of 1939, seek relief against a prior employer in whose employment he has been exposed for a period of six months or more ending after the effective date of the Act."

The Silva case raised no issue as to liability between successive employers after the effective date of the Act of 1939, as there was no change of employers. The act became effective on October 1, 1939, and Silva became totally disabled in December 1939. The prime question before the appellate court was whether Silva was entitled to compensation benefits under the Act of 1939 or under the Act of July 2, 1937, P. L. 2714, and the apportionment of liability between defendant employer and the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.

Claimant's counsel contends, in the brief filed, that claimant has been employed continuously as a miner at Steven's Shaft from August 30, 1945, to June 21, 1946, and that defendant, in "taking over the operation" on February 16, 1946, assumed all liability for the mine operation, including the work records of the men then employed there, at the date of such assumption of operation. Claimant further contends that a veteran miner, of 10 or 20 years employment, would be barred from an award of compensation, where the mine ownership changed less than six months prior to his total disability and that such a construction of the act is foreign to the legislative intent.

The act imposes liability upon the employer only, who is the "last employer in whose employment the employe was last exposed to the hazard of such occupational disease during a period of six months or more after the effective date of this Act". The act has now been in force for more than eight years and it may well be assumed that owner and employe are fully cognizant of liabilities and benefits under it. Clearly, if the instant claimant had changed his employer by some action on his part in accepting new employment at a different mine operation, the last employer would be relieved from liability under the agreed upon dates stated in this case. However, where claimant's employment is continuous in the same mine for the requisite period, although a new

ownership intervenes, he is entitled to compensation from the employer who is the owner at the date when disability occurs. It is our opinion that the statutory reference to liability of employers contemplates a change in employment by the employe rather than a change in ownership of the mine in which the employe is working. A new ownership acquires not only the chattels, equipment, fixtures and good will of the mine operation, but also assumes the contracts of employment as well, and the concomitant liabilities of wage scales, working conditions, seniority benefits and the workmen's and occupational disease compensation acts. An employe's status as such, with attending benefits, is not jeopardized by change in ownership, so long as there is no interference or change in the nature of his employment and substantially the same working conditions pertain. A change in corporate ownership may well contemplate the liquidation or dissolution of the selling corporation. Is an employe, totally disabled by silicosis shortly after the change in ownership, to be denied compensation benefits in a futile action against a "ghost" corporation? We believe that the liability of the grantor necessarily continues over to the grantee operator.

The record is silent as to the facts and circumstances attendent upon the change of claimant's employer from the 

Panzetti Coal Company to the instant defendant on February 16, 1946. Nor is there any testimony upon the record that claimant worked in the same mine from August 30, 1945 to February 16, 1946 and from the latter date to June 21, 1946 when disability occurred. It is, therefore, necessary to return the record to the referee for clarification of these necessary facts.

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of dismissal. The record is now remanded to the referee for further hearing and determination in accordance with the views expressed herein.

The appeal of claimant is sustained. 

The referee shall give this case priority over all other cases pending before him.

1948] 

 COMMON PLEAS NO. 1, PHILADELPHIA COUNTY DEFEO v. WILLIAMS AND MARCUS COMPANY et al. 

Workmen's compensation—Injury—Assault by fellow employe— Personal feud—Finding by board. 

An award of compensation, based on a finding that claimant, while working in defendant's employ, was severely assaulted by another employe, will be reversed where the finding was the sole basis for the award and where the testimony was to the effect that claimant had provoked the assault by using insulting and foul language in addressing his fellow employe; under the circumstances, the blow which injured claimant was due to a personal quarrel utterly unconnected with his employment.

Appeal from the Workmen's Compensation Board. C. P. 

No. 1, December term, 1947, no. 1544. Claim petition no. 

106,282. Exceptions sustained. April 14, 1948. 

L. Propper, for plaintiff. 

G. H. Detweiler, for defendants.

PARRY, J.: 

Appeal from the Workmen's Compensation Board. 

Claimant averred in his petition that while operating a silk screen process machine he was struck on the head by the machine and thrown to the floor. At the hearing he testified that he was struck by a silk screen and must have struck the concrete. He then assented to a statement by the referee that he understood him to mean that he came into contact with a portion of the machine and fell to the floor. 

There is nothing to indicate that the machine was out of order; it was operated by hand. The claimant said his duty was to mix colors. While he attempted to describe the machine and the way it worked, it is impossible to extract from his testimony, nor in fact does he attempt to

explain, in which way such an accident as he attempted to describe could have happened. 

Defendant called as a witness one Murray, an office employe who had occasion from time to time to go into the room where claimant worked but did not work with him and had no control over him. Murray testified that for a number of months whenever he went through that room claimant, while not addressing him by name, used insulting and foul language to him as he passed. That he had warned claimant that if he didn't stop it there would be trouble but the warning had no effect. As to this occasion he testified as follows: 

Murray (Testimony 23-24) "A. I warned him . . . and he just didn't pay any attention to it. However I don't like fights or anything like that so I just ignored him until July and with my ignoring he became more violent in his talk. On July 16 I was out back for a longer time than usual and I heard myself branded as everything vile under the sun, so I went up to him. "Q. I want to know what you heard. I want the words. "A. Well, the usual thing is a bastard and a son of a bitch and a cocksucker and all that kind of stuff so I went up to him. . . and warned him again, and with that he laughed at me and said he thought I was a double cocksucker and if I as much as laid hands to him he'd wipe up the floor with me and called me a cocksucker again and

I just couldn't take it and I hit him. I saw him hit the floor. "Q. Was he hit by any screen? "A. No."

The eyewitnesses employed in the same room as the claimant corroborated what Murray said. Claimant was afterwards recalled and said he had never used such language. Upon this the referee made the following finding: "2. On July 16, 1946 the claimant, while working in the employ of the defendant was severely assaulted by Welland 

R. Murray, 516 Morgan Avenue, Palmyra, New Jersey, another employe of the defendant company."

1948] 

This finding is the sole basis for an award of compensation. There was an appeal by defendant to the compensation board which affirmed the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and award in an opinion by its learned chairman, the pertinent part of which reads as follows: "Defendant attempts to deny liability under that part of section 301 (c) of the act which states, inter alia: 66 "The term injury by accident in the course of his employment . . . shall not include an injury caused by an act of a third party intended to injure the employe because of reasons personal to him and not directed against him as an employe or because of his employment.' "To substantiate its theory, defendant called as a witness an employe, Welland R. Murray, who testified that, though an office employe, it was necessary for him to occasionally be in the department where claimant was employed and though there was no reason for same, claimant for a period from January to July had continuously used vile and abusive language toward him and that on July 16, 1946, when claimant had again used vile language to him, he had punched claimant with such force as to knock him unconscious and cause him to be sent to the hospital. Two other of the defendant's employes, John Henry Morris and John

Joseph McCloskey, corroborated the testimony of the witness. "In our opinion the effect of this testimony is lost when in reviewing the testimony we learn that it was not unusual for employes of the defendant to address each other with vile language and there was no personal enmity or antagonism between claimant and the witness Murray. With this testimony before him the referee was justified in finding that the assault on claimant by a fellow employe was not an injury by an act of a third person intended to injure claimant for personal reasons and having so found, claimant is entitled to an award."

Now the referee made no such finding. We have already quoted his second finding and this, with his fourth to the effect that claimant was totally disabled "as a result of

being assaulted while in the employ of the defendant", comprises all he had to say on the subject. If he had made any such finding as that attributed to him by the learned chairman, it would not have been supported by anything in the evidence.

The Compensation Board accepts the testimony but holds that it has no effect because it was not unusual for the employes of defendant to use vile language. This regrettable practice is all too common and no doubt bad language may at times be heard in every industrial establishment in Pennsylvania but we are unable to discover what possible bearing it can have on the question whether the assault here was provoked or committed by reason of anything concerning, relating to or arising out of the employment or to the status of the belligerents as employes. 

By what process of reasoning the learned chairman reached the conclusion there was no personal enmity or animosity between these men, we cannot fathom. The incident speaks for itself; the words were in the highest degree injurious and their use provoked an assault. They are quoted only to show that by no process of interpretation or construction can they be deemed to have been directed to Murray by reason of his employment or anything arising out of it. There is not a line in the record that will support the notion that the blow that injured the claimant was due to anything but a personal reason utterly unconnected with the employment. 

In our opinion this case falls within the explicit terms of the exception in the statute and as the evidence permits of no other conclusion, the Compensation Board should have so held.

Defendant's exceptions to the decision of the Compensation Board are sustained and judgment is entered for defendant.

1948] 

 WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD PETRIGNI v. GRIFFIN MANUFACTURING CO. 

Workmen's compensation-Accidental injury-Death from pneumonia 

-Voluntary risk-Employe going to first aid room-Exposure to chill.

A referee's disallowance of compensation to claimant on account of the death of her husband will be affirmed where decedent sustained an accidental injury to his right thumb during his course of employment by defendant following which he went from the inside of the plant where he was working to the outside in order to reach the first aid room and as a result was exposed to a colder temperature receiving a chill which induced lobar pneumonia from which he died; under the circumstances, decedent's voluntary act in going to the first aid room without his overcoat thereby inducing pneumonia was a reasonably foreseeable risk and not an unusual circumstance such as would sustain an award for an accidental injury. 

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Smith. 

District No. 10, claim petition no. 108,698, accident no. 

5,015,484. Affirmed as amended. June 23, 1948.

Pennsylvania Manufacturers Association Casualty Insur ance Co., insurance carrier. 

Joseph V. Agresti, for plaintiff. 

Howard N. Palte and H. M. Engell, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This case involves a death claim. It is before the board upon an appeal by claimant, Josephine Petrigni, from the order of Referee Smith disallowing compensation for the death of her husband, William Petrigni, on February 22, 1947. There is no dispute that claimant's decedent sustained an accidental injury to his right thumb on February 15, 1947, during the course of his employment by defendant,

Griffin Manufacturing Company. It is claimed that decedent contracted pneumonia when "he ran from the warm foundry into the cold air without any headdress or outer clothing". The pivotal question is whether decedent suffered an accident within the contemplation of the Workmen's Compensation Act.

Dr. Frank A. Trippe, claimant's witness, testified that he has been the family physician since 1919 and that he saw decedent professionally on February 17, 1947, at which time he made a diagnosis of lobar pneumonia and had the patient hospitalized. Petrigni's condition became progressively worse until he expired. The doctor said he received a history from the patient that he got chilled going to the first aid office without an overcoat. Dr. F. W. Underhill, defendant's medical witness, testified that he treated decedent at his office on February 15, 1947 for a contused laceration of the right thumb. Upon word from decedent's home on February 17th that Petrigni was ill and could not come to the doctor's office for a dressing, the doctor's associate, Dr. A. T. Roos, made a house call, and from the report received, Dr. Roos was suspicious of pneumonia and suggested that the family physician be called. Dr. Underhill visited the patient in the hospital on February 20, 1947, and found the thumb wound in a perfectly clean condition and healing as well as could be expected. The doctor was of the opinion that decedent did not suffer from shock as a result of the injury, but only a nervous reaction. He had no record or recollection that the patient fainted in his office, nor was there any record that there was any undue sweating so that decedent's clothing was wet or soaked. 

Asked whether there was any causal connection between the accident and the death, Dr. Underhill testified: "From my record and observation, I would say that there is no direct connection. The only connection could be indirect, and that would be if there were undue exposure caused by having had an injury. In other words, if a man were working in an extremely hot place, if his clothes were wet with perspiration and then he was exposed to the ex-

1948] 

 tent that his clothing became chilled, then I would say there might be a real connection, but in the absence of any real exposure, I don't think there would be any connection, direct or indirect."

Henry Stringer, a witness called by claimant, testified in regard to decedent's employment duties and his activities at the time of the accident. Stringer explained that he and decedent were loading and unloading coils in the no. 2 annealing room, when the accident happened. He testified: ". . . We was hooking what I call a cover that fits over the coils when you put it in the oven, but we was figuring to unload that. We was hooking it up. The craneman went to back it up and he caught his thumb between the crane and the cover and he hollered and I yelled to the craneman to stop..

The witness stated that decedent had worn a sweater and cap, but no overcoat, when the foreman took him out of the plant to see the plant doctor. It was the same outfit in which decedent was working. Questioned as to the temperature of the work room at the time of the accident, Springer did not know the approximate temperature. He stated that three furnaces were going at the time and he placed decedent about 20 yards from the nearest one, handling coils. He did not know whether Petrigni was perspiring at the time. The witness estimated the size of the plant building to be about 40 yards in length, 20 yards in width and 18 feet in height. Umberto Ferri, also an employe in the annealing department, testified as a witness for claimant that he saw decedent when he returned from the doctor, with his hand bandaged, and that decedent then took his lunch bucket and went home. Ferri estimated the distance from the annealing department to the first aid office at about 600 feet. Although he was not working in the same annealing room with decedent when the latter was injured, he thought that the room temperature varied from 30 to 90 degrees, depending upon the place in the room where the employe worked, the outside temperature, and how often the large doors are opened to bring in coal and steel. There

are two annealing rooms. Decedent was working at the time in the coal annealing room, but his overcoat had been left in the coke annealing room. The shortest route between the two rooms was through an open alley way for a distance of about 25 feet. He said no salamanders were used so the men could get warm but that they sit down close to the furnaces at the opposite end of the building if they wanted to get warm. Claimant testified as to marriage and dependency. She stated that claimant returned home about 10:30 a. m. on February 15, 1947, appearing "white and shaking", and that her husband enjoyed good health prior to the accident. She said that he went to bed, was very nervous and developed a fever the next evening. Mary 

Kindle, a daughter, also testified that her father explained to her, after he returned home, how the accident happened and that he told her he fainted in the doctor's office. 

Defendant called Donald Jeffery, its maintenance foreman, who testified that the annealing room in question was 

78 feet by 145 feet in size and that windows, seven feet high, range both sides of the building's length. These windows, he said, are generally open at the furnace end of the building and at the other end are opened or closed depending upon outside weather conditions. He said a salamander is occasionally used by the men at the opposite end of the room, to keep warm. Around the furnaces, the foreman estimated the temperature around 90 degrees and at the other end of building he also agreed with Ferri that the temperature would drop to about 30 degrees. He estimated the longest distance from this annealing room to the first aid station at approximately 360 feet, depending upon which room exit was used. Jeffery said that he checked the distance on a blue print of the plant. He stated the cars are pulled from the furnaces at a high temperature, cooled as they are moved along the tracks and when the men unload the car at the far end of the room from the furnaces, they are cold. Carson Marsh, annealing room foreman, testified that decedent reported the accident to him around 8:30 a. m. on February 15, 1947, and that after taking Petrigni

1948] 

 to the first aid room, he returned to make arrangements to take the injured man to the doctor. He said "and when I had returned he had received his first aid and had went back to get his overcoat and was just in the process of leaving for the doctor". The witness stated that decedent was off two or three days about a week or two before the accident and was told by decedent it was because of a cold. 

The witness testified that Petrigni wore a sweater and cap at work and that the men kept a coke heated salamander going at the far end of the room from the furnaces to keep warm. The foreman accompanied decedent to the first aid room, which he estimated was around 125 feet away. He admitted that decedent wore no overcoat on the walk to the first aid station. Ray Wolowicz, an assistant foreman, testified that he drove decedent to Dr. Underhill's office and was present during the doctor's examination and treatment. 

Asked whether Petrigni had fainted, the witness testified: "The only thing I know of is that when his hand was being dressed the doctor was putting clamps in his hand, in his finger, and he appeared to be under pain, under stress, so the nurse asked him to lower his head while the doctor was working. Now if he fainted, it must have been for a very brief interval, that I wasn't even aware of it because he got up by himself, got off the chair by himself, and walked out to the car by himself, and at that timewell, I was rather pleased-I thought that the injury wasn't serious."

We have carefully reviewed the testimony in this case. 

We believe that it is fair to infer, after a very careful appraisement of all of the testimony, that decedent, in handling the cold cars, was working in a place of a cool to cold temperature and that he was not sweating. However, in going from inside the plant to the outside, he was exposed to a colder temperature and in walking a distance of approximately 300 feet to the first aid room, without an overcoat, he was chilled. The weather was not extreme nor unusual for February. There is testimony from both sides that the injury made decedent quite nervous and excitable.

We are of the opinion that the pneumonia symptoms which were recognized two or three days after the accident, had their origin in decedent's trips to and from the first aid station. The referee concluded that the pneumonia was not contracted as a result of going to the first aid station without adequate clothing, "inasmuch as decedent normally and habitually went from his working place to the place where his outer wraps were kept, which required going outdoors and across an alley, in his ordinary working clothes". We cannot agree with this conclusion as stated. Individuals react differently to trauma and the sight of blood. Hospital odors may produce nausea in some to the point of fainting, and upon others they have no effect whatsoever. In decedent's nervous and excitable state, it is logical to believe that his body became somewhat moist so that the sudden cold air would affect him adversely. This cannot be determined with exact certainty and it must be conceded that the pneumonia may have originated at home or elsewhere. 

The case does not turn upon this point. Admitting that the walk to the first aid station caused the pneumonia is claimant entitled to an award?

We have examined a number of authorities in this connection. In the cases in which compensation has been allowed, the facts show something fortuitous, undesigned or unexpected. The leading case of Parks v. Miller Printing 

Machine Co., 336 Pa. 455, comprehensively reviews and classifies cases involving pneumonia death claims. The first class comprises cases where "there is an involuntary, unexpected, fortuitous happening which causes the disease". 

It is not contended in the instant case that the pneumonia was caused by the lacerated thumb itself. It is attributed entirely by claimant to the intervening circumstance of the walk in the cold air. The second class of cases pronounced by the Supreme Court, "where the work or act performed by the employe is voluntary and not marked by any abnormal or unusual feature, but where there occurs an unexpected and unusual pathological result", likewise excludes an award in this case. If claimant is entitled to an award

1948] 

 here, her claim must fall within the third classification of cases, concerning which class, the court said: 66 "The third group, more indefinite but nevertheless well established, is where the exposure is, from a technical standpoint, voluntary, and the resulting pneumonia or similar disease reasonably foreseeable, but where the "accident" consists of an unusual and suddenly developed concatemation of circumstances which necessitates impulsive rather than deliberate action and under conditions markedly different from those attendant upon the usual course of the employe's regular work. For example, a workman was suddenly called upon to attempt a rescue of his father who had been buried by the slide of a cul bank; the effort lasted about 22 hours; a large quantity of water was used in the rescue work and the employe was drenched from his knees down; the result of this exposure was a cold which later took the form of pneumonia. The act thus performed by the employe was voluntary and under conditions from which a resulting pneumonia might readily have been anticipated, but compensation was allowed because of the extraordinary circumstances which demanded prompt action on the part of the employe under unusual and exceptionally unfavorable conditions (Jones v. Philadelphia and Reading Coal and 

Iron Company, 285 Pa. 317).'" (Emphasis supplied.)

Other examples cited in the court opinion likewise demonstrate exigencies which are distinguishable from intentional and deliberate exposure to the elements: Roth v. 

Locust Mountain State Hospital, 130 Pa. Superior Ct. 1. 

Mindful as we are of the humane purposes of compensation, we cannot say that there is present here such a series of unusual circumstances as will sustain an award under our decisions. There was no sudden exposure to intense cold. The injury in the first instance was not of fatal proportions. Decedent regularly walked in the open air from one annealing room to the other under all kinds of weather conditions. Decedent's voluntary act in going to the first aid room without his overcoat may well have caused the pneumonia, but that risk was reasonably forseeable. It is a

danger which people in all walks of life risk in frigid or inclement weather, if not properly and adequately attired. 

A common sense and realistic view of all the facts negatives an award of compensation.

We hereby amend the referee's findings of fact by the following additional 

Findings of fact 11. We find as a fact that the death of claimant's decedent on February 22, 1947, from lobar pneumonia was not caused by the accident on February 15, 1947. The referee's other findings of fact are affirmed. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's second and third conclusions of law and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following

2. Having found that claimant's decedent's death was not caused by accident, claimant is not entitled to compensation therefor. 

The referee's order of disallowance is affirmed. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD LEITCH v. STATE WORKMEN'S INSURANCE FUND et al. 

Workmen's compensation — Occupational disease 

Claim petition · 

Limitation-Total disability subsequent to one year after the date of last employment. 

A claim for compensation for total disability resulting from anthraco-silicosis was timely where claimant's last exposure to a silica hazard was on December 12, 1944, although total disability did not occur until February 25, 1947, and claimant's petition was not

1948]  filed until May 26, 1947, where the evidence supported the referee's finding that claimant was partially disabled as a result of the disease on December 12, 1944, the date of his last exposure; the provision in section 301 (c) of the Occupational Disease Act limiting payment of compensation to such disease "occurring within one year after the date of his last employment" means that the disease must develop within one year after the date of the last employment, not that the action must be started within one year after that date nor that the claimant must have been totally disabled within one year. 

Appeal by Commonwealth of Pennsylvania from award of Referee Carmalt, specially presiding in the third district. 

Claim petition 108,909, Accident no. 5,015,621. Affirmed. 

June 23, 1948.

State Workmen's Insurance Fund, insurance carrier. 

Pearson M. Judd, for plaintiff.

Ralph H. Behney, for defendant and Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

This is an appeal by the Commonwealth from an award made by the referee. 

The record discloses that, in his petition filed on May 26, 1947, claimant alleged that he became totally disabled, on 

March 1, 1947, as a result of anthraco-silicosis contracted in the course of his employment. The answers of defendant and of the Commonwealth, both filed on June 3, 1947, denied the material averments of claimant's petition. After hearings, the referee found that claimant's occupation in an employment having a silica hazard resulted in his being partially disabled on December 12, 1944, and that, on February 25, 1947, he became totally disabled as a result of anthraco-silicosis and, in accordance with such finding, entered an award in favor of claimant. This appeal followed. Defendant has also taken its appeal from the action

of the referee (A-33687) which appeal has been determined by us in a separate opinion. 

The testimony presented in this case is to the effect that claimant's last exposure to a silica hazard was on December 12, 1944, and the Commonwealth argues that, since total disability did not occur until February 25, 1947, more than one year after his last exposure, claimant is barred. 

We are unable to agree with such argument. 

Section 301 (c) of the Occupational Disease Act provides, inter alia: "Compensation for . . . occupational diseases . . . shall be paid only when such occupational disease is peculiar to the occupation or industry in which the employee was engaged . . . and occurring within one year after the date of his last employment in such occupation or industry." 

The referee has found as a fact, and such finding is warranted by the testimony, that on December 12, 1944, claimant was partially disabled as a result of anthraco-silicosis. 

It is to be noted that that was also the last date upon which claimant was exposed to a silica hazard. 

While it is, of course, clear that compensation is not payable for partial disability resulting from an occupational disease, there is nothing from which we can infer that it was the intention of the legislature to deny the payment of compensation to a claimant who, within the one-year period prescribed in section 301 (c) of the Occupational Disease Act, has become disabled as a result of an occupational disease but his condition has not reached the point of total disability. In our opinion, the words "occurring within one year after the date of his last employment" mean that the disease must have developed within one year after the date of last employment and not that the action must be started within one year after the date of last employment, nor that claimant must have been totally disabled within one year. In Agostin v. Pittsburgh 

Steel Foundry Corp., 354 Pa. 543, the Supreme Court said: "The time, therefore, when total disability occurred was the date which began the running of the statute under either the Act of 1937 or the Act of 1939."

1948]  Since it was properly proved that claimant's condition of anthraco-silicosis developed within one year after the date of his last exposure, the action of the referee was proper and must be sustained.

We, therefore, affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and award. 

The Commonwealth's appeal is dismissed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD GAYDOSH v. RICHMOND RADIATOR COMPANY 

Workmen's compensation-Occupational disease-Insurance carrier— Liability of carrier on risk at time of total disability. 

Where claimant became totally disabled from silicosis on January 31, 1947, as a result of his exposure to a silica hazard during his employment with defendant over a period of approximately 20 years, the insurance carrier for defendant at the time claimant became totally disabled was liable for compensation. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Foust, District No. 9, claim petition no. 108,423, accident no. 4,994,649. 

Affirmed. March 10, 1948. 

Travelers Insurance Company, insurance carrier. 

Wade K. Newel, for plaintiff. 

John R. Bredin, for defendant. 

V. C. Short and William M. Dreher, special appearances.

KNOLL, Commissioner: 

Claimant filed a claim petition alleging that he became totally disabled on January 31, 1947, as the result of silicosis after exposure to a silica hazard during his employment with defendant from May 7, 1927, to January 31, 1947.

After hearing, the referee awarded claimant total disability payments against the employer, the Travelers Insurance Company and the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. 

Defendant and the Travelers Insurance Company filed this appeal wherein the sole issue raised is the liability of the insurance carrier to pay compensation in this case. 

The record shows that the Travelers Insurance Company became the insurance carrier of defendant on January 1, 1947; that the Liberty Mutual Insurance Company was the insurance carrier from January 1, 1945, to December 31, 1946; and that the Pennsylvania Manufacturers Casualty 

Insurance Company was the insurer prior to January 1, 

Defendant insurance carrier denies liability, contending that the insurance carrier on the risk at the time claimant was afflicted with silicosis is liable for the compensation payments and it cites Anderson v. Schroeder Monumental 

Works, 159 Pa. Superior Ct. 620, in support of its contention. In that case, the liability of successive insurers was determined by the court and it was held that "the insurer's liability attached when the employee was afflicted with silicosis", and that exposure to the silica hazard gives rise to the ultimate liability.

Section 301 (g) of the Pennsylvania Occupational Dis ease Act provides, in part, as follows: "The employer liable for the compensation provided by this article shall be the employer in whose employment the employe was last exposed to the hazard of the occupational disease claimed, regardless of the length of time of such last exposure."

Defendant insurer accepted the liability of the employer "in whose employment the employe was last exposed to the

1948] 

 hazard of the occupational disease" on January 1, 1947, approximately one month before the employe became totally disabled. Undoubtedly, claimant was afflicted with silicosis during the period of his last exposure to the silica hazard and during the time of coverage by defendant insurance carrier. In a broad sense of the word "afflicted", claimant was first afflicted with silicosis at some undeterminable time during his long employment with defendant company. 

To accept that contention, it would mean the denial of the benefits of the statute to practically all employes since it would be impossible to establish the exact moment when claimant was first afflicted with silicosis. In our opinion, the court, in Anderson v. Schroeder Monumental Works, supra, correlated the words "afflicted with silicosis" with the last exposure of claimant to the silica hazard and did not in any way suggest that the commencement of the disease fixed the liability of the insurance carrier. See 

Krupka v. State Workmen's Insurance Fund, 33 Dept. Rep. 

468, an opinion by Commissioner Jacoby.

Accordingly, the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of award are affirmed. 

COMMON PLEAS OF SCHUYLKILL COUNTY DUPLAK ET UX. v. WILLIAM PENN COAL COMPANY ET AL. 

Workmen's compensation-Partial dependency-Evidence-Sufficiency. 

An order of compensation based on a referee's finding of partial dependency will be reversed where it appears that decedent, minor son of the claimants, contributed the sum of $80 a month toward a common family fund out of which, however, he received his board, lodging, and clothing, both parents testifying to the effect that such fund received by them from decedent was solely applied toward his maintenance.

Appeal from Workmen's Compensation Board. C. P. of 

Schuylkill County November term, 1947, no. 321. Appeal sustained. February 2, 1948. 

Roger J. Dever, for plaintiffs. 

Penrose Hertzler and E. Max Troutman, for defendants.

PALMER, President Judge: 

Joseph Duplak, the minor son of claimant, was killed in an accident on November 18, 1946, while employed by defendant company. A claim petition was filed on March 31, 1947, wherein claimant, his parents, alleged partial dependency. A hearing was held before Referee Enterline on 

April 29, 1947, and the referee sustained the claim of the parents for partial dependency and this decision was affirmed by the Workmen's Compensation Board. 

Defendant company appeals from the decision of the Workmen's Compensation Board, alleging that there was no competent evidence offered by claimants to sustain award. 

Defendant specifically takes exception to the fifth finding of fact of the referee and the second conclusion of law derived from this finding, as well as to the award. 

The fifth finding of fact and the second conclusion of law are as follows: "5. The petitioners lived with four children, two boys, Frank 21 years of age, and Joseph, the decedent, just short of 18 years of age; and two girls, Evelyn, aged 13, and Jean, aged 11. The father, Michael, was employed as a door tender in the mines, earning $80 every two weeks, or $160 a month, which amount he gave over to his wife, less a little spending money. Decedent, as noted, was also earning about the same sum of money and in like manner gave his earnings to his mother who ran the household, furnishing decedent with board, lodging, clothing, spending money, etc. The testimony is not clear as to the contributions of the son, Frankie, but we conclude from the meager testimony that while he was in

1948] 

 the service he made a monthly remittance of $49. However, at the time of decedent's death Frankie was evidently out of the service and was employed, bringing in enough money, however, to pay for his suits only. The total running expenses of the above family were $300 a month." "2. The deceased's parents, the claimants herein, being partially dependent upon their son, Joseph, at the time of his accidental death in the course of his employment, they, the said claimants, are entitled to be compensated therefor, and accordingly we make the following. "Award "The defendants, William Penn Coal Company, employer and Coal Operators Casualty Company, insurance carrier, are ordered and directed to pay compensation to Michael 

Duplak and Susan, his wife, from November 25, 1946, to 

April 29, 1947, a period of 22-1/7 weeks, at the rate of $6 a week, and amounting to $132.86, and to continue at said rate for a period of 300 weeks, to wit, to August 25, 1952. "Interest at the rate of six percentum per annum is to be paid in accordance with the act."

There are no disputed facts in this case. The testimony of the mother of the deceased shows that he was 18 years of age and lived at home with his parents and his two younger sisters. The parents own their own home and the father is steadily employed. The mother further testified she handled the finances of the family and her husband gave her $160 a month of his earnings, and she received an allotment check of $49 a month from the Government for her son, Frank, who is in military service. This constitutes all of the family earnings at the present time.

Prior to the death of decedent he contributed $80 a month toward the common family fund. However, for this sum he received his board and lodging and his mother purchased his clothing. The greater part of her testimony relating to family expenses is contradictory, evasive and incoherent. 

The portion of her testimony relating to the contribution

of the decedent toward the family support is as follows (p. 9 of testimony): "Q. The money Joseph gave you did that do more than pay for his clothing and spending? "A. Not so exact but it wasn't enough to keep the boy for a month. "Q. The money that Joseph gave you did that do more than buy his food and clothing and take care of his spending money? "A. Just enough for his own self."

The testimony of the father upon this pertinent matter is as follows (p. 10 of testimony): "Q. What did the boy do with his money? 66 "A. He didn't make more than for himself, for shoes, clothing and for spending and there was nothing left of his money. That is all he make." 

The term "dependency" in the compensation statute contemplates actual dependency and must affirmatively appear upon the record as a fact. It is not essential, however, to show that such a dependency constitutes sole and exclusive support; Morris v. Yough Coal and Supply Co., 265 Pa. 211.

The purposes of the compensation statute is to provide compensation for loss of support to the dependent of the deceased employe: Corcoran v. Pennsylvania Coal Co., 76 

Pa. Superior Ct. 325.

When a minor contributes to a family fund there exists a presumption that such contribution is made toward the support of his parents: Conroy v. Loew's Inc., 102 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 523. However, the question of dependency must be decided upon the circumstances in each individual case. 

The dependency of a parent need not be to a great or considerable degree but some contribution on the part of the deceased child must be shown toward the providing of ordinary necessities of life suitable to a person in their class: 

Smitti v. Roth Cadillac Co., 145 Pa. Superior Ct. 292.

In the case before us the evidence of the application of funds contributed by Joseph Duplak to his mother and

1948] 

 father does not show that such funds were applied toward the support of the mother and father in any manner whatsoever. The positive testimony of the mother and father is to the effect that such funds were solely applied toward the maintenance of Joseph Duplak himself. The testimony relat ing to the need of the family budget for such contributions from Joseph during his lifetime is so vague, evasive, and incoherent as to not support the claim of claimants. 

We are of the opinion that there is a complete lack of competent testimony to support the award of compensation in this case and that the presumption in their favor was destroyed by the testimony of claimants themselves. 

And now, February 2, 1948, the appeal of defendant is sustained; the award of the referee and the Workmen's Compensation Board is overruled, and judgment is directed to be entered for defendant. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD MATHOWSKY v. CONSAGRA COAL CO. 

Workmen's compensation—Occupational disease—Anthraco-silicosis— Degree of disability-Conflict of medical testimony. 

A referee's order disallowing a claimant's petition for compensation under the provisions of the Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act will be reversed and the record remanded for the appointment of an impartial physician to examine claimant and testify where there was a clear conflict of medical testimony as to the degree of disability resulting from anthraco-silicosis contracted by claimant in the course of his employment; where claimant is limited to work of a selective or highly specialized character as a result of silicosis he is entitled to compensation under the provisions of the act. 

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Carmalt, District No. 3, claim petition no. 108,867, accident no. 

5,015,591. Appeal sustained. June 9, 1948.

Lackawanna Casualty Company, insurance carrier. 

T. L. Kennedy, for claimant. 

Patrick J. Flannery, for defendant. 

KNOLL, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by claimant from an order of Referee 

Gladstone A. Carmalt, specially presiding in the Third Compensation District, dismissing claimant's petition for compensation under the provisions of the Pennsylvania Occupa tional Disease Act. 

The only issue in this case is the degree of disability resulting from the anthraco-silicosis contracted by claimant while working in the anthracite coal mines over a period of 38 years. From October 1943 to October 10, 1946, claimant worked in defendant's mines. 

Dr. M. J. Stec, called on behalf of claimant, testified that he examined claimant on October 31, 1947. He expressed the opinion that claimant was totally disabled as the result of a third stage anthraco-silicosis. X-ray reports dated 

February 22, 1947, showed a third stage anthraco-silicosis.

Dr. B. J. McGuire, an x-ray specialist, called by defendant, testified that he made clinical and x-ray examinations on June 13, 1947, and that, in his opinion, claimant had a first stage anthraco-silicosis and an old healed pulmonary tuberculosis and was not totally disabled. 

A report, signed by Dr. F. A. Muschlitz, of an examination of claimant on June 23, 1947, concluding that claimant was not totally disabled was offered in evidence by the defendant.

Defendant offered testimony showing that claimant registered for light work at the Bureau of Employment and Unemployment and that he was seen doing some work at his home. However, Dr. Stec, who testified that claimant

1948] 

 was totally disabled, also said that claimant was able to do very light and limited work. If claimant is limited to work of a selective or highly specialized character, as a result of his silicosis, he is entitled to compensation under the provisions of the Act: Hurtuk v. H. C. Frick Coke Co., 157 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 317.

In view of the conflict of medical testimony as to the degree of disability and the extent of the anthraco-silicosis, we believe that the referee should have the benefit of impartial medical testimony. 

Accordingly, the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law, and order of dismissal are hereby set aside and the record is remanded to Referee Gladstone A. Carmalt, specially presiding in the Third Compensation District, for the appointment, by the board of an impartial physician, expert of chest diseases, who shall examine claimant and the record and testify thereafter, subject to cross-examination, as to his opinion of the cause and degree of claimant's disability. At the conclusion of his testimony, the referee shall make such findings of fact, conclusions of law, and order as the entire record may warrant.

Hearing in this case is to be given precedence. 

The claimant's appeal is sustained. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD ROSENBERG v. ALLEGHENY RIVER MINING CO. 

Workmen's compensation-Dependency-Evidence-Sufficiency. 

A referee's order dismissing a claim for compensation based on dependency will be affirmed where it appears that claimant, father of the deceased, owned a farm free of debt, that he also worked for some coal companies in the vicinity, that the only item of income shown by him amounted to $850 for one year received from a coal company, that the farm income was not shown, although it appeared that the land was worked and produced both crops and stock.

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Dillman, District no. 8, claim petition no. 109,006, accident no. 

4,999,031. Appeal dismissed. June 9, 1948.

Coal Operators Casualty Company, insurance carrier. 

Peter Calarie, for claimant. 

R. W. Smith and R. H. Cunningham, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal from an order entered by Referee Dillman December 31, 1947, disallowing a death claim. 

Clair W. Rosenberger was killed March 21, 1947, when squeezed by a shuttle car in the course of his employment with defendant, Allegheny River Mining Company. The accident occurred at the end of the first week after he secured his job. His father, Edward Rosenberger, claimant, filed the dependency claim with which we are now concerned on 

June 3, 1947, for himself and in behalf of decedent's mother and three minor brothers and sisters. Defendant has paid the portion of the funeral bill for which it became liable but has denied its liability on the dependency which is therefore the sole issue in the case.

From the testimony it appears that the claimant father owned a considerable acreage of farm land on which the family home is situated and that this property is free of debt. As decedent grew up and became able to do so he helped claimant with the farming. The father also worked for some of the coal companies in the vicinity. After serving in the army from March 28, 1944 to May 11, 1946, decedent returned to helping on the farm until he undertook the work which led to his death. While the decedent was in the armed services in this country he did not send any money home but monthly, after he was sent overseas early in August 1944, a war savings bond purchased at $18.75 was sent home made out jointly to himself and his mother. While

1948] 

 working on the farm after he returned home, decedent drew 

40 weeks post service unemployment pay.

The claimant father and mother were the only witnesses who took the stand at the hearing and what they had to offer was patently insufficient to establish a family budget which would indicate dependency. The only item of income shown by the father amounted to $850 for the year 1946 received from one of the coal companies for which he worked. 

The farm income was not divulged although it is obvious from the testimony that the land was worked and produced both crops and stock. Further than this no evidence whatsoever of family needs and expenses was preferred. 

Rather than show a clear picture of family circumstances in the manner suggested, claimant relied upon raising an implication of dependency by showing that decedent did. actually contribute to the family support and it must be said that the evidence produced on this side of the question did not stand up as readily acceptible. Two of the letters written home by decedent at the time he expected to be shipped overseas were introduced to show that he intended his mother to cash the bonds which would be forthcoming for family expense. However, an examination of the exhibits leaves the reader with the clear impression that the expressions in them to the intended effect were most certainly interpolations in hand writing other than the son's. The witnesses, themselves, could not deny this.

The only other item in the phase of the matter just discussed has to do with small contributions to the family out of the post-service unemployment pay but the evidence in this connection is little more deserving of credibility than that which has been introduced with regard to the decedent's letters.

We have reviewed the whole record carefully and are constrained to hold that the referee did not abuse his discretion. We agree with him that the evidence is not factually competent to substantiate a claim of dependency. As to the applicable law we need but cite Orosky v. American Window

[84 Dep. Rep. 

Glass Co., 162 Pa. Superior Ct. 195 and the authorities therein referred to.

The findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of 

Referee Dillman dated December 31, 1947, are affirmed.

The appeal is dismisssed. 

COMMON PLEAS OF SCHUYLKILL COUNTY KALISH v. LEHIGH NAVIGATION COAL COMPANY, INC. 

Workmen's compensation-Occupational disease—Rejection of act by defendant-Subsequent acceptance.

An award to claimant for disability as a result of anthraco-silicosis, will be reversed where it appears that claimant was employed by defendant as a miner, that he ceased working on June 1, 1946, giving notice at that time that he was permanently disabled, that defendant had rejected the provisions of the Occupational Disease Act and did not accept the provisions of article III of the act until August 1, 1946; section 304 of the act provides the only method by which an employer who has previously rejected the provisions of the act can thereafter accept it; the fact that defendant entered into an agreement with the 

United Mine Workers of America on June 7, 1946, providing that the defendant would accept the provisions of the act and that the agreement should become operative on May 31, 1946, did not waive the requirements of notice as provided for in section 304. 

Appeal from the Workmen's Compensation Board. C. P. 

of Schuylkill County, January term, 1948, no. 158. Petition dismissed. February 24, 1948. 

Roger J. Dever, for plaintiff. 

George H. Kaercher, S. S. Riordan and W. J. Krencewicz, for defendant.

1948] 

 PALMER, President Judge: 

Claimant, Stanley Kalish, was employed by defendant company as a miner. On June 1, 1946, he ceased working for defendant and gave notice that he was permanently disabled because of anthraco-silicosis. He subsequently filed his claim for compensation under the Occupational Disease 

Compensation Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 566, as amended by the Act of May 18, 1945, P. L. 661.

The referee denied an award of compensation for the reason that the compensation authorities were without jurisdiction to entertain this claim. The Workmen's Compensation Board reversed the referee and made an award of compensation, from which ruling defendant has now appealed. 

The only question in this case relates to the jurisdiction of the compensation authorities.

Defendant company rejected the provisions of the Occupational Disease Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 566, supra, by having duly posted upon all of their properties notices to that effect, and by notifying the Department of Labor and 

Industry of this action on September 20, 1939.

This fact is not disputed and defendant, therefore, became a rejector of the statutory provisions. 

On June 7, 1946, the United Mine Workers of America and defendant company, together with the other anthracite operators, entered into a labor agreement which, among other provisions, contained a provision that the operating companies would accept the provisions of the Occupational Disease Act, and further, that said agreement should become operative on May 31, 1946. 

On May 31, 1946, defendant company had not changed its status as a rejector of the provisions of article III of the Occupational Disease Act. The manner provided for by the aforesaid statute by which an employer can change its status from an acceptor to a rejector or from a rejector to an acceptor is specifically set forth in section 304 of the Act of 1939, supra. This section is as follows:

"Any agreement between employer and employe for the operation or non-operation of the provisions of article three of this Act may be terminated by the posting of notice by the employer or by either party upon thirty days' notice to the other in writing, if a copy of such notice, with proof of posting or proof of service, be filed in the department as provided in Section three hundred and two of this article." 

In accordance with this section of the act, defendant company on July 2, 1946, caused notices to be placed upon all of its properties indicating that 30 days thereafter, they would accept the provisions of article III of the Occupational Disease Act. Thus, defendant company did not become an acceptor of this statutory provision until August 1, 1946. 

Section 304 of the act of assembly is the only manner prescribed by the statute whereby an employer who has previously rejected the provisions of the act can thereafter accept the provisions of the act, or vice versa. Although section 304 of the act provides that an employer and an employe may terminate their present status by following the procedure set forth in this section and it would, therefore, seem that this procedure is not mandatory but optional, it, however, remains the only manner prescribed by the act and is, therefore, unquestionably the procedure to be followed in order to bring about a change in status. 

As we have stated, there is no provision in the act whereby an employer rejecting its provisions can thereafter accept it by entering into an agreement with his employes or by any other means waive the requirements of notice as provided for in section 304.

The contention that a contract entered into by private parties can automatically and arbitrarily set aside a statutory provision is without precedent and, obviously, contrary to public policy.

Defendant company not having accepted the provisions of the Occupational Disease Act until August 1, 1946, the compensation authorities were without jurisdiction to entertain any claim against defendant founded upon this statute

1948] 

 prior to that date. Therefore, they were without jurisdiction to hear the claim of the claimant in this case. 

And now, to wit, February 24, 1948, the award made to claimant by the Workmen's Compensation Board is overruled; the findings of fact and conclusions of law as made by the referee are reinstated; the petition of claimant is hereby dismissed, and judgment is directed to be entered. for defendant.

COMMON PLEAS NO. 6, PHILADELPHIA COUNTY WALKER v. NU-CAR CARRIERS, INC., NEW AMSTERDAM CASUALTY COMPANY Workmen's compensation-Course of employment—Car driver—In jury while returning home after delivery of vehicle-Violation of company regulations at to means of transportation. 

An award of the compensation board based on its finding that claimant's decedent was within the course of his employment when he was fatally injured will be affirmed where it appeared that decedent was a driver employed by defendant in transporting motor vehicles to various destinations under a contract between the defendant and the United States Army, and that at the time of the accident which resulted in his death, decedent was returning to his home by motorcycle carrying with him documents needed by defendant as a means of getting payment from the Government for transporting vehicles; in such case, the fact that decedent violated a company regulation requiring drivers to use public transportation in returning to their homes did not take him outside the course of his employment, nor did the fact that decedent had received a "ticket" for excessive speed in the operation of a vehicle in the course of the trip but on a day prior to the accident terminate his employment, it being clear that the violation of the speed laws with which he was charged was not the cause of his death.

Appeal from Workmen's Compensation Board. C. P. No. 

6, December term, 1947, no. 5340. Dismissed. June 10, 1948.

W. W. Mentzinger and J. A. Palmer, for plaintiff. 

R. A. White, Jr., for defendant.

LEVINTHAL, J.: 

This case is before us on an appeal by defendants from a decision of the Workmen's Compensation Board. 

Claimant's decedent was employed as a driver for defendant corporation, which is engaged in the business of deliver-. ing motor vehicles from one place to another. At the time of the accident upon which this claim is based, April 1, 1945, defendant corporation had entered into a contract with the United States Army wherein it agreed to deliver certain Army vehicles to various destinations. Drivers were provided by defendant, and these drivers were required to be licensed by the State and also to have permits issued by the Federal Government. Drivers were paid on a mileage basis during the time they operated Army vehicles. They also received railroad or bus fare from Chambersburg to the place where they were to pick up vehicles, and from the point of destination back to Chambersburg, Pa. There is evidence that company regulations required the drivers to use bus, train or other public transportation.

Walker, claimant's decedent, was instructed, on March 29, 1945, to go to Richmond, Va., to service a motor vehicle and drive it to Newport News, Va. After arriving at Richmond, he was instructed to make delivery to Newport News and then to return to Richmond where he was to be given another vehicle for delivery to Carteret, N. J. While en route to Newport News, Walker, in violation of Government regulations, exceeded the speed limit and was given a "ticket" for driving 50 miles per hour. Under the Government regulations, this was cause for immediate revocation of the Government driving permit, without which defendant's drivers were unable to continue in its employ under the terms of the contract with the Teamsters' Union. Nevertheless, Walker completed the delivery and returnd to Rich-

1948] 

 mond, where he picked up a truck and drove to Carteret, N. J. From there he started the return trip to Chambersburg, Pa., by motorcycle which he had transported with him in the back of the Government vehicle, also in violation of Government regulations prohibiting the carrying of passengers or cargo. It was while returning to Chambersburg by motorcycle that Walker became involved in the accident which resulted in his death. At the time of the accident, Walker was carrying delivery receipts for the vehicles, which were required to be returned to defendant's office at Chambersburg.

The principal question raised in this case is whether Walker, by returning to Chambersburg by motorcycle, instead of by public transportation as provided by the company's rules and regulations, took himself outside the course of his employment. The compensation board, in affirming the award by the referee, found as a fact that defendant's drivers were entrusted with certain papers to be returned to the Chambersburg office. The board found as a fact that those papers were used by defendant as a means of getting payment from the United States Government for transporting the vehicles. Consequently, the board found that the drivers were furthering the interests of the employer in returning those papers to defendant and were within the course of their employment while returning to Chambersburg.

The question then arises, did the violation by Walker of the regulation regarding the mode of travel in returning to the home base, take him outside the course of his employment? The following cases indicate that even if this regulation were in full force and effect and not a dead rule more honored in the breach than in the observance (as there is much testimony to show), the violation of it by Walker would not disentitle him to a compensation award. 

Shoffler v. Lehigh Valley Coal Co., 290 Pa. 480 (1927), laid down the rule that "course of employment" does not include (a) injuries received while away from the actual

place of employment where the deviation or departure is wholly foreign to his duties and amounts to an abandonment of the employment; (b) injuries received in the commission of an act which is in direct violation of the law, or (c) an act contrary to the positive orders of the employer. 

Clause (c) of this rule was qualified and limited by the subsequent case of Dickey v. Pitts. & L. V. R. R. Co., 297 Pa. 

172 (1929), in which it was held: "Care must be taken not to confuse the principle enunciated, with negligent acts, wilful misconduct, or those acts in disregard of positive orders of the employer where the employee's duties included the doing of the act that caused the injury, or where his duties were so connected with the act that caused the injury that, as to it, he was not in the position of a stranger or trespasser. The violation of positive orders under these circumstances does not prohibit compensation for injuries sustained therefrom. "However, injuries resulting from those acts which are in direct hostility to and in defiance of positive orders of the employer concerning instrumentalities, places or things about or on which the employee has no duty to perform, and with which his employment does not connect him, are not compensable under the clause in question." 

This language was interpreted by the Superior Court in 

Walker v. Quemahoning Coal Co., 90 Pa. Superior Ct. 252 

(1930), to allow compensation on the following facts:

Claimant, an assistant foreman in a mine, was engaged in placing dynamite and setting it off. He used fuses to set off the explosive, though defendant company had posted notices prohibiting the use of fuses in the mine. Furthermore, as assistant foreman claimant had been told by the superintendent of the mine that the practice of using fuses was to be broken up and that he, claimant, was to see that everyone had batteries and caps instead. Claimant testified that he knew he was violating a rule of the company by using the fuse. It was held that despite the violation of positive orders, claimant was entitled to recover since he was injured in the

1948] 

 performance of a duty assigned to him and which was being performed by him in the furtherance of the interests of the employer. "Although in the method of performing the act he was acting in defiance of his employer's orders, he was not 'in the position of a stranger or trespasser', and was not acting in violation of law." 

Furthermore, in Karchut v. Helvetia Coal Mining Co., 110 Pa. Superior Ct. 200 (1933), a compensation claim was allowed where evidence showed that claimant's husband was employed as a "scraper", whose duty was to help load and unload a coal cutting machine from a truck and to turn switches when the machine was being moved along the tracks in the mine. Defendant contended that the "scraper" had taken himself outside the course of his employment by attempting to board the machine (as a result of which action he was killed) and also showed that the man in charge of the cutter had ordered decedent to get off the machine a short while before the accident. It was held that even though the injuries resulted directly from a violation of positive orders of the employer, since they were received while in the performance of duties incident to his employment, he was entitled to compensation. This opinion also cited the Dickey case and said that this case came within the qualification made by the Supreme Court relative to the effect of the commission by the employe of acts contrary to positive orders of his employer; decedent's duties were so connected with the handling and transportation of the cutting machines, that he was not in the position of a stranger or trespasser and had not taken himself outside the course of his employment.

Another decision of the same tenor is that of Barkenich v. Jeddo Highland Coal Co., 105 Pa. Superior Ct. 145 (1932).

There claimant was employed as a door boy in a mine. He was permitted to ride on a train of mine cars from one door to another, but was expressly forbidden to ride on the front of the train or between cars. When the accident happened, he was riding on the front of the train and as a result he

lost a hand. Defendant sought to distinguish the Dickey and 

Walker cases, supra, by stating that in those cases there had been a violation of general regulations, whereas here there had been positive defiance and transgression of a peremptory order to claimant not to ride on the front of the train; the order had been directly communicated to claimant on a number of occasions and he had frequently been driven away from the front of the train by the engineer and warned that if he continued in his violations of the order, he would be reported for insubordination. In sustaining the award, the court said: "The Dickey case is authority for the proposition that injuries resulting from acts which are in direct hostility to and defiance of positive orders of the employer are compensable if the employee's duties include the doing of the act that caused the injury, or where his duties were so connected with the act that caused the injury that, as to it, he was not in the position of a stranger or trespasser. "... there was sufficient evidence upon which to base the findings of fact of the referee and the board, that his conduct was negligent and a wilful misconduct in the performance of his duties, which was held insufficient (citing cases) to prevent compensation. Under our compensation law a forfeiture of compensation does not result from the employee's 'wilful misconduct'."

In the case now before us, the board found as a fact that part of the duty of defendant's drivers was to carry back to Chambersburg the delivery receipts after delivery of the trucks and that therefore, in returning to their office, the drivers were furthering the interests of the employer and they were still in the course of their employment. 

It might be persuasively argued that even if the drivers had no duty to perform with regard to returning the delivery receipts, they would still be in the course of their employment in making the return trip to Chambersburg. Since, however, the board found as a fact that the drivers were required to return these papers to the Chambersburg office,

1948] 

 it is not necessary to decide whether in the absence of such a duty, they would nevertheless be in the course of their employment while making the return trip.

There is no merit whatsoever, in our opinion, to the contention of defendant that the receipt by decedent of a "ticket" for excessive speed in the operation of the vehicle on a prior date automatically and immediately terminated his employment. Obviously, the operator of a vehicle should be entitled to contest in some appropriate proceeding the charge against him of violating the speed laws. As pointed out by the board, the charge directed against decedent did "not immediately sever the relationship of employer and employe. He continued in his work and it is equally clear that this violation was not the proximate cause of his injury and death.”

Order Defendant's appeal is dismissed and judgment is now entered against defendant, Nu Car Carriers, Inc., and its insurance carrier, as follows:

Compensation is awarded claimant, for herself and Edward Earl Walker, Audrie May Walker, Norman Lee Walker and Kenneth James Walker, at the rate of $18 per week from April 8, 1945, to January 6, 1951 (the end of the 300-week period), a period of 300 weeks... 

Accrued interest on payments from April 8, 1945, to June 8, 1948 ...

To claimant as guardian of Edward Earl Walker, Audrie May Walker, Norman Lee Walker and 

Kenneth James Walker, at the rate of $11.50 per week from January 6, 1951, to February 27, 1957 (when Edward Earl Walker becomes 16 years of age), a period of 320-3/7ths weeks... 

To claimant as guardian of Audrie May Walker, Norman Lee Walker and Kenneth James Walker, at the rate of $9 per week from February 27, 1947, $5,400.00 284.44 3,684.00

to September 24, 1958 (when Audrie May Walker becomes 16 years of age), a period of 82 weeks..

To claimant as guardian of Norman Lee Walker and Kenneth James Walker, at the rate of $6.50 per week from September 24, 1958, to November 

2, 1959 (when Norman Lee Walker becomes 16 years of age), a period of 57-5/7ths weeks...

To claimant as guardian of Kenneth James Walker, at the rate of $4 per week from November

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD COGLEY v. JONES & LAUGHLIN STEEL CORP. 

Workmen's compensation—Occupational disease—Silicosis-Total dis ability subsequent to one year after last employment. 

Where claimant became partially disabled from silicosis within one year after the date of his last employment with defendant in an occupation having a silica hazard, and filed his claim petition within one year from the date of his last employment, although total disability did not follow until three years thereafter, he thereupon became entitled to compensation under the Occupational Disease Act. 

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Dillman, District No. 8, claim petition no. 96,271, accident no. 

4,253,576. Reversed and remanded. June 30, 1948.

1948] 

John A. Robb, for plaintiff. 

W. A. Challener, Jr., for defendant. 

MURPHY, Chairman: 

This is an appeal by claimant from an order of disallowance of the referee.

The record discloses that claimant filed his claim petition under the Occupational Disease Act on July 12, 1943, alleging that he became totally disabled on June 23, 1943, as a result of anthraco-silicosis, contracted in the course of his employment with defendant from 1934 to 1943. Defendant's answer, filed on August 6, 1943, denied the material averments of claimant's petition. After hearings, the referee found that claimant was not totally disabled from silicosis, solely, at the time of the filing of his petition and that he did not become totally disabled therefrom within one year after the date of his last employment and, in accordance with such findings, dismissed claimant's petition. This appeal followed.

The testimony in the instant case is to the effect that claimant was employed by defendant, in its foundry, as a chipper and core digger, from 1934 to January 26, 1943; that, in this employment, he was exposed to a silica hazard; that, on the final day of his employment he became involved in a disagreement with his superior when, because of pains in his chest, he refused to "dig core"; that, three days later, on January 29, 1943, he commenced employment with the Machintosh-Hemphill Company, as a steel chipper, in which employment he continued until June 23, 1943; that he ceased his employment on that day and went to his father's farm and did no work until January 19, 1944, when he went to work as a solderer and welder for the Weimer Metalcraft Company where he remained until March 1944. On April 3, 1944, he was employed at light work for A. M. Byers Com-

pany, where his employment continued until July 18, 1946, since which time he has, admittedly, been totally disabled. 

Claimant's medical witness, Dr. John G. Bushman, testified that, as a result of an examination made by him on April 12, 1943, he was of the opinion that, at that time, claimant was totally disabled from silicosis. Dr. K. I. Fetterhoff, a lung specialist, testified that, as a result of various tests made of claimant between August 9, 1946, and October 23, 1946, he was of the opinion that claimant was then totally disabled as a result of silicosis. 

To the contrary, defendant called as a witness Dr. F. N. 

Groves who testified that he had examined claimant for the Byers Company, prior to his employment by them in 1944 and had passed him for employment. Under cross-examination, however, the witness admitted that, at the time of the examination, no examination was made for silicosis and that the only method of determining the presence or absence of silicosis would be by the history and X-ray findings. Through 

Irvin A. Brinkman, director of industrial relations of

Machintosh-Hemphill Co., defendant also introduced the original records of an examination of claimant made by Dr. 

Clark Wakefield, now deceased, on June 30, 1943, prior to claimant's employment by that firm, which records showed that claimant had then passed his physical examination prior to employment.

A careful review of the entire record convinces us that the action of the referee must be reversed. 

Section 301 (c) of the Occupational Disease Act provides, inter alia: "Compensation for the occupational diseases enumerated in this act shall be paid only when such occupational disease is peculiar to the occupation or industry in which the employee was engaged and not common to the general population and occurring within one year after the date of his last employment in such occupation or industry". 

Under this section of the act it is necessary, in order that a claim shall not be barred, that the disease occur within one year after the date of claimant's last employment, but

1948] 

 it is not necessary, as was erroneously held by the referee, that the disability become total within one year after the last employment: Agostin v. Pittsburgh Steel Foundry
