Corp., 354 Pa. 543. In the instant case, the medical testimony is to the effect that, on April 12, 1943, claimant was suffering from silicosis. The last date of his employment with defendant was on January 26, 1943 and on July 12, 1943, he filed the instant petition. It is, therefore, clear that he was suffering from partial disability at that time and that proper notice was given by him to defendant. 

At the time of the filing of his petition claimant, who was then suffering a partial disability, had merely an inchoate right against defendant which right did not ripen until July 18, 1946, the date upon which his disability became total. 

It is the occurrence of the disability which is the event that constitutes the compensable injury, although the disability is necessarily preceded by an exposure and an occupational disease of which it is the culmination: McIntyre v. Lavino & Co., 344 Pa. 168.

In view of what we have stated above, we amend the referee's 12th finding of fact to read as follows: "12. As a result of silicosis contracted in the course of his employment with defendant, claimant became totally disabled on July 18, 1946".

All other findings of fact are affirmed. 

We strike out the referee's second conclusion of law and, in lieu thereof, substitute the following: "2. Since claimant has proven by competent testimony and evidence that he became partially disabled from silicosis within one year after the date of his last employment with defendant in an occupation having a silica hazard and that, on July 18, 1946, he became totally disabled as a result thereof, he is entitled to recover the benefits of the Occupational Disease Act, as amended". 

All other conclusions of law are affirmed.

Since the record shows that claimant is now dead but there is no record of the date of his death and since it further shows that, in addition to his widow, he left surviving him

eight children, but there is no record as to the number of children entitled to receive the benefits provided for by the act, we are unable to enter an appropriate award in this case, upon the present state of the record. 

We, therefore, remand this case to Referee Alvin E. 

Dillman, District No. 8, for the sole purpose of determining the date of death of claimant and the number of children surviving entitled to the benefits of the Occupational Disease Act, with instructions to the referee to, thereafter, enter a proper award in accordance with this opinion. 

Claimant's appeal is sustained.

This case is to be given precedence. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD BERGMARK v. DOUGLASS CO. 

Workmen's compensation-Permanent injury-Industrial loss of use of one half of finger.

The industrial loss of use of one half of a finger is compensable and an award therefor will be affirmed where there is competent medical evidence which established that the distal joint was completely ankylosed and that the condition is permanent. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Curtis, District No. 8, claim petition no. 109,204, accident no. 5,015,700. 

Affirmed. June 23, 1948.

United States Fidelity & Guaranty Company, insurance carrier. 

Sidney Rosenblum, for plaintiff. 

O. W. T. Peterson, for defendant.

1948] 

 JACOBY, Commissioner: 

Claimant, William C. Bergmark, suffered an admitted accident to the right little finger on September 13, 1946, during the course of his employment by defendant, Thomas J. Douglass Company. Referee Curtis awarded compensation for the industrial loss of the use of one half of the finger and the defendant has appealed. There is competent and acceptable medical evidence which establishes that the distal joint of the right little finger remains completely ankylosed and that the condition is permanent. Is the industrial loss of the use of one half of the finger compensable. 

Section 306 (c) of the Workmen's Compensation Act of 

June 21, 1939, P. L. 520, provides, inter alia. "For all disability resulting from permanent injuries of the following classes, the compensation shall be exclusively as follows: . . . The loss of the first phalange of the thumb, or of any finger, shall be considered equivalent to the loss of one-half of such thumb or finger, and shall be compensated at the same rate as for the loss of a thumb or finger, but for one-half of the period provided for the loss of a thumb or finger."

Defendant contends there is no statutory authority for an award of compensation for the loss of use of one half of the member and that the act limits compensation to cases where there is an actual dismemberment. The case of Yaklich v. 

Union Collieries Co., 158 Pa. Superior Ct. 55, decides the question involved contrary to defendant's contention, and holds that the loss of use of one half of the thumb is compensable as being equivalent to the loss of one half of the thumb under section 306 (c). The court said (p. 59): "The appellant contends that 'loss of use' of one-half of the thumb is not compensable under this section, but with that contention we disagree. Section 306 (c) should be so construed that every reasonable intendment of its express language should be upheld in behalf of the employee. Ciotti v. Jarecki Manufacturing Company, 128 Pa. Superior Ct. 

233, 193 A. 323. The Workmen's Compensation Act is

remedial and is to receive a liberal construction. Ottavi v. 

Timothy Burke Stripping Company, 140 Pa. Superior Ct. 

389, 14 A. 2d 188. According to the testimony of Dr. Jamison, the claimant has permanently lost the use of the distal joint or first phalange of his left thumb. Therefore, for all practical purposes, he has lost the first phalange of his thumb to the same effect and extent as if it had been amputated or otherwise physically removed, and consequently, he has suffered a 'loss' within the terms of the Act and compensation therefore was properly awarded." 

This decision is controlling in the instant case. 

The appeal of defendant is dismissed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD SILVERTHORN v. AMERICAN CYANAMID & CHEMICAL CORP. 

Workmen's compensation—Award for disfigurement concurrent with award for disability.

Compensation payments for disfigurement under section 306 (c) run concurrently with disability payments under sections 306(a) and (b), hence a referee's order awarding compensation for a permanent facial disfigurement for an additional period following an award for a partial disability will be reversed.

Appeal by defendant from order of Referee Curtis, District No. 8, modifying compensation under agreement no. 

4,941,182. Affirmed as modified. June 30, 1948.

Employers' Liability Assurance Corp., insurance carrier.

1948] 

Harry A. Sherman, for plaintiff. 

Kim Darragh, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

Claimant, James Silverthorn, was accidentally injured on

December 4, 1946, during the course of his employment by defendant, American Cyanamid and Chemical Corporation.

He suffered severe burns to his arms, back, neck, ears and right hand. Claimant was totally disabled from December 

19, 1946, to February 29, 1947, at which date he returned to work without any loss of earnings, until April 1, 1947, when disability was 50 percent partial. Referee Curtis entered an appropriate award. On May 21, 1947, defendant filed a petition for termination alleging cessation of disability as of May 13, 1947. Upon hearing held, the referee found that claimant was entitled to compensation for an additional period of 25 weeks for a permanent facial disfigurement under section 306 (c) of the Workmen's Compensation Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 520.

Defendant's appeal poses two questions. First, did claimant suffer a serious and permanent disfigurement of the head or face, of such a character as to produce an unsightly appearance, and such as is not usually incident to the employment, within the contemplation and intendment of the act; and second, is claimant entitled to compensation for disfigurement in addition to compensation payments already made for disability. 

Dr. Charles F. Berg, called by defendant, testified that he examined claimant on March 13, 1947, and found the burn scars were all well healed and not incapacitating the patient in any way. The doctor also examined claimant on the date of the hearing. He stated that claimant has “akeloid scar on the posterior aspect of the left side of neck, approximately three inches in length and a half inch in width”. 

It is irregular in contour and "it is raised above the normal scar surface". It is reddish in color. Dr. Berg's opinion was the scars were permanent.

We have viewed claimant and we are satisfied that the disfigurement is serious, permanent and unsightly. There is no yardstick or measuring device for disfigurement claims: Matsko v. Haddock Mining Co., A-26909 (Board 

1941); Moore v. Marra Brothers, Inc., A-33040 (Board 

1944). Each case must necessarily depend upon its particular facts. Based upon our view of the disfigurement in question and upon our experience in many disfigurement claims, it is our considered independent opinion that the compensation of 25 weeks is fairly commensurate with the disfigurement suffered. Claimant has been paid compensation for total disability for 10-2/7 weeks and for partial disability for 10-3/7 weeks, or a total of 20-5/7 weeks. The referee erroneously found (third) that "claimant was paid compensation for 40 percent partial disability from March 1, 1947, until

March 13, 1947", when, as a matter of fact, claimant was paid compensation for partial disability until May 13, 1947.

Compensation payments for disfigurement, under section 

306 (c) run concurrently with disability payments under sections 306 (a) and (b): Madajewski v. Susquehanna Collieries Co., 135 Pa. Superior Ct. 181; Phillips v. Coxe

Brothers Co., Inc., 135 Pa. Superior Ct. 185. It is, therefore, necessary, under the decisions, to limit claimant's compensation in this case to 25 weeks.

We hereby amend the referee's findings of fact in the following respects: 

1. In the third finding of fact we substitute May 13, 1947, for March 13, 1947. 

2. We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's fourth finding of fact and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following: "Finding of fact "4. We find as a fact that claimant, as a result of the accidental injury, suffers a serious and permanent disfigurement

1948] 

 of the head of such a character as to produce an unsightly appearance, and such as is not usually incident to his employment."

As amended, the referee's findings of fact are hereby affirmed.

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's conclusion of law and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following: "Conclusion of law "1. Since claimant, as a result of the accidental injury, suffers a serious and permanent disfigurement of the head of such a character as to produce an unsightly appearance, and such as is not usually incident to his employment, he is entitled to compensation therefor."

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's order and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following: "Order "The board orders, adjudges and decrees that compensation payments under compensation agreement no. 4,941,182, executed by and between James Silverthorn, claimant, and against American Cyanamid & Chemical Corporation, defendant and/or its insurance carrier, Employers' Liability Assurance Corporation, be modified to provide for the payment of compensation payments for a total period of 25 weeks, or in the sum of $500, defendants to receive credit for 10 2/7 weeks of compensation at $20, already paid, or in the sum of $205.71,. and for 10 3/7 weeks of compensation at $17 per week already paid, or in the sum of $177.29; defendants shall pay to claimant compensation for 10 3/7 weeks at the rate of $3 per week, beginning May 14, 1947, or in the amount of $31.29, and thereafter, for a period of 

4 2/7 weeks at the rate of $20 per week, or $85.71, or in the aggregate amount of $117." 

The appeal of defendant is sustained.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD NICHOLS v. THE PENNSYLVANIA RAILROAD CO. 

Workmen's compensation—Injury while employed in interstate commerce- -Voluntary agreement for compensation-Final receipt— 

Voluntary resumption of payments—Jurisdiction of board-Petition for termination.

Where following an injury while claimant was engaged in interstate commerce, he and defendant entered into an agreement for payment of compensation which was subsequently terminated by a final receipt, after which defendant voluntarily resumed the making of total disability payments for a further period, the agreement, being voidable during its life if challenged on the grounds of jurisdiction, was voided by the final receipt, so that defendant was not liable to the claimant after the cessation of its voluntary payments and its petition for termination must therefore be dismissed.

Appeal by defendant from order of Referee Foust, District No. 9, awarding compensation under agreement no. 

4,310,617. Appeal sustained. June 30, 1948. 

John E. Evans, Jr., for plaintiff. 

Samuel P. Delisi, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal from an order entered by Referee Foust 

January 19, 1948, directing a resumption of compensation payments under an agreement. 

The agreement in the case was entered into under date of July 26, 1943, between claimant, Margaret M. Nichols, and defendant, the Pennsylvania Railroad Company. It provided for maximum compensation payments beginning July 8, 1943, reflecting total disability as a result of a sprain of the back sustained by claimant June 28, 1943, while shovelling pipe fittings from a passageway in defendant's shop at Pit-

1948] 

 cairn. The fittings were of the smaller variety and had just been dumped out of a basket after being cleaned in a vat of boiling lye. It is conceded that they were parts of rolling stock used in both interstate and intrastate commerce. 

The agreement was terminated by a final receipt dated November 11, 1943, which indicated that claimant was able to return to work October 15, 1943. However, work rehabilitation did not seem to have its intended effect and defendant voluntarily resumed making total disability payments May 

8, 1944, and continued them until June 24, 1945.

On December 21, 1945, claimant entered suit against defendant under the Federal Employer's Liability Act of April 

22, 1908, c 149, 35 Stat. at L. 65, as amended, August 11, 1939, in the District Court of the United States for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania at civil action no. 5494. This may have been prompted by a petition for termination filed by defendant in our own compensation bureau November 30, 1945, alleging recovery. The district court assumed jurisdiction and the case went to trial resulting in a verdict for defendant November 30, 1946. Defendant then filed an amended petition for termination November 26, 1947, raising the jurisdictional question before the Pennsylvania compensation authorities for the first time. This was supplemented by a petition for review filed on the same date (A-33724, a companion case to be decided herewith).

At the hearing in the case an extensive record of testimony was built up by witnesses, both lay and medical, called on each side. In addition to this the transcript of testimony taken before the district court was introduced into evidence as an exhibit and accompanies the record which is before us. 

We have read through all of it carefully and patiently but feel that we need not recount the details at this time because of the manner in which we believe the law must be applied on the face of the pleadings. 

So far as the substantive law is concerned there is now no compensation remedy open to employes such as claimant (Scarborough v. Penna. R. R. Co., 154 Pa. Superior Ct.

129; Trucco v. Erie R. R. Co., 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 398, 353 Pa. 320, 328 U. S. 843) where an original claim for workmen's compensation is lodged. The agreement in the present instance was voidable during its life if challenged on the grounds of jurisdiction and being voided by final receipt was not necessarily revived by defendant's voluntary resumption of payments. Under the decisions it would seem that anything designed to take its place would have to be in writing and signed by the parties (Busch v. Jones & Laughlin Steel Corp., 150 Pa. Superior Ct. 48), which was not done. In any event jurisdiction which does not exist cannot be conferred by consent, stipulation or agreement (Wolf et al. v. Lewisburg Trust & Safe Deposit Co., 305 Pa. 

583) nor by estoppel; Thompson v. Parke, 131 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 81.

What we have said so far circumvents the question of the plea in bar argued in claimant's behalf on appeal. 

She contends that the petition filed by defendant in this case and the companion case (supra) should be dismissed because they were filed more than a year subsequent to the last payment of compensation and cites the provision to that apparent effect in section 413 of the Act (77 PS §§771, 772). We have found no cases where such a defense has been raised against an employer and we doubt the legislative intent that the limitation should be so applied. But we do not think it necessary to decide the point. There being no agreement or order in existence to be terminated or reviewed defendant is not liable to claimant and the petitions therefore must be dismissed by reason of their abortive nature.

The findings of fact of Referee Foust dated January 19, 1948, are not inconsistent with the action we propose to take in this case and are therefore affirmed. 

The conclusions of law of Referee Foust dated January 

19, 1948, are vacated and set aside and the following substituted therefor:

1948] 

" "1. Claimant at the time of her accidental injury on

June 28, 1943, was working in interstate commerce. "2. The agreement entered into between the parties hereto under date of July 26, 1943, was terminated by final receipt dated November 16, 1943, and not thereafter revived. "3. Defendant is not liable to claimant for compensation payments under the Act of June 2, 1915, P. L. 736, as amended. "4. The petition filed in this case is entirely abortive and must be dismissed. "Order "The petitions for termination filed by defendant in this case November 30, 1945, and November 26, 1947, are hereby dismissed." 

The appeal is sustained.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD BARRETT v. M. A. BRUDER & SONS 

Workmen's compensation-Medical expense-Sacroiliac belt. 

An item of expense incurred by plaintiff for a sacroiliac belt and lift to relieve an injury suffered in the course of his employment did not come within the meaning of medical, surgical and hospital services provided for in the Workmen's Compensation Act and accordingly will be stricken out from an award which allowed it as a medical expense.

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Alessandroni, District No. 1, claim petition no. 104,412, accident no. 

4,378,912. Modified and affirmed. June 30, 1948.

American Mutual Liability Ins. Co., insurance carrier. 

Thomas J. Gaffney, for plaintiff. 

Frederick L. Fuges, for defendant.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

Claimant suffered a severe back strain on June 9, 1945, while in the course of his employment. He had been engaged in lifting cans of paint weighing 75 pounds when something snapped in his back and resulted in severe pain. Claimant only weighed 132 pounds and he was piling the cans, three high, when injured. This work required extreme exertion particularly when he was arranging the cans on the higher level.

The referee made an award and on appeal to the board by defendant the record was remanded for the purpose of offering claimant an opportunity of proving his medical expenses. These had been included in the award but not established by sufficient competent evidence. At the further hearing an agreement as to the amounts expended was reached by the parties. The referee restated his former findings of fact, conclusions of law and award. Defendant has again filed an appeal alleging that claimant has failed to establish the occurrence of an accident and that the award includes an item of $10.75 for a belt and lift as medical expenses.

We have carefully reviewed the entire record and we are of the opinion that the referee's award for partial disability was warranted. The occurrence of an accidental injury was established by sufficient competent evidence. The sudden injury suffered by claimant was an unforeseen occurrence which caused a sudden break or change in the physical

1948] 

 structure of claimant's body: Gavula v. Sims Co., 155 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 206,212.

We are of the further opinion that the sacroiliac belt and lift obtained by claimant is an appliance which does not come within the meaning of medical, surgical and hospital services. Accordingly, we strike the item of $10.75 from that portion of the award allowing medical expenses. 

The other findings of fact, conclusions of law and the award as modified are affirmed. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD SPEED v. THE DEVEREUX FOUNDATION Workmen's compensation—Injury in course of employment—House mother in private school—Injury in performance of personal duties. 

A referee's disallowance of compensation based on a finding that claimant when injured was not in the course of her employment, nor furthering the interest of her employer, will be affirmed where it appears that claimant was employed as a house mother at a school operated by defendant, that her duties as such were performed in a building separate from her living quarters, and that her injury occurred early in the morning while attending to personal duties in the building where she lived. 

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Graybill, District No. 4, claim petition no. 107,139, accident no. 

4,776,076. Affirmed. July 21, 1948.

Great American Indemnity Company, insurance carrier. 

Harry R. Kozart, for plaintiff. 

Harry Axelroth, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal from an order of disallowance entered by Referee Graybill, January 30, 1948.

Over the 1945 to 1946 school term, claimant, Virginia P. 

Speed, was employed as a house mother at a school property in Devon, Pa., operated by defendant, the Devereux 

Foundation. Her duties were performed in a building known as the Manor House and she was provided living quarters with other teachers in another building known as Spruce 

Cottage. On the morning of January 18, 1946, she rose early to be at work at 7 o'clock. At 6:30 o'clock while going to the bathroom in the cottage along a hallway where a light fixture had been out of order for some little time, she missed a turn and tumbled down steps to the first floor injuring her right forearm and sustaining some damage to her teeth.

She was treated by Dr. Ruth Duffy but eventually went to the Bryn Mawr Hospital. At the latter institution she insisted upon X-ray pictures which were taken about a week after the first examination. As a result splints were applied to her right wrist. She continued at her post at the school throughout the spring term complaining particularly that numbness in four of the fingers of her right hand prevented her from writing, then went home to Charleston, W. Va., where she consulted her physician, Dr. Anderson Hills. 

During July and August she went back to work with defendant at a summer camp maintained for its students in Maine. 

In the fall of 1946 she took a new job at the Woods School in Philadelphia but in a few months gave this up and returned to her West Virginia home.

At the hearing in the case claimant was the only witness who took the stand. None of the doctors to whom she submitted were called as witnesses and neither the X-ray pictures nor the clinical record made at the Bryn Mawr Hospital were produced. The referee therefore gave full credit to her testimony so far as the happening of an accident was concerned and accepted as genuine certain dental bills which claimant presented but he could not and did not find that

1948] 

 any disability reflected in loss of earning power had been suffered. Neither did he seem to be convinced that claimant's eventual retirement to her home was due to the consequences of her accident. Her testimony in this regard was uncontradicted but the referee was not required for that reason to accept it as significant of the true factual situation in the case: Walsh v. Penn Anthracite Mining Co., 147 Pa. Superior Ct. 328; Baston v. Stoehr & Fisher, 151

Pa. Superior Ct. 618. After a thorough review of claimant's testimony we cannot say that we disagree in this phase of the matter.

Neither are we disposed to differ with the referee in his application of the law which represents the true issue in the case on appeal. He found that claimant when injured was not in the course of her employment nor furthering the interests of her employer. In this we think he was right. 

In the narrow scope encompassed by the question the extremes are represented by Werner v. Allegheny County, 153 

Pa. Superior Ct. 10, wherein a hostess and guide on continuous call was found to be on duty while in quarters provided for her and Peoples-Pittsburgh Trust Co. v. Fidelity Trust 

Co., 149 Pa. Superior Ct. 444, wherein a claimant's decedent was found to have been serving his own purposes on his own time though he met with his fatal accident in rooms provided for him on defendant's property. The case before us falls in the latter category. Its classification thus is substantiated by a recent common pleas court case, Hood v. 

Penna. R. R. Co., 59 D. & C. 185, which involved an injury to a railroad worker in a bunk house supplied to him as a place to live by his employer there being no circumstance to show that the contribution of such accommodations was for the purpose of keeping him on call. 

We have reviewed this case carefully from both the factual and legal viewpoint and find that the referee has decided it without error.

The findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of 

Referee Graybill dated January 30, 1948, are affirmed. 

The appeal is dismissed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD DAVIS V. MERCK & COMPANY, INC. 

Workmen's compensation—Petition to review agreement—Finai receipt―Treating petition to review as petition to set aside final receipt. 

While a petition to review a compensation agreement filed under section 413 of the Workmen's Compensation Act may under certain circumstances be considered as a petition to set aside a final receipt under section 434, a petition to review filed nearly two years after the execution of the final receipt will not be considered as a petition to set aside the final receipt where no facts were averred in the petition that constituted good grounds for setting aside a receipt; therefore, a referee's order dismissing claimant's petition to review will be affirmed.

Appeal by claimant from order of Referee Foust, District No. 9, dismissing petition for modification under compensation agreement no. 4,740,013. Affirmed as amended. 

July 14, 1948. 

Anthony Cavalcante, for plaintiff. 

B. B. Whitehill, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This case dates back to September 7, 1944, when claimant, Thomas J. Davis, suffered accidental injuries to his left hand in the course of his employment by defendant, Merck & Company, Inc. A review of the record discloses that claimant received total disability benefits for 1 6/7 weeks under an open agreement which was terminated by a final receipt signed on October 5, 1944. Subsequently, on November 8, 1944, a supplemental agreement was executed to provide for payments for loss of the left little finger under section 301 (c) 

of the Workmen's Compensation Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 

520. Compensation was paid until December 27, 1944. This date is significant. Somewhat earlier, on December 19, 1944, claimant filed a petition (84098) for review of the supplemental agreement alleging further disability in the left hand other than loss of the little finger. Upon hearing before

1948] 

Referee Clayton on April 4, 1945, the petition was dismissed. 

The record shows that on June 12, 1945, a second final receipt was received by the bureau, dated December 28, 1944. No appeal was taken from the referee's decision filed on May 24, 1945, to the board until December 6, 1946 (A-32661). The claimant attributed the delay in taking the appeal to his failure to receive a copy of the referee's decision; he requested a rehearing. He also filed a formal petition for review (91384) on December 6, 1946, requesting a rehearing so that claimant could "produce medical testimony, not available at last hearing, by which he intends to prove that he has suffered the industrial loss of the use of the left hand as a result of this accident". In an opinion by Commissioner 

Knoll, filed May 28, 1947, we dismissed the appeal and petition for rehearing. The board hearing was held on February 

26, 1947. Prior to the filing of our opinion, claimant filed an amended petition for rehearing on May 17, 1947, setting forth various circumstances which may have been responsible for his not receiving the notice of the referee's decision and requesting anew an opportunity to present medical testimony. Attached to the petition is an affidavit of Dr. Sara H. 

Maiden. At the hearing before the referee on February 19, 1948, claimant's counsel stated: "Mr. Referee, I'd like to make an offer of proof in this matter. My position is, as set forth in my rehearing petition, which was executed by claimant on January 3, 1948, filed in this matter, claimant's position being that petition no. 

91,384 was filed within two years after the signing of the second final receipt, and therefore, if construed as a petition under 434, would be in time. My present petition—that is, the one executed January 3, 1948, is a petition which seeks to amend petition no. 91,384 to include therein the two matters which appear in that amended petition—one, an averment to set aside a final receipt, and, two, a request for a rehearing or hearing de novo."

The referee held that the matter was res adjudicata and that it was too late to consider a petition to set aside a final receipt. Claimant has appealed. Counsel for the interested parties have filed able briefs. We are sympathetic to claim-

ant's cause as it does not appear that he has had a full hearing upon the merits of his claim. However mindful we are of the humane purposes of compensation legislation, sympathy cannot usurp the requirements of the law and it must be fairly determined whether there is legal authority to reopen claimant's case at this late date. Strict adherence to the rules of evidence and procedure is not essential in compensation hearings. Our courts have uniformly held that a petition erroneously filed under one section of the act may, nevertheless, be considered under the proper section: 

Kissel v. Harbison-Walker Refractories, 157 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 37; Harrison v. Alden Park Manor Apts., 160 Pa. Superior Ct. 388 (1947). In the latter case, the court held it was error to dismiss a petition under the one year limitation of section 413 when it would have been timely under section 

434. Claimant does not challenge the propriety of our previous decision affirming the referee's dismissal of claimant's first petition to review the open agreement as it was filed too late under section 426. Claimant contends that if the second petition to review (91384), filed on December 6, 1946, had been considered as a petition to set aside the second final receipt, executed on December 28, 1944, it was timely. It is also urged that claimant's amendment to petition for rehearing, filed on January 5, 1948, avers sufficient grounds for avoiding the final receipt. Claimant's testimony at the hearing before the referee on April 4, 1945, discloses reference to compensation for total disability and for a specific loss. Davis testified: "Q. You have a final receipt? "A. I signed that before they paid for the loss of my finger. It was a misunderstanding. When the check came it was for the $18 and then for $15.49 and then I signed the final statement and then found out I had loss of the little finger. Then they sent a check for $110 which I refused to sign at that time.”

He later testified that he accepted all but the last check for $18.00. The second final receipt, dated December 28, 1944, was not a part of the record at that time, as it was not filed until June 12, 1945. The referee's fifth finding of fact

1948] 

 indicates that the referee considered the petition to review as a petition to set aside final receipt. He concluded there was "no disability beyond the industrial loss of the left little finger". Claimant did not offer any medical testimony and he was not represented by counsel at that hearing. 

Claimant's rights in this case dated from December 28, 1944, when the second final receipt was executed by him. 

Normally, he would have two full years within which to petition to vacate the final receipt: Section 434. Claimant's second petition to review (91384), filed on December 6, 1946, under section 413 of the act, if considered under section 434 as a petition to set aside final receipt would, as claimant contends, be timely. From the subject matter of the petition, there is nothing in its form or substance to indicate that the validity of the final receipt is challenged. The language in the petition for review is identical to that contained in the appeal. Both were filed on the same day, December 6, 1946. 

That petition was considered upon the appeal and dismissed, finally and effectively, by our opinion filed May 28, 1947.

The record is further confused by the filing on March 17, 1947, of an amended petition for rehearing to the original petition for review (84098) and still a later amendment to the second petition for review (91384), filed on January 5, 1948. The last petition must be considered as an original petition and it is, therefore, filed too late to set aside the final receipt. It is barred by the statute of limitations. A litigant cannot, indirectly, circumvent the direct provisions of the law by filing an amendment, which, in fact, raises an issue already adjudicated. In the case of Kochinsky v. Independent Pier Co., 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 15, the court said (p. 18): "The courts take a liberal attitude toward the pleadings in compensation cases and consider the substance of the relief prayed for rather than its form. (Citing cases) Of course, the parties are entitled to know the issue in any particular proceeding so that they may be prepared to meet it by proper evidence. There are certain minimum standards and the rules of pleading must be observed in a broad and general sense."

The petition in question (91384) gives no indication, in a broad or general sense, that it is a petition to set aside a final receipt. Claimant tacitly agrees such to be the case, by filing a so-called amendment on January 5, 1948. 

The case of Downs v. Linton's Lunch, 134 Pa. Superior Ct. 

248, stressed by claimant's counsel, involved a petition for reinstatement of compensation because of a recurrence, more than one year after the last payment of compensation, but within one year after the referee's order, erroneously terminating compensation. The referee, there, had terminated payments because claimant "had returned to work on December 22, 1931, at the same rate of pay and has been working since that time". That case is not analogous and is, therefore, not controlling. Claimant concedes that the referee's original dismissal was proper because of the inadequate presentation of his case. We are constrained to hold that this tribunal, under the instant facts, is without discretion in returning the record to the referee for further hearing and determination; to do so, at this late date, would be to reduce the statutory time provisions to meaningless words. 

We hereby affirm the referee's order of dismissal. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD FIGURA ET UX. v. GEORGE Workmen's compensation-Partial dependency-Burden of proof— 

Minor-Contributions to support of parents. 

1. Ordinarily the burden of proof of establishing dependency is upon a parent who claims compensation for the death of a child; however, where the child is a minor, dependency of the parent is presumed and the burden of proof rests upon defendant to overcome the statutory presumption. 

2. A referee's order of disallowance will be set aside and an award made in favor of claimants on the basis that they were partially dependent upon their minor son for support at the time of his accidental injury and death, where claimants introduced evidence uncontradicted by defendant, that the son regularly gave $15 or $20 per week to claimants during the period of his employment by the defendant, and that the father received wages of $44 per week for support of a family

1948] 

 of four; under the circumstances, the evidence clearly supported a finding of partial dependency upon the deceased son. 

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Gray bill, District No. 4; claim petition no. 109,135, accident no. 

4950160, Reversed. July 14, 1948.

Selected Risks Indemnity Company, insurance carrier. 

Donald L. LaBarre, for claimants. 

James C. Lanshe, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This case is before the board upon appeal by claimants, Barbara and Andrew Figura, from the order of Referee 

Graybill disallowing compensation for the death of their minor son, Frank Figura, during the course of his employment by defendant, Richard George, on December 18, 1946.

The appeal raises the single question whether claimants were partial dependents of the deceased son at the time of his death.

The record discloses that the son, Francis, was born on 

March 4, 1927. The father, Andrew Figura, testified that

Francis first worked when 16 years of age, during his school vacation, and later at a gas station and that he gave all his earnings to "Mom". The father stated that his son started to work for defendant when he was 17 years of age and turned over $15 or $20 each week to his mother. The son served in the United States military service from May 1945 until November 1946 and, according to the father, he sent four checks for $50 each during this period to his mother, as well as a monthly $50 bond, made out in the joint names of the son and mother. Claimant stated that the money was used for household purposes in the purchase of milk, clothing, coal and other necessities. Figura testified that the son also gave his mother $83 for Christmas and that he paid a $10 doctor bill for her. The family household, at the date of death, consisted of the two parents and two younger

children, who are unemployed. There are five other children, presently married, none of whom contribute to the family. 

The father stated that the children, prior to marriage, contributed a share of their earnings to the family budget. 

Claimant is employed at the Lehigh Portland Cement Company and draws a weekly gross pay of $44. Under crossexamination, the father testified: "Q. You could have supported your wife and your family without any money from Frank at that time, is that not right? "A. Yes, that is why the boy gives me helping when he is working, because the family is big and he worked to make a good living."

Barbara Figura, the mother, offered testimony of the same tenor as her husband. She also testified that she never asked the son for money for room and board, but that he always contributed out of his earnings to the family expenses. She testified: "Q. If Frank had not given you anything, your husband could have supported you and the children? "A. Yes, but it was hard."

Decedent was an unmarried minor at the time of his death. Therefore, section 307 (5), as amended by the Act of 

June 21, 1939, P. L. 520, and the Act of May 18, 1945, P. L. 

671, is applicable. The particular provision states: "If there be neither widow, widower, nor children entitled to compensation, then to the father or mother, if dependent to any extent upon the employe at the time of the accident, twenty-five per centum of wages, but not in excess of six dollars per week: Provided, however, that in the case of a minor child who has been contributing to his parents, the dependency of said parents shall be presumed: And provided further, that if the father or mother was totally dependent upon the deceased employe at the time of the accident, the compensation payable to such father or mother shall be forty-five per centum of wages, but not in excess of eleven dollars per week."

Ordinarily, the burden of proof is upon the parent to establish dependency: Todd v. Lehigh Valley Coal Co., 297

1948] 

Pa. 302. Contributions by a deceased child are insufficient; dependency upon those contributions for support and maintenance must be affirmatively established: Howard v. 

McClane, 146 Pa. Superior Ct. 212. But in the case of a deceased minor, the law expressly states that dependency of the parent is presumed and the burden of proof then rests upon a defendant to overcome this statutory presumption. 

Defendant called no witnesses. The discharge of its burden then, of necessity, depends entirely upon the testimony given by claimants. The family is of foreign extraction. As is customary in many such families, the father is the "titular" head but it is the mother who handles the family finances. 

The salary contributions are all made to her and she makes the disbursements as in her judgment are prudent and necessary. Here, the father testified that his earnings are turned over intact to the wife and prior to the deceased son's induction into the military service, his early wages were turned over in full to his mother, and she then made the disbursements and allowances. The uncontradicted testimony of the parents is that the son regularly turned over $15 or $20 per week during the period of his employment by defendant, up until the time of death. We are not concerned here with total dependency, but we are of the opinion that the parents were partially dependent upon decedent and the referee should have entered an appropriate award. The regular contributions made by the deceased son were in a substantial amount. We would indeed be blind to the realities of present every day economic conditions, were we to exclude the son's contributions to the family budget as a necessary part of the family support. A gross pay of $44 weekly, earned by the father, may be sufficient to provide a family of four with the bare necessities of life, but we do not believe that the legislature intended that dependency is to be excluded where the father is the sole home provider and is only able to eke out an existence for his family and provide his family with meager necessities. Furthermore, there is no definition as to the extent of dependency. Where there is dependency, even to a slight extent, dependency is established. With the statutory presumption existing in behalf of the parent of a

deceased minor child, we believe in the present case the contributions made by the son were necessary to adequately support claimants' family and therefore an award is warranted: Meily v. Keystone Sand Products Co., 14 W.C.B. 487; 

Hall v. Coal Co., 65 Pitts. L. J. 57; Lauer v. Flinn, 27 Dist. R. 

413. There is sufficient evidence upon the record from which we may logically and fairly infer dependency upon the deceased son: Magnate v. Julian, 19 Del. Co. 24. See Faucett v. Philadelphia Rapid Transit Co., 89 Pa. Superior Ct. 449. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's sixth, seventh and eighth findings of fact. In lieu thereof, we substitute the following 

Findings of fact 6. Claimant father is employed by the Lehigh Portland 

Cement Company at a weekly wage of $44, but his take home pay is from $35 to $37. 

7. We find that the deceased son was a minor, who contributed regularly out of his earnings to the household expenses, and that the contributions were necessary to maintain a fair standard of living for the family. 

8. We find that claimants were partially dependent upon their minor son, Francis, for support at the time of his accidental injury and death.

The referee's other findings of fact are affirmed. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's second conclusion of law and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following 

Conclusion of law 

2. Having found that claimants were partially dependent upon their deceased minor son at the time of his accidental injury and death, they are entitled to compensation under the act.

The referee's first conclusion of law is affirmed. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's order of disallowance and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following

1948] 395. 

Defendant, Richard George, by its insurance carrier,

Selected Risks Indemnity Company, is ordered and directed to pay to claimants, Barbara and Andrew Figura, the sum of $6 per week for the statutory period of 300 weeks beginning December 25, 1946.

This award to bear interest in accordance with section 410 of the act.

The appeal of claimants is sustained. 

SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA BEHANNA v. MEYERS and AMERICAN CASUALTY CO. 

Workmen's compensation-Claim petition Statute of limitations— 

Conduct of employer and insurance carrier-Estoppel. 

Where an injured employe on numerous occasions discussed his claim for workmen's compensation with his employer in an effort to secure information to enable him to file a timely report, was assured by his employer that the report would be filed, at the request of the insurer signed a statement of the nature and cause of the accident, and submitted to medical treatment furnished by the insurer over a period of several weeks, the board did not err in holding that the employer and insurer were estopped from asserting the bar of the statutory limitation where a claim petition was not filed until subsequent to the period of one year from the date of the accident. 

Appeal from the order of the County Court of Allegheny 

County, no. A 447 of 1947. Affirmed. July 23, 1948. Superior 

Court of Pennsylvania, April term, 1948, no. 149. 

Louis Vaira, for claimant. 

Dickie, Robinson & McCamey, for defendant.

FINE, J.: 

Where an injured employe has on numerous occasions discussed his claim for workmen's compensation with his

employer in an effort to secure information to enable him to file a timely report, has been continuously assured by his employer that the report would be filed, has at the request of the insurer signed a statement of the nature and cause of the accident, has complied with insurer's request for a medical examination and has submitted to 10 weeks' continuous medical treatment, did the board err in holding that the employer and insurer were estopped from asserting the bar of the statutory limitation? Raymond Meyers, employer, and his insurance carrier, appeal from an order of the court below affirming the conclusion of the board that they were estopped to deny the timeliness of the claim petition of Howard J. Behanna, the employe.

Claimant was injured in the course of his employment on August 21, 1942, but did not file his claim petition until May 19, 1944. The board affirmed the referee's dismissal of the petition for the reason that it had not been filed within the statutory period of one year from the date of the accident. The court below, pursuant to section 427 of the Workmen's Compensation Act of 1939, P. L. 520, as amended, 77 PS §877, remitted the case to the board for further inquiry and more specific findings of facts stating, inter alia: ". . . additional testimony should be taken to disclose the circumstances of the examination of the claimant by Dr. 

Linn, the physician of the insurance carrier, in the early part of February, 1943, and to bring to light the conduct of the insurance carrier subsequent thereto." The employer appealed. In Behanna v. Meyers, 158 Pa. Superior Ct. 208, 44 A. (2d) 600, this court held the order to be interlocutory and dismissed the appeal.

C. A. Dunn, agent of the insurer, was the only witness called at the second hearing. The referee again dismissed claimant's petition. The board, however, concluded that: "The conduct of the insurance carrier is such that it is estopped from asserting that the claim petition was not filed within the statutory period." The court below concluded that "The testimony clearly shows that the claimant made every effort to have a report filed with the carrier" and dismissed the appeal of the employer. This appeal followed.

1948] 

The scope of appellate review is limited to determining whether the acts and conduct of appellants are sufficient, as a matter of law, to estop them from invoking the statute of limitations as contained in section 315 of the Workmen's 

Compensation Act (77 PS §602): Kline v. Kiehl, 157 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 392, 395, 43 A. (2d) 616; Howard v. McClane, 146 Pa. Superior Ct. 212, 216, 22 A. (2d) 225; Meyers v.

Lehigh Valley Transportation Co., 138 Pa. Superior Ct. 569, 

573, 10 A. (2d) 879. The facts are so clearly recited and the law so ably enunciated by President Judge Baldridge in Behanna v. Meyers, supra, that there is no need to add to them nor to review the authorities there cited. Considering the record now presented there is ample evidence to support the conclusion that claimant's failure to file his claim petition within the one year period was brought about by misleading conduct of appellants such as tolled the statute and now estops them from invoking its provisions. 

Claimant on various occasions discussed his claim with his employer that a proper report would be timely filed with the carrier and was met with the reply that the employer "was too busy" but that "he would file the necessary report". 

In February of 1943 claimant was interviewed by Mr. Dunn, agent for the insurer and signed a statement pertaining to the injuries. He was requested to be examined by a Dr. 

Linn, employed by the insurer, and after a medical examination by Dr. Linn reported to the insurer. On April 26, 1943, claimant entered the Eye and Ear Hospital in Pittsburgh where he was treated for a period of 10 weeks. In September 1943 claimant again called on the insurer at which time he was advised that his claim was barred because not filed within the statutory period of one year. 

The principles enunciated in Meyers v. Lehigh Valley 

Transportation Co., 138 Pa. Superior Ct. 569, 10 A. (2d) 

879, are applicable here. In the Meyers case, the court, through Judge Rhodes, now President Judge, said: "If claimant was deceived or misled in connection with filing his claim petition by defendant and its insurance carrier, who are now seeking to take advantage of the limitation,

we think that the running of the statute would be tolled. 

Guy v. Stocklein Baking Co. et al., 133 Pa. Superior Ct. 38, 48, 1 A. 2d 839. The conduct of defendant and its insurance carrier may be such as to estop them from presenting the statutory limitation as a defense in bar of the claim for compensation, if the effect of such conduct was to mislead or deceive claimant, whether intentionally or not, and induce him to withhold or postpone filing his claim petition until more than a year had elapsed from the occurrence of the accident. Demmel v. Dilworth Co. et al., 136 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 37, 39, 7 A. 2d 50."

This court in Horton v. West Penn Power Co., 119 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 465, 180 Atl. 56, said, p. 473: "Proceedings under our compensation statute are not litigation in the ordinary sense of that word; it is neither required nor contemplated that claimants shall, in all cases, be represented by private counsel. . . . It does not follow, however, that the running of this statute of limitation may not be tolled by the declaration and the conduct of the parties invoking its protection."

It cannot be said that the board erred in holding that the conduct of the employer and his carrier during the one year subsequent to the accident, estops them from now asserting the bar of the statutory limitation. The court below aptly observed: "There is no doubt in our mind that the claimant was lulled into a sense of security which led him to postpone filing of his claim petition." 

Order affirmed. 

SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA JONES v. UNEMPLOYMENT COMPENSATION BOARD 

Unemployment compensation-Employe or independent contractor—

Collector of periodical subscription payments-Finding by 

Unemployment Compensation Board of Review. 

An award of compensation by the Unemployment Compensation

Board of Review based on its finding that claimant, who worked for appellant as a collector of periodical subscription payments, was subject to appellant's control in the performance of his duties, and that his services constituted employment as defined under section

1948] 

4(1) (1) (2) (B) of the Unemployment Compensation Law, will be affirmed where there was evidence to establish that appellant had the absolute right to terminate claimant's services at any time, and that it controlled claimant in the discharge of his duties, directing him as to where he should work, and as to the rendition of his reports; under the circumstances, the board was warranted in concluding that claimant was in the employment of the appellant and was not an independent. contractor.

Appeal from the decision of the Unemployment Compensation Board of Review at appeal no. B44-94-A-6073. Decision no. B-13168, in re Claim of Harry Blum. Decision affirmed. July 23, 1948. Superior Court of Pennsylvania, April term, 1948, no. 115. -, for claimant. 

Richard H. Wagner, Roland M. Morgan, William L. Hammond, and T. McKeen Chidsey, for defendant. 

RHODES, P. J.: 

Claimant in this unemployment compensation case worked for appellant from June 16, 1944, to June 2, 1947, as a collector of periodical subscription payments. The bureau denied benefits to claimant on the ground that he was financially ineligible to receive compensation under section 401 (a) of the Unemployment Compensation Law of December 5, 1936, P. L. (1937) 2897, as amended by the Act of May 29, 1945, P. L. 1145, sec. 8, 43 PS §801. The referee affirmed the decision of the bureau, having found that appellant exercised no control over claimant's time or activities, and that his only compensation was by way of commissions for services rendered. On appeal to the Unemployment Compensation Board of Review, the board substituted its own findings. of fact for certain findings of the referee, reversed the decision of the referee, and allowed compensation. The board found that claimant was compensated by retention of 20 percent on all moneys collected for appellant, and by payment of 10 cents for each account verified; that appellant did in fact control the performance of claimant's duties by giving him instructions as to the persons from whom he should collect, the amount to be collected, and as to how and when

reports should be submitted, and by directing him from time to time to ascertain the location of particular accounts, to verify the receipt of the publications by the subscribers, and to call upon subscribers to adjust complaints; and that claimant devoted all his time to his work and was actually dependent for his livelihood upon his association with and remuneration from appellant. The board also found that claimant received sufficient remuneration during his base year to meet the test of eligibility under sections 401(a) and 404. The board concluded that claimant's services constituted employment as defined under section 4(1), (1)- (2) (B) of the Unemployment Compensation Law, as amended, 43 PS §753, as claimant was not "free from control or direction over the performance of such services" regardless of whether the control referred to be general control or control over the method and means of performance, and as he was not "customarily engaged in an independently established trade, occupation, profession or business." This appeal was then taken by the claimed employer. 

Appellant's contention is that claimant's services were performed under such conditions as to make him an independent contractor, and that the conclusions of the board are not supported by any competent evidence. On appeal it is the function of this court to determine whether or not the evidence is sufficient to support the findings and conclusions of the board, as the board's findings of fact, if supported by the evidence and in the absence of fraud, are conclusive, and in such cases the jurisdiction of the court is confined to questions of law: Palumbo v. Unemployment 

Compensation Board of Review, 148 Pa. Superior Ct. 289, 

292, 25 A. (2d) 80; MacFarland v. Unemployment Compensation Board of Review, 158 Pa. Superior Ct. 418, 420 45 A. (2d) 423; Act of December 5, 1936, P. L. (1937) 2897, art.

V, sec. 510, 43 PS §830. 

The relevant portions of section 4 of the Unemployment 

Compensation Law, as amended, 43 PS §753, are the following: "(i) 'Employe' means every individual whether male, female, citizen, alien or minor, who is performing or subsequent to January first, one thousand nine hundred thirty-

1948] 

 six, has performed services for an employer in an employment subject to this act." "(j) 'Employer' means every—(1) individual, (2) copartnership, (3) association, (4) corporation (I) who or which employed or employs any employe (whether or not the same employe) in employment subject to this act for some portion of each of some twenty (20) days, each day being in a different calendar week, during the calendar year one thousand nine hundred thirty-six, or during any calendar year thereafter, to and including the calendar year one thousand nine hundred and forty-four, or who or which employed or employs any employe in employment subject to this act for some portion of a day during the calendar year one thousand nine hundred and forty-five or for some portion of a day during any calendar year thereafter, . . . 99 "(l) ... (2) The term 'Employment' shall include an individual's entire service performed within or both within and without this Commonwealth, if— . . . (B) . . . An individual performing services for remuneration in an employment subject to this act shall be deemed to be performing such services for wages, unless and until it is shown to the satisfaction of the department that (a) such individual has been and will continue to be free from control or direction over the performance of such services both under his contract of service and in fact; and (b) that such service is either outside the usual course of the business for which such service is performed, or that such service is performed outside of all the places of business of the enterprise for which such service is performed; and (c) that such individual is customarily engaged in an independently established trade, occupation, profession or business." "(x) 'Wages' means all remuneration for employment, (including the cash value of mediums of payment other than cash), .. ," with certain exceptions as enumerated in the act which are not here involved.

Appellant asserts that no right was reserved to control the manner and method of performance of appellant's work, that no control existed or was exercised, and that the relationship was therefore that of an independent contractor. 

We are of the opinion that the only ouestion presented for our determination is whether the evidence is sufficient

to support the board's findings which placed claimant within the coverage of the act. 

The issue raised is a narrow one and relates primarily to the question of control, and there is no doubt in our minds from an examination of the record that the evidence was sufficient to establish that appellant exercised a very definite control and direction over the performance of such services as claimant rendered to appellant; and that claimant was an employe and not an independent contractor. It has been said that the master and servant, or employer and employe, relationship exists where the employer has the right to select the employe, the power to remove and discharge him, and the right to direct what work shall be done, and the way and manner in which it shall be done: McColligan v. 

Pennsylvania Railroad Co., 214 Pa. 229, 232, 63 Atl. 792; 

Walters v. Kaufmann Department Stores, Inc., 334 Pa. 233, 235, 5 A. (2d) 559. The method of payment is not a determining factor in establishing the relationship of the parties. 

See Sechrist v. Kurtz Brothers et al., 147 Pa. Superior Ct. 

214, 219, 24 A. (2d) 128. But the power of an employer to terminate the employment at any time is incompatible with the full control of the work which is usually enjoyed by an independent contractor, and hence is considered as a strong circumstance tending to show the subserviency of the employee: American Writing Machine Co. v. Unemployment Compensation Board of Review, 148 Pa. Superior Ct. 

299, 304, 25 A. (2d) 85.

Appellant terminated claimant's services on June 2, 1947. 

He had worked for appellant continuously from June 16, 1944, and his duties consisted largely of collecting money due on accounts, for which he received a 20 percent commission. A secondary source of revenue was from a verification of accounts which appellant had with various individuals. The presence and the extent of supervision and control over the manner in which claimant performed his work for appellant are clearly established, and they are inconsistent with the relationship of independent contractor. 

Appellant acted on an absolute right to terminate claimant's services at any time, and his services were terminated on

1948] 

 five days' notice. The subserviency of claimant is obvious from the many exhibits offered by claimant and admitted in evidence. It suffices to quote from a few of them. On 

October 27, 1944, claimant received from appellant the following instructions: "Enclosed herewith you will find the contracts for West Newton. I will appreciate it if you will make the collections there Monday and Tuesday. In case you cannot make the collections, bring the contracts to the office Monday morning without fail. The man who was going to make the West Newton collections had to make collections in another town for me." Again, on November 14, 1945, he was told: "Please be sure and call on this subscriber and endeavor to collect the amount that is due. In case the subscriber will only pay 50¢ each month, accept the 50¢ until the account is paid in full." On March 14, 1946, he received the following: "We note that you have not reported as many collections or as much money during the current month as you did last month at this time. This should not be, in view of the fact you have quite a few new accounts. Call on this subscriber [Mrs. E. F. Clements] and in case you cannot collect the full amount tell the subscriber we will be satisfied with small monthly payments until the account is paid in full." On March 27, 1947, he was given the following instructions: "Please call on this subscriber [Mrs. Ann

Borovick] immediately and collect the amount due. Also make out change of address on this." On February 15, 1946, he received the following from appellant: "We have instructed you to use the first and third columns on your report. It was necessary for us to make up separate reports for you today. We do not have the time to do your work. 

Please see that this is done properly in the future." On 

May 15, 1947, this appears: "From time to time we will send you new orders for verification. Such orders are to be verified within 48 hours if possible. At least we should have them back here in the office on the following Friday morning. Return all verifications Special Delivery, deduct the cost of postage from your collection report, or, if you will let us know the amount of postage when you send the

verifications, we will include the amount in your check covering verifications."

Claimant was controlled in the discharge of his duties and was subject to the direction of appellant in the performance of his work. He was directed as to where he should work, and as to the rendition of his reports. The relationship was subject to termination at the will of appellant. Claimant (1) was not free from control or direction in the performance of his services; (2) his services were not outside the usual course of appellant's business; (3) he was not engaged in an independently established trade, occupation, profession, or business. The findings of fact of the board are supported by substantial evidence, and the board was warranted in concluding that claimant was in the "employment" of appellant within the meaning of the 

Unemployment Compensation Law, and therefore entitled to compensation.

This case is analogous to that of Leinbach Co., Inc., v. 

Unemployment Compensation Board of Review, 146 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 237, 22 A. (2d) 57. In that case we held that a traveling salesman selling on a commission basis within a certain territory at fixed prices was an employe and not an independent contractor. He paid his own expenses. He was free to come and go as he pleased within the assigned territory, and he was not under duty to work every day. We held that he was entitled to unemployment compensation, and said (page 241 of 146 Pa. Superior Ct., page 59 of 

22 A. (2d)): "We have no hesitation in holding that a traveling salesman, in the circumstances set forth in this case, is an employee within the provisions of the act and not an independent contractor."

Finally, it is to be remembered that the Unemployment Compensation Law is a remedial statute, and, excepting the sections imposing taxes, its provisions must be liberally and broadly construed so that its objectives may be completely achieved: MacFarland v. Unemployment Compensation 

Board of Review, supra, 158 Pa. Superior Ct. 418, 422, 45 

A. (2d) 423. 

Decision is affirmed.

1948] 

 SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA MANIKOWSKI v. MORRIS RUN COAL MINING CO. 

Workmen's compensation—Accidental injury-Coronary thrombosis— 

Unusual exertion in pushing coal car.

A finding by the Workmen's Compensation Board that claimant while pushing, with the aid of two other men, a loaded coal car weighing nearly 6,000 pounds, over-exerted himself, as a result of which he suffered a coronary thrombosis, and an award based thereon, will be affirmed where claimant was admittedly in sound health prior to his injury and the causal connection between his exertion and the coronary thrombosis was likewise established by uncontradicted testimony.

Appeal from the judgment of the Court of Common Pleas of Tioga County, August term, 1947, no. 144. Affirmed.

July 23, 1948. Superior Court of Pennsylvania, March term, 1948, no. 11. 

George Jerko, for claimant. 

Hopkins T. Rowlands, and John H. Hibbard, for defendant. 

Ross, J.:

In this workmen's compensation case, the referee made an award for total disabilty, the board affirmed the referee, the lower court affirmed the board and the employer took this appeal. 

Claimant, Enoch Manikowski, on May 29, 1945, while in the course of his employment in defendant's mine, suffered a coronary thrombosis while pushing a loaded coal car and, as a result, is totally disabled. The employer does not dispute the injury and its resulting disability but contends that the injury did not result from an accident within the meaning of Section 301 of the Workmen's Compensation Act. 

Claimant has the burden of proving by competent and substantial evidence, either direct or circumstantial, that his disabling injury resulted from "something undesigned, unexpected or fortuitous, outside of the ordinary course of events": Royko v. Logan Coal Co., 146 Pa. Superior Ct. 449, 22 A. (2d) 434. An injury gives rise to no inference that it

results from an accident. In Adamchick v. Wyoming Valley 

Collieries Co., 332 Pa. 401, 3 A. (2d) 377, the Supreme 

Court stated at page 410: "... to secure compensation there must be proof both of an accident and of an injury; an accident cannot be inferred merely from an injury. There must be some evidence of an accident, either direct or circumstantial, in the latter instance clearly and logically indicating it."

In this case, the board made, inter alia, the following findings of fact: "5. We find as a fact that on May 29, 1945 the claimant pushed a car with the aid of two men, Edward Olson and Frank Childs. The particular car was unusually difficult to move. . . . 7. We find as a fact that while the claimant was pushing said car on May 29, 1945 with all his strength that he felt a pain in his lower left chest and his both arms became numb and his wind got short. We find as a fact that as a result of using all his strength in pushing a loaded car with the aid of two men that the claimant over-exerted himself as a result of which he suffered a coronary thrombosis. We find as a fact that this set of circumstances constitutes an accident." If the findings of fact are supported by substantial and competent testimony and the "most favorable inferences" therefrom (Harris v. 

Meyers, 160 Pa. Superior Ct. 607, 52 A. (2d) 375) claimant's injury is compensable.

It is well settled that an injury resulting from overexertion or unusual exertion in the course of employment is compensable: Skroki v. Crucible Steel Co., 292 Pa. 550, 141 

Atl. 480. Cf. collection of cases in Royko v. Logan Coal Co., 146 Pa. Superior Ct. 449, at page 461, 22 A. (2d) 434, supra, and Foster v. State College Boro, 124 Pa. Superior Ct. 492, at page 497, 189 Atl. 786.

As the compensation authorities have found in his favor, we must review the evidence in the light most favorable to claimant (Hockenberry v. State Workmen's Insurance 

Fund, 133 Pa. Superior Ct. 249, 2 Atl. (2d) 536) and he is to be given the benefit of inferences reasonably deducible therefrom: Paulin v. Williams & Co., Inc., 122 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 462, 186 Atl. 415; Schubert v. Oswald & Hess Co., 161 

Pa. Superior Ct. 309, 54 A. (2d) 113.

1948] 

When claimant suffered his injury, he and two fellow employes, Olson and Childs, were attempting to move a loaded coal car weighing nearly 6000 pounds from a working face or room, over a knoll about 18 feet from the room, toward the main heading of the mine. Claimant and Olson attempted to "push that car, but we couldn't move that car" and then sought and secured the help of the motor runner, Childs. The three men moved the car over the knoll although it "stalled on us four times before we got it out we couldn't push it. . . . I was pushing with all my strength. . . . this car just simply stalled on us and we push for all we was worth, the three of us, to get it out". 

Claimant also testified that while pushing on the car after it stalled "I got the pain from pushing it . . around the heart my arms went numb on me and my wind got short on me"; and although he continued to push on the car until it was moved over the knoll, immediately afterwards "I pulled out my handkerchief and when I sat down one of my legs just shook and the sweat came out on me and I sat there for about 45 minutes” and that he has not been able to work since.

The causal connection between claimant's exertion and his coronary thrombosis is clearly shown by the uncontradicted testimony of claimant's family physician and of a heart specialist.

Appellant-employer contends that claimant is not entitled to compensation under the authority of Crispin v. Leedom & Worrall Co., 341 Pa. 325, 19 A. (2d) 400, but, in our opinion, that case does not govern the one before us.

In the Crispin case, claimant and another employe were engaged in pushing a loaded truck from an electric elevator. 

The elevator, operated by automatic control, stopped an inch to an inch and a half below the floor level of the store room where the contents of the truck were to be unloaded. The two men were unsuccessful in their first attempt to push the truck from the elevator, but by a second, stronger effort they were able to do so. Neither the disparity between the floor levels nor the effort required to overcome it were unusual circumstances. In denying compensation on the

ground that no accident had been shown, the Supreme Court, at page 329, summarized the Crispin facts as follows: "Here, a man with a chronic heart condition, engaged in his customary occupation, under conditions which were not unusual but ordinary, performing an act in which he had engaged on numerous other occasions, further damaged his already damaged heart, not as the result of an accident but in the normal performance of his employment." (Italics supplied.) 

That is not our case.

Here, the car on which claimant was pushing when he incurred his injury was the third loaded coal car he had helped to move over the knoll during that day. The other two cars were moved by claimant and one other man. Although sometimes it was necessary to have a third` man help in moving a car, claimant testified that he "saw something wrong with that car it seems that was the worst car we have had in there" and that never before had the claimant known a car that had "stuck" on him four times before it was moved over the knoll. The board's finding that the car "was unusually difficult to move" is supported by sufficient competent evidence and it would follow that "unusual exertion" would be required to move such a car. Furthermore, in this case, claimant in establishing unusual exertion is aided by an inference that was not present in the Crispin case. Here, claimant according to the uncontradicted testimony-and so found by the board-was in sound health prior to his injury on May 29, 1945. Consequently, claimant is entitled to the inference that his heart was injured by over-exertion-or unusual exertion-or exertion more severe than usual. "Where . a sound heart is affected by a severe exertion, and has not before been so affected, the inference is fair that the exertion which affected the heart, while it was of the same sort, must have differed in degree from that which was usual. It must have, as a fact, been more severe than usual and should be classified with those fortuitous physical violences of the bodily structure, which are properly described as accidents. The work may be of the same 'sort' or character as that called usual, but must have been harder than ordinary, or the

1948] 

 sound heart which had theretofore stood it would not have yielded to it. . . . If the heart is sound and has stood customary hard work for years, and if on a particular day it weakens, the inference is that the exertion was unusual, not that the heart was weak. Therefore, the inference is not that death was caused by a weak heart, but was caused by unusual exertion": Barr v. Atlantic Elevator Co., 124 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 57, 60, 187 Atl. 815; York v. State Workmen's 

Insurance Fund, 131 Pa. Superior Ct. 496, 501, 200 Atl. 230.

From an examination of the record in this case it is our opinion that the board's findings of fact are supported by substantial and competent evidence and that claimant's injury is the result of an accident within the meaning of the act and, therefore, compensable. 

Judgment affirmed.

SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA TURNER v. UNEMPLOYMENT COMPENSATION BOARD 

Unemployment compensation-Appeal from bureau to board— 

Limitation-Section 501(e) of Unemployment Compensation Law. 

amended, providing that unless the party aggrieved by a decision of the bureau files an appeal with the Unemployment Compensation Board within 10 days after receipt of notice thereof from the bureau, such decision of the bureau shall be final, is a mandatory provision; hence, an appeal taken by claimant from the bureau beyond the 10-day period was properly dismissed by the board where there was neither allegation nor proof that claimant was deprived of his rights by fraud or wrongful conduct of the administrative authorities.

Appeal by claimant from the decision of the Unemployment Compensation Board of Review, March 31, 1947,

appeal no. B-44-94-A-5206, decision no. B-9388. Decision affirmed. July 23, 1948. Superior Court of Pennsylvania, April term, 1948, no. 27. 

William G. Negley, for claimant.

R. Carlye Fee, T. McKeen Chidsey, for defendant. 

FINE, J.: 

Does section 501 (e) of the Unemployment Compensation law¹ permit a party aggrieved by a decision of the bureau to appeal to the board notwithstanding more than 10 days have elapsed since receipt of notice thereof from the bureau, where there is neither allegation nor proof that claimant was deprived of his rights by fraud or its equivalent, i. e., wrongful or negligent conduct of administrative authorities? That is the sole question to be determined on this appeal by Sylvester Turner from an order of the Unemployment Compensation Board of Review affirming disallowance of his appeal by the referee because it was not filed within 

1 Section 501 (e) provides: "Unless the claimant of last employer or base-year employer of the claimant files an appeal with the board, from the determination contained in any notice required to be furnished by the department under section five hundred and one (a), (c) and (d), within ten (10) calendar days after such notice was delivered to him personally, or was mailed to his last known post office address, and applies for a hearing, such determination of the department, with respect to the particular facts set forth in such notice, shall be final and compensation shall be paid or denied in accordance therewith. 

In the event that an appeal is filed with the board, the payment of any contested amount of compensation shall be withheld pending determination of the claim, but any uncontested amount of compensation allowed in any decision shall be paid notwithstanding any appeal which may thereafter be taken: Provided, That when a referee or the board affirms a decision of the department allowing compensation, such compensation shall be paid notwithstanding any further appeal. 

As amended 1942, Ex. Sess., April 23, P. L. 60, sec. 5; 1945, May 29, P. L. 1145, sec. 11." (43 PS §821 (e).)

1948] 

 the 10-day period required by the Unemployment Compensation Law, supra. 

Claimant, on May 10, 1946, was employed by the Carnegie

Illinois Steel Company, Homestead, Pa., as a laborer. On that date he was notified that because of a strike by coal miners the resulting lack of coal compelled a shutdown of the plant, and on May 17, 1946, he was laid off. After the strike ended, claimant did not return to work. Instead, he informed his employer on July 2, 1946, that he would seek work elsewhere.

On July 21, 1946, Turner filed his claim for unemployment compensation benefits for weeks ending July 28, August 4 and August 11, 1946. The bureau, on August 16, 1946, disallowed benefits assigning as the reason that claimant had disqualified himself by having voluntarily left his employment, without cause, within the meaning of section 

402 (b) of the Unemployment Compensation Law, 43 PS §802 (b). Nineteen days thereafter, on September 4, 1946, claimant filed his appeal and the matter was referred to a referee. The referee disallowed2 the appeal on January 13, 1947, because it had not been filed within the 10-day period prescribed by section 501 (e), supra, wherefore, he was "without jurisdiction to entertain the appeal." The board, on March 31, 1947, affirmed the decision of the referee. 

This appeal followed.

Claimant argues that the appeal should have been allowed for the reasons that (1) the tardiness was due to illness of his counsel, and (2) the board waived the provisions of the act by allowing the appeal in the first instance and referring it to a referee.
