The board contends the time limitation provision of the statute is mandatory and that it is without power to waive the provisions thereof except in circumstances not present here. The contentions of the board must be sustained. 

2 The referee, on October 23, 1946, originally allowed the appeal nunc pro tunc and awarded benefits but after reconsideration reversed his original decision.

[84 Dep. Rep. 

• • The language of section 501 (e), supra, that "Unless the [party aggrieved] . . . files an appeal with the board, from the determination contained in any notice required to be furnished by the department . . . within ten (10) calendar days after such notice was mailed to his last known post office address, . . . such determination of the department, with respect to the particular facts set forth in such notice, shall be final and compensation shall be paid or denied in accordance therewith." Such statutory provision is mandatory. "The mandatory or directory nature of a statute depends on whether the thing directed to be done is of the essence of the thing required: Singer v. Delaware L. & W. R. R. 

Co., 254 Pa. 502, 505; Socialist Labor Case, 332 Pa. 78; 

Deibert v. Rhodes, 291 Pa. 550; Norwegian Street, 81 Pa. 

349, 354. A mandatory provision is one the failure to follow which renders the proceeding to which it relates illegal and void. A directory provision is one the observance of which is not necessary to the validity of the proceeding. 

See Deibert v. Rhodes, supra. 'When a statute fixes the time within which an act must be done, the courts have no power to enlarge it, although it relates to a mere question of practice': Harris v. Mercur (No. 1), 202 Pa. 313, 318": 

American Labor Party Case, 352 Pa. 576, 579, 44 A. (2d) 48.

The essence of the thing required is that within 10 days after notice a party aggrieved by the determination of the bureau must file an appeal with the board. Failure so to do precludes him from thereafter challenging the facts set forth in such notice. The facts determined against claimant are that "Claimant separated himself from his employment when he failed to return after the industrial dispute of the coal miners was settled and further on 7/2/46 he informed the employer that he would seek work elsewhere." 

The provisions of the act being mandatory, the burden was upon claimant to show facts which would bring the case within the principle that where a party has been prevented from doing an act through fraud or its equivalent,

1948] 

 i. e., ignorance or negligent acts of an administrative official, power exists to allow an appeal nunc pro tunc if prosecuted within a reasonable time. See Nixon v. Nixon, 329 Pa. 256, 260, 198 Atl. 154; Tuttle Unemployment Compensation Case, 

160 Pa. Superior Ct. 46, 49 A. (2d) 847; Commonwealth v. 

Schneiderman, 162 Pa. Superior Ct. 461, 58 A. (2d) 196; 

Pittsburgh v. Ruffner, 134 Pa. Superior Ct. 192, 4 A. (2d) 

224. Mere hardship is not sufficient: Tuttle Unemployment 

Compensation Case, supra. A claimant's illness (Marcus v. 

Cohen, 94 Pa. Superior Ct. 383), or the neglect of an at torney (Wise v. Cambridge Springs Borough, 262 Pa. 139, 

104 Atl. 863) have been held to be insufficient to permit an appeal nunc pro tunc. Nor can the mandatory requirements be waived by agreement: Devlin v. Grabler Manufacturing 

Corp., 151 Pa. Superior Ct. 216, 30 A. (2d) 138. See 3 C. J. §1083, p. 1074; 4 C. J. S. §485. The rule of strict adherence to such mandatory provisions and the requirement of proof of extraordinary circumstances to warrant allowance of an appeal nunc pro tunc in matters relating to the time within which appeals must be perfected is a salutary one. If the rule were otherwise, finality of judicial and administrative procedure would be uncertain.

Claimant did not file his appeal within the time required by law; nor has he sustained the burden of showing that he was "misled by an officer who [was] authorized to act in the premises": (Tuttle Unemployment Compensation Case, supra); that there was neglect upon the part of an administrative officer; or any other circumstances from which fraud or its equivalent could be determined. Notwithstanding failure to seasonably appeal to the referee from the bureau's decision, the appeal to this court was properly taken.3 

3 Section 509 of the Unemployment Compensation Law as last amended by the Act of 1942, P. L. 60, sec 5, 43 PS §829, provides: "Any decision made by the department or any referee or the board shall become final ten days after the date thereof, unless appealed from, as hereinbefore provided; but any decision of the board or of

Decision affirmed. a referee, where an appeal has been disallowed by the board, shall nevertheless be subject to appeal to the Superior Court after the same has become final."

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD ANDERSON v. HOTEL SYLVANIA Workmen's compensation - Accidental injury — Hernia - - Notice - 

Sufficiency.

A referee's award of compensation based on a finding that claimant sustained a hernia as a result of lifting a crate of eggs in the course of his employment will be set aside where claimant gave no notice of the injury within 48 hours after the occurrence of the accident, other than to inform defendant's timekeeper that he was sick and had to go home and on the following morning told his boss that he was going into the hospital; under the circumstances, the notice required by section 306 (h) of the Act of May 18, 1945, P. L. 661, was not given. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Alessandroni, District No. 1, claim petition no. 109,977, accident no. 5,070025. Reversed. July 14, 1948. 

New Amsterdam Casualty Company, insurance carrier. 

Frank J. Eustace, Jr., for plaintiff. 

Raymond A. White, Jr., for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This case is before the board upon appeal by defendant, Hotel Sylvania, from Referee Alessandroni's award of compensation to claimant, Hubert E. Anderson, for a hernia claim. Claimant was not represented by counsel at the hear-

1948] 

 ing before the referee. The referee's examination of claimant discloses that he was employed as a cook by defendant on 

July 7, 1947, when he suffered an injury in lifting a crate of eggs from an icebox. He stated that he "got about halfway straightened up with those eggs" when he felt something give way in the left groin. Handling crates of eggs was claimant's regular duties, although he did not always lift the crates in the particular manner employed upon this occasion. 

Anderson denied any previous pain or discomfort in the left groin region. The incident occurred about 2 p.m. and claimant immediately went home by taxicab. Claimant testified that he told Tucker, the timekeeper, that he was sick and had to go home. The next morning he reported to the chef that "he would have to get somebody else, I wouldn't be there, I was going to the hospital". Claimant resumed his employment six weeks after the accident. He stated that he had been rejected for military service, being classified as 4F.

Elmer L. Elliott of the hotel staff, called by defendant, testified that he received no notice of the accident from claimant until August 2, 1947.

We are impressed by the series of events which the referee accepted as conclusive of an accident. Claimant testified that in lifting the crate of eggs on to his shoulder, he experienced the pain when he had almost straightened up. Claimant ceased work at once and was hospitalized the very next day. 

We are satisfied that the hernia resulted from lifting the crate in question in the manner described: Davis v. Jones & 

Laughlin Steel Co.,. 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 133. The absence of medical testimony is not fatal to the claim because the physical condition was the immediate, direct and probable result of the particular incident: Mohr v. Desimone & Sayers, 110 Pa. Superior Ct. 44; Testa v. National Radiator Co., 141 

Pa. Superior Ct. 206.

The only remaining question concerns notice. The legislature, in 1947, deleted the postulate requirements of a hernia claim, except in regard to notice within 48 hours. Section 

306 (h) of the Act of May 18, 1945, P. L. 661, now reads:

"Where claim is made for hernia, claimant must notify the employer or a representative of the employer within forty-eight hours after the occurrence of the accident." 

No formal notice is required so long as the employer has fair knowledge of the nature of the disability. Mindful as we are of the humane purposes of compensation, we cannot say that the employer had proper notice of the hernia injury within the contemplation of the act, until August 2, 1947. 

Claimant testified: "Q. What did you tell Tucker? "A. I told him I was sick and I had to go home. "Q. Did you tell him about the crate of eggs you were trying to lift? "A. No, sir. "Q. Why not? "A. Well, I didn't think it was serious, and I figured on coming back in, to work, the next morning. And that is what I told him."

Claimant stated that he told his boss the next morning thas he was going into the hospital. He testified: "Q. What did you tell him? "A. I told him he would have to get somebody else, I wouldn't be there, I was going to the hospital. "Q. Did you tell him why you were going there? "A. No, and he didn't ask me."

Being sick and going to a hospital could mean anything; certainly there is no implication of a hernia claim. Under these circumstances we are constrained to hold that required notice under the hernia section of the act was not given: 

Nemonich v. Pittsburgh Coal Co., 161 Pa. Superior Ct. 239 (1947).

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's sixth finding of fact and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following

1948] 

Finding of fact 

6. No notice was given to defendant until August 2, 1947, which was more than 48 hours after the occurrence of the hernia.

The referee's other findings of fact are affirmed. 

We hereby vacate the third paragraph of the referee's conclusions of law and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following 

Conclusion of law

Having found that claimant failed to give defendant notice of his injury within 48 hours of its occurrence, claimant is not entitled to compensation.

The remainder of the referee's conclusions are affirmed. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's award. In lieu thereof, we substitute the following 

Order of disallowance 

Claim petition no. 109,977 of Hubert E. Anderson is hereby dismissed. 

The appeal of defendant is sustained.

SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA UPDEGRAFF v. PENNSYLVANIA GAME COMMISSION Workmen's compensation—Death—Accidental injury—Coronary occlu sion-Game keeper-Performance of duties requiring unusual exertion.

An award based on a finding affirmed by the Workmen's Compensation Board that decedent, a game protector, suffered a coronary occlusion which resulted from overexertion in the course of his employment, will be affirmed where it appeared that decedent in response to a report that dogs were chasing deer, proceeded through unusually heavy

[84 Dep. Rep. 

snow and underbrush under conditions that required unusual exertion at the time he was stricken; the fact that decedent was afflicted with a preëxisting heart condition which did not prevent him from attending to his usual duties as game protector, did not prevent an award in view of the evidence as to unusual exertion. 

Appeal from the judgment of the Court of Common Pleas of Clarion County, February term, 1943, no. 13, and February term, 1946, no. 10. Judgment affirmed. July 23, 1948. 

Superior Court of Pennsylvania, April term, 1948, no. 45. 

A. A. Geary, for claimant.

S. H. Torchia, Ralph H. Behney and T. McKeen Chidsey, for defendants. 

Ross, J.:

Harry J. Updegraff, while in the course of his employment as a game protector, suffered a coronary occlusion which resulted in his death. His widow filed a claim for compensation on the ground that her husband's death resulted from overexertion in the course of his employment. 

The referee's award of compensation was affirmed by the board and the court below and this appeal was taken by the State Workmen's Insurance Fund. 

The facts are undisputed. At about 2:30 p.m. on March 5, 1942, someone called at the Updegraff home and told the deceased that two dogs were chasing deer at the foot of Baker Hill. Accompanied by his wife, the deceased left his home immediately in his automobile and they drove a distance of aboue one mile, parked the car and then proceeded on foot toward the place where it was reported that the dogs were chasing deer. On the previous day there was a fall of snow which covered the ground to the depth of from 14 to 17 inches. The deceased proceeded through the snow and underbrush and disappeared from the sight of claimant, who remained near the car. He failed to return for some period of time and claimant called to two boys who hap-

1948] 

 pened along and asked that they request someone to go in search of her husband. Dr. H. V. Swick, the family physician, and Frank Taylor came to the scene and followed the deceased's tracks until they came to the spot where they found him dead. Dr. Swick testified that deceased died as a result of coronary occlusion. He further testified that deceased had been suffering from a coronary condition of the heart prior to the date of his death.

The question before us is whether the death of the deceased employe was the result of an accident within the meaning of section 301 of the Workmen's Compensation Act. 

Claimant has the burden of proving by competent and substantial evidence, either direct or circumstantial, that her husband's death resulted from "something undesigned, unexpected or fortuitous, outside of the ordinary course of events": Royko v. Logan Coal Co., 146 Pa. Superior Ct. 449, 22 A. (2d) 434. An injury gives rise to no inference that it results from an accident. In Adamchick v. Wyoming 

Valley Collieries Co., 332 Pa. 401, 3 A. (2d) 377, the 

Supreme Court stated at page 410: ... to secure compensation there must be proof both of an accident and of an injury; an accident cannot be inferred merely from an injury. There must be some evidence of an accident, either direct or circumstantial, in the latter instance clearly and logically indicating it." If there is substantial and competent evidence of an accident, the mere fact that the employe was afflicted with a preëxisting physical defect or ailment which rendered him more susceptible to injury than an entirely normal person will not prevent an award: Gausman v. Pearson Co., 284 Pa. 348, 131 A. H. 247.

The causal connection between the deceased's exertion and his death is clearly shown by the testimony of Dr. Swick, who stated that it "was brought on by overexertion. There is very little doubt as to that", and in response to the question, "Your professional opinion is that the effort in going down there brought on this?" answered, "Yes, absolutely."

Although he testified that he had treated the deceased for approximately three years prior to his death, Dr. Swick

also testified that during that period the deceased had attended to his duties as game protector, and claimant testified that "he hadn't missed a day's work". Consequently, although Updegraff had a heart condition it did not prevent his performing his usual duties. Updegraff's superior testified that a game protector's general duties are "game protection and game management and all other activities which the Game Commission carry on", and in answer to the question, "And in the event that a report to him of dogs chasing deer what would be his duties in that respect?" answered, "It was his duty to go out and correct the condition." Of course, if—as contended by appellant-the deceased when stricken was performing his usual work in the usual manner and his death was the result of a normal amount of exertion, his death would not be compensable (Good v. Pa. 

Dept. of Property & Supplies, 346 Pa. 151, 30 A. (2d) 434; 

Crispin v. Leedom & Worrall Co., 341 Pa. 325, 19 A. (2d) 

400) but that, in our opinion, is not this case.

The referee, affirmed by the board, found as a fact, inter alia: "11. The death of decedent was the result of the unusual overexertion of plodding through the snow and brush on March 5, 1942, in the performance of his duties." It is well settled that an injury resulting from overexertion or unusual exertion in the course of employment is compensable: Skroki v. Crucible Steel Co., 292 Pa. 550, 141 Atl. 480. 

Cf. collection of cases in Royko v. Logan Coal Co., 146 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 449, at page 461, 22 A. (2d) 434, supra, and 

Foster v. State College Boro., 124 Pa. Superior Ct. 492, at page 497, 189 Atl. 786. Consequently, if the referee's eleventh finding of fact is supported by substantial and competent testimony, the award in this case must be affirmed. 

Dr. Swick, 29 years of age and in "perfect physical condition" (the deceased was 50 years old at the time of his death) testified as follows: "Q. Could you give us any idea of the conditions as they existed there in going down? A. Very, very difficult. I followed his tracks and I must say that I ran all the way down.

1948] 

When I got there I could actually taste blood in my mouth. 

Q. The tracks had been somewhat beaten when you went down? A. Yes, I didn't have to break the track. I used his... Q. Doctor, what would you say as to that particular snowfall as compared to others? A. It is the worst 

I ever saw," and testified further: "It was a heavy snow, so wet it would just ball up on your feet and you could hardly get one foot up from the other. Not the greatest depth but it was the consistency of the snow that packed but yet didn't give you any traction." 

Frank Taylor, who accompanied Dr. Swick to where they found the body, testified as follows: "Q. Do you remember about the condition of the snow there at that time? A. I would say it was better than 17 inches up there because I made the remark coming up through the brush and snow I was played out. . . . Q. Now in traveling through the snow how did it affect you? A. It just took my wind. I could hardly get through. It wasn't in a field-it was in the brush and most mighty hard to get through. It wasn't cleared out or anything and was terribly thick and hard to get through." 

R. L. Snyder, who attempted unsuccesfully to reach the deceased's body, testified: "Q. Had you had any experience in traveling through the snow? A. I seemed very anxious because they didn't get

Harry's body in, and I attempted to go up stream along the bank to find out what was wrong, and I just about played out. Q. How far did you get? A. Probably 40 or 50 feet. 

Q. It just about played you out? A. Yes, I got about 50 feet was all. Q. It wasn't on account of any inefficiency on your part, or was it? A. That was about the heaviest snow I ever tried to wade."

From this testimony it seems clear that the deceased, in the performance of his duties, encountered unusually difficult conditions ("worst snow", "heaviest snow I ever tried to wade", difficulty of "traction", brush "terribly thick" and "most mighty hard to get through") which required un-

usual exertion. This conclusion is inescapable when we consider the physical effect on those who traversed the same route through the snow or attempted to do so. 

In our opinion, this case cannot be distinguished from 

DeEsch v. Emmaus Borough, 143 Pa. Superior Ct. 225, 18 

A. (2d) 89, (allocatur refused, 143 Pa. Superior Ct. XXI).

In that case, a policeman, with a preëxisting ailment, while making an arrest, suffered a coronary thrombosis which caused his death three days later. In affirming an award of compensation, we quoted with approval from the opinion of Judge Henninger of the Court of Common Pleas of Lehigh 

County as follows: 

... Neither the referee nor the board decided that simply because decedent collapsed, the exertion must necessarily have been unusual. The finding was based rather on the testimony of the subordinate officer as to the conditions existing in this arrest that were not usually present in the ordinary course of their duties, that is, the heavy weight of the drunken man, his struggles and the necessity of carrying him down a narrow stairway. . . . The arrest of a drunken man may have been an everyday occurrence and certainly it was decedent's duty to do whatever was necessary to subdue him and remove him as a source of annoyance and danger to his family, but, as testified by Officer Sicher, the arrest of this particular inebriate necessitated a use of force far beyond that usually required." 

It is our opinion that the referee's eleventh finding of fact is supported by substantial and competent evidence and the inferences reasonably deducible therefrom (Paulin v. 

Williams & Co., Inc., 122 Pa. Superior Ct. 462, 186 Atl. 

415) and that the claimant's husband met his death as the result of an accident within the meaning of the Act. 

Judgment affirmed.

1948] 

 WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD WEINBERG v. WEIDMAN Workmen's compensation—Employe or independent contractor-Chem ist performing laboratory experiment-Control by defendant-Effect of claimant's admission of independent contractor relationship. 

1. A referee's award based on a finding that claimant was an employe of defendant and not an independent contractor will be affirmed where it appears that claimant, a graduate chemist, was injured while performing a laboratory experiment on defendant's premises pursuant to a specific technique laid down by defendant, for the purpose of establishing a defense in a patent infringement suit, that he was using materials and equipment supplied by defendant, that he was paid a specified weekly sum, and that the relationship could be terminated at any time by either party. 

2. A statement by claimant in a deposition in connection with a patent infringement suit to the effect that he was not employed by defendant in that suit, who was also defendant in his claim for compensation, but that he was an independent contractor, was not conclusive upon the question of whether claimant was in law an independent contractor or an employe.

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Alessandroni, District No. 1, claim petition no. 109,180, accident no. 

5,037,509. Affirmed as amended. July 21, 1947. 

New Amsterdam Casualty Company, insurance carrier. 

David L. Ullman, for plaintiff. 

Raymond A. White, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

Claimant, Sidney Weinberg, lost his right forearm on 

April 2, 1947, as a result of an explosion-fire in the laboratory of defendant, Harry Waldman, trading as Rona Company. The pivotal question is whether claimant at the time of the accident was an employe of defendant or an independent contractor. Referee Alessandroni held there was an

employer-employe relationship and entered an award in favor of claimant. Defendant has appealed. 

Although only four witnesses testified, the record is quite voluminous. Claimant, a member of the American Chemical 

Society, is a graduate of Temple University and holds a master of science degree from the University of Pennsylvania. He contributed articles on inorganic analytic chemistry in 1945 and 1946 to the analytical edition of the 

Industrial and Engineering Chemistry Journal. Defendant is a qualified assistant in pharmacy and has had various elementary courses in several branches of chemistry. He is engaged in the manufacture of pharmaceutical products for sale to the druggist trade. His manufacturing activities are confined to the manufacture of amphetamine products. The early relationship between the parties involved in this action is not particularly germane to the issue involved, but may be helpful to an orientation to the situation existing between these principals at the date of the accident on April 2, 1947.

The record establishes pretty clearly that in the summer of 1945 defendant approached claimant, a chemist employed at the United States Navy Yard, relative to the manufacture of dextro rotatory amphetamine base. Claimant undertook the assignment for the manufacture of the dextro product at an agreed upon price of $50 per pound. The arrangements were that the work was to be done in the basement of claimant's home and defendant would supply the ingredients of isopropyl alcohol, amphetamine and tartaric acid, as well as the equipment necessary for the manufacture. The amphetamine was combined with tartaric acid and dissolved in the alcohol, and redissolved through successive crystallizations. Claimant stated that he followed the technique prescribed by defendant for this manufacture. The work was to be done in claimant's spare time. Later in 1946 the same parties entered into an arrangement whereby claimant was to investigate the prospects for developing laevo amphetamine to produce racemic amphetamine. Rasemic amphetamine is known commercially as benzedrine. Weinberg testified that he was paid a salary of $25 per week during the period of investigation and experiment, until

1948] 

 he perfected the technique for the manufacture of the desired product. Following a fire in claimant's home, arrangements were made with defendant to transfer the activities to defendant's plant at 7 South Street, Philadelphia. The work was done in a room set apart and used exclusively as a laboratory. Claimant's duties were to render the amphetamine into a sulphate, or salt. Claimant was paid about a dollar a pound for the sulphate at the plant; defendant furnished all the materials, ingredients and equipment. 

Thus, claimant was engaged in making amphetamine sulphate and also amphetamine in its dextro optically-active form. According to claimant, acetone was later used in the manufacture of the two products, at the direction of the defendant. The acetone expedites the drying process, but constitutes an additional fire hazard. 

The testimony reveals that in November 1946 Waldman was made defendant in an injunction suit instituted in 

Federal court by Smith, Kline and French for infringement of its patent rights in manufacturing amphetamine sulphate in tablet form. The amphetamine base is not patented. As a result of the suit, the manufacture of amphetamine hydrochloride was undertaken by defendant. The hydrochloride is chemically different from the amphetamine sulphate but very similar in its physiological effects to benzedrine, so that it could be used as an alternate. Claimant explained that he neutralized the amphetamine base with hydrochloride acid and evaporated the material to a solid. Claimant was to be paid $2 per pound for the finished product and defendant was to furnish the ingredients and the equipment. 

When claimant began the manufacture of the sulphates, he testified that defendant gave him detailed directions, telling him "exactly how much alcohol, acid and amphetamine to use to make the sulphate", as well as showing him the method of filtering. He also testified that he "continually suggested methods of working out the hydrochloride". 

Under cross-examination, claimant testified in regard to the operations carried on by him in his basement as follows:

"The addition to that of the amphetamine base, the liquid, which was usually five pounds of base. It was in a six-gallon crock. The crock was obtained at Mr. Waldman's instance. 

He showed me what he used, and the alcohol was the same alcohol that he used and the amphetamine he brought, and the sulphuric acid he bought from Arthur Henry Thomas, and I used the same dilution, dilute sulphuric acid, that he specified, and mixed it the way he suggested and filtered it the way that he suggested, and used the pumps that he brought and urged me to use."

These activities give us the background of the relationship between claimant and defendant preliminary to the events immediately preceding the accident in question. According to claimant's testimony, a number of conferences were held by claimant, defendant and defendant's counsel, Arthur 

Cowan, in February 1947 relative to the patent infringement suit. It appears that defendant's strategy was to establish the existence of a published technique for the manufacture of the sulphates in question prior to plaintiffs' patent. The article, by Jones and Wallace, was published in 1926 in the Journal of the American Chemical Society. The claimant testified: "Q. . . . I ask you at this time whether, when you, Mr.

Waldman, and Mrs. Waldman were in Mr. Cowan's office, there was any further conversation in regard to your undertaking to follow the method of producing certain chemicals in accordance with the procedure outlined in the chemical literature that Mr. Waldman had discussed with you. "A. Yes. Mr. Cowan discussed the same thing. He stressed the importance of following a procedure that he would give me and not deviating from it; to follow it in cook-book fashion. He gave me a photostatic copy and impressed upon me the fact that I follow it literally and not deviate from it, so that a chemist of my standing, comparatively unknown, would be able to achieve the same outcome or end product as a well-known chemist or Ph. D. I mean, he stated that and told me that that was one of the purposes that he wanted me to do that."

1948] 

Defendant's testimony is to the same effect. Under crossexamination, Waldman testified: "Q. . . . So, in other words, if the Jones and Wallace procedure was practical, if it worked, that could have been used very effectively in your defense by showing that since Jones and Wallace had a practical method of making amphetamine hydrochloride in 1926, the patent issued to Smith, Kline and French, which they claimed you were infringing and which was issued in 1932, was itself no good? That's right, isn't it.? “A. Well, it was not a practical method. It didn't make any difference whether it was practical or not. "Q. All right. "A. Just to prove that Jones and Wallace made the dextro amphetamine hydrochloride six years previous to when 

Smith, Kline and French obtained their patent. "Q. Then that would knock their patent out? "A. It would invalidate the whole patent. "Q. And the suit against you would have been out the window? "A. That's right. "Q. And that is why it was important to show that this process would result in amphetamine hydrochloride? "A. That's right."

Claimant was to be paid $135 per week and was to devote as much time as possible to the project, in order to have the results available for the Federal court suit. He stated that one Robert W. Henry was to assist him in his work. 

Claimant started to work on this assignment early in March 1947 in defendant's laboratory. Defendant, as before, supplied the necessary material and equipment. The accident happened on April 2, 1947, while claimant was engaged in this work. Claimant had a solution in a flask or beaker, which was being stirred by an electrically operated motor when there was a sudden blinding flash and claimant's right hand "disappeared" in that flash. The accidental origin of claimant's injuries, and the extent thereof, are not challenged. The forearm was amputated just above

the wrist. While engaged in following the Jones and Wallace technique, claimant continued the manufacture of amphetamine hydrochloride.

Claimant started his work at the laboratory, following his regular day's work at the Navy Yard and stayed as long as necessary to complete the operation upon which he was engaged at the time. Claimant admitted no deductions were made from his earnings for social security, Federal income tax or the city wage tax. He also admitted that he paid 

Henry about 19 times from September 1946 to the end of March 1947, and that he made payroll deductions from 

Henry's earnings. Weinberg stated that defendant gave him all the money which he paid Henry. Claimant testified that in preparing the defense to the patent suit, it was understood that he would testify that he was an independent contractor rather than an employe, since defendant had made no payroll deductions for him. 

Tyson Hendricks, an employe of the Pennsylvania Hospital, produced the records of the hospital which showed that claimant was a patient in the hospital from April 2, 1947, to April 12, 1947, under the surgical service of Dr. 

Stanley E. Potter. Miss Paulene Henry, called by defendant, testified in regard to a certain deposition of claimant taken in connection with the patent suit. Henry, subpoenaed by defendant, testified that he was paid by claimant and that he received instructions as to his duties from both claimant and defendant. Henry worked in the laboratory from 9:30 a. m. until relieved by claimant around 5:45 p. m. He was engaged in making hydrochloride amphetamine salt; he said he gave defendant "a hand" when requested by defendant. He worked off and on from September 1946 until the middle of March 1947, when he became ill and was confined to his home for several weeks. Henry testified: "Q. Who gave you instructions as to the grinding of salts? "A. Well, when I first got there, in grinding the salts in the mortar, Mr. Weinberg showed me; and then, after 

I had been there for sometime, Mr. Waldman showed me

1948] 

 also how to grind it into the mortar, and filtered the salts in the filter. "Q. Did Mr. Waldman-you say Mr. Waldman showed you how to filter these saltse "A. That's right. "Q. Did Mr. Waldman show you anything about how to dry salts? "A. He did." "Q. Did Mr. Waldman at any time show you how to use the filter or how to pour this sulphuric acid into the amphetamine?

The witness also testified, in answer to questions of claimant's counsel, as to the variety of duties he performed in and out of the laboratory. He listed some of the duties performed for defendant, as follows: mixing the granulation in other parts of the plant; watching the tablet machine and grinding salts. In the deposition, Henry testified that all he did was fix solution. Henry admitted that in his deposition in the patent suit, he testified: "Q. You have been in the employ of Mr. Sidney Weinberg? "A. Yes; that is right.""

However, he explained this employment was prior to the patent suit. After a period of unemployment, he returned to work in the laboratory on the hydrochloride products and, according to Henry, worked for both claimant and defendant. Defendant later testified that following the injunction suit in November 1946 the plant was closed until January 1947 and that Henry was not employed there during the shutdown period. Defendant testified in regard to his dealings with claimant, that the latter "agreed to undertake the splitting of the racemic amphetamine into its dextro form and sell it to me at the rate of fifty dollars per pound" and that defendant then processed the material further. He said he supplied claimant with the necessary ingredients and equipment. He made no payroll deductions from the payments

due claimant. Defendant testified that while claimant was working in his laboratory, defendant had no control over his activities, records or hours. Waldman denied that he employed Henry or ever paid him. A number of checks drawn by defendant to claimant, as payee, were indorsed to and cashed by Henry. Whether Henry was an employe of claimant or defendant is relatively unimportant to the issue presented. There is acceptable testimony that he worked for defendant; especially so, since his hours of employment were during the day when claimant was absent from the laboratory. Defendant stated that the studies required for the court litigation were ordered by the attorney, Cowan, to whom claimant was to make his reports. He denied that he ever gave claimant any orders in this connection. Under cross-examination, defendant denied that he had ever given to claimant any oral or written instruction in the laboratory. 

Confronted with a memorandum to Weinberg which reads: "25 lbs. amine-continue with the HCL until I get some more. By that time you will be finished with the D. See if all the Procelin is accounted for," defendant admitted that he left the note for claimant, and that he left other similar notes or memos. Throughout the several manufacturing operations, defendant admitted that all of the materials and equipment were supplied by him to claimant. He stated that claimant was very secretive in his operations and never acquainted him with the processes. Defendant further testified that he could direct claimant as to which product he desired him to manufacture and that either party could have terminated the arrangements at any time. 

The deposition of claimant reveals statements by claimant that he was not employed by defendant, but was an independant contractor and that he employed Robert Henry to assist him as occasions required. We do not consider this testimony decisive upon the question whether claimant was, in law, an independent contractor or an employe. Incidentally, the deposition had reference to the situation between claimant and defendant prior to November 20, 1946, when the patent suit was filed. Clearly, it would be absurd to hold

1948]  that an employer could escape the liabilities and responsibilities of a principal by having an employe adopt the name classification of an independent contractor. A partner cannot relieve himself of the liabilities of a partner by stating in the articles of agreement that the parties thereto are not partners; so also, the parties to a contract may use the word partnership, and yet their contract may not really make them partners. In the instant case, the admission by claimant in his deposition, that he was an independent contractor, does not, per se, make him such. Certain criteria are well established in distinguishing an employer-employe relationship from that of contractor-contractee. The general rule is stated in Smith v. State Workmen's Insurance Fund, 

262 Pa. 286 to be: "Where a person lets out work to another, the contractee reserving no control over the work or workmen, the relation of contractor and contractee exists and not that of master and servant. 

If one renders service in the course of an occupation, representing the will of his employer only as to the result of his work, and not as to the means by which it is accomplished, it is an independent employment." See 

Simonton v. Morton, 275 Pa. 562, 568.

A master, generally, provides the tools and furnishes the means by which the work is accomplished, and directs what work shall be done and the manner and direction of its performance. Each case necessarily depends upon its own particular facts. In the case of Myers v. Maurer and Myers, 144 Pa. Superior Ct. 385, the court said (p. 392): "Neither the compensation authorities nor the courts

Should be solicitous to put claimants in the position of independent contractors when a reasonable view of the evidence warrants a finding that the injured person was an employee: 

Gailey v. State Workmen's Insurance Fund, 286 Pa. 311, 133 

A. 498."

In the Gailey case, the Supreme Court held that the mere fact that claimant was paid a certain price on each ton of coal taken from the mine, instead of fixed wages, did not. necessarily deprive him of the status of an employe.

We are in accord with the referee that claimant here was an employe of defendant and not an independent contractor. 

The work was carried on for the greater period of the relationship between Weinberg and Waldman upon the latter's premises. He furnished all of the materials and equipment as well. Furthermore, at the date of the accident, claimant was engaged in an operation precisely defined by defendant, or his attorney, in the interests of the defendant. He was required to follow meticulously, "in cook book fashion", the technique prescribed in the Jones and Wallace article; there was nothing left to his discretion or initiative. The specific instructions to follow the Jones and Wallace technique, without any variation whatsoever, dictated and determined the means, manner and direction of the work to be performed.

Defendant stresses the fact that claimant is a skilled chemist, a contributor of scientific articles to journals in the field of chemistry and, therefore, it is unreasonable to believe that he would be working under the supervision and control of defendant, whose scientific training did not extend beyond a qualified apprenticeship in pharmacy. This argument is wholly without merit. Ability and experience do not necessarily depend upon formal education. In the Pittsburgh area, leaders in the steel, glass and aluminum industry, to mention only a few, are not necessarily college trained. These leaders understand the technology of the manufacture of their product and speak and understand the scientific language of the industry. They have made a life work of their job. The record convinces us that defendant is well versed in the technical aspects of the manufacture of amphetamine products, in which he has been engaged and upon which his livelihood depended. He was not depending upon claimant to initiate him in these manufacturing processes. He was the proprietor of the establishment, he determined what product was to be made, and when; he provided all the tools and materials necessary to accomplish the desired ends. At the date of the accident, claimant received a weekly wage of $135, and it is signifi-

1948] 

 cant, too, that defendant admitted that the relationship could be terminated at any time by either party. If the employment was for the purpose of accomplishing a particular purpose, and that alone was the test of the relationship, the summary discharge of the employment contract could not lawfully occur: McColligan v. P. R. R., 214 Pa. 229, 232. The legal effect here of the cumulative incidents establish and constitute an employer-employe relationship within the contemplation of the Workmen's Compensation Act. 

Although there was no testimony offered as to the reasonableness of Dr. Potter's bill in the amount of $75 and the 

Pennsylvania Hospital bill for $128.60, it is our opinion, based upon long experience and sound common sense, that both are reasonable, within the statutory period and should be paid by defendant.

The referee's first finding of fact is hereby amended by substituting $135 instead of $50 as claimant's average weekly wage at the date of the accident. We add an addi tional finding of fact as follows: 

Finding of fact 

8. Claimant was under the surgical care of Dr. Stanley 

E. Potter for amputation of the right hand and general treatment of his injuries and we find that the doctor's statement of $75 for the professional services rendered to claimant is fair and reasonable. 

As amended, the referee's findings of fact are affirmed. 

We hereby affirm the referee's conclusions of law. 

We hereby amend the referee's award by adding thereto, the following paragraph:

It is hereby ordered and directed that, defendant and/or defendant insurance carrier, pay to Dr. Stanley E. Potter, the sum of $75 for professional services rendered claimant during the first 60 days following disability.

As amended, the referee's award is affirmed. 

The appeal of defendant is dismissed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD MYERS v. H. C. FRICK COKE CO. 

Workmen's compensation-Earning power after injury-Suspension of payments-Average wage for quarterly period. 

Where, following an injury, claimant received compensation for a period following which compensation payments were suspended as a result of his return to work, his receipt of an average weekly wage for a quarter-year period equal to that of his regular wages at the time of the accident precluded additional compensation for a period of several weeks during the quarter during which period claimant did not work because of his disability as a result of the injury. 

Appeal by claimant from order of Referee Clayton, District No. 1, dismissing petition to review under compensation agreement no. 4,538,686. Affirmed. June 23, 1948.

American Mutual Liability Insurance Co., insurance carrier. 

A. F. Barbieri, for claimant. 

Frederick L. Fuges, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

Claimant, Charles A. Myers, Jr., sustained accidental injuries on October 22, 1945, during the course of his employment as a brakeman by defendant, H. C. Frick Coke 

Company. An open agreement establishes the accident. On 

October 28, 1946, defendant filed a petition for modification of compensation payments, requesting suspension of payments, as of August 11, 1946. Subsequently, the interested parties entered into a supplemental agreement, agreeing "that compensation shall be suspended until such time as his wages change, all within the meaning of the Pennsyl vania Workmen's Compensation Act." On May 19, 1947, claimant filed his petition for modification alleging that "claimant is now unable to stand on right foot and leg”.

1948] 

Defendant filed a responsive answer. Referee Foust dismissed claimant's petition and this appeal has followed. 

Claimant, in support of his petition, testified that he was off work from the early part of May until June 1947 because his leg swelled up and bothered him. He had returned to other employment by defendant on August 11, 1946. He said that he experiences constant pain in the ankle and foot. 

Defendant admits that claimant was off work from May 

7th until June 2nd, both dates inclusive, but denies that claimant is entitled to compensation for that period on the ground that his average weekly wage was in excess, or equal to his regular wages at the date of the accident. Dr. 

George W. Teagarden, claimant's witness, examined claimant's ankle at the hearing and testified: "There is a bowing forward at the junction of the lower and middle third of the tibia. That is the big bone; and the tibia at that point is prominent. In addition, there is impairment of movement of the ankle. He only has about 50% flexion and extension at the ankle." 

Examination of the right hand and right knee at the hearing according to the doctor, demonstrated about a 75 percent grip of the hand. He could not elicit any crepitation in the knee joint. Under cross-examination, the doctor stated that there was swelling of the right ankle, but he had no tape measure to make an accurate measurement. 

William J. Eichar, defendant's payroll clerk, testified as to claimant's record of earnings from February 11, 1947, to August 11, 1947. The record shows claimant had total earnings of $625.19 for 51 working days during the quarter from February 11th to May 11th, or an average weekly wage of $48.09. Myers' average weekly wage at the date of the accident was $47.93. The second 13-weeks period from May 12, 1947, to August 11, 1947, showed total earnings of $622.05 for 42 days worked by claimant, or an average weekly wage of $47.85.

It appears that claimant did not work, as he claimed, from May 7, 1947, to June 2, 1947. Assuming that absence

[84 Dep. Rep. 

was due to the injury, is claimant entitled to compensation for the time missed from work. Or does his receipt of an average weekly wage for the quarter in which the absence occurred, equal to his regular wages, preclude additional compensation and modification of the agreement? 

The Superior Court, in construing "earning power" as contained in the Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 520, said in the case of Scipani v. Pressed Steel Car Co., 150 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 410, at page 415: "The 1939 amendment refers to the actual amount of wages received regardless of the rate of pay and the lack of opportunity for employment. "We do not agree that the phrase 'the weekly amount which the employe receives' contemplates a determination each week of the right to compensation for that period. 

Section 306 (b) refers to Sec. 309; both sections are a part of Article III and the latter section provides: 'Whenever in this article the term "wages" is used, it shall be construed to mean average weekly wages' ascertained, when fixed according to output and paid semi-monthly by computing the average weekly wage during a period of three consecutive months. "The weekly amount' of wages referred to in the 1939 amendment of Sec. 306 (b) means the average weekly wages for a like period. For any three-monthperiod, beginning with the date of claimant's return to work, when compensation is not payable because of the 1939 amendment, an order of suspension of payments will be appropriate."

In view of the fact that, based upon a quarterly basis, claimant received wages equal to the wages paid him at the time of the accident, the suspension agreement should not be disturbed.

We amend the referee's disposition of the petition by including the following 

Conclusion of law

Having found that claimant received wages during the quarter in which he was off work (May 7, 1947, to June 2,

1948] 

1947, equal to wages received at the time of the accident, he is not entitled to have the order of suspension of compensation changed.

The referee's findings of fact and order of dismissal are affirmed. 

SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA LAVELY v. UNEMPLOYMENT COMPENSATION BOARD 

Unemployment compensation—Unemployment due to voluntary suspension of work in industrial dispute―Inconsistent findings by board. 

An order of the Unemployment Compensation Board of Review disallowing compensation to claimant on the ground that his unemployment was due to his voluntary suspension of work in an industrial dispute will be reversed and the record remitted to the board where separate findings of the board were inconsistent with each other, one being to the effect that suspension of work was due to an act of the employer and another to the effect that suspension was due to claimant's decision not to work.

Appeal from the decision of the Unemployment Compensation Board of Review, dated October 21, 1947, at appeal no. B-44-91-C-123. Reversed and remitted. July 23, 1948. 

Superior Court of Pennsylvania, April term, 1948, no. 119. 

H. Ray Pope, Jr., for claimant. 

Roland M. Morgan, William L. Hammond and T. McKeen 

Chidsey, for defendant.

RENO, J.: 

This appeal underscores the statement in Stillman Unem ployment Compensation Case, 161 Pa. Superior Ct. 569, 

575, 56 A. (2d) 380:

"These principles governing appellate review of the decisions of administrative agencies were largely developed in workmen's compensation cases, a comparable area of the law, and are applicable to appeals from the Unemployment 

Compensation Board of Review." 

The board found against claimant, appellant here and disqualified him for four weeks following the one-week waiting period, holding that his unemployment during that period was due to his voluntary suspension of work in an industrial dispute.

In a workmen's compensation case, Walsh v. Penn Anthracite Mining Co., 147 Pa. Superior Ct. 328, 333, 24

A. (2d) 51, where a similar procedural situation prevailed, this court said: "Where the decision of the board is against the party having the burden of proof-in this case, the claimant-bearing in mind that a trier of fact is not required to accept even uncontradicted testimony as true (District of Columbia's 

Appeal, 343 Pa. 65, 79, 21 A. 2d 883, 890) the question before the court is whether the board's findings of fact are consistent with each other and with its conclusions of law and its order, and can be sustained without a capricious disregard of the competent evidence. Unless the answer is in the negative, the order must be affirmed." The court found the findings inconsistent with each other and upon that point said, p. 334: "But in such case it is not the duty of the court to decide which findings are to govern the case, but to refer the matter back to the board to make consistent findings and appropriate conclusions of law, and to enter an order in conformity with such findings and conclusions." 

These principles control the instant case. Admittedly, there was an industrial dispute at the plant where appellant was employed, and the question presented to the board was whether appellant's unemployment was due to his own decision or to an action of the employer: Stillman Unemployment Compensation Case, supra, p. 573.

The referee's first finding of fact affirmed by the board is: "1. Claimant was last employed by Climax Fire Brick Com-

1948] 

 pany of Climax, Pa., as a brick molder, at which plant he had been employed some 52 years. His last day of work was May 1, 1947, when he was told by his foreman that there would be no more work for him until further notice." (Italics supplied.) That finding means that the suspension of work was due to an action of the employer. 

The referee's tenth finding of fact affirmed by the board is : "10. On May 5, 1947, the entrance gates were open, work was available for the men and if any had reported for work they would have been employed. After that date, the employer locked up the plant for protection but any employe really wanting to return to work could have gained admittance. None applied during the period the plant was closed." (Italics supplied.) That means that the suspension was due to the employe's decision.

These findings face both ways, and are obviously inconsistent. From other findings, which need not be reproduced verbatim, it appears that the labor union, of which appellant was a member, following the War Labor Disputes Act, had given a 30-day strike notice to the employer "which expired on May 4, 1947", and that (finding no. 7) appellant and other employes "were laid off on May 1st and 2nd, as their services were not needed in view of the plant closing two or three days later". Unless it can be said that the strike notice in itself constituted a voluntary suspension of work, this is another finding that appellant's suspension was due to the decision of his employer.

No finding definitely reconciles these contradictory viewpoints. Furthermore, there is no finding of the ultimate fact, a finding that clearly answers the question of fact before the board: Was appellant's unemployment due to his decision or to an action of the employer? The board attempted to supply the deficiency and to harmonize the findings by a conclusion of law which, since we are not bound by the labels which administrative agencies attach to their determinations, might have been reviewed as a finding of fact: 

Carville v. Bornot & Co., 288 Pa. 104, 135 Atl. 652; Wahs v. 

Wolf, 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 181, 42 A. (2d) 166. However,

it is based, as we shall show, upon a fallacy, and it cannot be approved either as a conclusion of law or a finding of fact. In short, taken as a whole, the findings of fact do not adequately respond to the factual issue. 

The board's ultimate conclusion of law and its order rest upon the legal right of one party to a contract to declare it breached upon notice from the other that he will not perform his promise. We lay to one side the debatable question whether ancient contractual and property concepts, such as anticipatory repudiation of contracts and equitable estoppel, to which reference is also made in the decision, should govern controversies arising in this new and distinctive field of the law. Nor is it necessary to decide now whether a strike notice delivered pursuant to the Smith- Connally Act is an unlawful repudiation of a contract, warranting an employer to declare that the contract of employment has been breached. The point is that the notice could not possibly have been a repudiation of an existing contract. The board affirming the referee's fourth finding, and in its own second additional finding, distinctly found that under its own terms the existing contract expired on April 30, 1947. The strike notice was therefore not a repudiation of a contract whose obligations extended beyond the period covered by the notice, and at most amounted to the announcement that upon the expiration of the existing contract it would not be renewed upon the same terms. Hence the conclusion of law, even if sound, is not based upon the findings of fact, and is inconsistent with them. 

The inconsistencies of the findings with each other, and between the findings and conclusions, require us, following the Walsh case, supra, p. 335, to reverse the decision and remit the record with instructions to review all the evidence, taking additional evidence if deemed advisable, and to formulate consistent and adequate findings on all the factual questions raised by the controversy and on the basis of those facts to draw proper conclusions of law.

The decision is reversed and the record is remitted to the board for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

1948]  

SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA VON KAENEL v. UNEMPLOYMENT COMPENSATION BOARD 

Unemployment compensation-Appeal from referee to Unemployment 

Compensation Board-Time for taking-Section 502 of the Unemployment Compensation Law.

An employer's appeal to the Unemployment Compensation Board from a referee's decision granting benefits was not in compliance with the requirements of section 502 of the act providing that a referee's decision shall be deemed the final decision of the board unless within 10 days after the date of such decision the board permits any of the parties to institute a further appeal, where it appears that the employer did not file its appeal with the board until 22 days after the time for filing the appeal had expired, although prior to the expiration date the employer addressed a letter to the board expressing a desire to take an appeal and requesting that the board furnish appropriate papers for that purpose; under the circumstances, the board erred in concluding that the latter extended the time for filing an appeal, and lacking jurisdiction to hear it on the merits, an order of the board reversing the referee and disallowing benefits will be reversed.

Appeal from the decision of the Unemployment Compensation Board of Review, no. B-13289. Reversed. July 23, 1948. Superior Court of Pennsylvania, April term, 1948, no. 123. 

Jason Richardson and William L. Sixsmith, for claimant. 

Roland M. Morgan, William L. Hammond and T. McKeen 

Chidsey, for defendant.

FINE, J.: 

Charles Von Kaenel, claimant, appeals from the decision of the Unemployment Compensation Board which concluded that he was disqualified from receiving benefits because his unemployment was due to a voluntary suspension of work resulting from an industrial dispute [section 402 (d) of the 

Unemployment Compensation Law]. The question for de-

termination is whether the employer's appeal to the board from the referee's decision granting benefits was within the statutory period and in compliance with the requirements of section 502¹. The decision of the board must be reversed. 

Appellant was employed by the Pittsburgh Motor Coach 

Company, Pittsburgh, and was a member of Local 1084 of the Amalgamated Association of Street, Electric Railway and Motor Coach Employees of America, associated with the 

American Federation of Labor. On September 24, 1946, members of a union representing the employes of the Duquesne Light Company went out on a strike, as did maintenance employes of the Equitable Auto Company which performed maintenance work for the Pittsburgh Motor Coach Company. On September 27, 1946, appellant reported for work and discovered a picket line around his employer's garage. He crossed the picket line and took his bus out on schedule, but was later informed to return his bus to the garage because of threats of violence to the bus operators. 

Appellant complied with this request and on October 10, 1946, registered for work and filed an application for benefits effective September 27, 1946. Subsequent thereto, he filed a waiting week claim for the week ending October 3, 1946, and for subsequent weeks. On October 14, 1946, the strike was settled and appellant resumed his employment. 

On December 2, 1946, the bureau disallowed appellant's claim on the ground that claimant's employment was due 

1 Section 502 provides: "Where an appeal from the determination or revised determination, as the case may be, of the department is taken, a referee shall, after affording the parties reasonable opportunity for a fair hearing, affirm, modify or reverse such findings of fact and the determination or revised determination, as the case may be, of the department as to him shall appear just and proper. The parties shall be duly notified of the referee's decision and the reasons therefore, which shall be deemed the final decision of the board, unless within ten days after the date of such decision the board acts on its own motion, or upon application, permits any of the parties to institute a further appeal before the board. A memoranda of testimony of any hearing before any referee, shall be made and be preserved for a period of two years, as amended 1942, Ex. Sess., April 23, P. L. 60, sec. 5." (43 PS §822.)

1948]  to a voluntary suspension of work resulting from an industrial dispute and applied the disqualification provided by section 402 (d). On December 12, 1946, claimant appealed to the referee who, by decision of May 15, 1947, reversed the bureau and awarded benefits. On June 16, 1947, 22 days after the time for appeal had expired, the employer filed its appeal with the board. Thereupon a hearing was scheduled and held by the board, the notice of which set forth the issues involved as "Is claimant's unemployment due to voluntary suspension of work resulting from an industrial dispute within the meaning of section 402 (d) of the law? 

Has appellant filed a proper appeal from the decision of the referee within the meaning of section 502 of the law?" At that hearing counsel for the employer, duly sworn, testified that a letter was mailed to the Pennsylvania State Employment Service Office, Pittsburgh, Pa., on May 20, 1946, a copy of which was admitted in evidence, all without claimant's objection. The letter stated, inter alia: "We have received a copy of the referee's decision in the above entitled matter and it is our desire to take an appeal from that decision. Will you please furnish us with appropriate papers for this purpose. The entire testimony of counsel concerning the mailing is very brief, as follows: "By Mr. Fee to Attorney Anderson: Q. After you had prepared the letter of May 20, 1947, what did you do in order to have it go out? A. It was sent through our regular mail service. We have an office boy to put the letters in the mail. Q. You put it in the proper place to be picked up? 

A. I did. Q. Was the letter returned to your office? A. It was not. We made a search and there is no record that it was not mailed. The original letter is not in the office." 

A continued hearing was held on September 10, 1947, notice of which set forth the same issues as the previous notice. At the second hearing no testimony was taken on the validity of the appeal whereupon the parties proceeded to the merits of the case. The board by a decision dated October 16, 1947, reversed the referee, made no specific finding on the validity of the appeal and disallowed benefits. It is this

appeal by the employer to the board from the referee's decision which is the subject of the present controversy. 

Suffice it to say that the employer has not complied with the statutory requirement that an appeal be taken within 10 days from the decision of the referee. That statutory requirement is mandatory and cannot be waived by agreement: Devlin v. Grabler Mfg. Corp., 151 Pa. Superior Ct. 

216, 30 A. (2d) 138. It was incumbent upon the employer to meet the burden cast upon it of showing conduct emanating from the officers charged with administering the unemployment compensation law which misled the employer to his detriment: Tuttle Unemployment Compensation Case, 

160 Pa. Superior Ct. 46, 49 A. (2d) 847; Turner v. Unem ployment Compensation Board of Review, 163 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 168, A. (2d). Cf. Layton v. Unemployment Compensation Board of Review, 156 Pa. Superior Ct. 225, 40 

A. (2d) 125.

The burden was upon the employer to show facts which would place it within the principle that where a party has been prevented from doing an act through fraud or its equivalent, i. e., ignorance or negligent acts of an administrative official, power exists to allow an appeal nunc pro tunc if prosecuted within a reasonable time. The employer attempted to meet this burden by introducing into evidence the letter hereinabove recited. The compensation authorities have no record of receipt of that letter; nor is there satisfactory proof it was mailed; all the evidence thereon is negative. It is clear that the letter was not an appeal nor was it intended to serve as an appeal. It merely evidenced a present desire or intent to take an appeal which could either be perfected or abandoned before the expiration of the appeal period. Assuming that the letter was sent requesting forms of appeal, the employer could not thus so easily shed its burden of effecting a timely appeal; it should have pursued its request with alacrity and diligence. Moreover, it was not necessary for it to use the forms provided by the compensation authorities. Nor can the responsibility for the lateness of the appeal be shifted to the administrative agency, particularly where, as here, employer's counsel, ex-

1948] 

 perienced in the law, gave only passing attention to an expiring right.

The employer, instead of perfecting its appeal within the 10-day period as it should have done, waited until June 10, 1947, before making further inquiry. The delay was fatal in these circumstances. The board erred in concluding the letter of May 20, 1947, extended the time for filing the appeal and in permitting the appeal to be in effect filed nunc pro tunc. In Turner v. Unemployment Compensation Board of Review, supra, the board refused to entertain an appeal not filed within the 10-day limitation because the limitation provision is mandatory and it was without power to waive the provision except in circumstances not present there, and likewise absent here. If illness of counsel in the Turner case could not be excusatory of delay, surely the inattention of counsel in the present case cannot be successfully maintained in support of an appeal nunc pro tunc. 

True, section 501 (e) was involved in the Turner case, whereas in the present controversy section 502 of the act is the pertinent provision. There is a variance in the verbiage of the two sections and in the scope and purpose thereof, yet the reason for the rule of timely appeal is identical. 

The fact that claimant made no objection to the validity of the appeal at the hearings before the board is of no moment. Want of jurisdiction over the subject matter may be questioned for the first time on appeal: Patterson's Estate, 341 Pa. 177, 180, 19 A. (2d) 665. Claimant's silence could not confer jurisdiction, already lost to the board. Had he so desired, an agreement by him to contest the case on the merits could not breathe life into the expired power to hear and determine. Nor could the board, as here occurred, waive or dispense with the commands of the statute: In 

Devlin v. Crabler Mfg. Corp., 151 Pa. Superior Ct. 216, 30 

A. (2d) 138, we said: "We find no authority to the effect that the stipulation which was filed after the time for taking the appeal by claimant had expired could be a substitute for an appeal, or

[34 Dep. Rep.

· · 

It is the that it could act as an appeal nunc pro tunc. general rule that statutes requiring appeals to be taken and perfected within a certain time are mandatory and jurisdictional, and that the time cannot be extended by agreement or stipulation. 3 C. J. §1083, p. 1074; 4 C. J. S., Appeal and Error, §458."

The board lacked jurisdiction to hear the appeal on the merits and committed error in so doing. 

The decision of the board is reversed; the award of the referee is reinstated. 

SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA CRINER v. MCKEE GLASS COMPANY et al. 

Workmen's compensation 

Loss of eye Double vision 

Finding by board.

An award of compensation for the permanent loss of use of an eye will be affirmed where it appears that claimant so long as he had the use of his normal right eye was practically blind in the left eye as a result of his injury; the fact that the left eye could be corrected by lenses to provide claimant with normal vision in the event he lost the sight of his right eye but that the correction could not be made so that he could use his two eyes together did not affect the board's finding of loss of vision of the left eye for all practical intents and purposes.

Appeal from the decree of the Court of Common Pleas of 

Westmoreland County, February term, 1947, no. 250. Affirmed. July 23, 1948. Superior Court of Pennsylvania, April term, 1948, no. 101. 

Robert M. Carson, for claimant. 

Harold A. Stewart and H. Reginald Belden, for defendants.

1948] 

Ross, J.:

This is an appeal from an award of workmen's compensation for the permanent loss of use of an eye. 

Claimant, Joseph Criner, suffered an injury to his left eye on September 28, 1941, in the course of his employment with the McKee Glass Company. A traumatic cataract developed and an operation was performed for the removal of the cataract. After a hearing on claimant's petition for compensation for the injury to his left eye, the referee found as a fact that "as the end result of his injury and accident of September 28, 1941, claimant has lost the vision of his left eye for all practical intents and purposes" and awarded compensation for 125 weeks under section 306 (c) of our Workmen's Compensation Act for the permanent loss of use of the eye. The referee's findings of fact and the award were affirmed by the board, the employer's exceptions thereto were dismissed by the Court of Common Pleas of Westmoreland County, and this appeal was taken. 

The Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 520, 77 PS §513, was in force when claimant was injured. In Diaz v. Jones & Laughlin Steel Corp., 155 Pa. Superior Ct. 177, 38 A. (2d) 387, speaking through President Judge Keller, we said at page 183: "The amendment of June 4, 1937, P. L. 1552, had changed the Workmen's Compensation Act of 1915, P. L. 736, by providing that permanent loss of the use of an eye for industrial purposes should be considered as the equivalent of the permanent loss of the eye. But the Act of 1939, P. L. 520, which governs this case, struck out the words 'for industrial purposes', and restored the clause, in that respect, to the language of the original act, which had been correctly interpreted by Judge Horace Stern (now a Justice of the Supreme Court) when he was on the common pleas bench, to mean, not the permanent loss of the use of the eye for industrial purposes, but the permanent loss of its use for all practical intents and purposes." 

Cf. Wildman v. Pa. Dept. of Highways, 157 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 301, 43 A. (2d) 342. Consequently, in the instant case,

as in the Diaz and Wildman cases, the question before the compensation authorities was whether claimant had permanently lost the use of his left eye for "all practical intents and purposes", and they resolved this question in claimant's favor.

A medical witness for claimant, Dr. Curry, who had made an examination of claimant on June 21, 1945, testified that claimant has "vision amounting to only hand movements at a distance of six or eight inches, and that is most essentially loss of vision in that eye". He testified further as follows: "Q. Did your examination indicate whether by further operation the eye could be helped? A. I do not believe that any further operation would benefit him. Q. Is there any other method or procedure or treatment that could aid the eyesight in this particular left eye? A. No. . . . Q. Will time in any way aid or heal the present condition of that eye, doctor? A. It will not help it. Q. Doctor, what is his vision with a corrective lens if you tested it? A. Oh, it is practically nil-it amounts only to counting fingers. with corrective lenses what vision was present in accordance with Snellen's Chart? A. He had 4/200 with the correction. 

Q. What vision did he have without this corrective lens?

A. Counting movements, or distinguishing hand movements at a distance of six or eight inches. Q. what vision is that, according to Snellen's Chart? A. Practically none. 

what is your opinion with respect to whether or not that man has loss of vision in this injured eye for all practical purposes? A. He has lost it. Q. And is or is not the condition permanent? A. It is permanent."

Dr. McCaslin, an impartial medical expert called by the referee, after testifying that the vision in claimant's eye is 2/200 and that "the injury has reduced this man to one of monocular vision with the corresponding restriction of the field of vision which is characteristic of a monocular seeing person. It is impossible to develop with corrective lenses or other appliances binocular single vision", testified further: "Q. You say the vision in this eye, uncorrected is 2/200, but with a plus 12 sphere vision will be improved to 20/30? 

A. That's right. Q. Well, you say, doctor, it is impossible to

1948] 

... develop with corrective lenses or other appliances binocular single vision? A. That's right. Q. Then we would assume that his vision in reality is not correctible-we must assume that the vision in this eye you say can not be corrected with a lens? A. We can not develop binocular single vision—in other words he cannot use his two eyes together—with a len's on that eye he would see double. In other words, he has what is commonly classified as a reserve eye? A. That's right. 

Q. And how much reserve vision does he have? A. 2/200 if he has no aid to vision. . . . Q. . . . Now, how shall I classify your answer as to whether he has vision for all intents and purposes-do you think he has? A. He does not. 

Q. And this eye, as I understand your testimony, is not serving him to any extent now, but if he loses the good eye it will come back and give him some use and help him to carry on? A. If he loses the right eye he would be in about the same situation he is now he would have to repair the left and would not have the use of the right. . . . Q. . . . do you classify the present condition in this eye as being permanent? 

Is there some medical procedure that can make this eye more useful to the man? A. His condition as existing at the present time will stay that way."

Dr. Kutscher, who removed the cataract from claimant's eye, was called as a witness by the employer and after stating that claimant "has a reserve left eye" testified: "Q. You say if he wore glasses he would have what you term industrial vision? A. Yes, but he would have to wear a glass to have industrial vision. Q. Did you recommend him to do that? A. He should not wear a glass over his left eye because if he does he will have the likelihood of double vision-they all have double vision. Q. What do you mean by double vision? A. He would see one image with his right eye and he would see the same image with his left eye, but with the left eye the image would be small and it would be at a different place in space than the image with the right eye. 

Q. What do you mean when you say he has a reserve left eye, doctor? A. Well, if he should lose his right eye by virtue of some disease or injury, then he could have a • •

lens for his left eye that would allow him to see full normal. 

Q. Doctor, you say this man has a reserve eye? A. Yes. 

Q. Please tell us what reserve vision there is remaining in that eye? A. Without a lens? Q. Without a lens, yes, doctor.

A. Without a lens the vision would be about 3/200." 

It seems clear from the testimony of all the doctors that claimant, so long as he has the use of his undamaged and normal right eye, is practically blind in his left eye. However, defendant contends that the testimony shows claimant's left eye to be a "reserve eye" and, therefore, under the authority of Massett v. Armerford Coal M. Co., 82 Pa. Su perior Ct. 579, he cannot recover for the permanent loss of its use. 66 Defendant's contention would be sound-assuming that the compensation authorities found that he had a so-called reserve eye-if the law of the Massett case were still the law of this Commonwealth. However, it was decided before the amendment of 1939 and its construction by this court in Diaz v. Jones & Laughlin Steel Corporation, 155 Pa. Su perior Ct. 177, 38 A. (2d) 387, supra, and Wildman v. Pa. 

Dept. of Highways, 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 301, 43 A. (2d) 

342, supra. In the Diaz case, Judge Keller, who also had written the opinion in the Massett case, stated at page 183: . . counsel for the employer also persisted in asking the witnesses, as bearing on the permanent loss of the use of the left eye, whether claimant had sufficient vision in the left eye, prior to 1941, to do industrial work and paint, if he had no vision in the right eye. That was not the criterion. 

The standard was not, whether, before the accident in 1941, with the right eye gone, he could see sufficiently with the left eye to do his work as a painter; but, whether using both eyes he had better general vision than he would have with only the right eye. In other words, could he see better, in general, using the left eye in connection with his good right eye than by using the right eye alone? If he could, he had not lost the use of his left eye to such an extent as to be considered the equivalent of the permanent loss of the eye." 

Consequently, the Massett case was overruled at least inferentially-by the Diaz case.

1948] 

In this case, claimant with or without a corrective lens over his injured eye has no better vision than if he used his uninjured eye alone; he cannot use his eyes together, lens or no lens.

The finding of fact of the compensation authorities that claimant has "lost the vision of his left eye for all practical intents and purposes" is supported by evidence of the required quality and quantity. 

Judgment affirmed.

SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA MOORE v. HUNT MINING CO. et al. 

Workmen's compensation-Death-Coal miner-Violation of law- 

Finding by board.

Judgment for an award of compensation based on a finding by the board that decedent coal miner was not violating the law or positive orders of his employer at the time of the accident resulting in his death will be affirmed where there was competent and substantial evidence to sustain the board's finding that decedent at the time of the accident was not riding a coal car as defendant claimed; the burden of proving decedent's violation of law rested upon the defendant. 

Appeal from the judgment of the Court of Common Pleas of Lackawanna County, September term, 1947, no. 1680. 

Affirmed. July 23, 1948. Superior Court of Pennsylvania, February term, 1948, no. 18. 

L. D. Savige, for claimant. 

Nathan Hyman, Paul R. Orrson and Ernest D. Preate, for defendants.

FINE, J.: 

Frank Moore died June 25, 1945, as a result of injuries sustained in the employ of the Hunt Mining Company, appellant. Bessie M. Moore, his widow, filed a claim petition to which appellant filed an answer asserting that Moore, at the time he sustained the fatal injuries, was violating Rule 16 of the Anthratice Mining Law¹ as well as specific instructions of appellant not to ride the mine cars, which conduct barred recovery of compensation. The board affirmed the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and allowed compensation. The court below affirmed the action of the board and entered judgment on the award from which Hunt Mining Company and its insurance carrier appealed.
