Frank Moore, on the morning of June 22, 1945, at about 8:15 a.m., was engaged in the performance of his duties of supplying miners with empty cars and removing loaded cars from employer's mine to the outside. Leroy Walters, the only fellow-employe to witness the accident, was approximately 40 to 50 feet away from Moore at the time of the occurrence. He described the accident as follows: deceased was standing between two sets of cars on parallel tracks, one set was loaded with coal and the other was empty; Moore put his right foot on the bumper of the first car of the loaded trip and his left foot on the rope; that he was adjusting the clevice to untwist the rope when the rope suddenly jerked, whereupon Moore, lost his balance, fell over on the opposite side of the cars and was dragged approximately 10 feet. Walters immediately stopped the trip of cars and called the foreman who had Moore removed to the Mid-Valley Hospital. The referee found as a fact that "decedent at the time of the accident, which resulted in his death, was not riding the car or rope, but was straightening out the rope, and that decedent was not killed as a result of violation of the mining laws or of positive orders." The 

1 Rule 16 of the Anthracite Mining Law (Act of 1891, P. L. 176, 52 PS §287) provides: "No person shall ride upon or against any loaded car, cage or gunboat in any shaft, slope or plane in or about a mine or colliery."

1948] 

 board in affirming this finding stated: "The weight of the credible evidence negatives any violation of law or violation of positive orders by the decedent."

At the time of the accident Moore was either assembling a trip of loaded cars or supervising the movement of a trip already assembled, across no. 3 heading or level to the foot or bottom of no. 2 slope or plane, where in accordance with the usual practice it would be stopped preparatory to its ascent 1,200 to 1,400 feet up the said slope. The employe would then ascend the slope afoot and inform the engineer on no. 2 heading to hoist the trip as "everything is in the clear." The testimony of Walters is abundantly clear on the transportation practices: "Q. So if a man were carrying on the job of transportation man in the ordinary and regular manner of doing that he would couple the cars and attach the rope and walk up for three minutes and eight seconds? "A. Yes sir. . . 

"Q. He didn't walk up three minutes and eight seconds at the time of the accident, did he? "A. He didn't have a chance to. It was our practice in the mines to pull these cars up past the no. 3 engine in the mines where we had a head-block there and put the headblock over on the rail while the trip was standing there, go past the trip and walk up to the second engine and tell him the engine was okay to pull on up and from there on. "Q. Mr. Walters it wasn't done at the time of the accident because obviously from your testimony he gave the bell at the bottom of the trip, didn't he? "A. We always did that. "Q. What did you do, walk ahead or walk behind? "A. Stay right there until the cars are moved approximately 50 feet, stop the trip and put a head-block on so the cars can't come back, and walk past the cars and walk clear out, three minutes and eight seconds and tell the engineer to go ahead and pull it, everything is in the clear."

Appellants contend that violation of Rule 16 of the Anthracite Mining Law, supra, and deceased's conduct in direct hostility to specific instructions and in defiance of positive

orders of the employer not to ride loaded mine cars, so clearly appear that this court should declare as a matter of law that deceased had thereby removed himself from the course of his employment: Kirker v. W. M. McIntosh Co., 156 Pa. Superior Ct. 199, 39 A. (2d) 846. The Kirker case is easily distinguishable upon the facts and is not controlling. Cf. Soroka v. Philadelphia & Reading Coal & Iron Co., 138 Pa. Superior Ct. 296, 10 A. (2d) 904; Palla v. Glen Alden 

Coal Co., 105 Pa. Superior Ct. 96, 160 Atl. 157. To accept appellants' contention that the deceased was on the car presumably for his own convenience and to avoid walking the incline, we must reject all consideration of the usual practices of the employment, must discard as meaningless the reputation of the deceased as a careful workman and must assume not only that the deceased acted contrary to his usual conduct but that he violated the law and positive orders of his employer in which he was apparently joined to an extent by no. 2 engineman. The latter hoisted cars on the plane only after told to do so by the transportation man after he had ascended the slope; he did not start the ascent of cars on bell signal, as appellants here theorize. It seems illogical to assume Moore boarded the moving car to ride a short distance across no. 3 heading; rather, it is to be concluded, as testified by Walters, that he was on the front bumper, not for his own convenience, but pursuant to the usual practice and in the performance of his duties, for the purpose of straightening the twisted rope by adjusting the clevice with which it was attached to the front car of the trip. "Q. Is it the duty of the transportation man having hooked this rope on to the clevice of the loaded car to give the bells, two or four, whatever is required, and then watch that the hook doesn't fly out or the rope get snagged along the road? "A. Yes, sir. "Q. He should be near the head of the trip where he can keep that hook engaged in the clevice? "A. Yes, sir.

1948] 

"Q. And so far as you could see was Mr. Moore doing the right thing, the proper practice, in watching that the hook was in the clevice of the loaded car? "A. Yes, sir, Mr. Moore was very careful. 

"By the Referee: 

"Q. You said that he put his right foot on the bumper of the first car and his left foot on the rope. Was that the proper thing to do? "A. Well, Mr. Referee, as I see it, there may have been something wrong with the rope, the clevice gets twisted, and if you kick or push it, it will straighten itself out. I have done it myself several times, push that clevice around so it is straight, pull straight.”

When Walters was asked by the referee how he, as a transportation man, adjusted the twisted rope he replied: "While the cars were in motion, the same as Mr. Moore did." 

There is competent and substantial evidence to sustain the factual findings that Moore, at the time of the accident, was not violating the Anthracite Mining Law or positive orders of his employer. The testimony of Walters amply sustains the findings of the compensation authorities which will not be disturbed on appeal: Dunkle v. Baltimore & 

Ohio Railroad Co., 162 Pa. Superior Ct. 340, 57 A. (2d) 

714. Moreover, there was testimony that straightening the twisted rope or cable in such a manner is not unusual. 

There was no evidence of prior violations by Moore of either the law or any positive orders, nor that by so acting he was motivated by a desire to serve his own convenience. 

Deceased was doing what he was required to do-to make certain the cable was properly fastened so that the cars might be drawn up the slope.2 "Neither the lower court nor an appellate court can say that the board must find one way or another. Although it may feel that the weight of the evidence, as a whole, is against the finding of fact so made, it may not disturb that finding if it is supported by sufficient legally competent evidence: Hanlon v. Gulf Refining Co. et al., 115 Pa. 

2 Cf. Barkanich v. Jeddo-Highland Coal Co., 105 Pa. Superior Ct. 

145, 160 Atl. 137.

Superior Ct. 315, 317, 175 A. 724, 725. There can be no interference by the courts with such findings, whether they be based on proved facts or inferences therefrom. Flucker v. Carnegie Steel Co., 263 Pa. 113, 119, 106 A. 192, 194”: 

Paulin v. Williams & Co., 122 Pa. Superior Ct. 462, 466, 186 Atl. 415, affirmed in 327 Pa. 579, 583, 195 Atl. 40. The record does not so clearly establish that deceased was violating the law or a positive order of his employer to deny claimant compensation. As the board's findings are sustained by the evidence it was solely within their power to determine which of contrary inferences, fairly deducible from the basic facts found, they should adopt. Our revisory powers are limited to the ascertainment whether the findings are supported by evidence and if, upon such findings, the law has been properly applied. We may not alter the board's conclusions solely because we might well have concluded otherwise; Price v. Glen Alden Coal Co., 100 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 260; Labuck v. Mill Creek Coal Co., 292 Pa. 

284, 287, 141 Atl. 35; Stahl v. Watson Coal Co., 268 Pa. 

452, 454, 112 Atl. 14. Cf. Kolonik v. Hudson Coal Co., 160 

Pa. Superior Ct. 491, 493, 52 A. (2d) 384.

Section 301 of the Workmen's Compensation Act, as amended June 21, 1939, P. L. 520, 77 PS §431, provides "that no compensation shall be paid when the injury or death . . . is caused by the employe's violation of law, but the burden of proof of such fact shall be upon the employer." 

Likewise, where the employer suggests a violation of positive orders as the cause of the accident, the suggestion is of no effect unless the employer meets the burden of proving it: Hopwood v. Pittsburgh, 152 Pa. Superior Ct. 398, 33 

A. (2d) 658; Kolonik v. Hudson Coal Co., 160 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 491, 52 A. (2d) 384. Appellants have not met their burden with requisite proof of a violation of law or of a breach of positive orders or specific instructions of the employer.

It is unnecessary to pass upon the correctness of the admission, as res gestæ, of the statements made by deceased to appellee at the Mid-Valley Hospital approximately two

1948] 

 hours after the accident. The challenged testimony 3 we deem immaterial, for, ignoring it completely, the remaining evidence is sufficient to sustain the finding that the fatal injuries were the result of an accident sustained while in the course of employment. 

Judgment affirmed. 

3 The testimony admitted over objection reads as follows: "Q. Will you tell just what was the first thing your husband said to you about this accident? "A. Well I went in and he had his eyes closed and I walked up to him and said 'Dad what happened' and he looked up and said 'I guess they got me this time'. I said 'what happened to you' and he said 'there was a trip of cars off and I went up and got them on and gave the fellow the bell and it wouldn't start up, and then when they did start the cars the trip struck [me]."

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD COVELY v. READING AUTO ELECTRIC CO. 

Workmen's compensation-Partial disability—Sufficiency of evidence. 

A referee's order disallowing compensation for the death of claimant's minor son based on her claim of partial dependency will be reversed where it appears that decedent contributed an average of $10 a week to his parents and that his father's income in addition to that of other relatives who resided with the family did not equal the family expenses; the fact that claimant's other relatives did not pay a sufficient sum for their board and upkeep so that if claimant, her husband and decedent were living alone they would not have needed any contribution from decedent did not rebut the statutory presumption placed upon defendant by decedent's admitted contribution. 

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Graybill, District No. 4. Appeal sustained. July 21, 1948. 

Elliott B. Goldstan, for claimant. 

Allan K. Grim, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This case comes before the Workmen's Compensation Board upon an appeal by Mrs. Agnes E. Covely, claimant, from an order of disallowance filed by the referee for compensation for the death of her minor son, Clarence Covely. 

Decedent, Clarence Covely, aged 19, sustained fatal injuries on June 20, 1947, when an accidental explosion of an alcohol blow torch occurred, setting fire to his body, during the course of his employment.

The sole question before us is whether claimant was partially dependent on decedent.

The Workmen's Compensation Act, as amended May 18, 1945, P. L. 671, provides that in the case of a minor child who has been contributing to his parents, the dependency of such parents shall be presumed. In the instant case, the testimony clearly shows that decedent contributed upon an average of $10 per week to his parents. 

The burden thereupon shifted to defendant to rebut the statutory presumption.

It appears from the record that the family consisted of decedent, his parents, decedent's brother, Joseph, Jr., and his wife; a younger brother, Thomas, and claimant's widowed brother, Earl Frantz and his minor child. Claimant's husband earned around $2,900 net, the year prior to his son's death. Clarence contributed about $500, Joseph, Jr., who had been in the service, contributed about $400 for the year, and the elder Frantz paid $960 for himself and his boy, making a total income of about $4,760 for the year. 

According to claimant's Exhibit No. 2, which itemized expenses, there was an outlay of $5,140 for the year. The expenses listed thereon were not seriously questioned by defendant, the only contention being made that claimant's other relatives were not paying sufficient for their board and upkeep, that were claimant, her husband and minor son, Thomas, living alone, they would not have needed any contribution from decedent.

We feel bound to accept conditions as we find them. We cannot eliminate members of the household or change the

1948] 

 constituency thereof because they do not pay sufficient rent or board. Under the facts as presented, claimant was partially dependent on decedent as a matter of fact, and we so find. Nor do we believe that defendant was able to rebut the statutory presumption placed upon it in law: See Conroy v. Loew's Inc., 102 Pa. Superior Ct. 523; Kelly v. Hudson Coal Co., 119 Superior Ct. 405.

We vacate the referee's eighth finding of fact, second conclusion of law and order of disallowance, substituting and adding the following 

Findings of fact 

8. The Workmen's Compensation Board finds as a fact that the expenses of decedent's family exceeded their total income for the year preceding his death. 

10. The Workmen's Compensation Board finds as a fact that claimant was partially dependent upon him at the time of his death.

 2. The Workmen's Compensation Board concludes as a matter of law that defendant failed to rebut the presumption of dependency placed upon it by law. 

3. The Workmen's Compensation Board concludes as a matter of law that claimant is entitled to compensation for partial dependency. Award

The Workmen's Compensation Board hereby directs that 

Reading Auto Electric Co., defendant, pay to Mrs. Agnes E.

Covely, claimant, the sum of $6 per week beginning June 

20, 1947, and continuing for a period of 300 weeks, all within the limitations and intendment of the Workmen's 

Compensation Act, as amended.

This award shall bear interest at the rate of six percent per annum.

The balance of the referee's findings of fact and conclusions of law are affirmed. 

Claimant's appeal is sustained.

SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA ANGERHOFER v. UNEMPLOYMENT COMPENSATION BOARD 

Unemployment compensation-Voluntarily quitting work-Demand for double wages for operating with smaller crew. 

An order of the Unemployment Compensation Board of Review disallowing compensation on the ground that claimant voluntarily quit work without good cause within the meaning of section 402(b) of the Unemployment Compensation Law of December 5, 1936, P. L. 

(1937) 2897, as amended, will be affirmed where claimant's sole reason for quitting was the refusal of his employer to pay him double wages on account of extra work required by the fact that he operated two spinning machines with his fellow employes as a fourman crew instead of a five-man crew when one of the members was temporarily transferred, it appearing that claimant was not asked to do more work than his fellow employes and that he was not required to work any extra hours. 

Appeal from the decision of the Unemployment Compensation Board of Review dated June 9, 1947, appeal no. 

B44-99-B1598, decision no. B9944. Affirmed. July 23, 1948. 

Superior Court of Pennsylvania, October term, 1947, no. 230. 

William Vincent Mullin, for claimant. 

Richard H. Wagner, William L. Hammond and T. McKeen 

Chidsey, for defendant. 

Ross, J.:

This is an appeal by claimant, Edward Angerhofer, from a decision of the Unemployment Compensation Board of Review disallowing compensation on the ground that claimant voluntarily quit work without good cause within the meaning of section 402(b) of the Unemployment Compensation Law of December 5, 1936, P. L. (1937) 2897, as amended, 43 PS §802, which provides that an employe shall be ineligible for compensation for any week "in which his

1948] 

 unemployment is due to voluntarily leaving work without good cause".1

Claimant was employed as a "piecer" at approximately 

95 cents an hour for a 44-hour week. The work of a "piecer" consists of tending a spinning machine, called a "mule", which pulls the yarn from a frame, twists it and wraps it around cones, spindles or spools. The "piecer" removes the cones or spindles as they become filled, replenishes the mule with the yarn and pieces the yarn whenever it breaks. Claimant was a member of a five-man crew operating two spinning machines and, to replace a sick employe in another department, one of the members of this crew was temporarily transferred and for about three weeks the crew operated as a four-man unit. At the end of this three-week period claimant, contending that he was doing "two men's work", quit his employment with Sykes Brothers,

Inc., in Philadelphia because the employer refused to pay him for "two men's work", or double wages.

The referee in disallowing compensation made, inter alia, the following finding of fact: "2. Claimant was a piecer in a spinning mill and on occasions, when a fellow employe was absent, was requested to help to do the work of the person remaining away from work, along with the rest of the men who were present. Claimant felt that he was performing the work of two men and asked his employer to pay him for the work of two men. The employer explained the situation to claimant but claimant, nevertheless, walked off the job and did not return thereafter."

The board of review affirmed the referee's findings and made the following additional finding: "Claimant was not 

1 For able and comprehensive discussion of "good cause" see

Sturdevant Unemployment Compensation Case, 158 Pa. Superior Ct. 

548, 45 A. (2d) 898. 

2 Sykes testified: "The superintendent came in and told me that this man insisted that he was doing two men's work and he wanted two men's wages. I said to bring him down and I would talk to him. 

He came into the office and I explained to him that he was not entitled to it; that he was not doing two men's work and naturally we would not pay him for two men's work; that no one ever got paid when someone else was out and all pitched in."

required to do the work of two men but was expected to join with the rest of the crew to keep the machines operating when any of the crew members were absent. Claimant was paid on an hourly basis for the time actually worked and was not asked to do more work than his fellow employes. . . . 

Claimant's sole complaint-his only reason for quitting according to his own testimony ("I refused to work unless I got paid for two men's work")—was the refusal of his employer to pay him double wages. This complaint was based upon his contention that he was doing the work of two men a strictly factual question found against him by the triers of fact.

The board's findings of fact are supported by evidence that is real and substantial and are binding upon us: Un employment Compensation Law of December 5, 1936, P. L. 

(1937) 2897, sec. 510, 43 PS §830; D'Yantone v. Unem ployment Compensation Board of Review, 159 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 15, 46 A. (2d) 525.

It is in evidence that claimant "was not doing two men's work; he was not even doing his own; he would not help when someone was out"; and that claimant "was not doing his share of the work". According to the testimony, it was the custom of the shop observed by all who work there that "if one person is absent, everyone gets together and gets the work out". It is in evidence that if one of the five-man unit was absent, the others "might do a little more than they would if the other man were there" but that neither claimant "nor anyone else can do two men's work. The production suffers because of it", and that none of the other men objected to the "so called extra work" and that none of them asked for double wages. There is no evidence in the record that there was any change in claimant's working conditions that would justify his demand for double wages or even increased remuneration and he was not required to work any "extra hours".

Claimant for the first time now argues that he quit work because to continue in his employment would cause him to violate an agreement between the employer and the plant

1948] 

 union. This obviously is an afterthought, specious and without merit. There is no evidence in the record to show the breach of any agreement or to show that claimant in any way relied upon any agreement as a basis for his demand for double wages or as a reason for quitting. In fact, his own testimony shows that he quarreled with the officers of the union because they would not support him in his demand for "two men's pay".

The record clearly supports the decision of the board denying compensation on the ground that claimant voluntarily quit his employment without good cause. 

Decision affirmed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD GEARHART v. SUMMIT FAST FREIGHT, INC. 

Workmen's compensation-Employe or independent contractor- 

Owner driver of truck-Contract to transport steel. 

A claim for compensation arising from the death of claimant's husband was properly disallowed by the referee on the ground that the relationship between decedent and defendant at the time of the accident which resulted in decedent's death was that of an independent contractor and not that of employer and employe, where it appeared that decedent and defendant had entered into a written contract whereby decedent was to transport steel from a certain place in Pennsylvania to various points outside the State designated by the defendant, the contract further providing that the relationship between the parties was that of independent contractor, that the contractor should keep his equipment in first class repair and condition at his own expense, that the decedent would provide workmen's compensation coverage for his employes, and pay social security taxes, that he could take any route available under the defendant's ICC permit, and where it further appeared that decedent was not bound to transport for defendant exclusively, but in fact did some hauling for other freight lines.

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Carmalt, District No. 8, claim petition no. 108,468, accident no. 

4,972,976. Affirmed August 4, 1948.

Globe Indemnity Company, insurance carrier. 

John E. Evans, for plaintiff. 

John T. Conner, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This is a death case which comes before the Workmen's 

Compensation Board upon an appeal by Mrs. Beatrice G. 

Gearhart, claimant and widow of Norman D. Gearhart, deceased, from a decision by the referee disallowing any compensation.

There is little or no dispute as to the essential facts. It appears that on December 4, 1946, claimant's deceased sustained a fatal injury during the course of his employment with defendant, Summit Fast Freight, Inc., while driving his trailer-tractor near Bryan, Ohio. Gearhart had a written agreement with defendant to transport steel from Beaver Falls, Pa., to various points outside the State designated by defendant. Defendant had arrangements with other trailer-tractor owners similar to that entered into with decedent. Defendant also owned a number of trucks for which it employed drivers. Upon delivery of the load the driver-owned trucks were to be paid 75 percent of the freight rates charged. From this amount the owner, in this case decedent, paid for gas, oil and all repairs or expenses to the truck and for any employe or driver whom he might hire. 

Decedent was permitted to take any route that he wished to his destination as long as he took a route for which defendant had a permit from the Interstate Commerce Commission. Defendant carried public liability insurance, not only on its own trucks but on those owned by the individual owners.

1948] 

In the instant case decedent and defendant had entered into a written contract which provided, inter alia, that the relationship between the parties was that of independent contractor and not that of employer and employe; that the contractor should keep his equipment in first class repair and condition at his own expense; that he would furnish license plates and all registration certificates required for said equipment by the State of his residence; that said equipment would be operated at his expense by himself or by competent employes in a careful manner; that the first party to the contract, namely, the Summit Fast Freight,

Inc., should not be responsible for any fines or penalties which might be assessed against the second party (decedent) or against his employes by reason of any violation of law by him or them. Further terms of the contract provided that decedent would not display the certificate numbers or name of the Summit Fast Freight, Inc., on his equipment when it was not being used in the transportation service of the freight company; that decedent would provide workmen's compensation coverage for his employes, pay all such premiums, State and Federal taxes, unemployment insurance and social security.

This case presents two questions. First, was the relationship between decedent and defendant at the time of the accident that of employer and employe or that of an independent contractor? Second, if decedent was an employe, was he a "Pennsylvania Employe" within the meaning of the Workmen's Compensation Act as amended? The prin ciples of law involved, that of employer and employe, and that of an independent contractor are well established in law. The difficulty frequently presents itself in applying these principles to the particular factual situation. We conclude here that claimant's deceased was an independent contractor and that the decision of the referee should be affirmed.

The general rule is that the relationship of master and servant exists where the employer has the right to select the employe, the power to remove and discharge him and to

direct both what work should be done and the way and manner in which it should be done: McColligan v. Pennsylvania Railroad Company, 214 Pa. 229. Claimant's counsel has cited the case of Myers v. Maurer and Myers, 144 Pa.

Superior Ct. 385, as controlling here. We are rather of the opinion that the facts here are more similar to those set forth in the case of Harrison v. Greyvan Lines, 331 U. S. 704 and United States v. Mutual Trucking Co., 141 F. (2d) 655.

Here there is a specific written contract setting forth the relationship between the parties and it appears that the terms of the contract apparently were carried out. In the 

Myers case the contract was oral and defendant had hired an employe for the decedent who acted as his helper. Here defendant had no right to hire an employe for decedent, but decedent could hire whomever he wished to drive the truck or help him and he was obligated by his contract to carry workmen's compensation and pay social security. In this case decedent could take any route available under defendant's ICC permit but defendant's own drivers had to take a route designated by defendant. Defendant's drivers in the event of a breakdown were obliged to contact defendant, whereas decedent, in similar circumstances, had no duty to do so. Defendant's drivers were permitted to charge gas and oil to the company and the speeds in defendant's vehicles were controlled by a governor on each truck. Decedent was not obligated to put a governor on his truck nor could he charge gas and oil to the company. It does not appear that decedent had to report for work at any particular time and he was not bound to transport for defendant exclusively. In fact, the testimony shows that he did some hauling for other freight lines who had ICC permits; in fact the contract between decedent and defendant evidently contemplated this by requiring decedent to cover defendant's permit numbers on his equipment when he was not transporting for that company. Admittedly, there are many situations where the owners of trailertractors have been held to have been employes but from our study, we have concluded that decedent here was an independent contractor.

1948] 

In view of the foregoing we find it unnecessary to discuss the question of whether decedent was a "Pennsylvania Employe". We affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order. 

Claimant's appeal is hereby dismissed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD PELCZAR v. GLEN ALDEN COAL CO. 

Workmen's compensation-Dependency partial or total-Ability of children other than decedent to support parent. 

A referee's award of compensation to claimant based on his findings that she was partially dependent rather than totally dependent for support upon her deceased son, at the time of an accident which resulted in his death, will be affirmed where the evidence disclosed there were other children of claimant who were capable of contributing to her support, although it did not appear that any of them had actually been contributing to claimant's support. 

Appeal by claimant from award of Referee Gibb, District 

No. 2, claim petition no. 109,238, accident no. 5,022,591. Appeal dismissed. September 8, 1948. 

T. L. Kennedy, Jr., for claimant. 

F. B. Gelder, for defendant.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

Claimant has taken this appeal from the decision of the referee who found that she was partially dependent for support upon her deceased son, Carl Pelczar, at the time of an accident on May 3, 1947, which resulted in his death.

Defendant admits that decedent was the adult son of claimant and that he was fatally injured while in the course of his employment with defendant. Claimant contends that

the evidence presented justifies the finding that she was totally dependent for support upon him at the time of the fatal accident.

The extent of claimant's dependency was a mixed question of fact and law: Cardone v. Jennings, 133 Pa. Superior Ct. 

318. It is based on the particular circumstances of the case. 

Decedent was 38 years of age at the time of his death and the family at home consisted of claimant, a widow, her deceased son, a married sister and her husband. The married couple contributed to the food they consumed and paid the grocer's bill which amounted to $10 or $12 a week. The other children were, Jake, past 42 years of age, a widower, who was employed as a high school teacher and lived at Alden, Pa., a few miles away from claimant. A son, Walter, 40 years of age, lived in the same block with the mother and was employed by the Glen Alden Coal Co. A son, Felix, 36 years of age, who lived six or seven miles away from claimant, was employed by the Glen Alden Coal Co. A sister, Anna, was married and living at Glen Lyon. Her husband was employed. Josephine Edwards, another sister, was unemployed at the time. The husband of the married daughter, who lived with claimant, earned approximately $50 a week. 

It did not appear that any of the children other than decedent had been contributing to the support of the widowed mother who was an invalid. 

As stated in the case of Mattis v. Arcadia Coal Co., 148 

Pa. Superior Ct. 462, the Act of June 24, 1937, P. L. 2045 sec. 3, 62 PS §1973, required children, if of sufficient financial ability, to support their indigent parents. The other children of claimant who we believe were capable of contributing to the support of their parents should recognize their obligation to do so. Claimant was not without any other source of income or livelihood.

Accordingly, we agree with the referee's decision and in view of the principles set forth in the case of Mattis v. 

Arcadia Coal Co., supra, affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and award.

1948] 

 COMMON PLEAS OF SCHUYLKILL COUNTY WOLOSZYNSKI v. LOCUST COAL CO. et al. 

Workmen's compensation—Claim petition-Dismissal—Treatment as petition for rehearing. 

1. A petition presented under an improper section of the Workmen's 

Compensation Act will not be dismissed but will be deemed to have been presented under the proper section. 

2. A second claim petition filed within one year from the date of claimant's alleged injury and after a referee had entered an order dismissing a prior claim petition from which order claimant failed to appeal, may be treated as a petition for rehearing, especially where the referee in dismissing the first petition noted in his adjudication that should claimant's neurosis result in a later disability he might then bring up the case for further consideration within the period provided by law. 

3. Where a second claim petition is treated as a petition for rehearing the entire record under the first claim petition becomes a part of the record in the rehearing proceedings. 

Appeal by defendant from action of Workmen's Compensation Board. C. P. of Schuylkill County, March term, 1948, no. 167. Order reversed. May 3, 1948. 

Roger J. Dever, for claimant. 

Henry Houck, for defendant.

STAUDENMEIER, J.: 

On August 14, 1944, claimant filed a claim petition alleging that he was accidentally injured on March 3, 1944, the nature of the injury being that three sets of timber collapsed and knocked claimant down striking him on the back of the head and neck, and that he was also struck by a large rock. 

This claim petition further alleged that claimant was disabled from June 6, 1944.

Hearings were held by the referee on the petition, and on November 20, 1944, the referee made an order dismissing

the petition and denying compensation. No appeal was taken from the action of the referee by claimant. It is significant to note at this time that in the referee's adjudication, his second conclusion of law contained the following: "Should his slight neurosis result in a disability and loss of earning power within the limitations prescribed in the act, he may bring the matter up for further consideration within the periods prescribed in the act."

On January 30, 1945, claimant filed a second claim petition based upon the identical accident for which he claimed compensation in the first petition. The only difference being that in the second claim petition, he alleged that he was disabled from January 12, 1945.

Defendant filed an answer to this second claim petition averring that the matters alleged in his second claim petition were res judicata; and that compensation was disallowed by the referee; and further that no appeal was taken from the referee's disallowance; and that there were no provisions of law permitting a second petition for compensation following the referee's disallowance of the first petition based on the same accident and injury. 

At the first hearing on the second petition, defendant moved to dismiss the petition on the grounds stated in the answer. The referee overruled defendant's motion, and an exception was noted for defendant. 

Testimony was taken on the second claim petition, and on April 4, 1946, the referee gave claimant an award based upon his injury of March 3, 1944, and awarded compensation for total disability commencing on January 2, 1945.

Defendant appealed to the Workmen's Compensation 

Board which held that the matter was res judicata. It reversed the referee's findings of fact, and conclusions of law, and award, and entered an order of dismissal for defendant.

Claimant appealed to the Court of Common Pleas of Schuylkill County, and former Judge Paul suggested that the second claim petition filed by claimant could be treated

1948] 

 as a petition for rehearing, and thereby reversed the Workmen's Compensation Board's order, and remanded the record to the board for further hearing and determination. 

The record came before Referee Enterline, and at that time neither party offered any additional testimony. The referee then made the same findings of fact as he had made before, and again awarded compensation. 

Defendant again appealed to the Workmen's Compensation Board which affirmed the award of the referee. Thereupon an appeal was taken to this court, and in support thereof, defendant filed 11 exceptions which can be summarized into two questions as follows: 

1. Did the workmen's compensation authorities err in treating the second claim petition as a petition for rehearing? 

2. Are the findings of fact and conclusions of law of the workmen's compensation authorities supported by legally competent evidence?

In Werner v. Allegheny County, 153 Pa. Superior Ct. 

10, 19, 33 A. (2d) 451, 455, the court said: "It is now a well settled law that a petition presented under an improper section of the Act will not be dismissed, but will be deemed to have been presented under the proper section. Eberst v. Sears, Roebuck & Company, 133 Pa. 

Super. 427, 3 Atlantic 2nd Series 25."

In Kochinsky v. Independent Pier Company, 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 15, 18, 41 A. (2d) 409, 410, the court said: "Proceedings before the Compensation Authorities are not 'litigation' and the strict rules of pleadings and practice applicable to Common Law actions do not apply. The courts take a liberal attitude toward the pleadings in Compensation cases and consider the substance of the relief prayed for rather than its form."

In Kissel v. Harbison-Walker Refractories Company, 157 

Pa. Superior Ct. 37, 40, 41 A. (2d) 434, the court said: "In this respect the court below recognized that if the claimant is entitled to relief under any section of the statute,

his petition should be considered as filed under that section. 

Hill v. Booth and Flinn Co. et al., 146 Pa. Super. 575, 580.

Gardner v. Pressed Steel Car Company et al., 122 Pa. Super. 

592, 598." 

In the case of Downs v. Linton's Lunch, 334 Pa. 415, 134 

Pa. Superior Ct. 248, 254, 6 A. (2d) 515, 518, the court said: "In the administration of this humane legislation, it is not the policy of this court to impale a deserving claimant upon technicalities of pleading, or a mistake in filing his petition under an inapplicable section of the act, provided he adduces evidence showing that he is entitled to relief under any of its provisions." 

In the case of Mallory v. Pittsburgh Coal Co., 162 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 541, 546, 57 A. (2d) 912, 914, the court said: "But as this court said in Tubbs v. O. T. Oil Co., 114 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 375, 378, 174 A. 836, 837: ‘... it makes no real difference under which section a petition may have been filed, provided proper ground for action by the compensation authorities under either be proved.' See also Schrein v. 

Fleischmann's Vienna Model Bakery, Inc., 148 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 155, 24 A. 2d 661; Kissel v. Harbison-Walker Refractories Co., 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 37, 41 A. 2d 434; Harrison v. 

Alden Park Manor Apts., 160 Pa. Superior Ct. 388, 51 A. 2d 418."

The facts in this case fully warrant the action of the compensation board. The referee disallowed the original claim on the grounds that claimant at that particular time did not show that he had a resulting disability from his accident of March 3, 1944. He then stated that should a slight neurosis result in a disability and loss of earning power, claimant may then bring up the matter for further consideration within the periods expressed in the act. 

It may be said at this time that the referee's second conclusion of law was evidently misinterpreted by claimant, who should have filed a petition for rehearing with the Workmen's Compensation Board in order to reopen his case.

1948] 

But can we deprive a claimant of compensation justly due him if he failed to seek relief under a proper section of the Workmen's Compensation Act. It has been repeatedly held by our appellate courts that a technical approach should not be permitted to defeat a meritorious compensation claim. 

If compensation is to be granted, relief should be given under any section of the Workmen's Compensation Act. 

It is true that the proper procedure would have been to file a petition for rehearing under the Act of May 27, 1943, P. L. 691, sec. 1, 77 PS §871. However, the Workmen's Com pensation Board decided to treat the second claim petition as a petition for rehearing, and in so doing, we believe that the compensation board did not commit error. It must be borne in mind that the second claim petition was filed within one year from the date of claimant's accident. He was injured on March 3, 1944, and his second claim petition having been filed on January 30, 1945. 

It is apparent from the record that the same result would have been achieved if claimant had filed a petition for rehearing on January 30, 1945, instead of filing his second claim petition on that date. If we are to abide by the decisions of our appellate courts in their interpretation of the Workmen's Compensation Act, we can come to no other conclusion, but in construing this second claim petition as a petition for rehearing. We are giving the Workmen's Compensation Act a liberal and humanitarian interpretation, and we are not attempting to defeat a meritorious claim for technical reasons. We therefore conclude that the action of the compensation board in treating the second claim petition as a petition for rehearing was warranted and justified under the peculiar circumstances of this case. 

It should be noticed at this time that if the second claim petition in this instant case is to be considered as a petition for rehearing, then the entire record adduced under the first claim petition becomes a part of this record. See Serafini v. West End Coal Co., 131 Pa. Superior Ct. 476, 486. In other words, the testimony taken on the first claim petition

[84 Dep. Rep. 

can be taken into consideration by the compensation authorities in making their findings of fact and conclusions of law in the final determination of this case. There is no doubt that this is exactly what happened in the instant case, and we believe that under the law the compensation authorities were justified in so doing. Accordingly there is sufficient legally competent evidence that this claimant met with an accident on March 3, 1944, while in the course of his employment.

The only question remaining is whether or not there is sufficient legally competent evidence to show that claimant's accidental injury resulted in a disability.

We believe that there is sufficient competent evidence to support such a finding of fact; however, the difficulty with this record is that the seventh finding of fact is based upon incompetent and insufficient testimony, this finding reads as follows: 

"7. We find that the said injury to claimant was associated with a strong element of fear from which claimant has developed a severe traumatic neurosis totally disabling him on and since January 12, 1945.”

We have looked in vain for competent testimony to support that part of the seventh finding of fact which deals with "a strong element of fear". The only testimony of record supporting this portion of the seventh finding of fact, is the testimony of Doctor Matthews, an impartial expert, who on cross-examination testified as follows: "Q. Where did you get the fact stated in your report that that was a strong element of fear associated with the accident? "A. From the patient himself and his description of the situation where he had been working, that he had been compelled to extract himself from the fall of rock which allegedly injured him and he had been told had he been there a little longer he probably would have lost his life since the area in which he had been working had been filled with rock from a subsequent fall.

1948] 

"Q. Did you find that in the notes of testimony? "A. I did not."

Even though Doctor Matthews testified in this manner, claimant failed to offer any additional testimony to support his opinion dealing with "a strong element of fear". See

Keilbach v. Met. Life Ins. Co., 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 590, 594. 

We believe that the statements made by claimant to Doctor Matthews could be used by Doctor Matthews in reaching a diagnosis but they cannot be used to support a finding of fact such as we have here. In the case of Howarth et ux. v. Adams Express Co., 269 Pa. 280, 283 the court said: "An expert may express an opinion on an assumed state of facts, which the evidence tends to establish, but not on what some one told him, nor on what he learned from another doctor, nor from the history of the case, we know not what nor by whom communicated. An opinion based on such a question would naturally be misleading. . . . In such case, an expert opinion cannot be based upon facts not before the jury: Rogers on Expert Testimony (2d ed., p. 82); nor upon hearsay: Lawson on Expert and Opinion 

Evidence (2d ed., p. 266)."

This court is not desirous of prolonging this litigation, but under the record as submitted, it is the duty of the compensation authorities to find the facts and not that of the courts. This is the first time that the competency of the proof has been brought before this court and we therefore deem it necessary to remand the record to the compensation authorities for further hearing and determination. 

And now, May 3, 1948, the order of the Workmen's Compensation Board is reversed and the record is ordered to be remanded to the Workmen's Compensation Board for further hearing and determination.

[84 Dep. Rep. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD PANDOLPH v. SENECA COAL COMPANY Workmen's compensation—Insurance-Cancellation of policy—Failure to notify insured.

A policy of compensation insurance was held to be in force at the time of an accidental injury sustained by defendant's employe where there was evidence that it was the practice of the insurance company to renew automatically its insurance policies, unless contrary instructions were given either by the assured or an agent of the company, where it appeared that prior to the date of the accident the insurance company's general agent had advised it not to renew the policy but had not given notice to the insured of its cancellation. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Moore, District No. 8, claim petition no. 109,614, accident no. 5,023,426. 

Affirmed as modified. August 25, 1948. 

Rosen & Rosen, for claimant. 

Walter A. Kieler, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

The evidence in this case establishes, and it is admitted, that claimant, Victor Pandolph, sustained accidental injuries to his right foot on April 29, 1947, during the course of his employment by defendant, Seneca Coal Company. Referee 

Moore awarded compensation for 8-1/7 weeks, and later amended his findings, to provide compensation for "loss of use of the great toe of his right foot and amputation of the second toe of his right foot". The referee, accordingly, awarded compensation of 56 weeks, under section 306 (c) of the Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 520, as amended. Defendant, by its insurance carrier, Eureka Casualty Company, has appealed. The appeal poses two questions: First: Was the policy of insurance in force at the time of the accident?

1948] 

 and second: Does the medical testimony of record warrant an award of compensation for a specific loss injury?

W. G. Dick, branch manager of the Eureka Casualty Com pany, testified that the initial compensation policy no. 2271 was issued on April 1, 1946, for the term of one year and expired on April 1, 1947. Dick explained that a deposit premium is required at the issuance of the policy, which remains intact until the policy expires or an audit is made, which shows whether a return premium is due the assured. 

It appears that in coal mine cases, the policy premium is collected monthly, assessed upon the basis of wages expended during the month. The policy contained a 10-day cancellation provision by either party. The particular policy was written by the Williams-Cleveland Company of New Castle, general agents. Under cross-examination, the witness admitted that the company "generally renew all policies unless otherwise advised". The branch manager stated that the Williams-Cleveland Company, per W. Davis, advised the Eureka on February 26, 1947, not to renew the policy.

On May 7, 1947, after the accident, the carrier wrote defendant, "We regret to advise that we can be of no service to you in this captioned case for the reason that under date of February 26, 1947, we were advised that your company had rented out equipment, and we were requested to mark our records not to renew". Michael A. Barletta, secretary-treasurer of defendant company, called by defendant, testified: 

66 . . We had never received word from the Williams 

Cleveland Company or from the Eureka Casualty Company, nor from the Workmen's Compensation Board that we did not have Workmen's Compensation Insurance in force."

The witness also stated: "I'm aware of the custom in the industry not to cancel and not to fail to renew unless you notify the assured, and I relied upon that custom". 

Robert W. Thompson, an insurance agent, called by defendant as an expert, testified: "The ordinary practice is the policy is sent out at least

a month prior to expiration, and, if there's any adjustments due to the audit, that correction is made to the policy." 

Carl J. Lundgren, superintendent of the coal company, testified in regard to the insurance arrangements which he made with a special agent, Dale Mullin. He stated that the coal company ceased operations in September 1946 and rented the mine equipment to another concern. According to the superintendent, no monthly reports were then sent to the home office of the insurance carrier until advised by the Williams-Cleveland Company that reports should be continued marked "No Payroll". Lundgren stated that defendant company resumed mining operations in January 1947, for which month a report was made. The witness testified that insurance with the Eureka was placed about two weeks after the accident, which continued in force. 

After a careful review of the testimony, it is our considered opinion that the policy of insurance was in force on April 29, 1947, when claimant was injured. Our conclusion is based upon the particular factual situation in the instant case and the decision is limited to the facts set forth herein. We do not believe that we are establishing, nor do we intend to establish, any new principle of insurance law or that of principal and agent. We do not base our decision here upon any general custom in the insurance business as to automatic renewal of policies. We do base our opinion upon the practice of this specific insurance carrier of automatically renewing its policies, unless contrary instructions were given either by the assured or an agent of the company. 

If instructions not to renew were given by an agent, a duty then devolved upon the agent or insurance carrier to so notify the assured, who might rely upon the practice of the company.

The practice of the insurance carrier of automatically renewing its insurance policies created an arrangement or course of conduct upon which its policyholders were entitled to rely, and upon which, in this case, defendant did rely. 

Having created a situation of this kind, the insurance carrier, we feel, became duty bound to inform the assured of 1

1948] 

 its intention not to renew the policy. After the insurance carrier failed to inform defendant of its intention not to renew the policy, it thereupon became estopped from asserting that no policy of insurance was in force after the claim was made. In the absence of any word from Mullin, the special agent, the Williams-Cleveland Company, the general agent, or the Eureka Casualty Company, the other party to the contract, Seneca Coal Company had a right to believe and assume that the policy of insurance continued in full force and effect during the course of its mining operations: 

McGine v. State Mutual Benefit Society, 135 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 35. Accordingly, we hold that the failure of the insurance carrier or its agent, to give notice to the insured of cancellation of insurance is now fatal to its contention of nonliability.

We may next consider the extent of claimant's injuries in order to ascertain whether the referee's award under section 306 (c) is appropriate. Claimant testified as to the happening of the accident. Pandloph stated that he experiences a great deal of pain in the great toe, walks with a limp and that it interferes with working. He said that the toe is one and a half times as large as its normal size and that he has been able to wear only a tennis shoe. Claimant returned to work on July 2, 1947, which does not require any standing on his feet. Dr. Paul H. Wilson, called by claimant, testified that he was called on April 29, 1947, to attend claimant for "a compound fracture of his big toe, a mangling of the flesh and a crushing injury to the next toe". The doctor testified that the terminal phalanx of the great toe was amputated and between 1 and 2 of the next toe as well. At the doctor's last examination about one week prior to the referee's hearing, the doctor found "some limitation of motion in the joint of the big toe, and, alongside one of the cuts which were rather extensive, slicing down the toe, was a callus formation". The doctor stated that the big toe was about 1/3 larger than normal and "there will always be some impairment of function in that toe"; that “it will never be perfect". The doctor did not advise amputation

because he was fearful of the crippling after effects. The referee awarded compensation for 56 weeks under section 

306 (c).

From all circumstances, it may well be inferred that claimant has lost the industrial use of the two members in question, but there is no acceptable medical testimony to this effect. Dr. Wilson's prognosis was merely an impairment of function. This is not synonymous with total loss of use. 

We believe that the referee's award of December 3, 1947, is proper. Present medical testimony is insufficient to establish complete loss of industrial use. Claimant, may, within the limitations of the act, petition for a review if present or subsequent events demonstrate claimant is entitled to compensation for a specific loss.

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's amended findings of fact, amended conclusion of law and amended order dated January 16, 1948. In lieu thereof we hereby reinstate all the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order dated December 3, 1947, with the exception of the referee's thirteenth finding of fact. In addition thereto we add the following finding of fact: 

Finding of fact 

13. The Workmen's Compensation Board finds as a fact that defendant insurance carrier made a general practice of renewing all workmen's compensation policies unless advised by the agent or assured; that defendant company relied upon the same and believed that their workmen's compensation policy had been renewed, not having received any notice to the contrary.

1948] 

 WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD FOX v. BUTLER COUNTY MOTOR CO. 

Workmen's compensation—Accidental injury—Automobile mechanic— 

Seizure with pain while replacing axle on truck-Sufficiency of proof. 

A referee's award of compensation will be reversed where claimant's evidence was to the effect that he was performing his duties as an automobile mechanic engaged in putting on a new axle under a truck body, when he experienced a sharp pain in the back while pushing the housing in position, there being no evidence that he fell or twisted himself and no medical testimony presented as to what happened to claimant at the time; under the circumstances, there was no proof of an accidental injury.

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Moore, District No. 8, claim petition no. 110,456, accident no. 

5,071,522. Appeal sustained. September 1, 1948. 

Sidney Rosenblum, for claimant. 

F. S. McQuilkin, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This appeal, brought by defendant, Butler County Motor Company, from Referee Moore's award of compensation to claimant, Wilbur L. Fox, poses the single question whether claimant sustained an injury by accident within the meaning and contemplation of the Workmen's Compensation Act. 

Claimant, employed as an automobile mechanic on August 1, 1947, testified that he was under a truck body engaged in putting on a new axle, when he experienced a sharp pain in the back while pushing the housing in position. The housing and wheels, he said, weighed approximately 400 pounds. Claimant stated that he and James W. Groves, who was working with him at the time, finished the axle job. 

Claimant testified that he "just felt kind of funny at the time", but, upon inquiry by the referee, explained that it

was a sharp needle-like pain. Under cross-examination, claimant stated that he had been wearing a belt for injury from a prior accident, but he was not using it in the summer time. Grove, called by claimant, testified: "Q. What was he lifting? "A. Lifting on the housing, the differential housing, he had a bar to lift it in place. "Q. How much would that weigh? "A. Oh gosh, you got me there. I don't know just what it would weigh. "Q. Could you lift it yourself? "A. No sir, not with the wheels and everything on it I couldn't lift it. "Q. How did you know anything was wrong with him? "A. Well, he was lifting there and he said, 'I bet I hurt my back.' He said he felt something in his back, so he told me. "Q. You finished putting the housing on? "A. Yes sir."

The witness stated that "as near as" he could tell, the bar in claimant's hand slipped. No medical testimony was offered and defendant produced no testimony. Claimant was not represented by counsel before the referee. 

Defendant's counsel in the brief filed cites numerous cases in support of its contention that claimant did not sustain an accident, including the oft-cited cases of Lacey v. Washburn and Williams Co., 309 Pa. 574; Crispin v. Leedom and 

Worrall Co., 341 Pa. 325, and Good v. Department of Property and Supplies, 346 Pa. 151. Defendant contends that claimant was performing his regular duties in a usual manner and there was no fortuitous or undesigned event or happening responsible for his accident. In the case of Turek v. Damalak, 161 Pa. Superior Ct. 84, cited by defendant, the court reversed a compensation award for aggravation of a preëxisting arthritic condition while the employe was pulling a pedal operated sewing machine out from the wall in order to place the belt back on the treadle. Claimant there gave the machine a jerk in order to pull it out from the

1948] 

 wall and suffered a sharp pain in his back. The court held that replacing the belt and moving the machine from the wall "were acts within the normal and usual duties of an operator of a sewing machine and there is nothing in the evidence indicating either overexertion or other fortuitous happening as the cause of claimant's disability." 

The court said (p. 85): "The act of claimant in moving the machine was not an accident; it was merely an incident of the day's work." 

Claimant in the instant case testified that he did not fall or twist himself in any way. He could not recall whether he slipped or not. The work, while arduous, was claimant's regular work. The claimant admitted a history of an ailing back and because of hot weather dispensed with the belt which he ordinarily wore to support his back. Under the circumstances he may have made himself readily vulnerable to a recurrence of injury in the performance of his heavy duties as an automobile mechanic. In the absence of medical testimony, we cannot speculate as to what actually happened to the physical well being of the claimant at the time of the occurrence. Disability or death merely hastened by the performance of an employe's regular duties is not compensable: 

Crispin v. Leedom and Worrall Co., 341 Pa. 325; Good v.

Pa. Dept. of Property and Supplies, 346 Pa. 151. We would have to ignore the requirements of the Act and the pronouncements of our appellate courts, were we to sustain an award upon the evidence presented. The affirmative proof offered does not, in our opinion, meet the necessary burden of proof: Eckman v. U. S. Lock and Hardware Co., 146 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 513. The case of Buck v. Arndt, 153 Pa. Supe rior Ct. 632, cited by claimant's counsel in this appeal, stated (p. 534): "The real difficulty is in determining whether claimant has met the burden of establishing by substantial, competent evidence that an accident occurred during the course of his employment-the controlling question of law is whether there is evidence sufficient in quantity and quality to sup-

port findings that the injury resulted from the performance of the work and was unforeseen and unexpected." 

We are of the opinion that the necessary evidence is lacking in the present case. No medical testimony was offered; the preëxisting back ailment coupled with claimant's performance of his regular work in the usual manner precludes an award.

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's fifth and sixth findings of fact and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following 

Findings of fact 5. The repair work being performed on the truck by claimant on August 1, 1947, was his regular work, which he was doing in his usual manner, when he experienced the sharp pain in his back, and was not of accidental origin. 

6. Claimant had suffered a previous injury to the back and ordinarily used a belt to support his back, but had dispensed with the belt during hot weather because of skin irritation. 

7. Claimant returned to work on August 10, 1947, fully recovered.

The referee's other findings of fact are affirmed. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's second conclusion of law and in lieu thereof we substitute the following 

Conclusion of law 2. Having found that claimant did not suffer an accident on August 1, 1947, during the course of his employment by defendant, he is not entitled to compensation.

The referee's first conclusion of law is affirmed. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's award and in lieu thereof we enter the following 

Order of disallowance

The claim petition no. 100,456, filed by claimant, Wilbur 

L. Fox, is hereby dismissed. 

The appeal of defendant is sustained.

1948] 

 WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD DOLBIN v. LYKENS COAL COMPANY Workmen's compensation—Medical treatment—Refusal by claimant— 

Uncertainty as to effect of treatment. 

A referee's award of compensation to claimant for the loss of use of an eye will be affirmed as against defendant's contention that he had forfeited his right to compensation because he had refused medical treatment offered him by defendant, where claimant's medical experts testified that the proposed treatments would not restore vision, although defendant's experts were of the opinion that treatment would improve vision; under the circumstances claimant's refusal was not so unreasonable as to require a holding that he had forfeited all right to compensation.

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Enterline, District No. 5, agreement no. 4,803,942. Appeal dismissed. 

September 8, 1948. 

Roger J. Dever, for claimant.

Penrose Hertzler and J. G. Feinour, for defendant. 

KNOLL, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by defendant from an order of the referee awarding claimant compensation payments for the loss of use of an eye.

Claimant suffered an accidental injury to his left eye on March 21, 1946, the injury being described, in a compensation agreement entered into by the parties, as a secondary glaucoma. On July 29, 1946, compensation payments under this agreement were suspended by a supplemental agreement, pending determination of earning power and of the extent of the eye injury. On March 3, 1947, claimant petitioned to set aside a final receipt, although no final receipt had been signed by him. At the time of hearing, counsel agreed to accept claimant's petition as a peti-

tion to set aside a final receipt for the permanent loss of use of vision of the left eye.

The medical testimony of record shows that claimant, at time of hearing on April 9, 1947, had lost the vision of his left eye for all purposes. The sole issue before us is whether or not claimant had forfeited all rights to compensation because he had refused medical treatments offered him by defendant: Section 306 (ƒ). 

Dr. George Ricchiuti, an eye specialist, called on behalf of claimant, testified that he would not recommend surgery for the eye and he expressed the belief that no treatment could help the eye since claimant had had all the orthodox recognized treatments.

Dr. Walter A. Bacon, an eye specialist, called by claimant, testified that he examined claimant on June 10, 1947; that he found a blood clot of long standing in claimant's left eye and evidence of a secondary glaucoma; and that, in his opinion, due to the elapsed time since the injury, nothing could be done to improve the eye and surgery might cause involvement of the normal right eye. 

Claimant, on his own behalf, testified, upon cross-examination, that he had refused defendant's offer on April 8, 1947, of further medical treatment of his eye. 

Dr. W. T. Hunt, an eye specialist, called by defendant, testified that he first saw claimant on March 23, 1943; that he diagnosed an iridocyclitis with secondary glaucoma of the left eye; that the vision of the eye deteriorated progressively from 20/50ths on March 23, 1943, to light perception on 

April 8, 1947; that, without the recommended treatments, which would probably restore useful and industrial vision, claimant might eventually lose the eye. Dr. Hunt testified further that he felt that the loss of vision was not permanent and that with treatment there was a reasonable chance to obtain good vision of the eye. Concerning treatment while claimant was hospitalized from March 23, 1946, to April 18, 1946, the witness said that claimant was discharged from the hospital because "You can't give him that treatment too long at one period of time" and that he told claimant to return

1948] 

 for further treatment. The doctor refused to say what vision claimant may recover after the treatments, stating that there are no guarantees in medicine. 

Dr. Edmund B. Spaeth, an eye specialist, called on behalf of defendant, testified that he examined claimant on April 8, 1947, and found him suffering from a subacute iridocyclitis of the left eye. He recommended readmission of claimant to the hospital, the use of drops, injection of hypertonic salt solution beneath the conjunctiva, drainage of the anterior chamber and injections into the vein of a foreign proteid, saying that this was the accepted treatment for the eye condition. Dr. Spaeth was positive that the treatment would restore claimant's vision to a useful function for industrial purposes, testifying however, that he could not guarantee the treatment and only recommended it. Further, he denied the presence of a blood clot in the eye and concluded that if claimant had lost the vision of the eye, as testified to by Dr. Bacon, it was due to claimant's neglect and refusal to take the recommended treatment. 

The referee's decision is based on competent medical testimony and we find no error warranting a reversal of his judgment. Claimant's ophthalmologists testified positively and definitely that the proposed treatments would not restore the vision of claimant's eye. Defendant's experts were of the opinion that treatment would improve vision, but their testimony was indefinite as to the expected improvement. 

The very diversity of the medical opinions leads us to the conclusion that the success of the treatment is problematical and uncertain. Under the circumstances, and in view of the failure of the hospital treatments to effect a healing of the eye, we do not think it was unreasonable of claimant to refuse the proposed treatments upon the advice of his eye specialists. Clearly, claimant's refusal was not so unreasonable and unwarranted that we are required to rule that he had forfeited all right to compensation.

Accordingly, the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of award are affirmed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD MARTIN v. EVENING BULLETIN 

Workmen's compensation-Claim for medical expenses beyond 

60-day period-Necessity to petition board.

A claim for hospital and medical expenses incurred within an extra 30-day period beyond the 60-day period provided for in the Workmen's Compensation Act will be allowed, although defendant was furnishing medical services to claimant beyond the 60-day period, where it appears that claimant, being dissatisfied with the services, requested the defendant to hospitalize him, and upon the latter's refusal to do so, employed his own physician. Under the circumstances, claimant was not required to petition the board for further medical treatment before obtaining such services. 

Appeal by defendant from order of Referee Alessandroni, District No. 1, agreement no. 4,743,753. Appeal dismissed and referee's order affirmed as amended. August 4, 1948. 

Philip J. Franzese, for claimant. 

Louis Wagner, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This case comes before the Workmen's Compensation

Board upon appeal by the Evening Bulletin, defendant, from an order by the referee, rendering an award to Charles Martin, claimant, for further medical expenses. The case was before us on a prior occasion, at which time we rendered an opinion at A-32743, from which defendant prosecuted an appeal to the Court of Common Pleas of Philadelphia County. That court remanded the record to us for determination as to whether or not claimant had requested that the employer furnish additional medical and hospital service. That question goes to the crux of the instant case.

Claimant testified that he asked the insurance company physician to hospitalize him in January and he was told that he did not require hospital attention, that his own

1948] 

 physician subsequently sent him to a hospital where he procured relief. Claimant admitted that he was told that the medical services rendered by his own physician, Dr. Hawthorne, were to be at his own expense. He stated that he was dissatisfied with the medical treatments defendant's physician gave him, that he therefore went to his own physician.

Boiling down the testimony taken at both hearings, it appears that claimant was not satisfied with the manner in which his injuries responded to treatment, that he desired his own physician to treat him, that he requested defendant's physician, Dr. Snodgrass, to hospitalize him, but the latter refused. Claimant has apparently recovered under the care of his own physician.

Defendant's main contention is that claimant should have presented his petition for further medical treatment to the Workmen's Compensation Board, before such services were given him, for him to be entitled to medical and hospital treatment beyond the usual 60-day period.

Although the compensation authorities attempt to act upon petitions with promptness and diligence, and usually expedite such cases, it is not always possible to consider them with the same urgency which the situation may require. There may be occasions when life or death may depend upon further medical or hospitalization being given a claimant at once. Should a claimant lose additional medical benefits under the Workmen's Compensation Act, when he does not wait until he has filed a proper petition, and until the Workmen's Compensation Board has acted upon the same? We do not so believe.

Although defendant was furnishing medical services to claimant beyond the usual 60-day period, claimant was dissatisfied with those services. We do not believe, from the record, that claimant's position was arbitrary, capricious or unreasonable. He was anxious to make a speedy recovery and it appeared to him that his recovery would be furthered by a change in physicians and by his being hospitalized. His early recovery was to the benefit of defend-

ant, as well as himself, in that defendant would be paying less compensation payments.

From our careful study and reconsideration of the entire record, we have now reached the conclusion that claimant's medical and hospital bills for the period beyond the usual 

60-day period should be paid by defendant.

We desire to amend and enlarge on the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order and vacate the referee's first finding of fact, first conclusion of law and order, substituting in lieu thereof the following 

Findings of fact 

1. The Workmen's Compensation Board finds as a fact that claimant requested hospital treatment from defendant's insurance carrier for an extra 30-day period, but that his request was refused. 

2. The Workmen's Compensation Board finds as a fact that claimant entered the American Stomach Hospital on February 3, 1946, where he incurred a bill of $163.30 for a period of 30 days. 

3. The Workmen's Compensation Board finds as a fact that claimant procured additional medical treatment from Dr. Hawthorne at a cost of $35 for a 30-day period beyond the usual 60-day period. 

4. The Workmen's Compensation Board finds as a fact that claimant was dissatisfied with the medical treatments given him by defendant's physician.

 1. The Workmen's Compensation Board concludes as a matter of law that claimant is entitled to have his medical expenses and hospitalization bills paid by defendant for a period beyond the usual 60-day period, within the limita tions of the Workmen's Compensation Act. 

Order 

The Workmen's Compensation Board hereby orders and directs the Evening Bulletin, defendant, to pay to Charles Martin, claimant, for the American Stomach Hospital, the

1948] 

 sum of $163.30, and for Dr. Hawthorne, the sum of $35, for additional medical and hospital bills, beyond the usual 60-day period, all within the limitations of the Workmen's 

Compensation Act, as amended. 

Defendant's appeal is dismissed and the referee's order is affirmed as amended. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD BERTUOLA v. LATTIMER COAL CORP. 

Workmen's compensation-Evidence-Impartial medical witness— 

Contradiction of testimony by other evidence. 

A referee's order disallowing compensation notwithstanding the testimony of an impartial medical witness that claimant was totally disabled as the result of anthraco-silicosis will not be disturbed where the testimony of the impartial medical examiner was contradicted by other medical testimony, especially where the claimant himself admitted his ability to do general light work and where he had been employed as a janitor subsequent to the date of his alleged total disability. 

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Olexy, District No. 2, claim petition no. 105,964, accident no. 

4,863,519. Appeal dismissed. September 15, 1948. 

Coal Operators Casualty Co., insurance carrier. 

T. L. Kennedy, Jr., for claimant. 

Nathan Hyman, for defendant. 

MURPHY, Chairman: 

This is an appeal by claimant from an order of disallowance by the referee.

Claimant, in his petition filed on August 12, 1946, alleged that he became totally disabled on August 8, 1946, as a result of anthraco-silicosis contracted in the course of his employment. Defendant's answer, filed on August 26, 1946, denied the material averments of claimant's petition. After hearings the referee found that claimant was not totally disabled and, in accordance with such finding, dismissed claimant's petition. This appeal followed. 

In this case, after the taking of the testimony of the various witnesses, the matter was referred to an impartial examiner. Subsequently, the impartial medical witness testified before the referee that claimant was totally disabled as a result of anthraco-silicosis and, at the same hearing, rebuttal medical evidence was offered by defendant. 

It is important to note that, even though the impartial testified that claimant was totally disabled as a result of anthraco-silicosis claimant himself not only testified as to his ability and willingness to do general light work but also testified that he had been employed as a janitor from March 1947 to July 1947, at which time his employment ceased because the place of his employment ceased operations. Thus the testimony of claimant himself refutes the opinion testimony of the impartial physician. 

As we have previously stated in Moore v. Moshannon 

Smithing Coal Co., 2 W. C. R. 352: 

"An impartial having been appointed, there is nothing sacrosanct about the testimony he subsequently gives. 

Merely because he is appointed as an 'impartial' witness, does not imply that he cannot be in error as to his findings and conclusions."

Certainly where, as in this case, the conclusion reached by an impartial is exactly contrary to actual facts as proven or admitted, it cannot be said that the referee must, nevertheless, accept the opinion of the impartial medical witness and disregard facts which show such opinion to be erroneous. 

We, therefore, affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of disallowance.

1948] 

 WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD STUFFLET v. FRATERNAL ORDER OF EAGLES Workmen's compensation—Accidental injury-Detached retina of eye while lifting.

Evidence that claimant while moving a case of soft drinks for his employer suffered a detached retina of the eye, as a result of which he subsequently lost the sight of the eye, was sufficient to sustain an award based on a finding of accidental injury where there was competent evidence that the detached retina occurred, when claimant handled the case; the fact that claimant was performing his regular duties at the time did not deprive him of an award for an unexpected injury caused by the performance of his usual work in the usual manner.

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Graybill, District no. 4, claim petition no. 108,350, accident no. 

4,972,906. Appeal affirmed. July 14, 1948. 

Vincent Grant, for claimant. 

Allan K. Grim, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

Referee Graybill awarded claimant, Charles M. Stufflet, compensation for the loss of his right eye, and defendant,

Fraternal Order of Eagles, has appealed. 

The record discloses that on October 24, 1946, a cataract in the right eye was removed by Dr. John M. Wottring.

Claimant was hospitalized until November 3, 1946, and returned to his employment as a steward late in November. 

On December 5, 1946, while moving a case of soft drinks in the cellar, he suffered a detached retina of the same eye. 

An operation was performed but claimant lost the sight of the eye. Did claimant suffer a compensable accident within the meaning and intendment of the Workmen's 

Compensation Act?
