Dr. Wottring, called by claimant, testified as to the responsible cause of the loss, as follows: "The loss of the sight was the retinal detachment; he had no sign of it from the time I saw him on November 29th until I saw him on the 6th of December and, of course, he said it happened immediately while he was working, with a little pain, and that is presumably the time this thing came loose. I think the exertion, or heavy lifting, most likely caused it to start, or did cause it to start." 

Under cross-examination, the doctor stressed the fact that he found no evidence of any diseased part of the retina previous to the incident in question. Claimant's testimony establishes that his regular duties included lifting and moving cases of liquids from time to time. Claimant described the accident as follows: "I lifted one from the floor and carried it back to another cellar, and when I lifted that I got a sharp pain in the right side of my head and just kind of hit me dizzy and I told the other fellow I hurt my eye, I am all dizzy, I shouldn't have lifted this thing, I was dizzy all the time."

There is competent and cumulative evidence which convinces us that the detached retina occurred when claimant handled the full case as related by him. Defendant offered no testimony.

Defendant relies upon Brodbeck v. W. F. Trimble & Sons, 150 Pa. Superior Ct. 299, as controlling the instant case, where the court quoted from Rayko v. Logan Coal Co. et al., 146 Superior Ct. 449, 458, 22 A. (2d) 434, as follows (p. 301): "(1) Those in which the employee had a pre-existing disease which had progressed to the point where the continuation of his normal work was dangerous. Notwithstanding his physical condition, the employee continued at work until stricken while performing his usual work in the usual way and without the happening of any unexpected external occurrence."

The doctor's testimony in the present case establishes that there was no sign of a pre-existing disease or retinal detach-

1948] 

 ment from November 29, 1946, until the day after the accident. In the case of Gavula v. Sims Co., 155 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 206, the court said (p. 212) : 66 a compensable injury may occur in the course of the normal duties of an employee and without overexertion, when a strain, sprain or twist causes a break or sudden change in the physical structure or tissues of the bodythat is, a fracture of the bone or bony cartilage, or a rupture of the softer tissues (citing cases)."

Mindful as we are of the humane purposes of compensation legislation, we feel that claimant is entitled to an award "for an unexpected injury caused by the performance by the employee of his usual work in the usual manner is clear": 

Buck v. Arndt, 153 Pa. Superior Ct. 632.

The appeal of defendant is dismissed.

WORK MEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD MATTER v. HARRISBURG STOVE & FURNACE CENTER Workmen's compensation—Accidental injury—Hernia— 

Unusual exertion-Finding by referee. 

A referee's findings supported by the evidence that claimant, whose normal duties were that of a foreman rarely involving heavy work, attempted to move a coal heater weighing approximately 600 pounds from one location to another in the home of one of defendant's customers, and that in performing this work alone, although he usually had a helper, he tilted the heater forward on a hand truck and had to exert unusual effort to keep it from falling when he pulled the heater back on the truck, as the result of which he strained himself and suffered a hernia, was sufficient to support a finding of an accidental injury.

Appeal by defendant from order of Referee Patterson, District No. 6, claim petition no. 111,174, accident no. 

5,117,177. Appeal dismissed. September 15, 1948.

Employers Liability Assurance Corp., insurance carrier. 

Sidney Rosenblum, for claimant. 

Compton & Handler, for defendant.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

This is an appeal by defendant from an order of the referee suspending compensation.

The record discloses that, in his claim petition filed on December 10, 1947, claimant alleged that while attempting to move a coal heater, in the course of his employment on 

November 1, 1947, he strained himself, as a result of which he suffered a hernia of both sides. Defendant's answer, filed on January 7, 1948, denied the happening of an accident. After hearings, the referee found that though claimant had suffered a compensable hernia, by accident, in the course of his employment, he had lost no time or loss of earnings and, in accordance with such findings, suspended the payment of compensation. Defendant has taken this appeal arguing that there was no proof presented that claimant had suffered an accident in the course of his employment.

From all of the testimony presented, the referee has found as his fourth finding of fact, the following: "That about 4 p. m. on Saturday, November 1, 1947, claimant was attempting to move a coal heater weighing approximately 600 pounds from one location to another in the home of one of defendant's customers on Vernon Street, Harrisburg. Claimant was performing this work alone as his helper did not work on Saturday afternoons. He tilted the coal heater forward and placed a two-wheel, rubbertired, hand truck under the edge of it. As he pulled the heater back onto the truck he had the full weight of it on him-'it was more than I bargained for'-and it was

1948] 

 necessary for him to exert an unusual effort to keep the heater from falling. He managed to pull it back on the truck but at the same time he felt a burning sensation in his left inguinal region. . . ."

Defendant contends that these facts, properly gathered from the testimony of the witnesses, fall short of proving the happening of an accident. We are unable to agree. 

An injury by accident may occur in the course of the normal duties of an employe and without overexertion when a strain, sprain or twist causes a break or sudden change in the physical structure or tissue of the body: Rudy v. 

Motor Freight Express, 5 P. C. R. 12; Davis v. Lackawanna 

Linoleum Stores, 5 P. C. R. 58. Even where an employe is performing his regular work in the usual manner some unforeseen or undesigned circumstances may arise in its performance which would constitute a compensable accident: N. Y. E. v. H. M. Baker & Co., 5 P. C. R. 27.

To constitute a compensable accident, it must be shown that the work in which claimant was engaged at the time of the occurrence was of a different nature and required a materially greater amount of exertion than that to which he was ordinarily subjected, so as to justify a conclusion that the increased severity was the cause of the accidental injuries received: Rothwell v. Borough of Wesleyville, 5

P. C. R. 106. When we consider the testimony to the effect that claimant's normal duties were that of a foreman, rarely involving heavy work; that, when he did do heavy work he always had a helper, while on the occasion he attempted to do the moving without any help and that, while tilting the heater to place it on the truck, it was necessary for him to exert unusual effort to keep it from falling and while so doing he felt the burning sensation in his groin, we are of the opinion that claimant has sufficiently proven the happening of a compensable accident.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD STRAUB v. GLEN ALDEN COAL CO. 

Workmen's compensation-Course of employment-Riding loaded car in coal mine-Violation of employer's orders.

A referee's order disallowing compensation to claimant on account of the death of her husband will be affirmed where it appears that at the time he received his fatal injuries decedent was riding a car loaded with coal up a slope in defendant's mine in violation of defendant's order and in violation of a rule of the Anthracite Mine Law of Pennsylvania; although the violation of the rule of law was not the cause of decedent's injuries the violation of defendant's positive orders removed him from the course of his employment. 

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Gibb, specially presiding in District No. 2. Claim petition no. 

108,459, accident no. 4,978,154. Appeal dismissed. August 

4, 1948. 

Daniel J. Flood, for claimant. 

F. B. Gelder, for defendant.

KNOLL, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by claimant widow of Martin Straub, deceased, from an order of Referee Laurence V. Gibb, spe cially presiding in the Compensation District No. 2, dis missing her compensation petition. 

Decedent was fatally injured on February 10, 1947, in an accident which involved two loaded cars upon which decedent was riding up a slope in defendant's mine at the conclusion of his day's work.

The question before us is a legal one, whether decedent, while riding the loaded cars, was in the course of his employment.

The testimony established that decedent was ordered not to ride loaded cars nor to walk up the slope at any time.

1948]  He was employed as a runner to assist in hauling loaded cars to the foot of the slope and none of his duties required him to ride or walk up the slope. A manway, paralleling the slope, was provided by defendant for men to walk into and from the mine. The accident occurred about 700 feet from the top of the 2,200-foot long slope when the cars, upon one of which decedent was standing, became derailed and hit decedent.

It is evident from the record that decedent was riding in the loaded cars in violation of the positive orders of defendant and in violation of Rule 16 of the Anthracite Mine Law of Pennsylvania. While the violation of the rule of law was not the cause of decedent's fatal injuries (see Kolonik v. 

Hudson Coal Co., 160 Pa. Superior Ct. 491) decedent had removed himself from the course of his employment by his disregard of defendant's positive orders. We believe that the principles of law set forth in Demuzzio v. Latimer Coal 

Corp., 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 459; Garrahan v. Glen Alden 

Coal Co., 149 Pa. Superior Ct. 1, and Dickey v. Pittsburgh and Lake Erie Railroad Co., 297 Pa. 172, are controlling in this case. In the Garrahan case, page 8, the court, quoting from Dickey v. Pittsburgh & Lake Erie Railroad Co., 297 

Pa. 172, stated: "Here was a plain violation of positive instructions. . 

He had no duty to perform on the place of the accident or the instrumentality that killed him nor did his work bring him in any manner in contact with them; as to these he was a stranger. To sustain a different theory would weaken the beneficial effect of the law, take from the employer all opportunity to guard against accident and make discipline in a plant merely a thing of words only. Where an employee violates a positive rule as to entering forbidden parts of the owner's premises about which he has no duty to perform, or disobeys instructions against starting machinery or other dangerous agencies with which his work is not connected, and with which he has no business, and an injury results, he not only violates the orders of his employer, but is in the position of a trespasser, who without right, authority or permission, enters forbidden ground."

Accordingly, the referee's first conclusion of law is amended as follows: 

1. Since decedent had removed himself from the course of his employment by his direct violation of the positive orders of defendant, claimant widow is not entitled to compensation benefits. The findings of fact and order of the referee are affirmed. 

COMMON PLEAS COURT OF MIFFLIN COUNTY BINGAMAN v. BALDWIN LOCOMOTIVE WORKS, INC., et al.

Workmen's compensation-Occupational disease-Silicosis-Aggregate period of employment—Continuation of contract of employment—

Section 801(d) of Occupational Disease Act. 

To sustain an award for disability resulting from silicosis under section 301 (d) of the Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 566, the proof and findings must establish that the employe had an aggregate employment of at least four years in the Commonwealth during a period of eight years next preceding his disability, in an occupation having a silica hazard; proof of the silica hazard during all of the aggregate employment for four years of the eight-year period is essential, hence a finding of fact by the Workmen's Compensation Board that the decedent had an aggregate employment of at least four years in the Commonwealth during the period of eight years next preceding his disability, in an occupation having a silica hazard, is not supported by substantial evidence and an award based thereon will be set aside, where during the eight years next preceding his disability, decedent worked in defendant's steel foundry where he was subject to exposure to silica dust for a total aggregate period of 3 years, 6 months and 24 days, although his contract of employment with defendant was continuous over a period in excess of four years.

1948]  Appeal of defendant and Commonwealth of Pennsylvania from award of Workmen's Compensation Board. Claim petition no. 87,239, accident no. 3,679,861. C. P. of Mifflin 

County, May term, 1945, no. 287. Appeal sustained. January 5, 1945. 

F. Brewster Wickersham, with him Metzger & Wickersham, Huette F. Dowling and Henry J. Sommer, for claimant. 

Paul S. Lehman, for defendant.

S. H. Torchia, Ralph H. Behney and James H. Duff, At torney General, for Commonwealth.

UTTLEY, P. J.: 

The claim in this case is for total disability and death caused by silicosis, an occupational disease. The original claim petition was filed September 9, 1940, by Dallas M. 

Bingaman, who died December 6, 1940, before the final determination of his petition. On January 13, 1941, Dorothy

Bingaman, widow of Dallas M. Bingaman, filed a claim petition in her own right and for her dependent minor children, and the referee on December 17, 1942, awarded compensation on her petition, to be paid 50 percent by defendant and 50 percent by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. Defendant and the Commonwealth appealed from the award of the referee and the Workmen's Compensation Board set aside the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and award, and remanded the record to the referee to take the testimony of an impartial physician, appointed by the board, and make such disposition of the case as the facts and the law should warrant. The referee, after hearing the testimony of the impartial physician, again on August 31, 1944, awarded compensation, as before, on the petition of Dorothy Bingaman. Defendant and the Commonwealth again appealed to the board, which affirmed the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law, and award, and the

[84 Dep. Rep. 

appeal of defendant and the Commonwealth to this court followed. 

Dallas M. Bingaman left to survive him a widow, Dorothy

Bingaman, claimant, and four children, under the age of 

16 years, as follows: Eugene M. Bingaman, born March 

29, 1926; Genetti R. Bingaman, born November 20, 1927; 

Burnell Bingaman, born October 14, 1929, and Arlene Bingaman, born December 15, 1931, all of whom were living with Dallas M. Bingaman, at Middleburg, Pa., and entirely dependent upon him for support at the time of his death. 

In this opinion we will refer to Dorothy Bingaman as claimant, and her husband, Dallas M. Bingaman, as decedent. 

Appellants have filed five exceptions with their appeal. 

The first exception is that the Workmen's Compensation Board erred in finding as a fact that decedent had an aggregate employment of at least four years in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania during a period of eight years next preceding the date of his disability, within the meaning of the Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act, and the third exception is that the board erred in concluding as a matter of law that decedent had such an aggregate employment in an occupation having a silica hazard. As these two exceptions involve the same question, they will be considered together. The second exception is that the board erred in finding as a fact that Dallas M. Bingaman gave to defendant the notice required by the Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act. The fourth and fifth exceptions are respectively that the board erred in concluding as a matter of law that defendant employer and the Commonwealth are liable for compensation in this case and in dismissing the appeals of defendant and the Commonwealth. These last two exceptions involve the same questions raised by the first, second and third exceptions and will be considered therewith.

There are only two questions raised by this appeal, which may be stated as follows and will be considered in the order named:

1948] 

1. Was proper notice of disability given by Dallas M. 

Bingaman to defendant? 

2. Did decedent's employment satisfy the statutory requirement of "an aggregate employment of more than four years in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania during a period of eight years next preceding the date of disability, in an occupation having a silica or asbestos hazard"?

As to the first question, we agree with Commissioner Jacoby, who wrote the opinion in this case, that defendant had proper notice of the claim of Dallas M. Bingaman from the report of Dr. Paul H. Bickle, which, it is admitted, was received by Ray C. Yoder, defendant's personnel officer and representative for receiving notices and claims in compensation cases, within the time required by the Occupational Disease Act. This report, which is part of the record, is a printed form, designated "Doctor's Report of 

Disability, Employe of Standard Steel Works", was filled in and signed by Dr. Bickle and gives the name of the employe as Dallas M. Bingaman, with his address, age, marital status, color, and date of first and last treatments, and the diagnosis as "Pulmonary Tuberculosis and Silicosis", and estimates the temporary total disability as indeterminate. While this report was intended for the Aetna Insurance Company, carrier of the group insurance policy on defendant's employes, and is not exactly in the form suggested by section 312 of the Act of June 21, 1939, supra, it contains all the information required by that section, which concludes with the words "But no variation from this form shall be material if the notice be sufficient to inform the employer that a certain employe, by name, became disabled as the result of occupational disease, the character of which is described in ordinary language, in the course of his employment on or about a time specified". This, like all other sections of the Occupational Disease Act, should be liberally construed: Wilkinson v. United Parcel Service, 158 Pa. Superior Ct. 22, 43 A. (2d) 408, 411. Furthermore, the board's finding of fact that decedent gave defendant proper notice of his disability is supported by substantial, relevant and competent evidence and cannot be disturbed

by the court. Appellants' second exception, that the board erred in finding as a fact that Dallas M. Bingaman gave the required notice of his disability to defendant employer, is therefore unfounded.

The answer to the second question above stated involves the construction of subsection (d) of section 301 and subsection (a) of section 308, of the Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 566, as amended by the Act of June 12, 1941, P. L. 125, 77 PS §§1401, 1408, which reads as follows: "(d) Compensation for silicosis or anthracosilicosis and asbestosis shall be paid only when it is shown that the employe has had an aggregate employment of at least four years in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, during a period of eight years next preceding the date of disability, in an occupation having a silica or asbestos hazard. "(a) When compensation is awarded because of disability or death caused by silicosis, anthracosilicosis, asbestosis or any other occupational disease which developed to the point of disablement only after an exposure of five or more years, the compensation for disability or death due to such disease shall be paid jointly by the employer and the Commonwealth, in accordance with the following provisions: If disability begins between October 1, 1939, and

September 30, 1941, both dates inclusive, the employer shall be liable for and pay fifty percentum of the compensation due and the Commonwealth fifty percentum thereof. . . ."

The evidence in this case was sufficient to warrant the referee's finding of fact, confirmed by the board, that Dallas M. Bingaman, decedent, in the period of his employment with defendant as a chipper in its steel foundry, was engaged in an occupation having a silica hazard. While there was considerable medical testimony as to whether decedent died of silicosis, or tuberculosis, or silicosis and tuberculosis, there is no exception filed to the referee's finding of fact, confirmed by the board, that the disability and death of Dallas M. Bingaman, decedent, were caused primarily (as

1948] 

 definitely distinguished from a contributory or accelerating cause) by silicosis or silicosis accompanied by pulmonary tuberculosis. There was sufficient substantial, relevant and competent evidence from which the referee and the board could find both of the above facts. As the credibility of the witnesses, the conflicting evidence, and the inferences to be drawn therefrom, were for the board, the court has no power to reverse the above findings: Plaugher v. American 

Viscose Corp., 151 Pa. Superior Ct. 401. Therefore, the only portion of the above question, raised by appellant's first and third exceptions, is whether Dallas M. Bingaman, decedent, had an aggregate employment of at least four years during the eight years next preceding disability as a chipper in defendant's plant.

The referee and the board have found as matters of fact that during the period of eight years preceding December 8, 1939, the last day of his employment, decedent actually worked regularly as a chipper in defendant's steel foundry, where he was exposed to the silica hazard, during the following periods of time: May 11, 1934, to October 15, 1934; 

February 4, 1935, to June 13, 1935; April 9, 1936, to June 

13, 1938; and May 1, 1939, to and including December 8, 1939; and, in addition thereto, he worked for defendant company in 1923, 1925 to 1928, 1929 and 1930; that during these periods of time claimant was employed only in the capacity of a chipper, and during the eight years next preceding December 16, 1939, the date of his disability, he had no employment other than with defendant company, with the exception of lumbering and farm work, and that he accepted every call for work and continued working until laid off by defendant on account of reduction of force. The evidence also shows that during the period May 11, 1934, to December 8, 1939, claimant worked a total of 834 days, which, on the basis of a five-day week, was the equivalent of 166 4/5 weeks, or 3 years, 6 months and 24 days, the same as the other regular chippers worked, and he was carried all that time on defendant's personnel record and

never discharged, but that he did not work for defendant in the years 1931, 1932 and 1933. 

Appellants contend that because the total of the periods, which decedent actually worked in the occupation having a silica hazard, aggregated only 3 years, 6 months and 24 days, he has failed to satisfy the statutory requirement of an aggregate employment of at least four years. The contention of appellee, however, is that the term "aggregate employment" means the period during which the contract of employment, arising from the relationship of employer and employe, was continuously in force and that as this relationship between defendant and decedent was continuous at least from May 11, 1934, to December 8, 1939, the date when he quit work, a period of five and one half years, he has complied with the requirements of both sections of the statute above quoted. The duty of the court, therefore, is to determine the real meaning of the words "aggregate employment of at least four years" and "disablement only after an exposure of five (5) or more years", as used in the statute.

We are aware that our Superior Court has held that the Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act shall be liberally construed: Roschak v. Vulcan Iron Works, 157 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 227; 42 A. (2d) 280, 283; and that in borderline cases the court will resolve doubts in favor of claimant: York v. 

State Workmen's Insurance Fund, 131 Pa. Superior Ct. 496. 

This does not mean, however, that the court may ignore the clear intention and meaning of the legislature as expressed in the statute. The requirement of the statute is clear. It provides that compensation for silicosis shall be paid only when it is shown that the employe has an aggregate employment of at least four years during a period of eight years next preceding the date of his disability in an occupation having a silica hazard. Decedent must have not only an aggregate employment of four years but he must have actually worked at and been engaged in an occupation having a silica hazard throughout the four years to satisfy the requirement of the statute. It is the aggregate time claimant

1948] 

 has worked and been exposed in the occupation having the silica hazard rather than the length of his employment with defendant that is important. It is very significant that in subsection (a) of section 308 of the act, as amended, the Commonwealth can be held liable for a part of the compensation only where the occupational disease has developed to the point of disablement after an exposure of five or more years. This can only mean after claimant has actually worked in the occupation, having a silica hazard, five or more years, because to be exposed to the hazard five or more years he must have worked in the hazardous occupation that length of time. The use of the word "exposure" in subsection (g) of section 301 and subsection (a) of section 308 clearly indicates that the legislature also had in mind and meant exposure in subsection (d) of section 301 of the act. 

Decedent in this case actually worked as a chipper in defendant's steel foundry only 5 months and 4 days in 1934, 4 months and 9 days in 1935, 2 years, 2 months and 4 days in the period April 9, 1936, to June 13, 1938, and 7 months and 7 days in 1939, a total of 834 days, or 166 4/5 fiveday weeks, or 3 years, 6 months and 24 days, during the eight years next preceding his disability. We can understand how some allowance would be made for Sundays, holidays and sickness, but such breaks are included in the above periods. We are of the opinion that the intention of the legislature and the meaning of subsection (d) of section 301 of the Occupational Disease Act, supra, is that decedent, to be entitled to compensation for an occupational disease, must have worked and been exposed in an occupation having a silica hazard for a period of at least four years during the eight years next preceding his disability. This is the construction placed upon this section by the Superior Court in the very recent case of Tokash v. Early Foundry 

Co., 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 467; 43 A. (2d) 553, in which it was held that where a claimant worked for his employer for more than four years there must be evidence that at least four years had been put in in an occupation having a silica hazard before claimant would be entitled to compensation, and that "while a claimant may combine periods of

exposure in order to reach the required aggregate, he may not include, in the computation periods of employment, a different and non-hazardous occupation because he happens to have the same employer for both jobs". In the above case claimant worked the entire period of his employment for, and in the plant of, defendant employer, while in the case at bar decedent worked a part of the period of his employment for defendant employer and the other part at the openair occupations of lumbering and farming for another employer. The only difference, therefore, between the case above cited and the case at bar is that in the case cited claimant worked three and a half years in the occupation having a silica hazard and the remainder of the four years in a nonhazardous occupation, for the same employer, while in the case at bar decedent worked three and a half years in the occupation having a silica hazard for defendant employer and the remainder of the four years in the nonhazardous occupations of lumbering and farming for another employer. In both cases claimant was short of the period of exposure in an occupation having a silica hazard, required by the statute. The Supreme Court of Arizona in 

Magma Copper Company v. Gonsales et al., 152 Pacific Report (2d) 618, in construing a similar section of the Arizona Occupational Disease Law, have held that the total period of five years' exposure provided by the law must be shown to make out a prima facie case for compensation for silicosis.

The cases cited by counsel for claimant all bear upon the question of the continuation of employment. In the case of 

Wisconsin Granite Co. v. Industrial Commission, 242 N. W. 

191, the question involved was whether compensation for an occupational disease should be paid if claimant was not stricken while actually employed in the performance of his services. The length of the period of exposure to the occupational hazard was not involved. The effect of the court's opinion was that claimant was still in the employ of his employer when he was stricken: Cochrane v. William Penn 

Hotel Co., 140 Pa. Superior Ct. 323, 326, and Butera v. 

Western Ice and Utilities Co., 140 Pa. Superior Ct. 329, the other cases cited by counsel for claimant and Commissioner

1948] 

Jacoby, are not occupational disease cases but cases in which the distinction is drawn between a casual employment and employment in the regular course of the employer's business. These cases are only authority for the principle that it is the continuity of the employment rather than the regularity or the number of hours of actual work which determines the quality of the employment; that the quantity of work at any one time may be small, but if it recurs with regularity, with a fair expectation of its continuance for a reasonable period in the future, the employment is not casual. These cases are no help in the interpretation of the sections of the statute here under consideration. 

For the reasons above given we are of the opinion that, as a matter of law, the finding of fact of the Workmen's Compensation Board in the within case, that decedent had an aggregate employment of at least four years in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, during a period of eight years next preceding his disability, in an occupation having a silica hazard, within the meaning of the Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act, is not supported by substantial, relevant and competent evidence, that the board therefore erred in said finding of fact and in its conclusions of law that decedent was entitled to, and defendant and the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania were liable to claimant for, compensation for disability caused by the occupational disease of silicosis. This appeal will therefore have to be sustained, and the award of the Workmen's Compensation Board in this case set aside. Decree 

Now, January 5, 1945, after due consideration, the appeal of the Baldwin Locomotive Works, Inc., successor to Standard Steel Works Company, and the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, from the decision of the Workmen's Compensation

Board in the within case, is sustained, and the award of the Workmen's Compensation Board in the within case is hereby set aside.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD FISHER et ux. v. INDUSTRIAL EQUIPMENT COMPANY Workmen's compensation — Dependency Common-law marriage - 

Sufficiency of evidence.

An award based on a referee's finding that claimant was the widow of decedent, employe of defendant, killed in the course of his employment, will be affirmed where the evidence established the fact that on a certain date the decedent took the claimant as his wife and the claimant took the decedent as her husband, following which claimant's mother was advised and a celebration was held at claimant's home and they thereafter maintained a home as husband and wife, held a joint bank account, purchased and sold real estate and so held themselves out to the world.

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Sheldrake, District No. 1, claim petition no. 103,741, accident no. 

4,729,492. Appeal dismissed. January 14, 1948. 

David L. Ullman, for claimant. 

George H. Detweiler, for defendant.

KNOLL, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by defendant from the order of award of Referee John A. Sheldrake, of Compensation District 

No. 1.

On November 14, 1945, claimant filed her petition, averring, inter alia, that decedent, William T. Fisher, sustained certain injuries on October 11, 1945, while acting within the course of employment with defendant herein, which injuries resulted in the death of the said William T. Fisher on October 26, 1945. To this petition a responsive answer was filed by defendant, denying the material allegations of the said petition. 

The record discloses that decedent, William T. Fisher, sustained certain injuries on October 11, 1945, while acting within the course of his employment with defendant herein,

1948] 

 and as a result of the said injuries, a tetanus infection developed which resulted in the death of the said William T. 

Fisher on October 26, 1945. Hence, the issue in this case. is whether or not claimant, Madeline Fisher, was, in fact, the common-law wife of decedent, William T. Fisher.

Claimant, on her own behalf, testified that she and decedent frequently attended dances and other places of amusement; that in 1918 she was employed at a restaurant and decedent was employed by the Budd Manufacturing Company; that on Thanksgiving Day, 1918, both she and decedent were off from work by reason of the holiday; and that late in the afternoon of that day, decedent called at her home and she and decedent went for a walk, and during the walk the following occurrence took place: "Q. While you were taking a walk what if anything was said between you and him? "A. Yes there was-he said he wanted to talk to me about something; he said 'Madeline I love you and I have something to say to you' he said 'Now' he said 'I want to get married' and I said 'Yes' 'well', I said, 'I love you too and 

I want to get married to you' then he said 'You know, you are a Quaker. Us being different religions maybe we wouldn't want a Church wedding' so I said 'we being 

Quakers it is different' he said 'all right' he said 'now' he said, then he said 'Well I want you Madeline to become my. wife right here and now' so I said 'all right I will take you to be my husband right now'."

Claimant further testified that, following this occurrence, they returned to the home of claimant at which time decedent, in the presence of his mother-in-law, made the following statement: ". . . well I guess I can call you mother".

At the Thanksgiving dinner, the marriage of claimant and decedent was celebrated.

The record further discloses that shortly thereafter the parties set up housekeeping in an apartment, the furniture being provided by the mothers of claimant and decedent; that the rent books for the apartments occupied by the parties were in their respective names as husband and wife; that property was purchased and sold by them as husband

and wife; that joint bank accounts were kept as husband and wife; and that obligations were contracted from time to time as husband and wife.

The record also establishes that, at the time of his death, decedent carried a policy of life insurance with the Prudential Insurance Company, payable to claimant as his wife. 

Following the marriage, the parties lived together continuously as husband and wife and held themselves out to the world at large as husband and wife. 

The referee found as a fact that decedent left to survive his widow, claimant, Mrs. Madeline Fisher, who was dependent upon him for support at the time of his death. Based upon said finding of fact, the referee made an appropriate award. From this ruling defendant has appealed.

We have made a careful study of the record and are of the opinion that the ruling of the referee should be affirmed. 

The testimony in this case conclusively establishes the fact that, on Thanksgiving Day, 1918, decedent took claimant as his wife and claimant took decedent as her husband; that, following this occurrence, claimant's mother was immediately advised and a celebration was held at claimant's home. The testimony further establishes the fact that claimant and decedent maintained a home as husband and wife and that a substantial portion of the furniture was 'given to them by their respective mothers. In addition thereto, the evidence discloses that the parties contracted as husband and wife, maintained a joint bank account, purchased and sold real estate as husband and wife; also that they lived together as husband wife, and had held themselves out to the world as husband and wife. 

We, therefore, have all the incidents of a common-law marriage contracted by the parties without civil or religious ceremony and without prior license. Common-law marriages are valid under the common law of Pennsylvania and our appellate courts have held that there are no statutes which affect either the method of contracting a common-law marriage or its validity. In a workmen's compensation case, there must be substantial, credible and competent testimony sufficient to satisfy a reasonable mind as adequate proof

1948] 

 of a marriage at common-law. It is our opinion that claimant has met this burden and, by reason thereof, is entitled to the benefits of the Workmen's Compensation Act. See Buradus v. General Cement Products Co. et al., 159 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 501.

We, therefore, affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of award. 

The appeal of defendant is dismissed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD GREEN v. H. C. FRICK COKE CO. 

Workmen's compensation-Death resulting from injury-Payment to dependent widow-Deduction of payments to decedent in life time-Section 306(g) and section 307 (7) of the Act of 1939. 

Where claimant's husband suffered dermatitis as a result of an accidental injury in the course of his employment, for which injury he received compensation under an agreement until the time of his death, which resulted from the injury, claimant was entitled to an award for the balance of a 300-week period and not for the balance of a 500-week period, in accordance with section 306 (g) and section 

307 (7) of the Workmen's Compensation Act of 1939, in effect at the date of occurrence of the injury.

Appeal by claimant from award of Referee Foust, District No. 9, claim petition no. 109,307, accident no. 5,037,643. 

Affirmed. September 15, 1948. 

Anthony Cavalcante, for claimant. 

B. B. Whitehill, for defendant.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

This is an appeal by claimant from an award of the referee.

The record discloses that, on October 8, 1943, the parties entered into a compensation agreement providing for the payment of compensation at the rate of $18 per week commencing on June 8, 1943 and describing the accident of 

February 10, 1943, and the resulting injuries as follows: "Employe states that while loading coal the cable from his battery to head piece on cap, rubbed and irritated his neck. Dermatitis." 

On June 30, 1947, Hither Green, the widow of original claimant, Lemuel J. Green, filed her petition alleging that decedent's death, on June 5, 1947, resulted from exfoliative dermatitis for which, at the time of his death, he was receiving compensation under the agreement referred to above. Defendant's answer, filed on July 8, 1947, denied the material averments of claimant's petition. After hearings, the referee found that claimant was entitled to recover compensation under sections 306 (g) and 307 of the Workmen's Compensation Act and entered an award in her favor, for the balance of a 300-week period. Claimant has taken this appeal alleging that the award should have been for the balance of a 500-week period rather than for the balance of a 300-week period as awarded by the referee. 

From a review of the law applicable to the facts of the instant case, we are of the opinion that the action of the referee was proper and should be affirmed. 

The accident having occurred on February 10, 1943, the 

Workmen's Compensation Act of 1939 is the applicable act and is controlling in this case. 

Section 306 (g) of the said act provides: "Should the employee die as a result of the injury, the period during which compensation shall be payable to his dependents under Section 307 of this article, shall be reduced by the period during which compensation was paid to him in his lifetime under this Section of this article". 

Section 307 (2) provides the compensation to be paid in a death case, where the facts are similar to those in the instant case as follows: "In case of death, compensation shall be computed on the following basis, and distributed to the following per-

1948] 

 sons: To the widow or widower, if there be no children, forty-four per cent of wages, but not in excess of eleven dollars per week".

The length of time during which the said sum shall be payable is specifically covered by section 307 (7) of the act, which provides: "This compensation shall be paid during three hundred weeks, and in the case of children entitled to compensation under this Section, the compensation shall continue, after said period of three hundred weeks, until such child reaches the age of sixteen, etc."

Since, in the instant case there are no minor children surviving decedent, claimant widow is entitled to compensation in the sum of $11 a week for a period of 300 weeks, reduced by the period during which compensation was paid decedent. The award made by the referee is strictly in accord with this.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD MCGLYNN v. RICH HILL COAL MINING CORP. 

Workmen's compensation-Specific injury-Loss of one half of thumb 

-Section 306(c) of Workmen's Compensation Act. 

An award to claimant for the loss of one half of his right thumb, pursuant to section 306 (c) of the Workmen's Compensation Act, covered all disability as a result of the loss of the distal phalanx of plaintiff's thumb, including pain, annoyance and inability to work where claimant's injury was limited to the thumb.

Appeal by claimant from order of Referee Schwing, District No. 7, agreement no. 4,791,501. Affirmed. September 1, 1948.

for claimant. 

D. D. Griffith and R. H. Cunningham, for defendant. 

Coal Operators Casualty Co., insurance carrier.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

This is an appeal by claimant from an order of the referee awarding compensation under an agreement. 

The record discloses that, on May 31, 1946, the parties entered into an agreement providing for the payment of compensation at the rate of $20 per week commencing on February 23, 1946, and describing the accident of February 

15, 1946, and the resulting disability as follows: "Contused laceration of the right thumb, laceration of the right index finger, caused when claimant caught finger in machine box."

On January 15, 1947, defendant filed its petition to terminate, alleging that claimant's disability ceased on June 3, 1946, at which time he was able to resume his employment without further disability or loss of earning. Claimant's answer, filed on January 31, 1947, denied the material allegations of defendant's petition and alleged that he still suffered disability as a result of the accident. After hearings, the referee found that claimant had suffered the loss of one half of his right thumb as a result of the accident and, in accordance with such finding, dismissed defendant's petition and entered an award in favor of claimant for the loss of one half of his right thumb, giving defendant credit for the payment already made. This appeal followed. 

A careful review of the record in this case convinces us that the action of the referee must be affirmed. 

The compensation agreement and the testimony presented at the hearing upon defendant's petition for modification show that claimant suffered the loss of the distal phalanx of his right thumb, or one half of the thumb. This is a specific loss for which certain definite compensation is provided under the Workmen's Compensation Act.

1948] 

Section 306, subsection c, provides, inter alia: "(c) For all disability resulting from permanent injuries of the following classes, the compensation shall be exclusively as follows: . . . For the loss of a thumb, sixty-six and two-thirds per cent of wages during sixty weeks. . . "The loss of the first phalange of the thumb . . . shall be considered equivalent to the loss of one-half of such thumb 

and shall be compensated at the same rate as for the loss of a thumb or finger, but for one-half the period provided for the loss of a thumb. . . "

Compensation payable under section 306 (c) covers all disability as a result of specific loss, and includes pain, annoyance, inconvenience, inability to work and everything incident to the permanent injury: Constantini v. State

Workmen's Insurance Fund, 2 P. C. R. 110. This section fixes the total compensation for permanent injuries to certain parts of the body. It provides for all disability resulting from the permanent injuries and the compensation paid thereunder is fixed without regard to personal capacity to labor, or loss of earning power. Injury and not incapacity controls under section 306 (c): Meeder v. Rochester Pipe 

Products, 2 P. C. R. 161.

In view of what we have stated above, we affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD BARCLAY v. MOORE Workmen's compensation-Employe-Caretaker and gardener- 

Operation of greenhouse for own profit. 

A referee's award of compensation will be reversed where claimant, employed by defendant as a caretaker, gardener, and chauffeur, operated some greenhouses on defendant's property the profits of which, apart from expenses of maintenance claimant retained, it further

appearing that he sustained his injuries while preparing to deliver flowers from the greenhouses to a local store; under the circumstances, claimant in operating the greenhouses was in business for himself and while so engaged was not an employe of defendant. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Carmalt, District No. 8, claim petition no. 108,534, accident no. 

9,949,932. Appeal sustained. October 13, 1948. 

The Fidelity & Casualty Co. of N. Y., insurance carrier.

Sam R. Keller, for claimant. 

John F. Briley, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by defendant, P. M. Moore, from an award entered by Referee Carmalt, April 26, 1948.

On December 19, 1946, claimant, Roy F. Barclay, sustained injuries to the index and middle fingers of his right hand while attempting to get the fan belt to turn the waterpump of his automobile. As a result it is admitted that he has lost the use of half of his right index finger. The dispute in the case is over his relationship to defendant and whether or not the facts disclosed bring him within the protection of the Workmen's Compensation Law. 

With respect to the issue it appears from the evidence that defendant's business had to do with building supplies. He made his home on a sizeable country estate and hired claimant and his wife as caretakers. Claimant lived on the estate and took care of chickens, stock and the gardening, receiving for such work $125 per month. Aside from this remuneration he and his wife were favored with board and lodging. On the estate there were three greenhouses and quite some time before the accident complained of, defendant had indicated his intention to raze them. Claimant, having a horticultural propensity, induced defendant to spare the buildings and let him, claimant, operate them. 

This led to an arrangement whereby claimant produced

1948] 

 flowers in the greenhouses and sold them to those interested, mainly "old residenters" at prices far below the current market. He kept half of the income from this source and defendant used the other half to pay the upkeep expenses of the greenhouses. Both men evidently paid for seeds out of their respective shares. 

It appears from claimant's testimony that at the time of the accident, he was starting up the motor of his automobile preparatory to delivering some flowers to a local store and, on the way, taking a damaged clinker hook used in firing the greenhouse boilers to a machine shop to be repaired. Defendant had a different impression as to this trip. He understood that claimant was setting out to get some feed for the chickens at a nearby mill. 

The provision in the law (77 PS §22) which raises the question in this case excludes agricultural and domestic service employes from the benefit of the act and there is a corollary question as to a possible partnership status having been raised between the parties. 

We will deal with the latter question first. We think it least important and most readily susceptible of determination. Of course, if claimant was a partner in the floral enterprise, he would not be an employe and therefore not be en titled to compensation (Skinner's Pennsylvania Workmen's 

Compensation Law, 4th ed., p. 146). In our opinion he was not a partner. It is true that in a sense he shared profits but we do not think he engaged to share liability or responsibility. The Uniform Partnership Act of March 

26, 1915, P. L. 18, reads as follows in the subparagraphs to section 7: "(3) The sharing of gross returns does not of itself establish a partnership, whether or not the persons sharing them have a joint or common interest in any property from which the returns are derived. "(4) The receipt by a person of a share of the profits of a business is prima facie evidence that he is a partner in the business but no such inference shall be drawn if such profits were received in payment,

[84 Dep. Rep. 

"(a) As a debt by installment or otherwise "(b) As wages of an employee or rent to a landlord."

We think the last quoted phrase which we have italicized is doubly significant under the circumstances of the case before us. The portion of it referring to rent is important to the first of the questions comprising the issue. The evidence indicates that defendant was not disposed to make any use of the greenhouses. He wanted to get rid of them but relented to indulge claimant's desire to work on his own at something he understood. Since defendant's share of the return from this represented almost entirely the expense of maintaining the greenhouses it would seem logical to classify it as recompense for use and occupation and if such it was, it was, in our opinion, a rental. Claimant could not, then, be a partner.

The question of partnership being thus disposed of, to the best of our knowledge, we must agree that claimant was an employe but we do not agree that his endeavors in the greenhouses took him out of the exceptions in the act applicable to domestic and agricultural workers. He was either an entrepreneur as to them or they were an incidental adjunct to his regular employment as a caretaker and gardener. On appeal defendant would have us adopt the latter view and cites Jack v. Belin's Estate, 149 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 531, the only case which has gone before one of our higher courts on reasonably similar facts. But similarity is lacking on an important detail. In the Jack case claimant, a caretaker, was injured in a fall from a ladder while cleaning whitewash from the roof of a greenhouse. The distinguishing detail was that the greenhouse upon which he was working did not represent to him a source of independent income such as the greenhouses in the present case meant to Barclay. The better view as we see it is that in the present case claimant, so far as he was able to earn additional money by operating defendant's greenhouses, was in business for himself and not, in that phase of his work, an employe of defendant. 

The second, third, fourth, fifth and seventh findings of fact of Referee Carmalt dated April 26, 1948, are affirmed.

1948] 

The first and sixth findings of fact, first and second conclusions of law and order of Referee Carmalt of the same date are vacated and set aside and the following substituted therefor: 

Findings of fact 

1. Claimant, Roy F. Barclay, was employed on December 

19, 1946, by defendant, P. M. Moore, as a caretaker, handyman, gardner and chauffeur. 

6. On the date above set forth claimant operated greenhouses owned by defendant and situated on the home property of said defendant. 

7. Aside from the expenses of maintenance of said greenhouses, claimant retained the profits of the operation thereof.

1. Claimant and defendant were not associated as partners in the operation of the said greenhouses. 

2. The portion of the profits of the operation of the said greenhouses distributed at regular accounting intervals to defendant were in the nature of rentals for use and occupation of the same. 

3. Claimant was employed by defendant in a capacity excepted from the benefits of the Workmen's Compensation 

Act. 

4. The horticultural business in which claimant engaged involving the use of the said greenhouses was his own enterprise and in no way related to his employment by defendant as a caretaker, gardener, handyman or domestic servant. 

5. Article III of the Workmen's Compensation Act does not apply to the relationship existing between claimant and defendant with respect to the work being done by claimant at the time he sustained his accidental injury.

Order The claim petition filed by claimant in this case April 

24, 1947, is hereby dismissed. 

The appeal is sustained.

COMMON PLEAS OF WARREN COUNTY ROSSEY v. MAYBUR CHEMICAL COMPANY Workmen's compensation-Appeal from board-Time for taking 

-Notice to party of board's decision-Presumption as to service. 

1. Where there is evidence that a letter or notice has been mailed a presumption arises that it was properly stamped in conformity with the postal laws. 

2. Where there is evidence that a letter enclosing a copy of an opinion of the Workmen's Compensation Board, was mailed to claimant on June 26, 1946, a presumption of service on the claimant on the date when the letter was mailed arose, which presumption the claimant could not rebut by evidence that he had moved from the address to which the letter was mailed and did not receive it until July 1st, so that an appeal taken on July 17th, was not taken within the 20 days allowed by the act and since no application for an extension of time was made within the 20-day limit, the court will upon motion strike off the appeal.

In the Court of Common Pleas of Warren County, no. 37, September term, 1946. Appeal by claimant from the deci sion of the Workmen's Compensation Board. Appeal stricken. October 13, 1948. 

Harold S. Hampson, for claimant. 

Joseph H. Goldstein, for defendant.

WADE, P. J.: 

On June 26, 1946, the Workmen's Compensation Board handed down a decision in which the board affirmed the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of disallowance, thereby dismissing claimant's appeal. An appeal was taken from this order on July 17, 1946, to this court by Oren M. Rossey, claimant, by his attorney, Harold 

S. Hampson. The question is now before the court as to whether or not this appeal should be stricken upon the contention of Joseph H. Goldstein, counsel for the Mayburg

1948] 

Chemical Company, defendant, that said appeal was not filed within the 20 days provided by the Workmen's Compensation Act.

The position of Joseph H. Goldstein is that the appeal was not taken within the period allowed by the Workmen's 

Compensation Act, while the position of Harold S. Hampson, counsel for claimant, is two-fold: 

First: That the record is silent as to whether or not a notice that may have been directed to him as attorney of record was properly stamped and addressed. 

Counsel argues to the court that there must be affirmative evidence in the record that the opinion was enclosed in an envelope properly stamped and addressed. An examination of the record shows that on "June 26, 1946: Copy of Opinion mailed to parties". The first point, therefore, is the effect of evidence that a notice "was mailed" without precisely stating it was stamped. The law on this subject seems to be clearly established that where a letter or notice is mailed there is the presumption that it was properly stamped in conformity with the Postal Laws. Of course, this permits the objecting party to rebut this presumption, but until it is rebutted there is the presumption that a letter mailed was properly stamped. "The popular understanding of the word 'mailed' as applied to a letter is that it was duly stamped and placed under the control of the officers of the postal department whose duty it is to dispatch postal matter; and this is the meaning which should be attached to it in this case under the testimony. In the absence of evidence to the contrary or any inquiry as to the particular point, the witness might well be understood to mean that the letter was mailed in conformity with the requirements of the postal service": Reynolds v. 

Maryland Casualty Co., 30 Pa. Superior Ct. 456, 459 (1906).

Then counsel takes the further portion that there was "nothing in the record to show that the notice, properly stamped and addressed was mailed to the attorney for claimant". However, attached to the opinion, dated June 26, 1946, is a copy of a letter of notice to the parties. Since this

[84 Dep. Rep. 

point is made in this case the court quotes the letter in full as follows: 

"COMMONWEALTH OF PENNSYLVANIA DEPARTMENT OF LABOR AND INDUSTRY WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD HARRISBURG 

"H. M. Engell, Esq. 

1211 Finance Bldg. 

Philadelphia, Penna. 

Joseph H. Goldstein, Esq. 

Warren, Penna. 

Harold S. Hampson, Esq. 

Warren, Penna. 

Oren M. Rossey 

Mayburg, Penna. 

June 26, 1946.

A-31457 

OREN M. ROSSEY VS MAYBURG CHEMICAL CO. 

My dear Sir:

Enclosed find copy of (opinion) of the Workmen's Compensation Board, filed this day in the above captioned case. 

Very truly yours,

W. R. GALLAGHER 

W. R. Gallagher, Secretary

Workmen's Compensation Board" 

encl. er."

It seems to this court that it is apparent that the letter. was properly addressed to Harold S. Hampson, Esq., for, in the proper place at the heading of the letter, are found these words: "Harold S. Hampson, Esq., Warren, Penna.”

Certainly this is the proper address found on the very letter of notice of the filing of the opinion, and also, this letter indicated that there was enclosed therein an actual copy of the opinion. The court has already indicated that the opinion was dated June 26, 1946, and the letter is obviously dated June 26, 1946. Therefore, under these circumstances, since the notice was "mailed" in accordance with the record, this court will presume under the decisions that it was

1948] 

 properly stamped and an actual copy of the letter included in the record shows it was properly addressed to Harold S. 

Hampson, Esq., at Warren, Pa. This court must conclude that the Workmen's Compensation Act, which provides that "for the purpose of this article any notice or copy shall be deemed served on the date when mailed, properly stamped and addressed, and shall be presumed to have reached the party to be served . was complied with in the case at bar. 

If counsel for claimant desired to rebut this presumption he could have taken the stand and done so. However, counsel chose to stand upon the record as presented.

There is law to the effect that where a copy of a letter is found upon the desk of a decedent, there is the presumption that the original had been mailed. 66 '(3) However, where a copy of a letter which an official had the duty of sending was found in his desk after his death, the original was presumed to have been sent": 31 C. J. S. 

781, $136.

The second point in the case concerns notice to Oren M. 

Rossey, claimant himself. As quoted above, there was notice to Oren M. Rossey mailed June 26, 1946, which included a copy of the opinion dated June 26, 1946. Mr. Rossey desired to rebut this presumption of receipt of the notice in the due course of mailing on June 26, 1946, by showing that he had moved from Mayburg to Warren, Pa. The testimony shows that Mr. Rossey had been expecting such a notice and was watching the mails for this specific notice, but it was not received until July 1, 1946, at his home in Warren, Pa.

Therefore, Mr. Rossey contends, the statute was not complied with so far as giving notice to him personally to raise the presumption of service under the act. The act, in this regard, definitely states: ". . . any notice or copy shall be deemed served on the date when mailed properly stamped and addressed . . ." and in this case the record shows that the notice and copy of opinion were mailed June 26, 1946, to Oren M. Rossey, Mayburg, Pa.

Counsel for claimant takes the position that since his client moved from the address as given in the record, and

consequently there was some delay in receiving the notice, the time for taking an appeal should be extended. If it were the law that person could extend the time for an appeal by changing his address and by keeping from the board his current address, an appeal could thereby be extended at the will of claimant. 

Defendant in the case at bar complied with the act when it deposited in the mail the notice and copy of the decision on June 26, 1946, to Oren M. Rossey at Mayburg, Pa., the last known address of claimant, and also to Harold S. Hampson, Esq., Warren, Pa., the attorney of record for claimant. "Notice to an attorney of the time of trial of litigation which has been entrusted to him is notice to the client. 

See on the general subject of notice to an attorney as notice to his client: 7 Corpus Juris Secundum, page 853, Par. 69; 

2 Ruling Case Law, page 963, Par. 38; 1 Sadler's Criminal 

Procedure, page 412, Par. 335": Commonwealth v. Thompson and Bell, 29 Erie 98, 99. "Lawson was the agent of Cummins; and the service of the rule on him for the bail to justify, we think a sufficient service. It was the duty of the agent to give notice to his principal, and, if time were wanted, to apply to the magistrate for that purpose": Cummings v. Foreman, 6 Pa. 194, 195 (1847). See Newlin v. Newlin, 8 S. & R. 41 (1882),

A. L. I. Restatement of the Law of Agency, §385, Comment, subsec. 1, subsec. (a).

It is, therefore, the opinion of this court that the appeal taken July 17, 1946, was not in conformity with the provi sions of the Workmen's Compensation Act. This court is further of the opinion that since the appeal was not taken within the 20 days allowed and since no application for the extending of this time was made within the 20-day limit, this court has no equitable powers to grant any extension of time. "Where it affirmatively appeared from pleadings that appeal to Court of Common Pleas was not taken within twenty days after notice of Workmen's Compensation Board's de cision was deposited in mails, properly stamped and ad-

1948] 

 dressed to counsel for appellant, and no application for extension of time was made within the twenty day limit, the 

Court had no jurisdiction to entertain such appeal": Banks v. McClain, 156 Pa. Superior Ct. 512, 40 A. (2d) 905.

Therefore, the motion to strike off the appeal, filed September 5, 1946, by Joseph H. Goldstein, attorney for the 

Mayburg Chemical Company, must be granted.

Order 

And now, to wit, November 19, 1946, it is hereby ordered, adjudged, and decreed that the motion of Joseph H. Goldstein, attorney for the Mayburg Chemical Company, made September 5, 1946, be and the same is hereby granted, and the rule to show cause thereon granted be and the same is hereby made absolute, and the appeal taken by Oren M. 

Rossey, claimant, on July 17, 1946, be and the same is hereby stricken.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD ORRIS v. THE BERWIND-WHITE COAL MINING COMPANY ET AL. 

Workmen's compensation-Refusal of claimant to submit to medical examination Forfeiture of compensation 

Section 314 of Act of 1939. 

A petition by defendant to deprive claimant of compensation by reason of plaintiff's refusal to submit to an examination by defendant's physician will be granted where it appears that claimant has persisted in his refusal following a prior order of the board directing him to submit to such an examination. 

Petition to deprive claimant of compensation filed by counsel for defendant, before Referee Schwing, claim petition 109,041, accident no. 5,015,712. Petition granted. October 13, 1948.

Culbertson & Culbertson, for claimant. 

Francis A. Dunn, for defendant. 

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

The claim petition of John Orris, claimant, is presently pending and undetermined before Referee Schwing. Claimant has entered his medical testimony before the referee. 

It appears that defendant, the Berwind-White Coal Mining Company, has requested claimant on numerous occasions to submit to an examination at the hands of physicians of its selection. Claimant has failed and refused to accede to such requests. On June 21, 1948, defendant filed a petition with the board requiring claimant to submit to a physical examination. On July 14, 1948, we granted defendant's petition. 

We entered an order directing claimant to "submit to physi cal examination by Dr. W. S. Wheeling and Dr. H. B. Ander son, at the Windber Hospital, Windber, Pa., during week of July 26, 1948". Defendant has now filed a petition to deprive claimant of compensation, averring that claimant persists in his refusal to submit to an examination by defendant's physicians and requesting that claimant be deprived of compensation during the continuance of such refusal or neglect.

Section 314 of the Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 566, pro vides: "At any time after an injury the employe, if so requested by his employer, must submit himself for examination, at some reasonable time and place, to a physician or physicians legally authorized to practice under the laws of such place, who shall be selected and paid by the employer. If the employe shall refuse upon the request of the employer, to submit to the examination by the physician or physicians selected by the employer, the Board may, upon petition of the employer, order the employe to submit to an examination at a time and place set by it, and by the physician or

1948] 

 physicians selected and paid by the employer, or by a physician or physicians designated by it and paid by the employer; and if the employe shall, without reasonable cause or excuse, disobey or disregard such order, he shall be deprived of his right to compensation under this article. 

The Board may at any time after such first examination upon petition of the employer, order the employe to submit himself to such further examinations as it shall deem reasonable and necessary, at such times and places and by such physicians as it may designate; and in such case, the employer shall pay the fees and expenses of the examining physician or physicians, and the reasonable traveling expenses and loss of wages incurred by the employe in order to submit himself to such examination. The refusal or neglect, without reasonable cause or excuse, of the employe to submit to such examination ordered by the Board, either before or after an agreement or award, shall deprive him of the right to compensation, under this article, during the continuance of such refusal or neglect, and the period of such neglect or refusal shall be deducted from the period during which compensation would otherwise be payable. "The employe shall be entitled to have a physician or physicians of his own selection, to be paid by him, participate in any examination requested by his employer or ordered by the Board."

It appears to us that claimant has arbitrarily and wilfully refused to comply with the board's order of July 14, 1948. Defendant is entitled to the medical examination requested as a matter of fairness and justice, as well as under the law. Claimant's refusal is unreasonable and claimant is hereby deprived of any rights to compensation under the act. The prayer of defendant's petition is granted and we enter the following

Order It appearing that claimant, John Orris, has failed and refused to comply with our order of July 14, 1948, directing

him to submit to a physical examination by defendant's physicians, claimant is, therefore, deprived of his right to any compensation under the act. 

COMMON PLEAS OF SCHUYLKILL COUNTY FALATOVICH v. DELANO ANTHRACITE COLLIERIES COMPANY ET AL. 

Workmen's compensation—Occupational disease—Receipt by claimant of unemployment compensation-Estoppel from asserting total disability.

The receipt of unemployment compensation by a claimant does not bar the allowance of his claim for total disability resulting from an occupational disease for the same period, as a matter of law; nor do certifications of ability to work made by claimant on the weekly pay orders for unemployment compensation estop him from asserting as against the employer and insurance carrier that he was, at the same time, totally disabled within the meaning of the Occupational Disease Act, where there was no evidence that the employer or insurance carrier did or refrained from doing anything in reliance upon claimant's representations to the Unemployment Compensation Board. 

In the Court of Common Pleas of Schuylkill County, May term, 1946, no. 269. Appeal of defendant from award of

Workmen's Compensation Board. Exceptions dismissed and order of board affirmed. September 13, 1948. 

Thomas L. Kennedy, Jr., for claimant.

Penrose Hertzler and E. Mac Troutman, for appellant. 

DALTON, J.: 

The referee made an award for anthraco-silicosis against the employer and the insurance carrier at the rate of $16 a week and a separate award against the Commonwealth at the rate of $4 a week: Occupational Disease Act of June

1948] 531. 

21, 1939, P. L. 566, sec. 308, as amended, 77 PS §1408. On appeal by the insurance carrier, the Workmen's Compensation Board affirmed. The insurance carrier now appeals to this court. The Commonwealth has not appealed from the separate award against it.

Numerous exceptions have been filed, but appellant, in accordance with rule 26 of this court, has limited the scope of the appeal to a statement of two "Questions Involved". 

All other matters which might be suggested by the exceptions are deemed abandoned. 

The second "question involved" is stated as follows: "2.

Is a claimant entitled to the concurrent payment of unemployment compensation and occupational disease compensation, where the former is based upon his ability to work and the latter is based upon his inability to work?" For reasons hereinafter indicated, we think the question is too broadly stated. 

It appears that on December 31, 1946, which was approximately 212 months before the date of total disability as found by the referee and the board, claimant had applied for unemployment compensation. Pursuant to that application he was paid unemployment compensation at the rate of $20 per week for 20 consecutive weeks, beginning with the week ending January 13, 1947, and terminating with the week ending May 26, 1947. In the original application and on each of the subsequent weekly pay orders he certified his ability and availability for work. He did not file his claim petition for occupational disease until June 2, 1947. He has been awarded occupational disease compensation for total disability at the rate of $16 per week against the employer and the insurance carrier and at the rate of $4 per week against the Commonwealth; both awards run from March 25, 1947, that date being seven days after the beginning of total disability. It is now contended that occupational disease compensation should be disallowed for the period extending from March 25, 1947, to May 26, 1947, and for seven days thereafter, because claimant received unemployment compensation during the period mentioned.

It is immaterial to this proceeding whether claimant was or was not "entitled" to the unemployment compensation.

Our concern is whether he is entitled to the occupational disease compensation. Nor are we concerned with any credit or estoppel which the Commonwealth might possibly have asserted. The Commonwealth has not appealed from the award against it; its rights are not before us for adjudication. It is likewise clear that the employer and the insurance carrier cannot take advantage of rights and defenses peculiar to the Commonwealth. Their liability is primary, contractual and independent, whereas the statutory liability of the Commonwealth is assumed only in relief of the employer (Weyant v. General Refractories Co., 150 Pa. Superior Ct. 502), and the award against it is "several, and wholly distinct from that of the employer": Creighton v. 

Continental Roll & Steel Foundry Co. et al., 155 Pa. Supe rior Ct. 165, 176; Occupational Disease Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 566, sec. 308 (d), as amended, 77 PS §1408 (d). 

Defendant's argument really presents two distinct questions, which, limited to the matters properly before us, may be more precisely stated as follows: (a) Does the receipt of unemployment compensation bar the allowance of occupational disease compensation for total disability for the same period, as against the employer and the insurance carrier, as a matter of law; and (b) if not, do the certifications of ability to work, which claimant made on the weekly pay orders for unemployment compensation, estop him from asserting, as against the employer and the insurance carrier, that he was at the same time totally disabled within the meaning of the Occupational Disease Act? 

The first inquiry was answered adversely to defendant's contention in Bartels v. Ford Motor Co., 292 Mich. 40, 289

N. W. 322, but apparently has not been ruled upon by any court of this State.

Defendant's argument that, if the award is sustained, claimant will have received "dual compensation", overlooks the fact that unemployment compensation and occupational disease compensation arise out of two distinct statutes, serve entirely different purposes, are paid from entirely dif-

1948] 

 ferent sources, and are not necessarily the same either in weekly rate or in total amount. 

The purpose of the Unemployment Compensation Law of 

December 5, 1936, P. L. (1937) 2897, as expressed in section 

3 thereof, 43 PS §752, is to provide "Security against un employment and the spread of indigency . by the systematic setting aside of financial reserves to be used as compensation for loss of wages by employes during periods when they become unemployed through no fault of their own". Employers are therefore required to pay contributions, which are really excise taxes on the right to employ 

(Fidelity-Philadelphia Trust Co. et al. v. Hines, 337 Pa. 

48, 51), into the Unemployment Compensation Fund, which is "a special fund separate and apart from all public moneys or funds of this Commonwealth" and may be extended solely for the payment of unemployment compensation: Section 

601, 43 PS §841. The weekly rate and total amount of com pensation payable to an eligible claimant depend upon the wages paid him during his "base year".

Occupational disease compensation was first provided for by the Act of July 2, 1937, P. L. 2714, which was a supplement to the Workmen's Compensation Act. It is now provided for by an independent piece of legislation, the Occupa tional Disease Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 566. Employer and employe are free to accept or reject the compensatory features of the act, but when they elect to come under it, the statute becomes part of the contract of employment: 

Agostin v. Pittsburgh Steel Foundry Corp. et al., 354 Pa. 

543, 545. The employer then has a contractual obligation to pay compensation for disability or death in accordance with the schedule contained in the act: Occupational Disease 

Act, sec. 301 (a), 77 PS §1401 (a). The employe in return gives up his right to sue in tort "for the absolute certainty provided by the Act of receiving the compensation and bringing himself within its compensatory clauses" : Moffett v. Harbison-Walker Refractories Co., 339 Pa. 112, 116. The

Commonwealth assumes partial liability only in cases where the disease developed to the point of disablement after an

[84 Dep. Rep. 

exposure of five or more years, and in such case the Commonwealth's share is payable out of appropriations from the general fund in the State Treasury: Occupational Disease Act, sec. 308, as amended, 77 PS §1408. In cases of total disability, what the employe is entitled to be compensated for is not his loss of wages, but his loss of earning power: Jones v. Philadelphia & Reading Coal & Iron Co., 

154 Pa. Superior Ct. 513, 516; Keiser v. Philadelphia & Reading Coal & Iron Co., 134 Pa. Superior Ct. 104.

Claimant contends that the question is ruled by section 204 of the Occupational Disease Act, 77 PS §1304, which provides, inter alia, that: "The receipt of benefits from any association, society or fund shall not bar . . . the recovery of compensation . . ." As was explained in Zbirowski v. 

J. T. Lewis & Bros. Co., 130 Pa. Superior Ct. 222, 237, that section was directed primarily toward employers' disability plans. In view of the genesis of the provision, we prefer to rest our decision on the ground, also stated in the Zbirowski case, at p. 240, that "There is no statutory provision permitting the allowance of the credit claimed by the defendant in the case". Section 306 (a) of the Workmen's Compensa tion Act, as reënacted June 4, 1937, P. L. 1552, contained a provision terminating the monthly payments for life therein provided for, "if the person receiving compensation accepts other public funds contributed to by the employer which equal or exceed the amount of compensation payments". Although the legislature was cognizant of this provision when it amended and reenacted the act in 1939, because it struck it out, it wrote no such limitation into either the Workmen's Compensation Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 520, or the Occupational Disease Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 566. Arguments drawn from a supposed public policy are futile. There is no public policy as to workmen's compensation or occupational disease compensation except as expressed in the statutes providing for them: Shindledecker v. New Bethlehem Borough et al., 145 Pa. Superior Ct. 77, 

80. "When employer and employe accept compensation legislation their relation in regard to it becomes contractual and their rights are to be determined under its provisions":

1948] 

 McIntyle v. E. J. Lavino & Co. et al., 344 Pa. 163, 168. The courts cannot write into the contract an additional term not authorized by the legislature. Neither the employer nor the insurance carrier has as yet compensated claimant for his loss of earning power; all the employer has done is to pay unemployment taxes which would be payable in any event. To disallow occupational disease compensation for the period in which claimant received unemployment compensation would not only be to allow the employer and the carrier an unearned credit not authorized by statute, but would also, in effect, be sanctioning the diversion of public funds, earmarked for a special purpose, to the relief of the employer's private and independent contractual obligation to pay compensation under an entirely different statute.
