If the unemployment compensation was wrongfully received, the Unemployment Compensation Fund may recover it by civil action in the name of the Commonwealth: 

Unemployment Compensation Law, sec. 804, as amended, 43 

PS §874, read together with section 309, as amended, 43 PS §789. We therefore conclude that the receipt of unemployment compensation does not, in itself and as a matter of law, bar claimant from receiving from the employer or the insurance carrier occupational disease compensation for the same period.

The remaining inquiry is whether claimant is estopped, as to the employer and the carrier, from asserting that he was totally disabled within the meaning of the Occupational Disease Act during the period of time he received unemployment compensation. Whatever representations he may have made on his original application for unemployment compensation need not be considered, because that application was made prior to the date of total disability. We are concerned solely with his receipt of unemployment compensation after the date of total disability, which was based on his certifications on the weekly pay orders that he was able to work and available for work. Since these certifications were not made as formal judicial admissions in the course of the present proceeding, they are not conclusive in the absence of facts constituting an estoppel : 4 Wigmore

[84 Dep. Rep. 

on Evidence, 3d ed., §§1059, 1066; Commonwealth v. Monongahela Bridge Co., 216 Pa. 108, 115-116; Morrett v. Fire 

Association of Phila., 265 Pa. 9, 14; Greek Catholic Congregation v. Wilson Coal Co., 329 Pa. 341, 349; Nusbaum v.

Warwick Hotel Co., 112 Pa. Superior Ct. 277, 282-283. To constitute an estoppel, it must appear that the statement is clearly inconsistent with the evidence sought to be given; that the other party has acted in reliance upon the admission; and that the latter will be injured by allowing the truth of the admission to be disproved; Eldred v. Hazlett's 

Administrator, 33 Pa. 307, 316. A party who relies on an estoppel must establish every essential fact entering into that doctrine by clear, precise and unequivocal evidence: 

Peoples National Bank v. Bartel et al., 128 Pa. Superior Ct. 

128, 131.

The exact language of the certifications does not appear, but it may be assumed that they were substantially in the language of the statutory requirement that claimant be "able to work and available for suitable work": Unemploy ment Compensation Law, sec. 401, as amended, 43 PS §801. 

"Suitable work" is defined by section 4 of the statute, 43 PS §753, as "all work which the employe is capable of performing". In determining what is suitable work, the statute requires that among other factors the "physical fitness" of the employe shall be considered. In Sturdevant 

Unemployment Compensation Case, 158 Pa. Superior Ct. 

548, 561, it was said: "Nor does our statute require that the employe be available for full-time work, or for permanent, as distinguished from temporary, employment. So long as the claimant is ready, willing and able to accept some substantial and suitable work he has met the statutory requirements. By the same token, the availability rule does not necessarily require that a claimant be available for his most recent work or his customary work. It is sufficient if he is able to do some type of work, and there is reasonably op- .portunity for securing such work in the vicinity in which he lives."

1948] 

The certifications of claimant, therefore, were in legal effect simply representations that he was able to do some work, but only such work as he was capable of performing within his limitations. Whether that ability was sufficient to entitle him to the unemployment compensation was a matter which, if contested, could only be decided by applying the tests required by the Unemployment Act and the decisions construing it. If the contest were decided in his favor it would adjudicate only that he had sufficient ability to work to entitle him to the unemployment compensation. 

It would not necessarily be an adjudication that his ability to work was such as to disentitle him to occupational disease compensation, for even a judgment is not conclusive evidence of any matter to be inferred by argument from the judgment: Commonwealth v. Monongahela Bridge Co., 216 Pa. 108, 116. On the contrary, when a claimant applies for occupational disease compensation his right thereto is to be determined, not by the test of ineligibility for unemment compensation, but solely by the decisions of the appellate courts relating to occupational disease or workmen's compensation. Within the meaning of the latter statutes, a claimant may be totally disabled even though he may be able to do casual odd jobs (Forsythe v. Harrison Twp., 157 

Pa. Superior Ct. 433, 436), and even though he has actually earned wages after the disease has disabled him: Jones v. 

Philadelphia & Reading Coal & Iron Co., 154 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 513, 516. So, whether the assertion of total disability for occupational disease compensation purposes is clearly inconsistent with the representations made to the unemployment compensation authorities, is at least open to question.

Be that as it may, there is no evidence that the employer did or refrained from doing anything in reliance on those representations. In fact, there is no evidence that the employer even knew about them until after the present petition was filed. Furthermore, in order to make out an estoppel it must not only be shown that the party relied on the statements but that he had been "substantially injured" by so doing: Schwab v. Edge, 214 Pa. 602, 605. The employer

has shown no such injury. The unemployment compensation paid claimant was not the employer's money; it was the property of the Unemployment Compensation Fund. It is argued that the employer's "experience rating" has been adversely affected and that in turn the employer may have to pay a higher rate of contribution. In answer to this, it is sufficient to say that the rate of contribution to the Unemployment Fund does not depend on the "employer's experience" alone, but on the "State experience" as well. The effect of the receipt of unemployment compensation by this claimant on the employer's contribution rate, if it affected it at all and there is no proof that it has, can only be conjectured and may be extremely insubstantial. "An argument or an inference will not support an estoppel": Peoples 

National Bank v. Bartel et al., 128 Pa. Superior Ct. 128, 131. There is nothing in the record on which to base estoppel in favor of the employer and the insurance carrier. As to them, therefore, the receipt of unemployment compensation and the certifications made in connection therewith were of evidential value only. The weight to be given this evidence was exclusively for the compensation authorities. 

And now, September 13, 1948, the exceptions are dis missed and the order of the Workmen's Compensation Board is affirmed. Judgment is given in favor of claimant and against defendants, Delano Anthracite Collieries Company and Eureka Casualty Company, in the sum of $3,200, together with costs; subject, however, to a credit for the aggregate principal sums of compensation which may have been paid heretofore under this claim; subject also to any termination, modification, suspension or reinstatement justified by the Occupational Disease Act; and subject further to liquidation, at any time and from time to time, of the aggregate installments then due and unpaid, together with interest thereon at the rate of six percent per annum, calculated in accordance with the provisions of the act.

1948] 

 COMMON PLEAS OF SCHUYLKILL COUNTY KOCKER v. LEHIGH NAVIGATION COAL COMPANY, INC. 

Workmen's compensation-Premises of employer-Employe on way home after finishing work.

An award of compensation by the Workmen's Compensation Board to claimant, on account of the death of her husband, employe of defendant, will be reversed where it appears that decedent, who was employed as an outside laborer at defendant's colliery, had finished his day's work and was on his way home when he was struck by a railroad locomotive while walking on the tracks of a railroad, it appearing that the site of the accident was not owned, leased or contracted by defendant but was on the main line of the railroad, at a distance of 190 feet from the breaker where decedent worked and 400 yards from the nearest building used in connection with defendant's operation.

In the Court of Common Pleas of Schuylkill County, November term, 1946, no. 291. Appeal of defendant from award of Workmen's Compensation Board. Sustained. July 26, 1948. 

CURRAN, J.: 

On January 19, 1944, claimant's decedent was employed as an outside laborer at No. 6 Lansford Colliery of defendant corporation.

The no. 6 breaker of defendant company is located on the north side of the main tracks of the Lehigh and New England Railroad Company, in the borough of Summit Hill. 

A path used by employes of the company begins at a point south of the breaker about 400 feet, more or less, from the breaker and extends across property owned by defendant across the main line tracks of the Lehigh and New England Railroad and then extends along other lands of defendant in an irregular line along the east end of the breaker, and then extending around the breaker on its north side in a

westerly direction to a point, and then parallel to the breaker on the west side again to the main tracks of the Lehigh and New England Railroad, and then continuing after crossing said tracks along other property of defendant company in a southwesterly direction to a street designated as Front Street in an adjoining town. 

After completing his employment on January 19, 1944, decedent was on his way home and at a point on the above described path, 190 feet west of the breaker, while walking on the tracks of the Lehigh and New England Railroad, he was struck with a locomotive and killed. The path used by decedent was the most convenient route to his home. While the path itself was not maintained by defendant company, the company had placed concrete pipes in a section where the path had been washed out, and at the request of the employes, had erected a hand-rail over the pipes in order to make it easier for the employes to reach the adjoining higher ground along the path. 

There was a roadway leading from the breaker used by automobiles and employes and available for all of the employes, which highway crossed the main tracks of the Lehigh and New England Railroad by an overhead bridge and traversed a spur track of the Lehigh and New England Railroad and some narrow gauge tracks owned by defendant company.

The roadway was maintained by defendant. To use this route decedent-employe would have had to travel about two miles farther to get to his home. 

There is no dispute as to the facts in the case. Decedent had finished his day's work and was on his way home. The only question to be determined is whether or not he was still on the "premises" of defendant company. The referee and the Workmen's Compensation Board found that decedent was on the "premises" of defendant and engaged in the furtherance of the business of his employer, his presence being required on that part of the premises in which the accident occurred.

1948] 

The appellate courts have frequently defined the word "premises" as used in interpreting section 301 of the Workmen's Compensation Act, and the question whether or not a claimant is on the "premises" of his employer within the meaning of the term as used in the Workmen's Compensation Act is a legal question: Wolske v. American Bridge 

Co., 158 Pa. Superior Ct. 339, 44 A. (2d) 873. "The word 'premises' in the Act is limited to the property of the employer used in connection with the actual place of work where the employer carries on the business in which the employer is engaged. Meucci v. Gallatin Coal Co. et al., 279 Pa. 184, 123 A. 766; . . .": Fedorko v. Pennsylvania 

Electric Co., 161 Pa. Superior Ct. 279, 54 A. (2d) 103; 

Young v. Hamilton Watch Co., 158 Pa. Superior Ct. 448, 45 A. (2d) 261. "In the Molek case the referee found that the place where the claimant was injured was included within the operating premises of the employer and this court held that the referee's finding was 'amply supported by the evidence'. 

Speaking through Judge Cunningham, we stated, at page 

98 of 120 Pa. Superior at page 843 of 181 A.: 'It is, of course, true that the word 'premises' must receive a more narrow definition than that of 'property'. At the same time, we must give a common-sense meaning to the term. The line between what is to be considered premises and what is not must necessarily be drawn in a somewhat arbitrary manner when considering a large mine property. The referee has drawn this line at the state highway. We believe this to be a finding in accord with established facts. Obviously, the premises did not terminate at the actual mouth of the mine": Fedorko v. Pennsylvania Electric Co., supra.

In the case before us the accident did not actually happen on the property of defendant company. The accident occurred on the right of way of the Lehigh and New England Railroad. From the record it would appear that the site of the accident was not owned, leased or controlled by defendant. It is true that the Lehigh and New England Railroad is used by defendant company in shipping its coal

and receiving coal cars, but the record also indicates that the accident occurred on the main line of the Lehigh and New England Railroad, which runs from Hauto, Pa., to 

Campbell City, N. Y., and not on any spur of the railroad that enters the breaker or operation of defendant company, so that it is difficult to conclude that the main track of the Lehigh and New England Railroad forms a component or integral part of defendant's operation.

The line between what is considered "premises" and what is not must necessarily be drawn in a somewhat arbitrary manner when considering a large mine property. The employe at the time of the accident was 190 feet from the breaker and 400 yards from the nearest building located on the south side of the main tracks, and used in connection with the operation of defendant company. He was not on the property of the company at the time he was struck. 

In the case of Shickley v. Philadelphia & Reading Coal 

& Iron Co., 118 Atl. 255, the employe slipped on a loose stone on a path leading to his place of employment 900 feet from the operation of defendant's mine. The path was upon property owned by defendant and habitually used by defendant's employes, there being no bridge to defendant's mine except by this and other paths over defendant's property. It was there determined that the path was not part of the premises of defendant. 

In the recent case of Young v. Hamilton Watch Co., 158 

Pa. Superior Ct. 448, 45 A. (2d) 261, defendant employer maintained a parking lot for the use of its employes. The parking lot was separated from the plant by a public highway. Claimant was injured on a portion of the parking lot and the appellate court determined it was not part of the premises. A similar conclusion was reached in the case of Sheridan v. Glen Alden Coal Co., 160 Pa. Superior Ct. 

115, 50 A. (2d) 540. In the latter case the entrance to the mine was 250 feet from the point on the parking lot where appellant sustained his injury. 

Claimant relies upon the case of Tigue v. Forty Fort Coal 

Co., 264 Pa. 590, 107 Atl. 862, and Tolan v. Philadelphia &

Reading Coal & Iron Co., 270 Pa. 112, 113 Atl. 67.

1948] 

In the Tigue case it would appear from the opinion as reported that the accident to claimant occurred while the employe was traversing a route along the railroad tracks on the property of defendant company, enclosed by a fence. 

And in the Tolan case the accident occurred on a private road leading into the workings of defendant company, the road being located on the property of defendant and maintained by defendant.

We believe the above cases are distinguishable on their facts from the case at bar. We are of the opinion that decedent in this case was not upon the "premises" of defendant at the time he was injured. The appeal is sustained. 

And now, to wit, July 26, 1948, the appeal is sustained and the award of the Workmen's Compensation Board is reversed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD HEUMANN v. PENN BEEF COMPANY Workmen's compensation-Death—Accidental injury-Sufficiency of evidence.

A referee's award to claimant as widow of decedent based on his findings that decedent sustained an injury by accident as a result of stepping on a rusty nail, following which he developed septicemia, will be affirmed where there was evidence by a fellow worker of the decedent that on a certain date he and decedent were in defendant's locker room when decedent pulled off his rubber boot and the witness noticed a red spot on the instep of the foot as to which decedent told him he had stepped on a nail, and that another fellow worker on the date in question heard the decedent make an exclamation and noticed him limping an hour and a half later; there being other evidence to the effect that decedent was in apparent

good health and walked without any disability on the morning of the day in question, that later in the afternoon he was limping and that on the floor of the premises, at the place where he worked, wooden planks with nails and wires were strewn around. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Alessandroni, District No. 1, claim petition no. 106,466, accident no. 

4,830,521. Affirmed. August 4, 1948.

Henry Temin, for claimant. 

J. Paul Erwin, for defendant.

KNOLL, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by defendant from the order of award of 

Referee John Alessandroni, of the First Compensation Dis trict.

On October 8, 1946, claimant, as the widow of Karl Heumann, filed a claim petition on behalf of herself and her minor children, averring, inter alia, that decedent, Karl 

Heumann, sustained certain injuries on May 10, 1946, while acting within the course of his employment with defendant herein, which resulted in his death on May 23, 1946. To this petition a responsive answer was filed by defendant denying the allegations of the said petition. 

Claimant, on her own behalf, testified as to her marriage with Karl Heumann; that two children were born of the said marriage, and that she and the two children were totally dependent upon decedent for support. Claimant further testified that decedent had been employed by defendant herein for a period of two to three years and had worked steadily during that period of time; that on the morning of May 10, 1946, decedent left home on or about 7 a.m., in good spirits and apparently in good health, and returned home about 6:30 p.m. limping, and, in answer to her query, stated that he stepped on a nail while at work. 

Following dinner, decedent went to bed, complaining of

1948] 

 pain in his foot and an examination by the witness disclosed that the foot was swollen with a red spot on the left leg. The following morning decedent went back to work although his foot hurt and he returned home about 4 o'clock, which was earlier than usual, and, previously thereto, had called the witness to arrange for a doctor to come to their home. 

When decedent returned home, he was unable to walk and it was necessary for him to crawl on his knees up the staircase. Decedent was placed in bed where he remained until he was admitted to the hospital on or about May 20, 1946. 

John Montague, a fellow worker of decedent, was called as a witness on behalf of claimant, and testified that, in the establishment of defendant, cattle were kept on the first floor, were slaughtered on the second floor, and were transferred from the first to the second floor by a ramp leading from the first to the second floor. On May 10, 1946, he and decedent were undressing in the locker room maintained by defendant on the second floor of the establishment, when decedent pulled off his rubber boot, and he noticed a red spot in the area of the instep of the foot. He asked decedent what had happened and the decedent said, ". . . he had tread on a nail in the pens," and he advised decedent to see a doctor. The witness was unable to recall whether the red mark was on the right or left foot; and further testified that, immediately prior to the time decedent and he started their usual duties, decedent appeared to be in good health and walked without any apparent disability. 

Dr. Berthold M. Stern, called on behalf of claimant, testified that he first examined claimant on May 11, 1946, which examination disclosed a sore spot on the sole in the midfoot region, a little toward the heel. The doctor made a diagnosis of localized cellulitis. The doctor again examined decedent the following morning, at which time decedent complained of pain in the popliteal region and the doctor administered tetanus antitoxin. The doctor continued to treat decedent thereafter and, while the local condition seemed to heal up superficially, the pain in decedent's knee became more severe and decedent developed a swelling in the left inguinal region together with red spots all over the body. The doctor

then consulted with Dr. Bernstein and arranged for decedent's admission to the hospital. 

Following the death of decedent, an autopsy was performed, and the doctor made a diagnosis of septicemia. The autopsy also revealed that decedent had myocarditis, pericarditis, endocarditis and an overwhelming infection of streptococcus throughout his body. The doctor was of the opinion that the streptococcus entered the body of decedent through the puncture wound which decedent had received prior thereto. The doctor fixed septicemia as the cause of death, and also testified that there was no evidence of infection from any other source. 

Eli A. Goldberg, the general manager and supervisor of defendant company, was called as a witness on behalf of claimant, and testified that there were wooden planks with nails and wires from the bales of hay and straw on the floor of the premises of defendant company; that, on the morning of May 10, 1946, he was driven to work by decedent, who was apparently in good health and walked without any apparent disability, and that later in the afternoon of the same day, he saw decedent limping.

Joe Gratz, a fellow worker of decedent, was called as a witness on behalf of claimant, and testified that, on the morning of May 10, 1946, he changed his clothes at the same time decedent was changing his, and decedent appeared to be in good health, without any marks on his foot or body; that straw and hay, wires from the hay and straw, and nails in the wood were on the floor of defendant's premises; that after lunch he and decedent were driving the cattle out and he heard decedent exclaim, "Oop"; that he noticed decedent limping approximately 12 hours later. The witness further testified that the men at the plant wore rubber boots with light soles and no shoes.

No testimony was offered on behalf of defendant. 

The referee found as a fact that decedent, on May 10, 1946, sustained an injury by accident as a result of stepping on a rusty nail which entered decedent's left foot, causing

1948] 

 decedent to become totally disabled from May 12, 1946, to 

May 23, 1946, on which day decedent died; and that the cause of death was septicemia, resulting from accident heretofore referred to. Based upon said findings of fact, the referee made an appropriate award. From this ruling defendant has appealed.

We have made a careful study of the record and are of the opinion that the ruling of the referee should be affirmed. 

The testimony in this case discloses that decedent had been employed by defendant herein for a period of at least two years, during which period of time decedent was a steady worker and was able to perform his duties without any apparent disability; that, on May 10, 1946, claimant went to work in apparently good health and came home limping and suffering pain in the left foot. It also appears from the testimony that decedent went to work the following morning and endeavored to perform his usual duties, but, by reason of the pain and disability from which he was suffering, he was compelled to terminate his employment at an earlier hour and to return home to obtain medical attention. Following his return home, decedent was confined to his bed and was subsequently removed to a hospital approximately 

10 days after the accident, where he died three days thereafter as a result of septicemia or blood poisoning.

Thus we have a natural sequence of events beginning with the exclamation by decedent of the word "Oop", which is the natural exclamation of a person who steps on a nail or other object, resulting in pain to the individual, following which decedent suffered pain and limped, and died as a result of septicemia. We believe that these events clearly and logically indicate that decedent suffered an accident incurred as the result of stepping on an object while acting within the course of his employment with defendant herein. 

In addition thereto, the uncontradicted evidence is to the effect that, when decedent went to work on the morning of 

May 10, 1946, he was not suffering from any foot injury, and when he returned home, he was limping and there was a bright red spot in the area of the instep of the left foot,

leaving a reasonable and well-balanced mind to conclude that an accident did occur on May 10, 1946, while decedent was acting within the course of his employment with defendant herein.

In addition to this testimony, we have the testimony of decedent's fellow workers to the effect that, on the morning of May 10, 1946, decedent was in good health and was able to walk without any apparent disability and that, following the day's work, decedent's foot was swollen and, in the words of one of the witnesses, required medical attention. 

The medical testimony in this case clearly establishes septicemia as the cause of death; and the fact that the streptococcus germ must enter the body through a break in the skin, and that the germ invaded the body through the puncture wound which the decedent had received. In addition thereto, there is no evidence of any other source of infection. This testimony, in our opinion, was sufficient to establish causal connection between the foot injury and the cause of death.

Defendant has contended that much of the testimony offered on behalf of claimant, to prove the accident, was hearsay evidence and, by reason thereof, was inadmissible. We are of the opinion that sufficient direct and circumstantial evidence was presented to warrant a finding that decedent sustained an accident within the meaning of the Workmen's 

Compensation Act, resulting in decedent's death. Therefore, hearsay evidence, relevant and material to the issue and consistent therewith, may be considered for the additional light, if any, that it throws on the entire matter and the referee did not err in admitting this testimony. 

Considering the testimony in its entirety, we are of the opinion that sufficient testimony was presented to warrant the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of award. See Lambing v. Consolidation Coal Co., 161 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 346, and Ceccato v. Union Collieries Co., 141 

Pa. Superior Ct. 440.

We, therefore, affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of award. 

The appeal of defendant is dismissed.

1948] 

 WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD DOYLE v. I. T. E. CIRCUIT BREAKER CO. 

Workmen's compensation—Accidental injury—Unusual move 

-Injury to knee. 

1. A referee's award based on his finding that claimant suffered a torn cartilage of his knee as a result of an accident will be set aside where claimant's testimony was to the effect that while kneeling on his left knee with his right foot on the ground in the course of his employment by defendant, he made a "quick" turn to the left to get a tool and that as he did so his right knee locked, there being further evidence that claimant had a "trick" right knee acquired as the result of a prior injury; under the evidence, claimant's quick turn to pick up a tool could not be considered of itself an accident. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Clayton, District No. 1, claim petition no. 112,284, accident no. 5,186,470. 

Reversed. October 27, 1948. 

Liberty Mutual Ins. Co., insurance carrier. 

Philip J. Franzese, for claimant. 

J. Paul Erwin, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal from an award entered by Referee 

Clayton on May 8, 1948.

The undisputed facts in this case indicate that claimant, Andrew Doyle, had a "trick" right knee acquired in a basketball game during the 1946-1947 season; that on February 13, 1948, while kneeling on his left knee with his right foot on the ground in the course of his employment with defendant, the I. T. E. Circuit Breaker Co., he made a "quick" turn to the left to get a tool or welding rod; that as he did so his right knee locked; that he immediately ceased work, reported to defendant's dispensary, was ex-

amined by his family physician, then by the physician of defendant's insurance carrier and finally operated upon at the Chestnut Hill Hospital on March 8, 1948; and that he returned to work without loss of earning power on March 29, 1948. It may here be noted that the original injury to the knee was sustained while claimant was playing on a team supported by defendant. 

At the hearing in the case claimant was the only witness called. No supporting medical testimony was offered. Yet, as objected to by defendant, the referee has conjured a diagnosis of "torn cartilage" of the right knee in his second finding of fact. This is an untenable position. Where a preëxisting condition is a factor, competent and unequivocal medical testimony is necessary: Schubert v. Oswald & Hess, 

161 Pa. Superior Ct. 309. Incidentally, claimant paid his doctor bill out of his own pocket and his hospital bill was covered almost entirely by Blue Cross insurance. 

Aside from the above, however, we believe that the principal issue relates to the nature of the occurrence alleged as an accident. In this phase of the matter we disagree with the referee. It is our opinion that the quick turn to the left to pick up material or a tool cannot be considered in and of itself an accident. The motion was voluntary and there are no concomitant circumstances to show emergency or stress or that the position from which it was made was unusual. It is true that we have held certain quick reactions to constitute an accident (Harris v. Abbotts Dairies, Inc., 26 W. C. B. 55-1945) but only when the situation which necessitated them contained the elements of a fortuitous incident. In the last analysis, then, this case, as defendant contends, is ruled by the principle enunciated in Adamchick v. Wyoming Collieries Co., 131 Pa. Superior Ct. 72, and compensation must be denied. As claimant states, by reason of his views on substantial justice, defendant may have in some measure, maybe morally, been responsible for his acquisition of a "trick" knee but our system of jurisprudence does not follow that principle. We are bound by the law and the claim thereunder in this case has not been

1948] 

 proved. The basketball game injury is not being tried in this instance and we feel certain that the onset of disability as of the date alleged was unquestionably a recurrence of the condition occasioned by claimant's former mishap. We do not think that the "quick" turn to which he has testified was an aggravating factor. 

The first, third and fifth findings of fact and first conclusion of law of Referee Clayton dated May 18, 1948, are affirmed.

The second finding of fact of Referee Clayton of the same date is modified, deleting therefrom the words "and suffered a torn cartilage".

The fourth finding of fact of the same date is modified by deleting therefrom the words "as a result of the accident of 

February 13, 1948". 

The following finding of fact is supplied: 

Finding of fact 6. Claimant has not proved that he was disabled by accidental injury on February 13, 1948.

The second conclusion of law, award and bill of expense of Referee Clayton dated May 18, 1948, are vacated and set aside and the following substituted therefor: 

Conclusion of law 

2. Since claimant has not proved an accidental injury in the course of his employment with defendant on February 13, 1948, his disability complained of is not compensable. Order The petition filed in this case on March 29, 1948, is hereby dismissed. 

The appeal is sustained.

[84 Dep. Rep. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD VERNOSKY v. BUCK RUN COLLIERY CO. 

Workmen's compensation-Death-Cause-Sufficiency of evidence. 

A referee's order dismissing a claim for death will be affirmed where there was evidence that claimant's husband was found dead between car rails in a mine operated by defendant where decedent was employed, there being no further evidence of any unusual event which could have caused or contributed to the death. 

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Enter line, District No. 5, claim petition no. 112,024, accident no. 

5,179,967. Dismissed. October 27, 1948.

Lackawanna Casualty Company, insurance carrier. 

Isadore E. Krasno, for plaintiff.

Penrose Hertzler, for defendant. 

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal from an order entered by Referee 

Enterline April 8, 1948 dismissing a death claim.

Claimant, Mary Vernosky, is the dependent widow of Harry Vernosky who on March 10, 1947 was found lying dead between car rails in a mine operated by defendant, the Buck Run Colliery Co. The claim petition filed March 

8, 1948 gives the cause of death as a heart attack by way of restatement from the death certificate covering the case and alleges exposure to smoke and fumes as the accident. 

Defendant filed an answer in the nature of a general denial on March 19, 1948.

At the hearing in the case nothing of a substantial nature was presented as proof in support of the claim. All that claimant could testify to was that the decedent was a man in apparent good health up to the time of his death. She obviously had no knowledge of any unusual happening

1948] 

 which could have caused or contributed to the fatality. In this phase of the matter she called two of the decedent's fellow workmen, John Wartella and Harry Loyko. These witnesses could only testify that they found the decedent lying dead and both of them stated that they found no marks of any kind on the body. 

With so little to go on there was nothing for the referee to do but dismiss the claim. The collapse of an employe while at work does not create a presumption that death is accidental (York v. State Workmen's Insurance Fund, 131 

Pa. Superior Ct. 496). In the absence of eye witnesses there must be circumstantial evidence sufficient to satisfy reasonable and well balanced minds (Piatrowski v. Dey Co., 123 

Pa. Superior Ct. 29). The burden was on claimant to prove death by accidental means (Doloff v. Wilkie Buick Co., 158 

Pa. Superior Ct. 453) and the evidence we have reviewed is so barren in this regard that we must agree with the action taken by the referee.

The findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of 

Referee Enterline dated April 28, 1948 are affirmed. 

The appeal is dismissed.

SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA LYNN v. POTTSVILLE BOX CORPORATION Workmen's compensation — Hernia Descent immediately following Findings by board — Effect of. 

accident 

An order of the court below awarding claimant compensation for disability as the result of a hernia sustained in the course of his employment will be affirmed, although the order reversed a decision of the compensation board, where the case turned on the determination whether the hernia was at once precipitated and whether it followed the cause without intervening time within the meaning of section 306 (b) of the Workmen's Compensation Act, as amended by the Act of June 21, 1939, and where the findings of the board did not reveal when the hernia was precipitated but only that in the opinion of the

board it was not precipitated according to the statutory requirements; in such case where the material facts found by the board established that the hernia was compensable, a so-called finding of fact by the board that the hernia was not at once precipitated by the accident, was a conclusion of law without binding effect upon the court. 

Appeal from judgment of the Court of Common Pleas of 

Schuylkill County, March term, 1943, no. 147. Judgment affirmed. November 9, 1948. Superior Court of Pennsylvania, October term, 1948, no. 2. 

Henry Houck, for appellee.

E. MacTroutman and Penrose Hertzler, for appellant. 

DITHRICH, J.: 

In this workmen's compensation case the learned judges of the court below sitting en banc reversed the decision of the referee which had been affirmed by the board and awarded claimant compensation. The claim has been pending eight years. It has been before the board three times and before the Court of Common Pleas of Schuylkill County twice. Claimant sustained a hernia in the course of his employment, and the sole question involved is whether it is compensable under section 306 (h) of the Workmen's Compensation Act of 1915, P. L. 736, as amended by the Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 520.

The compensation authorities have consistently held that it is not compensable. They rely on the referee's seventh and eighth findings of fact which have been affirmed by the board. They are: "7. We further find that the hernia was not at once precipitated by the occurrence on August 20, 1940. "8. We further find that the descent of the hernia did not follow the cause without intervening time." (Italics supplied.)

In its opinion affirming the action of the referee, the board states in part:

1948] 

"Claimant has presented no testimony showing that his hernia was at once precipitated by the strain of his lifting and that the hernia descended without intervening time. 

Beyond his testimony that he first noticed the hernial lump on August 21, 1940, we have no evidence indicating the time of descent."

As we shall later point out, that would be sufficient evidence of descent within a reasonable time, which is all that is required under the 1939 amendment. 

The court, in reversing the board and allowing the claim, said: "The evidence offered in this case does not sustain the seventh and eighth finding [s] of fact and the second Conclusion of Law . . ." It is as follows: "2. Claimant having failed to establish by incontrovertible proof that the hernia was at once precipitated or that it followed the cause without intervening time, we conclude that claimant's petition must be dismissed and compensation denied. . . ." The words which we have italicized in quoting the referee's findings of fact are taken verbatim from section 306 (h), the new language in the Act of 1939 being in italics and the supplanted words of the earlier act being in brackets.* The board and the learned court below both fell into error in treating the referee's seventh and eighth findings of fact as such, when they are literally conclusions of law based on an incorrect or improper application of the law to the facts. 

The material facts as found by the referee and affirmed by the board are as follows: Claimant on August 20, 1940, while stacking rolls of paper in his employer's stockroom, suffered a "severe strain, in that the rolls which he was then * "Hernia shall be considered as a physical weakness or ailment, which ordinarily develops gradually, and shall not be compensable, unless incontrovertible [conclusive] proof is offered that the hernia was at once [immediately] precipitated by sudden effort or severe strain and that: first, the descent of the hernia followed the cause without intervening time [immediately]; second, there was actual pain in the hernial region at the time of the descent; third, the above manifestations were of such severity they were noticed at once [immediately] by the claimant, necessitating immediate cessation of work, and communicated to the employer or a representative of the employer within forty-eight hours after the occurrence of the accident."

was stacking were heavier than the ones he generally worked upon..."; they weighed approximately 175 to 180 pounds per roll; the ordinary paper weighed about 120 pounds. He reported to his foreman that he had "a distressed feeling in the back". He "ceased work for about ten minutes white and . . . looked sick. About an hour later he vomited". He continued to work that day and the next on the evening thereof, namely, August 21st, went home "feeling sick with pain. While bathing himself that evening, he noticed a lump in his right inguinal region. He then went to the office of Dr. Wm. A. Burke, who diagnosed his condition as a right inguinal hernia. At or about eight o'clock on the morning of the 22nd he reported the hernia to his foreman". (Italics supplied.)

Appellant has made much of an apparent confusion by claimant and Dr. Burke as to the date on which Dr. Burke first saw him. In his surgeon's report, Dr. Burke reported it as August 23rd, but his office record shows it was August 

21st. Claimant first said he went to see the doctor three days after the occurrence, but later corrected it to one day. 

His foreman testified that he reported the hernia to him on the morning of August 22nd, which was within 48 hours as required by the act, and in any event the referee found that claimant "noticed a lump" on the twenty-first and that he "then went" to the office of Dr. Burke. He further found as a fact that claimant reported his hernia to his foreman on the morning of the twenty-second; and, to make the findings consistent, "then" must be taken to mean August 

21st. If taken to mean August 23rd, it would be inconsistent with the referee's other findings. 

Appellant seeks to make it appear that when Dr. Burke first examined claimant on August 21, 1940, "he found a 'sac' which was at least a month old". The record discloses that the surgeon made that discovery on October 9, 1940, when he operated on claimant, and not on August 21, 1940, as appellant would have us believe. 

In Hopp v. Taub, 117 Pa. Superior Ct. 55, 177 Atl. 214, where claimant first discovered a "lump" two days after the happening of an accident and the injury was not diagnosed

1948] 

 as a hernia until three days later, but claimant's employer had been notified within 48 hours of the happening of the accident, the court said (page 58): "Here, the evidence does not show that the 'descent of the hernia immediately followed the cause'. On the other hand, it does rebut the statutory presumption that the hernia from which this claimant suffered was a 'physical weakness or ailment' which developed gradually. . . . In this case we have proof of an accident and of pain immediately following the slipping of the barrel while being unloaded by claimant and a fellow workman from the truck. By reason of the severity of the pain, claimant was obliged to quit work and return to his home. When visited there by his employer, within forty-eight hours, claimant communicated to him the fact that the accident had occurred and that he was suffering from pains in his 'stomach'."

That case arose prior to the 1939 amendment, but in 

Drumbar v. Jeddo-Highland Coal Co., 155 Pa. Superior Ct. 

57, 37 A. 2d 25, where appellant's principal argument was that certain differences in the language in section 306 (h) of the Act of 1939 and the earlier Hernia Amendment of 1937 indicated an intention on the part of the legislature to impose, by the Act of 1939, a greater burden of proof than was required by the earlier act, it was held (pp. 59-60): "With the single exception that an entirely new element of proof was introduced by the Act of 1939, viz., that the manifestations of the hernia must necessitate immediate cessation of work, the differences in the language are, in our opinion, insignificant. [That new element of proof is not lacking in the instant case.] We have already held there is no substantial difference between incontrovertible proof and conclusive proof (Grant v. Wark Construction Co., 152 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 214, 31 A. 2d 739); by the use of these expressions it was not intended that proof must be either incontrovertible or conclusive in the literal sense. Such a construction would make it virtually impossible for an employe to secure compensation for a hernia. When given a reasonable construction (Stat. Const. Act of May 28, 1937, P. L.

1019 art. IV, §52, 46 PS 552), they mean merely 'clear and convincing proof.' [Citing cases.] (Italics applied.) "In the new act, proof is required that the hernia was 'at once' precipitated, that the descent followed the cause 'without intervening time' and that the manifestations of the hernia were noticed 'at once', whereas the earlier act used the word 'immediately'. We think there is no substantial difference between 'at once' and 'without intervening time' on the one hand and 'immediately' on the other. The standard dictionaries indicate no appreciable difference. We have held that 'immediately' does not mean instantaneously, but within a reasonable time; that for a hernia to be compensable it is not necessary to prove that the injured workman removed his clothing and discovered it on the spot but he is within the requirements of the law where it was noticed for the first time several hours afterwards."

It was further held that an immediate cessation of work for "two or three minutes" was sufficient to meet the requirement of the amendment. Here, the referee found as a fact that claimant had immediately ceased work for 10 minutes.

The case turns then on a determination of whether the hernia was "at once" precipitated, and whether it followed the cause "without intervening time" within the meaning of section 306 (h) of the amendment of 1939. 

The findings, which the learned court below held were not sustained by the evidence, are negative, not positive, and are phrased in the exact language of the statute. They do not reveal when the hernia was precipitated, but only that in the opinion of the referee and the board it was not precipitated according to the statutory requirement. They are not supported by any affirmative testimony, but rest rather on an inference that since claimant himself did not notice any abdominal swelling or protrusion until the day following the accident, it had not descended "at once". In the recent case of Nemonich v. Pittsburgh Coal Co., 161 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 239, 54 A. 2d 73, speaking through Rhodes, P. J., we said (p. 242) :

1948] 

"It is not necessary that claimant should himself be aware of, or notice, the protrusion. Romesburg v. Gallatin Market et al., supra, 114 Pa. Superior Ct. 388, 393, 174 A. 805.

In the Romesburg case the claimant did not notice the hernia, but the company doctor who examined claimant within forty-eight hours after the accident saw the hernia, although the doctor did not inform claimant of his condition. We said (114 Pa. Superior Ct. 388, at page 394, 174 A. 805, at page 

807): "That a protrusion must exist is one of the conditions of the act if it is a hernia of the character intended to be covered by the amendment but the protrusion may not have been such as the employe could have discovered, yet if notice of the protrusion comes to the employer either through the employe or his representative or is observed by the employer or notice thereof is communicated to him or to his representative, we believe the act has been complied with."" 

What we said, speaking through Judge Hirt, in Davis v. 

Jones & Laughlin Steel Corp., 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 133, 136, 42 A. 2d 83, is most appropriate here: "In this case under the findings, every statutory presumption against an award has been overcome. And the facts which remove the presumption constitute 'incontrovertible proof' within the intent of the amendment (Grant v. Wark 

Const. Co., 152 Pa. Superior Ct. 214, 31 A. 2d 749); there is no denial of them. Since the hernia was precipitated by sudden effort or severe strain, a pure question of law is presented in this appeal which requires a reversal of the judgment."

Whether on the facts as found by the compensation authorities claimant is entitled to compensation is a question of law and as such open to review: Strunk v. E. D. Huffman & Sons, 144 Pa. Superior Ct. 429, 19 A. 2d 539. In that case this court said, in an opinion by Rhodes, J., now P. J. (p. 436): "Appellant has discussed at length and criticized the opinion of the court below. We are not necessarily concerned with the court's comments on the findings of fact or appellant's criticisms of some of the statements in the opinion,

for we all agree that the conclusion of the court below that deceased was in the course of his employment when fatally injured was correct, and followed from the facts found by the compensation authorities. It was proper to enter judgment for claimant. Berlin v. Crawford, 86 Pa. Superior Ct. 283; 

Hein v. Ludwig, 118 Pa. Superior Ct. 152, 157, 179 A. 917." 

See Buck v. Arndt, 153 Pa. Superior Ct. 632, 34 A. 2d 823.

In Hein v. Ludwig, supra, the referee made no award and the evidence did not show clearly the full amount of claimant's wages at the time of accident. For that reason the record was remitted with direction to make a definite award. 

But here, all the evidence necessary for framing an award was before the court and, since the amount was not in controversy, the court was justified in making the award. To send the case back for that purpose would only have further delayed a cause already too long delayed. 

Judgment affirmed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD LACAVAGE v. STATE WORKMEN'S INSURANCE FUND ET AL. 

Workmen's compensation-Dependency-Wife separated from husband 

-Failure to show support.

A petition for compensation by claimant as dependent widow of a decedent was properly dismissed by the referee, where it appeared that claimant had separated from decedent in 1937; that she had obtained a support order on her husband in 1944 and that in 1945 she had received the sum of $2,000 upon agreement that she would not seek support from her husband and that she had not received any support from him after that date until the time of his death two years later in 1947; under the circumstances claimant failed to show she was actually dependent upon her husband at the time of his death and was then receiving from him a substantial portion of her support.

1948] 

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Foust, specially presiding in District No. 5, claim petition no. 

110,120, accident no. 4,863,560. Dismissed. October 20, 1948. 

Roger J. Dever, for claimant. 

Ralph H. Behney, for defendant.

KNOLL, Commissioner: 

On September 11, 1947, claimant filed a petition alleging that her husband, William Lacavage, died on May 15, 1947, from anthraco-silicosis and that she was the dependent widow of the deceased. The referee dismissed her petition upon concluding as a matter of law that claimant was not a dependent within the contemplation of The Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act. This appeal of claimant followed.

Claimant's right to compensation is determined by section 307 (8) of the act, which provides: "No compensation shall be payable under this section to a widow, unless she was living with her deceased husband at the time of his death, or was then actually dependent upon him and receiving from him a substantial portion of her support." 

It is not sufficient to show that a wife living apart from her husband was actually dependent upon him at the time of his death; she is also required to show affirmatively that she was receiving from him a substantial portion of her support at the time of his death: Kelly v. Star Auto Painting 

Co., 161 Pa. Superior Ct. 503.

In this case, the record establishes that claimant had separated from her husband in 1937; that divorce proceedings were initiated by the husband in 1941; and that later, in 1941, an agreement for alimony at the rate of $50 per month was entered into by counsel for the parties. On 

April 3, 1944, claimant obtained an order of court directing the husband to pay her the sum of $50 per month as alimony pendente lite from April 7, 1941, less $150 already paid. 

On May 10, 1945, the order of court was revoked upon agreement and stipulation of counsel for the parties. The

record further shows, from admissions of claimant, that she received $2,000 on May 10, 1945, upon agreement that she would not seek support from her husband, and that she had not received any support from him from May 10, 1945, to the time of his death on May 15, 1947.

Claimant has failed to show that she was actually dependent upon her husband at the time of his death and was then receiving from him a substantial portion of her support. 

She had repudiated her right to support and had not received any support for more than two years prior to the 

Idate of her husband's death.

Accordingly, the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of dismissal are affirmed. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD DEE v. I. T. E. CIRCUIT BREAKER COMPANY Workmen's compensation-Hernia-Accidental injury-Lifting. 

An award for disability from inguinal hernia will be sustained where claimant's evidence was to the effect that he had to lift a welding gun weighing approximately 40 pounds about five feet, that a counterbalance normally used to facilitate the handling of the welding gun was not working very well, that the services of a helper were usually called for and that when he straightened himself up, after lifting, he felt pain subsequently diagnosed as hernia. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Alessandroni, District No. 1, claim petition no. 107,578, accident no. 

4,934,867. Appeal dismissed. February 11, 1948.

Bernard I. Shovlin, for plaintiff. 

J. Paul Erwin, for defendant.

1948] 

 JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by defendant, the I. T. E. Circuit Breaker

Company, from an award for hernial disability entered by 

Referee Alessandroni on September 16, 1947. 

Claimant in the case is Frank J. Dee and the incident he has alleged as an accident occurred on November 15, 1946, which fell on a Friday. The following Monday morning, he reported to his foreman that his back was hurting him, presented a certificate from his own physician, Dr. Carl M.

Winter, and requested lighter work. Later the same morning he saw Dr. Herbert Shimer, the plant physician, after which he finished his work for the day at 4:30 in the afternoon.

Much of claimant's testimony at the first hearing in the case, held April 22, 1947, has to do with the nature of the occurrence to which he attributed his trouble. He explained that he had to lift a welding gun, weighing approximately 40 pounds, about five feet to get it up over a form in preparing to weld some cleats. There was a counterbalance to facilitate the handling of the gun and claimant stated that it had not been working very well. He insisted he had complained of this to his foreman but it was difficult to get him to make a direct statement to the effect that the recalcitrance of the counterbalance was involved in the lifting incident which is alleged to have caused his disability. He finally stated that though the counterbalance was working to some extent, he could not get enough lift out of it. Another point in his testimony to be noted is his declaration that the handling of the particular gun involved, usually called for the services of a helper but that he was working alone under pressure to complete the week's production. The pain from the injury did not make itself felt so much at the time of the lifting as when he straightened himself up afterwards.

The medical testimony was introduced through Dr. Winters and, at a second hearing held on September 10, 1947, through Dr. Charles S. Shafer, who operated on November 

26, 1946, to correct a right direct inguinal hernia and a

smaller bulge on the left side. Dr. Winters was unwilling to express an opinion. His only specialty was obstetrics. 

Dr. Shafer, faced with a hypothetical question containing all the facts reasonably to be inferred from the evidence, finally did express a competent opinion in the words "I think it did", after attempting to stay on the safer ground of possibility and probability (see Elonis v. Lytle Coal Co., 134 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 264). He was equally definite on crossexamination.

On appeal defendant relies upon the construction of the law which has revived the necessity of proving the happening of a truly fortuitous event and has thrown into some confusion the principles followed in earlier cases basing an award on a twist or sprain suffered while doing regular work in the usual way (Crispin v. Leedom and Worrall Co., 341 Pa. 325, and cases therein cited). Claimant points to 

Bird v. Brown, 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 49, wherein a workman twisted himself while unloading a truck under pressure of time without the help that such effort usually warranted. 

The happening in that case occurred on September 9, 1938, during the time that the law (Act of June 4, 1939, P. L. 1552) did not contain the strict statutory requirements with relation to proof and, except for the 48-hour notice provisions which has been reënacted (Act of May 18, 1945, P. L. 671, sec. 306 H), the law on the subject must be construed as much the same now. We think the cases are parallel to a sufficient degree and that the award in the present instance must therefore be sustained. In the Bird case the court said "While working under unusual conditiones he (claimant) turned his body when lifting a heavy load and suffered a strain, which resulted in a hernia." In the case before us the load being lifted was heavy enough (Camilli v. Penna. 

Railroad, 135 Pa. Superior Ct. 510) and was being hoisted without the assistance of the usual helper or the inefficient counterbalance. Hence the fortuitous element in the matter. 

As to notice within 48 hours (Act of 1945, supra) we cannot overlook the fact that the statutory period expired on Sunday, a holiday. Under the circumstances notice on 

Monday morning was soon enough (76 PS § 172).

1948] 

In conclusion we must state that we do not think the present status of the referee's findings of fact are quite sufficient. There should have been reference to evidence showing freedom from hernia prior to the incident which forms the basis of this case. Also the description of accidental elements should have been more complete. We will cure this oversight to the best of our ability by supplemental findings. 

The findings of fact, conclusions of law, award and bill of expenses of Referee Alessandroni, as hereinafter supplemented, are affirmed. 

Findings of fact 9. The lifting of the gun as above set forth was done on tiptoe, under pressure of hastened production, without the assistance of a helper as was usual, and accompanied by failure of operation of a faulty counterbalance. 

10. Claimant had never, before the incident complained of as an accident, known himself to have a hernial lump in his groin. 

The appeal is dismissed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD MILLER v. C. H. WHEELER MANUFACTURING CO. 

Workmen's compensation—Partial disability not reflected in loss of earnings.

A referee's award of compensation to claimant based on a finding of 20 percent partial disability will be set aside and compensation payments will be suspended where it appears that claimant suffered an injury to the right index finger, which did not amount to loss of use of the finger and where claimant's weekly earnings upon his return to work were substantially the same as his average weekly wage, at the time of his accident.

Appeal by defendant from order of Referee Clayton, District No. 1, dismissing petition for termination under com-

pensation agreement no. 5,084,835. Sustained. October 27, 1948.

American Mutual Liability Insurance Co., insurance carrier. 

Wm. V. Mullin, for plaintiff. 

Frederick L. Fuges, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal from an order entered by Referee Clayton on May 5, 1948, dismissing a petition for termination filed by defendant, C. H. Wheeler Manufacturing Co., on

March 4, 1948, and awarding compensation to claimant, Robert Miller, on a 20 percent partial disability basis. A cross-appeal, with which we will deal in a separate opinion, raises the question as to whether or not the referee erred in not awarding compensation to claimant for loss of use of a right index finger.

The accident in the case involved the tool of a lathe. It occurred August 25, 1947, and, according to an agreement entered into under date of September 8, 1947, resulted in multiple lacerations of the right hand. Claimant immediately came under the care of Dr. John Hand, who at first debrided the wounds, and then after an intervening infection repaired the tendons affecting the index finger, as best he could, in an operation performed September 29, 1947.

Claimant returned to work December 8, 1947, and has been employed ever since operating a milling machine.

At the hearing the question posed had to do with whether or not there was residual partial disability or loss of use of the right index finger, claimant contending for the latter and defendant denying that either condition prevailed and as to these questions Dr. Hand, called by claimant, and C. F. 

Brooks, defendant's personnel manager, were the most important witnesses. Dr. Hand at first stated that claimant had sustained a total loss of the index finger but later on in

1948] 

 his testimony admitted that there was partial motion in all of the joints of the member involved and that the situation was not comparable to one in which amputation would be indicated. Brooks testified as to claimant's earning record subsequent to the return to work stating that claimant's hourly rate of pay increased from $1.35 prior to injury to $1.45 after reëmployment. Claimant in his own behalf testified that there was some significance in the change of work from his lathe to a milling machine particularly with regard to the necessity for help but could not deny that the difference was minimal. 

On appeal defendant rightly calls attention to Dr. Hand's admission that the use of claimant's finger was not lost to such an extent as to be equivalent to surgical removal (Bauman v. Spokas, 146 Pa. Superior Ct. 530), to the misconception entertained by Dr. Hand relative to "industrial" loss of use of a member (Snyder v. Hoffman, 159 Pa. Superior Ct. 

392) and to the uncontrovertible portent of claimant's earning record after he returned to work. 

We fully agree with the position taken by defendant on the first two phases of the issue, both of which relate more intimately to claimant's appeal. We will deal more particularly here, however, with the last point suggested, which has to do with earning power measured by wage periods. 

Prior to injury claimant earned for four consecutive 

13-week wage quarters $671.50, $731.91, $687.13 and $545.40. Taking the most favorable quarter his compensation was set by agreement in accordance with a calculated average weekly wage of $56.30 and this must be accepted as the gauge of his earning power under the clear terms of the act (77 PS § 582). There were only two working days remaining in the week that he returned to work and for these he was paid $23.20. For the following 13-week period he had a weekly earning overage of $54.40 but for the last 

13-week period of which Brooks had a record claimant averaged $56.73, which is in excess of the figure upon which his compensation was calculated. Under such circumstances it cannot be said that the slight physical disability which remains because of the condition of claimant's right index

finger is reflected in a loss of earning power. In our opinion, then, the case calls for the application of the rule in Scipani v. Pressed Steel Car Co. (150 Pa. Superior Ct. 410), and in applying that rule we are also disposed to find that claimant suffers slight disability of an undetermined degree rather than 20 percent over-all disability.

The first, second and third findings of fact of Referee 

Clayton dated May 5, 1948, are affirmed.

The fourth finding of fact, conclusion of law and order of Referee Clayton of the same date are vacated and set aside and the following substituted therefor: 

Findings of fact 4. Claimant still suffers a slight disability of undetermined degree. 

5. Claimant's disability is not reflected in any loss of earning power. 

Conclusion of law

Since claimant suffers a slight undetermined degree of disability not reflected in any loss of earning power compensation must be suspended.

Order The prayer of defendant's petition for termination is denied but compensation payments under the agreement in this case are hereby suspended as of December 8, 1947. 

The appeal is sustained.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD MILLER v. C. H. WHEELER MANUFACTURING CO. 

Workmen's compensation-Specific loss-Finger-Partial motion. 

Medical testimony that claimant suffered an injury to his right index finger, so that there was only 20 percent motion in the metacarpal phalangeal joint and 15 percent motion in the proximal and terminal interphalangeal joints would not sustain a finding of loss of use of the

1948] 

 finger, especially where it was admitted that the claimant was better off than he would be if the finger had been amputated. 

Appeal by claimant from order of Referee Clayton, District No. 1, dismissing petition for termination under compensation agreement no. 5,084,835. Dismissed. October 27, 1948.

American Mutual Liability Ins. Co., insurance carrier. 

William V. Mullin, for plaintiff. 

Frederick L. Fuges, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by claimant, Robert Miller, from an order for payments of partial disability compensation entered by Referee Clayton on May 5, 1948. A cross-appeal by defendant, C. H. Wheeler Manufacturing Co., has been dealt with in a separate opinion to be published herewith. 

The facts in the case, set forth more fully in our other opinion, above referred to, have to do with an accident occurring August 25, 1947, in which claimant's right hand was lacerated by a lathe tool; with an agreement entered into to cover immediate disability; with claimant's return to work at a commensurate wage on December 8, 1947, and with the ultimate consequences signalizing claimant's condition with regard to compensability as of the time defendant requested termination in its petition filed March 4, 1948. 

In this appeal claimant contends that he should have been awarded compensation for the loss of use of a right index finger rather than for partial disability, but as suggested in our opinion in the cross-appeal, supra, we cannot agree. The evidence on the issue which is most important was introduced through Dr. John Hand, the attending physician. On direct examination Dr. Hand testified that there was a total loss of the finger but cross-examination brought out a different situation. He thought that, by reason of the condition of the index finger and the presence of scar tissue in

the palmar surface of the right hand, there was a 50 percent impairment in the use of the hand but admitted that so far as the injured finger was concerned there was 20 percent motion in the metacarpal phalangeal joint and 15 percent motion in the proximal and terminal interphalangeal joints. He seemed to base his opinion as to the loss of use of the index finger on the grounds of functional awkwardness and readily admitted that claimant was better off than he would be if the finger had been amputated. This settles the matter so far as our understanding of the law is concerned. The loss of use has not been "practically equivalent to removal" (Bauman v. Spokas, 146 Pa. Superior Ct. 

530) and compensation under section 306 (c) of the Act of 

May 18, 1945, P. L. 671, is out of the question.

By reference our findings and conclusions set forth in our opinion to be published herewith in the cross-appeal as hereinafter supplemented, are restated as applicable in the present instance and so adjudged. 

Finding of fact 

5. Claimant did not sustain a loss or loss of use of his right index finger. 

The appeal is dismissed.

SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA MICHALSKY v. UNEMPLOYMENT COMPENSATION BOARD OF REVIEW Unemployment compensation-Voluntary unemployment-Employe— 

Imprisonment for refusal to comply with support order.

Where a claimant was confined to jail for a period of six months because of noncompliance with a support order and deliberately prolonged his term in jail in defiance of the court, which had committed him for contempt and failure to comply with the order, the effect of his voluntary unemployment under the circumstances amounted to an abandonment of his employment and the termination of relationship

1948] 

 of employer and employe, so that he was disqualified from receiving benefits under section 402 (b) of the Unemployment Compensation Law. 

Appeal from decision of the Unemployment Compensation 

Board of Review, appeal no. B-44-93-K-3497, decision no. 

B-14243. Order affirmed November 10, 1948. Superior Court of Pennsylvania, October term, 1948, no. 78.

E. MacTroutman and Penrose Hertzler, for intervener. 

William L. Hammond, Special Deputy Attorney General, and T. McKeen Chidsey, Attorney General, for appellee. 

HIRT, J.: 

Claimant, appellant here, had been employed by Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company as a miner in the Maple Hill Colliery for many years. December 7, 1946, was his last working day. On that date his person was attached and he was committed to Schuylkill County Jail because he then was $55 in arrears in his payments on a court order under which he was obliged to pay $70 monthly for the support of his wife and six of his nine children who were under 16 years of age. His regular average earnings were then, and for some time had been almost $53 per week. Claimant remained in jail until June 2, 1947, when he contacted his attorney and was released. He then was able to work and he immediately reported at Maple Hill Colliery for reëmployment. During the whole of the six months' period of claimant's incarceration, Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company, his employer, had no knowledge of his whereabouts, with the result that in the interval he had been replaced by another employe and no work was available for him at the colliery upon his release from jail. He thereupon filed claims for unemployment compensation benefits. These were denied by the bureau on a finding that "claimant was responsible for his idleness" and was ineligible for benefits within the meaning of section 402(b) of the Unemployment Compen sation Law of December 5, 1936, Second Ex. Sess., P. L.

[84 Dep. Rep. 

[1937] 2897, as amended, 43 PS §802. The decision of the bureau was affirmed by the referee on a like finding that claimant had voluntarily left his employment without good cause. On further appeal the board of review affirmed the findings and decision of the referee. In the course of its opinion the board held: "An essential element of the employment relationship is the regular attendance by the employe in order that the employer's business be not disrupted. Where an individual is unable to report for work, it is incumbent upon him in order to maintain the employment relationship to make a reasonable effort to notify his employer when he is compelled to be absent and to give some indication of when he expects to be able to return."

The board in effect also found that claimant did not make a "sufficient effort to communicate with his employer" during his six months' term in jail, and concluded: "The claimant by his voluntary act in having failed to communicate with the employer during his extended absence, voluntarily left his work within the meaning of section 402 (b) and is disqualified thereunder."

Section 3, art. 1, of the Unemployment Compensation 

Law, 43 PS §752, is a declaration of public policy as to the purposes and aims of the legislature in establishing our system of unemployment compensation. It specifically recites that the setting aside of unemployment reserves are made compulsory under the police power "for the benefit of persons unemployed through no fault of their own". The public policy so declared must be considered in construing every provision of the act and in determining eligibility for compensation in every case: Barclay White Co. v. Unemployment Compensation Board, 356 Pa. 43, 50 A. (2d) 336.

In Department of Labor and Industry, etc., v. Unemployment Compensation Board, 148 Pa. Superior Ct. 246, 24

A. (2d) 667, we emphasized a limitation on the right to the benefits intended by the act, thus: ". . . the basic principle at the root of the Act, justifying the exercise of the police powers of the Commonwealth in its enactment, is that the reserves thus set aside from the enforced contributions of

1948] 

 employers are to be used for the benefit of persons unemployed through no fault of their own."

In the present case, therefore, if claimant's unemployment resulted from his own fault he is not eligible for compensation. One who voluntarily leaves his work (Mandel v. Unemployment Compensation Board, 141 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 580, 15 A. (2d) 479) or unreasonably refuses proper employment (Brilhart Unemployment Compensation Case, 159 Pa. Superior Ct. 567, 49 A. (2d) 260) or has become unemployed by reason of his conviction and imprisonment for crime (Department of Labor and Industry, etc., v. Unemployment Compensation Board, supra) is ineligible for unemployment benefits. The present appeal differs from the above cases only on its facts; essentially it is of the same character and falls within the class of cases where ineligibility for compensation is chargeable to claimant's fault.

While claimant here did not formally quit his employment, he must have known that his job would not be kept open for him if he stayed away from his work indefinitely. He deliberately prolonged his term in jail as a "sit-down strike" against his wife and in defiance of the court which had committed him for contempt in failing to comply with its order. The fact that claimant's self-imposed six months' sentence was not directed against his employer does not alter the fact that he is responsible for the situation which compelled his replacement by another productive worker in the mine. If this delinquent husband at any time had indicated a sincere intention of making good his arrears. on the support order, he undoubtedly would have been released from jail to return to his employment. However, in any view, though he had no resources other than his earnings, he could have secured the payment of his arrearage at any time after he was served with the attachment. 

He owed $55 on the support order but he had a credit with his employer for two weeks' wages earned in an amount more than sufficient to discharge the arrearage. This comment from Dawkins Unemployment Compensation Case, 358 

Pa. 224, 238, 56 A. (2d) 254, therefore is pertinent:

. "If every reason which appeals to an employe's head or his heart is to be accepted as a 'good cause" for his or her voluntarily leaving a job in a locality where there is no other work available, the Unemployment Compensation Law will become in many instances an invitation to a compensated rest."

Claimant was maintained by the county during his six months' sojourn in jail and he is attempting further to extend his "compensated rest" period in this appeal at the expense of the unemployment compensation fund. We are in agreement with the bureau, the referee and with the board that claimant is ineligible for benefits within the meaning of section 402(b) of the act (43 PS §802). 

Claimant tacitly admits that his unemployment was voluntary during the whole of the six months' period of his confinement in jail. He did not file a claim for benefits until after his release and the first compensable week for which he claimed compensation ended on June 29, 1947.

We agree with the conclusion of the board, but we differ as to the significance which the board attached to claimant's failure while in jail to give notice to his employer as to his whereabouts. The solution of cases of this class is not so simple and they cannot be decided in all instances by the application of a convenient rule. A timely notice to an employer by an employe of his whereabouts and his reason for his absence from his employment in some cases will preserve his right to benefits. In others, the employeremploye relationship cannot be preserved by such notice alone Each case must be viewed in the light of its circumstances and on its own facts Here, to have given such notice without making any effort to get out of jail would not have improved claimant's position He had the key to his own release from confinement and, as we have indicated, he wilfully refused to use it. The legal effect of his voluntary unemployment for the period of six months under the circumstances of this case, amounts to an abandonment of his employment and a termination of the relationship of employer and employe. Claimant is not entitled to benefits. 

Order affirmed.

1948] 

 WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD 

BELL v. LIT BROTHERS Workmen's compensation—Injury in the course of employment—Sales lady entering employer's store-Instructions to use another entrance—Injury on sidewalk.

A referee's award, based on his determination that claimant was injured during the course of her employment, will be affirmed where it appears that claimant, employed as a saleslady in a department store, entered the store at the employes' entrance shortly before the hour she was scheduled to begin work, that she carried with her a package containing an article similar to that sold by defendant's store as the result of which she was stopped by a store guard and directed to another entrance, that she thereupon left the store to gain entrance and enroute thereto, she fell on the sidewalk adjoining the store sustaining an injury; conceding that the sidewalk where she fell was not a part of defendant's premises, having once entered the store, her leaving the premises temporarily was not for a purpose foreign to her employment but to further it. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Sheldrake, District No. 1, claim petition no. 108,889, ac dent no. 

4944290. Dismissed. November 17, 1948. 

New Amsterdam Casualty Company, insurance carrier. 

Howard Wallner, for claimant. 

Raymond A. White, Jr., for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This case, in which Ada Bell is claimant and Lit Brothers, defendant, is before us upon an appeal by defendant on an award made by the referee to claimant. 

There is little dispute as to the essential facts. It appears that on December 7, 1946, claimant, employed by defendant as a saleslady in its store, entered the store at the employes'

entrance shortly before the hour she was scheduled to begin work. She carried with her a bag of soap chips; the store guard stopped her and directed her to another entrance, to be used by employes who carried packages with articles similar to those sold by defendant store.
