Claimant thereupon was obliged to leave the store to gain entrance where designated by the guard, and enroute thereto she fell on the sidewalk adjoining the store, sustaining a fracture of the right elbow and bruises to her left ankle. She was totally disabled for a period of 9 2/7 weeks. 

The only question raised by defendant on its appeal is whether claimant was in the course of her employment, or on defendant's premises when injured.

It may be conceded that the sidewalk where claimant fell is not part of defendant's premises. However, claimant contends that having entered on defendant's premises proper, she remained in the course of her employment when she went out on the sidewalk to gain entrance to the store, as directed by defendant's guard.

While defendant had issued printed regulations to employes as to the entrance to be used when carrying articles sold by the store, claimant had not been employed by defendant when such regulations were distributed to employes. 

She did not receive a booklet with the regulations. 

It is clear that claimant entered defendant's store proper, leaving it only at the instance of the store guard. Had she not been so directed, she would not have been injured. 

Having entered the store about the time scheduled, her leaving the premises temporarily was not for a purpose foreign to her employment, but to further it. When the guard stopped claimant, she was no longer en route to work, she was on defendant's premises.

We conclude that claimant was injured during the course of her employment.

We affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and award.

1948] 

 WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD DAUBE v. STOECKLEIN Workmen's compensation-Occupational disease—Dermatitis—Partial disability.

Where a claimant was awarded compensation for total disability for a certain period due to dermatitis incurred in the course of his employment as a baker, his claim for further compensation as a result of an alleged partial disability following his return to employment as a carpenter at a wage substantially less than his averge weekly wage as a baker at the time of his accident was properly denied by the referee; the fact that claimant could not resume his employment as a baker because of his allergy to baking ingredients would not substantiate a finding of partial disability nor is an award of compensation for such disability authorized by the Occupational Disease Compensation Act.

Appeal by claimant from award of Referee Gibb, District No. 8, claim petition no. 109,608, accident no. 5037845. 

Dismissed, November 17, 1948. 

Maryland Casualty Company, insurance carrier. 

Arnold D. Wilner, for claimant. 

Robert L. Loehl, for defendant. 

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

Referee Gibb awarded claimant, Clarence Daube, compensation for total disability due to a contact dermatitis incurred in the course of his duties as a baker. The award of compensation for the period from July 14, 1947, to September 11, 1947, is entered only against defendant, George

F. Stoecklein. The present appeal is by claimant, who contends that he has been partially disabled since September 

11, 1947, and is entitled to compensation therefor.

The record discloses that claimant's average weekly wage at the time of the accident was $75 per week and since September 11, 1947, he has been employed as a carpenter's assistant at $52 per week. It is contended that claimant is allergic to some ingredient in the baking mixture and therefore is unable to resume his regular employment, without suffering a recurrence of the dermatitis. Under the circumstances, is the contention of claimant that he is entitled to an award for partial disability because of his lowered earning power, sound?

We do not believe that the determination of this case. rests upon the question of the wage differential. In order for the board to take cognizance of the claim for partial disability, it is first incumbent upon claimant to prove an existing residual disability. When that fact is established, then the propriety of the order of termination, or a suspension order may be inquired into: Holtz v. McGraw and 

Bindley, 161 Pa. Superior Ct. 271. It is true that claimant at the present time cannot resume an employment in which he has gainfully engaged for more than 20 years. As a baker, claimant, in a sense, is totally disabled. But he has no substantial distress or disability in following other remunerative employment. Although at times, claimant stated, his hands become itchy and bother him somewhat, nevertheless claimant has failed to present any competent or acceptable evidence as to the extent or degree, if any, of over-all disability resulting from the dermatitis. There is no authority in the Occupational Disease Compensation Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 566, for an award of compensation for partial disability based entirely upon a difference in wages, nor has any case been cited in this Commonwealth or elsewhere in support of this proposition. 

While claimant has worked as a baker for more than 20 years, it does not appear that the dermatitis was due to an exposure of more than five years. Dr. S. R. Perrin, claimant's witness, attached no importance to the long period of exposure. He was of the opinion that the dermatitis started early in June 1947. The referee found (sixth finding of

1948] 

 fact) that all disability from the contact dermatitis ceased and terminated on September 11, 1947. The doctor was uncertain whether claimant would lose his sensitivity to the flour ingredients in the course of time. There is no support in law for claimant's contention that his allergy to the baking ingredients constitutes partial disability. In the case of Kusevich v. Heinz Co., 149 Pa. Superior Ct. 232, the court said (p. 235): "Concededly he had dermatitis and there was evidence that it was caused by the soap. Whether it was the result of the use of the soap on that particular date or due to a daily use for a long period the medical authorities said frankly they could not state. But mere proof of an injury apparently attributable to claimant's skin being allergic to this soap, does not justify a conclusion that the injury resulted from an accident."

This case is analagous to the one under consideration and decisive of the question against claimant. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD WOODINGTON v. CRAMP SHIPBUILDING COMPANY Workmen's compensation—Partial disability following total-Credit for overpayment made by employer. 

1. A referee's order giving effect to a modification of compensation payments for disability from total to partial as of a date prior to the date as of which compensation had been paid to claimant for total disability, thereby setting up a credit in favor of defendant for overpayments of compensation will be affirmed where claimant did not deny

that his disability had changed but contended that such a credit was not authorized by law. 

2. Under section 306 (b) of the Workmen's Compensation Act, com pensation for partial disability is payable for a period of 300 consecutive weeks; where partial disability follows total, the period of 

300 weeks will be reduced by the number of weeks for which compensation was paid for total disability. 

Appeal by claimant from order of Referee Alessandroni, District No. 1, granting petition for modification under compensation agreement no. 4,079,353. Affirmed. June 22, 1948.

Pershing N. Calabro, for plaintiff. 

J. Paul Erwin, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal from an order entered by Referee 

Alessandroni June 22, 1948, giving effect to modification of disability from total to partial as of January 5, 1947, and by reason thereof setting up a credit in the amount of $452.55 in favor of defendant, the Cramp Shipbuilding Company, against claimant, Charles Woodington, for overpayments of compensation made up to March 11, 1948. The case was before us on two prior occasions. In the first of these (A-30569), in an opinion published October 13, 1944, we affirmed an order of suspension of an agreement as supplemented May 17, 1943, because of claimant's return to work without loss of earnings on July 13, 1942. In the second instance, in our opinion (A-32668) dated April 23, 1947, we affirmed an order reinstating compensation on a total disability basis as of October 10, 1945. Defendant filed the petition instituting the present proceeding on April 

10, 1948.

The basic facts in the case are that claimant sustained a stellate fracture of the frontal bone in an accident which oc-

1948] 

 curred on June 4, 1942, in the course of his employment with defendant. The injury affected the vision of his right eye and, since he was qualified as a civil engineer, his skill in operating instruments was impaired. A high percentage of visual acuity was spared to him by an operation performed by Dr. V. M. Ellis, defendant's witness, May 3, 1943, and he went back to work June 13, 1943 (see A-30569, supra). However, he was laid off October 9, 1945, and, pursuant to the second proceeding in this case (A-32668, supra), it was found, on testimony of Dr. Samuel T. Gordy, an impartial neurologist, that he was totally disabled by reason of a post-concussion syndrome due to the fracture. 

In the present status of the case it is not denied that claimant went to work for Earl R. Davis, a new employer, and his earning record in this new job shows an average for the first 13 weeks beginning January 5, of $35.19 per week; for the next 13-week period of $60.69 per week; for the following 13-week period $62.24 per week, and for the last quarter of 1947, $56.17 per week. This indicates that a commensurate earning power was regained and claimant states in his testimony that he notified defendant's insurance carrier to that effect. There is no evidence in the most recent record as to change in physical disability but defendant has alleged a change to partial in its petition and, since claimant has not filed an answer denying the allegation, it is wholly proper to assume that it is admitted (77 

PS §821), there being no proof to the contrary.

The ultimate issue on appeal has to do, therefore, with the credit granted to defendant by the referee's order. It is contended that such a credit is not authorized by law; that suspension would be the only remedy open to defendant and that claimant would in any event be entitled to 300 weeks of compensation cumulatively. In answer to these points, we may say that the power of the compensation authorities to grant credits has never been questioned; that the partial disability in the instant case has been, to all intents and purposes, admitted and that the 300-week period set forth in section 306 (b) of the act (77 PS §512)

has from the beginning been construed to mean a period of 

300 consecutive weeks (Ludington v. Russell Coal Co., 90 

Pa. Superior Ct. 318).

The findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of Referee Alessandroni dated June 22, 1948, are affirmed. 

The appeal is dismissed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD LEYER v. McCORMICK CO. 

Workmen's compensation-Occupational disease-Silicosis sole cause of death-Pneumonia caused by silicosis.

Evidence that silicosis contracted in the course of his employment by defendant was the sole cause of death of claimant's husband, notwithstanding the fact that pneumonia induced by the silicosis was the final disease causing death, was sufficient to sustain a referee's award of compensation to claimant and her two children. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Moore, District No. 8, claim petition no. 96,958, accident no. 4,253,939. 

Affirmed November 17, 1948.

Pennsylvania Manufacturers' Association Casualty In surance Co., insurance carrier. 

Samuel Keller, for plaintiff. 

James J. Burns, Jr., for defendant. 

MURPHY, Chairman: 

Claimant is the widow of Edwin Francis Leyer, who died on February 8, 1943. She filed the present petition for compensation on behalf of herself and two minor children alleging that her husband's death was the result of silicosis

1948] 

 contracted during 43 years of employment with defendant.

The referee awarded compensation. On appeal by defendant the award was set aside because it was based on a finding that silicosis was the "primary cause" of death. This finding although responsive to the issue as developed by claimant's proof did not, however, meet the requirements of section 301 (c) of the Act of 1939, which provides that "compensation shall be payable . . . for death resulting solely by silicosis." A rehearing was granted and held. The referee again made an award. Defendant has taken the present appeal.

Claimant's evidence indicates that decedent had been employed by defendant from 1900 to 1933 as a grinder of anthracite coal and from 1933 to January 30, 1943, as a grinder of various materials which contained silica. Decedent became ill on January 30, 1943 and complained of severe cough, chest pains and fever. Dr. Harry I. Miller was called on February 3, 1943. He found Leyer to be suffering from dyspnea, marked weakness and a chest infection. Decedent's condition became aggravated and on February 7, 1943, he was admitted to the Montefiore Hospital. 

X-rays taken at the hospital showed broncho-pneumonia involvement. Death occurred on February 8, 1943. An autopsy disclosed generalized pneumonkoniosis, terminal pneumonia, congestion of the liver, cardiac degeneration, adhesion of the pleura and extreme fibrosis of the lungs due to anthraco-silicosis. Dr. Miller stated that decedent had such a severe infection of pneumonkoniosis that even though pneumonia was the terminal cause of death it was actually caused by pneumonkoniosis. 

Dr. C. Howard Marcy, who had examined the record in the case was called by defendant and testified that in his opinion the immediate cause of death was pneumonia because of the absence of any prior disabling illness. The symptoms described, the duration of the last illness and the autopsy findings were not consistent with death caused primarily by anthraco-silicosis. On cross-examination he admitted that the autopsy showed extreme fibrosis due to

anthraco-silicosis; that decedent had advanced silicosis; that persons so afflicted rarely die from the silicosis itself and that some other condition is usually the terminal cause of death and that here it was pneumonia. 

Dr. W. I. Fetterhoff, a specialist in chest diseases was called by claimant and testified that he had examined the records in the case, including the X-rays. He was of the opinion that the X-rays taken prior to the death of Edwin Francis Leyer showed bilateral third degree silicosis. That even though decedent had not been disabled or complained prior to January 30, 1943, he must have suffered prior to his last illness with the amount of silicosis found in his lungs. The silicosis was the sole cause of death and was due to decedent's employment. This witness was asked "What is the single factor in your opinion that caused his death, doctor?" and in reply stated "I think the cause of Mr. Leyer's death was silicosis."

We have carefully reviewed the entire record and are satisfied that the evidence is sufficient to support the referee's decision. Decedent was exposed to a silica hazard during his employment with defendant and his death was the result of silicosis and caused solely thereby. This is not a case where the silicotic condition contributed to the death of claimant's decedent along with pneumonia. Here the third degree silicosis was the active agency finally which caused the death even though the final and terminal disease was the pneumonia. As stated by claimant's attending physician, Dr. Miller, the generalized pneumonkoniosis (silicosis) led to the terminal pneumonia which killed decedent. 

Thus the pneumonia was caused or superimposed by the silicosis and as stated in Treaster v.. North American Refractories Co., 156 Pa. Superior Ct., 567,572," the disease or weakness is a passive factor without effect in depriving the silicosis of its character as the sole producing cause of death." See also, Anderson v. Schroeder Monumental Works, 159 Pa. Superior Ct. 620.

A more recent case of particular interest in the present claim is Oskin v. Wheeling Steel Corp., 162 Pa. Superior

1948] 

Ct. 568. There the issue was whether claimant's total disability was due to silicosis or arthritis. There too, Dr. C. 

Howard Marcy testified for the defendant and Dr. K. I. 

Fetterhoff for claimant. The appellate court in affirming the award held the evidence sufficient to support our finding that the total disability was the result of silicosis and caused solely thereby even though claimant also suffered from arthritis.

We believe that claimant has met the burden of establishing her claim and she and her children are entitled to receive compensation. No useful purpose would be served by further delaying the case for impartial medical testimony.

Accordingly, we affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and award. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD BRANDT v. ELLWOOD CITY FORGE CO. 

Workmen's compensation—Partial disability-Return to work at higher wage-Suspension of compensation. 

A referee's order suspending compensation where claimant still suffered a partial disability but returned to work at wages in excess of those received at the time of his accident will be affirmed, notwithstanding the fact that claimant was unable, because of his injuries, to resume his former work, for which he would have received a higher wage because of an increase in the hourly rate; where a partially disabled employe is given lighter work at wages equivalent to those he received at the time of his injury compensation payments must be suspended.

Appeal by claimant from order of Referee Moore, District No. 8, suspending compensation under agreement no. 

4,897,107. Affirmed. November 17, 1948.

Pennsylvania Manufacturers Association Casualty In surance Co., insurance carrier. 

J. H. Cohran, for plaintiff. 

H. M. Engell, for defendant.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

This is an appeal by claimant from an order of the referee suspending compensation.

The record discloses that, on October 7, 1946, the parties entered into a compensation agreement providing for the payment of compensation at the rate of $20 a week, commencing on September 24, 1946, and describing the accident of September 16, 1946, and the resulting injuries as follows: "Employe was firing furnace when he turned his back to furnace to put shovel of coal when his clothes caught fire causing first degree burn to back."

On October 22, 1947, defendant filed a petition to terminate in which it alleged that claimant had completely recovered and returned to work on July 7, 1947, but that he refused to sign a final receipt or cash the final check. Claimant's answer, filed on October 29, 1947, denied the allegations of defendant's petition and alleged that, as a result of the injury, claimant has only half the use of his left arm. 

After hearings, the referee found that, though claimant still suffers a partial disability, he returned to work on July 7, 1947, without any loss of earning power and, in accordance with such finding, suspended the payment of compensation until such time as the partial disability should be reflected in loss of earning power. This appeal followed. 

Claimant argues in this appeal that, though his wages, at the time of the accident, were $1.05 per hour and are presently $1.11 per hour, he was unable, because of the injuries suffered by him in the accident, to resume his former work where, if he were able to do it, he would now be receiving $1.25 per hour and, thus, he has shown an actual loss in earning power for which he is entitled to an award.

1948] 

We are unable to agree with the argument advanced by claimant. Under the act, where a claimant receives the same wages he was paid prior to the accident, it cannot be said that his disability has reflected itself in a loss of earning power. However, it is still possible for one to have a partial disability despite the fact that he is not entitled to compensation. Thus, the definition of earning power has been changed under the act, but the meaning of partial disability has in no way been affected: Wright v. Fullerton 

Textile Co., 2 P.C.R. 82.

Where it is apparent that claimant has a partial disability and such disability is not presently reflected in a loss of earning power, the board has made a practice of suspending compensation rather than granting an order of termination since the possibility of future loss is present: 

Policicchio v. Emerald Coal & Coke Co., 6 P.C.R. 42.

Under the act, no compensation is payable, regardless of loss of earning power when an employe receives as much for his services as he earned before his injury: Shaw v. Woolridge Coal Co., 4 P.C.R. 72; Scipani v. Pressed Steel Car 

Co., 150 Pa. Superior Ct. 410; Kelemora v. Reiber, 161 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 169.

Nor does the fact that claimant is earning his present wages in the doing of work different or lighter than that which he was doing at the time of the accident affect our conclusion since, in Holtz v. McGraw and Bindley, 161 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 371, our appellate court held that, where a partially disabled employe was given lighter work at equivalent wages, the board was bound to suspend payment of compensation under the agreement until claimant's earnings were less than before the accident. Thus, during any period in which his wages exceed those received prior to the accident, an employe even though he may still suffer a disability, is not entitled to compensation.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD BENNET v. STATE WORKMEN'S INSURANCE FUND Workmen's compensation-Injury in course of employment-Employe leaving premises during rest period.

A referee's award to claimant based on his determination that she was injured in the course of her employment and in furtherance of the business of her employer will be affirmed where it appears that claimant was employed as a checker and sorter by defendant, that defendant provided a 15-minute rest period in the afternoon, during which time plaintiff left the premises and proceeded across the street to a confectionery store and was injured after she left the sidewalk, there being evidence that the employer had allowed the rest period to increase the efficiency of the employes and that they were paid for the time involved. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Smith, District No. 10, claim petition no. 111,972, accident no. 5,155,110. 

Dismissed. November 17, 1948.

State Workmen's Insurance Fund, insurance carrier. 

Sidney Rosenblum, for claimant. 

Ralph H. Behney, for defendant.

KNOLL, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by defendant from the order of award of 

Referee Jesse G. Smith, of the Tenth Compensation District.

On March 4, 1948, claimant filed a petition, averring, inter alia, that she sustained certain injuries on December 19, 1947, while acting within the course of her employment. To this petition a responsive answer was filed by the State 

Workmen's Insurance Fund, denying the allegations of the said petition.

Claimant, on her own behalf, testified that she has been employed as a checker and sorter by defendant employer for a period of approximately one year; that the company pro-

1948] 

 vided a 15-minute rest period between 2:25 and 2:40 p. m.; that on December 19, 1947, during the said rest period, she left the premises and proceeded across the street to a confectionery store and had just left the sidewalk when she fell and sustained a fracture of the left forearm. Claimant further testified that, as a result of the aforesaid occurrence, she was disabled to March 30, 1948, and that, on the following day, she resumed her regular employment.

Forty Concilla, the proprietor of the cleaning establishment, testified that the nature of his business required his employes to stand all of the time and that an investigation on his part disclosed that in the afternoon the employes tended to become "sluggish" and the efficiency of operation was impaired; that, to overcome this condition, he provided a 15-minute rest period in the afternoon, when the employes went outside for fresh air and to a confectionery shop known as the "Sugar Bowl", located across the street from his premises, to procure sandwiches and soda pop; that the employes were paid for the time involved in the rest period; and that this procedure has resulted in increased efficiency in the operation of his establishment. 

The referee found as a fact that claimant was injured while acting within the course of her employment, as a result of which claimant was totally disabled from December 

19, 1947, to March 30, 1948, inclusive. Based upon said finding of fact, the referee made an appropriate award. 

From this ruling the State Workmen's Insurance Fund has appealed.

We have made a careful study of the record and are of the opinion that the ruling of the referee should be affirmed. 

Section 301, art. III, of the Workmen's Compensation 

Act, as amended, 77 PS § 411, provides that compensation shall be payable to an employe for injuries sustained while the employe is engaged in the furtherance of the business or affairs of the employer whether upon the employer's premises or elsewhere. The testimony in this case discloses that, in order to bring about a more efficient operation of his plant, the employer provided a 15-minute rest period and

that it was customary for the employes to cross the street to a confectionery shop for the purpose of obtaining refreshments; that this procedure was with the employer's approval and consent-and that the employes were paid for the rest period.

We are of the opinion that claimant, at the time of the accident, was actually engaged in the furtherance of her employer's business or affairs for the reason that the rest period and the procuring of refreshments resulted in a more efficient operation of the employer's plant and to the direct advantage of the employer. An accident is in the course of employment even though it occurs off the premises of the employer where the act has some connection or is concerned in some manner, although not necessarily close, with the business of the employer. Since claimant was injured while acting within the course of her employment and in furtherance of the business of her employer, she is entitled to the payment of compensation. See Maketa v. Butcher, 158 Pa.

Superior Ct. 519; Hohman v. George H. Soffel Co. et al., 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 274.

We, therefore, affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of award. 

The appeal of the State Workmen's Insurance Fund is dismissed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD ROBINSON v. SUN SHIPBUILDING CO. 

Workmen's compensation-Causal connection between injury and death -Award-Credit for compensation paid to decedent in lifetime. 

A referee's finding of a causal connection between an accidental injury sustained by claimant's husband and his subsequent death will be affirmed where the medical testimony as to such connection was conflicting; however, the referee's award of compensation to claimant for a period of 300 weeks will be set aside and an amended award entered where it appeared that decedent received compensation for a period during his lifetime; in such case section 306 (g) of the Work-

1948] 

 men's Compensation Act of June 21, 1939, still in effect, requires that the period of compensation to the widow be reduced by the period during which payments were made to decedent. 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Clayton, District No. 1, claim petition no. 106,250, accident no. 

4,738,996. Affirmed as amended. November 17, 1948. 

Lester L. Dolfman, for plaintiff. 

J. Allen Hodge, for defendant.

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This claim petition was filed by Gladys B. Robinson, widow of Alfonso Robinson, alleging that he sustained an accidental injury during the course of his employment with Sun Shipbuilding Company, defendant, on August 20, 1945. Robinson filed a claim petition during his lifetime, but died before the taking of testimony had been completed. The referee made awards in both cases, and defendant has appealed from both awards. In this case we have disposed of defendant's appeal in the claim petition filed by Robinson's widow. In a companion case at A-33973 we have considered the appeal filed by defendant in the claim petition filed by Alfonso Robinson. 

The testimony taken is applicable to both cases. The record was before us upon a prior occasion at which time we remanded it to the referee for the testimony of an impartial medical expert.

The questions here are whether Robinson sustained an accidental injury during the course of his employment on August 20, 1945, and, if so, whether the accident caused his death.

The testimony as to an accident is rather meager, being furnished solely by Robinson, who, it must be pointed out, was not in the best mental condition. The record clearly reveals that even before the alleged accident he was absent minded and forgetful, being afflicted with paresis. Robinson, in his claim petition, alleged that he sustained an injury to

[84 Dep. Rep. 

his knee, that he was struck by and knocked down by a hand truck. He testified that he was struck on the left side by a flat iron object on a hand truck, as he was going down a grade and could not stop. He gave hospital histories of falling while at work, and being knocked from a truck, when it was struck by another truck. The trucks referred to, it appears, have two wheels in front, and two handles in the rear. Robinson stated that he left work for home after the occurrence and did not report to the dispensary, that he boarded a street-car but rode too far. The conductor, he continued, inquired whether he was ill and upon receiving an affirmative answer secured two boys to take him to the hospital.

Louis Recupito, a police officer, found Robinson sitting upon a doorstep at Woodland Avenue and 58th Street about 

4:30 p. m. on August 20, 1945, upon answering a radio call.

Robinson was unable to walk and the witness took him to the Mercy Hospital. There Dr. George P. Marshall, who testified in claimant's behalf, examined Robinson and noticed a swelling of the left hip. X-rays of the skull vertebrae, left knee and shoulder girdle were negative for fractures. 

A tentative diagnosis of paresis was made, and final diagnosis was meningeal cerebral irritation, due to hematoma of the spinal cord. This, the doctor believed, caused a paralysis, rendering Robinson unable to walk. The doctor admitted that meningeal infection can be due to syphilis as well as trauma. 

Dr. Benjamin P. Weiss, a neurologist, defendant's witness, examined Robinson on June 21, 1946, making a complete neurological examination. He concluded Robinson had paresis and arthritic changes in the knee joints, that he was suffering from a syphilitic infection of the brain, spinal cord and coverings. The doctor examined all the hospital records and concluded that Robinson's death was due to the progress of the paresis and had no connection with the alleged accident. An injury to the hip would have no affect on paresis, he stated. There was no evidence, Dr. Weiss testified, of hematoma of the spinal cord.

1948] 

Dr. Samuel T. Gordy, the impartial medical expert appointed by the Workmen's Compensation Board, felt that there was a causal connection between the alleged accident and Robinson's death. The doctor concluded that Robinson must have had a spinal injury, because he was unable to walk.

The sole testimony as to an accident was given by Robinson. While the various histories that he gave did not correspond precisely, they all were to the general effect that he had sustained an accidental injury through the use of a hand truck. We are satisfied, as was the referee, that 

Robinson's testimony was credible and that he sustained an accidental injury during the course of his employment on 

August 20, 1945.

We have already reviewed the medical testimony of the record at some length. The impartial expert, Dr. Gordy, and claimant's witness, Dr. Marshall, whom we erroneously stated, in our prior opinion at A-32962, was not a licensed physician when he treated Robinson, both felt that the accident had caused a paralysis of the legs probably due to a hemorrhage or concussion of the spinal cord. This, Dr. 

Gordy stated, caused Robinson to be bedridden and a good subject for bronchopneumonia, which caused death. 

The referee had all the medical testimony before him, and saw fit to elect to accept that given by Dr. Marshall and 

Dr. Gordy. We cannot conclude that any obvious error was made in so doing. Robinson worked until the day of the accident; he never worked thereafter. We do not believe that by mere coincidence, his paresis progressed to a stage where it and of itself disabled him, on a day when he sustained an accidental injury. While there appears to be some doubt as to whether Robinson had a hematoma of the spine as has been suggested by claimant's witness, Dr. Marshall, we believe, nevertheless, that the accident was the direct cause of his disability and death. The referee awarded claimant compensation for a period of 300 weeks. Defendant contends that this period should have been reduced by that period during which Robinson was entitled to compensation in his lifetime, according to section 306 (g) of the Work-

men's Compensation Act of June 21, 1939, P. L. 520. We believe defendant's position to be correct. While counsel for claimant maintains that this particular subsection was repealed by the legislature in amending this section by the Act of July 10, 1945, P. L. 671, it appears upon examination that subsection (g) of section 306 was neither repealed nor amended, and we conclude that it is still in force. Accordingly, we will vacate the referee's award and substitute the following 

Amended award

Compensation is awarded, and defendant is ordered to pay to claimant, Gladys B. Robinson, widow, and Gary 

Edward Robinson, dependent minor, compensation at the rate of $15 per week (being the maximum under the act), beginning August 8, 1946, and continuing for a period of 254-4/7 weeks or until the remarriage of claimant. 

Defendant is ordered to continue payments of compensation following the period of 250-4/7 weeks to claimant on behalf of Gary Edward Robinson, dependent minor, at the rate of $4.50 per week (being the maximum under the act) until Gary Edward Robinson becomes 16 years of age. 

Together with interest in accordance with section 410 of the act.

Defendant is further ordered to pay to claimant, Gladys B. Robinson, widow, the sum of $200 to reimburse her for expenses connected with the burial of decedent. 

Defendant is further ordered to pay to Dr. Samuel T. 

Gordy, 4312 Spruce Street, Philadelphia, Pa., the sum of $150 to reimburse him for his services as impartial medical expert in this case.

We affirm the referee's findings of fact and conclusions of law.

Defendant's appeal is sustained as to the period of compensation due claimant, but its other exceptions are dismissed.

 SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA PHILLIPS v. UNEMPLOYMENT COMPENSATION BOARD OF REVIEW 

Unemployment compensation-Voluntary suspension of work- Refusal to cross picket line maintained by another union. 

Claimant's refusal to cross a picket line at his employer's plant maintained by a union of which he was not a member nor eligible for membership, amounted to a voluntary suspension of work, under section 402 (d) of the Unemployment Compensation Law as amended and consequently he was disqualified for benefits for the four-week period provided by the act.

Appeal from the decision of the Unemployment Compensation Board of Review, dated January 16, 1947, at appeal no. B-44-99-E-2485. Decision affirmed. November 9, 1948. Superior Court of Pennsylvania, October term, 1947, no. 102. 

Louis H. Wilderman, for appellant. 

William L. Hammond, Special Deputy Attorney General, and T. McKeen Chidsey, Attorney General, for appellee. 

RENO, J.:

The Lanston Monotype Company employed 429 persons on May 20, 1946. Office Employees Union, Local No. 14, comprising 50 members, called a strike. Appellant was a member of Local No. 1216 of the Machinists International

Association which consisted of 260 members. The remaining 

119 employes were not members of either union. When members of the machinists' union appeared for work on May 20, 1946, they discovered the office employes had established a picket line. Appellant and other members of the machinists' union refused to cross this picket line. On 

August 12, 1946, the dispute between the office employes' union and the employer was settled, and appellant returned to work. The referee, reversing the bureau, ruled that

appellant's unemployment was not due to a voluntary suspension of work resulting from an industrial dispute, and was qualified for compensation within the meaning of sec tion 402 (d) of the Unemployment Compensation Law. The board reversed the referee and held that appellant's leaving constituted a voluntary suspension of work, and that under section 402 (d) he was disqualified for benefits for the week ending May 25, 1946, and the four weeks immediately following. This appeal followed.

The question raised by this appeal is whether appellant's refusal to cross the picket line maintained by a union of which he was not a member, nor eligible for membership, amounts to a voluntary suspension of work under section 402 (d), as amended by the Act of April 23, 1942, P. Ľ. 

60, sec. 4, and the Act of May 29, 1945, P. L. 1145, sec. 9. (The further amendment of June 30, 1947, P. L. 1186, sec. 

2, 43 PS sec. 802, is not involved in this appeal.) That section provides: "An employe shall be ineligible for compensation for any week... (d) In which his unemployment is due to a voluntary suspension of work resulting from an industrial dispute, at the factory establishment or other premises at which he is or was last employed: Provided, That this disqualification shall apply only to any week of unemployment which, in whole or in part, includes any part of a period beginning with the day on which such suspension occurs and ending with (1) the last day of the fourth calendar week immediately following the calendar week in which such suspension occurs, or (2) the day on which such suspension was terminated, whichever is the earlier."

It is conceded that claimant's unemployment resulted from an industrial dispute. However, appellant contends the suspension of work was involuntary since his decision not to cross the picket line was made for him and not by him. 

It should first be pointed out that in section 402 (d) the word "voluntary" had not been changed, and that only in section 402 (b) was "voluntary" amended by adding the words "good cause". When we referred to "voluntarily leaving" in Teicher Unemployment Compensation Case, 154

1948] 

Pa. Superior Ct. 250, 35 A. (2d) 739, and the Sturdevant

Unemployment Compensation Case, 158 Pa. Superior Ct. 

548, 45 A. (2d) 898, we were concerned with "voluntarily leaving work without good cause" under section 402(b), and those decisions are here irrelevant. 

A voluntary act is one done intentionally and proceeding from the will of the actor. The fact that appellant may have had good cause for refusal to cross the picket line is not important so long as the decision was his own. We stated in Stillman Unemployment Compensation Case, 161 

Pa. Superior Ct. 569, 572, 56 A. (2d) 380, in defining "voluntary" within the meaning of section 402 (d) that "Voluntary' in this context connotes a suspension of work resulting from the decision of the employe, as distinguished from a dismissal or discharge or lay-off by the employer". 

The testimony discloses that appellant's reason for failing to return to work was that he "didn't like to try crossing the picket line and causing trouble". When he was asked who decided whether the members of his union would or would not cross the picket line he replied: "No decision was made. They just saw a picket line there and didn't cross it." Even though extraneous factors may have influenced the decision, still it was made of his own volition. If an employe is prevented from working through no act of his own, as where he is forcibly barred from working, he would be entitled to compensation. But if a picket line is maintained within the limits permitted by law and there is no physical compulsion exerted to prevent employes from passing the picket line, nonstrikers are unemployed solely by their own choice: Bodinson Manufacturing Company v. 

California Employment Commission, 17 Cal. (2d) 321, 109 

P. (2d) 935. Appellant was not what President Judge

Keller in Miller v. Unemployment Compensation Board of 

Review, 152 Pa. Superior Ct. 315, 321, 31 A. (2d) 740, termed an "innocent bystander". His adherence to union principles dictated his decision not to cross the picket line, and he made the strikers' cause his own by voluntarily suspending his own work.

Appellant's second assignment of error concerns board's additional finding of fact: "Work was at all times available to the claimants throughout the suspension of operations and on May 28, 1946, the company so notified the employes, when notices to this effect were mailed together with pay checks. Such notice contained in part the following statement: 'For your information the plant of the Lanston Monotype Machine Company is open and will continue to remain open during regular working hours.'"

There was testimony that on the day of the strike the front door was opened about the middle of the morning, that the factory manager had the door open every day, and that the employer sent notices to all employes that the plant would remain open during regular working hours. 

There also was testimony that at least five supervisory employes were at the plant after May 28th to direct the work of the employes. This evidence supports the finding, and is binding upon us: Unemployment Compensation Law, section 510, 43 PS sec. 830; Hall v. Unemployment Compensation Board of Review, 160 Pa. Superior Ct. 65, 49 A. (2d) 872; D'Yantone Unemployment Compensation Case, 159 Pa. Superior Ct. 15, 46 A. (2d) 525.

Appellant further contends that the board erred in finding the entrances to the company were unlocked and that those desiring to enter experienced no difficulty in this respect. The testimony clearly indicates that appellant and the other members of his union made no attempt to cross the picket line to determine if the doors were locked. 

Appellant states that after the hearing before the referee a further investigation showed that when the doors were closed they could not be opened from the outside. The doors to the Locust Street entrance, where members of the machinists' union were accustomed to reporting, were usually in the charge of a member of that union and therefore on the morning of the strike these doors were not open. Later, that morning, when officials of the company got inside, they opened the doors on the 24th Street side and several employes of the company entered the building. Therefore we

1948] 

 find that there is a rational basis for the board's conclusion that the entrances were unlocked, and that those desirous of entering experienced no difficulty. Our review is confined to questions of law and we cannot disturb the board's findings of fact where they are predicated upon substantial and competent evidence: Stillman Unemployment Compensation Case, supra. 

Decision affirmed.

SUPERIOR COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA MCGANN v. UNEMPLOYMENT COMPENSATION BOARD OF REVIEW, DEPARTMENT OF LABOR AND INDUSTRY 

Unemployment compensation-Voluntary suspension of work-Refusal to cross picket line-Absence of threats of violence. 

Claimant's refusal to cross a picket line maintained in a dispute between steamship companies and two unions, neither of which claimant was a member, constituted a voluntary act so as to disqualify him from unemployment compensation benefits, under section 402 (d) where there was substantial competent evidence to support the board's finding that appellant was not threatened with any injury nor violence to prevent him from passing the line, and that his refusal to work was voluntary. 

Appeal from decision and order of the Unemployment 

Compensation Board of Review of June 25, 1947, reversing the decision of referee in re appeal no. B-44-99-E-4313.

Decision affirmed. November 9, 1948. Superior Court of 

Pennsylvania, October term, 1947, no. 241. 

William L. Hammond and T. McKeen Chidsey, Attorney 

General, for appellee. 

Robert G. Kelly and Bernard J. Duffy, Jr., for intervenor appellees.

[84 Dep. Rep. 

RENO, J.: 

Appellant is a member and the president of Local 1242, Steamship Clerks and Checkers, International Longshore men's Association, and had been employed for three months as a checker and clerk by J. A. McCarthy Company. He is one of over 2,400 claimants who are members of various unions of the Longshoremen's Association. They had been employed by various steamship and stevedoring companies along the Philadelphia waterfront.

A labor dispute arose between the steamship companies on one side and the Marine Engineers Beneficial Association and the Masters, Mates and Pilots Union on the other. 

The unions called a strike against the various steamship companies by which their members were employed in New 

York, Philadelphia and Baltimore. Appellant and other claimants are not members of either of the two striking unions. On October 1, 1946, the striking unions stopped all imports and exports, and picketed both American and foreign ships along the entire Philadelphia waterfront. In 

New York and Baltimore the loading and unloading of foreign ships was continued without interference and only American ships were picketed. 

As a result of the labor dispute claimants became unemployed. The bureau decided their unemployment was not due to a voluntary suspension of work within the meaning of section 402 (d) of the Unemployment Compensation Law, and were entitled to benefits without imposing the prescribed disqualifying period. The employer appealed to the referee who affirmed the bureau's decision. The employer then appealed to the board, and the prior determination was reversed. It held that the unemployment was voluntary, and claimants were temporarily disqualified under section 402 (d). Claimants have appealed from that decision, and the employer was allowed to intervene as an appellee. The employer's brief supports the decision of the board. 

To facilitate this appeal and to avoid separate appeals of the more than 2,400 cases, the board vacated its decision as to all claimants except Joseph Kushman (no. 240, October

1948] 

 term, 1947), Frank H. McGann (no. 241, October term, 1947) and Thomas J. Byrne (no. 242, October term, 1947).

It has been agreed between counsel that our decision on this appeal shall determine the Kushman and Byrne appeals and in turn also decide the eligibility of all other claimants for benefits.

The questions which we are called upon to decide are: (1) Whether appellant's refusal to cross the picket line constitutes a voluntary act so as to disqualify him from unemployment compensation benefits during the period prescribed by section 402(d), and (2) whether there is substantial, competent evidence to support the board's findings that such refusal was voluntary under the circumstances. 

It is admitted that appellant's unemployment "resulted from an industrial dispute". The pertinent provision of the 

Unemployment Law, sec. 402 (d), as amended by the Act of 

April 23, 1942, P. L. 60, sec. 4, and the Act of May 29, 1945,

P. L. 1145, sec. 9, provides in substance that an employe is ineligible for compensation for any week in which his unemployment is due to a voluntary suspension of work resulting from an industrial dispute. The disqualification applies only for the period of unemployment and for not more than four calendar weeks. (The further amendment of June 30, 1947, P. L. 1186, sec. 2, 43 PS sec. 802, is not involved in this appeal.)

We have previously discussed at some length the meaning of the word "voluntary" as used in section 402 (d): Stillman Unemployment Compensation Case, 161 Pa. Superior 

Ct. 569, 56 A. (2d) 380; Phillips v. Unemployment Compensation Board of Review, 163 Pa. Superior Ct. 374, A. (2d) —. In both instances we denied compensation on the ground that the employe's refusal to cross a picket line was a voluntary suspension of work within the meaning of section 402(d).

Appellant would have us distinguish the Stillman case, supra, and like decisions, mainly on the basis that in the Stillman case there was no evidence of violence and that

there is such evidence here. We agree with the argument that if he was prevented from peacefully pursuing his employment "because of the militant attitude of the picket line, because of incidents of violence, and because of threats of physical violence", his unemployment would be involuntary.

The board found that claimants were not threatened with any injury nor were there any threats or attempts at violence to prevent him from passing through to work. 

Its seventh finding of fact follows: "7. The claimants would have been willing to work on the foreign ships had the striking unions been willing to confine their picket line exclusively to American ships. The claimants were not, however, willing to cross the picket lines. They were not prevented by violence, threats or intimidation from crossing the lines; no violence was practiced or threatened on the picket lines and the only 'violence' which took place was when some of the claimants went to a picket line and ridiculed some of the pickets. The pickets followed them to a nearby taproom and a 'scuffle' ensued. The failure of the claimants to cross the picket line was due almost entirely, if not altogether, to their unwillingness in principle to cross a picket line and the unemployment for which claims were filed during the period in question was due to their determination to refrain from working rather than to cross the picket line."

The board's findings of fact, if supported by substantial and competent evidence, are binding upon us in the absence of fraud: Unemployment Compensation Law, sec. 510, 43 

PS sec. 830; Miller v. Unemployment Compensation Board of Review, 152 Pa. Superior Ct. 315, 31 A. (2d) 740;

D'Yantone Unemployment Compensation Case, 159 Pa. Su perior Ct. 15, 46 A. (2d) 525; Hall v. Unemployment Compensation Board of Review, 160 Pa. Superior Ct. 65, 49 A. (2d) 872.

The testimony shows that when appellant reported for work he found pickets at the gate and "to avoid any kind of conflict or violence with them [he] turned around and went home." No attempt was ever made to cross the picket

1948] 

 line. His testimony was that he would not do so mainly because he did not want to create any violence or risk of harm to himself and secondly as a matter of principle. There was not a single act of violence, or any threat to do bodily harm to appellant or other claimants. 

Stress is laid upon the testimony of the vice president of the Longshoremen's Association, and it is contended that upon his testimony alone a finding of violence at the picket line could and should have been predicated. He was asked by counsel for the employer whether at a strikers' meeting he had stated: "Piers 19 and 38 was picketed. Pier 38 at

Allegheny Avenue we advised them to go in regardless and we are working those places." Before the witness could answer the question, claimants' counsel interjected: "Why don't you go through the whole thing. The next sentence is that 'We asked them to withdraw pickets at Pier 5. They doubled the pickets and knocked us out at Pier 5.'" Whereupon the witness answered: "That's right. They doubled it." It cannot be said that his testimony amounts to more than an assertion that the pickets were doubled at Pier 5. 

However, even if this testimony could be taken to include the statement that claimants were "knocked out at Pier 5", a finding of violence would not necessarily follow. Webster ascribes that meaning to the phrase in boxing jargon, but it has likewise other connotations. The board very properly refused to base a finding upon this equivocal evidence, an isolated statement, amounting at most to a mere scintilla of proof.

At the hearing before the board additional testimony was offered. A member of the strike committee of the Masters, Mates and Pilots testified that his union had announced that it would resist with violence any attempt to break its picket lines. He testified to an occurrence where some men had been drinking, and that they had "ridiculed" the pickets who followed them back to a taproom where there was a "scuffle". The witness did not identify any of claimants as members of that group. His statement that the striking unions would have repelled any attempt to cross the picket line amounts only to an undisclosed intention to do violence.

There is no evidence of any attempt to cross the picket line peacefully or by force. We conclude that the board's findings that claimants made no effort to cross the picket lines, that they were not actually threatened, and that there was no attempted violence are supported by substantial and competent evidence.

The mere statement by a claimant that he refused to cross a picket line because of fear of bodily harm is not enough to demonstrate that his unemployment was involuntary in a situation where there was not a single overt act of violence of any character, leading a reasonable person to believe that he would be in physical danger in the event he attempted to cross the picket lines. A nonstriker's fear of injury must be real and substantial and not nebulous. Strike and picket lines are not always accompanied by violence, intimidation and physical restraint. In the absence of evidence to the contrary we may assume that picketing is carried on peacefully and within the limits permitted by law. 

Steamship Trade Assn. of Baltimore, Inc., v. Davis, et al., Md., 57 A. (2d) 818, illustrates the principle.

Seemingly it relates to the Baltimore counterpart of the same labor dispute with which this appeal is concerned. 

The Masters, Mates and Pilots Union and the Marine Engineers Beneficial Association called the strike. Claimants were members of the Longshoremen's Association who became unemployed due to the labor dispute. The board found the longshoremen had attempted to cross picket lines but withdrew when the threatening attitude of the strikers indicated that there might be considerable trouble. The 

Superior Court of Baltimore City and the court of appeals affirmed the board's decision that claimants' unemployment was due to a fear of physical violence, and they were allowed compensation. The evidence disclosed the pickets were armed with clubs and other weapons. They dared the longshoremen to go through the picket lines and threatened the lives of the longshoremen on various occasions. Appellants, who were the employers, admitted that claimants had good reason to fear violence. Had the record before us disclosed that the strike in Philadelphia had developed a similar

1948] 

 situation, appellant would have made out a case for benefits. 

We find appellant has not overcome the board's finding that the suspension of work was voluntary, and therefore appellant was properly denied benefits during the disqualifying period fixed by section 402(d).

The decision in this appeal and those at nos. 240 and 242, October term, 1947, are affirmed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD LIMPERT v. PITTSBURGH EQUITABLE METER COMPANY Workmen's compensation—Injury—Subsequent removal to hospital— 

Injury in hospital resulting in death-Causal connection. 

A referee's order disallowing a claim for compensation based on a finding that decedent's death occurred as a result of hypostatic pneumonia which was not the result of an accident admittedly sustained by decedent in the course of his employment will be affirmed, where it appears that decedent subsequent to his injury was removed to a hospital where he suffered a fall sustaining a fracture of the hip requiring him to be confined to bed thus bringing about hypostatic pneumonia, which resulted in death; under the circumstances, the pneumonia and death were not the approximate result of his original injury.

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Dillman, District No. 8, claim petition no. 102,779, accident no. 4,253,- 

797. Affirmed. December 1, 1948.

American Mutual Liability Insurance Co., insurance car rier. 

L. Pat McGrath, for claimant. 

Daniel S. Newman, for defendant.

KNOLL, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by claimant from the order of disallowance of Referee Alvin E. Dillman, of the Eighth Compensation District. 

On July 31, 1945, claimant, Catherine A. Limpert, filed a claim petition, averring, inter alia, that her husband, Anthony D. Limpert, sustained certain injuries on March 

17, 1943, while acting within the course of his employment with defendant, which injuries resulted in his death on 

March 22, 1945. To this petition a responsive answer was filed by defendant, denying the allegations of the said petition.

A study of the record discloses that decedent, Anthony D. Limpert, filed a claim petition on September 20, 1943, averring, inter alia, that he sustained certain injuries on March 17, 1943, while acting within the course of his employment with defendant herein. Testimony was duly taken before Referee Alvin E. Dillman, District No. 8, who, by decision dated April 14, 1944, found as a fact that claimant sustained injuries by accident while acting within the course of his employment with defendant on March 17, 1943, and as a result thereof claimant became totally disabled. Based upon this and other findings of fact, the referee awarded compensation to decedent herein. From this ruling claimant appealed to this board, which, by opinion dated January 12, 1945, affirmed the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of award and dismissed the appeal. No appeal was taken by defendant from this opinion. Pursuant to the aforesaid award, compensation was paid to decedent, Anthony D. Limpert, to March 21, 1945, the date of his death.

In support of her claim for compensation, claimant called 

Grace Hauck, a stepdaughter of Anthony D. Limpert, who testified that she spoke to decedent prior to his death, at which time decedent stated that an attendant had taken him into the bathroom and left him there and, while he was trying to get from the commode to the wheelchair, he slipped and fell. This conversation took place the night of

1948]  March 20, 1945, which was one day prior to the date of death. On cross-examination, the witness further testified that she had visited decedent three or four times a week prior to the date of his death and that decedent had made no mention of the accident prior to the conversation heretofore referred to. 

Dr. Joseph M. O'Brien, called on behalf of claimant, testified that he was the attending physician following the accident of March 17, 1943; that he continued to treat decedent thereafter until December 7, 1943; and that he made a diagnosis of multiple polyperipheral neuritis. Based upon the examinations heretofore referred to and upon statements received from other doctors subsequent thereto, the doctor stated that the approximate cause of death was multiple polyperipheral neuritis, the primary cause was hypostatic pneumonia, superinduced from fracture of the left hip. The doctor testified that hypostatic pneumonia is caused generally by age, as a result of being put in an absolute resting position, which causes a secretion that fills up the lungs with fluid, as distinguished from the normal type of pneumonia which is caused by a bacilli or virus. On cross-examination, the doctor testified that the fracture of the hip caused decedent to be confined to bed which, in turn, induced the pneumonia.

Elizabeth A. Berthold, a nurse attendant at the Woodville 

Allegheny County Hospital, testified that she was called by another patient and went into the bathroom and found decedent lying on the floor, at which time she arranged to have him removed to a bed; that the following day, decedent was transferred to the Mayview General Hospital, Mayview, Pa.; that she did not see decedent fall, and when she saw decedent he was on the bathroom floor by the commode.

Dr. Harry Lerner, of the Mayview General Hospital, called as a witness on behalf of claimant, testified that decedent was admitted to the hospital on February 7, 1945; that 

X-ray examination disclosed a fracture through the trochanter region, shaft fragment displaced slightly upward

on the head of the fragment; that claimant was treated from 

February 7, 1945, by means of a Roger-Anderson splint; and that from that date until March 21, 1945, the date of death, decedent was confined to bed or placed in a wheelchair. 

The doctor further testified that, on February 11, 1945, decedent developed hypostatic pneumonia. The doctor fixed hypostatic pneumonia as the primary cause of death and the fracture of the left hip as the secondary or contributory cause of death.

Dr. Shaul George, called on behalf of claimant, testified that he examined decedent on December 22, 1943, and March 5, 1944, but administered no treatment to decedent. Due to the fact that decedent was unable to receive proper care, the doctor recommended that decedent be admitted to the Woodville Hospital and executed the necessary papers for transfer of decedent to the hospital.

Defendant offered in evidence a copy of the statement of claim filed by claimant against the Continental Casualty Company in the Court of Common Pleas of Allegheny County, which set forth that decedent fell on a bathroom floor and fractured his left hip as a result of which he contracted hypostatic pneumonia, and, as a result of said accident, died on March 22, 1945. Defendant also offered in evidence affidavit of claim for indemnity for death; affidavit of undertaker; affidavit of attending physician; and coroner's inquest report.

The referee found as a fact that decedent came to his death March 21, 1945, as a result of hypostatic pneumonia, following an accident on February 6, 1945, and not as a result of the accident of March 17, 1943, alleged by claimant. Based upon said finding of fact, the referee dismissed the claim petition. From this ruling claimant has appealed. 

We have made a careful study of the record and are of the opinion that the ruling of the referee should be affirmed. 

The testimony in this case discloses that decedent, on March 17, 1943, sustained certain injuries while acting within the course of his employment by reason of which he was paid compensation to March 21, 1945, the date of his death.

1948] 

[ The testimony further establishes the fact that, as a result of the aforesaid occurrence, decedent suffered from multiple polyperipheral neuritis; that, by reason of this condition, decedent required care which he was unable to receive from any member of his household, which resulted in Dr. Shaul 

George's arranging for decedent to be transferred to the Woodville State Hospital. The hospital records, which were offered in evidence on behalf of claimant disclosed that decedent, at the time of his examination on February 2, 1945, complained of a weakness of the legs but was not confined to bed and was able to walk without any aid, and that the legs were never swollen or painful; that he had occasional dizziness, no headache, no cordy or respiratory symptoms, appetite fair, pulse regular, no genito-urinary symptoms. 

The testimony further disclosed the fact that, on February 6, 1945, while confined to the Woodville State Hospital, decedent fell while walking from the commode to a wheelchair, resulting in decedent's suffering a fracture of the left hip which, in turn, required decedent to be confined to his bed bringing about the hypostatic pneumonia, which, in turn, resulted in death.

Considering the testimony in its entirety, we are of the opinion that the accident of February 6, 1945, which resulted in the pneumonia and death, was not the proximate, natural and probable result of the original injury of March 17, 1943, and that there is no causal connection between the original injury of March 17, 1943, and the subsequent death and, by reason thereof, claimant, as the widow of Anthony D. Limpert, is not entitled to the payment of compensation. See Kolyer v. Westmoreland Coal Co., 149 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 473.

We, therefore, affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of disallowance.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD MALYTORIS v. THE MURRAY CORPORATION OF AMERICA Workmen's compensation-Claim petition Statute of limitations- 

Conduct of defendant.

A referee's order denying claimant's petition for compensation filed more than two years after the date when claimant sustained his injuries will be affirmed where claimant testified that he did not file his petition sooner because the person in charge of the insurance department of defendant company had told him about three weeks after the accident when he signed a statement pertaining to it, that he would be taken care of, it further appearing that claimant was disabled for a period of about three weeks following his accident, after which he returned to his employment for a period of several months before he was laid off; under the circumstances, the evidence did not support a finding of fraud nor intention of deception on the part of defendant so as to estop it from pleading the bar of the statute. 

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Phillips,

District No. 3 claim petition no. 107,882, accident no. 4,594,- 

421. Dismissed. November 17, 1948.

Hartford Accident & Indemnity Company, insurance carrier. 

Milton J. Kolansky, for plaintiff. 

Frank M. Walsh, for defendant.

KNOLL, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by claimant from the order of disallowance of Referee David W. Phillips, of the Third Compensation District.

On February 24, 1947, a claim petition was filed by claimant herein, averring, that he sustained certain injuries on December 23, 1944, while acting within the course of his employment with defendant herein, as a result of which he has sustained the loss of vision of the right eye. To this petition a responsive answer was filed by defendant, aver-

1948] 

 ring, inter alia, that the said claim was barred by reason of the statute of limitations.

We are of the opinion that sufficient testimony was presented to warrant findings that claimant sustained an injury on December 23, 1944, while acting within the course of his employment with defendant herein; and that claimant has sustained the loss of use of the right eye for all intents and purposes as a result of said accident. The sole issue in this case is whether or not the claim is barred by reason of the statute of limitations and whether or not defendant is estopped from asserting the bar of the statute of limitations. 

The testimony discloses that the accident occurred on December 23, 1944, and that, following the accident, claimant reported to the first aid office of defendant herein, and was referred to Dr. Curtin for examination; that two or three days following the accident, claimant reported at one of the offices of defendant company where he was asked questions pertaining to the accident by Claude Martin, who was in charge of the insurance department of the defendant company, and signed a statement concerning the accident and his injuries incident thereto. Claimant, at the request of defendant, was examined by Dr. James S. Jordan on or about December 26, 1944. There is also testimony by claimant to the effect that, at the time he appeared at the office of defendant company and signed the question and answer statement, he was told by Mr. Martin that "I would be taken care of if I would sign the papers". This was denied by Mr. Martin, who testified that a statement was obtained and an examination conducted by Dr. Jordan for the purpose of ascertaining whether or not claimant had a compensable claim and was at no time advised that he would be taken care of. It likewise appears from the testimony that, following the accident, claimant was disabled for about three weeks and returned to his employment with defendant herein following the said three-week period, doing a different type of work but receiving wages equal to those received prior to the accident, and continued to work continuously thereafter until August 15, 1945, when the work, for

which claimant was employed, was terminated and other employes of defendant were laid off. 

The testimony further discloses that in February 1947, in response to a letter received from defendant company, claimant returned to report for work, at which time a physical examination was made of claimant following which he was advised that, by reason of the condition of his eye, he could not be reëmployed. On or about February 24, 1947, claimant filed the instant petition. 

It also appears from the testimony that, following the conversation with Mr. Martin, about two or three days after the accident, claimant contacted no one to ascertain whether or not his claim had been recognized or rejected, nor did he at any time endeavor to ascertain what, if anything, defendant company would do.

In August 1946 claimant obtained employment as a salesman earning $28 to $30 per week and while employed by defendant company, earned from $55 to $65 per week. 

The referee found as a fact that the claim petition had not been filed within the statutory period of one year and that claimant had failed to produce sufficient evidence to warrant the tolling of the statute and, based upon said findings of fact, dismissed the claim petition. From this ruling claimant has appealed.

We have made a careful study of the record and are of the opinion that the ruling of the referee should be affirmed. 

Section 315 of the Workmen's Compensation Act, 77 PS 

§602, provides that all claims for compensation shall be filed within one year after the date of the accident, otherwise the claim for compensation shall be forever barred. However, this section is subject to the legal proposition that where a defendant or its representatives so deport themselves in their dealings with a claimant as to mislead or deceive him, whether innocently or with fraudulent purposes, and induce him to postpone the filing of his petition until the period of limitation has expired, the defense of delay is not available, as a defendant cannot be permitted

1948] 

 to benefit from a neglect for which he is himself primarily responsible. See Mackanitz v. Pittsburgh and West Virginia 

Ry. Co., 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 359. However, the burden of proof is upon claimant to show, by evidence clear and persuasive and of more than doubtful weight, that defendant's conduct was the cause of delay: Rowles v. State Workmen's Insurance Fund, 141 Pa. Superior Ct. 193. 

The testimony in the case at issue discloses that a few days following the accident, claimant was questioned as to facts concerning the accident by a representative of the defendant company who also arranged for a physical examination of claimant to determine whether or not claimant has suffered a compensable accident. There is nothing in the record, in our opinion, to warrant a finding that claimant was lulled into a sense of security and, by reason thereof, did not file the claim petition within the statutory period of one year. It is our opinion that claimant decided to file the claim petition after his job was finished by reason of the fact that the work which claimant was employed to do was terminated and claimant and other employes of defendant company were laid off at that time. This is supported by the following statement of the claimant: "Q. Will you tell us, if you can, why you did not make out a claim petition similar to the one you made out on 

February 14, 1947, in this office, before the date you did make it out? "A. Well they told me they would take care of me, I had a job, I was willing, what more does a fellow want? So when they refused to hire me again . . .”

We are of the opinion that claimant, as long as he was employed by defendant herein, had no intention of filing a claim petition and that he decided to file the claim petition after he was refused employment in September 1947. We are likewise of the opinion that claimant was not deceived by reason of any statement made by defendant herein. The statements attributed to Mr. Martin to the effect that claimant would be taken care of if he signed the papers are

alleged to have been made in December 1944. The medical examinations of claimant to ascertain whether or not he sustained a compensable injury were also conducted in December 1944. The claim petition, however, was not filed until February 24, 1947, or approximately a period of 26 months thereafter. In Guy v. Stoecklein Baking Co. et al., 133 Pa. Superior Ct. 38, the court held that the employe must file his petition within one year of the declarations or conduct relied upon by the employe and by which the employer is estopped.

We are of the opinion, considering the testimony in its entirety, that the testimony offered on behalf of claimant is not of such character as to warrant a finding of fraud or its equivalent on the part of defendant nor is there any evidence of intentional deception so as to estop defendant from pleading the bar of statute of limitations. We are also of the opinion that the referee properly disallowed the claim petition filed in this case.

We, therefore, affirm the referee's findings of fact, conclusions of law and order of disallowance. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD STOUDT v. HAGER & BROS., INC. 

Workmen's compensation-Occupational disease-Dermatitis-Period of exposure-Liability of Commonwealth-Section 308(a). 

An award to claimant for compensation will be upheld under the provisions of section 108 of the Occupational Disease Act where claimant became disabled from dermatitis as the result of his working with a soda solution while in defendant's employ as a painter and paperhanger after a short period of exposure; in such case since claimant's disability did not follow an exposure of five or more years, the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania was relieved from liability for joint payments with the employer by section 308 (a) of the act.

1948] 

Appeal by defendant from award of Referee Graybill, District No. 4, claim petition no. 111,471, accident no. 

5,018,822. Affirmed. December 1, 1948.

Penna. Manufacturer's Association Casualty Ins. Co., in surance carrier. 

Sidney E. Rosenblum, for claimant. 

Paul A. Mueller, for defendant. 

KNOLL, Commissioner: 

This is an appeal by defendant from an award of compensation payments to claimant under the provisions of The 

Pennsylvania Occupational Disease Act. 

Claimant's petition, filed January 24, 1948, alleged, inter alia, that he became disabled from dermatitis on September 10, 1947; that he was last exposed to the occupational hazard on September 9, 1947; and that he gave notice of disability to defendant on September 10, 1947. Defendant and the State Workmen's Insurance Board, custodian of the Occupational Disease Fund, filed separate answers denying the material allegations of the claim petition. 

The record shows that the parties entered into a compensation agreement on April 16, 1947, providing for maximum compensation payments to claimant, wherein it was agreed that claimant suffered a chemical dermatitis and caustic burns to his hands on March 18, 1947. Claimant received compensation for one week and the agreement was terminated by final receipt of claimant. A supplemental agreement, executed on August 22, 1947, provided for recurrence of disability and claimant was paid compensation from April 19, 1947, to May 11, 1947. This agreement was terminated by final receipt signed by claimant on August 

22, 1947.

Claimant, a painter and paperhanger, testified that he worked with a soda solution for about eight days in March

1947, washing and preparing for painting; that he became disabled for two weeks; that his disability recurred about two weeks after he returned to work; and that he again resumed work in May 1947, and worked until September 9, 1947, when he became disabled for the third time and was idle to March 2, 1948, the date of hearing. He admitted that his physician advised him to return to work on January 9, 1948, but said that defendant employer would not give him work until his hand was completely healed. Claimant testified further that he had not worked with soda water from May to September 1947, and that the only work he did during that period was incidental to paperhanging and scraping and no painting at any time. 

Dr. A. M. Congello, an osteopath, called on behalf of claimant, testified that he first treated claimant on March 24, 1947, for chemical burns of the hands; that this condition cleared up and claimant returned to work; that he treated claimant on April 18, 1947, and on September 10, 1947, for chemical dermatitis which, he thought, was in its origin caused by the exposure to the soda water and which was subsequently brought on by exposure to paint products. 

In his opinion, claimant was able to return to work on 

January 9, 1948.

Defendant offered no testimony before the referee. 

Defendant excepts to the referee's findings of fact that claimant's disability had resulted after an exposure of more than five years and contends that claimant's dermatitis is not compensable under the act. 

We agree that claimant's disability had originated during March 1947, after claimant's hands had been burned in the caustic solution and was not the result of exposure to an occupational hazard over a period of five or more years. It is our opinion that claimant's disability is compensable under section 108, which relates to specific diseases which may or may not develop in a short period of time. 

Section 308 (a), providing for joint payments of compensation by the Commonwealth and by the employer where disability develops after an exposure of five or more years, makes the employer solely liable where disability occurs in

1948] 

 fewer than five years: Reichart v. Pennsylvania R. R. Co., 156 Pa. Superior Ct. 213; Kuntz v. Alliance Sand Co., 156

Pa. Superior Ct. 563. The occupational diseases which are compensable only upon proof of exposure over a fixed period of time, silicosis, anthraco-silicosis and asbestosis, are specified in section 301 (d) of the act in clear distinction from the first 10 subsections of section 108. It was required of claimant to prove only that his disability arose out of and in the course of his employment and not that he had been exposed to the occupational hazard for five or more years. 

We believe that the record warrants an award under section 108 (i) of the act, which provides as follows: "Infection or inflammation of the skin due to oils, cutting compounds, lubricants, dust, liquids, fumes, gases or vapor, in any occupation involving direct contact with, handling thereof, or exposure thereto."

On April 16, 1947, the parties had agreed that claimant had suffered a chemical dermatitis during the course of his employment on March 18, 1947. In August 1947 a supplemental agreement was executed for a recurrence of disability.
