In addition to this evidence, we have the testimony of claimant's physician, undenied by defendant, that claimant's chemical dermatitis had resulted from exposure to paint products.

Accordingly, the referee's seventh finding of fact, and order of award are hereby set aside and, in lieu thereof, we substitute the following 

Findings of fact 7. That claimant contracted an occupational chemical dermatitis while in the course of his employment with defendant from March 18, 1947, to September 9, 1947, and that he was totally disabled as the result of a recurrence thereof from September 10, 1947, to January 9, 1948.

3. Since claimant's occupational disease and resulting disability had developed after an exposure of less than five

years, the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania is not liable for joint payments of compensation to claimant. Award

Compensation is, accordingly, awarded and Hager & Bros., Inc., defendant, and/or its insurance carrier, are hereby ordered and directed to pay to Victor Stoudt, claimant, compensation at the rate of $20 per week from September 17, 1947, to January 9, 1948, a period of 16 2/7 weeks or the sum of $325.71, with interest at the rate of six percent on all deferred payments.

The referee's remaining findings of fact and conclusions of law are hereby affirmed. 

COMMON PLEAS OF MERCER COUNTY HUNTER v. SHARON STEEL CORPORATION 

Workmen's compensation - Injury - Loss of eye- Causal connection between injury and disability-Expert medical testimony-Sufficiency. 

1. On an appeal from an order of the Workmen's Compensation 

Board where the decision of the board is against the party having the burden of proof, the question before the court is whether the board's findings of fact are consistent with each other and with its conclusions of law and its order, and can be sustained without a capricious disregard of the competent evidence 2. Where the sequence of events does not strongly indicate a connection between an injury and a subsequent disability so that it cannot be said that the injury was immediately and directly the result of the accident, claimant has the burden of establishing causal connection by expert testimony. 

3. An order of the board denying a claim for disability resulting from the loss of vision in an eye allegedly the result of an accident sustained by claimant when he struck his head against a beam, hitting the corner of his eyebrow, will be affirmed where claimant did not notice any immediate disability but about six weeks after the occur-

1948] 

 rence lost all vision in the eye, and where claimant's medical expert testified that the injury could cause the loss of vision, but gave no positive testimony that in his opinion it was the cause. 

In the Court of Common Pleas of Mercer County, June term, 1948, no. 46. Appeal from the order of Workmen's 

Compensation Board. Appeal dismissed. November 19, 1948. 

Philip Brockway, for claimant. 

Emrys G. Francis, for defendant.

ROWLEY, P. J.: 

This matter is before the court upon claimant's appeal from an order of the Workmen's Compensation Board which rejected claimant's petition for compensation for loss of an eye.

The referee's findings of fact include the following: "4. That claimant during his course of employment with defendant company, on June 26, 1948, struck his head against a beam, hitting the outer corner of the left eyebrow; there was no blood as a result of this injury, but it merely caused the eye to get black and blue. "6. That about six weeks later claimant noticed that his left eye started blurring, and he had the sensation that there were "flies in the air", and on August 28, 1946, normal vision in the eye disappeared entirely. "7. That on August 29, 1946, claimant of his own accord went to Dr. R. J. Riddle, eye surgeon, and claimant was informed that he had a detached retina of the left eye; claimant at that time was unable to tell the doctor of any accident which might have caused the detached retina; he did not tell the doctor of the bump he had received on June 26th; claimant then went to Dr. S. P. Sampson of New 

Brighton, who rendered the same diagnosis, but did not suggest surgery. "8. That claimant went to an official in the office of defendant company on August 30, 1946, and made an applica-

tion for relief payments from the company, and it was not until October 9, 1946, that the claimant recalled the bump of June 26, 1946, to his left eyebrow, and this was the first time that claimant reported the occurrence to anyone in the company. "9. Your referee finds as a fact that claimant, as a result of the accident of June 26, 1946, sustained a detached retina of the left eye, causing him to lose the vision of that eye. "10. Your referee finds as a fact that claimant did not report the occurrence of the accident as the cause for the detached retina within 90 days from June 26, 1946."

The referee drew the following conclusion of law: "Second: Since claimant sustained an accident on June 

26, 1946, resulting in a detached retina on August 28, 1946, but since claimant did not report the occurrence of the accident or the connection between the bump on the head and the detached retina, he is not entitled to recover compensation under the provisions of the Workmen's Compensation Act."

Upon appeal, the Workmen's Compensation Board set aside the referee's eighth and ninth findings of fact and his second conclusion of law, and in lieu thereof substituted the following "Findings of fact "8. That claimant made application for relief payments from defendant employer on August 30, 1946, and reported the occurrence of June 26, 1946, to defendant on October 

14, 1946. "9. That claimant is suffering from a detached retina of the left eye, the cause of which is undetermined, resulting in the loss of vision of the eye. 

"Conclusions of Law 

"2. Since claimnt had not suffered a compensable injury on June 26, 1946, and since he had not reported the accident of June 26, 1946, within 90 days thereafter, he is not en-

1948] 

5 titled to compensation payments under the provisions of the Workmen's Compensation Act." 

The following is a brief history of the instant case: 

In mid-August 1946 claimant became aware of defective vision. On August 28th he lost all vision in the left eye. 

He visited Dr. R. J. Riddle on August 29th and was informed that the retina of his left eye was detached. On that occasion, claimant had no recollection of any accident or injury that might explain the condition of his eye. On 

September 2nd, claimant visited Dr. S. P. Simpson, who confirmed the diagnosis of Dr. Riddle. Dr. Simpson informed claimant that the conditions "comes from bumps or falls." At that time, claimant could recall none. On October 

9th, claimant called upon a Miss Smith in New Castle, whose mother had sustained a detached retina. Miss Smith informed claimant that her mother's injury was the result of a fall. Upon return to his home, claimant began "thinking back over a period of time as to when I had a bump" and "it was then I discovered, or remembered, that I had a bump before the 4th of July." Thereafter, on October 14, 1946, claimant reported to his employer the accident of 

June 26th.

The question presented to us by this appeal is stated by claimant thus: "Is a claim compensable under the Workmen's Compensation Act when a notice of injury is given by an employe to his employer within 90 days after the occurrence of the injury, but more than ninety days after the accident which caused the injury?"

Claimant's brief, however, also discusses the testimony of Dr. Simpson and urges that it establishes that the detached retina was due to the bump suffered by claimant on June 26th.

Upon appeal, the findings of the Workmen's Compensation Board can be attacked only on the ground that they are unsupported by competent evidence. The court may not weigh the evidence and change findings according to its own belief: Vorbroff v. Mesta Machine Co., 286 Pa. 199. 

The court has jurisdiction to consider only questions of

law, including determination of whether the record contains competent and substantial evidence to justify the Board's findings, but the court may not reverse the board and substitute its own findings for those of the board: Galinski v. 

Odin Stove Mfg. Co., 159 Pa. Superior Ct. 457.

Where the decision of the board is against the party having the burden of proof-in this case, claimant-the question before the court is whether the board's findings of fact are consistent with each other and with its conclusions of law and its order, and can be sustained without a capricious disregard of the competent evidence. Unless the answer is in the negative, the order must be affirmed: Walsh v. 

Penn Anthracite Mining Co., 147 Pa. Superior Ct. 328; 

Richards v. Fraim Lock Co., 158 Pa. Superior Ct. 414. 

Where the compensation authorities refuse to find facts in favor of the party having the burden of proof, the question on review is not whether competent evidence would sustain such a finding if made, but whether there was a capricious disregard of competent evidence in the refusal so to find: Kostello v. Kostello, 159 Pa. Superior Ct. 

194, 196.

In order to recover compensation, instant claimant had the burden of proving to the satisfaction of the board-the ultimate fact-finding body-the affirmative of three questions of fact: 

1. Did claimant sustain a blow on the head on June 26, 1946, while in the course of his employment? 

2. Was such a blow on June 26th the cause of the detached retina and his subsequent loss of vision? 

3. Did claimant give employer the required notice of injury?

The board adopted the referee's finding of an accident on June 26th, but declined to attribute claimant's disability to that accident. Therefore, our first problem is to determine whether the board capriciously disregarded competent evidence that the accident of June 26th caused the injury of which claimant now complains. 

We shall need to consider by what type of evidence claimant is required to establish the causal connection between

1948]  . the accident and the injury. Where an injury is so immediately and directly, or naturally and probably, the result of the accident that the connection between them does not depend solely on the testimony of professional or expert witnesses, the causal connection may be shown by lay testimony: Davis v. Davis, 80 Pa. Superior Ct. 343; McCoy v. Spriggs, 102 Pa. Superior Ct. 500; Tabuteau v. London 

Guarantee & Accident Co., 351 Pa. 183.

It was not until October that claimant referred his injury to the accident of June 26th. He had then come to assume that the injury was due to a blow. Having searched his memory for recollection of a fall or blow, and recalling only the accident of June 26th, he concluded that the latter was the cause of the injury.

In the light of this circumstance, we think it cannot be said that the injury was so immediately and directly the result of the accident as to relieve him of the obligation to produce expert testimony on the point. 

Where the sequence of events does not strongly indicate a connection between the injury and the disability, so that it cannot be said that the injury was immediately and directly, or naturally and probably, the result of the accident, claimant has the burden of establishing causal connection by expert testimony: Anderson v. Baxter, 385 Pa. 443, 446;

Bunnell v. State Workmen's Insurance Fund, 124 Pa. Supe rior Ct. 171 and cases there cited. Where there is no obvious causal relation between the accident and the injury, unequivocal medical testimony is necessary to establish causal connection: Baughman v. Bockensmith, etc., 161 Pa. Superior Ct. 601, 602; Rich v. Philadelphia Abattoir Co., 160 Pa.

Superior Ct. 200, 203. Therefore, the paramount question which arises is, whether the medical testimony, offered by claimant to establish causal connection, meets the required standard. Whether there is such legally competent evidence is a question of law: Anderson v. Baxter, 285 Pa. 443;

Loeffler v. Western Electric Co., 107 Pa. Superior Ct. 336; 

Bunnell v. State Workmen's Insurance Fund, supra. 

Dr. R. J. Riddle, ophthalmologist, testified that his examination of claimant revealed that "The whole upper anterior

portion of his left retina had become detached and that was the reason this patient did not see well from that eye." 

The doctor stated that for all practical purposes claimant had lost the sight of his eye.

Claimant's counsel put to Dr. Riddle the following questions: "Q. Assuming that Mr. Hunter's testimony as to the blow he received on June 26, 1946, is true, and assuming also that his testimony is true and correct as to his physical condition and no other accidents or diseases affecting his eyes, other than the one he mentioned as having happened 18 years ago, assuming those facts, would it be your opinion that the detachment of the retina was caused by the blow he received on June 26,. 1946? “A. I can't answer that directly. The only way I could answer is by saying it could be a factor, but I don't know that anyone could give you a definite answer as to that. "Q. Is it true, doctor, that a detachment of the retina can occur at much longer intervals, that is, intervals between the time of the trauma and the time of the actual loss of sight; is it true that the time interval can be extended over a period of several months to possibly a year? "A. That is true and such cases are on record, but they are much in dispute. The ones I have seen usually come in hours or days or perhaps weeks after the accident, but not months. There are cases on record as having followed months or years after, but they are rare and they are exceptions." 

Upon cross-examination, Dr. Riddle was asked: "Q. Now, doctor, knowing what you do about this case, both from today and the examination of the eye and from the history given you in the case, would you be able to individuate the causal factor in this detached retina? "A. No, I don't think I could."

The other expert witness for claimant is Dr. S. P. Simpson, a specialist in eye, ear, nose and throat, who examined claimant in September and October 1946. The physician testified that claimant had a detached retina, which developed further between the examinations.

1948] 

The following is included in the direct examination of 

Dr. Simpson: 

"Q. Did he give you any history? "A. No, I didn't ask him for any history. . . . "Q. From your examination do you think you can. 

Strike that. First let me put it this way. My understanding of the causes of detached retina is that they are approximately six: myopia, trauma, senility, some kind of infection, a hemorrhage or a tumor. Is that approximately right? "A. Yes, a tumor would be very rare . . hemorrhage, I don't know . . . I have a lot of hemorrhage in the vitreous without any detached retina. "Q. Now, from your examination of Mr Hunter, can you eliminate any of these causes? "A. I would just make a broad statement of that kind, see, but I cannot exactly eliminate . . . what I wanted to tell you in the first place to shorten this business was this. 

I have had a great number of these cases, my share of them, or probably more than my share. In this case, to my mind, I would have to believe him when he said he was hurt, because ordinarily a detached retina, even from coughing, sneezing or a jolt of some kind, would become detached first at the upper margin of the retina. This did not. The reason it was slow was because detachment started in the upper interquadrant, which is very unusual; one of the usual things when we get a detachment is from an infection. Well, some of these will get well, because it's a serum that makes the detached retina, but that serum sometimes is absorbed, but if the edge of the retina was detached that wouldn't happen, but you can see it sometimes, and by checking the field can tell the parts affected, what parts are detached due to the serum behind it. "Q. If Mr. Hunter had told you a blow? "A. Yes, he told me afterwards. did he tell you of "Q. Would you be willing to say that that blow . . "A. Could do it. Now I will tell you why that would be

true. You hear them talk about it can't happen this way and that way, but from my examination of these eyes, you may have a detached retina and know nothing about it for a long time because it's a very slight detachment, and as the detachment becomes greater it becomes more rapidly detached, so that he might be right. "Q. It could go on over a period of three to six months? "A. Oh, my yes, even a longer period than that. I have had them that way, that they would be detached enough that it would interfere with their vision, they would notice it, but yet, after lying down a while, it would come back. 

You know, we don't know what holds the retina, by what means it's attached-it's due to the vitreous, that's why you talk about myopia being the cause of it. There's no cause of detached retina. "Q. Let me ask you this question, doctor. I listed some of these other causes and you yourself probably know of other things, just like this cataract operation that causes a detached retina. Now, in your examination of Mr. Hunter, did you find anything else that might have caused this detached retina? "A. Not a thing. "Q. Then it's your opinion, if his history is correct, that the blow probably caused . .

Mr. Francis: I object to that, Mr. Referee, to the use of the word probably. "A. I can't hold that down too tight. I have people come in here, quite a few people, and I would say, 'Do you know your left eye is blind?', they never knew it, because they would lose their vision gradually . . . if a person has a left eye go bad they are not as apt to notice it."

The following is quoted from the cross-examination of 

Dr. Simpson: 

"Q. With these various causes of a detached retina, Dr. 

Simpson, and seeing Mr. Hunter several months after the date that he testified he had a blow, you cannot individuate the cause, can you Doctor, as to the detached retina? "A. I could in most cases, yes.

1948] 

"Q. But in this case could you, any more than saying that a blow could cause it? "A. I could say that the blow could cause it.”

Dr. Riddle did not undertake to assign the cause of the injury. The essence of Dr. Simpson's testimony is that the accident of June 26th could cause the injury. To the question whether the blow caused (the injury), he answered, "I can't hold that down too tight," because, as he stated, sometimes the vision is so gradually lost that the individual is not aware of the loss.

In the instant case, the loss of vision was so remote from the accident that common observation would suggest no connection between them, consequently the burden was on claimant to establish the connection by expert evidence: 

Anderson v. Baxter. "Both the courts and the administrative authorities have, very properly, been most liberal in construing the Workmen's Compensation Law, holding that claims thereunder need not be made out with the same exactness of proof required in suits at law. It must be understood however, that when, in cases of this class, expert testimony is relied upon to show the connection between an alleged cause and a certain result, it is not enough for the doctors to say simply that the ailment might have resulted from the assigned cause, or that the one could have brought about the other; they must go further and testify, at least, that, taking into consideration all the attending data, it is their professional opinion the result in question most probably came from the cause alleged. Here the strongest expert evidence to sustain the claim is that Fink's paralysis 'could be due to a blow on the head;' and, as just indicated, this is not enough to justify or support a finding that the blow, or jar, testified to in this case caused the paralysis which affects plaintiff": 

Fink v. Sheldon Axle & Spring Co., 270 Pa. 476. 

"The sixth assignment is based on the admission of the testimony of Dr. Kuntz to the effect that the 'condition from which plaintiff suffers today could have originated in the accident of 1928.' The admission of this testimony was error and the assignment is sustained.

"In Vorbnoff v. Mesta Machine Co., 286 Pa. 199, 206, 133 A. 256, this Court said: '. . . The witness would have to testify, not that the condition of claimant might have, or even probably did, come from the accident, but that 'in his professional opinion the result in question came from the cause alleged;' for, according to our latest pronouncement on this subject, a less direct expression of opinion would fall below the required standard of proof, and therefore would not constitute legally competent evidence.' This rule of law is applicable not only to compensation cases but to actions at law: Fink v. Sheldon Axle & Spring Co., 270 

Pa. 476" Nestor v. George, 354 Pa. 18, 24.

In the instant case, no expert witness testified that taking into account all the attending data, it is his professional opinion that the loss of vision did in fact result from the accident of June 26th, or any other expression tantamount thereto. Hence, it was not sufficient under the rule stated in Fink v. Sheldon Axle & Spring Co., 270 Pa. 476; Zimmerman v. Weinroth 272 Pa. 537; McCoy v. Jones & Laughlin

Steel Co., 275 Pa. 422; Manchline v. State Insurance Fund, 

279 Pa. 524; McCrosson v. Philadelphia Rapid Transit Co., 283 Pa. 492; Gausman v. Pearson Co., 284 Pa. 348.

In cases such as this, there must be a probable, direct relation shown between the accident and the disability, otherwise liability would be fixed by surmise: Morgan v. Phila delphia & Reading Coal & Iron Co., 273 Pa. 255, 258. 

The testimony that the disability is likely the result of the accident is not equivalent to an assertion of his professional opinion that in fact it actually did so: Anderson v. 

Baxter, supra. "The statement of proof required is medical testimony to the effect that the accident 'caused the injury' not that it 'could have' or 'probably'": Barkus v. Thornton-Fuller Co., 157 Pa. Superior Ct. 239, 243.

At one point in his testimony Dr. Simpson seemed to indicate an opinion that the injury was the result of the accident. He stated that the point of detachment and the development of disability were unusual and tended to rule out some of the usual causes of detached retina; however,

1948] 

 this comment was modified by his declaration, "He (claimant) might be right" (in attributing the disability to the accident). Furthermore, when asked directly whether the blow probably caused the injury, he answered, "I can't hold that down too tight." The doctor added that loss of vision of the left eye sometimes occurs so gradually that the patient is not aware of it (and seemingly, is unable to assign any date for the onset). The nearest that Dr. Simpson came to referring the disability to the injury of June 26th, was the declaration that the accident "could cause it." 

For the reasons hereinbefore set forth, we are constrained to hold that there is not competent and substantial medical evidence, i. e., expressions of expert opinions, measuring up to the test prescribed in Elowa v. Lytle Coal Co., 134 Pa. 

Superior Ct. 264 and affording a substantial basis (Wilbert v. Commonwealth of Pennsylvania Second Injury Reserve 

Acct., 143 Pa. Superior Ct. 37) to support a finding that the accident of June 26th materially contributed to the disability which claimant now suffers, in the sense of being, either the sole cause or the superinducing cause. 

In view of our conclusion as to the cause of the disability, it is unnecessary to consider whether claimant gave the required notice of injury.

The order of the Workmen's Compensation Board must be affirmed.

Order 

And now, November 19, 1948, this matter came on for argument upon appeal by claimant from an order of the Workmen's Compensation Board, and same was argued, whereupon, after due consideration, it is ordered, adjudged and decreed that the order appealed from be affirmed, and the appeal dismissed.

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD SAFIN v. JONES & LAUGHLIN STEEL CORP. 

Workmen's compensation—Occupational disease—Silicosis—Primary cause of death ·Pneumonia as immediate cause. 

Medical testimony to the effect that silicosis was the primary cause of death of claimant's husband although pneumonia was the immediate cause entitled claimant to an award for compensation where decedent had been employed as a motorman and coal loader inside defendant's mine, where he had been exposed to a silica hazard over a long period of time, and where silicosis rendered him unable to continue his work within three weeks prior to his death. 

Appeal by claimant from disallowance of Referee Gibb, District No. 8, claim petition no. 82,854, accident no. 

9,132,905. Sustained. December 1, 1948. 

Samuel Krimsly, for claimant. 

Wm. A. Challener, Jr., for defendant. 

JACOBY, Commissioner: 

This case is before the board upon the second appeal by claimant, Elizabeth Safin, from the order of Referee Gibb disallowing compensation for the death of her husband, George Safin, who died on April 20, 1939. When the case was first before the board (A-32236), we remanded the record to the referee for the appointment of an impartial physician, because there was conflicting medical opinion as to whether silicosis was the primary cause of death. There was unanimity of opinion that the terminal cause of death was bronchial pneumonia. There was a difference of opinion whether the extensive silicosis found was a passive agent or the active agency which terminated the life. 

Dr. C. Howard Marcy, appointed by the board as an impartial physician, testified that he had reviewed the record

1948]  and was of the opinion "that the primary cause of death was acute massive bilateral pneumonia, and that the silicosis was a contributing factor". Dr. Marcy explained that by "a contributing factor”, he meant that "if a man has appreciable damage to his lungs and then contracts pneumonia he has a poorer chance of recovery with that reduced breathing space from the results of silicosis than he would had he had normal lungs". In other words, the doctor believed that the silicosis might have had an adverse influence, through interfering with normal breathing, upon the course of the pneumonia.

Claimant called Dr. Algernon N. Alpern, who testified that he reviewed the record, and was of the opinion that decedent died of "silicosis of the lungs, severe, complicated by terminal pneumonia". Dr. Alpern elaborated that the silicotic fibrosis that occurred in the lymphatic system destroyed entirely the defenses to the infection or infected fibrosis of the lymphatics, which drain off the excess fluid and also counteracts infection, and meant an inability on the part of the patient to fight back against the pneumonia. In substance, Dr. Marcy testified to the same effect, that the silicosis lowered or weakened decedent's resistance to the pneumonia. 

After a careful review of the entire record, it is our considered opinion that the silicosis was the active agency which terminated the life. Certain significant incidents prompt this conclusion. As a motorman and coal loader inside the mine, he was exposed to a silica hazard over a long period of time. Defendant's medical witnesses admitted the presence of silicosis and Dr. T. H. Helmbold acknowledged that it was a third stage silicosis, productive of cough upon exertion. Despite a weakened condition due to a shortness of breath, coughing and the like, Safin continued in defendant's employ until March 31, 1939, when he became ill. Death from pneumonia occurred on April 20, 1939. The testimony of Dr. K. I. Fetterhoff, claimant's witness, is entirely credible and acceptable that decedent was a sick man before the advent of the pneumonia, to which he succumbed. The doctor expressed the opinion that decedent "died primarily of silicosis, and pneumonia was an accelerating condition or

coup-de-grace; in other words, it was the final blow that really caused his death". In spite of the fact that pneumonia claims a great many victims from all walks of life, nevertheless, we believe, in the instant case, that the silicosis was the active agency and constituted the primary cause of death, within the contemplation of the act and the pronouncement of our appellate courts. In the frequently cited case of Stauffer v. Hubley Mfg. Co., 151 Pa. Superior Ct. 

322, the court clearly distinguishes between primary cause and immediate cause. The court said (p. 325): "By primary cause is meant the main, chief, principal or predominant cause of the death that had then occurrednot some serious disease which would probably have caused the patient's death in the future, but was not the principal cause of his death at that time. "By immediate cause is meant the direct, present, instant or proximate cause of the death that had taken place; that which produced the result without any intervening agency." 

In the case before us, we consider the silicosis as the primary cause and the pneumonia as the immediate or terminal cause. The case of Treaster v. North American Refractories 

Co., 156 Pa. Superior Ct. 567, is authority for the proposition that "where the silicosis is itself the active agency which terminates the life, there is compliance with the statute, notwithstanding the victim displayed disorders unconnected with the occupational disease which might in themselves have produced death had they been allowed to traverse their expected course".

In the recent case of Askin v. Wheeling Steel Corp., 162 

Pa. Superior Ct. 568, the issue before the court was whether claimant's total disability was due to silicosis or arthritis. 

There, the court held the claim was compensable even though claimant also suffered from arthritis. Each case necessarily depends upon its own facts. In this case, decedent's long exposure to a silica hazard, his inability to continue work after March 31, 1939, death within three weeks, leads us to conclude that the death was due primarily to the admitted advanced silicosis. Claimant is, therefore, entitled to an award.

1948] 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's fifth finding of fact and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following 

Finding of fact 

5. That George Safin, claimant's decedent, died on April 

20, 1939. We find that the immediate cause of death was lobar pneumonia but that the primary cause of death was third stage silicosis from which claimant suffered, and which was incurred in the course of claimant's employment as a motor operator and coal loader by defendant. 

The referee's other findings of fact are hereby affirmed. 

We hereby vacate the referee's second conclusion of law and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following 

Conclusion of law 2. Having found that silicosis was the primary cause of the death of claimant's decedent, claimant is entitled to compensation in accordance with the provisions of the 

Occupational Disease Compensation Act of July 2, 1937, 

P. L. 2714.

We affirm the referee's first conclusion of law. 

We hereby vacate and set aside the referee's order of dismissal and in lieu thereof, we substitute the following Award

The board accordingly awards to claimant, Elizabeth Safin, dependent widow of George Safin, and to her minor dependent children, George, Elizabeth, Anna, Frank, Margaret, Paul, Julia, Catherine and Joseph Safin, and against defendants, Jones & Laughlin Steel Corporation and the 

Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, Department of Labor and

Industry, Bureau of Workmen's Compensation, compensa tion at the rates for the periods and in the amounts as imposed by section 5(b) of the Act of 1937, P. L. 2714, and also section 307 of the Act of 1937, P. L. 1552, payable as follows: Twenty percent by the Jones & Laughlin Steel 

Corporation and 80 percent by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, Department of Labor and Industry, Bureau.

This award to bear interest in accordance with section 

410 of the act. 

No bill of costs taxed.

The appeal of claimant is sustained. 

WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION BOARD TAMBLYN v. DELMONT FUEL COMPANY Workmen's compensation-Suspension of payment-Partial disability without loss of earnings.

A referee's order suspending rather than terminating compensation will be affirmed although claimant suffered no present loss of earning power where it appeared that he had lost from 20 to 25 percent of the motion of his jaw as the result of his accidental injury, which interfered with his eating so that he had to remain on a liquid diet until his jaw improved.

Appeal by defendant from order of Referee Foust, District No. 9, suspending compensation under agreement no. 

4,885,081. Affirmed. December 1, 1948. 

Coal Operators Casualty Co., insurance carrier. 

Joseph M. Loughran, for claimant. 

R. W. Smith, Jr., and R. H. Cunningham, for defendant.

MURPHY, Chairman: 

This is an appeal by defendant from an order of the referee suspending compensation.

The record in this case discloses that, on September 12, 1946, the parties entered into a compensation agreement, providing for the payment of compensation at the rate of $20 a week, commencing on August 23, 1946, and describing

1948] 

 the accident of August 15, 1946, and the resulting injuries as follows: 

"Claimant was struck by drill handle, causing laceration of chin and fracture of mandibile".

On September 4, 1947, defendant filed its petition to modify alleging that all disability resulting from the accident had ceased on January 23, 1947, to which date compensation had been paid and, though claimant alleges a functional disability resulting from his accidental injuries, defendant denied that the alleged functional disability resulted in a loss of earning power. In his answer filed on 

September 16, 1947, claimant denied the averments of defendant's petition and averred that, though he had returned to work, he was still "permanently and totally disabled". After hearings, the referee found that, though claimant had returned to his regular occupation on January 

27, 1947, with no impairment of wages, the condition of his mouth, which was a result of the accident, was such that he must eat soft foods at all times which causes stomach distress, causing claimant to vomit on many mornings and, on the basis of such findings, the referee suspended the payment.of compensation. This appeal followed.

The basis of defendant's appeal is that "there is absolutely no testimony upon which he (referee) might find that claimant has a partial disability reflected in any way in his ability to following his regular and usual occupation" and, therefore, the referee should have entered an order of termination rather than an order of suspension. With this argument we are unable to agree. 

On a petition to terminate or modify, the burden of proof is on the employer: Ludwig v. Union Collieries Co., 2

P. C. R. 222. In our opinion, defendant has not met the burden of proof imposed upon it such as would warrant our terminating the compensation payments. 

There is no doubt from the testimony presented that, while claimant presently suffers no loss of earning power, he does have a partial disability. Dr. Forest Thomas, a dental surgeon who treated claimant and who was called as a witness by claimant, testified that claimant has lost

from 20 percent to 25 percent of the motion of his jaw, as a result of his accidental injuries and defendant's medical witness, Dr. Richard S. Cole testified that "it was recommended that he (claimant) return to work January 27, 1947, on a temporary basis with notation that he might require some later treatment".

Claimant testified that his diet is mainly a liquid diet, as a result of which he suffers pains in the stomach and, upon awakening, is sick in the stomach with the result that he has lost occasional time from work. It is, therefore, obvious that claimant has not totally recovered from his injuries and that all disability has not ceased. There is always the possibility that, if the condition of claimant's jaw does not improve and he must continue upon his liquid diet that, as a result thereof, his physical condition will be impaired to the point where he will be unable to continue in his regular employment as a miner. As long as this partial disability continues, within the limit of the act and while claimant suffers no loss of earnings, defendant is entitled to a suspension but not to a termination.
